# GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO

### GOLD-MAKING, BOOK III.

I shall seem to bring forth something of great moment for the human race,
since, as if I wished for everyone to grow rich with gold,
I shall attempt to teach the very method by which it can be made;
a secret which nature has thus concealed deep beneath the lowest
mountains, so that the human race might seek it through all lands,
enduring and exhausted by great labors.
It was hidden so that mortals might possess a single standard and limit for price,
by which the exchange of goods would be
more just, and trade among various nations
more suitable. But if anyone, by a certain art, should bring
this secret into the light, and make it pass into common use,
so that what is precious is thought of as cheap as dirt,
immediately the remaining arts would fall away in sloth,
just as this one untiring art would raise its head; nor perhaps
would the **Father** <note>original: *pater*. Referring to Jupiter or God as the ultimate arbiter of order.</note> himself sharpen mortal hearts with cares
any longer. From that point, he would allow all things to grow numb 
in a heavy lethargy, or rather, he would soon command 
the wicked race to change every form of human beauty.
As for the author of such a great crime, after he has been tossed 
through various dangers, the Father will either thrust him down to **Orcus** <note>The Roman Underworld.</note>
with a thunderbolt, or bind him to a high rock
to pay eternal penalties forever. For why else would the anger of 
dreadful **Jove** <note>Jupiter.</note> have struck those who piled **Ossa** upon **Olympus**,
and **Pelion** upon **Ossa** <note>References to the Giants who attempted to storm heaven by stacking mountains.</note>, 
and the more savage **Coeus**, **Iapetus**, and **Typhoeus**,
shaping them into creatures worthy of his lightning?
Or why was the fire stolen from the ethereal seats, 
and **Prometheus** <note>The Titan who stole fire from the gods to give to humanity, punished by being chained to a rock in the Caucasus.</note> punished on the Caucasian rock by the bird,
more than he who, through this art, would imprudently make gold common?
Such a man would be worthy to be punished by both penalties at once.
Perhaps the Emperor **Claudius** <note>Referring to an anecdote found in Pliny the Elder, where an inventor presented "flexible glass" to the Emperor, who had the man executed so the value of gold and silver would not collapse.</note> provided for this one thing:
that when flexible glass was made through a wondrous trial,
it should not detract from the prices long ago established for metals.
A later **Caesar** <note>original: *inferior... Caesar*. This likely refers to the Emperor Diocletian (reigned 284–305 AD).</note>, a long time afterward, 
perhaps saw the same thing himself, when he wished to destroy 
the practitioners of so great an art, and commanded that a heap 
of many gathered books be burned <note>Diocletian reportedly ordered the burning of Egyptian alchemical texts in 296 AD to prevent the Egyptians from becoming wealthy enough to finance revolts against Rome.</note>, while he happened to traverse 
the wealthiest kingdoms of **Egypt** with an assembled army.
Being provident for the Roman Empire, he feared that art 
and the great riches then prepared by its means.
Indeed, in vain did **Faunus**, the son of **Picus**, and the nourishing [offspring] of Jove...

<note>original catchword: *Ipse* (He himself)</note>

# GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO

### GOLD-MAKING, BOOK III.

Even the grandson <note>Likely referring to a mythological figure like Cadmus or a descendant of Atlas, credited with early mining.</note> himself would be carried with deserved praise because, long ago,
he was the first to draw forth wide veins of silver from deep caves
for the **Westerners** <note>original: *Hesperios*. Refers to the peoples of Italy or Spain.</note>, and was the first to open
such great approaches to gold itself in the deepest earth—
if the value of these things were to decrease because of some art.
But we are not doing that: for we do not write everything for everyone;
instead, having detested the common crowd in this whole matter,
we play <note>The poet uses "ludimus" (we play/jest) to describe his poetic composition, suggesting it is a refined intellectual exercise.</note>, and it is certain we must keep the uninitiated far from here,
and frighten them off: even with our writings, so that they do not hope
to grasp with their understanding what we sing for a few wise men, and what
we speak of—not as mere craftsmen, but as those who (like other things of old)
are investigating this work of nature—and those things which
are scarcely revealed even with great labor to those
who, warned by us, are called as worthy of such great things.
Especially since some things are rightly intended to be left unsaid;
indeed, it is an unspeakable crime to speak them
unless they are thoroughly wrapped in obscure riddles.
And even some false things (which we ourselves have done sparingly
of our own accord) are sometimes scattered; you should not
believe that everything reported to you is especially true
where the **Art** <note>term: *Ars*. Here referring specifically to Alchemy, the human imitation and perfection of nature's processes.</note> is attempted for secret uses,
and where we disclose in what manner experience reveals itself,
being bound by the laws of this intricate art.
Indeed, where we reveal the forces of nature, and judge
<image-desc>A vertical brown ink line is drawn in the right margin alongside lines 25 to 30.</image-desc>
**Art** to be her handmaid, and where we first show
that this art exists, and then what it is, everything thereafter
will occur to you as more and more true; from there,
you will perceive everything that must be put into practice,
more than in those places where we seemed to teach
the method of the art itself, and make it subject to our instruction.
Nor was this just a way of speaking, but rather
some unknown **inspiration** <note>original: *furor*. A reference to the "divine madness" or poetic frenzy that strikes the author.</note> fell upon me here, by which—with a favoring 
divinity—I was led along a path not worn by use under the high
summits of the **Pierides** <note>The Muses, the goddesses of inspiration.</note>, and I hoped to visit the joyful hills,
and drink from the sacred springs, and pluck the leaves—
the honorable rewards for a learned brow,
loved by me and sought through many years.
For these comforts restrain anxious cares;
this love, this delight, and this grace occupy the empty mind,
and this one pleasure, having embraced the soul,

# GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO

[Page 248]

**GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO**

It fulfills, and from here joys run through the whole breast,
Joys granted by the gift of the **Castalian sisters** <note>original: *Castalidum sororum*. The Muses, who were said to live on Mount Parnassus near the Castalian Spring.</note>.
Therefore, departing from this point, I command that no one
Should remove from the fire the work it has guided, lest by chance
The heat—conceived through a long-enduring **virtue** <term>virtue: here meaning the inherent power or "potency" of the alchemical substance</term>—should slacken.
Instead, let the artist rather intensify it, until his own hand,
When touching the vessel, can only just endure it; yet he must see
That the heat never exceeds its own driving force, but remains
So continuous and level that joyful Nature may follow it.
Therefore, let no delay hold you back from proceeding
When you have ceased to further the brilliance
Of the hoped-for **whiteness** <note>original: *candoris*. This refers to the *Albedo*, the second major stage of the alchemical process where the matter is purified.</note> you have finally attained.
But still, let **patience**—that faithful companion—always stand
Against your haste; let her ensure that the long days themselves
Do not weary you, for you should not hope for such great things
To be produced in a short time; if you are able to seek these out,
You would leave nothing else equally worth seeking or wishing for.
And so, after the fire has proceeded further here,
It is not just one color or appearance you must watch for;
But before the **purple** <note>original: *purpureus*. The *Rubedo* or Red Stage, the final goal of the work.</note> presents itself to your sight,
A whiteness, gradually bathed in a **saffron cloak** <note>original: *croceo perfusus canduor amictu*. This refers to *Citrinitas*, the yellowing stage that traditionally sits between the white and the red.</note>,
And changing in various ways, will endure for a whole year,
Until the **red** soon begins to show itself, and to bloom 
Clearly beneath the deep skin, like a blushing violet,
And shining next to **Tyrian hyacinth** <note>original: *Tyrio hyacintho*. A reference to the precious deep-red or purple dyes of ancient Tyre.</note>.
Yet do not stop even here, but proceed immediately
Further, and do not wander from the straight path where it leads you.
Then, let it not come to your mind, nor let anyone persuade you,
To change the fire in any way, unless by chance you intensify it 
Slightly—only so much as you can bear to touch while remaining
Unburned and unharmed; let this be your goal and your measure,
Than which you should believe nothing in this whole time
Is more important to keep. For in this alone you will imitate Nature;
As for the rest, if you make some mistake or leave something out,
Nothing prevents you from correcting it or composing it again,
Provided these things were rightly observed and sought after before.
But if you stop, whereby that **fiery force**—which feeds the
Offspring with continuous fuel—dies away,
You achieve nothing; and suddenly, as soon as the fire stops,
Everything will collapse, and you will not be able to repair it by any art.

# PHILOSOPHY
<page-num>149</page-num>

...sharp. And this is what the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or a generic alchemical authority</note> says: whiten it, and sublimate it quickly with fire, until the spirit goes out from it, which you will find within it, which is called the "bird" or the "ash of Hermes." Wherefore Morienus also says: Do not despise the ash <note>original: "Cinerem ne vilipendas"</note>: for it is the crown of your heart, and the ash of things that endure. And in the *Book of the Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> it is said: Increase the control of the fire: and through whiteness one arrives at incineration, which is called calcined earth <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or oxidize it</term>, which is of a fiery nature: and you have in the previously mentioned proportions the four elements, namely dissolved water, whitened earth, sublimated air, and calcined fire. Concerning these four elements, Aristotle also says in the *Book on the Governance of Princes* <note>original: "lib. de Regim. principum," a reference to the pseudo-Aristotelian *Secretum Secretorum*</note> to Alexander: when you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then you will have the full art of philosophy.

And here is the end of the first composition, as Morienus says. Now let us pass to the second composition, which must breathe life into, tint, and quicken the first composition. Wherefore the philosopher Calindus says: No one ever could, nor later will be able to tint the foliated earth <note>original: "terram foliatam"; a specific state of the alchemical matter that appears flaky or layered like leaves</note> except with gold. Therefore Hermes commands, saying: Sow your gold in the white foliated earth, which through calcination is made fiery, subtle, and airy. Into this earth, therefore, we place the "feminine gold" <note>likely referring to silver or a receptive form of gold</note> along with the tincture of gold. But gold can never perfectly tint another body than itself; certainly this cannot happen unless it is perfected by art. Wherefore Raymond <note>Raymond Lull, a famous medieval philosopher and purported alchemist</note> says: Although this stone of ours already contains the tincture within itself naturally—for it was created perfectly in the body of "magnesia"—nonetheless, it does not have it of itself unless it is perfected by art and labor. 

Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of Arabic chemistry</note> says in the *Operation of Roots*: To this end the operation is performed, so that the tincture of gold may be improved in the gold more than it is in its own nature: and also so that it may become the Elixir according to the allegory of the wise, that is, a clear compound made of various species—a condiment, an antidote, and a medicine for all bodies that are to be cured, purged, and transformed into true "Lunar-maker" <note>original: "Lunificum"; something that creates silver</note> and "Solar-maker" <note>original: "Solificum"; something that creates gold</note>. 

But do we need only gold and no other body? Hear Hermes saying: Its father (that is, the father of the first composition) is the Sun <note>Gold</note>, its mother is the Moon <note>Silver</note>. The Father is hot and dry, generating the tincture; the Mother is cold and moist, nourishing that which is brought forth. Therefore the Sun by itself, and the Moon by itself, are of very difficult fusion. But when they are joined in the manner by which soldering is done to gold, they melt very quickly. Therefore Maria <note>Maria the Prophetess, an early alchemist often cited in medieval texts</note> says: Take the projected body, or the small mountain...

It cites legendary figures like Hermes, Geber, and Maria the Prophetess to explain how the purified "ash" must be "tinted" to gain the power of transforming metals.</summary>

->## IOANNES AVRELIVS AVGURELLVS<-

Whether the intense heat exceeds the proper measure by a little more or a little less, or whether the time or place varies: from here, if you look at the logic, the cause will be clear to you why it has led the births through so long a duration, or made them shorter. For the birth which the seventh month brings forth will not be a false human delivery; nor could you say that this one, which the eleventh has produced, is not true—though such matters are usually attributed to the gods above and the stars. <note>Augurello compares the "gestation" of the alchemical Stone to human pregnancy, noting that the timing can vary based on heat and planetary influence.</note>

There are some who then keep the matter parched in the furnace with no small fires for seven nights and days, until it is thickened more, as they say; yet the wise man would not approve of this in every respect. For nature seems to do nothing similar to this: but once she has begun something, she soon always maintains one steady course and rejects whatever is different from her beginning.

I advise you, so that these things may complete the whole circle for you which you drive around more rightly, do not despise observing the seasons throughout the year in your affairs. And, if you desire to hear anything from me, you will begin precisely under **Spring** itself, when the whole world is in labor, and when nature opens herself for all things to be created. You should arrange all things according to her secret course, with me as your guide—as I have always advised—lest, having abandoned her path, you attempt to depart from the right way.

In **Spring**, therefore, give the order to fuse your glass; in **Spring** also, form your vessels from clay and fit your furnaces, when winter’s rage has ceased and while the summer heat does not yet hinder you, so that you may handle even the most powerful fires at close range.

Perhaps here you might seek the numbers and the weights of things which you must establish for yourself before you finish that work. But if you consider it, there are only three first principles <term>primordia: the "Three Principles" or *Tria Prima*—Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt—which alchemists believed composed all metals</term>: then two, then even—if you see correctly—there will be only one, and it will consist as a triple nature in **gold** alone. Indeed, you may comprehend all these in a single weight: for they differ in nothing among themselves when joined, and each one exchanges its own weight for another in turn. Yet you should handle all these things so exactly that those by whom gold is marvelously separated from silver do not care to subtract from so small a number, nor to weigh so minutely with such a modest balance.

->### THE POEMS OF OLD AGE, BOOK I<-

But those things <note>Referring to the technical alchemical matters discussed in previous volumes.</note> are now in the past. Now we proceed with what is at hand, stirred by your favoring divinity <note>original: "numine"</note> to begin, and to deliver those things which I promised, as we are able, and as the spirit, powerful in heaven, breathes upon the lowly. You look upon these things with serenity—this we pray with a suppliant mind, as you are accustomed to do with whatever is offered to you—nor should you refuse to grant me a little delay from time to time, until, looking inward, you have inspected whether perhaps we are heading on the right path through the steep way <note>A metaphor for the difficult intellectual and spiritual climb of the author's work.</note> which we now enter toward these ascents.

The madman, heartless and out of his mind, lacking counsel, reason, and all piety, has said to himself that there is no God. But the wise man first conceives in his mind that He exists: then, crying out with a splendid voice, he makes it known that He not only exists, but that He holds and rules all things with His powerful right hand, and by His nod tempers <note>original: "temperare" — meaning to regulate or bring into balance.</note> all that He has made, and is present everywhere to all, and commands each thing.

Truly it is no light thing to see what steps he climbs; whoever turns these things over in his mind and reaches above that which no power of mortals could ever attempt to be carried, unless a heavenly breeze <note>original: "superna... aura"</note> breathed from above, and unless His favor were present—He whose deeds we seek to tell, moved by no small fervor. Fear and trembling, accompanied by reverence, than which no other is greater, press from every side, and warn us little ones not to undergo a heavy burden unequal to our shoulders. But love, once powerful to make inaccessible ways passable, when hope and faith come to meet it, encourages and almost compels one to enter the hidden path of inward prayer <note>original: "Orationis intimae" — this refers to a deep, contemplative form of communication with the divine.</note>.

Command me then what I should do, my God, the one King of all, and my only Master. Do you command, Lord? Perhaps indeed you do: for I do not see how these things could be breathed from elsewhere. I will try, therefore: you, I pray, favor my undertakings,

->### GERONTICON, BOOK I<-

# THE POEMS OF GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO
## To Pietro Lipomano, son of Girolamo, of Venice
### THE POEMS OF OLD AGE
### BOOK I

The Muses are close to my heart, and poems are my chief concern. All other joys, which once might have occupied my idle mind, are now set aside; this single pleasure brings back to me whatever sweetness I once perceived with every sense. Therefore, I place a secluded altar to these Muses in a grateful spirit. Here are Ivy and Laurel, as well as pleasant greenery among sunny hills; here is a grove of Myrtle. There is a grove sacred to Venus, and the mild vine <note>original: "vua" — referring to the grape cluster</note>, so pleasing to Bacchus <note>original: "Lyæo" — an epithet for Bacchus, the god of wine</note>, hangs there in thick clusters.

Before all else, I must pave a courtyard with much gold; then, columns of solid adamant shall rise. Upon these, I shall ordain that a high roof be placed, adorned with great gems and bound with the eternal fastenings of thick bronze. No length of time shall ever harm these joined structures, though it may oppose them with its powerful efforts. The Goddesses <note>The Muses</note> shall stand in the middle and hold the temple. Henceforth, accompanied by an honorable assembly of bards, I shall bring them gifts—not the common things we are accustomed to offer them, but the rarest of all noble things, such as only the greatest poets, chosen from the whole number, have been able to set aside.

And you, O worthy offspring of the Lipomano family, a young man increased in rare virtue and distinguished character—things which, having proceeded from the highest seat of heaven, are usually stored within a righteous mind—give yourself to me now, free of care and with a pure heart. I desire you to be admitted to these sacred rites and to perform the duties which are now prepared and entrusted to us for you alone. Therefore, first clothe your shining shoulders in this white garment, and gird yourself with me for such great matters. Standing by me, draw the divine liquid <note>original: "laticem" — often referring to water from a sacred spring</note> from pure springs, and take up lilies with full hands, along with flowers gathered together from the varied turf.

<summary>Augurello opens his first book of "Geronticon" by dedicating his remaining years to the Muses and inviting his patron, Pietro Lipomano, to join him in a symbolic, sacred ritual of poetic creation.</summary>

Finally, while I pour out these words of prayer far and wide, 
As the long-standing priest of these Muses and of Phoebus <note>original: "Phœbi" — Apollo, the god of light and poetry</note>,
Scatter the ground and fill all things with sweet vapor.
O Phoebus, whom the nine holy spirits of the sisters <note>The nine Muses</note>
Always surround; by singing a Paean <note>original: "Pæana" — a song of praise or healing</note> to the gods there,
They occasionally scatter an eternal aura among mortals.
From this, the vigorous spirit takes divine strength for songs
And leads the poet <note>original: "vatem" — a visionary poet or prophet</note> down from the highest ether.
May it be right for this petitioner to hope for a draft of that spirit—
He who has served you with his whole soul from his earliest years.
He shall establish for you a shining bull and a snowy heifer
Sacred to the Muses, and every year he shall hang
A green Laurel beneath the very center of the temple’s roof.
And he shall both give you this fire, by which the fervent altar shines,
And shall cherish its light through a long age.
Now, with a benign nod, you shall make all these things fulfilled.
These things I pray: but you also, O youth, whom the gods 
Will soon reserve for greater things, as a suppliant join in these 
Vows and prayers, since all things have been performed 
Rightly for you; for the god has nodded with a certain omen,
And the altars have shone with clear flames.

# TO LEO X, SUPREME PONTIFF
## *The first ascent to God.*

Now I try many things with myself, and have long pondered
Whether the promises I once made to you, holy father, 
Might be fulfilled in any part—
Back when I held your occupied ears with a little book, 
Perhaps being foolish, though I was setting forth there 
The secrets of Daedalian Nature <note>original: "Dedalæ Naturæ" — referring to the intricate, maze-like complexity of nature, often associated with the craftsman Daedalus</note>
And the gifts of a most powerful art <note>This likely refers to Augurello's interest in alchemy and his work "Chrysopoeia"</note>.
Did I not indeed seem to act foolishly?
Since I, senseless, then considered that those things 
Would be wonders to you, to whom nothing can seem a wonder;
Since you have surpassed the measure of humanity
And immediately made little of all human things,
Nor have you thought of anything humble or low
Since you approached the steps of the highest seat,
And, so great a man, entered upon the role of the gods on earth.

The insane man <note>A reference to Psalm 14:1: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God."</note> has said to himself that there is no God—senseless and out of his mind, devoid of counsel, of reason, and lacking all piety. Truly, it is no light thing to see which steps he climbs, whoever turns these things over in his soul and strives above that to which no mortal force can ever be carried, unless a celestial breeze should blow from above, and unless the favor of Him is present, whose very deeds we seek to describe, moved by divine frenzy <note>original: "furore" — referring to the classical concept of poetic or prophetic inspiration</note>. Fear and trembling, accompanied by reverence—than which none is greater—press upon me from every side, and warn us, little as we are, not to undergo a heavy weight unequal to our shoulders <note>A poetic convention of modesty, common in Latin literature</note>. 

But love, powerful enough to make once inaccessible paths passable, when hope and faith come forward to meet it, encourages and almost compels me to enter the hidden path of inward reason. Therefore, command me what I should do, my God, the one King of all, and my only Master. Do you command it, Lord? Perhaps indeed you do: for I do not see how these things could be inspired from elsewhere. I shall try, therefore: you, I pray, favor my beginnings,

Who, again, seeing the other parts of the world and moving among them, could cease to marvel at the wide-reaching circuit of the earth lying below? Like every kind of plant <note>original: "stirpium genus" — referring to all botanical life</note> that raises itself from the ground, and those that clothe the earth’s skin with blossoms that rival precious gems? 

How the multiform and wandering offspring of living creatures, scattered everywhere through the wide stretches of earth and sea, grows and is always carried by its own singular force, where it can, and where nature first gave it its own impulses. Add to these the clear and flowing streams of springs, and the courses of rivers in deep channels between pleasant banks, among sunny hills, and the green fields of the plains with sweet, growing herbs. 

But who, endowed with a serene mind, does not wonder at the deepest valleys sinking down from the mountains, and other mountains rising from the depths of the valleys? Or at clear lakes spread beneath the peaks of greening cliffs? Or to whom is the immense vastness of the seas and shores, and the varied and pleasing positions of the islands, not also a miracle? Pour out from the very depths of your heart voices to Him, whose grace will soon be fully present for you; He will embrace you, and on all sides in heaven there will be joys, than which no greater could anywhere exist. For there, it happens that there is more rejoicing for one who has turned from vices to the celestial kingdoms of the powers above <note>original: "superûm" — a classical term for the gods, here used in a Christian context to mean the heavenly host or God.</note>, than if many, whose life on earth was most holy, were carried up to the heavenly heights.

---

### EASTER <note>original: "PASCHA" — The celebration of the Resurrection of Jesus.</note>

This is that day which the Creator of all things established: come, everyone, with me, and favor the occasion with your tongues and your minds <note>A ritual formula calling for holy silence or respectful speech during a ceremony.</note>. Let all be joyful with me, singing praises and happy songs; in this way, return your thanks to the King of the Heavens. 

And you, holy father, especially—to whose heart much religion and the observance of true faith are always dear—proceed joyfully to lead the day with a solemn procession, full of the immense honor of a celestial gift. As is your custom, follow with royal ornament and a pure heart, and finally embrace this day with every devotion among the Christian leaders <term>proceres</term>, in the midst of the faithful council, and highly placed in the chosen order of the fathers <note>The "holy father" and "order of fathers" likely refer to the Pope and the College of Cardinals.</note>. 

Enough has been given to tears and mournful grief for the season—though it is never enough for our wickedness and our crime—but nonetheless, we have lamented these things with a constant voice and added prayers. These prayers, the merciful Redeemer is believed to have heard, and He now spares the weary affairs of men.

->GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO<-

### EASTER (Continued)

We also perceived how the wicked crowd once violated Him in wretched ways, and how He, in His holiness, bore a thousand mockeries; we are accustomed to recall these very things every year. We saw—while all the disciples He had chosen for Himself fled in distress—how He was surrounded on all sides by the savage madness of robbers, bound with hard knots, and foully dragged through the streets to the high priests and leaders. How the insane mob laughed at Him here, how they spat upon Him, afflicted Him with whips, and how they harassed His divine body with profane rituals, we have drawn in abundance from the holy writers <note>The four Evangelists of the New Testament.</note>; meanwhile, we filled everything with copious weeping, bringing forth the heavy grief of an afflicted mind from the depths of our hearts.

Finally, we saw the Almighty, the Author of all things, lifted upon the cross to endure sorrows and the hard tortures of death, which no one on earth ever bore or felt before. And—alas, alas!—so that we might not die eternally, He fell, though He was the eternal one who had created all things, who always remains and is always to be the same, who moves all by His nod and governs all that exists. Clothed in the form of a mortal man, He fell for our sake.

Let these things have been celebrated thus in the days just passed, following the sacred rite and mixed with pious sorrow. But today, there is a need to bathe the mind with joyful gladness instead of tears, and to show on a serene face joys that yield to nothing. For the Greatest Himself—who allowed Himself to be mocked by sickly mortals and had died by an unspeakable slaughter—now, with death subdued and the human condition overcome, has broken the gates of the Underworld <note>original: "postibus Orci" — Augurello uses the classical Roman name for the underworld, Orcus, to refer to the Christian Hell or Limbo.</note>. As a victor wishing to return to the heavenly realms, He suddenly presented Himself as both God and true man—yet no longer mortal as He was before. On the contrary, while His mortal nature remained, it was now entirely united with the divine; He offered Himself to be seen by us so that no doubt might remain. Thus, on that light <note>The dawn of Easter Sunday.</note> when He rose again as He had foretold, we might all know Him as the master of both death and life.

What of us? Shall we not also rise with the Lord? Let us rise: first, let this be a passage <note>The word "Pascha" (Easter) is derived from a Hebrew word meaning "passage" or "pass over."</note> from vices to the highest peaks—to virtue and religion.

...Soon to the heavenly powers above, and the celestial fatherland: for no other reason did He depart from His high seat and come to the human race here, than that He might lead us with Him, eager and willing to go.

# TO TRIFON GABRIELE
### *A Venetian Patrician.* <note>Trifon Gabriele (1470–1549) was a celebrated Venetian humanist and cleric, often called the "Socrates of Venice" because he taught primarily through conversation rather than published books.</note>

To what place, O companions, do you allow me to be carried now, wandering through these deserted places? To what dark caves do they lead me now, among thick briars and sharp rocks? They drive me, perplexed by various wandering paths, and they always oppress and constantly fatigue me. Nor does any of you, in such great danger, extend a right hand and stop my wandering on this deceptive path, or guide my way in person and lead me back to level ground.

Yet once many used to call me back—or you especially, dear Trifon—if by chance I seemed to turn aside even slightly from the right path. I had begun, as far as my small strength for songs allowed, to follow from afar the secret footsteps of ethereal song, which the prophet <note>Refers to King David, traditionally the author of the Psalms.</note> once brought forth with inspired breath to the lyre. All those who approach the sacred thresholds—moved by the secret divinity of the true Phoebus <note>original: "Veri... Phœbi." While Phoebus is the Greek god Apollo, here the poet uses the name as a humanist metaphor for the Holy Spirit or the source of Divine Truth.</note>—openly confess that he sang an inimitable song, one far beyond the grasp of men.

And so, looking up, and worshipping in a humble and prone position, I was trying to see if he might show himself favorable to me, being burdened by my frequent prayers; whether he might be moved by this affection of mine, or rather by the kind assent of his own [will], and by the sole gift of the mind.

Finally, persisting in this hope alone, I was then entirely immersed in those things which he had once sung; nor, meanwhile, did I leave aside the other precepts of the Old Law <note>original: "Legis... vetustae," referring to the Old Testament or the Mosaic Law.</note>, but I continued to read the works of grave authors. I occupied myself among things that were pleasing to me and suited to my senses and my years. But now, captured by I know not what subtle sweetness, I play at youthful things beyond my usual age. Will you permit me to be led through these empty matters? Things which, to me, are not suitable for our studies...

# GIOVANNI AURELIO AUGURELLO
### [To Trifon Gabriele]

They immediately offend even purified ears.
Why do you cease to call me to my former harmonies?
Those songs which you used to approve with no small praise,
you often applied swift spurs to me as I ran.
Why do you not begin to exhort? Why not, as before, advise?
Or—since you have the power—compel me to these pious
duties? These are always deservedly most pleasing to you.
Either because the service of the Muses <note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration, here used by the humanist poet to describe his creative work.</note> is no small matter to you,
as often as you aspire toward their peaks:
Or because you hold our sacred rites with the wonderful effort of a pious mind,
and you venerate them with equal honor.
Come then—for I ask it—let us try what could befit us both,
if perhaps that burning melody might inspire us,
that song which never modulated anything except by divine grace.
Looking always toward the open heavens, the King himself <note>King David, traditionally the author of the Psalms.</note> sang of the King of Kings,
and offered praise to the One, and honor to the One.
You go first, I will follow; for thus, my friend, you will call me
back once more, not to things abandoned, but to things interrupted.

**Trifon:** What joys took hold of the desolate fathers <note>The "fathers" refers to the Patriarchs and righteous souls of the Old Testament awaiting salvation.</note>—
whom a horrible fear had driven and dispersed before—
when they saw the one they had mourned as dead emerge from the tomb,
their hearts struck with a marvelous wonder.

**Augurello:** What joys took hold of the prostrate mothers,
when the messenger <note>The angel at the tomb.</note> sent from the heavenly height of heaven
presented himself to the fearful women with a cheerful face,
to soothe their sorrowful hearts with peaceful words.

**Trifon:** When terror was cast into the ranks of the guards,
when a trembling invaded the earth, and suddenly the stone
which clung firmly to the tomb was torn away from its covering.

**Augurello:** At which noise the evil Spirits <note>original: "Manes." In classical mythology, these are the spirits of the dead, but here the poet uses the term to describe the demons or shadows of Hell.</note> fled beneath Tartarus <note>A classical name for the underworld or Hell.</note>,
when they realized they were overtaken by such great light,
and could no longer be hidden under even the smallest cover.

**Trifon:** But the good turned their senses and eyes suddenly
toward the Lord, toward the very Father of things and God,
and toward Christ, who had been expected for so long.

**Augurello:** Indeed, they all came eagerly into the thresholds of light,
following the outstretched banners of the eternal leader;
but they left the deserved darkness to the miserable guilty ones.
But cease now: for certain things are prepared for the good...

<meta>This page continues the poetic dialogue between Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (Aurelius) and his friend Trifon Gabriele (Tryphon). The previous page ended with a description of the mothers' joy at the Resurrection; this page concludes their exchange by describing the eternal peace of the soul in Heaven and introduces a new poem addressed to Antonio Vonica.</meta>

# GERONTICON, BOOK I.

There are rewards for those who will eventually see the blessed seats,
as soon as they have left behind on earth that fleeting
and mortal weight of the self. No force of labors,
no pains harass them; no fear,
no fraud, no deceit. Indeed, that dire pleasure
always accompanied by a countless tumult of errors—
and the other things that vex mortals and distress them in vain—
none of these approach or come near that place.
But a secure rest remains, and a life
tried by no cares, utterly without need of our earthly goods.
They live content for ages with the sight of the All <note>This refers to the "Beatific Vision," the ultimate Christian hope of seeing God face to face.</note> alone,
nor is any rest from seeing granted to them,
yet this is their highest rest: for in this the blessed
rejoice in that eternal age, world without end.
**Try.** Thus may celestial favor prosper your undertakings here,
through which you seem to me to have sung so great a song;
Aurelius, do not abandon these studies or these songs.
**A.** Rather, do not refuse to hand back these many aids, 
Tryphon, which you have now given to me by your own rhythm
when I seek them again: for thus you will breathe honor upon our works,
just as a craftsman's hands add beauty to ivory; and much
gratitude shall one day remain for you in our poem.

---

## TO ANTONIO VONICA
### Of Treviso.

Where, O where do you Silidian Nymphs <note>The "Silides" are nymphs associated with the river Sile near Treviso; Augurello often uses them as local Muses for his poetry.</note> snatch me through the rivers?
I no longer hold the reins of my floating horse, nor am I 
master of my own mind, able to discern in which 
direction I should steer myself; on one side greater floods terrify me,
on the other a muddy marsh stands in the way, sluggish and clinging,
where the hoof of a four-legged beast could scarcely be pulled free.
These were my thoughts while I was led into the river by the force of my carrier:
yet every fear was that I might be submerged in the deep
whirlpool, and be carried hopeless beneath the waves.
For there was no hope for me, nor any certain or faithful
plan for help, but everything was full of immense dread,
and manifest dangers were exposed on every side.
And not even the one whom the Greek poets once imagined—
he upon whom Arion <note>A legendary Greek harper who was saved from drowning by a music-loving dolphin.</note> was carried while holding his lyre and plectrum—
could a Dolphin then show itself to aid me.

Not content to swim within the narrow banks of a river,
a monstrous Whale <note>original: *Cetus*</note> with its throat raised high would
swallow me, just as it once took the prophet Jonah in its 
gaping mouth and hid him within its vast belly.
That man, not at all obedient to the warnings of God—who had 
ordered him to seek the city of Nineveh <note>An ancient Assyrian city; in the Bible, Jonah is sent there to preach repentance.</note> at once and carry 
dreadful commands—fled toward Tarshish. He thought that 
he might hide from God Himself, who sees all things.
Fearful, he boarded a ship and withdrew himself beneath
the very rudder, where he hid in trembling.
Meanwhile, the sea began to be stirred with a great roar;
the sailors shuddered, the captain himself grew afraid,
and now, as a suppliant with his companions, he offers vows in prayer.
Then he tries to seek out the cause of the sudden storm
and casts lots; at the same time, he prays to Jonah—
on whom the lot itself had fallen—that he might look out
for his own life and the lives of everyone equally. Jonah says
he offers a path to safety, if they would all form a group
and throw him headlong into the sea: for he said it was 
in his own name that they suffered all these troubles—
he, the fool who did not immediately fulfill the commands of God.
Therefore, as the power to save themselves in their trembling
is offered, they seize him and hurl him from the high
stern into the deep sea. Immediately, a huge monster 
devours him in its wide mouth and hides him in its vitals.
What could he do? Where, through those hiding places and dark entrails,
could he go? On whose help could he rely, so that he might 
escape from there? Or see the lights of heaven from so far away?
As for what remained, the wise man soon performs the only thing possible:
he begs for mercy as a suppliant in prayer. And God, of His own accord,
gives the command; Jonah is cast out upon the light and dry seaweed,
unharmed, although he had been held within that savage belly
for three days and three nights together.
Therefore, having been ordered again, he approaches the city powerful
in people and affairs, and openly delivers his threatening words.
The people immediately tremble and carry out the commands,
and God duly remits their sins, now purified.
The Father knows how to spare the humble; and in His mercy,
He once spared the human race for the crimes we committed,
and He paid an unmerited penalty for our sin. <note>This concludes the poem by linking Jonah’s three days in the whale to Christ’s sacrifice and three days in the tomb—a common theme in Renaissance "typology" where Old Testament events prefigure the New Testament.</note>

<page-num>263</page-num>
<header>THE GERONTICON <note>Literally "The Book of the Old Man."</note> BOOK I.</header>

He <note>Referring to Christ, whom the poet views as the fulfillment of the "Sign of Jonah" mentioned on the previous page.</note> approached death, and endured lying in the tomb for three days; soon after, He brought salvation to all people and reopened the way to the vaulted heavens above. To Him, in whatever place and at whatever time you might desire things either great or small, all things are a concern. For who could have kept me from such great dangers, had not heavenly favor and God Himself been present then?

I pray you, Antonio <note>Antonio Vonica, a humanist and physician from Treviso to whom this poem is addressed.</note>, look upon these matters with me, and turn them over in your prudent mind for a long time. For while I was being tossed about in such narrow straits, behold, two young men stood by me immediately. One leapt into the currents rejoicing, while the other remained diligently upon the bank. The former took the fierce horse by the right hand and held its ear. And to me he said, "Do not fear." He proceeds, and the horse, previously wild, goes along mildly; and so he approaches the bank. From there, the one who had stood waiting before calmly reached out his hand and helped me out; and so both of them placed me safely on dry land. 

Then they quickly departed, while I attempted to return to them—and to the gods above—deserved thanks from the bottom of my heart. I do not remember seeing these men in any other region. They were seen by me then for the first time, nor did it happen that I saw them elsewhere again. If by chance you wish to know their appearance, both flourished in green youth. But the one who stayed close to me in the midst of the waves was taller, so as to match me as I rode, a great Hero <note>original: *Heros*</note> walking with broad shoulders. But the one whom I said waited attentively on the edge of the bank, offering his hand to me as I asked, was agile and dexterous, fit for all tasks, and his face excelled in every honor. 

Why should the ancient age boast of the twins **Pollux** and **Castor** <note>In Greek mythology, the Dioscuri, who were often said to appear to save sailors and travelers in distress.</note>, that they were often present to help many? Might I not be permitted to imagine these two as gods for myself, based on their appearance and every virtue? But, my friend, let us not invent such tales; rather, let us believe that God often helps our affairs—He who, in His piety, pities the afflicted and the sick among men, and repays us with good deeds even when we deserve ill.

## TO BARTHOLOMEW AGO-
## *lantus of Treviso.*

I would have invited you to these feasts too, my friend,
Had I not known, Agolantus, that you are held by many obligations,
Which you must certainly taste first,
Before you would wish to come here to our midday meals.
Perhaps they advise that this is how it should be done—that we devour
Certain appetizers first, which sharpen the appetite and are pleasing;
Then we may sit at a healthy table after some delay.
You have begun to discern the causes of things more closely,
And where human power is able to carry itself, you labor
To stretch, and to fill yourself with this study of a blessed mind—
If indeed there is anything in human affairs that you would deem
Worthy of such a great name. For what has been handed down in both languages <note>original: "linguis... vtrifq;" — This refers to the standard humanist mastery of both Latin and Greek.</note>
Is already known to you; only other great matters remain for you,
Which you turn over, and upon which you now alone
Diligently lean for a long time, so that eventually, returning satisfied
And filled by them, like a guest of a keen
Intellect, you may see whether you have perhaps only tasted the scent
Of the feasts, while remaining free and devoid of the flavor.
These things are undoubtedly superior to all other things
Which mortal hearts desire and even seek.
But both toward these and in these, we always strive under a spiteful light,
And we fall into such varied darkness, surrounded as we are,
That you could hardly say you found a likeness of truth by chance—
Which you wish to have sought by reason and attempt by the investigation of your own mind.
How much better it was that the wise man <note>Referring to the Greek philosopher Socrates, whom the Roman writer Cicero famously described as the first to bring philosophy down from the heavens to the earth to focus on human life and ethics.</note> was said to draw Wisdom <term>Sophia</term> <note>original: "Sophiam"—the Greek word for wisdom.</note> down from heaven
To the lands; he, leaving behind things to be contemplated—
Which the others who were present were eager to search with all their
Strength—taught us to look at what is closest to us,
To embrace virtue, to pursue <note>The Latin "infectarier" here carries the sense of "tracking" or "following," implying the active effort to hunt down and eliminate vice.</note> vices, and finally
To arrange one's whole life by an eternal law.
But what can he, or anyone, though they followed better paths
Than others, contribute to our affairs? For what empty shadow of things
Would compete with the things themselves?
This is the one wisdom we follow, and the unique virtue.
Devoted to the study of this now, and free from other cares, we are held.
This you also, when the time comes (though that too always...

To look up at them with frequent affection, and to seek them with the whole mind.
From this comes that powerful Love, which, as soon as it has left
Its companions, fervent Hope and Faith, behind on the earth,
Finally accompanies the chosen through the whole of Olympus. <note>original: "Olympo" — Here used by the Christian humanist poet to signify Heaven.</note>

## TO PIETRO LIPOMANO <note>Pietro Lipomano (c. 1491–1548) was a member of a prominent Venetian family who later became a Bishop.</note> ON THE
### *death of his sister Clara.*

The pleasant places, Pietro, which you see as you wander,
Think that you are seeing vain dreams,
That they do not truly exist, but only seem to, and are glimpsed
From every side through the deep, slippery, and empty void.
The singing birds, and the light tresses of the trees,
And the sharp murmur and sounding of the leaves,
As the West Wind <note>original: "Fauonio" — Favonius, the gentle spring breeze.</note> moves them gently,
The fervent dogs across the plains, the fleeing hare,
The girl binding her head with a fresh flower,
The boy joyful and wandering with light love,
And everything that you seem to see here so vividly,
They are entirely the shadow of an empty eternity,
Rather than of things which are able to endure
Through all time. But riches, fields, houses,
Even these are vain, and do not possess...

*What part of itself is whole, or what of itself is powerful,*
*And ever firm, and ever consistent with itself?*
*Beauty, strength, and grace avail nothing,*
*Nor can honor preserve a thing, so that it might long endure;*
*Everywhere, whatever you see brought forth*
*Beneath the heavens, all things are fleeting, all are flowing,*
*Save for that which the nurturing grace* <note>original: "alma... gratia"</note>
*Of the God <note>The Latin "Deorum" (of the Gods) is a classical plural used by humanists to refer to the Divine or Providence.</note> has given as a gift*
*To you, to me, and to others to whom it is granted*
*To be strong in mind: for only the mind flourishes,*
*Ever to be in the future; and at the same time, it leaves*
*The heavy weight of itself upon the ground, and to the sacred*
*Dwellings of the eternal pole, it immediately flies, light.*
*Where the pious enjoy, in a golden cycle,*
*Every vigor and innermost salvation;*
*There is no other vigor, nor any other salvation,*
*Nor any other Good; nor is there any other*
*State of blessedness or rest for the others*
*In that place; but beneath the moving sphere all things*
*Fluctuate everywhere. Yet that one man is somewhat*
*More firm, who, though dwelling in the depths, looks*
*To what is above his head, and readily puts himself forth,*
*And while he lingers here, heavy, he yet unfolds*
*His wings, light and high in the manner of a bird,*
*And seeks heaven with his mind, as if released from the body.*
*But this is the blessed life of an exceedingly perfect*
*Man, which few are able to enjoy,*
*And which that (if it can be said so) your*
*Most great priest, who is to be honored above all,*
*Strives for; and having willingly spurned all things*
*Which the World of its own accord seeks with all its strength,*
*Having followed this one path, he embraces it utterly.*
*And now, hiding far off in the high mountains,*
*Away from his country, his friends, and all his dear ones,*

*Exhorts, and promotes them in wonderful ways—*
*Their vices abandoned—toward what is decent, toward what is right, toward that*

They say there is a hill dedicated to Phoebus <note>The god Apollo, patron of the arts.</note> and the Muses, where all poets alike strive to compete, and they hasten there to drink the sacred liquid. <note>Poetic inspiration was often symbolized by the waters of the Hippocrene or Castalian springs on Mount Parnassus.</note> They believe the Laurel <note>The evergreen symbol of poetic victory and immortality.</note> grows forever green upon its peak, from which they might bind their heads with the desired crown. Therefore, one may see some individuals bring themselves to the very foot of the mountain; and staying there at the base, they wear away the best part of their younger years. These are content to gaze at the high summits from afar, if only they might touch some of the divine stream with the very edge of their lips, or by some stroke of luck gather any fallen leaves from the blessed branches of that nourishing tree.

There are also those, as they say, who labor to crawl at the enclosure of the mid-point of the cliff with great effort, within which so few are admitted that only one or another in these places can seem to be sufficient. But what of him who, daring to despise those placed below, raises himself up and stands as he climbs upon the highest peak? And there, among the laurels and at the very threshold of the fountain, he establishes an altar to the Muses and to Phoebus as their priest; he addresses the gods there, and hears and sees them—happy man! 

O, if it were granted to me at least to dwell within a nearby valley, what more fortunate thing could I wish for? # TREATISE OF LORD THOMAS AQUINAS OF THE ORDER OF PREACHERS, ON THE
## Philosophical Stone, and first concerning Super-celestial Bodies. <note>Though attributed here to Thomas Aquinas, modern scholars generally consider this alchemical work to be "pseudo-Aquinas"—written by a later author using the famous theologian's name to lend authority to the text.</note>

### CHAPTER I

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a man in a scholarly robe seated at a writing desk, framed by ornate foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>**Aristotle** says in the first book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "meteororum." Aristotle's *Meteorologica* was the standard textbook on the elements and natural phenomena.</note> that it is beautiful and laudable to investigate the cause of the intention of causes; for the wise, seeing the effect of things, scrutinize the causes. We, however, see that **celestial bodies** act upon the elements, and from the potentiality of the matter of one element—for instance, from the matter of water—they **educe** <note>original: "educere." A technical term in Scholastic philosophy meaning to bring out or manifest a form that was previously latent in matter.</note> the form of air and fire. For every agent in nature acts so as to produce something similar to itself, just as fire acts upon wood and produces fire; and I speak here of the principal natural agents. For the **Super-celestial Bodies** seem to be not without the matter of an element or an elemental form, and especially because we see by our senses that the sphere of the planets is of a simpler nature,

<header>SECRETS OF ALCHEMY</header>

than the planets themselves, and that the planets are denser and more composite bodies. But for the evidence of this truth—not just according to what I have proved concerning the influences of natural things. And Roger <note>Refers to Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), the English philosopher and scientist whose theories on optics and "species" were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> explains this best. Every natural agent acts through its **likeness**, by projecting that likeness into the passive subject; this likeness is not different in kind from the agent itself. For example, if tow <note>original: *stuppa*—the coarse, highly flammable fibers of flax or hemp.</note> is placed near a fire, even if it is not touching the fire, the fire (like other agents) will multiply its **species** <note>In medieval science, a "species" is the visible or invisible power/image emitted by an object through a medium like air.</note> through the medium. This species will be multiplied and received into the tow through the continuous natural action of the fire and the tow's own readiness to be affected; the species will be strengthened within it until it exists as a completed fire. Because of this, it is clear that the likeness of the fire was not different in kind [species] from the fire itself. 

But certain things are highly active in their specific action, so that they can draw forth [new things] through their likeness, conforming and multiplying things exactly like themselves, just as fire does. There are others, however, which cannot draw forth a likeness of themselves into a subject as a complete version of their kind, such as a human. For a human could not conform the likeness that is in the medium enough that it becomes an actual human, because a human is occupied with other actions. Hence, according to what Roger proves in his book *On Influences* <note>Referring to *De multiplicatione specierum* (On the Multiplication of Species), often circulated as part of Bacon's larger works on influences.</note>, if a human had as strong an action in his likeness as fire does, there is no doubt that this species would become a true human; hence it cannot be said that the likeness of a human is entirely "not-human," because he places it under that same kind. 

<margin>|</margin>Therefore, since the celestial bodies act upon the elements, they act through their likeness. Since they draw forth something similar to themselves, and as if of the same kind, it follows that when they draw forth an element from an element, <margin>|</margin> and elemental things from elements, they must necessarily <margin>|</margin> possess something of the elements within themselves. 

And so that you may see this more fully, consider this in the **sun**, which draws forth fire through the body of a glass vessel <note>original: *urinalis*—a round-bottomed glass flask, here used as a lens to focus sunlight.</note> full of water and from a spherical crystal body. Hence you ought to know that, although the agent (according to what was proven in the book <margin>|</margin> *On Influences*) multiplies its likeness through a straight and very strong **perpendicular line**—as is clear with the <margin>|</margin> tow and the fire, which are first joined at the point of that line considered perpendicularly—nevertheless, when the vessel full <margin>|</margin> of water or the crystal is placed toward the sun, the solar rays (which are their likeness, as is clear if a mirror is applied, <margin>|</margin> showing the sun to be multiplied there through a perpendicular line)...

...straight line, which, passing through the whole body, is not refracted <note>original: *frangitur* - literally "broken," the standard medieval term for the bending of light or refraction</note> in the water because of the strength of its action. Those rays that pass through straight lines that are not perpendicular, or those which are refracted in the body of a glass vessel <note>original: *vrinalis* - a spherical glass vessel, often used in medicine and alchemy, which acts as a lens</note>, become oblique in the water and pass to another part, where they are joined together at a point on the perpendicular line. That point becomes combustible, so that if tow <note>original: *stuppa* - coarse, flammable fibers of flax or hemp</note> is applied, it is immediately ignited, as is shown here. Because of this, the likeness of the sun or the ray of the sun is confirmed: through the continuous action of the sun, fire is produced. Therefore, the sun has a fiery nature within itself; this is also seen in burning mirrors. I propose that a mirror can be made of such a composition, position, and form from highly polished steel <note>original: *chalibe*</note>, that an entire line becomes combustible, so that when directed at a village or city or any place, it burns it incessantly. Thus says Athanasius <note>referring to a medieval authority on optics, likely drawing on traditions attributed to Archimedes</note> in the book *On Burning Mirrors*.

<margin></margin>Because of this, it is manifest that the sun and other super-celestial bodies are not without elemental matter; yet they are not, for this reason, corruptible, nor heavy, nor light. Therefore, a distinction must be made concerning the elements: some are most pure and simple, having no power to change one into another, because their matter is perfectly contained by its own form. These "pure" elements can be the super-celestial bodies. For we literally place "water above the firmament" <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis, interpreted by medieval scholars as a physical crystalline or "watery" sphere in the heavens</note> and a watery or crystalline heaven. Similarly, we can speak of the other elements, and say that the super-celestial bodies are composed of these elements through divine power or the Intelligence that governs them. Gravity or levity cannot be generated from these celestial elements—meaning that "celestial earth" is not heavy or weighted—because weight only belongs to that thick and heavy earth which is purely elemental.

<margin></margin>Nevertheless, colors are generated in the super-celestial bodies by these very elements. Since the super-celestial bodies are, as it were, "gilded," they sparkle from the ray striking them, just as a gilded shield sparkles when it is struck by the sun. Thus the Astrologer <note>A general reference to the consensus of astronomers or a specific authority like Ptolemy</note> posits this when explaining the cause of the twinkling of the stars. And because such a color or gilding must be generated, Isaac <note>likely Isaac Israeli, the influential Neoplatonic philosopher and physician</note> and Roger <note>Roger Bacon</note> in the book *On Sense* <note>original: *De Sensu*</note> prove from certain elemental qualities that an elemental nature must exist within them. But because those elements are most pure in their natures and are not mixed with various accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like size or temporary color</note>, it is necessary that they exist in these bodies either corporally or proportionally, so that they can never be overcome by another. Do not wonder at this, because I, through my art...

# THE SECRETS OF ALCHEMY

<margin>|</margin>With nature cooperating, I separated the four elements from certain lower bodies <note>original: *corporibus inferioribus* — a term for earthly materials as opposed to celestial ones</note> so that I held each part separately: namely water, fire, and earth <note>The author likely assumes air is captured or inherent in the process</note>, and I purified each of them from accidental qualities <note>original: *accidentibus* — in Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential characteristics like color or smell</note> as much as I could through a certain secret operation. Finally, I joined the purified elements together, and there resulted a certain wonderful thing which is not overcome by any of those lower elements. For if it were to stay in the fire forever, it would never be consumed, and never be changed. Therefore, do not wonder if the super-celestial bodies <note>The planets and stars</note> are incorruptible, even though they are composed of elements. Thus, there is no doubt that the mentioned nature participates greatly in the celestial body. Whence says Hermogenes <note>original: *Hermogenes qui triplex fuit* — a reference to Hermes Trismegistus, the "Thrice-Greatest," the legendary foundational figure of alchemy</note>, who was threefold in Philosophy: "Concerning that air and earth, when I had reached perfection, I felt a joy such as I never had, seeing the fifth essence <term>quintessence: the pure, fifth element that exists beyond the four earthly elements and makes up the heavens</term> without elemental matter, as we shall say below." 

<margin>|</margin>A handful of fire has more power than perhaps a hundred of air; because of this, one handful of fire will strongly enter into a thousand parts of earth. However, we do not know how the weights of these elements behave in a mixture. Yet through craftsmanship, with nature cooperating, I saw that when I had separated the four elements from certain bodies and purified each by itself, in joining them I placed an equal weight of air, water, and earth. Of fire, indeed, I placed a sixteenth part. And although this mixture <note>original: *confectio*</note> is composed of elements, it nevertheless has more of a fiery nature than of any other element. For when one part was cast upon a thousand parts of quicksilver <note>original: *argenti viui* — literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>, we perceived that it coagulated it and made it red. Because of this, it rightly 

<margin>|</margin>appears that this nature has something of the nature of the celestial bodies, for in transmutation <term>transmutation: the alchemical process of changing one substance, usually a base metal, into another, such as gold</term> it behaves almost as a form or a most powerful agent.

## *Concerning lower bodies, and the being and essence of Minerals, and first concerning Stones.*

### CHAPTER II.

Minerals are divided into stones and metals. Therefore, being <note>original: *esse*</note> is in these for the same reason as in other creatures, except that the being of the essence is drawn out in these into the act of the individual <note>original: *suppositi* — a technical scholastic term for a distinct, self-subsisting individual</note>, and many trans-

...changes than in the elements or the super-celestial bodies, for their matter is composed of many forms. The matter of stones, however, is water, both mixed and thick, having either much earthiness or very little, depending on the purity of the stone. Whence, according to what Aristotle says in the book *Meteorology* <note>original: *Meteorum* — Aristotle's treatise on natural philosophy and atmospheric phenomena</note> (though others think the chapter belongs to Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian polymath whose works on minerals were often appended to Aristotle's</note>), pure earth does not become stone, but rather "watery earth." This is just as we see stones generated in rivers, or salt generated from salt water which contains much earthiness, and stone formed through the heat of the sun and fire.

Furthermore, the matter of stone is "thick water," while the acting agent is heat and cold, which congeal that water and bring the essence of the stone into reality. For the nature of stone is found in plants and in animals; you should consider that these stones are not without great power. For some of them are congealed in animals by the power of heat, and among many other powerful stones, it is believed that those which proceed from animals are more powerful than others. Others, truly, are congealed by a mineral power with nature cooperating.

For as Aristotle says, some people make a certain water composed of two waters, which they call **Virgin’s Milk** <term>Virgin's Milk (lac virginis): an alchemical term for a white, milky suspension produced by mixing two clear liquids—usually lead acetate and a carbonate or sulfate—causing a precipitate to form</term>, and they coagulate it into a stone. It is said to be made from **litharge** <term>litharge: a natural mineral form of lead(II) oxide, used in ancient and medieval chemistry</term> dissolved in vinegar and the water of **alkali salt** <note>original: *aqua salis Alkali* — likely a solution of potassium or sodium carbonate</note>. Although each of these waters is very clear, when both are joined together, they immediately become—through a certain mineral effect—one water, thick and white like milk. When they soak into this whatever they wish to coagulate into stone, it is indeed coagulated; for instance, if the **lime of silver** <term>calx: the powdery metallic oxide or "ash" left after a metal has been burned or corroded</term> or of another body is soaked in water of this kind and afterwards placed in the **alchemical furnace** <note>original: *Kimia* — here referring to the laboratory apparatus or the art of chemistry itself</note> over a slow fire, it will become stone. For that "milk" has the nature of coagulating "limes" into stones.

We also see that from blood, eggs, hair, brain, and other parts of animals, stones of wonderful efficacy and power can be made. For example, concerning blood: human blood was taken and left to putrefy in warm dung <note>A common medieval method for providing steady, gentle heat for fermentation or chemical breakdown</note>; afterward, it was placed in a **distillatory** and a white water was distilled, in the manner of milk. Afterward, the fire was increased and an oil was distilled. Then the dregs <note>original: *fæces* — the solid residue remaining after distillation</note> which remained in the distillatory were **rectified** <note>purified through repeated heating</note> until they became white as snow. Then we poured its oil back over it, and it became a clear and red stone of wonderful efficacy and power, such that it was able to bind a flow of blood and expel many infirmities. From plants we also extracted waters in this way: namely, we burned the plants in a furnace of **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or oxidation</term>; furthermore, we converted the ash into water, and we distilled and coagulated it...

Because I have separated the four elements from certain bodies, purified them, and joined the purified parts, there came to me a stone of such great efficacy and power...

->*On the being and essence of metals, and first concerning their being and essence or natural composition and the being of the individual substance.*<-

### CHAPTER III.

The being of the individual metal <note>original: *Esse suppositi* — a Scholastic term referring to the actual, individual existence of a specific thing</note> is drawn out from the matter of its planet and from natures, and likewise through artifice. Therefore, since there are seven metals, each specific metal is drawn from its own planet, namely: Gold from the Sun (and it is called Sol), Silver from the Moon (called Luna), Iron from Mars, Quicksilver from Mercury, Tin from Jupiter, Lead from Saturn, and Copper and Bronze from Venus; and they are called by the names of their planets.

->*On Substantial Matter.*<-

The substantial matter of all metals is quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum* — literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>, which is why in some metals it is coagulated by a weak freezing, and in others by a strong one. Thus, there are degrees among metals according to the degrees of the action of the planets and of entirely pure sulfur congealed with quicksilver. Those metals in which there is little congealed or earthy matter behave as "matter" and "in potency" <note>An Aristotelian concept meaning the metal has the potential to be transformed into something else</note> when compared or opposed to other metals. For instance, lead is earthy quicksilver that is only slightly coagulated, coming from a subtle and small amount of sulfur; and because the action of its planet [Saturn] is distant and weak, it exists "in potency" to become tin, copper, iron, silver, or gold. Tin, however, is clear quicksilver coagulated slightly by a gross and impure sulfur, because of which it exists in potency to copper, iron, silver, and gold. Iron, indeed, is gross quicksilver...

[...lead] is terrestrial, [formed] from a very coarse terrestrial sulfur, strongly coagulated by the action of its planet <note>Referring to Saturn</note>; therefore, it possesses the potential to become copper, silver, and gold. **Copper** <term>cuprum</term>, however, is coagulated from much sulfur and a moderately coarse **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the traditional name for mercury</term>, with its own planet <note>Venus</note> cooperating; for this reason, it possesses the potential to become silver and gold. **Silver** <term>argentum</term> also is [formed] from a white, clear, subtle, and non-burning sulfur, and from a subtle, coagulated, limpid, and clear quicksilver, with its planet, the **Moon** <term>Luna</term>, cooperating; therefore, it only possesses the potential to become gold. **Gold** <term>aurum</term> truly is more perfect than all metals, and it is made from a red, clear, subtle, and non-burning sulfur, and from a subtle and clear quicksilver, strongly congealed by the cooperation of the **Sun** <term>Sol</term>, so that it cannot even be consumed by sulfur, which consumes all other metals. ...subsequently deceiving kings and princes, and to such an extent that kings, despairing of the truth of this science, neither seek it out nor desire to know it. For so many erroneous books, so many follies, and so many variations in operations have been written by these ignorant men that, once you have spent all your resources working according to their instructions, you will achieve no result at all, falling instead into a despair of the science.

I, however, considering all these things—and how kings had attempted subtle operations and yet could hardly or never reach perfection—once believed this science to be nothing at all. But returning to my senses, I considered the books of Aristotle or Avicenna regarding the **Secrets of Secrets** <note>original: *Secretis Secretorum* — a widely circulated medieval text of pseudo-Aristotelian advice and alchemy</note>, and I found them to be lacking in reason, insofar as they declare the deed or the science in a confused manner and somewhat in riddles. I considered the books of those who contradicted them and found their delusions to be similar. For I saw **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the traditional name for mercury</term> penetrate and pass through other metals; for instance, if you touch copper with quicksilver mixed with a little blood and clay, it will penetrate it externally and internally and make it white, although that color does not last. Thus, it is clear that quicksilver possesses a capacity for mixture with bodies and for penetration. 

Therefore, I considered: what if it were held so that it did not fly away <note>The author is describing the "fixation" of mercury, preventing it from evaporating when heated</note>, and were in a fixed state with [metallic] bodies? It would then do what copper and other bodies do, but would not be burned by those things which consume copper but do not consume silver. It would then be as silver and possess such power. 

I therefore **sublimated** <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then allowing it to solidify again, used for purification</term> quicksilver many times, so that it might be brought into a fixed state—namely, so that it would not fly away from the fire. This sublimated substance I dissolved in water, so that a reduction to the **first matter** <term>prima materia: the fundamental, formless base of all substance in Aristotelian physics</term> might take place. From the aforementioned water, I many times saturated **lime of silver** <term>calcem argenti: silver that has been reduced to a powder or oxide through heat</term> and fixed sublimated **arsenic**. Once it was dissolved, I congealed it, and there resulted for me a stone as clear as crystal, having the nature of cutting or pounding, of penetrating, and of remaining fixed within [metallic] bodies. 

The result was such that if you project a small amount of this stone upon a large quantity of copper, it will immediately draw out from it the form of pure silver, than which none better is found. However, to convert it into gold, I took the redness of our **sulfur** <term>sulphur</term> by boiling it in **sharp water** <term>aqua acuta: likely a strong acid or distilled vinegar</term> over a slow fire. This I congealed with the aforementioned white stone, so that it was made red; and a little of this...

### CHAPTER V.

There is, however, another more noble method of transmuting—namely, turning quicksilver into gold or silver by the power of red and white sulphur, which is most clear, simple, and non-burning. For I have not published this book for common folk, but for the perfected. 

I urge, however, that no one presume to begin the work because of these things which are to be said, unless they are highly skilled and experienced in natural principles, and very discerning in the methods of distillation, dissolution, and congelation, and especially in the management of fires. A man who wishes to prepare this out of greed does not know what he does; one must act with discernment and diligence. There is, therefore, a certain mineral stone from which such power is drawn—namely, of clear white or red sulphur that is not consumed by fire—and it is drawn out through the separation of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, and through their purification and conjunction.
