### *Concerning the mineral, animal, and vegetable stone of this sixth division or treatise.*
# CHAPTER VI.

There is also another stone, which according to Aristotle <note>Aristotle was the primary philosophical authority for medieval alchemists, though many texts attributed to him were actually written by later authors</note> is a "stone and not a stone." For it is mineral, vegetable, and a rational animal <note>This refers to the "Universal Stone," which was believed to be found within all levels of creation: minerals, plants, and humans</note>; it is found in every place, at every time, and within every person. You must rot <note>original: *putrefacere* — to undergo putrefaction, a stage of breaking down matter through gentle heat</note> this substance under dung, and once rotted, place it in a glass gourd <note>original: *cucurbita* — a round-bottomed flask</note> with its alembic <term>alembic: a hood or cap placed on a flask to catch and condense vapors during distillation</term>. Extract the elements in the same manner as described above and join them together; there will result for you a stone of less power and virtue than the one mentioned before. 

And do not be surprised that I told you it should be rotted under warm horse dung; an artisan ought to test this, for if he places wheat bread under it for nine days, it will be turned into true flesh mixed with blood. Because of this, I believe God chose wheat bread to be transubstantiated into His body <note>A reference to the Eucharist; alchemists often drew parallels between the transformation of bread into the body of Christ and the transformation of base matter into the Stone</note> rather than anything else; perhaps from this substance, the four elements can be drawn out and some good work can be performed. 

From all that has been said, it is clear from what things the actual substance of minerals is composed, and how it is produced not by nature alone, but also by artifice <note>Alchemy was often defined as "art imitating nature," completing what nature left unfinished</note>. Blessed be God, who gave such power to men that, existing as an imitator of nature, he can change natural species—a task that sluggish nature performs only over a vast amount of time. Behold, there are other ways of transmuting metals which are set down in the books of Rhazes <note>original: *Rasis* — a famous 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note>, Archelaus, and in the seventh book of precepts, and in many other alchemical books.

### *Concerning the method of operating through the spirits.*
# CHAPTER VII.

There is also a method of operating through the "spirits." To understand this, note that there are four spirits; they are called spirits because they fly away from the fire <note>The "spirits" are volatile substances that sublimate or vaporize when heated</note>, and they possess the nature of the four elements. They are these: Sulphur, which has a fiery nature,

Sal ammoniac <note>original: *Sal Armoniacum*</note>, Mercury <note>original: *Argentum viuum*</note>—which possesses a watery spirit and is known by another name as the "fugitive servant" <note>original: *servus fugitivus* — an alchemical nickname for mercury because it evaporates or "flees" when heated</note>—and orpiment <note>original: *Auripigmentum*</note> or arsenic, which possesses an earthy spirit. Some people work with one of these by <term>sublimating: heating a solid until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify substances</term> it, converting it into a liquid, distilling it, and congealing it. By then casting it upon copper, they claim it is transformed. Some work with two of these, others with three, and some with all four: namely, by sublimating each one individually many times until it is <term>fixed: rendered stable and no longer volatile when exposed to fire</term>, then distilling each one individually, dissolving it into a liquid with sharp dissolving waters <note>likely referring to strong mineral acids</note>, soaking it many times, and then joining all the liquids together. By distilling and congealing them once more, one obtains a white crystalline stone. If you cast a small amount of this upon any metal, it would transmute it into true Silver <note>original: *lunam* — the Moon was the alchemical symbol for silver</note>. At that point, some say the four elements are present and purified; others say it is one spirit combined with the bodies. Although I have not tested this method myself, it seems natural, and I suspect and believe it is almost unknown to everyone—though Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher whose works were fundamental to medieval alchemy</note> touches upon this method somewhat in his letter addressed to his father. I, however, will test this method when I have the time and place.

It will be entirely dissolved into a liquid; distill this liquid three or four times and congeal it, and you will have a stone,

->CHAPTER IX.<-

For Gold, however, take purified <term>vitriol: a glassy mineral, typically iron or copper sulfate</term> that has been <term>calcined: heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile substances, turning it into a powder</term> until it is red. Dissolve this in the urine of boys <note>A common source of nitrogen and phosphorus in early laboratories</note> and distill the entire mixture. Repeat this process as many times as necessary until the resulting water is deep red. Then, combine this liquid with the aforementioned water <note>Referring to the liquid from the previous chapter used for silver</note> before it solidifies. Place both waters under dung <note>A common method for providing gentle, consistent heat through natural fermentation</note> for several days so that they may be better incorporated. Distill and congeal them both together, and you will possess a red stone similar to a <term>hyacinth: a reddish-orange gemstone, likely a variety of zircon</term>. If you <term>project: the act of casting an alchemical substance onto a molten base metal</term> one part of this stone upon seven parts of Mercury or of purified and solid Saturn <note>original: *Saturni* — the alchemical name for Lead</note>, it will be transformed into pure Gold <note>original: *Solem obrisum*</note>, for the stone possesses a nature similar to a ferment. 

Many other operations may also be found in books—nearly infinite and confusing ones—which lead men into error and the loss of their wealth without any benefit, especially regarding the "preparations," which would take too long to recount. As for me, I was moved not by greed for profit, but by a desire to witness with my own eyes the marvelous effects of nature and their causes—not just the general ones, but the most specific and immediate, looking upon not only their accidental qualities but their essential ones. I have tested many of these things in the separation of elements from bodies. Although that work is true and perfect, I suffered such great labor and stench <note>original: *fœtorem*</note>, as well as the weakening of my own body, that I resolved never to attempt this work again unless forced by necessity. Let these words suffice regarding minerals.

# THE TREATISE OF SIR THOMAS AQUINAS
->*given to Brother Reginald, on the art of Alchemy.*<-
<note>While traditionally attributed to the great philosopher Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), most modern scholars believe this and similar alchemical texts were written by later authors using his famous name to gain authority.</note>

Overcome by your constant requests, dearest brother, I propose to set down for you a brief treatise on our art. It contains certain rules, easy and effective operations, and the truest <term>tinctures: substances used to "dye" or transform the color and nature of a metal</term>. This is divided into eight chapters. I wish for you to be warned in three matters: First, that you should not care much for the words of the modern or ancient philosophers who speak of this science. For the entire alchemical art has established its seat in the capacity of the intellect and in experimental demonstration. The philosophers, wishing to hide the truth of the science, spoke almost entirely in figurative language. Second—

# OF SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS.

Second, do not value a plurality of things, nor the mixing of diverse species, for nature never produces anything except what is like itself—although from a horse and a donkey a mule is generated by an imperfect production, just as some who imitate science produce a certain multiplication from many things. Third, do not be talkative, but set a guard over your mouth, and like a son of the wise, do not cast pearls before swine. Maintaining peace with your God, always fix the ordained end of your work in your mind. Believe for certain that if you keep these rules—passed down to me by Master Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the famous 13th-century theologian and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, who was also rumored to practice alchemy</note>—before your eyes, you will not need to seek Kings and Great Men, but Kings and Great Men will bestow all honor upon you. For anyone in this art serving Kings and Prelates is held in suspicion, since he himself is not only able to help them, but all those in need step by step; however, what he has received for free, he should never provide for a price. Therefore, let the aforementioned rules be undoubtedly marked and sealed in your heart with a secret seal; for in the previous book intended for the common people, I spoke philosophically, but to you, my most secret son, I have written more openly, trusting in your silence.

->*On the operation.*<-

## CHAPTER II.

Since, according to Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational in the Middle Ages</note> in his letter to King Assa: We seek to make a true and single substance forced from many into one fixed thing, which, when placed over fire, may withstand it; which will be penetrating and indwelling, tinting Mercury and other bodies with a most true <term>tincture: a concentrated substance used to transform base metals into gold or silver</term> of the proper weight, the nobility of which tincture exceeds all the treasure of the world. For our one thing makes three, three makes two, and two finally exist as one. How this single substance is finally made, as Avicenna says, one must have patience, time, and the proper instrument. Patience, because according to Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath often regarded as the father of early chemistry</note>, "haste is from the devil." Therefore, let him who does not have patience stay his hand from the operation. Time is also necessary, because every natural action, which our art follows, has its own determined manner and time. Instruments, indeed, are necessary, yet not many, as will become clear in what follows, since our work is completed in one thing, one vessel, and one way, according to Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the origins of alchemy are attributed</note>, and through a single operation. Although this <term>medicine: the alchemical agent of transformation, also called the Philosopher’s Stone</term> is gathered from many things, it is nonetheless one single material, needing no other external thing except for white or red <term>ferment: a substance added to the alchemical mix to "leaven" or trigger the transformation into silver or gold</term>. ...natural thing never placed in any other work, from which, in the governance of the work, diverse colors will appear according to the timing. In the first days, it is also necessary to rise early in the morning and see if the vineyard has blossomed <note>An alchemical metaphor for the first signs of successful chemical reaction, often related to the "white" stage</note>; in those following, the raven's head <note>original: *corvinum*; the black stage of the alchemical process, known as the *nigredo*</note> transformed in the solitude of the blind, and manifold colors, among all of which an intense white color is to be looked for. Follow, therefore, Saint Albertus Magnus <note>The famous 13th-century theologian and teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note>, my master, and work with mineral quicksilver, for it is the perfecter of our work against burning, the preserver, and the producer of melting. For when it is "fixed" <note>Made solid, stable, or non-volatile so that it no longer evaporates when heated</note>, it is a tincture of whiteness or redness of most abundant restoration, of shining brilliance; and it does not withdraw from what it is mixed with, for it is friendly to metals and the medium for joining tinctures, since it mixes with them, entering into their depths and penetrating naturally, which means it adheres to them.

->*On the composition of Mercury and its separation.*<-

### CHAPTER III.

And although our work is perfected from our Mercury alone, it nonetheless requires a red or white ferment <note>An additive, usually gold for the "red" work or silver for the "white" work, that acts like yeast to "leaven" the mercury into the Stone</note>. It is therefore more easily mixed with the Sun [gold] and the Moon [silver], and becomes one with them, since these two bodies participate more in its nature; they are therefore more perfect than others. The reason is that those bodies which contain more Mercury are of greater perfection. Therefore, the Sun and Moon, containing more of it, are mixed for the red and the white; they are "fixed" by standing in the fire, since Mercury itself is the only one that perfects the work. In it we find everything we need for our work, to which nothing foreign should be added.

to be joined, Sun <note>original: *Sol*; alchemical gold</note> and Moon <note>original: *Luna*; alchemical silver</note> are not foreign to one another, because they are reduced at the beginning of the work into their first nature—that is, Mercury—which is why they took their origin from it. Some, however, strive to complete their work from Mercury alone, or from simple Magnesia <note>A term for the "prime matter" or essential base of the Stone</note>, washing it in the sharpest vinegar, cooking it in oil, subliming, roasting, calcining, distilling, and extracting the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated form of a substance</note>, twisting the Mercury itself with the elements and other infinite martyrizations <note>A term used by alchemists to describe the violent chemical processes—like heating or dissolving—used to break down a substance</note>, and believing by their operations that something great will be found from them; in the end, they find little profit. But believe me, son, that our entire mastery consists solely in the governance of fire through the capacity of industry. For we perform nothing, but the power of a well-directed fire works our stone with little labor and few expenses; provided that our stone, when it has been once dissolved into its first nature—namely, into the "first water," or "virgin's milk," or the "dragon's tail"—then the stone itself calcines, sublimes, distills, reduces, washes, and congeals itself. Through the power of proportionate fire, it perfects itself in a single vessel without any other manual operation.

Recognize therefore, son, how the philosophers have spoken figuratively about manual operations. So that you may be certain of the purging of our Mercury, I will teach the true operation for our common Mercury to be very gently prepared. Take, therefore, mineral Mercury, otherwise called Spanish earth, or our Antimony, or the "black, many-eyed earth"—all of which are the same thing and not inferior to their kind—and which has not been placed in any work before. Take twenty-five pounds at most and make it pass through a thick linen cloth three times; then make it pass through the skin of a hare, and finally make it pass through a thick linen cloth again. This is the true washing. Pay attention: if any of its thickness remains in the skin, or any density of filth or foulness, then that Mercury is not valid for our work. If, however, nothing appears, it is good for you. Note that with this Mercury, and with nothing else added to it, both works <note>Likely referring to the "White Work" (silver) and the "Red Work" (gold)</note> can be perfected.

### CHAPTER V.

Take two ounces of common purified **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*; gold</note>—that is, gold heated in the fire, which is the <term>ferment of redness</term> <note>A substance added to the "work" to induce the final red color of the Philosopher's Stone</note>—and cut it into small pieces with shears. Add fourteen ounces of Mercury and make the Mercury smoke in a tile; dissolve my Sun and stir it with a wooden rod until the gold is well-dissolved and mixed. Then pour the whole mixture into clear water in a glass or stone bowl, and wash it often by wiping and changing the water until all the blackness recedes from the water. Then, if you wish to pay attention, **the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land** <note>A biblical quote from the Song of Solomon, used by alchemists to signal the appearance of certain chemical changes or "signs of life" in the matter</note>. Once it is cleansed, make the <term>amalgam</term> <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal</note> pass through a well-bound leather, squeezing out the whole amalgam except for two ounces. 

<note>The text contains a likely error here: it first says 14 ounces remain in the leather, but then commands that exactly 2 ounces must remain. Logically, the 14 ounces of mercury are squeezed out, leaving the 2 ounces of gold-rich amalgam.</note> 

Fourteen ounces will remain in the leather <insert>this likely refers to the mercury squeezed out</insert>, and those fourteen ounces are things suitable for our operation; and attend that there should be neither more nor less than two ounces of the total matter remaining in the leather. If there is more, decrease it; if there is less, add to it. And those two expressed ounces, which are called **virgin's milk**, reserve for the second operation. 

Therefore, let the matter from the leather be placed into a glass vessel, and the glass into the <term>furnace</term> <note>original: *furnellum*; a small alchemical stove</note> described above, with a lamp lit beneath it, burning continuously day and night so that it is never extinguished. Let the flame, once enclosed, strike in a direct path, yet it should not touch the pot, with all parts of the furnace being well-sealed with <term>lute</term> <note>original: *lutatis*; a clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels</note> in a similar fashion. If, after a month or two, you wish to look upon the **flowers of life** and the principal colors—namely, the black, white, yellow, and red—then without any work of your hands, through the governance of the fire alone, the hidden shall be made manifest, and the manifest shall become hidden. In this way, our matter brings itself to the perfect **elixir**, turning itself into a most subtle powder, which is called the **dead earth**, or the **dead man in the tomb**, or **magnesia** <note>A term for the "prime matter" or base of the Stone</note>. Know then that the spirit is hidden within him in the tomb, and the soul...

### CHAPTER VI.

In the same way, the process is done for the **white** <note>The "White Work" or *Albedo*, the stage in the Great Work that produces silver</note>, that is, for **Moon** <note>original: *lunam*; the alchemical name for silver</note>. This is the <term>ferment of whiteness</term>. When you have mixed it with seven parts of purified Mercury, proceed in the same manner as you did for the red. For in every white work, nothing enters except the white, and in every red work, nothing but the red ought to enter. From the same water of ours, both red and white are made, yet with a different ferment added; and once the aforementioned time has elapsed, it can tinge Mercury to white, just as you did for the red. 

Note, however, that **soldered silver** <note>original: *Argentum solitatum*; likely silver that has been refined or prepared for a specific metallurgical use</note> is more useful in this matter than bulk silver <note>original: *argentum massale*</note>, because it contains within itself a mixture of certain dregs of Mercury, and it must be amalgamated with cold Mercury, not hot. Otherwise, those working this way err greatly by dissolving the <term>amalgam</term> <note>A mixture of mercury and another metal</note> in **strong water** <note>original: *aqua forti*; nitric acid, used to separate metals</note> to purify it; if they would consider the nature of the composition of strong water, they would see that the matter is more destroyed by it. 

Some also wish to work with mineral **Sun** or **Moon** <note>i.e., raw gold or silver found in the earth, rather than chemically prepared</note> according to the rules of this book, and they err, saying that the Sun has no humidity and is manifestly hot, and therefore best; indeed, the **quintessence** <note>original: *quinta essentia*; the "fifth essence" or the most purified, spiritualized core of a substance</note> is extracted by the subtle skill of fire in a vessel of circulation, which is called the **Pelican** <note>original: *Pellicanus*; a unique alchemical flask with two side-arms that feed back into the base, symbolizing the bird that feeds its young from its own breast</note>. Mineral Sun and Moon, however, have such a great amount of impure dregs mixed with them that their purification for our purpose would not be "the work of women and the play of children" <note>A common alchemical phrase suggesting a simple or easy task</note>, but rather the labors of a most strong elder man, persisting through dissolving, calcining, and other operations of the great art.

# THE BOOK OF LIGHT BY JOHN OF ROQUETAILLADE,
## *a brother of the Order of Friars Minor.* <note>The Franciscans</note>

### CHAPTER ONE.

First, I considered the future times which were foretold by Christ in the Gospel, namely concerning the tribulations in the time of the Antichrist, under whom the Roman Church will be scourged and stripped of all its riches by tyrants. And although the Church of God shall then be so desolate and confused, it shall nevertheless be delivered from such great tribulations by Christ. Therefore, to deliver the chosen people of God, to whom it is given to know the mystery of God and the mastery of truth, I wish to describe without long-windedness the work of the Great <term>Stone of the Philosophers</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note>, both for the <term>white</term> <note>Albedo: the stage for creating silver</note> and for the <term>red</term> <note>Rubedo: the final stage for creating gold</note>. And this is against the custom of the philosophers who were before us, who, because of malice and envy, concealed this art from their own sons. And my intention is to benefit the good [members] of the holy Roman Church, and to openly and briefly narrate its whole truth.

### *Concerning the matter of our stone.* CHAPTER II.

The matter of the stone is one and the same thing, of low price, which is found everywhere in viscous water, which is called **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note>. And since they say that it is found in vile places, many brutish men who do not understand the true intention of the Philosophers have sought this stone in dung. And know, my son, that the matter is prepared by removing the earthiness which **Mercury** has, and by adding to it the **Sulfur of the Philosophers**, which is not common sulfur; rather, our sulfur is invisible, and I shall name it by its own proper name, which is **vitriol** <note>A sulfate mineral, often iron or copper sulfate; a vital substance in alchemical laboratory work</note>...

### Concerning the Aforementioned Operation. CHAPTER III.

Take one pound each of Saltpeter and Roman Vitriol—that is, one pound of each, ground and mixed. Dry them in a golden pan over a slow fire, stirring constantly so that the moisture departs. Next, take one pound of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>, from the mine and not [extracted] from lead, and wrapped in a leather cloth, squeeze it over the heated matter of the vitriol and saltpeter. Because it is sown through the pores [of the cloth], stir the matter with a stick so it is well mixed, until no trace of the Mercury appears. Place it in a vessel to be <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form</note> over a gentle fire. If the matter has been well dried, keep the vessel closed; however, keep it open until the moisture has departed, which you will know by placing a metal blade or sword over the opening [to check for condensation]. Afterwards, strengthen the fire for twelve hours, and at the end make it even stronger so the work is well sublimated. 

When the vessel has cooled, extract it, and you will find the Mercury sublimated, white as snow. In this way, sublimate the Mercury itself three times with its own dregs, and once without the dregs. Thus, in this operation, you have achieved two things: you have purged the Mercury of its earthiness, its blackness, and the moisture it held; and you have congealed it, making it white as snow. You have made it fit for grinding and mixing, fit for <term>digestion</term> <note>slow, steady heating over a long period</note> in a dry stove, and fit for converting it into "water," as we shall describe below. 

You have placed within it invisible sulfur, which is the <term>tincture</term> <note>The essence or coloring principle capable of transforming matter</note> of redness; it is the spirit of Roman vitriol, and it provides a great aid. For that spirit has the nature of staining things red and congealing Mercury into a solid substance, and yet it makes it white as snow. 

And this is what the great philosophers wrote: that our Stone is made from prepared and separated Mercury and sulfur. Concerning this work and substance, Master Arnold <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist frequently cited in later medieval texts</note> speaks parabolically in his treatise: *unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies*, and so forth <note>original: "nisi granū frumenti in terram cadens mortuum fuerit"; a reference to the Gospel of John 12:24 used here to describe the alchemical process of "death" and "rebirth" of materials</note>. He understands the "grain dead in the earth" to be Mercury killed with saltpeter, Roman vitriol, and sulfur; there it is <term>mortified</term> <note>The stage of 'killing' or chemically breaking down a substance</note> and there it is sublimated with fire, and thus it brings forth much fruit. 

And this is the *Greater Stone* of all, which the philosophers sought and, once found, hid away. The sign [of success] is that the spirit of vitriol is incorporated into the Mercury, and that the sublimated Mercury leaves many dregs at the bottom of the vessel, while the spirit of vitriol ascends because...

### CHAPTER IV.

Afterward, break the vessel and extract the fifth essence or spirit of Mercury, and you will find burnt black substances in the bottom of the vessel, separated from the spirit of Mercury. ### On the fifth operation, which is the preparation of the matter or Virgin’s Milk for the "white" stage, by its reduction into powder.
## CHAPTER VII.

This operation concerns how the matter is prepared for the white stage <note>albedo, the second major phase of the alchemical Great Work</note>, and how the <term>Virgin’s Milk</term> <note>a term for the purified mercurial distillate</note> is <term>digested</term> <note>heated gently over a long period</note> and reduced by the power of fire into a powder so subtle that it cannot be felt by touch. Receive this, therefore, with the blessing of Jesus Christ. Some philosophers have said that an "animal" should be taken with all its blood; it is called an "animal" because it "grows" when it is <term>sublimated</term> <note>the process of a solid turning into vapor and then back to solid</note>, and because it has a bloody soul—namely, the aforementioned invisible spirit of <term>vitriol</term> <note>a sulfate mineral, usually of iron or copper</note>. Place this in a round-bottomed <term>ampoule</term> <note>a sealed glass vial</note>; heat its neck and "strangle" it—that is, squeeze it shut with forceps while the glass is hot so that nothing can escape. Place a metal plate between the fire and the flask, which must be well-prepared (meaning perforated) so that the Virgin’s Milk is not destroyed by the direct heat. Place it in a <term>philosophers’ furnace</term> <note>also called an athanor, designed for constant heat</note> so that it receives equal heat from every side, lest the Milk fly away due to uneven firing. It is a great task of service to provide the fire temperately so the work is not destroyed. Let as many coals burn as allows a man’s hand to be held inside the walls of the furnace. Within is the vessel containing the material of the shining Virgin’s Milk. You shall continue the fire until you see the matter turn black; rejoice then, for you have the beginning of digestion. Continue the fire until all the colors have passed, and you will see the matter begin to whiten. When you see the matter perfectly whitened, you possess the completed Stone for the white stage.

### On the sixth operation, namely the reddening of the white stone.
## CHAPTER VIII.

The sixth operation of the Stone continues until the stone, already completed at the white stage, is perfected to the red <note>rubedo, the final stage of the alchemical process</note>, with absolutely nothing added or removed. Thus, extract it from the aforementioned vessel, which is called the <term>Philosophers’ Egg</term> <note>an oval glass vessel symbolizing the womb of creation</note>. Master Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist</note> says that our Stone is enclosed in this vessel just as Christ was in the tomb. Then, take one part of this powder and keep it aside; with it, you will be able to convert all imperfect metals into true silver <note>original: *verā lunam*, literally "true moon"</note>.

<page-num>303</page-num>
<header>### THE BOOK OF LIGHT</header>

...and seal the other part in the aforementioned vessel as before, and strengthen the fire, as Master Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist frequently cited in medieval texts</note> says; he states that after the stone has reached perfect whiteness, it does not fear the punishments of fire, because there is no danger to it if you apply a strong fire, since such a fire is necessary for it. The reason for this is that if it is <term>digested</term> <note>heated slowly to mature the substance</note> by a slow fire, the invisible sulfur hidden in the <term>vitriol</term> <note>a sulfate mineral; here referring to the "soul" or "fire" of the matter</note>—namely, the spirit lurking beneath the whiteness of the stone—cannot be boiled down. Instead, the spirit of Mercury in that fire is digested to the white stage; therefore, it is necessary for the fire to be increased so that it may reach more deeply and digest the tincture of redness <note>original: *tincturam rubedinis*</note> of the hidden sulfur of vitriol. This brings the redness to the surface through the strengthening of the fire, and thus, by the power of the fire, the matter is turned into red without adding anything else to it. In this way, the **greatest king** <note>a common alchemical metaphor for the finished Philosopher's Stone</note> rises from the closed tomb and is resurrected from the dead, with a most brilliant crown upon his head, as Master Arnold says. 

But note that in two vessels, this work of the stone can be performed and operated toward both the white and the red stages with one fire and one furnace—except that you should withdraw the vessel for the white stage once it is "clothed in whiteness," while the vessel for the red stage must be notably increased in heat, as I have said. Note also that some perform this work using only the **Virgin’s Milk** <note>a term for the purified mercurial distillate or "mercury of the philosophers"</note> and do not care for the elements of fire and air; their work is done solely through the most noble Virgin’s Milk. Others mix three elements together: one weight of fire, four weights of air, and eight weights of Virgin’s Milk. This method is stronger for the red stage but weaker for the white stage. In these three ways, it can be done simultaneously in one vessel from the Virgin’s Milk alone for the red stage, and in another vessel from the three elements, using one furnace and one fire.

If you test these various methods, you will see the great miracles that have been bestowed by God Most High. Concerning this work, there has never been anyone before me who spoke the truth so clearly. For indeed, the great philosophers to whom this secret and mastery were revealed were bound by a horrible curse from God, that they should in no way declare this divine work to any man, lest this secret fall into the hands of wicked men. But I do not care for such a curse; for I do not reveal this secret to villainous men, but I reveal it to the Church of God, to perfect Christians, and to those who fear God, so that they may succor the poor—and especially the evangelical brothers and the churches—so that they may visit widows, wards, and orphans in their necessities and tribulations. 

And this is the **sixth operation**.

### *Concerning the seventh operation, which is about projection.*
### CHAPTER IX.

The seventh part of this work concerns the practical application of the power of the <term>elixir</term> <note>the "stone" or transformative substance</note>—namely, the perfect medicine. The power of this elixir for the "white" stage is that it converts <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note>, <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note>, <term>Mars</term> <note>iron</note>, and <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note> into true <term>Moon</term> <note>silver</note>. And the power of the perfect medicine for the "red" stage is that it converts the aforementioned bodies and silver into <term>Sun</term> <note>gold</note>. 

It is done in this way: Place Mercury in a <term>crucible</term> <note>a vessel for melting metals</note> and heat it until the Mercury almost boils and smokes. Afterward, cast upon it while it is thus boiling the White or Red Medicine, whichever you wish. Give it a strong fire as if you intended to melt silver, and after a sufficient <term>decoction</term> <note>heating or boiling down</note>, draw it out. If it possesses much color, or if it is breakable, then it is the perfect medicine. Then, project it upon other Mercury until the color and the malleability please you; experience will teach you upon how many weights it may fall, for sometimes it will fall upon many weights, and sometimes upon few, just as one method of operation will surpass another, and according to the skill of the Master of the art. 

Upon lead and tin, the melted medicine is projected, and the fire is increased as described above. Upon <term>latten</term> <note>a brass-like alloy</note>, iron, and steel, it is projected in this manner: First, the powder is cast upon glowing plates, and it is weighed for refiring; or those bodies are melted, and the medicine is cast into them while they are molten. These bodies do not require a preceding purification, because the medicine is like a **fire of hell** <note>original: *ignis inferni*; a metaphor for its intense, purifying power</note>, virtually consuming every imperfection of all bodies and converting them into its own nature—which is their good and ultimate end. 

Some Philosophers, when they wish to work toward silver, project the medicine upon bronze or iron; and when working toward gold, they project the medicine upon the purest melted gold, and this "medicated gold" then becomes the medicine to convert bronze or silver into gold. The medicine can also be dissolved in a <term>bath</term> <note>bain-marie or water bath</note> and congealed by the fire through repeated turns; in this way, its power is increased infinitely.

Likewise, ensure that the side of the plate does not rise to the head of the pot, lest the fire reverberate against the vessels from the middle air above the cups and the tripod. See that the fire is on every side of it, for more fire rises through three holes than through one; thus you will be able to increase or diminish the fires as it seems best to you. 

Note that upon the tripod where there is a gap in the plate, you can fit an earthen bowl, and beneath the bowl a tripod, and there place the **philosophical egg**, and place another bowl beneath it. It is thus appropriate to raise or erect two bowls in the air, so that it does not touch the sides of the bowls, etc.

### THE DESCRIPTION AND FORM OF THE PHYSICAL FURNACE FOLLOWS.

*This furnace shall be three and a half feet in total height, and one and a half feet wide inclusive, and divided as follows.*

*First, the furnace shall be so composed that the space through which the ashes fall through an iron grate is one foot high. From the iron grate to the middle—the space where the hearth is built—it shall be nine <term>digits</term> <note>an ancient unit of measurement approximately equal to the width of a finger, or about 0.75 inches</note> high. Thus, having a height of two feet minus three digits, a plate of clay or iron is to be placed in the middle, in the center of which there is a round hole four digits in diameter, through which the heat of the fire may ascend into the upper part where the work is performed. Then, over that hole, there shall be three removable lids, slightly wider than the hole of the intermediate plate, just as is marked with the letter A. Each lid will also have a round hole of a different size. In the first, the hole will be three digits; in the second, two; and in the third, finally, one; so that one may be used in place of another as the heat of the fire requires a change of the lids.*

*The space where the work is performed, namely from the intermediate plate to the very top cover, shall be one foot and three digits high. In this space, an earthenware or iron <term>tripod</term> <note>a three-legged stand used to support the glass vessel above the heat source</note> is placed directly over the hole of the intermediate plate, as is marked with the letter B. This tripod shall be three and a half digits wide at its upper part, and six digits high; upon it, you will place the glass vessel which contains all the matter intended for the operation.*

## THE LITTLE KEY OF RAYMOND LULLY OF MAJORCA, also called the "Opener," in which all things required for the work of Alchemy are clearly declared. <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315) was a philosopher and mystic. We have called this work of ours the **Little Key** <term>Clauicula: Latin for "little key." In alchemical literature, a "Clavicula" is a text intended to explain or unlock the secrets hidden in more complex, "locked" manuscripts.</term>, because without this present book, no one can understand what we have written in our other books. In those works, we completed the entire art, though we used words that were quite obscure for the sake of the ignorant. I have written many long books divided into sections and under obscure names <note>original: "dijs" – likely a variant of "dictis" (sayings/terms) or a reference to planetary "gods" used as code.</note>, as appears in our **Testament** <note>original: "testamento" – the *Testamentum* is one of the most famous alchemical works attributed to Lully.</note>, where we dealt with natural principles. All things pertaining to the art are placed there, though they are "under the hammer" <note>original: "sub martello" – a metaphor likely meaning the knowledge is still in a raw, forged, or encrypted state.</note> in the first text of Philosophy. 

Likewise, I have written in our chapter on the **quicksilver** <term>arg. viuo: "argentum vivum," or Mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "spirit" of all metals.</term> of the Philosophers, and in the second part of the *Testament* regarding the abundance of physical minerals, and in our book on the **fifth essence** <term>quinta essentia: the Quintessence or "ether," the purest fifth element that transcends the standard four (earth, air, fire, water).</term>—that is, on the fifth essence of gold and silver—and then in other books made by me, where the whole art is completed. 

But we have hidden the secret as much as possible. However, because without this secret no one can enter the "minerals of the philosophers" <note>A metaphorical term for the hidden base materials needed to begin the Great Work.</note> nor do anything that might benefit them, I will declare the whole art without any deception, with the help of the Most High, who was pleased to reveal this secret to us. And therefore, beware of revealing this secret to the wicked; share it only with your intimate friends. Even then, you should give it to no one lightly, since it is a gift of God, who will give it to whom He wills. He who possesses it will have an eternal treasure. Know, therefore, how to correct the imperfect by means of the perfect. The **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the Sun (Sol) always represents Gold.</note> is the father of all metals, and the **Moon** <note>In alchemy, the Moon (Luna) always represents Silver.</note> is the mother, although the Moon receives her brightness from the Sun. ### *On the difference between common quicksilver and Physical quicksilver.*

## CHAPTER ONE.

We say that common quicksilver cannot be the quicksilver of the philosophers, by whatever artifice it may be prepared, because the common kind cannot be held in the fire except by another corporeal quicksilver that is hot, dry, and more highly "digested" <term>Digestion: A process of slow, consistent heating used to mature a substance, similar to how the body processes food.</term>. Therefore, I say our Physical [mercury] is of a more fixed and hotter nature than the common. 

And this is because our corporeal quicksilver has been converted into a running quicksilver that does not stain the fingers; and when it is mixed with the common kind, they join and embrace each other in a bond of love so that they are never separated from one another, just like water mixed with water, for so it pleases nature. Indeed, our quicksilver enters and actually mixes with the common kind, drying out its phlegmatic moisture and removing the coldness from the body, blackening it like coal, which it afterward converts into powder. 

Note, therefore, that common quicksilver cannot perform those operations which our Physical [mercury] can, for our mercury possesses the heat of nature’s true temperament in all its qualities; therefore it turns the common kind into its own tempered nature. Furthermore, it does something else: for after its transmutation, it converts [the substance] into pure metal—that is, into the Sun or the Moon.

These, being free, will multiply their species into infinity; for from one ounce of this powder, you will make infinite Suns, and you will reduce it into a Moon better than any metal from the mine.

### *Regarding our Great Work for the white and for the red.*
#### CHAPTER VII.

Reduce your living lime <term>calx viva: a purified metallic ash, not common quicklime</term>, as was previously stated regarding the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; alchemical code for silver</note>, into quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note>, which is our secret. You can reduce this lime into the finest Gold, as was said above regarding the Silver.

...[multiplied] units, place 4 ounces of our living lime <term>calx viva: here referring to a purified metallic substance rather than common lime</term> in the menstrual solvent <note>original: *menstruali*; an alchemical solvent used to break down substances</note> so that it may be dissolved, and it will immediately be dissolved into green water. Likewise, in 13 ounces of the same fetid menstrual solvent, you shall dissolve 4 ounces of common quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note> that has been well-washed. And when the quicksilver has been dissolved, join both solutions together, and place the vessel, well sealed, in digestion in horse dung <note>a traditional alchemical method for providing gentle, consistent heat</note> for 30 days. When these are finished, cause it to distill in a water bath <note>original: *balneo*; a vessel of hot water used for indirect heating</note> until you have retrieved everything. Then take the residue in another vessel, so that the oil may be extracted from it over a charcoal fire; then the remaining matter will be black. Place this in the furnace over ashes to distill for two hours. After cooling, open the vessel and pour the water distilled via the water bath over it. Wash it well. Distill the menstrual solvent through the water bath, and all the water that can rise, and the oil through the ashes just as you did above. And by doing this, you shall repeat the process so many times until the matter remains like coal, black in the bottom of the vessel.

Son of the doctrine, you will then have the "Crow's Head" <note>original: *caput corvi*; the symbol of the *nigredo* or black stage, representing the death of the material</note>, which philosophers have sought so much, and without which nothing is accomplished in the Mastery. Therefore, son, keep in mind the divine supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, who died, was buried and entombed, and on the third day rose again into a permanent earth. <note>Alchemists frequently used Christ's death and resurrection as an allegory for the chemical process of purification and the "rebirth" of the stone.</note> Son, keep in mind that no being can be made perpetual in life unless it has first died. Take, therefore, your black body and calcine <note>heat to a high temperature to drive off volatile substances</note> it in the same vessel for three days; afterwards let it cool, and upon opening the vessel you will find a spongy and dead earth, which you shall keep until it is necessary to perform the union of the body with the soul.

Take the water that was distilled through the water bath, and distill it many times until it is purified and reduced into a crystalline matter. Imbibe, therefore, your body—which is the black earth—with its own proper water, gradually sprinkling and cooking it until the body is made white and very shining. And then the water is infused into it, which vivifies and clarifies it. Then apply a vehement fire in its same luted <note>sealed with airtight clay</note> vessel, as if you wished to sublimate common mercury, for 12 hours. Open the cooled vessel, and you will find your white matter sublimated, which we call "sealed earth" <note>original: *terra sigillata*; traditionally a medicinal clay, used here for the purified White Stone</note>. This is our body, exalted and placed in great dignity: our sulfur, our quicksilver, our arsenic, wherein you must keep our gold—which is our ferment—and our living lime; and between them it begets the "son of fire," which is the love of the philosophers.

### *Multiplication of the aforesaid sulfur.*
## CHAPTER IX.

Place that matter of yours in a strong measuring vessel <term>metreto: a glass or ceramic vessel used for precise chemical measurement</term>, upon which you should place an amalgam made from our living lime <note>original: *calce viva*; in this context, it refers to a purified metallic substance rather than common quicklime</note>, which was prepared in our first practice, where we reduced it into silver. Let them be mixed together, as described above; and place them over a fire of ashes <note>a method of heating where the vessel sits in a bed of hot ashes to distribute heat evenly</note>. You will see the matter move; then increase the fire, and in 4 hours it will become a very white sulfurous substance. When this has been fixed <note>made resistant to evaporation by heat</note>, one ounce of it will coagulate and fix 100 ounces of any common quicksilver into a true medicine, and this can be repeated upon a thousand, and so on unto infinity.

### *Fixation of the aforesaid multiplied sulfur.*
## CHAPTER X.

Take the sulfur that has now been multiplied and set it down in the measuring vessel. Pour the oil over it which had been saved during the separation of the elements, and let it sit until it becomes soft. Afterwards, place it upon the ashes for fusion <note>melting together</note>, applying fire of the first, second, and third degrees <note>referring to the alchemical scale of heat intensity</note> until it reaches a state of whiteness. Then break the vessel, and you will find a white crystalline plate. Place a piece of this upon a hot metal plate, and if it flows without smoke, project <note>add the medicine to a base metal</note> one weight of this substance upon 1,000 weights of Mercury, and the whole will be converted into silver. If the medicine is not flowing and fusible, set it back into a crucible, adding the oil drop by drop until it flows like wax; then your medicine will be perfected at a ratio of 1 to 1,000, and it can be multiplied infinitely.

->*A recapitulation of the whole mastery in a brief form.*<-

## CHAPTER XII.

Everything we have treated in this book, we have learned to be true, and we testify to it; we have seen it with our own eyes, felt it with our hands, touched it and performed it. This recapitulation encompasses our entire mastery in a brief discourse and without fiction. We therefore command the stone which we name: that you refine it as much by the ingenuity of nature as of art, and reduce it into quicksilver <note>original: *arg. viuum* (argentum vivum); philosophical mercury</note>. To this quicksilver let a "white body" be added, which is of the same nature, and let it be boiled until it reaches the true preparation of the mineral. And let that mineral be multiplied according to your will. And once again, let the aforesaid matter be reduced into quicksilver, and dissolve it in our solvent <term>menstruali: a philosophical solvent, not common acid, used to break down metallic bodies</term>, until the stone becomes volatile, divided from all its elements. And finally, let both the body and soul be perfectly purged to the ultimate perfection, so that a good conjunction of the body with the spirit can be made, by means of tempered natural heat. 

And let the stone be made into a mineral, and let the fire be continued until it is reduced into a white powder, which we call the sulfur and quicksilver of the philosophers, and then by the vigor of fire it is made fixed or volatile. It is changed to such an extent that the volatile part flies away from its coarse earths and ascends on high, whiter than snow, and the dregs should be cast away, because they are worth nothing. Then take our sulfur and the aforesaid oil, and you shall multiply it with its stated distillation vessel <term>alembico: a traditional alchemical still with a cooling "beak"</term>, until it is once more reduced into a white powder whiter than snow. Let the powders be fixed, having been multiplied by the ingenuity of both nature and practice, by boiling with water until all things remain stable in the test of the fire, flowing like wax without smoke. And the water of the first solution must be added; once that solution is made, let some yellow substance be added—which is gold—by way of conjunction, with the distillation of the whole soul. Afterward, let the fire be given in the first, second, third, and fourth degrees.

### C H A P T E R XIII.

Take <note>original: *Rec.* (Recipe); the standard opening for an alchemical or medical formula</note> one ounce of fine Silver <note>original: *Luna*; the Moon, the alchemical symbol for silver</note> refined by cupel <note>original: *de copella*; a cupel is a shallow porous cup used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead</note> and three ounces of quicksilver, and let an amalgam be made. First, let the silver leaf be heated in a crucible, then let the quicksilver be cast in, stirring with a rod, and let both be heated well. Then let it be placed in vinegar with salt, grinding them together in a wooden mortar with a pestle, washing away and removing the impurity, doing this until it is finally amalgamated. Then let it be washed with clean, warm common water; afterward, let it pass through a clean linen cloth. That which remains in the cloth, having the nature of a "body" <note>the solid part of the mixture</note>, should be added again with three parts of salt and one part of the body, grinding and washing well; let it be strained and calcined <note>heated to a powder without melting</note> for 12 hours. Grind it again with salt, repeating this three times and adding new salt. Let it be powdered again until it is an impalpable dust, and wash it with warm water until all saltiness has departed. Then let it be strained through a cotton filter, and let your lime <note>original: *calx*; the powder resulting from calcination</note> be dried. It will be a white lime; let it be put away until the hour of necessity, lest the coldness touch it.

->*To make Oil of Tartar.*<-

### C H A P T E R XIV.

Take good Tartar <note>original: *tartarum*; the crystalline crust found in wine barrels, potassium bitartrate</note> that is "shining in the fracture" <note>meaning it has a bright, crystalline interior when broken</note>, and let it be calcined in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note> for ten hours. Afterward, let it be powdered and placed upon marble to dissolve in a cold place; there it will dissolve into a liquid oil. And when it has all been dissolved, let it be distilled through a cotton filter and kept neatly for the "imbibition" <note>the soaking or saturation</note> of your lime.

### C H A P T E R  XVI.

Take <note>original: *Rec.* (Recipe); the traditional imperative for the start of a formula</note> three pounds of reddish Roman vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfate, a key acidic component in alchemical recipes</note>, one pound of saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and three ounces of cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide, known for its bright red color</note>. Then let them be placed in a large and strong glass vessel <note>original: *metreto*</note>, and let there be added water of life <note>original: *aquæ vitæ*; typically a highly rectified alcohol or a potent distilled spirit</note> rectified seven times; then let it be placed in horse dung <note>original: *fimo equino*; decomposing horse manure provided a steady, gentle heat for long-term digestion or fermentation</note> for 15 days, in a vessel well sealed. Afterward, let the fire be increased until the cap <note>original: *cappæ*; refers to the head of the alembic or the top of the furnace</note> reaches a red heat. Then let the fire be strengthened until the cap reaches a white heat; afterward, let the vessel cool, and let the receiver be removed and sealed very well with wax, and kept until needed. Note that the solvent <note>menstruum</note> ought to be rectified seven times by distillation, always throwing away the dregs, before it is put to use in the work.

# THE MINERAL 
## WORKS OF MASTER JOHANN ISAAC
### HOLLANDUS, OR CONCERNING THE
### Philosopher's 
### Stone,
->BOOK ONE.<-

NOW I wish to teach my son the first method discovered in Alchemy for restoring all metals which are dead and impure to the true Sun and Moon <note>original: *Solem & Lunam*; alchemical metaphors for Gold and Silver</note>: and my son shall know that this method is called the "first order" in Alchemy: because it is the first that was discovered in the nature of things for perfecting imperfect metals.

->The Work of the First Order.<-

When finished, let it cool, and having removed the alembic, take out that which has been sublimated. Remove the dregs <note>original: *fæces*</note>; you may test whether anything but dregs remains by placing it upon a burning coal or a glowing plate of copper or iron.

### CHAPTER IV.

Then you shall sublimate again that which was once sublimated, using fresh material <note>reagents like the salt and alum mentioned before</note>, proceeding in all ways as described above. You shall repeat this sublimation a third time, always with fresh material. Finally, you shall sublimate it by itself—that is, without any other material—until nothing more remains [in the bottom]; then the Stone is pure. For first, it has been purged of all its combustible sulfur <note>alchemists believed "combustible sulfur" was an impurity that caused metals to be destroyed by fire</note>, so that it is no longer consumable by fire. It is also thoroughly purged of its earthiness <note>original: *terrestritate*; the gross, solid impurities</note>, which prevented it from entering <note>penetrating or transforming other metals</note>; for both that earthiness and the combustible sulfur were left behind with the dregs. Previously, the combustible sulfur burned its body when it was moved to the fire, and the earthiness prevented its entry so that it could not penetrate into metals; it is now separated and free from these two, as has been said.

## CHAPTER V.

<margin>
The Stone contains certain subtle spirits.

The Stone is partly fixed and partly not fixed.
</margin>

Now my son shall also know that this Stone still contains matter within itself which takes away its <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates or escapes when heated</note>. For as long as it contains that matter, this Stone can never be fixed. And in this, many are deceived who do not know this matter. My son might ask, what is that matter? Let my son hold this as a great secret: there exists within this Stone—both the white and the red—a certain most subtle spirit <note>original: *spiritum subtilissimum*; refers to extremely volatile vapors</note>, so fleeting and subtle that the Stone could never be fixed even if it were in the fire for a thousand years. For when it is to be fixed, whether with a <term>ferment</term> <note>an additive, often gold or silver, used to "seed" the Stone’s transformative power</note> or with some other body, such a tiny fire must be applied that nothing at all is sublimated upward; otherwise, it will not become fixed with the ferment or the body, and it would then have to be joined together again and again. How could it ever be fixed in that way? Truly, this Stone possesses those subtle spirits, none of which can be allowed to ascend. Therefore, the subtle spirit must be separated from the Stone, just like that coarse earthiness or earthy matter that prevents "entry" <note>original: *ingressum*; the ability of the alchemical medicine to penetrate and transform a base metal</note>. Thus, these two matters must be separated from the Stone before the Stone can be fixed with any ferment or body.

<margin>
The Stone must be purified of three superfluities: namely, combustible sulfur, earthiness that prevents entry, and the subtle spirit that hinders fixation.
</margin>

<margin>
Superfluous things are to be removed from the Stone, but tempered things are to be preserved within it.
</margin>

The "middle spirit" or matter is to be taken, which is always found in the middle place; and that is the spirit we seek, which is between the fixed and the non-fixed. For if you place that matter in a glass crucible, it will melt before it begins to fly away; nor will it fly quickly, but rather in the manner of pure wax, rising slowly from the fire. Thus, the matter of the Stone is "tempered" <note>balanced or harmonized</note> between the fixed and the non-fixed once its superfluity has been taken away—that is, first the combustible <term>Sulfur</term> <note>not common brimstone, but an oily, flammable impurity thought to cause "burning" or blackening in chemical reactions</note>, then its earthiness that prevents or takes away entry, and finally its subtle combustible spirits that rob the Stone of its fixation. And in this all Alchemists err, because they do not know the Stone nor its nature, and they do not take away its superfluity. That is to say, they do not remove the superfluous parts, nor can they preserve the tempered parts between the fixed and non-fixed; and this is the greatest secret in this art. Therefore, learn to know the Stone and its nature, and you shall not err.

...sublimation <note>The text begins mid-word, completing the term "sublimationis" from the preceding page</note>, with the receiver <term>luted</term> <note>sealed with airtight clay or paste</note> firmly to the beak of the vessel, he shall add a very tiny fire, only a little warmer than the sun in midsummer. But the matter of the Stone, which is likened to all natures, is found in the middle, sublimated to the neck of the pot; it does not ascend as high as those subtle, combustible spirits. For the matter of the Stone is neither able nor strong enough to rise to that height to which that subtle spirit ascends. This is because the matter of the Stone possesses certain "fixed" parts in its nature which hold back those volatile parts, so that they cannot rise as high as those subtle, "intemperate" <note>unbalanced or overly volatile</note> spirits, with which no fixed parts are mixed. 

Truly, take out and save the noble matter of the Stone, for it is that true Stone which Almighty God has given us freely, and it is prepared for our work. Indeed, it is equal in its power to operate in all the works of the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>the "Philosophers" refers to historical alchemists like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber</note>. For if you place this Stone in a glass <term>crucible</term> over the fire, it will melt like wax before it begins to ascend; then it will rise gradually, like wax or anything else that rises by fire. Its fixed parts, which it contains within itself, bring this about; they hold those volatile parts near them so that they must melt along with the fixed parts before they ascend. Thus, even those fixed parts sometimes ascend together with them. For the volatile parts of the Stone are greater than the fixed parts; therefore, the volatile parts partially lift the fixed parts with them by the force of the fire. 

Know this, my son: the knowledge of this Stone will lead your work to a happy conclusion by the help of God, the Best and Greatest; but truly, ignorance of the Stone gives birth to many errors.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>How the prepared materials are to be mixed.</margin>
You shall know moreover, my son, that you must take 10 lbs of prepared <term>Saturn</term> <note>Lead</note> and 1 lb of prepared <term>Luna</term> <note>Silver</note>, which together make 11 lbs; then take 12 <note>the unit is likely ounces or a proportional measure</note> of your prepared spirit, and mix them well together. Then grind them upon a stone with common water, so that a painter might be able to paint with that material using a brush. Then evaporate the moisture over a <term>balneum</term> <note>a water bath used for gentle heating</note> until it turns to powder, and then place it in a large glass or stone jar <note>original: "olla"</note> made in this fashion:

You shall smooth the jar upon an even stone and place a smoothed lid upon it, and with a lead weight placed on top, you shall set it in the <term>Furnace of the Philosophers</term>. Place it in a ceramic bowl with ashes, with three openings set above the furnace, so that it receives heat from both above and below. And whatever you do, add only a small fire at first for six weeks. When these have passed, increase the fire gradually until it can endure a great fire. Test this often by removing a little on a plate <note>original: "laminae"</note> to see if it is <term>fixed</term> <note>chemically stable and no longer evaporating when heated</note>. If it is not yet fixed, let it remain. When you see it has become fixed, take out one <term>drachm</term> <note>a small unit of weight</note>, put it into a glass crucible, and place it in the fire. Let it glow for a quarter of an hour, then let it cool and weigh it to see if you have your [original] weight. If you do not have it, put it back in until it becomes fixed. 

Then you have good Silver <note>original: "Luna"</note> by all tests, and that Silver could be reduced to good Gold <note>original: "Solem"</note> with little labor. In this same way, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin</note> is reduced to Silver, just as was taught here regarding Lead. And if you place Gold <note>original: "Solem"</note> in the position of the <term>ferment</term> <note>a substance added to trigger the transformation of the whole mass</note>, Gold shall be made from Lead. But in the work of Tin, you can produce nothing except Silver. This is the book of the first order concerning the reduction of Tin and Lead to Silver and Gold. But if you wish to reduce Lead to Gold, the <term>Red Stone</term> <note>the higher-grade version of the Philosopher's Stone used for making gold, rather than the white stone used for silver</note> must be prepared, just as was taught concerning the white; and Gold must be taken in its essence, or at least reduced to a <term>calx</term> <note>a fine powder produced by roasting a metal</note>.

<header>MASTER JOHANN ISAACUS</header>

Apply such heat from above that the <term>spirit</term> <note>In alchemy, the "spirit" refers to the volatile, vaporous part of a substance</note> exits through the <term>ferment</term> <note>The "ferment" is the substance added to the base material to trigger a transformation, much like yeast in bread</note> and settles itself below in the bottom of the glass. Therefore, the fire must be governed in this way: so that there is equal heat in the upper and lower parts of the furnace. You would be greatly deceived if you raised more heat in the upper than in the lower part of the furnace, such that the spirit would subside below through the ferment, and then you were to take some from there for testing. Therefore, do as you were taught above—namely, that you test and weigh. For if you were to take it out and test it, but did not weigh it; when you took from your ferment (from which the spirit had been <term>sublimated</term> <note>Sublimation is the process where a solid turns into a gas and then back to a solid, often rising to the top of a vessel</note> below or above), you would find it to be of full weight. Then you would judge it to be <term>fixed</term> <note>A "fixed" substance is one that has become stable and will no longer evaporate or change when exposed to high heat</note>, but you would be deceived: for the spirit would be lying below at the bottom, and the ferment would be above the spirit, and you would have tested nothing other than the ferment alone. For this reason, look forward accurately so that you rule the fire in such a way that the heat below and 

<margin>It is better to err on the side of too little rather than too much fire.</margin>

above, and in the sides, is equally great. And whatever you do, apply a smaller rather than a larger fire: thus you cannot be deceived, and even though a much longer time will be needed before it is fixed, it is nonetheless much more certain. Therefore, be wise, my son, and take care for yourself in building the fire, lest you must begin again from the start, exactly as if it had never been moved to the fire. For in the whole of the <term>Art</term> <note>A common term for the practice of alchemy</note>, nothing must be more carefully attended to than this fixation. For the spirit and the ferment ought to remain joined and united if they are ever to be fixed at last. For how could two become one when one withdraws itself from the other, and when they are separated from each other in turn? Therefore, my son, see prudently that you moderate your fire so that you do not drive the spirit, soul, and body away from each other by too vehement a fire, but always build a small fire, so that they remain joined, that both the soul and body may be able to be one. Read this lesson again and again, and 

<margin>Note: in the space of a Lord's Prayer the fire can be neglected, such that one must begin again from the start: therefore these things are to be read and remembered often.</margin>

impress it upon your mind, for by the negligence of the fire many works are lost. ### Projection. CHAPTER X.

You shall also take, my son, pure cleaned <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper</note>, and you shall melt 4 parts of it over one part of <term>Luna</term> <note>The alchemical name for silver</note>. ### The third work of the medicine of the 3rd order. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>The difference between the work of the second and third order.</margin>
You shall now also know, my son, that there is furthermore another work or medicine, and it is the work of the <term>third order</term>. There is no difference between the work of the second and third order except this alone: that the third is prepared more subtly and strongly. The second order makes no <term>projection</term> <note>The act of casting a small amount of alchemical agent into a larger mass of base metal to transform it</note> except upon purified metals, but the third makes a projection upon impure metals. > *Our medicine removes the rust from metals, and gives an eternal <term>tincture</term> <note>A permanent color or quality imparted to a substance</note>, which they preserve forever.*

OF MINERAL WORKS

### *On preparing the Stone from Silver alone.*

<margin>The nature of all those things which exist beneath the Lunar circle <note>original: "sub circulo Lunari"; referring to the "sublunary" realm of Earth, which in medieval cosmology was the realm of change and decay, governed by the Moon.</note> must be understood.</margin>
Next, my son, I wish to teach you the composition of the Stone of the Ancients, and first how you shall arrive at it: You shall study diligently in this art, my son, and with a sharp mind you shall comprehend the sayings of the ancients. You must also learn the nature of all things, and how nature works in all things, and especially whatever lies beneath the <term>Lunar circle</term> <note>The sphere of the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> and its course: and when the Moon first began its course in the Sphere, and from where. Furthermore, you must hold fast to the knowledge of where metals in the <term>mines</term> <note>original: "fodinis"</note> derive their origin, from where they first grow and increase, and how, and toward what state the nature of metals loves to be reduced—and would have reduced itself, had nature not been hindered by other things so that it could not finish its work. You must know the causes of these hindrances, and know also (if you wish to be a worker in this art) in which works you should not imitate nature, and in which you ought to imitate it. I tell you this must be known, or I do not advise you to undertake the work. Those who are ignorant of this are far from the art, being without foundation or root upon which their thoughts or the perceptions of their minds can lean; and for this reason, they do not know whether they act rightly or wrongly. Indeed, unless you know their essence and nature, their beginning, growth, and defects—the reasons why nature cannot reach its goal—and if you do not know their inner parts, you will accomplish nothing in our art. Therefore study diligently before you approach the work, and if you are sick or of weak health, do not begin; for the work, once it has been started, can by no means be interrupted. You must also excel in sharpness of wit, for here one must work with subtlety.

<margin>The chemical art is an enemy to the poor.</margin>
Furthermore, he who wishes to put his hands to this work can practice nothing else. Likewise, it must by no means be undertaken out of greed, for you could not wait for the end; for the greedy always think of profit. And if you are poor, you will not even be able to pursue it, for this art is an enemy to the poor. The expense is great, and the work cannot be done with a small amount of material, and the time required is long. Unless you know yourself to be provided with such wealth that you can provide for yourself and your companions for two years—the expenses, vessels, glasses, and other utensils—do not begin, for you cannot carry out the work alone. Likewise, you must have much material from which to complete your work; for to finish it, you must have at least 3 pounds <note>original: "3 ℔."</note> of material, and prepared from the start, so that if anything...

MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC

...that nothing be lacking to you in the work, so that you may have enough material to correct the work. Now, my son, since you feel yourself properly instructed in these aforesaid matters, and fit for performing our work and bringing it to its conclusion—so that nothing is missing, as was said before, and you have knowledge of all things and know the nature of metals—you must also recognize the material from which this most excellent work ought to be made.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>The error of many <term>sophists</term> <note>In alchemy, "sophists" were those who practiced "false" chemistry, using deceptive or superficial methods rather than following the true laws of nature.</note> who desire to extract the stone from other things.</note></margin>
You know, moreover, that all metals grow from the mixture of <term>Mercury</term> and <term>Sulfur</term>, both the clean and the unclean. It is also established that metals can be produced from no other thing in the nature of things than from these two. Therefore, it is clear that no foreign things enter into our stone which have not drawn their first origin from these two. 

All those err who presume to extract the stone from hair, eggs, blood, living creatures, or from any of the four <term>spirits</term> <note>The "four spirits" of alchemy were typically mercury, sulfur, orpiment, and sal ammoniac.</note>, and those who seek it from urine <note>original: "lotio"</note>, or from Mercury or Sulfur which were not bodies <note>He refers to mercury and sulfur in their common, volatile state, rather than the "fixed" or "philosophical" versions required for the Work.</note>; all these are the ravings and dreams of men ignorant of nature. Others amalgamate the <term>Sun</term> (gold), the <term>Moon</term> (silver), and purified Mercury, and they set them to be cooked. When they have cooked them for a long time, they obtain a red powder, like brick dust; but when they desire to test whether the Mercury is "fixed" <note>original: "fixus"; meaning stable and resistant to evaporation by heat.</note>, it goes off in smoke, and carries away with it the best part of the metal’s body. That which is fixed remains as a dry matter which cannot be melted, so thoroughly has it been dried out by the fire. 

There are others still who wish to draw out the stone from the Sun and Moon, as if they thought they could extract the red or white stone from these perfect bodies, which are hard and solid; wherefore that is also impossible for us. For our natural fire harms these bodies very little, and could do nothing to them, even if the stone could be led out from there. They are hard and fixed, and nothing foreign can be added to our stone; only those things which are superfluous in it are to be taken away, and it must be made subtle, and more than subtle. Those are the hard and fixed bodies which, if they were to be reduced so that the stone could be elicited from them, would have to be "un-fixed" <note>original: "defixanda"; a process of breaking down a solid substance to make it volatile or liquid again.</note>, and spirits would have to be made from them, if anything can be produced from them. Thus it becomes clear that our stone cannot be extracted from hard, fixed bodies.

Now my son may truly ask: from where is our stone to be extracted? Let my son know, however, that the Sages have sought something...

<summary>Isaac Hollandus explains that the Philosopher's Stone must originate from the principles of Mercury and Sulfur, rejecting the use of organic materials or common metals in their solid, "fixed" state. He warns that trying to extract the stone from gold or silver alone is impossible because their "fixed" nature resists the subtle alchemical fire.</summary>

You know now the material from which you will elicit the stone; you also know that I have here clearly demonstrated and named the material to you under other words.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>That there is only one method for the red and the white stone. * Or, that there is only one material.</margin>
My son shall know for certain that there are not several methods, but only one, for the red and for the white stone <note>In alchemy, the "white stone" (albedo) was capable of transmuting metals into silver, while the "red stone" (rubedo) was the final perfection, capable of making gold.</note>. However, there were once those who could not extract this stone except from the two <term>luminaries</term> <note>The "luminaries" refer to the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver).</note>, that is, from the aforementioned material. When they had already drawn out the stone, they first produced the stone for the white, using no white <term>ferment</term> <note>A "ferment" in alchemy acts like yeast in bread; it is a small amount of "perfect" metal (gold or silver) added to the alchemical medicine to "fix" it and give it the specific quality of the desired metal.</note>, and they produced the stone with great labor. Then they additionally produced the same for the red, with no red ferment used, and produced it with great labor, over a long time, and with great subtlety. For the stone thus produced performed a wondrous and infinite projection <note>"Projection" is the final stage where a small amount of the Stone is cast upon a molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note>. They did not know how to make the stone otherwise than from both materials for the red and white without any ferment. Therefore, they wrote in their secret books that the stone cannot be made except from both those materials, as much for the red as for the white. In this they wrote the truth: but the stone for the red cannot be made unless you add ferment, and the material for the white must be present. Similarly, the stone for the white cannot be extracted unless a ferment is used, and the material for the red must be present. These were the first who found the material for making the stone.

### CHAPTER XVI.

But afterwards other Philosophers emerged who inspected the matter more deeply—namely, that there is a double material created by God, one for the red and the other for the white. Progressing further, they saw that God created two lights to illuminate the world: one by day and the other by night, just as we see with our eyes. The Moon shines by night as the Sun by day, one without the [other...]
