->CHAPTER LXXXI.<-

<margin>
There are 3 methods of cleansing or separating a thing from its dregs.
All things that are dug up in the earth are converted back into earth.
</margin>

Know, beloved, that there are 3 ways and methods of cleansing or separating a thing from its dregs. The first method is that which has been spoken of, according to nature or through nature. For nature repels from itself whatever is imperfect. Just as we see daily in all things that are dug up in the earth, all are converted together into earth, which is their **medium** <note>Hollandus uses "medium" here to mean the intermediate state or the base substrate from which things come and to which they return.</note>. And look at whatever is daily exposed to the air, whether it be iron, steel, lead, copper, wood, or stone: and all that is exposed to the air day and night perishes and is worn away, and is consumed over a long period of time. Bulwarks and fortresses, however strong, perish by the length of time, and are **calcined** <term>calcined|Reduced to powder or ash by heat or long exposure to the elements, representing a return to the state of "earth."</term> into earth, which is their middle stage.

---

->CHAPTER LXXXII.<-

<margin>
An excellent explanation of why all things are converted into earth, and not into air, water, or fire.
One element is more impure than another, but earth is the most unclean of all.
</margin>

You may ask: how does it happen that all things are converted into earth, and not into air, water, or fire? Know this: whatever exists here below under the **lunar circle** <note>The "sublunary" sphere; in the medieval worldview, this was the region between the Earth and the Moon, where all things are subject to change and decay.</note> is composed of the four elements. And all four elements are unclean and full of dregs. One element is more impure than another, as is taught in the "Vegetable Work." And earth is the most unclean and the driest element, having the most dregs. Thus all things must first be converted into earth before they can be converted into air, water, or fire. It must be so, because nature works without the aid of art <note>Here "art" refers to human alchemical intervention.</note>. For nature does not move further than to work from step to step. And therefore nature works for a long time. For you cannot reach from the beginning to the end unless you first cross the intermediate space; nor can you complete a journey of 100 miles unless you first cross the path in between. You cannot reach the fourth step unless first [you reach] the second...

Hollandus explains that all things naturally return to earth—the most "dross-filled" element—as a necessary first step in their purification or transformation.</summary>

...the second and third methods previously mentioned. And for he who does not understand this, I would not be the author who advises him to work in our art. Thus, my son, from the aforesaid reasoning it is clear that all things which are purified by the course of nature are converted into earth. For when anything is converted into earth, it is then opened and resolved, so that each element may draw its like to itself, just as is sufficiently demonstrated in the **vegetable work** <term>vegetable work|Alchemical processes involving plant matter, often used as an analogy for the growth and "seeding" of metals.</term>. And to lead a thing from the first degree into the next, it is necessary for it to be converted into another nature; and it cannot be converted into another nature unless it first becomes earth, because of the dregs <note>original: "fæces"</note> which it contains within itself. Look at **lead** <note>original: "plumbum"</note>: whatever is moved toward the fire in a pot must first be converted into ashes or earth before the potter can **vitrify** <term>vitrify|The process of turning a substance into glass through intense heat.</term> it. For lead cannot become glass before it is transferred into another nature; nor can it be converted into another nature unless it first becomes earth, because of the dregs it contains. Nor can you by force make **silver** <note>original: "argentum"</note> out of lead unless it first becomes glass, as is rightly taught in many places—although it can indeed be brought to silver by another method, by gradually removing its dregs, as is taught in its proper place. For lead, in its outward parts, is silver; thus nothing else is lacking for lead to be brought to silver except that its dregs be drawn away, and its terrestrial sulfur, and then it is silver. Just as nature converts it daily, as may be seen.

Observe ancient fortresses which were once roofed with lead, and upon which it has lain for five hundred or six hundred years, so that all that lead is converted into earth, or into **cerussa** <term>cerussa|White lead, a white pigment produced by the corrosion of lead; historically used in cosmetics and paint.</term>, as is still found daily on old leaden roofs, which falls off in shavings. And if it could lie there longer, Nature would at last cook it thoroughly into silver and cleanse it. Just as I myself saw, when an old roof of this kind, covered in lead that had easily lain there for two or three thousand years, was being removed; that leaden roof broke apart into crumbs, just as if it had been **calcined** <term>calcined|Reduced to a powder or ash through prolonged heating.</term>. And when it was broken apart, it glittered as if silver filings had been in it, and it was white as cerussa ought to be. But it appeared as if that cerussa had been sprinkled with silver. And that lead was placed in **scoring dishes** <note>original: "testis"</note> with other lead and was purified through the **cupel** <term>cupellation|A refining process where ores or alloyed metals are treated under high temperatures to separate noble metals, like gold and silver, from base metals like lead.</term>, and the whole mass together was pure **Luna** <note>original: "Luna"; alchemical code for silver.</note>. Thus nature had cleansed it by long **digestion** <term>digestion|A process of slow, gentle heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance over time.</term>. Thus it stands by the aforesaid reason that nature works, cleanses, and repels all dregs from itself, reducing them to nothing, and reducing the **marrow of the sun** <note>original: "medullam solis"; likely referring to the essential gold-principle or the highest state of metallic purity.</note> into powder.

Even if that water were to stand until the very last day, it would never spoil, provided you kept it properly sealed. The same judgment applies to **oil**. For if any oil were kept in a stone jar or vessel for several years, it would push its own dregs away from itself to the bottom, and would become clear and thin, just as was said of the water. And look at old **wine**, or well-preserved **beer** <note>original: "ceruisiam"</note> that is firmly sealed—how it pushes the dregs from itself to the bottom; see those old and clear wines, which have often been clarified from their dregs, how effective and clear they become: Indeed, if they were left for several years and properly sealed, they would cleanse themselves so much that in the end no dregs would be found in them; thus in the end they would be **rectified**, and even if they were distilled, they would leave no dregs. Then that which was further rectified would be red and as clear as crystal. But a long time would be needed before nature could bring wine to that point; yet in the end, it would happen. And this is how the matter stands in all things that have dregs, as was said before. Thus it is clear by the reasoning already stated: nature herself, by the course of nature, rejects all dregs from herself. And if you desire to be taught more clearly on this matter, seek it in the **vegetable work** <note>original: "opere vegetabili"; alchemical processes using plant matter used as an analogy for the growth of metals.</note>, where you will be taught manifest truths.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII.

<margin>2. A method of purification performed by art, through dissolving and congealing.</margin>
There is, moreover, also another method of purifying whatever has dregs in nature: this is indeed done by **Art** <note>In alchemical texts, "Art" refers to the human-assisted acceleration of natural processes, often using heat and laboratory apparatus.</note>: in this, Art assists nature; and it is done by **dissolving and congealing** <term>dissolving and congealing|The alchemical cycle of "solve et coagula," where a substance is broken down into liquid and then reformed into a solid to purify it.</term>, as is partially declared in the **Great Work** <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) is the legendary process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. Therefore, I do not wish to write perfectly concerning it—that is, concerning the purification or separation of dregs. If you desire to understand this plainly, seek it in the **vegetable work**, where the **rectification of the elements** is treated, where the elements are purified to the extreme without the separation of the elements; there you will be taught at length and plainly regarding these things.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV.

<margin>
3. The method of purification <note>original: "Mundificandi ratio"</note> which is done by fire, and is called burning or calcination.
</margin>

Next, you shall know that there is another purification <term>rectification|In alchemy, this refers to the process of refining a substance to its purest, most potent state, often through heat.</term> for the dregs of all metals and mineral things, which is performed by fire. We shall discuss this purification somewhat and teach as much as is necessary; but if you desire to be taught more clearly about it, look in the treatise on the vegetable stone <note>original: "in vegetabili"</note>, where the shaping of precious stones and the making of precious enamels <note>original: "amaulis"</note> are discussed. There you will be taught at length and clearly. Here, we do not wish to deal with it more extensively or in more words than is necessary and required for our work. You shall know that all metals can be purged of their dregs by fire: and the elements will remain perfectly together without separation, and thereafter without fixation. And all shall be done by fire. Truly, this burning <note>original: "ustio"</note> is done in various ways. For Gold <note>original: "Sol"</note> must be burned or cemented differently than Silver <note>original: "Luna"</note>; Silver differently than Lead <note>original: "Saturnus"</note>; and Copper <note>original: "Venus"</note> must be burned differently than Iron <note>original: "Mars"</note>.

### CHAPTER LXXXV.

<margin>
A twofold burning is employed in metals.
</margin>

Furthermore, you shall know that there is a twofold burning used in metals: one by **cementation** <term>cementation|A process where a metal is surrounded by powdered chemical reagents and heated, allowing the metal to be purified without melting it.</term>, of which we shall speak further below; and one cementation is done with salt and mineral spirits, without the conversion of the metals into glass; and one way is done differently than another.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI.

<margin>
A question with its solution.
</margin>

Now you might ask: Can all metals be converted into glass without any addition, and then be reduced back into metal? You shall know that all metals can be converted into glass without any addition, with the single exception of Gold <note>original: "Sole vno excepto"</note>. It refuses to be converted into glass, even if it were burned until the Day of Judgment. Something must be added to it, which is not necessary for other metals. For Gold is pure by nature, and although it may have some dregs in itself, they are not so many that they can cover its body. Thus, however much Gold is burned, the dregs do not become glass; rather, it is purely scorched by great and strong combustion, so that it does not become glass. Truly, that cannot happen with other metals; they become a "natural glass." Now you might say: once something has become glass, it has been brought to its final state. For when a thing is glass, it can be brought back to no other material. <margin>Glass is the end of all things, which is proven.</margin> Because glass is the end of all things, and after the Judgment, whatever is contained beneath the firmament shall all be converted into glass by divine ordination. It is clear, therefore, that glass is the final state of all; and glass can be brought back by art to no other thing than to glass, or to burnt material, or to dregs. For I have often seen glass, by long and vehement burning, reduced to blackness <note>original: "ni-", catchword: "gros"</note>...

You shall know therefore that glass is the extreme and final state of all things, except for metal and metallic things. The reason is this: In all combustible things, the oil and natural moisture are separated from their earth by violent and long-lasting burning; except in metals and metallic mineral things, in those the oil is not separated from the earth: but it always clings to the earth in the fire, even if they were burned forever. For if the oil were separated from the earth of metals, the **Elixir** <term>Elixir|The 'philosopher's stone' in liquid or powder form, believed to be capable of transmuting metals.</term> could by no means be made from the earth, and the **salt of metals** <note>In this context, 'salt' refers to the solid, purified essence of the metal left after calcination.</note> could not be melted: how then would they give entrance into imperfect bodies, or give tincture?

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.

<margin>
Question with response.
</margin>

You may ask: does salt give the **tincture** <term>tincture|In alchemy, the spiritual essence or 'color' of a substance that allows it to transform the properties of another material.</term> of metals? Know this: take the oil of the metal, that gives the tincture. Know that when salt is extracted from a metal and prepared as it should be for making a **projection** <term>projection|The final step of the alchemical work, where the prepared substance is cast upon molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</term>, it does not produce any tincture, but it makes the projection toward the white <note>original: "ad album" — meaning it transmutes the metal into silver.</note>. And the matter is this: Its oil is enclosed in its interior, like the yolk in the white of an egg. But when we wish to make the red projection <note>original: "ad rubrum" — meaning it transmutes the metal into gold.</note>, the fire or oil must be placed on the outside, and its salt or earth on the inside; and thus this same thing will produce a projection toward the red, just as it previously did toward the white. Previously it was the salt of metals, and it made one part in 100; and when the fire or oil is placed on the outside, then it is the oil of metals, and it makes 1 part in 1000. And although the material is the same, nevertheless its interior is placed on the outside, and its exterior on the inside.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.

<margin>
Another question. Air gives entrance, fire the tincture, oil makes it melt, earth fixes. 2 Reasons.
</margin>

You may also ask: when the salt or earth of metals are drawn out from the metals with their oil by the burning of fire, then their **Mercury** <term>Mercury|Here used as the 'Air' or the volatile, spiritual element of the metal rather than the liquid metal itself.</term> or air is separated from the earth and from the oil; how can that salt or oil give entrance? For the Philosophers say: air gives entrance, fire the tincture, oil makes it melt, earth fixes <term>fixation|The process of stabilizing a substance so it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire.</term>. And this air has flown away during the long burning of the fire. Know that enough air remains in the oil within the fire as much as may suffice for it. For the elements are so glued together that you can never separate them from each other without them remaining mixed among themselves.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX.

<margin>Another question likewise.</margin>
You may ask: How is it that all metals become glass, except for the **Sun** <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) always refers to gold, which was considered the only "perfect" metal that could not be further changed by fire.</note>? You should understand it this way: All [other] metals are impure and full of dross, and therefore they are easily **calcined** <term>calcined|The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile parts and reduce it to a powder or "calx."</term>. For all the parts of these metals are full of impure, sulfurous dross which they acquired in the mines; and when they encounter a violent fire, they are easily calcined, and the moisture of the thick sulfurous dross is burned away. For their sulfur is not **fixed** <term>fixed|Stable in fire; a substance that does not evaporate or escape when heated.</term>, in the way that the **sulfur of the Sun** <note>The "sulfur of gold" was believed to be the most stable and pure form of the active principle in matter.</note> is. And once the fattiness of the sulfur is burned off, the dross of the sulfur becomes so dry that the whole metal is converted into a **calx** <note>A fine powder remaining after a metal has been burned.</note> or earth. And for this reason, every metal must be converted into a calx or earth; for it cannot be transformed into glass unless it is first a calx. <margin>Nothing can be transferred from its own nature into another nature without a middle state.</margin> Nothing can be transferred from its own nature into another nature without a **medium** <note>A middle step or transitional substance.</note>. For it was first a metal, and then it becomes glass. Now, metal and glass are two [different] natures; and for this to happen, it must happen through earth or calx, which is the medium. And then, by even more intense burning and over a long period of time, that earth or calx is converted into glass—as is well taught where the making of **artificial gemstones** <note>original: "lapides effigiari" — the creation of imitation gems using glass and metallic oxides.</note> is described. Indeed, these artificial stones are easily ten times more beautiful and clearer than the **Oriental ones** <note>Natural gemstones imported from the East, which were the standard of luxury at the time.</note>, and much more pleasing to the sight. Look, for instance, at the **enamel** <term>amausa|A type of glass paste or enamel used to imitate gemstones or decorate metalwork.</term> with which encaustic work is painted: how beautiful the greens, blues, yellows, reds, and whites are! And one is half again as beautiful as another, even though they are of the same color, and even twenty times more excellent. And yet they were all made from the same metal.

### CHAPTER XC.

<margin>Why some enamels are more precious than others, even though they are made from the same metal.</margin>
You may ask: How is it that one is more precious than another, since they are made from the same metal? Know this: when the metal has been reduced to a calx or earth, and then placed in a **vaulted furnace** <note>A furnace with an arched roof designed to trap and concentrate heat.</note> or a **reverberatory furnace** <term>reverberatory furnace|A furnace that reflects (reverberates) heat from the roof onto the material, allowing for extremely high temperatures.</term> in which glass is burned, it must have the most intense heat before it can become clean, clear, and transparent glass, and before the dross is converted into glass. You shall know that glass produced in this way is like a **glorified body** <note>A theological metaphor for matter that has been purified of all "corrupt" or "heavy" qualities.</note>, because the dross of the metal, which was previously a black, foul, and impure body, becomes glass. And beneath that body lies hidden the **quintessence** <term>quintessence|The "fifth essence" or purest, most potent part of a substance, believed to be indestructible.</term> of the metal, which is incombustible,

## CHAPTER XCI.

<margin>Calcined metal is a calx or earth.</margin>
You shall know that when a metal is **calcined** <term>calcined|Reduced to a powder by the action of intense heat.</term>, it is a **calx** <note>original: "calcem" — the dry, crumbly powder left after heating a metal.</note> or earth. If the craftsman wishes to produce an excellent green enamel, he must burn it from the calx of **Venus** <note>In alchemy, Venus represents Copper.</note>. And if he then wishes to have a distinguished greenness, which surpasses all other greens in color and clarity, he must grind the calx upon a marble slab with salt water until it is an impalpable powder, and then wash it with clean, common water until the water flows off the calx clear and pure. He should grind it as before until no more earthy filth remains. From this, the burned glass becomes a much more beautiful and excellent enamel, and it also melts much more easily than if you had made glass from it without grinding and purging it of its earthy dross. The same is true for the other calxes of **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> and also of **Mars** <note>Iron</note>; these produce a yellow glass. **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note> produces a white enamel, **the Moon** <note>Silver</note> a sky-blue, and **the Sun** <note>Gold</note> a red. If they desire other colors, they mix one color with another.

## CHAPTER XCII.

<margin>A question regarding enamels: whether they can be reduced back into their metallic body.</margin>
Now my son may ask: once enamels have been made from metals, is it possible to reduce them back into their [metallic] body, since glass is the "extreme" or final state of all things, as was mentioned before? You shall know that a body can indeed be made from them again, since that burning happens easily with a vehement fire. For within the space of twelve hours, either glass or enamel can easily be made from the calxes of metals in a **reverberatory furnace** <term>reverberatory furnace|A furnace that reflects (reverberates) heat from the roof down onto the material being heated, preventing direct contact with the fuel.</term>. The calxes of the metals are not "resolved" <note>i.e., not fully broken down into their constituent elements</note>; they are a dry matter in which the earthiness or dross has been brought out, and it is dry. ### CHAPTER XCIII.

<margin>More concerning Enamels.</margin>
Therefore, take and pulverize **Enamel** <term>Amausa|Also known as 'glass pastes' or 'artificial gems,' these are colored glasses used to imitate precious stones.</term> very finely, and take good distilled vinegar in which **sal ammoniac** <term>sal armoniacum|Ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to dissolve metals or act as a flux.</term> has been dissolved—one *loth* <note>A 'loth' was a small unit of weight, roughly half an ounce.</note> of sal ammoniac in each pound of vinegar. With this, grind the powder upon a stone as finely as if a painter were using it. Put that ground material into a glass or a stone jar, and pour a good quantity of distilled vinegar over it. Place it in a **water bath** <term>balneo|A 'Bain-marie' or water bath used to provide gentle, even heat.</term>, and apply fire beneath the bath so that it boils. Stir it four or five times a day with a wooden spatula, and keep it this way for four days and nights. Then let it cool, and pour the vinegar dregs into a clean stone jar. Pour fresh vinegar over the remaining dregs again, and do as before. Repeat this a third time, always adding the first vinegar. 

Then all that 'body' is dissolved from those dregs, or from the glass. Next, evaporate the vinegar, or distill it through an **alembic** <term>alembic|A specialized lid or 'beak' used in distillation to collect and cool vapors.</term>; at the bottom, the body of the metal will remain as a fine powder. Mix a little **borax** <note>Borax was used then, as now, as a 'flux' to help metals melt more easily.</note> with it, place it in a crucible, and melt it in a vehement fire with the body. If it was **Mars** <term>Mars|Iron.</term> or **Venus** <term>Venus|Copper.</term>, they are rendered clean and pure, so that they are no longer infested by tarnish or rust, and are free from their dregs. If, however, it was **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter|Tin.</term>, its 'stench' and 'shriek' <note>original: "fœtor ac stridor" — 'Stridor' refers to the 'tin cry,' the crackling sound pure tin makes when bent.</note> are taken away, and it is clean and strong like **Luna** <term>Luna|Silver.</term>. If it is fixed Luna, it remains so; if it is **Sol** <term>Sol|Gold.</term>, it becomes a medicine; and if it was **Saturn** <term>Saturn|Lead.</term>, it becomes Silver. But it is not useful to do this except for the purpose of investigating nature. For I have seen an ounce of red enamel sell for 20 ducats, blue for 8, and another for 2 ducats. Therefore, beloved, it would not be profitable to reduce it back into a metal body. <margin>The art of making enamels is distinguished.</margin> The art of making enamels is distinguished. For it is easily done when they are made only roughly from calces. An unpolished pound of Copper, Iron, Tin, or Lead is easily sold for a ducat. But when the calces are most pure...

...[as is] taught in the **vegetable work** <note>original: "opere vegetabili"; in alchemy, the "Vegetable Work" refers to processes using organic materials or plants, often considered a preliminary or parallel path to the mineral work.</note>, from which are fashioned precious stones that are placed in the vessels of princes; and from it, the vessels of Kings are made. Thus, metals are purified by burning, or by **reverberating** <term>reverberando|Heating a material in a furnace where the flame is deflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the substance, rather than touching it directly.</term>, or by calcining, and by washing the **calces** <term>calces|The dry, powdery remains (oxides) left after a metal has been burned.</term> repeatedly, and by reducing the calces back into a metallic body; and then by calcining again, and once more washing with common water, until no more dregs are produced.

### CHAPTER XCIV.

<margin>
Note that there is also another burning called **cementation**, which is another form of calcination. The difference between them.
</margin>
Know also, my beloved, that there is another burning which is called **Cementation** <term>Cæmentatio|A process where metal plates are packed in a powdered mixture (the "cement") and heated, allowing the mixture to chemically act on the metal surface.</term>, which burning is a second type of calcination. However, there is a difference. When common calcination is performed, it is tempered with common salt; the plates of metal are hammered out, and a **crucible** <note>A ceramic or graphite container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</note> or another earthy vessel is taken, and they are placed layer upon layer until the crucible is full. Then, the crucible is properly **luted** <note>Sealed with "lute," a clay-like paste used to make vessels airtight.</note> and placed in the fire, and a natural white-heat is applied. If it be **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, for 2 days; if **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, 6 days; if **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, 24 hours; if **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, 8 days; if **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, 2 days; and so on. This is the method of calcining. Likewise, the method of cementation is done in the same way as calcination. But this is the difference: it is aided by certain **mineral spirits** <note>Volatile chemicals like sulfur or arsenic that "attack" the metal.</note> which assist the fire in the burning of the metals, helping to crush them into powder, and even adding a certain **tincture** <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is a substance that can color or "stain" a metal to change its properties or appearance.</note> to the bodies, making them melt more easily afterward. These spirits are mixed with prepared salt and arranged in the same way as was said regarding calcination. Know that I have said all these things so that you may know and understand how the purification of metals through fire was discovered. There are also many other ways to bring metals to perfection through fire which are not necessary for our work here; enough is handed down about them in the vegetable work, where it is taught what must be done with fire and water. You will find this in the sixth and eighth chapters; if you desire to be taught more clearly and plainly about it, seek it there.

### *On the Philosopher's Stone*, CHAPTER XCV.

<margin>
There follows the explanation of the work done once by the author's own hand.
</margin>
Now I wish to teach my beloved a certain work which I once performed with my own hand; it is a work easy to do without great care or much anxiety, and it is one of my greatest secrets. For he who does not know how to prepare this work will never make any progress in the art. For here is taught which **Mercury** <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers" is not common quicksilver, but the hidden, life-giving essence or "soul" of the metals required for the Great Work.</note> the Philosophers have in mind, and how it is to be extracted from the bodies, along with many other secrets that will be mentioned in the work...

### Fixed Silver, CHAPTER XCVI.

<margin>First, pure cupelled Silver and pure Gold must be taken.</margin>
First, you shall take pure **cupelled** <term>cupellatam|Purified in a cupel, a shallow porous bowl used to separate precious metals from base metals like lead through high-heat oxidation.</term> Silver and pure Gold as you please, and beat them into thin plates the thickness of a ducat and the width of one palm. And to your Silver you shall add prepared common salt and **arsenic** sublimated to white—that is, by the **calces** <term>calces|The dry, powdery oxides or "ashes" left after a substance has been burned or calcined.</term> of eggshells and **calamine stone** <note>original: "lapidis calaminaris"; a zinc ore.</note>, of each an equal portion. 

<margin>Calamine stone is called **Cadmia** by Pliny.</margin>
And for every three pounds of these, take one pound of arsenic sublimated three or four times, always grinding it over the dregs; then the arsenic is prepared. Then take one pound of prepared salt, half an ounce of the aforesaid arsenic, and two ounces of white **calcined tartar** <note>original: "tartari albi calcinati"; potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking, burned to a white ash.</note> that is properly clear and transparent. Mix the tartar and the arsenic thoroughly with the salt. Then have a **crucible** <term>crucibulum|A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</term> and place the materials to be **cemented** <term>cæmentanda|A process of heating metal plates packed in a powdered chemical mixture (the "cement") to alter the metal's properties without melting it.</term> layer upon layer, as you know, to the thickness of a finger. When the crucible is full, **lute** <term>luta|To seal a vessel with "lute," a clay or paste used to make it airtight.</term> it firmly and let it dry well. Then set it to be cemented, applying a moderate flame so that your Silver does not melt. Let it glow gently for 36 hours, then let it cool. Then break open your crucible, and your Silver will be calcined; your Silver will be black and brittle, in the manner of glass. 

Then have clean common water, distil it, and wash away all the saltiness from your Silver, and let it dry. Then grind it finely in a mortar, and grind that powder very finely upon a marble slab with distilled common water. Then have a glass bowl and put your ground Silver into it, and add clean distilled water. Wash your powder and let it settle. That which is good will seek the bottom, and that which is worth nothing will remain in the water. Gently pour that off into another glass bowl; pour clean distilled water over the powder again and stir it, and wash it anew, and again let it settle. Gently pour the water off once more into the other bowl with the first water. Then once more pour distilled water over the powder, wash it, and do as before. Repeat this workmanship until your water returns from the powder as entirely clear as it was when you poured it in. Then it is properly washed and as white as snow. Then evaporate all your water which you poured off from the powder, in case any of your powder was poured out with it...

Then your Silver is clean and relieved of all its dregs <term>fęcibus|The impurities, sediment, or "worthless" matter left over in a chemical process.</term>; and the elements are rectified <term>rectificata|Purified or brought to their highest, most balanced state.</term> without separation.

<margin>The Proof.</margin> **The Proof:** dissolve 1 part of that white powder in rectified **aqua vitae** <term>aqua vitæ|Literally "water of life," usually referring to highly distilled alcohol or a potent solvent.</term> or distilled vinegar, and congeal it again, and dissolve it once more: you will find no dregs, even if you did it a hundred times. I myself have tested it. 

<margin>A great mystery.</margin> What do you think of this secret? It is a **great mystery** in the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work."</note>, greater than can be rightly understood. Because the elements are rectified without separation. Truly, I tell you in good faith, it is the greatest, most perfect mystery performed in the Art for creating the **elixir** <note>The transformative substance or "medicine" used for transmutation.</note> from a single metal alone. For it possesses its own proper proportion of weight. 

When elements are purged by dissolving and congealing, it is excellent. But this method is much more certain. For when it is done or managed by dissolving and congealing, the element of **Earth** is separated with the dregs from the three remaining elements <note>The four classical elements are Earth, Air, Fire, and Water; the author argues that separating them is risky compared to his unified method.</note>. It is good when it is done correctly, and diligent care is taken that the dregs are well-preserved so that nothing of them is lost, and the fire is controlled in **reverberating** <term>reuerberando|Heating in a furnace where the flame is deflected or "reverberated" onto the material rather than touching it directly.</term> it in the proper manner. 

And in rectifying the Earth to extract Fire, Water, and Air from the dregs is very dangerous; for one must be extremely cautious. Something is always lost, and if anything is lost or neglected, you do not have the right proportion of your weight, nor what you ought to have of your elements. And thus you will never achieve your desire. Impress this well upon your memory so that you never forget: there can be no defect. The elements must have their own proper proportion. 

Therefore, it is very dangerous to perform works in which any elements are separated. It is good when done properly, and it even allows for an infinite **projection** <term>proiectio|The final stage of the alchemical work where the medicinal "Stone" is cast upon a base metal to transmute it into silver or gold.</term>, much higher than when the elements are not separated. And so, beloved, our ancestors erred much and spent much time in vain before they had knowledge of rectifying elements without separation. Indeed, this is clearly shown here. Therefore, do not expose yourself to danger by doing anything in which any elements must be separated from one another. I fear you might err, and [lose] any ele- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with "elements" on the next page.</note>

Therefore, beloved, keep these instructions, and in this way you will be able to err very little. You may indeed lose a tiny bit of your powder during washing, but whatever remains is perfected, for Nature does not err. The elements remain bound together there, for in the work they are bound even more strongly than before. When they are pure and clean from their dregs <term>fæcibus|The impurities or "worthless" sediment remaining after a chemical reaction.</term>, and then set to be cemented for the space of 3 days, they are then fixed together so that the **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical symbol for silver.</note> becomes fixed. It is tested in **strong water** <term>aqua forti|Nitric acid, used by alchemists to test the purity of metals as it dissolves most base metals but leaves gold and "fixed" substances untouched.</term> and does not dissolve. And whatever is done regarding calcination <term>calcinatione|The process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder.</term> or cementation can all be done with prepared common salt, without arsenic or tartar. But it lasts longer. For when it is calcined with common salt alone, the plates of Silver do not want to be calcined so easily a second time. Sometimes they must be put in two or three times before they are entirely calcined for pulverizing.

<margin>Why arsenic and tartar are used.</margin>
This is the one reason why arsenic and tartar are mixed in: they are so fierce and sharp with the salt that they easily corrode the plates, so that they can be easily pulverized the first time. Furthermore, they consume the dregs, so that there is no need to repeat the calcination too often. Thirdly, they give a white tincture when we wish to use them in the "white work" <note>The *Albedo* or white stage of alchemy, aimed at producing silver.</note>. But if the work were to be "red" <note>The *Rubedo* or red stage, aimed at producing gold.</note>, it would be better to take Mercury sublimated to red in place of arsenic, just as is done in the cementation of **Gold** <note>original: "Solis"; literally 'the Sun'.</note>. That is the reason why these are used. But if one wished, he could do it with prepared salt alone. I myself have often experienced this.

<margin>The difference between the cementation of Gold and Silver.</margin>
Know that between the cementation of Gold and Silver there is no other difference than this: you shall take in place of arsenic Mercury sublimated to red. And you ought not to crush the Gold into powder, nor wash it, as was said regarding the Silver. For Gold has no blackness in it that must be washed away. The Mercury, salt, and tartar consume all its dregs. And you ought not to cement it longer than until you no longer lose anything in the powder. Then the Gold is unburdened of its dregs. And if you wish to cement it better, cement it for the space of 3 days, like the Silver. My beloved, use no other preparation or purification <term>mundificationem|A cleansing or 'world-making' purification of the material.</term> than that which I use by fire, as I have taught you here. See to it yourself that you have your elements perfectly together; although that other method of dissolving and congealing is excellent, and although the elements become much subtler and the **projection** <note>The final act of transforming base metal into gold by casting the Philosopher's Stone upon it.</note> much higher, it does not matter to receive so much advantage. This is the purification...

## CHAPTER XCVII.

<margin>
How the Mercury of the Philosophers is to be extracted.
</margin>
Now, my son, we wish to teach you how we extract the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <term>Mercurius Philosophorum|Not the common quicksilver found in shops, but a purified "essential" mercury that alchemists believed was the root of all metals.</term>. Know first that I have told you of many works which other craftsmen have done, and which I myself have seen performed by others: some are perfect and some are imperfect. But whether they be perfect or imperfect, the Mercury of the Philosophers must be obtained so that the end goal may be reached. For Mercury coming from the mines is nothing other than a **crude sperm** <note>Alchemists viewed metals as organic entities that "grew" from seeds or sperm within the earth.</note>, not yet sufficiently cooked out in the mines: perhaps it would easily lie there for another two hundred or three hundred years before it would congeal. And when it was already entirely congealed, it would still have to lie for several more years before the matter could be converted into a subtle powder; and once converted into powder by the long cooking of natural heat, it would still have to become red. For when Mercury is first converted into an exhalation, it evaporates through the opening of the mine, and if it then encounters the **Sulfur of the Philosophers** <note>The active, masculine principle in alchemy, contrasted with the passive, feminine Mercury.</note> with its spiritual nature so that they become one body—and if then that sulfur has been rightly separated from its combustible fatness—it becomes a perfect body, whether white or red. And to the ignorant, that sulfur is merely dross, and dregs, and the **combustible fatness of vitriol** <term>vitriolum|A group of glassy sulfate minerals. "Combustible fatness" refers to the impure, oily sulfur that alchemists sought to remove.</term>; and it is separated from it because all things in nature desire to unburden themselves of their dregs. Thus, crude sulfur is the scum of vitriol: from crude vitriol comes red sulfur, and from white vitriol comes white sulfur, as is taught in the "vegetable" work <note>Likely referring to Hollandus's other writings on the "Vegetable Stone" or organic alchemy.</note> where the sulfurs present in all things are discussed.

<margin>
In all things in which the four elements are present, there is combustible and incombustible sulfur.
</margin>
In all things in which the **four elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> are present, there is within them both combustible and incombustible sulfur, as is clearly shown there. And when the aforementioned vapor is then gathered with the Sulfur of the Philosophers and made into one body, it must be cooked for a long time in the "belly of the mines" with a tempered heat before that Mercury and sulfur become **fixed** <term>fixa|Substances that are stable under heat and do not evaporate.</term>; and this takes place over a thousand years, as God and Nature work these things. Therefore, beloved, Mercury coming from the mines is the "crude blood" from which, by the work of nature, the sperm of metals is cooked before it becomes a vapor. 

<margin>
Mercury is the instrument and the hammer for working in our art.
</margin>
And for that reason, metal is not found in the mines of Mercury, nor is Mercury found in metallic mines. The matter is crude and is not useful to our art. But it is the instrument and the hammer for working in our art. ### *The Extraction of Mercury from Silver, etc.*
## CHAPTER XCVIII.

<margin>A moderate fire must be used.</margin>
Now my son shall learn how to extract Mercury from the bodies [of metals]. First, you shall make **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis|Literally "strong water," a historical name for nitric acid, used by alchemists to dissolve metals like silver.</term> from equal parts of vitriol and saltpeter, and in it you shall dissolve **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver.</note> in the usual manner. Then cause it to be precipitated with common water. Then wash away the saltiness of the *aqua fortis* from your **calx** <term>calx|The powdery residue left after a metal has been dissolved and precipitated, or roasted; essentially a metallic oxide.</term> with clean water. Then dry the *calx*, and place it in a flat glass vessel having a flat bottom. Then place it on a tripod or in an **athanor** <term>athanor|A "slow-cooker" furnace of the alchemists, designed to maintain a steady, uniform temperature for weeks or months.</term>, and set it to be calcined in the furnace in which you calcine your spirits. And apply a moderate fire, just as if you wished to keep lead in a melted state without it solidifying. And keep it in that heat for six weeks; meanwhile, your Silver will be so resolved that its Mercury is separated from the earth, and from the oil that remains with the earth. And you may do the same with **Gold** <note>original: "Sole"; the alchemical name for gold.</note>. But its *calx* must remain for at least 18 weeks, or 24, or sometimes 32, before the Gold allows its Mercury to be separated from the earth and oil, which always remain joined. For the oil and earth of metals cannot be separated from one another, as was said before. And because Gold has a united and solid body, its *calx* must remain so long to be opened before it is willing to release its Mercury. Therefore, it is better to leave it for 32 or 40 weeks in the furnace. For the longer it is held in the furnace at a moderate heat, as is proper, the more the body becomes opened into a **death of a sponge** <note>original: "mortem spongiæ"; likely describing the material becoming extremely porous, light, and losing its metallic nature.</note>, and it swells up, becoming so light that it is incredible to those who have not seen it. Likewise, take 1 ounce of the *calx* of Gold, and a glass bowl capable of holding three quarters of a liquid. The bowl will become so full that the *calx* will easily stand two or three fingers' breadth above the edges of the bowl—so much is that body opened. But it must easily remain for a year to be opened to that extent. And if it were so resolved, Mercury would easily be sublimated from it with a small fire, just as one would sublimate **sal ammoniac** <term>sal armoniacum|Ammonium chloride, a salt known to alchemists for its ability to sublimate (turn directly from solid to vapor) when heated.</term>. And in this way, you can open all metals so that you may have or draw their Mercury from them by sublimating, as is taught where it treats of salt. And you shall know that when Mercury is drawn out from metals by sublimation, the Mercury then ascends, as has been said.

## The Purification of Mercury. CHAPTER XCIX.

And if you sublimate it again even three or four times through vitriol or arsenic, it will ascend clear as a crystal, concerning which there is no need for us to say more here. Know that when **Gold** <note>original: "Sol"</note> and **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> are dissolved in this manner in a calcining furnace, or in an **athanor** <term>athanor|A "slow-cooker" furnace of the alchemists, designed to maintain a steady, uniform temperature for weeks or months.</term>, or on a tripod: finely grind them upon a stone with **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac|Ammonium chloride; a salt used in alchemy to help volatile substances "ascend" or sublimate.</term>. To 1 pound of silver **calx** <term>calx|The powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or dissolved; the "ash" of the metal.</term>, add a quarter pound of sal ammoniac, which should be clear and transparent as crystal, without moisture; and once ground, place them into a stone jar. Then take vinegar distilled five or six times from its **phlegm** <term>phlegm|The watery, inactive part of a substance that remains or is removed during distillation.</term>, so that it leaves no more dregs. Pour this vinegar into another stone jar, and with an **alembic** <term>alembic|A glass or ceramic still-head used to collect and condense vapors during distillation.</term> placed on top, set it in a **water bath** <term>balneo|Also known as a 'bain-marie,' a vessel of hot water used to heat another container gently and evenly.</term>. And lute the jar containing the ground calx securely to the beak of the alembic, and let the **luting** <term>lute|A clay or paste used to seal the joints of laboratory equipment to make them airtight.</term> dry well. Then build a fire under the bath, and gradually distill the vinegar over the silver calx. For every pound of silver calx you have, distill 4 pounds of vinegar over it.

<margin>Why it must be allowed to cool for so long.</margin>
When all the vinegar has been distilled: allow it to cool easily for 3 days before you remove the jar. For if you were to remove the vinegar sooner, the Silver and the sal ammoniac would escape you, and you would retain nothing, so violent is that matter: for cold and heat meet there at the same time. And when you wish to remove it, have a glass lid ready for the mouth of the jar, polished smooth, which you shall immediately glue to it with lute, so that its **virtue** <note>original: "virtus"; the active essence or spiritual power of the alchemical substance.</note> does not escape you. Then place the jar in the water bath: and apply no hotter fire than your hand can comfortably bear in water up to the **knuckles** <note>original: "condylos"</note>, or than can be drunk without danger of burning. Keep it in this state for six weeks: then let it cool. Break it open, and immediately fix an alembic to the jar very firmly with lute: and place a receiver at the beak. Distill in a moderately warm bath whatever wishes to distill. And when it no longer distills, then take it out and place it in a vessel with **ashes** <term>testa cum cineribus|An 'ash-bath,' where the vessel is heated by hot ashes or sand to reach higher temperatures than a water bath allows.</term>. Lute the receiver to the beak again: and at the beginning apply a tiny fire: then a stronger one at intervals, until your Mercury begins to **sublimate** <term>sublimate|The process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collects as a solid again on a cooler surface, effectively purifying it.</term> upward with the sal ammoniac, as white as snow: and hanging in clear fibers to the white matter. Keep it so until you see it no longer sublimates, at that same whiteness, so that the Mercury is properly extracted from the earth. Afterward, let it cool, and having removed the alembic, take out the sublimated Mercury along with the sal ammoniac.

->CHAPTER C.<-

<margin>
What kind of heat is to be applied.
</margin>

Then take your sublimated Mercury, and the sal ammoniac, and your clear salt, and grind them together dry upon a marble slab. Then put all that has been ground into a glass bowl, and place it in a tripod or **calcining furnace** <term>fornace calcinatoria|A furnace designed for high-heat roasting of substances to reduce them to a powder.</term>, and let it stand there for six weeks: and apply heat, just as if you were keeping lead in a melted state without it solidifying <note>This implies a steady, moderate heat just above the melting point of lead.</note>. And when those six weeks have passed, let it cool, and then place it in a cold cellar, and put a linen cloth over it, so that no dust falls in. In the space of 6 or 8 days, it will be entirely dissolved into clear water.

Take 3 parts of **Silver** <note>original: "Lunæ"</note> prepared in the fire as I have taught you here, and one part of **Gold** <note>original: "Solis"</note> also prepared in the fire as I also taught you before, and dissolve each one in **strong water** <term>strong water|Nitric acid, used to dissolve metals.</term>, and cause them to be precipitated, and wash the saltiness from them, and dry them. ### *The Mixing*
## CHAPTER CII.

<margin>How the aforesaid are to be mixed.</margin>
Then take 3 parts of the **Silver calx** and one of the **Gold calx**, and mix them together, and place 1 ounce or 2 ounces into that water, according to how much water you have, or according to how great you wish your work to be. And stop up the glass with cork or another lid that is solid: and allow it to be dissolved, and sometimes unstop it, and let it finish dissolving: and when it is almost dissolved, add a little more, 1 ounce or less, according to how much it seems will dissolve in it. And when it is again almost dissolved: add more once more. Repeat this until nothing more wishes to be dissolved in it, so that it remains there. Then it is enough, and your water is saturated with its own food: it has drunk its fill of its **mother's milk** <note>An alchemical metaphor for a substance being nourished or "fed" by its primary solvent until it can hold no more.</note>.

## CHAPTER CIII.

<margin>Nature does not err.</margin>
You shall also know that this is the best dissolution that was ever discovered in the world; in this there is no error of proportion or weight. For **Nature does not err**. For when the **Mercury** <term>Mercury|Here referring to the "Philosophical Mercury" or the specialized solvent prepared earlier.</term> is dissolved, it further dissolves other metals, as is rightly taught in other places. Nor will it dissolve more than it is able, nor will it receive more body into itself than its nature can bear. For whatever it has no need of, it is not able to dissolve at all. And it is the best **amalgamation** that can be found.

->### CHAPTER CIV.<-

You should also know that those small fibers sometimes do not show themselves. And when they no longer show themselves, the matter has been made fixed by the preceding heat. Let this not trouble you at all. <margin>He recommends a small fire.</margin> It is better for the work to become fixed by a small heat than by a great one. If at the beginning you were to add heat such as that of the Sun shining in mid-summer, small fibers would arise as wide as a hand, but this would not be useful. It is better for the **stone** <note>The "Philosophers' Stone" or the alchemical matter in progress.</note> to be cooked with such a small heat that no small fibers arise. For when the fibers are born, if you then applied a greater heat, then all the **spirit** <note>The volatile part of the substance.</note> would ascend and fly up into the upper part of the glass in the manner of white smoke. And if by chance that should happen, open the glass and wipe away the white matter from inside, and stop up the glass again. And beware not to apply such great heat again; otherwise your matter would become black or red, like brick dust. And then it would be corrupted, and you would have to begin all over again from the start. Therefore, see that you moderate your fire so that you do not acquire a saffron color <note>original: "croceum"; a yellow-orange hue</note> instead of whiteness, nor redness instead of a saffron color. <margin>It is better to err on the side of too little than in the violence of the fire.</margin> It is better for the fire to be too small than if it were too great. And when it is now perfectly white, and no small fibers arise from that heat, your matter is fixed. Then you will be able to divide the matter into 2 parts, so that you may cook one part to the **red** and the other to the **white** <note>These represent the two final stages of the Work: the White Stone for silver and the Red Stone for gold.</note>. Then empty the other part into another glass, and stop it up tightly with lute, and place it in the same furnace in the ashes, and you shall draw it toward the red. And as for that which is for the white...

### CHAPTER 105.

<margin>The method of extracting the water of paradise from Silver.</margin>
Now you shall learn to extract the water of paradise from Silver. And you shall know that **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> is drawn out from Silver in two ways: I have taught you the reasoning in the [previous] work. And when you have ground the **calx** <note>The fine powder resulting from the burning or oxidation of a metal.</note> of Silver with the tartar, you do not have much need to put the matter in the furnace to be dissolved. Instead, put it into a jar or glass, and over it [pour] vinegar, as before; and do it in all ways as you were taught before. And the Mercury shall distill through the beak of the **alembic** <term>alembic|The top part of a still, used to catch and cool vapors so they drip into a receiving vessel.</term> as living [liquid] mercury; and the nature of the Tartar which it has within itself performs this. Put that Mercury into a glass pot, and draw the **phlegm** <term>phlegm|The watery, inactive liquid that comes off first during distillation.</term> from it, as I have sufficiently taught you in another place.

### *The Reddening of the Stone.*

### CHAPTER 108.

<margin>How the stone is to be made red.</margin>
<margin>The fire must be increased according to the colors.</margin>
You know that when I commanded you to take a half-portion from the glass vessel from which you fashioned your first **medicine** <note>In alchemy, the "medicine" refers to the Philosopher's Stone itself, which "heals" base metals into gold.</note>, I told you then: save the other half-portion for the red work. You took that half-portion and poured the **water of paradise** <term>water of paradise|A highly purified alchemical solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve and nourish the stone.</term> over it; and you placed it next to that glass in which the stone for the red work stood. And you applied a single fire until the stone was perfectly white; and meanwhile, the matter became saffron-colored. And when you see, my son, the matter becoming saffron, like saffron powder, you must increase your fire a little for 8 or 10 days. And observe whether your color does not become darker. That is a sign that the stone does not wish to progress at that heat, and that your fire is not sufficiently powerful. Therefore, increase your fire a little more even now, and see if you do not yet make any progress in the color. Thus, increase your fire a little more still. And do this for as long as it takes until you make progress in the color. And do this step by step until your stone begins to turn entirely red. Then you shall increase your fire every 5 or 6 days until the stone is perfectly red, like a **Ruby**, and radiates in the glass like the eyes of fishes: then you cannot increase the fire too much, even if you were to make the stone entirely white-hot. For when this sign is observed, the stone is completed and **fixed** <note>original: "fixus"; meaning the substance is now stable and will no longer evaporate or change when exposed to intense heat.</note>. These things I have told you so that you may use moderation in managing the fire. For if you were to apply a fire that is too fervent to acquire the red color in place of the saffron or white, you would have to start over from the beginning; or if you produced whiteness instead of blackness, you would have to begin anew.

<margin>The manner of fire is to be maintained not only here, but in all chemical works.</margin>
For this reason, it is better at the beginning, and always, to build a fire that is too small rather than one that is too large, and to follow it degree by degree. Just as the colors change through stages and become deeper and deeper, so too shall the fire be increased. And the **regimen of fire** <note>The "regimen" is the systematic control of heat, considered the most difficult secret of alchemy.</note> is to be maintained not only in this work, but in all works that are performed in the **art** <note>original: "opere"; referring to the Great Work of alchemy.</note>. For to rightly moderate the government of the fire is the other half of our art. When the proportions of the weights are not rightly introduced into the work...

### CHAPTER CX.

Now I will teach you the foundation of the art and of all perfect works. Although one craftsman works this way, and another that way; and even if each has a particular work with which he is occupied, according to the books of the Ancients, and each has a particular opinion and a particular method of operation. And all will arrive at a good end. But one way is short, another is long: and one makes a higher <margin>Precision in working.</margin> projection than another. And everything is good. One is easy, carried out without much labor, and another with great labor, according to the precision of the craftsman. Therefore I will teach you the true foundation of every work, in one principal operation and with much reasoning, which I shall mention in the work. And you shall know that I, Isaac your father, performed this work with my own hand, as well as many others. And I have also seen many, and heard of even more. And among all, I never performed, nor saw, nor heard of one which I trust so firmly as this, and in which I found so high a projection. Therefore, understand this work thoroughly.

For **Nature works through Nature**, as has been sufficiently demonstrated above. And if more...

### CHAPTER CXIII.

<margin>Water of the clouds.</margin>
Take, therefore, in the name of God and all the celestial hosts, 4 pounds of Roman blue vitriol <note>original: "vitrioli Romani cærulei"; copper sulfate, prized for its purity and deep blue color</note>, of the best and clearest quality, and 4 pounds of saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate, used here to create a corrosive acid</note>: and evaporate them together until they are so dry that they may be turned into powder, stirring them with a wooden stick in an earthen pan. Then take one pound of Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, from which the superfluous moisture has been removed. And take half of the material which you have dried, and grind the Mercury with it while dry, as finely as you are able. This is most conveniently done in a dry stove-room, with the stone [mortar] and pestle slightly warmed, so that no moisture may reach the material. Then place it into a large glass pot, with a wide alembic <note>A cap or lid used in distillation</note> placed on top for extracting the strong water <note>original: "aquam fortem"; nitric acid</note> from it. And seal the large alembic to the pot with lute <note>A clay-like paste used to make laboratory seals airtight</note>, and attach a receiver to the alembic, and let it dry thoroughly. Build a small fire at first, increasing it more and more at intervals, as you know how, every 4 hours, until the material glows white-hot. And keep it glowing in this manner for 4 hours; then let it cool. Now you shall know that the strong water passes over in the space of 16 hours, or 20, or more, according to how you know to govern your fire. And it is better to be occupied with this work for 36 or 40 hours than if you were to hurry and the spirits did not pass over well; and also because of the great danger to the vessels, as they are less likely to crack under a tempered heat.

### CHAPTER CXIV.

<margin>Sublimation of Mercury. Tincture of vitriol.</margin>
Therefore, follow the common rule for making the water; and when all the strong water has distilled, the Mercury will sublimate <note>The process where a solid turns into gas and then back to solid on a cooler surface</note> upwards into the alembic, and even quite solidly: and it will take with it all the tincture of the vitriol. And when it sublimates no further, let it cool; and having removed the receiver, put your strong water into a glass vessel and stop it up tightly. Then take your sublimated Mercury from the alembic, and grind it again with the other half of the material. When all has been duly mixed as before, place it again in the glass pot, and distill once more as before; and when all these things are finished, remove it. Then take another 4 pounds each <note>original: "ana"; a medical term meaning equal parts of each ingredient</note> of vitriol and saltpeter, and do as before. And then you will have enough strong water: and the Mercury will have been sublimated four times, and you will have the whole body full of tinctures.

### Proportions.

### CHAPTER 115.

<margin>The true proportion of weights.</margin>
<margin>1st Reason. A note on proportion.</margin>
Now you shall know and understand the weights of the Sun <note>Gold</note>, the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and Mercury. Take 8 *lothones* <term>loth: a unit of weight common in Germanic lands, roughly equal to half an ounce</term> of pure Moon purified by cupellation <note>A refining process where silver or gold is heated in a shallow vessel (a cupel) to oxidize and remove impurities like lead</note>, and 4 *lothones* of pure Sun that has been cemented <note>Refined by being packed in a "cement" of salts and heated, which removes silver and other impurities</note>; these together make 12 *lothones*. And 6 *lothones* of Mercury which you have sublimated <note>Purified by turning it into vapor and then back into a solid</note> together make 18 *lothones*. This is the true proportion of weights. Question: Why is twice as much "body" <note>The solid, stable metals—in this case, gold and silver</note> given as "spirit" <note>The volatile substance, Mercury</note>? You should know that when the body is stronger and more subtle than the spirit and they are moved to the fire, then the body will retain the best and most subtle part of the spirit within itself: it will convert it and lead it to its own likeness and nature. Then it will consume, spit out, and reduce to nothing the coarse parts or dross <note>original: "fæces"</note>. But if the spirit is in a greater quantity and more subtle than the body, the spirit will ascend and carry away the best part of the body with it, and leave the coarse parts or dross at the bottom; for they are not of its nature. That is the first reason.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
The second reason is: if there were more spirit than body, or an equal amount <note>original: "ana"; used in prescriptions to mean "of each the same amount"</note> of both, when it is set to be fixed <note>To be made resistant to the heat of the fire so it no longer evaporates</note>, it would be fixed with great difficulty, and the time required would be very long. Therefore, it was done for these two reasons. However, once the spirits and bodies are already fixed together, then enough spirit can be added.

<margin>3rd Reason.</margin>
For whatever is placed with it is easily fixed. For when bodies and spirits are fixed together, they are the Elixir. And if many weights of spirit are added, it is easily fixed. This is the third reason.

<margin>4th Reason.</margin>
<margin>Spirit of aqua vitæ.</margin>
The fourth reason is, if more spirit is given than body, or even an equal amount: the spirits of the strong waters <note>original: "aquarum fortium"; nitric acid or similar corrosive mineral acids</note> remain with them in the work. And those are very oily, volatile spirits; such also are the spirits of *aqua vitæ* <note>original: "aquæ vitæ"; literally "water of life," referring to concentrated alcohol</note>, and they are fixed with great difficulty; and these remain for the most part with the work. For it is only drawn out from a warm bath <note>original: "balneo"; a water-bath or "bain-marie" used for gentle heating</note> during the process of congealing. And if there were already as much spirit as body, because all those other spirits would remain with the work, it could not be fixed at all, or the time would be far too long. Now the proportion of weights has been demonstrated by reason.

Thus it is clear that each thing has its proper proportion of water. ### CHAPTER CXVIII.

<margin>
Which nutrients are to be taken.

All corrosive power removed from the strong water. A great secret.

For in all dissolved **Silver**, the powder of **Gold** is found. Indeed, every **Silver** contains **Gold**, whether a little or a lot. Keep this here. And when you have poured each individual part into a glass jar in this manner, place an **alembic** <note>a pointed cap used in distillation to direct vapors into a beak</note> upon each one, and place them in a basin with sand in a **bath** <term>original: *balneo*; a method of gentle heating, like a double boiler or sand bath</term>. And when it is so dry, pour over it good **rectified** <note>purified and strengthened by repeated distillation</note> ***aqua vitæ*** <term>literally "water of life"; high-proof alcohol or brandy used as a solvent</term>, until the liquid stands three fingers wide above the matter. In this way, you would not need to put on or take off the alembic each time; instead, the dissolved matter would simply be emptied from one to another to avoid losing too much of the **spirit** <note>the volatile, gaseous essence of the substance</note>. This is also the least amount of trouble. 

Therefore, obtain twelve or more such glasses for yourself, both small and large. For although they stand in the furnace or upon the ashes, not much distills out of them; whatever rises up sinks back down to the bottom, and not much passes through the beak. This is because there is no downward slope through which the moisture can collect. Thus, these glasses are very good for dissolving, congealing, and **rectifying** <note>purifying</note>. There is no need to seal them with lute; one simply pours from glass to glass and stops the top with a cork or a tiny round glass that fits and is polished. 

Therefore, I advise you to work your task in this manner until you gather the materials. Then they must be placed in a **fixing glass** <term>original: *vitro fixatorio*; a vessel designed to withstand long, steady heat to "fix" a volatile substance into a solid state</term>. Then, put each matter into its own glass, each in its own particular furnace or bath, in a basin with sand or **sifted ashes** <term>original: *cineribus cribratis*</term>. Pour your ***aqua vitæ*** over it so that it stands four fingers above the matter, seal the receiver to the beak of the vessel, and let it be dissolved with a tiny heat—so gentle that you could keep your hand in the bath. And it will be dissolved; below, in the bottom of the glass, certain **dregs** <term>original: *fax*; literally "lees" or "sediment"</term> will remain. Then have another three glasses of the same composition: pour the clear liquid from all three glasses, each into its own particular glass, and stop it up tightly. Once more, pour ***aqua vitæ*** over the dregs of each glass—just enough so they are again covered by four fingers—close it, and place it again in the bath as before...

...with the receiver sealed to the beak with lute <note>a paste or clay used to make joints airtight</note>: and when it has stood for three or four days in the bath, if anything still remains in the dregs <term>original: *fæcibus*; the solid residue or sediment left after distillation or dissolution</term>, it may be dissolved. And repeat that work as many times as necessary, until no more dregs remain for you from any of these three, but all three are dissolved so that they leave no dregs. And at least always put the dregs into the same jar, each by itself, for the element of Earth is in those dregs. You shall still calcine <term>original: *calcinabis*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> all three of these dregs: and you shall extract the Earth from each of the dregs, and you shall bring each one to its own matter, before they are gathered together.

## CHAPTER CXIX.

<margin>How the Earth is to be calcined.</margin>
Now you shall know, my son, that your 3 matters are subtle and rectified <note>purified and refined</note>—namely, 3 elements—and the element of Earth still lies in the dregs, each in its own glass. Now keep your 3 matters firmly sealed until the dregs have been calcined. And after the calcination of all three Earths extracted from them and rectified: and then also the Earth having been brought into its own nature: then we shall bring the work together and set it to be fixed <note>in alchemy, "fixing" refers to making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat without evaporating</note>, as we will teach later.

->Calcination of the Earth.<-

## CHAPTER 120.

Take, beloved, your 3 glass jars in which the dregs <term>original: *fæces*; the solid residue or sediment left after distillation or dissolution</term> remain; and you shall evaporate them until they are entirely dry. Then have over each jar a round glass lid—the jar should be smoothed evenly on top—and also a cover, so that they fit one another perfectly. Then seal the cover over the jar with lute <note>a paste or clay used to make joints airtight</note>, and place each in a basin with ashes, each upon its own specific furnace.

<margin>Gold must be calcined longer than silver.</margin>
For Gold [Sol] must be calcined longer than Silver [Luna]. The dregs of Gold should easily be calcined for the space of 6 refections <note>original: *refectionum*; in alchemy, these are specific cycles of heating or periods of processing</note>, while Silver is easily calcined in 30 hours. And the dregs of Mercury are easily calcined in 18 hours. Therefore, each glass must stand upon its own furnace: and you shall add only enough fire to each so that the dregs glow with a common heat. You shall keep the dregs of Gold for 6 days in a natural glow <term>original: *candore*; the state of being white-hot or incandescent</term>, then let them cool: and the dregs of Silver for 30 or 32 hours in a single glow: and those of Mercury for 18 or 20 hours in a single glow: then let them cool. Then remove all 3 glasses: and if anything has been sublimated <term>the process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid on a cooler surface</term> upward into the cover or to the edges of the jar, wipe it off with a feather. Then pour distilled common water over each of the dregs, and place the jars upon the furnace in a pot with ashes: and let the water boil for an hour, then let it cool. Then have 3 other glass jars, and pour off each water by itself gradually from its dregs, or distill it through a filter.

<margin>Extraction of the Salt.</margin>
Then again pour other common water over the dregs which remained in the jar, and do so again for an hour: then again let it cool: and again carefully pour each into its own water, as before. Then again pour fresh water over it. In this way, you have drawn the element of "earth" out of the dregs. Then cast away the dregs, for they are entirely useless. Then set your 3 jars to be congealed <note>here meaning to allow the liquid to evaporate or sit until the salts crystallize</note>, and in the bottom of each jar you will find salt that is between white and ash-colored: pour distilled water over it, and let it boil again for an hour: then let it cool and settle, and pour the liquid away from its dregs, and cast those dregs away. Then evaporate your water from each jar, and once again a salt will remain for you in each jar, and it will now be a little whiter. Pour water over your salt again, as before, and do as you did before.

<margin>The earth rectified and cleansed.</margin>
Repeat this work as many times until your salt no longer leaves behind any dregs. Then your "earth" is rectified <note>purified and refined to its proper state</note>, and cleansed of all uncleanness: and these are the Earths of the Philosophers.

<summary>This page describes the calcination of the solid residues of gold, silver, and mercury through prolonged heating and subsequent water-leaching to extract pure "philosophical salts." This process of repeated boiling, filtering, and evaporating "rectifies" the elemental earth by removing all useless dregs.</summary>

### CHAPTER 121.

Now add all the earth to its own purified <term>original: *rectificatis*; referring to substances that have been distilled or refined to their purest state</term> elements. These have now been properly purified together and made subtle <note>refined into a very fine or volatile state</note>, without the separation of the elements. You have brought them so far that they are now a medicine due to their great refinement: <margin>Medicine.</margin> for you have placed their exterior within, and their interior without <note>a classic alchemical phrase meaning to turn the hidden qualities of a substance outward</note>, and you have stripped them of all impurity. <margin>Morienus.</margin> Therefore Morienus the Philosopher says: Unless you make the impure bodies pure, and clean from all dregs, you have found nothing in our art. <margin>Hermes.</margin> Hermes says: The body is dissolved by the eternal water, and that water congeals the eternal Mercury <note>the "Philosophical Mercury," not common quicksilver</note> through coagulation. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle says: Prepare the bodies and dissolve them, and then join them with the washed and cleansed spirits, and an eternal coagulation and fixation <note>the process by which a volatile substance is made to resist the fire</note> occurs. Geber says: Afterwards, join to it the prepared soul; in this way, the eternal color is imprinted upon it, which it will retain forever. <margin>Rhazes.</margin> Rhazes says: Turn the bodies into water, and cleanse that water of all its impurity, and from it make earth once again, and from the earth, water: and then add the spirit and the soul to it; then you have acted correctly in our art. <margin>Danthynus.</margin> Danthynus says: Purge the bodies and whiten them, and add the prepared spirit to them, and pour life or the soul into them: thus occurs the eternal bonding and eternal fixation. <margin>Plato.</margin> And Plato says: Destroy the imperfect body and reduce it to water, and wash away its leprosy <note>a term for the "diseased" impurities or corrosion found in base metals</note>, and cleanse it, and add the prepared spirit to it, so that fire will not separate them: and then add the prepared soul to it, so they will resist every test and pass through. <margin>Hermes.</margin> Hermes further says: Dissolve the bodies and whiten them, and strip them of all impurity; bring the washed spirits to the bodies, so they cannot be separated. Then add the ferment <note>a substance that triggers the transformation of the whole mixture, much like yeast in bread</note> to them: thus the eternal tincture <note>the final alchemical agent capable of transmuting metals</note> is imprinted upon them, so that fire cannot separate them. <margin>Kalid to Morienus.</margin> Kalid asked Morienus: What is the best gathering together? Morienus replied: A perfect, fixed body dissolved into eternal water, with the prepared spirit immersed in it, is a perfect work and a firm union, such that they are not at all separated by fire afterward.
