### CHAPTER 125.

<margin>
The greatest secret lies in the joining.
</margin>
<margin>
The <term>amalgamation: the process of mixing mercury with another metal to form a paste or alloy</term> of the Moon <note>Silver</note> with Mercury.
</margin>
You shall know that in this joining <note>original: *coniunctione*</note> lies the greatest secret that exists in the entire art. It is certainly true that perfection is finally reached after a long duration of time by those who work with amalgamations, joining bodies such as the Moon <note>Silver</note> and Mercury in a single glass vessel and cooking them over a tiny fire until they are made perfect. You shall know and rightly understand that all who work in this way—with amalgamations of the Moon and Mercury—are fools. Whether they distill them with <term>strong water: usually nitric acid, used to dissolve and separate metals</term>, or distill part and let part remain, thinking they can prepare a <term>medicine: in alchemy, a substance used to "heal" base metals into gold or to restore human health</term> from them in a short time, they are fools; they understand neither the art nor themselves. And even if the material were perhaps perfected at the very end, as it would be (as has been shown in many places above), the time required would be so long that it would weary them to wait, and they would abandon the work. The Reason: the Moon <note>Silver</note> is cold and moist, not <term>fixed: rendered solid or resistant to evaporation by heat</term>, dirty, impure, and volatile—and Mercury is even more so. These two join: which will make the other perfect? For both are imperfect. I tell you, I have seen many learned men sitting at their work who performed such operations, and they had been occupied with these works for many years; yet I never saw any of them achieve perfection. Although perfection is to be expected at the end, they could not endure the wait; then they would ruin their work with the fire, or they would seek some strange advice to reach the end. No matter what method they entered upon, in the end they ruined everything. But if they had allowed it to stand for some years, and followed through day and night with a tiny fire, it would have emerged perfect at last, so that they or their descendants might have seen its art.

<margin>
The Reason:
</margin>
The reason, beloved, why it must stand for many years is this: Nature does not work except through nature, although it is helped a little by a tiny fire which is added to it continually day and night. The Moon <note>Silver</note> is imperfect, and Mercury is even more imperfect; which will make the other perfect? Neither has that power. How can an unclean garment be washed and cleaned in dirty water? Truly, no one can do it. So it is with the Moon and Mercury: when they are joined, neither has the power to help the other. But Nature consumes the dross <note>original: *fæces*; the impurities or sediment</note> by the help of a constant <term>decoction: a long process of heating a substance to extract its essence or refine it</term> over a small fire. And even now, when all the dross has been consumed, both are still not fixed; which will fix the other? Nature, with a tiny fire and constant decoction, fixes the Moon; and even after a long time and constant decoction, the Moon becomes a medicine.

### CHAPTER CXXVI.

### CHAPTER 129.

<margin>The making of the Elixir.</margin>
**N**ow you shall take a fixatory glass <note>a specialized vessel designed to withstand long periods of heat to "fix" or stabilize volatile substances</note>, and place into it those little stones of Silver <note>original: *Lunae*; literally "of the Moon," the alchemical name for silver</note>, and you shall seal it with the seal of Hermes <note>an airtight, "hermetic" seal made by melting the glass neck of the vessel shut</note>. You shall place it upon the furnace in the ashes, and add a fire so hot that you are only just able to hold your finger in the ashes without burning it. And when the glass feels the heat, immediately those little stones will melt like oil, and they will easily ascend in 1,000 tiny fibers; and then they will descend again. And day by day they will become thicker, as the matter becomes more "fixed" <note>rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by heat</note>. And at the end they become so thick that they can hardly return down again. And though before they seemed to be 1,000, now they are scarcely 15 or 16. When I see this sign, increase your fire just enough so that you can hardly hold your finger in the ashes for the length of time it takes to recite a *Hail Mary* <note>original: *aue Maria*; a common way for medieval and early modern craftsmen to measure short durations of time before precise clocks were available</note>. And when you see that no more stones ascend and descend, increase your fire so that you cannot bear your finger in the ashes by any means. Keep it in this way for 24 hours; and if during that time you see nothing more ascending or descending, your matter is fixed. And that will happen in 40 days: and then your perfected body is ready, finished, and is a "medicine." Here now the body is no longer imperfect; rather it is a "glorified body" and a high medicine: for it has the power to convert all imperfect bodies into perfect Silver. And what is more, if you project it upon pure Gold <note>original: *Solem*; literally "the Sun"</note>, it will convert it by its own nature into true Silver. For this reason Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "He who cannot make Silver from Gold, can make Gold from Silver." Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy</note> says: "He who knows not how to make white from red, knows not how to make red from white." And you shall know by this same reasoning that the Elixir can be made from all imperfect metals; and thereafter you shall know that the crystalline stones of Gold <note>original: *Solis*</note> must also be put into the fixatory glass and set to be fixed, just as was said regarding the Silver. It is the same workmanship, the same construction, and the same fixatory glass. And if your furnace is large enough, all those

Place those three glasses together upon the same furnace, and give to all of them the same regulation of fire. You should likewise know that the Mercury <note>original: *Mercurium*; quicksilver</note> must be cooked until it has been clarified of all impurity, before it is added to the prepared body. For it still possesses within itself the spirit of wine <note>distilled alcohol</note> which it took up, and also the spirit of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note> and saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> which it carried up during sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it vapors and then collects as a solid again</note>. It also contains its own rectified earth; and all these things are not yet fixed <note>stable under heat</note>, nor are they gathered into a single thing, nor are they yet a simple substance, but a composite. Therefore, the Mercury must also be driven until it is a simple substance: one part fixed in its nature, and also one part not fixed. 

You shall understand it in this way: You have heard much concerning the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver</note>—that when the little stones <note>crystals formed during the process</note> no longer rise up, then it is enough, and the Silver is fixed. And when no more little stones rise up in the Mercury's glass, then likewise it is enough. And then it is partly fixed and partly not fixed. Understand it thus: the spirit of vitriol and the earth have fixed one part of the Mercury, so that it does not have the power to rise up or produce little stones through heat. But if it were placed in a crucible <note>original: *testa*; a heat-resistant pot</note> with ashes and a great heat were added to it, one part would indeed still rise or sublimate; but not the whole of it. The greatest part would remain fixed at the bottom. Thus, when the Mercury no longer rises in the fixatory glass, or does not produce little stones under such heat as we described for the Silver, it is partly fixed and partly not fixed, according to the aforementioned ratio. And when it is such, it is ready to be joined to the Silver.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin> 
For Aristotle says: Prepare the body until it is perfect, then join to it the prepared spirit; and together they become one, so that they cannot be separated by fire.

### CHAPTER 130.

<margin>Gold is a much more perfect medicine than silver.</margin> 
You should know that these little stones of the Sun <note>original: *Solis*; the alchemical name for gold</note> must also be prepared before they can be added to the body. For Gold also possesses the spirit of wine and its own earth, and these are not yet fixed with the three elements. In this state, it is not yet a ferment, nor a soul <note>original: *anima*; the vitalizing principle in alchemy</note>; it is still a composite. Therefore, the little stones of Gold must also be placed in the fixatory glass and fixed just as the Silver was. When the Gold is fixed, it is also a perfect medicine, like the Silver, and yet much more perfect. For by as much as the Sun surpasses the Moon, by so much is this medicine more perfect. Then this medicine has the power of transforming all imperfect metals into Gold.

<margin>
Once the materials are prepared, they are finally ready to be placed together, so that the stone may be fashioned from them.

Those who seek shortcut paths will be deceived: they will spoil everything they set aside for the purpose of making the stone. There are many "fixations" <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> and other minor works from which some fruit might eventually be gained, provided the practitioners reach the end and can rightly endure the long wait. However, such people are like a cook who wishes to cook all kinds of food in a single pot—vegetables, bacon, fish, and so on. This would result in a foul pottage. The same would happen if someone were to bring together Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note>, Mercury, Gold <note>original: *Sole*</note>, along with other spirits and "strong waters" <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; mineral acids like nitric acid</note>, and imagine they could cook it all at once in a single glass; the same fate as the cook’s stew would befall them.

<margin>
The simile of a cook wishing to cook all kinds of food in one pot.
</margin>
For in nature, one thing is cold, another hot; a third is moist, a fourth dry, and a fifth is fixed. One is clean, another unclean; one is combustible, another incombustible. Yet the foolish believe they can bring all these materials, residing together in one vessel, to a single end—either the "Stone" or some other potent medicine—in a short time. For them, it is impossible. They merely cook slimy materials. They do not grasp the obscure words of the Philosophers; their entire undertaking is madness. Therefore, beloved, read this lesson often, lest you fall into such error.

### CHAPTER CXXXII.

Now we wish to return to our work. Beloved, when your Silver, Mercury, and Gold have been prepared in that manner, you shall open the fixation-glass <note>a specialized glass vessel used to stabilize chemicals</note> containing the "body" of your Silver, and you shall pour the Mercury into it while it is still warm; for if it were cold, it would be too thick. The same must be done with the Gold. Once the "spirit" <note>here referring to the volatile components like Mercury</note> has been poured over the "body" <note>the solid metal, Silver</note>, seal your glass with strong lute <note>original: *luto*; a reinforced clay sealant used to make vessels airtight</note> and place it once more in the ashes. Apply heat for 7 days, so hot that you can scarcely keep a finger in the ashes, in order to properly gather, mix, and unite the spirit with the body. Then let it cool. Now the body and spirit are prepared to receive the "soul" <note>the vitalizing principle, often identified with the Gold or the 'ferment'</note> or the ferment.

<margin>
The body and spirit prepared to receive the soul.
</margin>

### CHAPTER CXXXIII.

Then, in the name of God, take the ferment <note>a substance used to 'leaven' or transform the mixture</note> and pour it warm into the glass with the Silver and Mercury. Cover it with strong lute and place it upon the furnace. You shall apply fire for 7 days, as described above, so that it may be properly incorporated with the others. What were previously three things are now one. Then let it cool, and pour it—while still warm—into the glass vial for the "Regimen" <note>the final stage of controlled heating</note> or into a "glass egg" <note>an ovoid alchemical flask</note>, and seal it. **Fire.** Place it in the secret furnace, the athanor <note>a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature</note>, or upon a tripod for 40 days, maintaining a fire so warm that you can comfortably hold your hand there.

### *Multiplication.*
## CHAPTER CXXXIV.

<margin>Mercury to be prepared.</margin>
Prepare your Mercury <note>the metal Quicksilver, though often referring to a specialized alchemical "Mercury of the Philosophers"</note> in the same manner as taught in this work, until it forms into small crystalline stones. Add 100 parts of this to one part of your pulverized Stone, and place them together in a "fixing" glass vessel. Seal it firmly and place it upon the furnace, adding such heat that you can barely keep your finger in the ashes. Let it stay in that heat for 15 days; then empty it into a glass vial or "egg." Seal it with the Seal of Hermes <note>an airtight seal created by melting the glass neck of the vessel shut</note> and place it on a tripod for 40 days, adding such heat that you can hold your hand there, or endure it for the duration of a Lord's Prayer, measured from the interior wall of the furnace to the exterior. When the 40 days are finished, take it out and break the glass. Take out the noble Stone; this one performs as high a projection as the previous one. Give thanks to God for all His wonderful gifts which He has bestowed upon His servants and sons.

### *Another work.*
## CHAPTER CXXXV.

Know, beloved, as a secret: when you wish to perform any "fixation" <note>making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> or multiplication, so that you may quickly perceive fruit and reach the end, you must first cleanse the spirits by "sublimation" <note>a process of vaporization and solidification used for purification</note>. The "bodies"—whether Gold <note>original: *Sol*</note> or Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note>—must also be cleansed beforehand: Gold by "cementing" and Silver by "calcining" <note>two different methods of high-heat chemical purification</note>, as I will teach below. No union can be made between the soul and the body so that they remain together as long as any impurity remains in either the soul or the body. Furthermore, the soul can in no way remain in the body without the spirit.

<margin>The spirit as mediator between soul and body.</margin>
And you shall know that the spirit is the mediator <note>a go-between or reconciling agent</note> between the soul and the body, which binds both together, unites them, and so mixes itself with those two that there is such a firm bond of love between these three that they can never be separated, neither now nor at any time hereafter; and what had previously been three are now nothing but one. But as long as any impurity remains, no union <note>original: *congregatio*</note> can happen by any art. It is the ignorance of this fact that causes all men to wander in error. If, however, they possessed this knowledge, all their works would succeed well and they would not err. For if they applied themselves to fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate when heated</term>, they would fix the substance quickly. And if they applied themselves to multiplication <term>multiplication: the process of increasing the quantity or the transmuting power of the alchemical medicine</term>, the Mercury would quickly unite itself into the body. And however little Mercury remains with the body, when more is added again, it is quickly fixed with it; for one part further fixes the other, and with each turn more and more, and more quickly. <margin>The spirit always grows in the body.</margin> For the spirit always grows in the body: for the more the body increases, the more the subtle spirit grows with it and becomes stronger, and it retains more Mercury with itself, and does so quickly. Indeed, multiplication could easily be performed for so long, and held in the fire, until the matter became so subtle that it would melt in the manner of wax and penetrate glass, just as oil penetrates leather; and it would become a perfect Elixir for transmuting <note>original: *transferenda*, to transfer or transform</note> metals into the Sun <note>original: *Solem*; Gold</note> or into the Moon <note>original: *Lunam*; Silver</note>. And the subtle spirit performs all of this, being the mediator between the soul and the body. For the subtle spirit grows so abundantly in the body that it makes the whole thing a medicine. It increases in metals just as air grows in an apple. <margin>A comparison of the apple.</margin> Place an apple in the world, exposed to the air and in a dry place, as soon as you pluck it from the tree, and let it lie there for a whole year; the longer it lies, the more fragrant it becomes. By what reason does this happen? One or two apples are not large, and yet they give off a scent through the whole room. That scent comes from a noble spirit which keeps the apple in its essence, and which grows more in it every day; indeed, it remains until the body begins to decay, at which point the noble spirit departs from it, and the apple rots and stinks. How much more, then, does the noble spirit grow in the work where the spirit and body are entirely pure? Therefore, beloved, purify the soul and body completely before you apply or join the spirit to them.

You shall furthermore know the weights of all multiplications and fixations that must be observed. And in this many people err. For if you add too much of the volatile matter to the fixed part, the volatile part will carry the best of the fixed part away with it...

And if the fixed part is stronger than the volatile, the best part of the volatile remains with it. In this, all Alchemists err. You should know, therefore, that in performing your multiplications <term>multiplication: the process of increasing the transmuting power or quantity of the Elixir</term> or your fixations <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term>, you must take three parts of the body, one part of the soul, and one part of the spirit. Mix these thoroughly together, and apply such a heat that the body draws the soul to itself, and the spirit becomes a participant in both of them. Thus, the spirit and the body become thick and dense, while the body becomes subtle <note>refined or purified</note>; in this way, your work will be successful. But if you apply such heat that the spirit and soul become more subtle than they were before, while the body becomes thicker and darker, then everything is ruined. You shall proceed in this way: apply a slow fire, so that the body draws the soul to itself and the spirit shares in both, penetrating through the body and the soul, heating them both so that they both become one single body.

### CHAPTER 137.

<margin>
For generation to occur, a contrary must be present.
</margin>
You shall know why the spirit is joined to the soul and the body; the reason is this. Luna <note>Latin: *Luna*; refers here to Silver, representing the "Body"</note> is the body, and Mercury is the soul. Both are cold and moist in their outer qualities, but hot and dry in their inner natures. Since they are composed this way, how could a union occur? A contrary nature must be present if any generation <note>the birth of a new substance</note> is to take place; yet fools are unable to grasp this. Nevertheless, the Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical text</note> says that nature must be followed, just as a child is conceived in a mother. They speak plainly and without hidden words, yet men can neither perceive nor understand them. They place Luna and Mercury together, amalgamating <note>mixing mercury with another metal</note> them, and they think they are fixing those two together. They fail to notice that both are of the same nature—cold and moist—and they try to marry them without a medium <note>a middle or reconciling agent</note>. Fire would sooner be extinguished by fire, which is impossible. So it is with Luna and Mercury: before you could fix them together, you would first make them both volatile. For Luna is so cold and moist when it is not fixed that the Mercury can drag it away from the earth by subliming <note>heating a solid until it turns into vapor</note> it, so that nothing remains except earth and salt. And when a large quantity of Mercury is added to it, and a more vehement fire is applied, one becomes volatile along with the other. The volatile parts carry the earth or salt up with them, leaving nothing but dregs at the bottom of the vessel.

<margin>
What the spirit accomplishes when joined to the body and soul.
</margin>
Fools, however, cannot understand this reason, nor do they notice that two similar things cannot be joined without a medium, which is the spirit. The spirit is extremely hot and dry, while Mercury and Luna are cold and moist in their outward parts. Now, when the spirit is added to these in the correct proportion, it warms the coldness of both...

With its heat and its dryness, it tempers the moisture, so that through it the one may enter the other; thus the spirit becomes one body with both. To these, proportion must also be added. For if there were too much spirit, such that it made them too hot or dry, generation <note>the alchemical process of "birthing" a new substance</note> would not occur. For they are hot and dry within; if they were also made hot and dry on the outside, both would become a red powder, in the manner of earth that has been stripped of its moisture. And if you were to apply too great a fire, it would also be corrupted. 

Even so, beloved, you must rule it in this way: that they may rest quietly among themselves without separation, so that they can enter into one another by resting without separation. You shall increase the fire no more than so that you can endure the heat with your finger for the space of a "Hail Mary" <note>original: *Aue Maria*; a common medieval way to measure time, roughly 15-20 seconds</note>. If Alchemists understood this principle fundamentally, all their works would proceed without obstacle; whether amalgamations, fixations <term>fixation: making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>, or multiplications <term>multiplication: increasing the power or quantity of the transmuting agent</term>, whether in the Stone or other medicines, all would have a good success without great labor and without great expense. Imprint this upon your memory, and read it through often, and understand every word fundamentally before you begin any work; in this way, you will neither err nor be deceived.

### Of Sulphurs
### CHAPTER 138.

<margin>There are as many sulphurs as there are metals.</margin>
Now, my beloved, you shall hold as a great secret that there are as many Sulphurs as there are metals. And according to how each is clean and pure, so too are the metals pure. Thus it happens that lead, iron, and copper are so impure: for their sulphurs are impure, fatty, and foul-smelling. Therefore they are unclean, rusty, black, stinking, and full of combustible sulphur. 

And you should know that in every thing there is a combustible fire, as has been said in many places, and this corrupts all things that exist in the nature of things. For in whatever thing combustible fatness <note>the "oily" or flammable part of a substance</note> dwells, that thing is imperfect and must quickly perish and be reduced to nothing. For the spirit cannot rest in it for long: for it does not find a clean place there in which it might rest. Therefore, impure metals are imperfect; for in them there is as much combustible sulphur or oil as there is in all growing things, whether in the vegetable or the animal. Indeed, even in Luna <note>original: *Luna*; refers to Silver</note> there is combustible sulphur or oil. For this reason, it holds no cement <note>a chemical paste used to purify metals</note>, nor colors, nor antimony: the combustible sulphur or oil within it causes this. And then Luna is purged of its sulphur...

...combustible [sulfur], Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note> is fixed, it holds its colors, and withstands cementation <term>cementation: a high-heat refining process used to separate gold from silver and base metals</term>, and passes through antimony <note>antimony was used as a purifying agent in gold refining</note>, and it is effectively a white Sun <note>the "white Sun" refers to silver that has reached a high state of purity and stability, resembling gold in everything but color</note>. Likewise, Gold <note>original: *Sol*</note> has no combustible sulfur within itself; therefore it is fixed and pure, and passes all tests. Therefore, my beloved, you shall know that wherever

combustible sulfur is present, the spirit cannot rest. For this reason, all who work with combustible sulfur go astray. Thus Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit</note> says: "Our sulfur is not the common sulfur: our sulfur is incombustible and clean."

### CHAPTER 139.

<margin>Many kinds of sulfurs.</margin>
You must know that there are many kinds of sulfurs, such as common sulfur, from which gunpowder is made; this is entirely useless for our work because of its odor and its overflowing oiliness. Nevertheless, there is a noble spirit within it that is entirely useful for our work, but it must be drawn out from it by art, such as by sublimation <term>sublimation: heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term>, through the means that shall be described below. There is also another sulfur having much combustible oil in itself, and it is called orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*, a yellow arsenic mineral</note>; and it is better than the former. This truly has a noble spirit in itself, which likewise would have to be extracted by sublimation. There is also another, which is better than those two, and it is called red arsenic <note>likely realgar</note>, and it likewise has a very noble spirit in itself. There is also yet another sulfur, called white arsenic: and it is the best of all our works; but it must be purified even better by sublimation, as will be taught later.

### CHAPTER 140.

<margin>Sulfur is in all things created by God.</margin>
Furthermore, nothing has been created by God that does not contain sulfur, in which sulfur there is a noble spirit that serves in the animal or vegetable work, when it has been drawn out from the combustible oil or fire. And without that spirit, no vegetable or animal stone <note>the "stone" or elixir derived from organic materials</note> can be perfected, nor any other work. Thus you shall learn to know the sulfurs. For if you take crude sulfur that still possesses combustibility within it, it will corrupt your work. Or if you take into your white works a red spirit coming from orpiment, or from red saffron-colored arsenic, you would corrupt your work. And if you also take into your red work a white spirit proceeding from white arsenic, or from calamine stone <note>a zinc ore</note>, or from white vitriol <note>zinc sulfate</note>—all of which contain white sulfur—you will also corrupt your work. And if you mix a white spirit with a red body, you will destroy everything." Therefore be prudent and circumspect. And furthermore, when you wish to prepare the stone, or...

### CHAPTER 151.

<margin>The ratio of proportion.</margin>Take 6 parts of the body, and 1 part each of the soul and the spirit. The reasoning is this: Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note> is not fixed, and it contains much Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> within itself, which is one body with the body of Silver; and one body is not willingly separated from itself. Although it is purified upon the cupel <note>original: *testa*; a shallow vessel used in assaying</note>, the Mercury remains with the Silver. But in cement <note>refining paste</note> or antimony, there it flies away with the antimony, which is a spirit, and by burning it reduces the body of Silver to nothing. For this reason, people often take too much of the spirit, and one part of the soul (which is Mercury), and one part of the spirit. This is too much, so that it becomes volatile. For as soon as the Mercury approaches the Silver, the Mercury which is already in the Silver mixes with the Mercury which was never a body <note>the "Mercury which was never a body" refers to crude or "running" quicksilver, as opposed to the metallic mercury integrated into the silver</note>. And they are mixed together; and the spirit, which is the mediator between these three—that is, between the Mercury and the body of Silver—mixes itself with them. If too much Mercury and spirit were added to the Silver, and they were mixed together and moved to the fire, they would fly away together; they would snatch away the best part of the body with them and leave nothing behind except dregs. Therefore, take 6 parts of Silver and one part each of the soul and the spirit, so that the body remains strong and fixes the soul and the body <note>original: *corpˢ* (corpus); likely referring to the metallic substance</note> within itself.

<margin>Danthinus.</margin>Therefore the philosopher Danthinus <note>likely John Dastin, a famous 14th-century English alchemist</note> says: "When the body draws the soul and spirit with it, or into itself, rejoice; for your work will reach its desired end. But when the soul and spirit draw the body, you retain nothing but ashes." For when Mercury is added to your Silver, both of those aforementioned Mercuries are gathered together and become one. Then comes the spirit, which is the mediator between the two Mercuries and the body, and it mixes itself with those three; just as before the Mercury of the Silver was one body, it is now gathered with the Mercury which was never a body. And this is what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "When Mercury is a body, it further embodies; when it is dissolved, it further dissolves; when it is fixed, it further fixes." Therefore the Mercury of the Silver draws the Mercury which is added to it (and which is crude, for it never was a body) toward its own nature. The Silver makes a body out of it. ### CHAPTER 142.

<margin>Commonly called rock alum.</margin>

### CHAPTER 144.

<margin>The rule of fire.</margin>
Take Silver <note>original: *Lunam*; literally "the Moon," the alchemical name for silver</note> that has been cupelled <note>original: *cupellatam*; refined in a shallow ceramic cup called a cupel to remove base metals like lead</note> and thoroughly purified, and then even now refined from lead in a crucible; then hammered into thin plates, and then cemented <note>original: *cæmentatam*; a process of heating a metal with dry chemicals, often salts, to further purify it</note> with common salt, layer upon layer, and sealed with lute <note>original: *lutatam*; a clay sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>, and then calcined, as you know. First use a small fire, then one somewhat stronger, until the crucible glows red, but so that the Silver does not melt. And leave it thus for 24 hours in a single glow or heat. Then open the crucible and wash the salt from your plates until everything is clean and pure. And grind your plates upon a stone and wash them as is fitting. Then reduce your Silver back into a body, and again make plates as before, and cement as before. Do this and repeat it until your Silver comes out of the cement clean and bright: so that the water poured over it flows away as clean and clear as it was when poured on. Then set it aside until you have need of it.

### CHAPTER 145.

Now I have taught you how to prepare your Silver, Mercury, Arsenic, and sal ammoniac for the white stone <note>the "White Work" or *albedo*, the stage of the Great Work that produces silver</note> or for fixation. And once one fixation is done, you must always add living Mercury, and you shall fix it again for a short time, taking it out and putting it back in. But if you were to always add Mercury and never take anything out, your fixation would become meltable like wax <note>original: *fusilis vt cera*</note> and become a medicine; and it would perform a projection <note>original: *proiectionem*; the final act of transmutation where the alchemical medicine is cast upon a base metal to transform it</note> upon Mercury that has life, as was said regarding projection, and as will be taught hereafter.

# MASTER JOHANNES ISAAC.

If alum <note>original: *alumen*; a mineral salt used as a mordant to fix dyes to fabric</note> were not added, the red color would not enter the cloth and remain fixed; it would fly away invisibly, and the cloth would turn pale. For the color is the spirit of the red, and the alum partakes of both <note>meaning it shares the nature of both the dye and the fabric</note>, so that once gathered, they enter one into the other. You must also have water of the clouds <note>original: *aqua nubium*; likely rainwater, considered pure by alchemists</note> in which all three of these things may boil; and when, through boiling, they have entered into one another and are properly gathered together, the cloth is hung up to be dried, the water recedes, and the fixed color remains in the cloth. So it is with our Stone. Although we have rightly prepared the bodies, the soul, and the spirit: unless they enter into one another, they will not remain together now or at any other time without the medium of water.

### CHAPTER 149.

<margin>Geber. Aristotle. Hermes. Danthynus. Morienus.</margin>
Likewise, now beloved, where shall we find that water? For Geber says: Our water is not the water of the clouds. Aristotle says: Our water is a dry water <note>original: *aqua sicca*; a paradoxical term for a substance that acts like a solvent but is not a common liquid</note>. Hermes says: Our water is gathered from foul and stinking menstrual matter <note>original: *menstruali materia*; in alchemy, this refers to a base, "unrefined" starting material, not necessarily biological blood</note>. Danthynus says: Our water is found in old stables, latrines, and foul sewers <note>a reference to the source of saltpeter or nitre</note>. And Morienus says: Our water grows in mountains and valleys.

And the foolish do not understand these words, thinking it is Mercury. It is not Mercury; it is a dry water which causes all the mineral spirits, the soul, and the body to enter and gather together. And when it has gathered them, it recedes from them and allows them to remain fixed together. And this water is found in all things that exist in the world. For if this water did not exist, we would strive in vain to make the Stone. For how would we make our prepared materials enter one into another? It is just as when Apothecaries <note>original: *Pharmacopolæ*</note> gather their herbs together. And we must do the same, whether in the vegetable, animal, or mineral kingdom; to perform the perfect work, or to make the quintessence, we must have the dry water from each distinct thing.

<margin>Dry water is in all things.</margin>
Therefore, dry water is present in all things so that they may make themselves perfect.

<margin>Galen.</margin>
Thus Galen says: all things have their own proper medicine for making the Stone, whether in the mineral, animal, or vegetable kingdom, without the addition of any foreign things. Therefore, when we wish to make the Stone or any fixation, we must perform that conjunction with our dry water, just as was said of the dyer and the Apothecary. It is for this reason, my beloved, that so many fall into error, because they do not understand nature, nor do they follow it. I have mentioned the dyer and the Apothecary to you so that through that reasoning you might understand raw nature, so that

### CHAPTER 150.

**T**ake 6 parts of your prepared Moon <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for silver</note>, and one part each of your sublimated spirit and soul, and half a part of your dry water. Maintain this same heat for 6 or 8 days, until you see that nothing more is raised by sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again at the top of the vessel</note> at that temperature. When nothing more sublimates, increase the fire slightly every eight <margin>A fierce fire must be used.</margin> days, until your material is fixed <term>fixed: a state where a substance no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to high heat</term>. Then apply a fierce fire. Remove the sal ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, used here as a volatile agent</note> by sublimation, and weigh it. If you have the correct weight—the same amount as you initially added and no more—then your material is fixed. But if you find it weighs more than what you put in at the start, the material is not yet fixed. Mix it again with the material and continue increasing the fire until it is fixed. Then, by sublimating your dry water <note>original: *aquam siccam*; likely a potent chemical solvent like a strong acid or mineral spirit</note> again, draw off the dry portion, take out your material, and weigh it to see if you have your full weight. 

And if you then wish to make the medicine from it, add only half as much live mercury <note>original: *Mercurij viui*; liquid quicksilver</note> as the material weighs, and also only half as much dry water: namely, where there were 2 parts, add one more, so they make 3 parts in total. At the same time, grind them together upon a stone with water of life <note>original: *aqua vitae*; high-proof distilled alcohol used as a solvent</note>, as was said before. Place it back into the glass jar in every way as described above, until your material is fixed. 

Then once more draw off your dry water by sublimation, and weigh your material. Take only half as much mercury as your material weighs, and 5 lots <note>original: *lothones*; a historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce</note> of your dry water; grind it again upon the stone with water of life as before. Proceed as before until your material is fixed. 

By sublimation, draw off your dry water again, and weigh the material for a third time: take half as much live mercury and 6 lots of dry water; mix and grind with water of life, and proceed as before until your material is fixed. It will become fusible <term>fusible: capable of being melted</term> like wax before it becomes entirely fixed. 

At that point, you can no longer draw off your dry water by sublimation. For when the stone reaches a high enough heat, it melts and encloses that water within itself, so that it can no longer fly upward. Nevertheless, that dry water is not fixed, nor can it be made fixed. Thus, it is necessary for the medicine to be partly fixed and partly not fixed. But the ignorant are unable to understand this. They always strive to make their material entirely fixed. But when they finally have it fixed, they have made no more progress than before; for when they went to perform the projection <note>the final alchemical act of casting the Stone onto base metals to transform them into silver or gold</note>, they achieved nothing. All their work was lost because they did not understand the words of the Philosophers. They abandoned the work exactly where it needed to be started anew, as was shown above. 

Now therefore, beloved, after you have made your medicine fusible, you shall place your medicine in a glass crucible melted from Venetian glass <note>highly prized, high-quality heat-resistant glass from Venice</note>, and you shall melt it. And once your medicine is melted, it is the stone.

# MINERAL WORKS
<meta>catchword: to make</meta>

...clear, white, and transparent in the manner of a crystal, retaining within itself that **dry water** <term>dry water: a potent alchemical solvent, often a mineral acid, that does not "wet" the hands like common water</term> which is not fixed, as it ought to be. For if it did not contain that dry water within itself, it could not perform **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of alchemy where the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon base metals to transmute them</term>. For when it is cast upon prepared **live mercury** <note>original: *Merc. vivum*; quicksilver</note>, or upon dead, foul, and impure metals (even those that have been "revived"), it would perform no projection at all. Indeed, there would be nothing to draw the medicine and the mercury together, just as was shown before with the example of the dyer and the pharmacist. Therefore, my dear, the dry water in the stone must not be fixed, but must remain volatile if projection is to occur.

### CHAPTER CLI.

<margin>
The dry water in the stone must be volatile and not fixed.

<margin>
What the dry water achieves.

You shall know, my dear, that when you perform projection, that water is present in the stone; and when the stone begins to melt over the mercury or over the impure metals, then that dry water draws the medicine and the metals together into one, and causes the one to enter into the other. And once it has joined them, it flies away during the melting process. For in projection, the medicine must flow together with the mercury or the impure metals into which the projection is made. And then the work is perfected. What do you think, my dear? Is this not a great secret hidden from all men? You shall further know that the work for the **Red** <note>the "Red Work" refers to the creation of gold</note> is the same as for the **White** <note>the "White Work" refers to the creation of silver</note> regarding the craftsmanship, except that the furnace, the weights, and the time are somewhat longer. And whoever seeks other ways to fashion the mineral stone shall go astray. Many and varied are the paths, but they are not firm, and many errors fall into them. However, this method must be present for the work to emerge perfected.

## *Reddening Water.*
### CHAPTER CLIII.

<margin>Fire regimen.</margin>
<margin>White water.</margin>
<margin>The likeness of a man exhaling breath.</margin>
Take **saffron of Mars** <term>saffron of Mars: iron oxide, often used to give a red color to the work</term>, **antimony** as it comes from the mines, and **red arsenic**, one pound of each; 1 pound of **orpiment** <note>original: *auripigmenti*; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>; 3 pounds of **Roman vitriol** <term>Roman vitriol: iron or copper sulfate crystals</term>; and **saltpeter** in a weight equal to all the others combined. Grind them all together and dry them until they can be powdered. Then mix in 1 pound of **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used as a flux and to carry spirits over in distillation</term>. When it is thoroughly mixed, put it into an earthenware vessel that can easily withstand the fire and is not glazed on the inside. Place an **alembic** <term>alembic: the "cap" or head of a still used for distilling vapors</term> on top of it, and **lute** <term>lute: a clay or paste used to hermetically seal the joints of alchemical apparatus</term> it firmly and tightly; place it upon the furnace with a receiver attached, and distill the **strong water** <note>original: *aquam fortem*; a mineral acid</note> as is proper: first with a small fire, and always increasing it.

A white water will distill for you; when it has finished distilling, the alembic will begin to turn red or become saffron-colored. Then quickly remove the receiver and add another, sealing the work tightly with lute. Increase your fire until the **white spirit** passes over—this is the sal ammoniac, which passes over last of all. Keep the fire going until the alembic becomes entirely clear. When the red spirit now passes, nothing else passes with it. But as soon as it has passed, the spirit and the water pass together. Then the alembic becomes white inside, as if it were full of snow. Then maintain the fire until the spirit and the dry water are led out through the beak by exhalation—just as a man exhales his breath with force, so the spirit and the dry water expire through the tube of the alembic into the receiver, and they increase the fire.

And when the spirit and the dry water have passed over, the alembic becomes clean, clear, white, and transparent. Then allow it to cool and remove it from the fire, and put the water into a glass and stopper it tightly. Then take the **dead head** <term>dead head: *caput mortuum*; the solid residue remaining in the vessel after distillation</term> and grind it into a very fine powder; place it in clean, clear water for 2 hours, allow it to settle, and pour off the clear liquid from the top. Then pour fresh, clean, clear water over it again, as before.

# PREFACE TO THE BOOK ON THE CONDITIONS OF THE PHYSICAL STONE.

->In which the diverse and various labors of the craftsmen are reviewed,<-

<margin>Various studies of the Alchemists.</margin>
WHOEVER devotes themselves to Chemistry <term>Chemistry: in this context, the term refers to Alchymia or Alchemy, the art of transmuting metals and preparing medicinal elixirs</term>, they all propose one goal to themselves: of converting mercury <note>original: *hydrargyrum*</note> or base and impure metals into gold or silver; but to achieve this, they enter into various paths, and nearly every individual assumes a material different from others. <margin>Those supposing the art lies in animals.</margin> For some seek it in animals, and therefore believe it must be drawn from basilisks, salamanders, vipers, toads, and other venomous creatures; because the Philosophers <note>the "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities</note> sometimes applied these names through a certain similarity to their Stone <note>original: *Lapidi suo*; the Philosopher's Stone</note>. To such an extent has the insane hunger for gold invaded the minds of men that, in their desire to possess it, they neglect life itself—for whose prolongation and preservation all things are prepared—so that the Poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid* (3.56)</note> not undeservedly exclaimed, though in another respect:

> To what do you not drive the hearts of mortals,
> O accursed hunger for gold? <note>original: *Quid non mortalia pectora cogis / Auri sacra fames?*</note>

<margin>In parts of animals, humors, and excrements.</margin>
Those others, not so dangerously insane, yet no more prudent, examine those things which have their origin from animals, and spend their labor in vain on eggs, blood, honey, milk, hair, and—foul to say—semen, menstrual blood, urine, and other excrements. For let it be far from the Wisdom of God, glorious and sublime, that the seed of gold and silver, and so precious a treasure, should be found in vile things of this kind

# PREFACE.

...and hidden away, cast off against the order of nature. I would not deny that some of nature's most beautiful secrets lie hidden in certain of the things mentioned above; however, I firmly assert that they are useless for the metamorphosis of metals <note>original: *metamorphosin*; the transformation of base metals into gold or silver</note> unless they are first reduced into quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> and sulfur <note>original: *sulphur*</note>, which are the principles of metals; which is unlikely to be possible. For although some people have claimed to me that they extracted small grains resembling mercury <note>original: *hydrargyro*</note> adhering to the sides of the vessels from the salt of urine, one must believe that it was a certain appearance of mercury rather than the true substance, since those grains did not merge together like liquid Mercury <note>original: *Mercurii*</note>, nor did they reflect its other properties.

<margin>Why the Philosophers adapted the names of various things to the Stone.</margin>
If, however, the Philosophers have sometimes called the physical stone <note>original: *lapidem physicum*; the Philosopher’s Stone</note> or its principles or elements by these or similar names, it should be judged that it was not done without reason. For they did not use these names only to conceal the art and exclude the unskilled and unworthy, but also to attract the more learned and prudent, and to teach and openly declare the properties of that same art through the characteristics of unusual words and things.

<margin>Those who suppose the art lies in Vegetables.</margin>
Others believe that vegetables are to be preferred, and they anxiously investigate the "Philosopher’s Moonwort" <note>original: *Lunariam*; a plant often associated with the moon and silver due to its seed pods</note>, along with mercury-plant <note>original: *mercuriali*</note>, celandine <note>original: *chelidonia*</note>, and the like; they run through mountains, valleys, forests, plains, slopes, dewy and arid places, and when they have tried everything, they complain that they have lost their labor and expense. Then they turn to the gums, "tears" <note>sap or resins</note>, and resins of various trees, yet no one rejoices in having found the fruit of their labors even in these. For although the aforementioned things are theoretically possible according to nature, yet more quickly, as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath; he was considered the "father of chemistry" by medieval alchemists</note> says, they will pass away from this life failing from their toil before they are able to lead their undertakings to the end.

...quicksilver and the more impure metals into silver or gold; or so that, by a not-at-all small or profitable shortcut, they might inseparably mix copper or iron, or even what they call <term>precipitated quicksilver</term> <note>original: *arg. viuum præcipitatum*; mercury that has been chemically reacted to form a solid powder</note>, into gold with the help of these substances. <margin>Those who suppose the Art is found in <term>marcasites</term> <note>original: *marchasitis*; iron pyrites or similar metallic ores often mistaken for gold or silver because of their luster</note>.</margin>

...adheres to impure metals and brings about an alteration of form, they believed that these properties of the <term>Elixir</term> <note>the transformative substance capable of changing base metals into gold</note> could be found in nothing better than in <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *spiritibus*; volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that vaporize when heated</note>. Therefore, they cleanse them from "earthiness"—which hinders entry into metals and produces a foul color—through <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: *sublimationem*; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind</note>. For in this way, they are rendered more brilliant, more transparent, and much more subtle, allowing them to more easily enter and penetrate the density of metallic bodies. However, a double disadvantage is discovered in them: namely, because they are not <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *fixi*; stable and resistant to the action of fire</note>, they withdraw from the bodies during the <term>examination</term> <note>the process of testing a metal's purity in a furnace</note>. They cannot adhere to bodies firmly or profitably because of their volatile nature and flight; indeed, sometimes they even lift the bodies up with them and fly away together <note>a reference to the way volatile mercury can cause other metals to vaporize during heating</note>. If, however, they are fixed, they are reduced back into an earthy substance, as is apparent in the fixation of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argenti viui*; mercury</note> which is performed through <term>precipitation</term> <note>the process of turning a liquid or vaporous substance into a solid through a chemical reaction</note>. Consequently, they do not have "entry" into the metal's core, nor do they liquefy, unless perhaps into glass.

<margin>Those who place the Art in base metals.</margin>
Observing these things, others believe that the material of the Elixir should more usefully be sought in "bodies" <note>solid metals</note>. Thus, they reduce impure metals into a <term>calx</term> <note>original: *calcem*; a dry, powdery oxide produced by heating a metal</note>, so that they may destroy the corrupting, <term>combustible sulfurity</term> <note>original: *sulphureitatem adustiuam*; the alchemical principle believed to cause metals to tarnish or be consumed by fire</note> by means of fire. Then, they reduce it back into a body, and they repeat this many times. Finally, they attempt to bring these bodies—thus purified according to their intention—to the highest degree of perfection by fire alone, or by joining imperfect metals with perfect ones to complete them simultaneously. But since it is not enough for the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>the term used for alchemists following the "true" chemical tradition</note> to simply create a piece of gold or silver, but rather they seek an Elixir which is ten, a hundred, or a thousand times more perfect than gold or silver itself, these labors seem rightly to be avoided and rejected as being of little use.

<margin>The opinion of those who place the Art in perfect metals.</margin>
For this reason, some more prudent seekers—seeing that imperfect metals are impure at their very root and cannot easily be cleansed except by an external, adventitious <term>medicine</term> <note>another name for the Elixir, used here in the sense of a healing agent for "sick" or "impure" metals</note> that removes their superfluities and consolidates and fixes their quicksilver—have decided that this same thing must be sought in more perfect bodies...

...judged that they should be deservedly retained. But since no <term>generation</term> <note>the creation of a new substance</note> occurs except after <term>corruption</term> <note>the breakdown or "death" of the original material</note>, and because these metals are very difficult to break down due to their strong composition and the difficulty of their resolution, they decided that <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note>, which is of the same nature as the metals, should be logically adopted. By this means, through frequent methods of <term>digestion</term> <note>prolonged heating at a gentle temperature</note> and <term>sublimation</term>, they refined the "perfect bodies" <note>gold and silver</note> and brought them, as they believe, into a "vegetable" nature. In this state, they not only grew into a "golden or silver tree" <note>a reference to "Diana's Tree," a dendritic growth of crystals in a flask</note> within the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note>, but they also converted and coagulated other quicksilver into their own nature through perpetual <term>augmentation</term> or <term>fermentation</term>. This is truly an astounding miracle of nature, provided that they later know how to properly <term>fix</term> these substances <note>make them stable under heat</note>, grant these fixed substances entry into others, and achieve an easy melting with unchangeable transformation.

<margin>Another opinion of the practitioners.</margin>
There are some, however, who are not satisfied with the aforementioned secret. They cannot persuade themselves that two extremes in the work of nature—namely quicksilver on one hand, and a most perfect metal on the other—can be properly joined or remain together and <term>tinge</term> <note>original: *tingere*; to dye or transform the nature of a metal</note> effectively. Therefore, they sought a certain middle state between the softness of quicksilver and the hardness of the metal to serve as the cause of their union. This middle substance they called the **sulfur of nature**. They hope that this sulfur—swollen with <term>Mercury</term> drawn from the more perfect bodies through frequent <term>imbibitions</term> <note>the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note>, and separated from earthy dregs through "philosophical sublimation" until pure—might easily embrace the "perfect body" as something similar to itself because of its purity. Thus stabilized and frequently soaked in its own Mercury, they hope it can be brought to the completion of the <term>Elixir</term>.

<margin>Locating the art in the spirit of gold.</margin>
Certain others, attempting a more secret investigation, observed the purer part of gold after the thicker and impurer part had been cast aside. This they call the "true seed of gold," the "spirit of gold," or the "sulfur of gold." They claim it possesses such power that, when cast upon <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *hydrargyro*</note> boiling over a fire, it transforms it into gold,

# PREFACE.

->PREFACE.<-

## BOOKS ON THE DISCOVERY OF TRUTH *or perfection.*

### CHAPTER I.

*On the six properties of things from which the Medicine is drawn.*

We have considered in our volumes, based on the secret powers of natural principles, and indeed through our own experience and the entirely certain investigation of our discovery, that those things from which our <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "medicina"; in this context, the Philosopher's Stone or the agent of transmutation</note> for transmuting bodies is drawn, must possess these properties of qualities within themselves.

First, that they contain within themselves a most subtle earth, which is incombustible <note>original: "incombustibilem"; meaning it cannot be destroyed or consumed by fire, a vital trait for a substance intended to stabilize metals</note> and fit for fixing <term>fixing</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</note>, being fixed in every way with its own radical moisture.

Second, that they possess an airy and fiery moisture uniformly joined to that earth, such that if one part is volatile, the other is as well; and that this moisture itself, surpassing all other moistures, can withstand the heat of the fire until the limit of its sufficient thickening is complete, according to the requirements of its perfection, remaining inseparably with the earth attached to it without evaporating.

Third, that the natural disposition of the moisture is such that, by virtue of its oiliness in all the differences of its properties, it soothes the earth attached to it in an oily manner—converting both into one another homogeneously—through a total union and a bond of inseparable conjunction equally, so that after the final stage of preparation, it provides a good fusion <note>meaning the substance will melt and flow easily like wax or oil when heated</note>.

Fourth, that this oiliness be of such purity of essence, and artificially cleansed of every combustible or burning thing, that it does not burn the things with which it is joined at the smallest level, but rather preserves them from combustion.

Fifth, that it possesses within itself a clear and splendid <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura"; the concentrated essence or color that "dyes" base metal into the appearance and nature of gold or silver</note>, white or red, pure and incombustible, stable and fixed; and that fire can in no way change it, nor can burning sulfurous substances or sharp, corroding ones corrupt and defile those bodies.

Sixth, that the whole compound, once <term>waxed</term> <note>original: "inceratum"; the stage where the alchemical medicine reaches a waxy consistency, allowing it to penetrate metals</note> with its final completion, be of such subtlety and thinness of matter that, after the final limit of its decoction <note>the process of heating or "cooking" the substance over a long period</note>, it remains in a state of the thinnest fusion like water when <term>projected</term> <note>the "projection" is the final step of casting the Stone onto molten base metal to transform it</note>, and pe- <note>The text continues on the next page: "penetrable"</note>

# ON THE SEVEN PROPERTIES OF THE MEDICINE.

## CHAPTER II.

Having considered these things, we have found through our investigation seven properties of things necessary and opportune in our <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapide"; here referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note>, and they are these: **Oiliness**, **thinness of matter**, **affinity**, **radical moisture**, **clarity of purity**, **a fixing earth**, and **tincture**.

The first property of these differences is **oiliness** itself, which provides universal melting and opening of the matter during <term>projection</term> <note>the final step of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them</note>. For the first thing that is necessary after the projection of the medicine is its sudden and suitable melting, which is accomplished and incorporated through mineral oiliness.

The second is the **thinness of the matter**, or its spiritual subtlety, flowing very thinly in the melt like water, penetrating into the depths of the changeable thing; because second, after the melting of the medicine, its immediate entry is necessary.

The third is **affinity** or proximity between the <term>Elixir</term> <note>the perfected substance of transmutation</note> and the thing to be transformed, providing adherence when it meets its like, and retention; because third, immediately after the entry of the medicine, a suitable adherence is both fitting and necessary.

The fourth is **radical moisture**, fiery, congealing, and consolidating the retained parts with the adherence of its like, with a union of all similar parts inseparably forever; because fourth, after the adherence, the consolidation of the parts is opportune, with its viscous and necessary radical moisture.

The fifth is the **clarity of purity** which cleanses, giving an eminent splendor, preserving from combustion, and not scorching. It does not remain after the consolidation of the purified parts, so that the actual fire may burn away all foreign <term>superfluities</term> <note>original: "superfluitates"; impurities or unnecessary elements that do not belong to the perfected metal</note> that are not consolidated; therefore, purification follows immediately and is necessary.

These qualities—such as oiliness and radical moisture—ensure the Stone can withstand fire while purifying the metal it touches.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER I.</header>

<margin>The viscous moisture of metals.</margin>
It evaporates from fire, however slow it may be, as the learned distillations of the <term>Spagyrists</term> <note>original: *Spagirorum*; followers of the alchemical tradition, particularly those practicing the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" substances</note> testify; for water, raised by the heat of fire, drips through the spout of the lid, while the dry earth remains at the bottom of the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: *cucurbitæ*; a gourd-shaped chemical flask used in distillation</note>. Metals, however, preserve their moisture in burning furnaces. We understand clearly, therefore, that this moisture is not that of simple water, but is oily and sticky. For we do not see other humors separated with difficulty from those things to which they are natural, unless they are gluey; in that case, their parts cling together so closely that they cannot easily be pulled apart. Thus, by a certain singular divine providence, the moisture innate in living creatures was made "fat" or oily, so that it might not be quickly dried out by natural heat, by which grace they live and thrive for a long time. Therefore, so that the nature of water might remain in metals with such durability, it could be nothing other than viscous and sticky. But because we see oily moisture in many things catch fire and burn, yet the moisture of metals is not dissipated or consumed by fire—or only with great difficulty—

<margin>Why the oily moisture of metals is not consumed.</margin>
it does not seem that the oily and viscous moisture alone is the matter of metals. Rather, as it has been acted upon by the thinnest earthy parts, it is so balanced and joined by a strong union that the smallest particle of one has become the same as the smallest of the other, and the greatest of one with the greatest of the other. Thus it happens that the earth does not permit the moisture to cling to anything but itself, nor to flow away entirely, but to consist as if in globules; meanwhile, the moisture so tempers the dry earth that it flows and runs on a flat surface, protecting it on all sides so it is not consumed by fire. Consequently, the moist part does not abandon the dry part, nor vice versa, but either recedes from the fire with its entire substance, or remains with the whole.

<margin>The primary matter of metals.</margin>
Therefore, the first matter of all metals is a viscous or oily moisture, incombustible and subtle, incorporated with a subtle earth, equally and strongly mixed through the <term>smallest particles</term> <note>original: *per minima*; a term in natural philosophy referring to the smallest possible units of a substance that still retain its character</note> in the caverns of the earth. But just as in many things there is a double "oiliness"—one of which is internal, retained in the roots of a thing so that it cannot be torn out by fire except by the consumption and destruction of the substance in which it inheres; the other as if external, having something drossy and combustible mixed in—so in all metals except gold, we also establish a double oiliness. One is indeed external, sulfurous and flammable, which reached them by accident and does not belong to the total union with the earthy parts of the thing; 

<margin>Double oiliness in metals.</margin>
the other is truly internal, very subtle, and not burnable, because...

<header>ON MINERAL OIL</header>

<margin>Why certain metals tolerate fire more or less.</margin>
...it belongs to the substantial composition of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argenti vivi*; mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" or "moisture" of all metals</note>, and therefore it cannot be rooted out by fire except with the loss of the entire substance. From this, it is clear why some metals endure longer in fire than others: for those that abound more in that internal unctuosity are consumed less, as is evident in silver, and especially in gold. Those, however, that abound in external unctuosity are consumed more, such as lead and iron; for the scorching sulfur enclosed in their substance diminishes them through inflammation and drives them out into smoke.

Hence the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 14th-century alchemical treatise</note> says:

> In no way were we able to find, nor could the Philosophers in any way find, any thing that persists in fire, except alone that perfect, oily moisture which is non-combustible.

<margin>From *The Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 5.</margin>
<term>Geber</term> <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early alchemy</note> also implies both types [of moisture] in these words: "Imperfect bodies have superfluous humors and a scorching sulfurousness that generates blackness in them and corrupts them; they also have an unclean, dreg-filled, and combustible earthiness that is too thick, hindering their entry and melting. And because these superfluities have come upon these bodies accidentally, and not fundamentally, and the stripping away of accidents is possible, we must—using artificial fire—remove these aforementioned accidental superfluities from the cleansed bodies, so that only the substance of quicksilver and the fundamental sulfur remains."

<margin>From *The Summary of Perfection*, chapter on the nature of <term>Venus</term> <note>original: *Veneris*; the alchemical name for copper</note>.</margin>
And elsewhere: "From the preceding discussions, it is concluded that there is a double sulfurousness in bodies: one indeed deep within the quicksilver at the beginning of its mixing, and the other coming upon it from the outside." In these places, although he does not mention "unctuosity" by name, yet since he names both sulfurs—namely, the combustible and the fundamental—he declares his intention sufficiently, since sulfur cannot exist without unctuosity.

<margin>In the *Commentary on the Emerald Tablet*. In the *Codicil*.</margin>
The Blessed <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> <note>the famous theologian to whom several alchemical works were apocryphally attributed</note> also mentions this pure and clean unctuosity: "Earth," he says, "that is, the turbulence of earthiness, is separated from the intrinsic, fundamental, pure, and non-combustible unctuosity." And the eminent <term>Raymond Lull</term> <note>a Majorcan philosopher and mystic; like Aquinas, many alchemical texts were later attributed to him</note>: "This is that intrinsic unctuosity, very subtle and non-combustible, containing a subtle earthy mixture brought to a fiery or airy state through strong digestion, which is retained in the roots of the thing in such a way that it can no longer be torn out by fire."

<margin>Internal unctuosity is called oil. *The Testament*, chapter 15.</margin>
Therefore, this internal, pure unctuosity, retained in the roots of metals and not subject to the violence of fire, is called "Oiliness" by Geber, or rather by his translator; other Philosophers call it "Oil" and "Ointment." Just as the venerable Lull says in his first...

...first in this opinion: The extremes of the <term>Stone</term> <note>original: *lapidis*; the Philosopher’s Stone, the goal of the alchemical work</note> in the first degree are quicksilver and sulfur; in the second degree, it is the complete <term>Elixir</term> <note>a substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note>. But the middle ground between these two extremes are the ointments and oils, some of which are more cooked, more pure, and more digested than others; and these we call the "perfection-making medicines" and the "ferments of the Elixir." <margin>Epistle to Asten concerning the Rule.</margin> And Avicenna says: This is the Elixir, which is dyed by its own tincture, and submerged in its own oil, and fixed by its own <term>calx</term> <note>original: *calce*; the chalky powder or ash left after a metal has been burned or "calcined"</note>. We find its water just as we find water in minerals; its oil is like sulfur or arsenic in minerals; and its calx is like the lime found in minerals.

<margin>Why Geber speaks of Oiliness in the first place.</margin> Therefore, <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> places oiliness in the first position among the properties of medicine. This is not because it is the first in the order of the physical work—since other preparations must necessarily come before it—but because it is the most noble, the queen of the rest. Upon this oiliness the entire secret of the Art depends, and within it, the Sages have hidden the whole of their science under the names of various things. Parmenides, marvelling at its nature, exclaims in the *Assembly*: "O that celestial nature, multiplying the natures of virtue! O strong nature, overcoming all things with its own victory!" The greatest property of this nature is a natural one: God has granted that fire shall not harm it. For this reason we magnify it, because nothing is more precious than it. In all of nature, nothing similar is found; when it is joined by liquefaction with its own cleansed bodies, it performs the most profound works. Of this nature Hermes also says: "O strong nature, conquering and overcoming natures, and making its own natures rejoice." Likewise, Aros says: "She is the all in the all, and that 'all' which is sought and which is thought of; for in her is the fleeing and the fixed, the dyeing and the dyed, the white and the red, the male and the female, joined together in an inseparable composition." <margin>The Testament, ch. 4</margin> Commending this same nature to us, <term>Lullius</term> <note>Ramon Lull, a 13-century philosopher and purported alchemist</note> says: "The secret spirit is the <term>second water</term>, from which every thing receives nourishment, every seed its growth, and every light its illumination. This water carries with it light, life, and spirit." Now, the reason he calls it "second water"—which he himself and other Philosophers in many places have called "oil"—is because it is extracted in the second place, namely after the spirit, as will become clear from what is said below.

<margin>The first definition of Oil.</margin> What then is this oiliness, or this oil precious to God, to which nothing similar is found in the nature of things? I could propose its true definition in a few words and say, as above, that this oiliness is nothing other than a <insert>radical</insert> moisture...

<margin>*The fourth definition of oil.*</margin>

<margin>*A comparison of the definitions.*</margin>
From these definitions, we gather that the **Oil of the Philosophers** is nothing other than water—not indeed from a spring or rain, which is foreign to the nature of metals, but a <term>Mercurial</term> <note>derived from the essence of mercury, the 'universal' metallic principle</note> water that is highly oily, smoothed by frequent distillations, and reduced in some way to the nature of air. Within this oil, the <term>radical</term> or formal heat of the metals lies hidden, cooking their purified matter into true silver and gold, provided that nature is assisted and the internal heat is moved and excited by an artificial fire applied from the outside. Alternatively, it is the highly sticky, hot, and subtle <term>radical moisture</term> of the calx of any metal (which is the true seed of gold and silver), dissolved and refined by Mercury so that it no longer contains any oiliness, or any evaporable or <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>watery or sluggish</note> moisture that can be felt; for it is otherwise impossible to empty the calx entirely of its powers, which consist in that oily moisture.

# ON MINERAL OILS

<margin>Lunar Oil. *The Testament*, chapter 52.</margin>The second is the Lunar oil, concerning which he speaks in the following chapter and book. The water of dissolved Moon <note>original: *Lunae*; alchemical code for silver</note> is the ferment for the white <term>Elixir</term> <note>the substance intended to transform base metals into silver</note>, having been made spiritual. Regarding both, <term>Raymond Lull</term> <note>a major 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note> says: "The ferment shall not be of this or that, but of the Sun <note>gold</note> and Moon <note>silver</note> only; for we seek nothing except that the stone be converted into its own like, because the entire temperament is from them, and the ferment does not exist until the said bodies are converted into their <term>prime matter</term> <note>the original, undifferentiated state of a substance</note>." Moreover, <term>Geber</term> <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though these works are often attributed to a "Pseudo-Geber"</note> shows that the ferment is not different from the oil in these 
<margin>*The Book of Furnaces*, chapter 27. Chapter 25.</margin>words: "Take the ferment of the Moon, which is its oil, and add to it double the amount of sublimated arsenic, etc." And in another place: "The ferment of the Moon for the 'white work' is made when the Moon has been dissolved in its own corrosive water; and if you decoct <note>boil down</note> this water to a third, and place it in the air by itself, or in a <term>bath</term> <note>a water bath</note>, or in dung <note>horse manure was used to provide steady, gentle heat</note> for several days, it will be the oil of the Moon, and the ferment itself, which you should keep for the white work."

<margin>The secret of the Art.</margin>In this passage, a beautiful and admirable secret of the Art is revealed, which all the Philosophers have most especially concealed. Namely, that the body of the Moon simply resolved is not—nor is it called—the Oil which the Philosophers so greatly praise, but only its third part, which is more gluey and pure, in which the 
<margin>The words of Geber are interpreted.</margin>essence and <term>tincture</term> <note>the color-changing principle</note> of the Lunar body chiefly consists. However, when he says the water of the Moon must be decocted to a third, do not understand it as being decocted in the way a meat broth is, until two-thirds have evaporated; rather, the Lunar water must be accustomed to a vapor-bath so that two parts of the <term>mercurial water</term> <note>original: *aquæ argenti*; literally "water of silver," referring here to the solvent</note> ascend together with the spirit and are united at once, while the remaining one part becomes that which obtains the name and properties of oil.

<margin>Preparation of Solar oil.</margin>Solar Oil: although Geber, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the same book, says it is decocted and prepared in the same way as the Moon, I do not deny that its <term>digestions</term> <note>the process of heating a substance slowly</note>, or decoctions, or preparations are the same. But there is no need for it to be reduced to a third part of its tincture, nor can it be done without damage and corruption of the spirit, since gold is much more digested and decocted by nature. It is probable that little of it ascends with the spirit after preparation unless it is urged by a 
<margin>*Practice of the Testament*, chapter 13.</margin>vehement fire, which does not result in a benefit for the craftsman. Indeed, Raymond Lull asserts that the body of the Sun <note>gold</note> is entirely "essential" compared to silver. 
<margin>All gold passes into oil.</margin>He calls it essential because gold is nothing other than the pure substance of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argenti vivi*</note>, fixed and incombustible, equally tempered and proportioned with its own internal <term>sulfur</term> <note>the active, combustible principle in alchemy</note>, such as the Philosophers desire for the easy fusion and tincture of their Elixir.
