# CHAPTER 50

<margin>Oil of sulfur. *The Testament*, chapter 10.</margin>Which he himself confirms in the *Art of Intellect* <note>original: *in arte intellect.*; likely referring to a work by Raymond Lull</note>, saying: "In the composition of gold there is a greater quantity of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and consequently less corruption, because its entire matter is purely essential and incorruptible." The third Oil is nothing but the tincture of sulfur, about which <term>Geber</term> <note>the Latin name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy</note> says: "Sulfur is light, alum, and tincture." And <term>Lull</term> <note>Raymond Lull, a major 13th-century philosopher whose name was often attached to alchemical texts</note> says: "This is the quicksilver which fitly and usefully receives the tincture of our sulfur, in which our stone is dissolved." Likewise in the *Codicil*: "The tincture is separated from its coarse, earthy dregs by slow distillations." However, when I say "oil of sulfur," I do not mean only the sulfur of gold and silver—which is clear from the testimony of all the Philosophers to contain the tincture within itself, and which we admit is even more effective in the composition of the <term>elixir</term>—but also the sulfur of the <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>base metals like lead, tin, or copper, as opposed to "perfect" gold and silver</note>. The <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the essential, life-giving liquid believed to exist within all matter</note> and primordial nature of these metals consists chiefly in the earth and adheres to it more stubbornly. Although this moisture is small and meager in itself, it can nevertheless be increased in a marvelous way by the addition of the oil of perfect metals. The experts of the art have taken care not to reduce these perfect metals into sulfur because of their strong composition (especially that of gold), as much as into Mercury, which may suffice for the sulfurs of ignoble metals to be restored to their own nature and substance.

<margin>The sulfur of gold is more perfect than the others.</margin>
<margin>The oil of imperfect bodies is not different from the oil of perfect ones except in quantity.</margin>
Nevertheless, if the sulfur of gold can be obtained, it is not to be despised, since by it the way is a little shorter, more absolute, and more perfect. The oil of sulfur could likewise be divided into as many species as there are metals; but because the primordial moisture of metals that is sought is not diverse, but the same in its principles and qualities—although it abounds a little more in one and less in another—we deliberately pass over this distinction. Yet it must be advised that the oil or radical humor of the imperfect metals, although it is very meager and of the smallest quantity, can nevertheless be extended and increased at will according to the quantity of prepared <term>calxes</term> <note>the powdery metallic residue or oxide remaining after a substance has been heated or "calcined"</note>. The method for which is as follows.

<margin>The preparation and increase of the oil of sulfur.</margin>

Then apply a very gentle fire, so that the Mercury does not rise <note>evaporate or sublime</note>, until you see an oil like a film of various colors rising above the Mercury; separate this and set it aside. Then, having closed the vessel, light the fire again for several days, until all the oil

This must be refined by itself through twelve or fifteen distillations, so that it may cast off any earthy dregs it might contain and flow as thinly as common oil when it is heated.

<margin>Why the oil is required in the Art.</margin>
Nor was there any other reason why the Philosophers sought with such great effort to extract this oil, or primordial unctuous moisture, from its watery or <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>referring to the "cold and moist" humor; here meaning watery impurities</note> parts and coarse earthy dregs, except so that it could be most perfectly refined and cleansed of the superfluous sulfurous impurities naturally inherent in it. Thus, it can be further "digested" by art than it ever was by nature. Afterward, it can be joined more effectively to the purified, whitened earth, which it then tints, solidifies, and causes to flow; for the unctuous moisture abundant in metals is the primary cause of their ability to be extended under the hammer <note>malleability</note> and their proper melting.

<margin>The powers of the oil are explained below.</margin>
But we shall explain the powers of this oil toward the end of this chapter and in other places; for now, since <term>Geber</term> <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> desires easy fusion <note>melting</note> as the primary property of the "Medicine," which is achieved through mineral oiliness or the "Oil of the Philosophers," we shall focus our discourse primarily on that.

# CHAPTER I.

...nay, rather, the powder is consumed and vanishes along with the imperfect metals. Thus, struck with amazement, they judged that something was missing from the medicine; and at last, they noticed that the **radical moisture** <note>original: *humorem radicalem*; the fundamental, life-giving fluid thought to hold the elements of a substance together</note> of metals is the principal cause of their melting. Therefore, they separated this same moisture from the metals with great diligence, and frequently "imbibed" <note>the process of soaking a dry substance in liquid until it is absorbed</note> their dry and non-flowing powders with it. Finally, they discovered that these powders were not only melted when cast upon imperfect bodies, but also entered into them, bringing about a transformation. Because they desired the Medicine to melt as easily as wax brought near a fire, they called this part of the work **ceration** <note>original: *cerationem*; from the Latin *cera*, meaning wax</note>, as I indeed believe.

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter on ceration. What ceration is.</margin>
This is defined by Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure whose writings formed the foundation of medieval alchemy</note> as the softening of a hard, non-fusible thing until it reaches liquefaction. Therefore, a body that is dry and hard—having been deprived of its moisture and dried out through **calcination** <note>the process of roasting a substance to reduce it to a fine powder</note>—must be softened and restored to a state of fluidity by the repeated imbibing of oil. This continues until it flows like wax over a fire and penetrates and enters other bodies. This is what Geber calls the "opening of the matter" in this passage, and it induces a silver or golden perfection through the "ferment" of gold or silver, brought about by a greater or lesser **decoction** <note>the process of heating or "cooking" a substance over a long period</note>. And this is what the Master requires, saying: the first and most necessary thing after the **projection** <note>the final step of casting the alchemical "philosopher's stone" or powder onto base metals to transform them</note> of the Medicine is its sudden and suitable fusion, which is accomplished by "mineral oiliness."

He specifies "mineral oiliness" so as to exclude all other oils—fats, resins, and greasy substances—which are drawn from plants, animals, or things originating from them, whether by distillation, pressing, or any other method, or which flow out spontaneously. For all those organic substances retreat from the fire or are quickly burned away. However, the **radical moisture** of metals, because of its likeness in nature and the strong union of its elements, is not consumed, but remains **fixed** <note>original: *fixum*; stable and resistant to change when exposed to heat</note> and incombustible.

<margin>The oil must be "fixed."</margin>
<margin>Part 1, chapter 12.</margin>
Whence the author of the *Rosarius Minor* <note>original: *Rosarium minus*, or "The Lesser Rose Garden," a famous alchemical treatise</note> says: No matter how much something is "waxed" with oils, it is worth nothing unless the oil has first been fixed.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But someone might say: Does not Geber himself, in this same book (on the *Discovery of Perfection*, final chapter), teach how to compose white "waxing" oils for the White **Elixir**, and red ones for the Red Work? And for the white work, does he not say that one should take the oil of egg whites, and grind it with half a portion of **saltpeter** <note>potassium nitrate</note> and equal parts of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>, or with alkali salt, and distill it anew, and repeat the process several times? Or that the aforementioned oil of eggs should be joined with oil of tartar and distilled together? Likewise for the Red Elixir...

<summary>This page defines "ceration," the process of making a dry alchemical powder fluid like wax so it can penetrate metals. It emphasizes using "mineral oil" rather than organic oils because only mineral moisture is "fixed" and can withstand the heat of the furnace.</summary>

# CONCERNING MINERAL OIL

Does he not command that the oil of egg yolks or human hair be taken, and an equal amount of sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum; a salt used as a flux and cleaning agent in alchemy</term> be added and distilled, and this repeated three times? And in the same place, does he not also command that oil of verdigris <term>viridis æris; the green pigment or "rust" that forms on copper</term> and gall be composed? Similarly, Raymond Lull and others prescribe—not just once—oil of tartar, blood, balsam, and many similar things.

<margin>Response.</margin>
We admit that these and many other things were indeed written by them, but only to deceive the incautious and imprudent, who involve themselves in such arduous works of nature without any prior reason or exploration of causes. For it was not fitting for the Art to be handed down in such a way that the imprudent might seize it as unworthily as the prudent; for then, according to Rhasis <note>Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, a famous Persian physician and alchemist</note>, the wise would be made equal to the foolish, and the learned to the unlearned, which would be unjust. 

<margin>Chapter on ceration. No oil other than mineral is required.</margin>
Indeed, Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> in his *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: *sum. perfect.*; the most influential medieval work on alchemy</note> rebukes this error in express words. "Some have thought," he says, "that **ceration** <note>the process of making a substance soft and flowable like wax</note> ought to be done with liquid oils and waters, but that is erroneous and entirely remote from the principles of this natural mastery, and is refuted by the manifest works of nature." 

And consequently, he adds the reason: because we do not see that nature placed a "quickly terminable" moisture in metallic bodies themselves, but rather a "long-lasting" one, for the necessity of their fusion and softening. For if nature had placed such a [fleeting] moisture in them, it would necessarily follow that the bodies would be totally deprived of moisture by a single ignition <note>heating a substance until it glows</note>. From this it would follow that after one ignition, any body could neither be hammered nor melted. 

<margin>Book of the Invention of Perfection.</margin>
And in the last chapter previously cited, he similarly affirms that these oils do not provide the **radical mineral moisture** <note>the fundamental, essential fluid believed to exist within minerals</note>. If they do not provide this—and it is certain they do not—then there will surely be no use for them. 

As for what he adds—that these oils "save" the tincture <note>the alchemical agent used to transform or "tinge" metals</note> from burning until it enters [the metal], and afterwards flee by the pressure of the fire—the reasoning is plainly frivolous. It is added only to deceive the improvident, and could easily be exploded by even a mediocre mind. For how shall they save the tincture from burning when they cannot preserve themselves from being consumed by fire? But they say, "they will save it for a time." That too is no less absurd: for two bodies, however related, cannot come together and be mixed unless the third thing that hinders their mixing is removed. 

Yet oils of this kind infect both the tincture and the body to be tinged with their "oiliness," and they prevent them from mixing until they have completely receded by the heat of the fire. Therefore, you will have accomplished nothing more with those things added than if they were not added, since it is necessary that they [be removed] first...

### CHAPTER ONE.

...be consumed before the dyeing agent and the object to be dyed can become one and the same. Plainly, the same judgment must be made regarding any other oils, salts, vitriols <term>atramentis; metallic sulfates used in making inks and acids</term>, antimony, and the rest of the marcasites <term>marchasitis; various sulfide minerals like iron pyrite</term> and mineral media melted by the force of fire. <margin>Oils of mineral media are useless to the work.</margin> Although these do not catch flame—since they possess the nature of "parting waters" used for separating gold and silver <note>referring to corrosive acids like nitric acid</note> rather than the nature of oils properly called flammable—nonetheless, even these do not persist in the fire, but recede through evaporation. Furthermore, the tinctures cannot be mixed through their innermost parts, but only moisten the surface; hence they do not facilitate the tincture's entry into other metallic bodies, but rather hinder it. However, the oil that renders the **medicine** <note>the alchemical Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> meltable must not only enter its smallest parts, but also be incorporated into them through union and—as Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous medieval authority on alchemy</note> says—"become its viscera" <note>original: *inuisceretur*; to be thoroughly enmeshed in the internal guts or structure</note>, so that one does not leave the other during the melting process.

<margin>Oils of metals are invalid.</margin>
But perhaps the oils of metals will provide what is sought—namely, to soften a hard, non-meltable body, make it flow, and enter with alteration? For like things are easily joined to like, and nothing is more akin to another than metal to metal. Accordingly, for the **ceration** <note>making a substance soft and flowable like wax</note> of the **White Elixir** <note>the substance meant to transform base metals into silver</note>, some prescribe the oil of quicksilver, tin, and silver—or, to use the planetary names, Mercury, Jupiter, and the Moon. For the **Red Elixir** <note>the substance for gold</note>, they prescribe the oil of lead, copper, iron, and gold—or, to use the terms of the Chemists: Saturn, Venus, Mars, and the Sun. But truly, even these oils will not remove the rigidity and hardness of a non-meltable tincture, nor make it flow more quickly, since they do not penetrate its inner parts any more than the previously mentioned substances. This is because they are plainly removed from the nature of metals; they have utterly cast off the **Mercurial essence** through which metallic bodies exist, and have assumed another essence entirely contrary to it. Furthermore, they too—no less than any of the things mentioned above—are consumed and vanish by the violence of the fire.

<margin>Question</margin>
But someone might perhaps rise up and say: You previously attributed an airy and volatile nature to the "philosophical oil," ordering it to be purified and raised up by distillation. But if it has been made volatile by Art—even if it was naturally fixed before, in whole or in part—surely even this will not be able to tolerate the fire, <margin>Solution.</margin> without fleeing from its face? I respond that this **radical moisture** <note>the fundamental, life-giving liquid essence of a substance</note>, which we call oil, is either the purer and more sticky part of "Lunar" or "Solar" quicksilver, which [is the life] of bodies...

...reflects the nature of its own components, which are fixed, according to that saying of Ramon Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan polymath whose name was frequently attached to alchemical treatises on the transmutation of metals.</note>:
> The quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; Mercury</note> of the perfect bodies is fixed, since it has been decocted <note>original: *decoctum*; cooked or ripened</note> in the belly of the earth by the action of a tempered heat. Indeed, the "silver-ness" <note>original: *Argenteitas*; the essential quality that makes silver what it is</note> fixed in the depths of the substance of gold and silver is a fixed substance; it is a substance most subtle and pure, of an extremely easy and thin liquefaction in the manner of wax, and it is fixed against the assault of fire.

Or, it may be called the "radical moisture" <term>radicale humidum; the essential, life-sustaining fluid thought to exist within all matter</term> of imperfect metals—subtle and impenetrable by fire—which can be extracted from their calxes <term>calcibus; the crumbly powder or ash left after a metal has been roasted or oxidized</term> only with great difficulty and by great artifice, because of its firm and very tenacious adherence to the remaining parts constituting the metals. Therefore, a large quantity of quicksilver is added to it, so that the volatile part might overcome the total amount of the fixed part many times over, thus drawing it out and retaining it as something similar and kindred to itself.

<margin>The Book of Figures.</margin>
It is of this that Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabian alchemist Muhammad ibn Umayl</note> seems to have spoken when he says:
> The Stone is living and immortal, which fire cannot burn, and because of this the true tincture <note>the concentrated essence used to transform base metal into gold</note> is extracted—that is, the fixed and incombustible part, whose grain was previously incombustible. It was "combustible" only because it was immersed in an imperfect body and dispersed through its entire substance, and thus could not defend itself against the fire; but afterward, when united, it can. For a virtue united is stronger than one dispersed.

Moreover, this "radical moisture" of imperfect bodies, which Senior calls a "grain," is like a certain seed of silver and gold which nature has inserted into them. This is so that, given the opportunity, they might be ripened into gold and silver by nature over a long time, or by art in a short time. Regarding this grain and seed, the most learned author of the *Lesser Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium minus*; a famous medieval alchemical text</note> writes in Part 2, Chapter 3:
> Bodies submerged in Mercury through a suitable putrefaction <note>the alchemical stage of breaking down a substance into a black, fermented mass</note> return into the quicksilver which they were before; and the metallic grains, projected into their own cleansed earth, are multiplied and grow wonderfully.

And in Chapter 4 of the same work:
> Let the seed or ferment be most purely cleansed, of which one part suffices for twelve parts of the cleansed stone.

<margin>A grain of gold or silver exists in all metals.</margin>
And that seed of gold and silver can be visibly shown and extracted from lead, in which gold or silver is found (as we have learned from experts), just as gold is found from silver, and similarly one or the other from various metals, if the craftsman is not lacking. In substance, this is nothing other than natural gold and silver, retaining all the conditions and characteristics of gold and silver. # CHAPTER ONE

...is extracted. It is not required in the art, however, that gold and silver be extracted in their specific physical form from imperfect bodies, but only that a calx <term>calx; the powdery remains of a metal after it has been roasted or oxidized</term> of those purified bodies be obtained. In this calx, this grain or seed lies hidden until it is dissolved and led forth by Mercury <note>original: *Mercurium*; refers here to the alchemical principle of fluidity and transformation</note>, which, being pure, absorbs the pure Sun <note>Gold</note> or pure Moon <note>Silver</note>. Ramon Llull indicates this clearly enough when explaining that saying of an unnamed author:

<margin>*The Testament*, chapter 62.</margin>
> *For beneath its shadow lies this fifth substance.* <note>original: "Nam sub eius ombra latet hac substantia quinta." The "fifth substance" or quintessence was considered the purest, most potent part of a material.</note>

The "fifth substance" of Mercury, he says, is nothing other than that which is pure and incombustible; it is nothing but gold and silver, which are bodies liquefied and melted—inside and out—by the power of the "menstrual fire" <note>original: *ignis menstrualis*; in alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent, and the "menstrual fire" refers to the corrosive, dissolving heat of a liquid catalyst</note> (understand this to be Mercury). Afterward, they are purified and separated from it, and from all their original stain and blemish. For gold, which is incombustible, remains melted and liquefied, and is "gold-making" <note>original: *aurificans*</note> within the said Mercury. Furthermore, the Mercury is entirely fermented in the seminal matter because of the "sweetness" of the gold, which nourishes the seed, moves it, and multiplies it.

<margin>Earth aiding the fixation of the oil.</margin>
Besides the fixed radical moisture, we also have in the work a "fixing earth" <note>original: *terram figentem*</note>, to which the moisture is returned as if to its own proper body. The body indeed embraces that moisture as its own nature, thickens it, and fixes it, so that finally it can endure all the violence of fire. In turn, the oil or radical humor grants fusion <note>the ability to melt and flow</note> and entry into melted metals to its own body (which is otherwise not fusible and is deprived of its native moisture), so that it may convert them into its own nature. Therefore, we say that the Oil of the Philosophers is indeed made volatile by art, yet possesses in itself the nature of the fixed, which is able to fix it—namely, with the slight assistance of the body or earth into which it is poured back. Otherwise, if it were mixed with a foreign body that is heterogeneous to itself, it could be fixed no less than any of the oils mentioned before, because it will not be mixed into another body "through its smallest parts" <term>per minima; a philosophical term meaning mixing at the level of the most basic, indivisible particles</term>, as Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit of Jerusalem.</note> testifies: *The soul quickly enters its own body, but if you strive to join it to a foreign body, you will labor in vain.* We shall show more extensively below that the "soul" is nothing other than the Philosophers' Oil.

<margin>Four ways of rendering the medicine fusible.</margin>
But perhaps someone will desire to know how this easy fusion <note>melting</note> of the tincture <note>the alchemical substance capable of changing the color and nature of metals</note> is achieved, so that it can be mixed without difficulty with the bodies to be transmuted, suddenly enter them, and induce alteration. Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in Arabic alchemy.</note>, in his *Summa of Perfection* <note>original: *Summa perfectionis*</note>, hands down three ways by which we can most conveniently attain this; Ramon Llull and Arnaldus de Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> add a fourth...

# ON MINERAL OIL

<margin>
[Rubric]
How the entry [of medicines] is achieved through the art.
</margin>

<margin>
First, through dissolution.
</margin>

...the new. We shall first examine the methods of Geber <note>original: *Gebri*; refers to the author of the *Summa Perfectionis*, a foundational medieval alchemical text</note>. One method is through the solution of that which "enters," and through the dissolution of that which "does not enter," and by the mixing of both solutions. This passage seems difficult to understand at first glance: for what is that which enters, and what is that which does not enter? But Geber will easily explain himself if we remember that the "medicine" <term>medicine; in alchemy, this refers to the "Philosopher's Stone" or "Elixir" used to "heal" or transmute base metals into gold</term> consists of fixed and non-fixed <note>volatile</note> parts. If one part exceeds the other in proportion, the medicine will flow either more easily or with more difficulty: for the flow and "entry" <note>original: *ingressio*; the ability of the alchemical agent to penetrate the internal structure of a metal</note> are granted to the medicine by the addition of a non-fixed substance. 

But because someone might suspect that the solution of a tincture is not the way to transform another body into gold or silver—since solution makes a tincture volatile—Geber meets this unspoken objection by adding later: *Yet let the solution not be of all parts, but of certain ones.* However, that the Philosopher <note>meaning Geber</note> is speaking of the solution of the medicine, even though he inserted many other things in his usual manner, is sufficiently declared by his own immediately preceding words: *Let those things be dissolved whose intention is to enter with alteration.* 

Now, for which parts does the Philosopher require solution? It is an easy guess. Namely, for those less-fixed parts which adhere to the fixed tincture that cannot penetrate. Is the Physical tincture, then, part fixed and part non-fixed? Not at all. For we seek a tincture that is entirely fixed and "fixing" <note>stable in fire and able to make other substances stable</note>; otherwise, it would not radically change base metals into gold and silver, which are fixed metals. Rather, it is a substance whose parts can be "re-rawed" <note>original: *reincrudari*; returned to a workable, liquid, or "crude" state</note> and dissolved again by the chemical art, and then condensed and fixed again by the fixed parts, until one inseparable compound is made from them. For if the medicine does not penetrate or does not flow, it is a sign that its parts are not sufficiently refined or perfectly mixed.

<margin>In the *Codicillus* <note>A famous work attributed to Ramon Llull</note>.</margin>
Whence Ramon Llull <note>original: *Raim. Lul.*</note> says: *He does not refine who does not join through the smallest parts, nor can he join through the smallest parts who dries before he moistens.* <note>original: *per minima*; refers to the alchemical theory that substances must be broken down to their smallest particles or atoms to truly bond</note> But, what should be done with the fixed parts? For Geber hints at these when he says that the solution must be made "of that which does not enter." This will be clear enough if we return to other places and chapters of the *Summa Perfectionis*, especially those regarding Calcination <term>calcination; the process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a fine powder</term> and Solution: for we shall see that the fixed parts we wish to resolve must necessarily be calcined, since calcination is the cause of easier solution.

<margin>
Calcined things are more easily dissolved.
</margin>

For thus he adds in the chapter cited above: *Through solution, fusion is completed in things that are not fusible, and this is the reason why we calcine certain things,*

...we determine, namely, so that they may be better dissolved; and for this reason they are dissolved, so that bodies may better receive an impression from them. <margin>
Method of operation.
</margin>
Therefore, the method for this is that an Elixir that cannot be melted should be dissolved as much as possible, while its fixed <note>stable and heat-resistant</note> parts should be calcined <term>calcination; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state, usually to a powder</term>; after calcination, let them be dissolved by the heat of a bath <note>original: *balnei*; likely a water bath or *balneum Mariae*</note> or dung <note>original: *fimi*; decomposing manure was used as a steady, low-heat source in alchemy</note>. If indeed all its parts are not yet dissolved, let the calcination and solution be repeated upon them until the greater part is resolved. Let the solutions be poured together and then coagulated again, and let them be fixed until the Elixir enters <note>original: *ingrediatur*; penetrates the metal</note> and tints <note>original: *tingat*; changes the color and nature of the metal</note>. Geber himself is the author of this interpretation.

<margin>
In the *Summa Perfectionis*. <note>The most famous work attributed to Geber, the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan</note>

After this, mix all the solutions together and coagulate them; then, by roasting gently, keep them in a moderate fire until a greater heat can be applied to it, according to its requirement. And this is indeed the first method of inducing sudden liquefaction in the Elixir; but because it is of much labor and long time, Geber adds a second, easier method, saying:

<margin>
The second method, Ceration.

*Either we grant entry to those things which, by their own thickness, are not permitted to enter, by the multiple repetition of the sublimation of non-flammable spirits over them—namely, of arsenic and of non-fixed quicksilver* <note>original: *argenti viui*; mercury</note>. And in the Chapter on Solution: *To the end that the medicine might penetrate and transmute, it is not achieved without the mastery* <note>original: *magisterio*; the specialized alchemical process</note>, *which is, namely, that after its solution and coagulation, one of the purified, non-fixed spirits should be administered to it, and be sublimated from it so many times until it remains with it, providing it with a faster fusion and preserving it from turning into glass during fusion.* Likewise, in the Chapter on Ceration <term>ceration; an alchemical process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</term>: *The method of ceration is that the sublimation of the aforementioned spirits be repeated many times over the thing to be waxed, until, remaining in it with their humidity, they provide a good fusion.* And he describes these spirits in the same place with these words: *In no things is this cerative humidity found better, more possibly, or more closely than in these, namely, sulfur, and...*

Question.
</margin>
If someone should say: We do indeed grant that in the aforementioned spirits <note>volatile alchemical substances that "fly" from the fire, like sulfur, arsenic, and mercury</note> there is a very strong union of the earth with humidity; for the humidity of sulfur does not depart from its earth until the whole is consumed, nor can its "oil" be removed through distillation <term>distillation; the process of purifying a liquid by heating and cooling</term> as it can from other things containing oil. The same occurs in arsenic. Even quicksilver, though sublimated <term>sublimation; the process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid, used here to purify mercury</term> many times, leaves no dregs at the bottom; for it either departs from the fire with its entire substance, or remains with its entire substance, as all the Chemists assert and as experience—the mistress of things—teaches. But how can these things, which flee so easily from the fire, provide the easy fusion <note>the ability to melt into a liquid state</note> required for a tincture, when Geber (in the chapter on *Ceration* <note>the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>) and Lullius, and other Philosophers, require for this a humidity that, above all other humidities, remains to withstand the heat of the fire?

<margin>
Solution.
</margin>
We respond: Geber is not speaking of common sulfur or common arsenic as they exist in their natural state, since he says those things corrupt and blacken everything; for this reason, in his chapter on *Sulfur*, he warns that we should not use them without "mastery" <note>original: *magisterium*; the skilled alchemical process of purification or transformation</note>, without which they provide nothing of what we seek. Rather, he speaks of their "middle substance" <note>the refined essence or pure core of the material</note> which, as he says, is not disturbed by the entry of earthiness, which is perfected through good fusion, and whose impression is not easily removed due to its subtlety. 

<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 58.
</margin>
<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 17.
</margin>
Furthermore, his words are not to be understood as referring to common quicksilver, since he explicitly says that in the fusion of bodies, spirits abandon them and do not adhere; rather, they flee the harshness of the fire. And in the preceding chapter: *All spirits have the tendency to flee: quicksilver and sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum; ammonium chloride, often used as a flux in alchemy</term> do so more, sulfur less, and its companion, namely arsenic, even less so.* What then shall that quicksilver be? Clearly, that which has been prepared by art, as we have taught above. Hence the *Lesser Rosary*, chapter 12, part 1: *Calcined bodies are "waxed" <note>softened or made fusible</note> with resolved bodies (namely, perfected ones), and this is done by soaking and sublimating.* Or, it is the "middle substance of Mercury," whose property—as Geber says—is not to be burned, but to defend against burning, and even to "fix" <note>to make a volatile substance resistant to fire</note> and render things fixed. 

<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection*, *Testament of Practice*, chapter 25.
</margin>
Regarding this, Lullius says: *Nature, at its root, does not cease to wax its body with the humidity of fusibles—namely, sulfur and quicksilver—because it finds no other body more suitable to nature than in sulfur...*

### ON MINERAL OIL

...[natu]re, but you may well believe that the whole proceeds from quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term>, and this humidity is neither limiting nor consuming, but rather a radical perfecting power, very subtle, in which the natural heat of all liquefiable things rests. <margin>Mode of operation.</margin> Raymond Lully pursues this second mode of inceration <term>inceration; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency to allow it to penetrate metals</term> more extensively in his *Codicillus*, to this effect: Let the "stone" be taken—namely, the body to be incerated—and by grinding it, soak <note>original: *imbibe*</note> it in its vessel through "imbibition by the smallest parts" <note>the practice of adding liquid in very small, gradual increments so the solid absorbs it completely</note> in turns; afterwards, cook it with a gentle fire until that part has been congealed into the substance of the stone. Then, gradually strengthen the fire of the coals until whatever has been released is sublimated <term>sublimation; heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then collecting the purified solid as it cools</term> from it, both from the "dry water" of sulfur and from the "moist water" of quicksilver. Then, return whatever has been sublimated back onto its dregs <note>original: *fæces*; the solid residue or "earth" left at the bottom of the vessel</note>, grinding and soaking it with the aforementioned spirit which abounds more exuberantly in humidity; and do this with repeated soaking, "dewy" cooking, congealing, and sublimation with its successive and diligently continued fires, until through the constant repetition of sublimating non-flammable spirits over them, and continuous motion, the whole is "fixed" <term>fixation; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it no longer evaporates</term> at the bottom.

<margin>The mode of ceration.</margin> A third way of achieving fusion <note>the ability to melt into a liquid state</note> is handed down by Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure regarded as the father of chemistry/alchemy</note> in these words: "To allow entry to things that cannot be mixed, a good precaution is that the body—which is intended to be changed and altered by these things—be dissolved, and those things whose purpose it is to enter with alteration should also be dissolved." Therefore, the Philosopher <note>referring to Geber</note> wants both the "Physical tincture" <note>the Elixir or transforming agent</note> (which is not normally mixable) to be dissolved, and similarly the body which we desire to alter, and both solutions to be mingled and coagulated together. We have shown that this can be done because the completed Elixir, although not naturally meltable <note>fusile</note>, possesses the nature of the "fixed" within itself. The reason for this is evident: For every thing enjoys its own nature and embraces it more than a foreign one; just as we see in water, for if you pour it into other water, both will easily mix. If, therefore, both the "medicine" <note>another term for the Elixir</note> is dissolved and likewise the metallic body to be transmuted, both will be converted into "Mercury" <note>here meaning a liquid, metallic state</note>; since there is Mercury on both sides, one will easily mix with the other.

<margin>Question.</margin> But someone might ask whether the non-meltable Elixir and the metallic body will be changed through this kind of solution into Elixir, or into gold or silver? <margin>Solution.</margin> We answer: into Elixir; for in this passage Geber is not dealing with "projection" <term>projection; the final stage of the Great Work where the Elixir is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold</term>, but rather how the entry of the medicine may be achieved through the art. But once the medicine is thus dissolved and coagulated again with the body (which was likewise dissolved), it afterwards en-

->### ON MINERAL OIL<-

[...to re]turn and be able to alter the species of the metal into which its spirit has been mixed, about which more will be said below. <margin>The fourth mode of Inceration.</margin> The fourth mode of inceration <term>inceration; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency so it can penetrate metals</term> described by Lully and Arnaldus <note>Raymond Lully and Arnaldus de Villa Nova, two of the most influential figures in medieval alchemy</note> is this: That the white or red medicine <note>the alchemical elixir in its silver-making or gold-making state</note> be placed in a small dish over a light fire, and a drop of oil be dripped upon it one after another, until it is melted as required.

<margin>Heading on the preparation of the medicine used so that it may acquire the proper differing properties.</margin>
But for the fusion <note>melting and blending</note> of metals, knowledge of the aforementioned things is not enough; one still desires a perfect understanding of the administration of fire during the coagulation of the medicine, or its "return into earth" after its dissolution. Whence Geber in his *Summa Perfectionis* <note>The Sum of Perfection, a cornerstone of Latin alchemy attributed to Geber</note> does not grant a perfect fusion unless caution is used in its fixation <term>fixation; the process of making a volatile substance stable in heat</term>. Specifically, the craftsman must be practiced in the administration of fire during its fixation, so that the humidity can be removed from it just enough to allow for a complete and perfect melting.

<margin>Caution in achieving fusion.</margin>
And it is this: namely, if you seek to soften bodies that are hard to melt by using this process, a slow fire should be used at the beginning of the inceration. For a slow fire preserves humidity and brings fusion to perfection. If, however, you wish to harden soft substances, a vehement fire should be prepared, for such a fire consumes humidity. See how diligent the Philosopher is, and how he omits nothing that is necessary for the craftsman to know for the perfect preparation of the medicine—even if, according to the custom of authors teaching this art, he does not teach everything in order and in a continuous series of speech, but scattered and through different chapters, so that the art is not equally open to everyone.

<margin>Why the fastest fusion is required in the Elixir.</margin>
The reason why the Philosophers require such rapid fusion in the Elixir is because they seek to convert not only imperfect metals, but also quicksilver <term>hydrargyrum; mercury</term> into gold and silver. If the Elixir does not liquefy with the greatest ease, the quicksilver—being unable to tolerate the violence of the fire—will evaporate before the Elixir can enter and tint it.

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, Chapter on the medicine coagulating Mercury.</margin>
For so says Geber: Since quicksilver is easily fugitive <note>volatile; tending to evaporate quickly</note> without catching fire, it requires some medicine which suddenly, before its flight, adheres to it in its depths, joins it in its smallest parts, thickens it, and preserves it through its own fixation in the fire. This continues until it gains a tolerance for a greater fire that consumes its humidity, and by this artifice, converts it in a moment into true Sun-making <term>Solificum; the power to transform a substance into gold</term> and Moon-making <term>Lunificium; the power to transform a substance into silver</term> material, according to what the medicine was prepared for.

The Philosophers—and especially Lully and Arnaldus—describe the sign of perfect inceration for us: if upon a heated plate

# CHAPTER ONE

...it shall resolve itself <note>original: "se resoluerit"</note> very quickly like wax without smoke. Another test: When you wish to test the medicine, place the weight of one grain of wheat upon a glowing plate of copper; if, entering the plate with little heat, it spreads itself throughout, both inside and out, it is perfectly tinting <note>capable of transforming the metal's color and nature</note> and persistent in the fire.

<margin>Various names and powers of the oil.</margin>
Hitherto we have spoken of how the ease of fusion <term>fusion; the ability of the alchemical medicine to melt and penetrate a metal</term> of the medicine is attained; now let us explain several different names of the "oil," and certain other of its powers. To this end, let us first hear Raymond Lully <note>a major 13th-century philosopher and purported alchemist</note> speaking in the *Codicillus* in this manner:

<margin>On the beginning of the second practice.</margin>
> However great the quantity of oil shall be, so great also will be the quantity of the tincture <note>the concentrated essence that changes the metal</note>, because this oil is the tincture, the gold, and the soul, and the ointment of the philosophers, by which the whole mastery <term>mastery; the complete alchemical process or Great Work</term> is completed.

Likewise in:
<margin>Testament, chapter 46.</margin>
We call the better part of the whole composite, digested and separated, the ointment, the soul, our gold, and the oil. And in the following chapter: Our well-tempered and moist secrets into which bodies are turned by the art of the mastery, are ointments, oils, ferments, the soul, and suns, which do not cease to shine upon our earth and radiate.

<margin>The Rosary, part 2, chapter 10.</margin>
In the same vein, Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says:
> Keep the air thus washed aside, since it is the oil, tincture, and gold, soul and ointment of the philosophers, which colors and tints, and fixes and makes [the metal] to flow.

The Oil of the Philosophers, therefore, as is evident from the above, is called the tincture, the soul, the ferment, the ointment, gold and silver, and is distinguished by many other names.

<margin>Why the oil is called a tincture.</margin>
It is named a "tincture" because it colors and tints the earth <note>the solid matter remaining in the flask</note> when it has been cleansed and purified of all filth, whether earthy or phlegmatic <note>watery or sluggish impurities</note>. It is compared to the dye used by cloth-dyers: the dye is carried in water onto the cloth; then the water recedes through drying, and the tincture remains fixed in the cloth because of its oiliness. In a similar way here, the spirit in which the tincture of the dissolved perfect bodies <note>usually gold or silver</note> is carried is brought back upon its white and purged "earth," and is dried there; the tincture remains in that earth and is called "oil."

<margin>Why the oil is called the soul.</margin>
The same substance is called the "soul" <note>original: "anima"</note>, because just as all animals and plants live, grow, are nourished, and multiplied by their soul, so the Physical Stone <term>Physical Stone; another name for the Philosophers' Stone</term>, when this oil is poured upon it after its "birth," is illuminated by a metallic splendor. It is decorated, nourished, grows, is increased, and produces its own likeness, with the craftsman ministering to it and aiding nature. This is not because the soul of the stone is a vegetable soul, like a plant, or a vital soul, having the power of life in itself—which nature...

<margin>Testament, chapters 83 and 49.</margin>

Raymond Lully affirms the same thing: "The soul is in the seed of nature like a master in his craft." Also: "The whole effect proceeds from the soul, because no form except the soul is a mover of nature according to its own proper act; and without motion, a thing cannot be generated." Yet you should not understand this to mean that it is a physical, organic body possessing vital or animal power <note>meaning it is not "alive" like an animal, but carries a formative "spirit"</note>, but rather it acts just as a worker does in his craft.

<margin>
Testament, chapter 83.
Oil is the form of the metal.
Oil is called the ferment.
Testament, chapter 38.

By the same Lully, this oil is called the "form of the metal" elsewhere. It is furthermore called the "ferment" <note>original: "fermentum"</note>, because just as leaven <note>ferment</note> converts the whole dough into the nature of the leaven, so also this oil turns the whole "stone" <term>stone; the Alchemical Philosophers' Stone or medicine</term> into its own nature, and impresses upon it its own power and action of tinting <note>changing color</note> and flowing. To this purpose, Raymond Lully writes most fittingly: "The property of the ferment is to turn the stone into the nature of the ferment—namely, into a liquefiable and flowing nature—by reason of its subtle oiliness, and its incombustible and fermentable oil, which gently enters the parts of the said matter, which is submerged in the permanent liquid."

<margin>
Oil is called the Gold and Silver of the Philosophers.
Testament, chapter 47.
</margin>
It is similarly named the "gold of the philosophers," not that of the common people, because it is clearly no longer a solid body as it was before, but has been made thinned and spiritual; the same is to be understood regarding "silver." For so Lully says: "You must labor in the thinning of nature to form the body of philosophy, until it is clear water, which is called the 'water of wisdom'; for it is entirely gold and silver brought into the action of elemental spirits, in which the spirit of the fifth essence <term>fifth essence; the quintessence, or the purest, most refined state of matter</term> rests and rejoices, which does everything."

<margin>* Oil is called an ointment.</margin>
* It is also called an "ointment," because just as all fats and ointments soften and make slippery those things to which they are applied, similarly this oil softens the hard parts of the stone, smoothes the rough ones, and makes them flow. Geber <note>an 8th-century authority often called the "Father of Chemistry"</note> mentions this faculty most especially and in the first place, in his chapter on the properties of medicine; however, as for the fact that it tints, colors, and fixes <term>fixation; the process of making a substance stable in fire so it does not evaporate</term>, he remains silent according to his custom, though he indicates the same thing in other places, but under a changed name. For what he calls "oiliness" here—a name very well suited to the action of inducing an easy flow—

# CHAPTER I

<margin>
Why Geber called the oil sulfur, light, and alum for the tincture.
</margin>
...with its companion it becomes a tincture, and gives full weight to each of the metals, and it purifies and brightens it from filth <note>the "filth" refers to the metallic impurities or "leprosy" that alchemists believed made metals "base" like lead or tin</note>. He calls it **light**, in respect to the soul, which illuminates the dead and dark body; for a body is said to be dark as long as the soul is absent from it. Thus says Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note>: 
> Every body, as long as it lacks a soul, is found to be obscure and dark.

He calls it **Alum**, in respect to its fixation <term>fixation; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term>, or as the medium joining the spirit with the body. This is an analogy taken from dyers, who often add alum to their dyes so that the colors in cloth and other things are fixed and adhere more stubbornly. He calls it a **tincture** <gloss>a transformative dye or medicine</gloss> because of the fixed red or white color it induces. And this indeed can serve as a most beautiful example for us: how the Philosophers, under various names of things, 
<margin>
How the Philosophers teach and hide the art under various names of things.
</margin>
openly describe the power and nature of the matter to the learned, while with that same variety of names, they keep the unlearned and imprudent away from the art. In the same chapter, he says that "Sulfur becomes a tincture with its companion." In many places, Geber calls the "Companion of Sulfur" **arsenic**; this is also how it can be understood in this passage—namely, that arsenic is the tincture of whiteness, while sulfur is the tincture of redness. The following chapter on arsenic openly testifies to this, saying: "Arsenic is of a subtle matter and similar to sulfur; therefore, it ought not to be defined otherwise than sulfur. However, it differs from sulfur in this: it is easily a tincture of whiteness but very difficultly of redness, while sulfur is easily a tincture of redness but very difficultly of whiteness." Nevertheless, in this place, the companion of sulfur can also most conveniently be called the **Mercury** <term>Philosophical Mercury; a purified, spiritualized form of the metal</term> that is homogenous to it, under whose appearance—or absorbed in whose womb—it lies hidden, until by the action of decoction <note>prolonged heating</note> it brings forth its firm color, whether white or red. 
<margin>
In the *Codicillus*, the Oil takes on the figure and color of the spirit or Mercury.
</margin>
Suggesting this same point, Raymond Lully says in the *Codicillus*: 
> This oil, waxing <gloss>softening like wax</gloss> and joining natures, and bringing individuals into the medicine, retains the color of the spirit until its own re-thickening <note>original: "reinspissationem"; the process of becoming thick or solid again</note>, and then it puts on yellowness <note>original: "citrinitatem"; a golden-yellow color signifying a high degree of perfection</note> and metallic form. 

And the *Lilium* <note>likely referring to the *Lilium inter spinas*, or "The Lily Among Thorns," a popular alchemical text</note> says: "The spirit is the bearer of the virtues of the soul—that is, of sulfur—through the body of magnesia <term>magnesia; here used as a term for the "crude" matter or the "mother" of the stone</term> or earth." That this could be Geber’s intention is clear from this: because a little earlier he had said, "He who seeks to elicit the work from it should not elicit it by preparing it by itself, since it is perfected with a mixture, and without that, the mastery <gloss>the alchemical process or Great Work</gloss> is prolonged even unto despair." By its "companion," therefore, understand the spirit or Mercury in which it is hidden, or under whose appearance the sulfur (the dissolved perfect body) lies concealed.

### ON MINERAL OILINESS
<meta>catchword: ...is</meta>

<margin>
The perfected stone is called sulfur. 
*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 28.
</margin>
...by whose airy and fiery power the stone is digested and fixed <term>fixed; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term>, and takes on the form of silver or gold. However, when Geber adds that sulfur becomes a tincture <gloss>a transformative dye</gloss>, and gives full weight to each of the metals, and purifies and brightens them from filth <note>impurities believed to cause the "leprosy" or corrosion of base metals</note>, he was looking toward the end of the completed decoction <note>the long heating process in a sealed vessel</note>. For at that point, the perfected stone is called **sulfur** by Lullius <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and writer to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> and by Geber, who writes in this manner: "He who knows how to mix sulfur and make it friendly with bodies has found one of the greatest secrets of nature." It is as if he were to say: he who has brought the stone to such a point that, through its easy melting <note>original: "fluxione"</note>, it can be mixed and joined with imperfect metals, and firmly adhere to them, penetrate, and transmute them, has found the path of perfection.

<margin>Letter to Thomas of Bologna.</margin>
From this same condition of oiliness, to which the whole stone is brought through ceration <term>ceration; softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>, it is also very often called a **gum**. Hence Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist</note> says: "The perfected stone is gum and sulfur."

<margin>On some other properties.</margin>
From what has been said above, it is clear that this oil not only brings about the easy melting of the Medicine <note>another name for the Philosopher's Stone</note>, but also dyes it. This is also attested by Aschane or Astano in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," an influential early alchemical text</note>: "The imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of a ferment <note>a substance that, like yeast, spreads its qualities through a mass</note>, which ferment is the soul of the imperfect body." It also fixes the body, by reason of its dry and fiery quality, even though this oil appears outwardly to be moist in the form of a spirit. Regarding this, more will be said, God willing, in Chapter 4. The author of the *Scala* <note>The *Scala Philosophorum*, or "Ladder of the Philosophers"</note> encompasses some other powers of the oil in these few words: "Oil is a living tincture, consolidating, multiplying, coloring, brightening, purging, perpetuating, and confirming." And Richard the Philosopher, King of the Persians <note>likely a pseudonymous reference to an ancient authority</note>, says: "The stone becomes a running leaf, penetrating, coloring, perpetuating, a living oil, persevering, purifying, a living and life-giving color, making the dead rise again." Something has been said about tincture and color, and more will be said more extensively, God willing, in the final chapter.

<margin>Oil consolidates.</margin>
It **consolidates**, by reason of its meltability <note>original: "liquabilitatis"</note>, through which it dissolves those parts of the stone that do not flow—those which have been broken apart by calcination <term>calcination; heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> and deprived of moisture—and makes them run, so that the moist part does not leave its dry part, nor vice versa. And this is perfected through ceration, the method of which we have described.

<margin>It penetrates.</margin>
It **penetrates**, by reason of its subtlety and its similarity and affinity, by which it easily enters its own body but rejects a foreign one.

<margin>It multiplies.</margin>
It **multiplies**, because it is the pure food and nourishment of sulfur, which is also converted into the true substance of sulfur.

<margin>Practice of the Testament, chapter 27.</margin>
Whence Lullius says: "From the substance of the blood, which is an exuberated moisture <note>original: "humidum exuberatum"</note>, the spirit is generated."

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>Why oil is called blood.</margin>
<margin>Chapter on Ceration <note>Original: "Cap. de Cerat." Ceration is the alchemical process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax (cera).</note></margin>
...is expressed in the substance of the medicinal body, and is nutritionally strengthened by it. He calls this oil "blood," both by reason of its color—which is potentially blood-red—and by reason of similarity. Just as blood in animals pervades all parts of the body, nourishing and warming it, and creating life-giving spirits, so too does the oil—or the "radical humor" <term>radical humor; the innate, vital moisture believed to be the source of life and flexibility in all things</term>—act within the Stone. Hence the author of the *Lesser Rosary* says: "The water of the body, when the body is reduced into Mercury, is called blood." And to explain himself, he adds: "And this oil is not obtained except from fixed <note>non-volatile; stable under heat</note> metals." Because of this nourishing and nutrient-providing power, Hermes says in the *Smaragdine Tablet* <note>The Emerald Tablet, a foundational text of Hermetic philosophy</note>: "Its nurse is the earth." This should not be understood as common earth, or sulfur (which is nourished rather than nourishes), but of the radical moisture into which a subtle and pure earthiness is mixed. Without this, as St. Thomas Aquinas <note>Many alchemical works were pseudonymously attributed to the famous theologian Thomas Aquinas</note> says, the spirit of the Stone could in no way be held back, nor would it possess the completion of its power.

<margin>In the commentary on the same tablet.</margin>
<margin>Oil clarifies and purges.</margin>
Oil clarifies the character of the soul illuminating the body, as we have said. It purges and cleanses by removing the impediment which prevents the Stone from generating its own kind, and by providing the force and power of generation. Alternatively, it is because at the end of the completed decoction <note>the process of long, steady heating</note>, the Stone—of which the radical moisture is the largest and most vital part, and the total cause of its perfection—purges and cleanses imperfect things from their filth <note>impurities or "leprosy" in base metals</note>, transforming them into gold and silver.

<margin>Oil gives life.</margin>
It vivifies <note>gives life</note>, because the form of the Stone depends on the soul and its entire effect; otherwise, it would have no name in the nature of things, nor could it subsist by itself, because the united parts would be separated.

<margin>It perpetuates.</margin>
It perpetuates and confirms, because since it is itself incorruptible and does not fear the fire, it pours that same property into the body. And because it joins the spirit with the body—for it is a certain medium between them, retaining the nature of both within itself—without its help, they would easily slip away from each other.

<margin>Oil joins contrary natures.</margin>
Whence the Philosopher in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," an ancient alchemical dialogue</note> says: "One joins, two compose the medicine." And Astanus says in the same place: "The spirit is joined and bound with the body by means of the soul, and with it is simultaneously converted into the color of the ferment; and it becomes one with them." And Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> says: "The soul has the power to give life to and bind two contraries—namely, body and spirit—by refining and mixing the body with the spirit, and by congealing and retaining the body in the spirit, and the spirit in the body, with a permanent fixation."

<margin>In the *Apertorium* <note>A work attributed to Lull</note>.</margin>

### ON MINERAL OIL

...with the spirit, and the spirit with the body. *The Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text</note> says: "The soul is the bond of the spirit, just as the body is the bond of the soul; the soul joins, couples, and tints." And to conclude with Senior <note>original: *Senior*; referring to Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were foundational to Latin alchemy</note>, the preparation of things from the beginning to the end is an honored, fixed water <note>a "fixed water" is a liquid substance that does not evaporate when exposed to heat</note>, for it manifests the tincture <term>tincture; the transformative essence capable of changing the color and quality of metals</term> during projection <term>projection; the final step of the Great Work where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transmute it</term>, and it is the mediator between opposites, being itself the beginning, middle, and end.

<margin>
Epilogue of the first chapter.
</margin>

Having explained the uses and benefits of this Oil which it brings to medicine, who—along with the Philosophers—would not admire its nature, cherish it, and deem it more precious than gold and silver? While gold and silver are dead bodies, and nothing of benefit is found in them except the common use they have in human life, this nature is entirely spiritual gold and silver. It tints the physical body, fixes it <note>makes it stable under heat</note>, and makes it flow <note>original: *fluere*; to melt easily like wax</note>, joining and uniting the tinctures; furthermore, it increases its own kind and extends and multiplies infinitely. If gold is commended by the Philosophers for its brightness, solidity, and eternity, this nature—as if born from gold and being, as it were, the daughter of gold—possesses that same brightness within itself, although it is not visible to the eyes while it lies hidden under the form of Mercury <term>Mercury; the "Philosophical Mercury" or the volatile, liquid principle of matter</term>, as we have said, until it manifests itself to the eyes of all through decoction <note>long, slow heating</note> and the power of fire. It is endowed with that same solidity, since it consolidates a calcined <term>calcined; a substance reduced to powder through high heat</term> and broken-down body, bringing it to the weight of gold. It has achieved a durability and permanence in fire no less than that of gold itself, since it was born in fire, and for that reason is in a way called the daughter of fire—rejoicing in fire and remaining perpetual within it, if it is returned to a cleansed and whitened earth; for unless it were fixed and had the power of fixing within itself, it would not fix. Therefore, since it possesses the same properties as gold—and many more—and excels common gold as much as the spirit excels the body, this oil must be most diligently investigated above all by any student of true chemistry <note>original: *chemia*; at this time, chemistry and alchemy were often used interchangeably to describe the "sacred science" of matter</note>. It should be compared with the oils of any other things taken from animals, vegetables, or intermediate minerals to see if anything similar can be found in the nature of things. But if it is not found—as it is certain not to be found—let the seeker cling to this one alone, having rejected the rest.

## CHAPTER II.

*In which a more secret discussion is established concerning Philosophical Solution, and the ways in which the body and spirit are thinned are enumerated: and the advantages of the thinness of matter are recounted.*

<margin>Why the thinness of matter is required.</margin>
Having examined the first property of the Elixir, which depends on the Oil or the radical moisture of metals, I transition to the second, which consists in the thinning of the matter or its spiritual subtlety. The Philosopher <note>original: *Philosophus*; typically referring to Aristotle, though here it implies the collective wisdom of alchemical authorities</note> requires this so that the medicine may flow not only easily, but moreover most finely, like water penetrating into the depth of a substance that is to be altered. But before we pass on the methods of thinning, it must first be known which things are to be thinned; for once the subject to be thinned is known, the methods of operation will more easily become clear. <margin>Which elements supply the matter and which the form for the Stone.</margin> All the elements of the stone <term>the Stone; the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> must be thinned, some of which will provide us with the matter, others with the form. The heavier and denser elements—namely, earth and water—will supply the matter; the light and rare ones—namely, air and fire (or fire hosted in the air)—will provide the form. For fire cannot subsist by itself, but it is necessary that it take up and enter another body in which it may move and exercise its action. Water and earth are the passive elements <note>original: *patientia*; in the Aristotelian sense, these are the elements that receive action</note>, while air and fire are the active elements. According to the Philosopher, the acts of active things are within a well-disposed passive subject: therefore, the better the matter has been prepared and the more it has been thinned, the more fit it will be for receiving the form. And the more noble the matter, the more noble will be the form. And conversely, the more compact and earthy the matter is, and the further removed from a sublime nature, the weaker it will be for receiving the form. <margin>*On the Intent of Alchemy*, chapter 6.</margin> And so the Philosophers diligently warn us that the matter of the Elixir must be thinned, and especially Raymond Lully <note>Raimundus Lullius (c. 1232–1315); a Majorcan philosopher to whom many influential alchemical works were later attributed</note>. "Unless the things," he says, "from which the Elixir is composed are reduced to the most perfect and greatest thinness, there cannot be gradually increased or introduced into them such a high degree and exaltation above nature, so that they might surpass nature tenfold, a hundredfold, or a thousandfold." <margin>In the *Apertorium*.</margin> The same author says: "Matter that is not well prepared cannot perform or create the cause of preparation. Therefore, first prepare your matter,"

But the elements of the stone <term>the Stone; the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of alchemy</term> cannot be thinned—indeed, they cannot even be obtained, according to the testimony of all the Philosophers—except from dissolved bodies: therefore, the bodies must first be thinned through dissolution, which is the first step of the work.

<margin>Dissolution is the first step of the work.</margin>
Moreover, this dissolution is nothing other than the return of bodies into the Mercury and sulfur from which they took their origin. However, no body can be resolved back into Mercury except for a metallic one, consisting of Mercury and sulfur. But since metals are either perfect or imperfect, it may rightly be doubted 

<margin>Which metals are more or less fit for solution.</margin>
whether these or those should be taken as the matter of the Elixir to perform this solution. Indeed, the imperfect metals <note>Imperfect metals usually referred to lead, tin, iron, or copper, which were seen as "diseased" versions of gold.</note> seem easier to dissolve, while the perfect ones are more difficult, because the latter have a nature so dense and compact that fire or art can scarcely act upon them, whereas the former are the opposite. But since imperfect metals contain impure and unclean sulfur and quicksilver, we seem justified in avoiding the labor of their preparation and purification, as we possess bodies that are pure by nature <note>original: *a natura muda*; referring to gold and silver</note>, and which can be thinned by art and led from corporeality to spirituality. And indeed, the greatest consensus of the Philosophers is found in this: they instruct that **Sol** <note>original: *Solem*; the Sun, representing Gold</note> and **Luna** <note>original: *Lunam*; the Moon, representing Silver</note> be dissolved and reduced to their first matter. # CHAPTER TWO.

and had been acted upon by nature: for the vapor of the natural mixture of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"; the common name for mercury</note> and sulfur, carried upwards, first occupies whichever nearby places are suitable for generation; then, once those are filled, it passes to others, and thus finally after several centuries it is carried to the highest parts of the mountains, until at last on their surface or sides it is revealed by a flood of water or some other chance, or even detected by the industry of skilled miners and those experienced in such things, or by the rod which they call "divine" <note>the divining rod or dowsing rod, used to find ores</note>.

<margin>How there are two stones.</margin>
The Philosophers also expressly affirm that there is no gold which was not first silver. If, however, someone tries to perfect the elixir with the Moon <note>In alchemy, the Moon (Luna) represents silver</note> alone, he will not be able to progress beyond Lunar whiteness, nor convert imperfect metals into gold, but only into silver. And thus there will be two medicines: one Solar <note>representing gold</note>, the other Lunar. And the reason is evident enough, because every like produces its like: just as a human is generated from a human, or a lion from a lion, nothing can give the form of gold unless it first possessed the form of gold.

<margin>Every form proceeds from its like. *The Sounding Trumpet* <note>original: "Clang. buc.", referring to the alchemical text *Clangore Buccinae*</note>.</margin>
For it is the property of the form of gold alone to generate gold, and of the form of silver alone to generate silver. Whence Morienus says: "Every tincture <term>Tincture: the transformative essence or "dye" that changes the quality of a metal</term> proceeds from its like." What I have said is confirmed by the authority of Raymond Lull, cited by the Anonymous author. His words are these: "The spirit, that is, the water, is not coagulated <note>thickened or solidified</note> except by means of a body that has been dissolved in it, since bodies are the 'rennet' of this 'milk' <note>Alchemical bodies act like rennet in cheese-making, curdling the liquid mercury into a solid state</note>, and such rennet ought to be the Sun [gold] and Moon [silver], dissolved in Mercury itself: but only the Moon for the white work, and the Sun for the white and red work." Yet I would not deny that the calx <note>original: "calcem"; the powdery residue left after a metal is burned or calcinated</note> of silver as well as other metals passes into gold, and becomes a Red Elixir, if it is afterwards imbued with solar oil and fully decocted <note>boiled or concentrated</note>.

<margin>On the intention of the Alchemists.</margin>
Regarding the Sulfur of the Moon, Raymond Lull openly testifies to this, saying: "When the sulfur of the Moon has been circulated, you must imbibe it little by little with the water of the solar body, and cook it until it has its proper weight." And regarding the calx of other metals in the same place: "My son, you can make the elixir from the calx of whichever body you wish, for the white or the red work, in this way: Take the said sulfur for white or red, and wax it <note>original: "incera"; a process of making a substance soft and pliable like wax</note>, or imbibe it with the oil of the body of the Sun or Moon, according to whether you wish to make the white or red [medicine]." But the calx of the Moon by itself—that is, decocted with Lunar Mercury and waxed with its oil—is only digested into the "Moon" <note>silver</note> or a Lunar Elixir; it cannot overstep whiteness, nor [reach] yellowness...

And although this can happen through nature, humans are not granted such a long lifespan that they can wait for the change from silver into gold—or from white sulfur to red, as the Chemists <term>Chemistae: early practitioners of chemistry and alchemy</term> say—by decoction <note>the process of heating a substance to extract its essence or change its state</note> alone. Therefore, if the Lunar medicine <note>the tincture used to make silver</note> is to be converted into the Solar <note>the tincture used to make gold</note>, it must be done by mixing it with a coloring substance of its own nature, which can be none other than gold. Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath whose Latin-attributed works were foundational to alchemy</note> understands this when he says: "The medicine of the third order is twofold, yet it is one in essence and similar in its manner of action, and therefore it is called a single medicine. However, there is the addition of a citrine <note>lemon-yellow</note> color, which is perfected from the purest substance of fixed sulfur; the difference between this and that—namely the Lunar and the Solar—is that the latter contains that color within itself, while the former does not." Since these things are so, and the white elixir becomes red not by its own power but by an external one, the Philosophers very correctly established two different works and distinguished the white from the red; yet no less truly, regarding the Solar work, they affirmed a single medicine for both white and red.

<margin>
All bodies can supply the material for the elixir.
*The Rosary*, part 1, chapter 7.
*On the Perfection of the Magistery*.
*On the Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 5.
</margin>
I said earlier that we might be excused from the dissolving of imperfect metals. I would not want this understood as if their solution were entirely useless, or that their purified substance does not enter into the white or red elixir. That would be contrary to the opinion of the Philosophers, who teach that both the mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> and the sulfur of these metals must be purified; however, their mercury cannot be obtained except through dissolution. Indeed, Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>Arnald of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> is a primary witness that the material for the elixir can be sought from all metals. He states: "From the bodies of the Sun and Moon <note>gold and silver</note> prepared with their sulfur and arsenic, our medicine is drawn, and it can likewise be drawn from other bodies." Next, Aristotle—not the Stagirite <note>the famous Greek philosopher</note> himself, but a later author like Auicenna or Rhasi <note>Avicenna and Rhazes, famous Persian physicians often cited in alchemical texts</note>—says: "I know most truly that any of the bodies and spirits, if prepared with a perfect preparation, is a white and red elixir by itself alone." And Geber, after showing the method for preparing and purifying imperfect bodies, finally adds: "This is the general method for the improvement and refinement of their pure substance. First, this purged and reduced body must be <insert>to be</insert> calcined <note>reduced to a powder through heat</note> again with fire and the aforementioned cleansing aids, then dissolved with those things that are solvent. For this water is our stone, and it is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> from quicksilver, and sulfur from sulfur..."
