<header>ON THE SUBTLETY OF MATTER</header>

Those who devote their effort to alum <note>a specific type of mineral salt used as a corrosive or astringent</note>, or similar substances that imitate the nature of these, seem to satisfy quite beautifully the definition of solution handed down by Geber in his <margin>*Summary of Perfection*, ch. 52.</margin> *Summary of Perfection*, who says that Solution is nothing other than the reduction of a dry thing into water. And after a few lines he adds: <margin>Errors of the practitioners.</margin> "Everything that is dissolved must necessarily have the nature of salt, alums, or their likeness." Likewise: "From the works of nature we can prove that only those things which preserve the nature of salts and alums and the like are soluble; for in considering all her works, we do not find other things dissolved except these." Likewise, those who work with the gums of trees and plants seem to grasp Geber’s meaning in some part, just as do those who extract waters by distillation from animals and vegetables (or things originating from them). They calcine <note>reduce to ash through dry heat</note> the earth or dregs left at the bottom of the vessels, then soak and dissolve that lime <note>the powdery residue of calcination</note> with its own water; they do this especially because Geber adds that every perfection of solution is brought about with subtle waters that are highly sharp, acrid, and pungent, having no dregs. But who would deny that in such a vast diversity of animals and vegetables, waters of this mark are not found?

But the Philosophers do not labor with waters that cling to the touch <note>original: "aquas tangenti adhærentibus," referring to ordinary wet liquids</note>, or transparent waters, which cannot be mixed with metals. Whence we read in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or *Assembly of the Philosophers*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Beginners, hearing the word 'water,' think it is rainwater or spring water, but if they had read our books, they would surely know it to be permanent water <note>original: "aquam permanentem," a term for the metallic solvent that does not evaporate like water</note>." 

Furthermore, it is certain that those err no less who obtain "strong waters" <note>original: "aquas validas seu fortes," referring to mineral acids like nitric acid</note>, as they call them, by distillation from saltpeter, vitriol, and common salt, with sal ammoniac added or other similar things. In these, they corrode metallic bodies; they do not dissolve them (as they think) by a natural and physical solution, which requires the reduction of the body into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>. Nor do those sin any less who, by the force of a strong fire, draw out a water from running quicksilver, or from quicksilver mortified through sublimation with salts, and hope they can reduce gold and silver into the "first matter" with it. They seem indeed to come closest to the knowledge of solution, which ought to be done through things related and homogeneous <note>sharing the same essential nature</note>; for Mercury and the perfect metals do not differ, except that the metals are fully decocted <note>ripened or cooked by nature's heat</note> by nature, while Mercury is only begun and left imperfect. But nevertheless, they do not sufficiently grasp what they are doing, for they corrupt the "spermatic" nature and proportion of the Mercury, which none is able to restore

<margin>The most secret dissolution of the Philosophers.</margin>
What, then, will the Philosophical Solution finally be? Concerning the knowledge of this, most brilliant minds have sweated much, and yet they could not attain it. For it is the most secret <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: *arcanum*; a hidden mystery or profound secret</note> of the entire chemical work. If anyone should know it—having investigated it by his own industry or through the teaching of another—surely the remaining regimens of the art will not be hidden from him, provided that books are not lacking and he does not cease to apply himself to them diligently. Indeed, the Philosophers assert that perfect bodies must be converted into <term>prime matter</term> <note>the fundamental, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</note>, that is, into Mercury; but this cannot be done except through corruption, for the "corruption of one is the generation of another" <note>A common medieval scientific maxim derived from Aristotle, meaning that for something new to be born, the old form must be destroyed</note>. But these same philosophers say that corruption must be induced through paths contrary to nature. Just as perfect metals are cooked by a slow heat in the bowels of the earth, and there their humidity is gradually thickened and fixed, so if they are to be reduced back to prime matter, it will be necessary for them to be calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, dissolved, and <term>re-incrudated</term> <note>returned to a "crude" or raw, liquid-like state</note>. 

<margin>*The Testament*, chapter 19.</margin>
Ramon Llull <note>A 13th-century polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> calls calcination and solution "operations contrary to nature." This re-incrudation—or rather, the separation of bodies—will not seem to be the way toward construction. And even if it were the way, the Philosophers have not described the manner in which it can or should be done. They certainly command that gold and silver be dissolved by "water of their own kind," or through Mercury into Mercury, but I have tried this for many years, and others have tried it, yet I do not hear of anyone who has gained the fruit of his labors, unless the method of the work was changed. Some have sublimated quicksilver from gold with strong and vehement firing, so that its subtlety might ascend and create a very yellow color with it; they thought they had achieved something great, when yet they had not even reached the first regimen of the Physical work. 

<margin>*On the Intention of Alchemists*.</margin>
For they are deceived, as Ramon Llull says, who think that spirits <note>volatile substances like mercury or sulfur</note> can be joined with bodies <note>solid metals</note> while they remain in their raw thickness and diversity of nature. This cannot happen until they are reduced to a single equality of form. By which most beautiful sentiment—to be noted in golden letters—the Philosopher proposes to us two reasons by which bodies are most aptly joined with spirits. For if...

...they must be led to an equality of form. It will be necessary first to cook the spirit into a solar or lunar body <note>original: *corpus solare vel lunare*; in alchemy, "solar" refers to gold and "lunar" to silver</note>, and thus join it with gold and silver, which seems difficult to do; or to reduce the body of gold or silver into a Mercurial nature and add it to quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, which will be easier. For God has given us mineral means by which this can be conveniently performed. This is why Geber <note>a Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure considered the father of Islamic and European alchemy</note> says that the perfection of the mastery consists in the consideration of both material things and those that assist. Which things are the "assistants," he clearly enough declares in the book *On the Investigation of Perfection*, Chapter 4. "The things," he says, "assisting the preparation are these: namely, all kinds of salts, alums, and <term>atraments</term> <note>original: *atramentorum*; vitriols or black metallic sulfates used in making ink and in alchemy</note>, etc." And Ramon Llull says: "In the first order there are four practical principles, of which two are natural, and the remaining two are against nature. The natural ones are sulfur and quicksilver, and from these two the 'metallic love' is born, through which the generation of the sought-after thing occurs." And a little later: "Against nature are the nature of <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid or sulfate salts</note> and the nature of common salt, from which a love of another kind arises—nevertheless of a near generation—and under these, the corruption of the sought-after thing occurs." Vincent [of Beauvais] in the *Mirror of Doctrine*: "The property of salt is that it liquefies gold and silver with the violence of fire, and increases their color—namely, redness in gold and whiteness in silver—and converts them from corporality to spirituality <note>meaning the transformation of a solid metal into a liquid or vaporous state</note>, and washes away filth from the bodies, and corrodes their sulfurousness." He says that salt leads gold and silver from "corporeity to spirituality," which is nothing other than reducing them into their prime matter, or into Mercury. When he adds that salt washes filth from the bodies, understand this to mean "imperfect bodies" <note>base metals like lead or copper</note>, for the perfect ones <note>gold and silver</note> do not have external filth or sulfurousness. From these things one may gather how sparingly and in how few words the Philosophers describe the greatest secret of this art, without the knowledge of which no one can reduce gold and silver into prime matter, or into running Mercury.

<header>CHAPTER TWO.</header>

...coagulation, nor that the spirit is coagulated, except with the dissolution of the body; yet in this dissolution of the metal, no coagulation of the spirit can take place, since no spirit is joined to the body, but rather salts, which only resolve the thickness of the body and are then separated from it. <margin>Response to objections.</margin> I respond that the Philosophers indeed teach the truth, but we must look carefully at which dissolution they are speaking of. For the Philosophers, after the manner of Poets, very often begin their books with a <term>hysteron proteron</term> <note>original: *ὕστερον πρότερον*; a Greek rhetorical device where the natural order of things is reversed, putting the "last" thing "first."</note>, placing the beginning at the end. <margin>Three solutions in the work.</margin> We say, therefore, along with *Ramon Llull*, *Marsilio Ficino*, and others most skilled in this science, that there are three primary solutions in the Chemical work. The first is of the crude metallic body; the second is of the physical earth; and the third is that which consists in the nutrition or increase of the Stone. Nor do the Philosophers mean anything else when they say the work is nothing other than perfect dissolution and congelation—not just once, but repeated quite often. <margin>Demonstrating that the solution of the crude metal is not the formal "solution" of the Philosophers.</margin> Moreover, it is clear from this that the dissolution so widely celebrated by the Philosophers is not that first one of the crude body, because immediately after the dissolution of the body, they command that the elements be separated and purged, and once purged, joined together again. Yet these same authors say that in a true dissolution, the spirit is so united with the body that one cannot afterwards be separated from the other. If this is true—as can be proven by countless testimonies of the authors of this art, which I will omit for the sake of brevity—what separation or purging of elements should we expect in a hard and solid body that cannot be divided? Furthermore, the Philosophers assert that a true union of body and spirit does not occur unless both have first been most perfectly cleansed. But if no union of the body with the spirit occurs before their perfect cleansing, surely no suitable dissolution can take place, since their union occurs only through dissolution. <margin>In the physical solution, everything is turned into powder.</margin> If anyone should attempt a middle way, and think that in the physical solution the spirit is not coagulated into a dry body but only thickened or rendered more dense—not unlike someone adding flour to milk or water to boil a porridge that is neither entirely thin nor thick—let him hear the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium*; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, one of the most famous alchemical texts</note> and *Assoten* in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, an ancient alchemical dialogue</note>. "Unless all things are turned into powder, you have not yet crushed them; therefore cook and grind them until they are converted and by nature become powder." They are speaking here of the physical solution. And *Zeno* says in the same place: "Unless you turn bodies into non-bodies, and the incorporeal into bodies, you have not yet found the work."

# ON THE THINNESS OF MATTER

...you have learned: moreover, bodies become incorporeal <note>original: *incorporea*; referring to a state where the solid metal is transformed into a vapor or a non-solid essence.</note> when the *ethelia* <note>original: *ethelia*; an archaic alchemical term often referring to the "spirit" or volatile part of a substance, or a specific mineral vapor.</note> is ground down until it becomes a powder; a state which cannot be achieved except through the strongest boiling and continuous grinding. But if, in a true solution, everything must be turned into powder, then no room remains for the separation of the elements. This separation must occur in a liquid body; it cannot happen in a dry one, especially since it must be carried out through distillations and sublimations, separating fire from earth and the subtle from the dense, according to the precept of Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>.

<margin>The physical solution that occurs.</margin>
Therefore, when the Philosophers say that the dissolution of the body does not happen without the coagulation of the spirit, and vice versa, we must understand them to be speaking either of the *second solution*, in which the water is so united to the earth that one does not easily leave the other, or of the *third solution*, in which the volatile elements are fixed and reduced into a "tinging, flowing, and penetrating" earth.

<margin>What the first solution is like.</margin>
However, we shall consider the *first solution* to be the simple [dissolving] of gold or silver, or another metal, into quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; *argentum vivum*</term>. Because the "form" of these metallic bodies has already been brought to an equality with that of common quicksilver, the quicksilver embraces the metal very easily and is joined to it at the smallest level, just as milk is joined to milk. Regarding this, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century chemist/alchemist.</note> says:

> One quicksilver adheres more to another quicksilver and is more "friendly" to it; then comes gold, and then silver; but the remaining bodies do not have such an affinity or conformity with it, because they participate less in its nature.

<margin>In the *Codicillus*.</margin>
And Ramon Llull <note>A 13th-century philosopher and purported alchemist.</note> says:

> Dissolution occurs in our Stone so that it may make the Stone entirely subtle [fine and refined], so that it may afterwards be better joined with the spirits; for that which is of a subtle and rare substance is joined more quickly with what is subtle and rarefied, and increases more swiftly than that which is thick, hard, and opaque.

<margin>The dissolved body must be joined to the spirit, and not the other way around.</margin>
Do you see how the eminent Doctor Llull judges that the spirit should not be joined with a hard and solid body—as almost everyone today does, and as I myself once did in a great error—but on the contrary, the thinned and dissolved body should be joined with the spirit? Geber also expressly confesses that no body, no matter how much it agrees with Mercury in nature, can firmly adhere to it or be able to coagulate it [on its own].

<margin>In *The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 33.</margin>
For he says:

> We do not see any of the bodies in their own nature coagulate quicksilver; rather, it flees from them, no matter how great their suitability might be. Therefore, we have considered that no body adheres to it in its depths.

What could be more open than these words of Geber, what could be clearer, or even truer?

> No body, he says, no matter how much it agrees with Mercury, coagulates it; but it [Mercury] agrees most particularly with

# CHAPTER SECOND

<margin>
No body coagulates <term>Mercury|The chemical process of turning a liquid or vaporous substance into a solid</term> unless it is first dissolved. From the *Book of Secrets*.
</margin>
<margin>
Solution and coagulation are one single work.
</margin>
...gold, as is witnessed everywhere: for if gold is not powerful enough to coagulate Mercury, assuredly neither will Mercury be effective enough for dissolving gold, since the work of <term>coagulation|solidification</term> and <term>solution|dissolution into liquid</term> is one, and there is no difference of time between these two. For in this way says Calid, son of Sasichi <note>original: *Calid, filius sasichi*; referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince and famous legendary figure in alchemy.</note>: *The solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit are two things, but they have one operation, because the spirit is not coagulated except with the solution of the body, and similarly the body is not dissolved except with the coagulation of the spirit.* <note>original: "Solutio corporis & coagulatio spiritus sunt duo, sed habent vnam operationē..."</note> And a little later: *Know that between the solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit, there is no difference of time, nor a different work, such that one might be without the other, but they have one limit, and one deed, and one and the same operation circles over those two.* He says in Chapter 1, no less clearly than Raymond Lull or <term>Geber|The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential medieval alchemist</term>, that bodies must be made subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to refining a substance until it is very fine, pure, or even vaporous.</note> before the spirits are joined with them. In these words: *I say that the spirit will not dwell in the body, nor be in it, nor remain with it in any way, until the body itself possesses such subtlety and thinness as the spirit has; and when it has been thinned and made subtle, and has passed from its density and thickness to thinness, and from coarseness and corporality to spirituality, it will then be mixed with the subtle spirits, and thus they will come out as one and the same, and they shall not be separated, just as water mixed with water cannot be.* From the things said above, it is clear enough how great an error they have lived in until now, and even live in today, who hope that 
<margin>
Gold and silver cannot be dissolved by common Mercury.
</margin>
gold, silver, or other metals can be dissolved with common <term>quicksilver|Ordinary liquid mercury found in shops, as opposed to the specialized "Philosophical Mercury" of the alchemists</term>, and they pass by the true solution of the Philosophers. Whence it is no wonder if those laboring at the very beginning do not achieve the desired end.

<margin>
The third objection.
</margin>
But another will say: "Nothing foreign enters into our <term>Stone|The Philosopher's Stone</term>, nor is anything mixed with it which is not of its own metallic nature; why then do you persuade us to add <term>salts|Chemical compounds often used as fluxes or cleansing agents</term> and <term>atramenta|Vitriols or dark metallic sulfates</term> to the bodies, which are foreign to the nature of metals?" 

<margin>
The Response.
</margin>
I respond: it is one thing simply to add something for the purging or thinning of the spirits or bodies, and quite another for it to enter and be mixed through the smallest parts at the root while both remain there permanently. Thus the Philosophers indeed add salt to the spirits so they may be purged, and to the bodies so they may be dissolved, but they do not enter the inward substance of those same things, nor do they increase their weight, nor do they stick to them in any way; rather, they are removed by the lightest washing or rinsing. Nothing except the metallic and Mercurial nature is joined together in the work, from which alone the whole work is completed.

<summary>This page argues that the dissolution of solid metals and the solidification of volatile spirits happen simultaneously as one single process. It also defends the use of external "cleansing" agents like salts, explaining they act as temporary tools rather than permanent ingredients in the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

# ON THE THINNESS OF MATTER

<margin>
The method of solution is twofold.
</margin>
Perfect and imperfect bodies are thus dissolved, but for different reasons: the imperfect ones are dissolved so that we may obtain the <term>Mercury|The alchemical principle of fluidity and transformation</term> with which the earth is soaked, washed, and <term>sublimed|The process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</term>. The perfect ones, however, are dissolved so that the <term>spirits|Volatile substances like sulfur or mercury</term> may be fermented, fixed, and <term>tinged|Given the power to transform other metals</term>, because spirits cannot be fixed in the earth except through the "water" of perfect bodies.

<margin>
What the difference is between the solution of perfect and imperfect bodies.
</margin>
There is also this difference between the metals: the perfect ones do not require any <term>depuration|The removal of impurities or "cleansing"</term> before solution, because they are already perfect and clean; they only require <term>attenuation|The process of making a substance thinner or more subtle</term>.

<margin>
From *The Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 2.
</margin>
<margin>
Perfect bodies do not need preparation before solution.
</margin>
Geber <note>original: *Geber*; the Latinized name for the 8th-century chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note> himself teaches us this. To prepare, he says, is to remove superfluities and to supply what is absent, and thus to impart to them a known perfection. But perfect bodies do not lack this preparation. They do, however, require a preparation by which their parts are made more subtle, and are reduced from their "corporeality" (physicality) to a "spirituality."

<margin>
From *The Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 5.
</margin>
<margin>
How imperfect ones are to be prepared before solution.
</margin>
In contrast, because imperfect bodies contain an unclean, drossy, and incombustible earthiness that is too thick—preventing both penetration and melting—as well as a similarly combustible and corrupting humidity that is of a sparse and porous substance, having a melting point without proper <term>ignition|The state of glowing with heat</term> or none at all, and not tolerating sufficient extension under the hammer: these must be purified before solution. These superfluities, which have come upon them accidentally rather than being part of their core nature, must be removed by the craft.

Geber explains the method of this most elegantly in the following sense. First, all the superfluous and corrupted humidity in their essence, as well as the subtle and burning superfluity, must be raised up with a proportional fire, and this is done by <term>calcining|Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term>. Then, the total corrupted substance remaining in their "calx" (powdered remains) of burning humidity and blackness must be eaten away with cleansed, corrosive, sharp, or sour "waters," until the calx is white or red, or colored according to the nature and property of the body, and is clean and pure from all superfluity or corruption. 

Afterward, the total unclean, drossy, combustible, and thick earthiness must be erased or cast down with the aforementioned cleansed or pure things that do not have a metallic melting point—by this he means <term>salts|Chemical compounds used as fluxes or reagents</term>—mixed and well-ground with the purified calx. In the melting or the reduction of the calx, these salts will retain the thick and unclean earthiness within themselves, while the body remains pure, cleansed of every corrupting superfluity. This is all done through <term>descension|A process where a substance is melted so that it drips down through a filter into a lower vessel, leaving dross behind</term>. Since Geber provides the method and reason for descension openly and clearly—contrary to his usual habit—we shall send the reader there so as not to be overly long.

### CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>On the thinning of the elements of the stone.</margin>
Having explained the attenuation of metals, which is carried out through reduction into the first matter—that is, <term>Mercury|The alchemical principle of fluidity and potential, not just the common metal quicksilver</term>—let us begin the discourse on the work of the stone. The Philosophers have commanded that this stone be refined no less than the hard and compact metallic body itself. <margin>How many modes of operation there are.</margin> Indeed, there are six primary ways in which this is achieved: <term>Putrefaction|The process of breaking down and "rotting" a substance to its base state</term>, <term>distillation|Heating a liquid to create vapor and then cooling it back to liquid</term>, <term>calcination|Heating a solid until it turns into a fine powder or ash</term>, <term>solution|Dissolving a solid into a liquid</term>, <term>sublimation|Heating a solid so it turns directly into vapor and then back to solid in a purer form</term>, and <term>ceration|The process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>. Some of these serve the "upper" part of the stone, some the "lower," and others serve both. <margin>The stone divided into an upper and lower part.</margin> For thus Hermes <note>original: *Hermes*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and the author of the *Emerald Tablet*.</note> divided the parts of the stone, saying: "That which is above is like that which is below." <note>original: *Quod est superius, est sicut quod inferius.*</note> Now, I call the "upper" part the spiritual part—the non-fixed, light, and volatile part—namely, the spirit and the soul, which vivifies the dead stone and causes it to rise again. I call the "lower" part the earth, which remains fixed; once all superfluities are removed and consumed, it is mixed with the upper part. From these joined and united parts, the perfect work is made. <margin>Operations serving the upper or lower part of the stone.</margin> Distillation thins the upper part; calcination, solution, and ceration thin the lower part; putrefaction and sublimation thin both. To these could be added filtration through a filter, or <term>depuration|The removal of impurities</term> through cloth strips, since those things that are purified are also further refined. Likewise, <term>maceration|Steeping or soaking</term> and infusion may be added, by which the virtues and more refined parts of dry things are called out and infused into liquids such as wine, water, or oil. Similarly, one might add <term>circulation|A process where a liquid is continuously distilled and condensed in a closed vessel</term>, by which, through a perpetual rotation or continuous ascent and descent, certain liquids are thinned beyond measure so that they deposit the <term>calx|The chalky residue or powder left after heating</term> that could not be removed from them by any other distillations, leaving it at the bottom and assuming a somewhat airy nature. But because these and similar processes are more suited to vegetables and things derived from animals than to metals (though the same works are sometimes applied to metals by analogy), we will deliberately pass over them, especially since they have been clearly handed down by others who wrote about the extraction of the <term>Quinta essentia|The "Fifth Essence" or Quintessence; the most purified and potent form of a substance</term>. Yet, they are not to be entirely rejected in the art of metallic metamorphosis: for although they are not strictly part of the perfection of the Elixir, they nevertheless sometimes help not a little in the preparation of things. For filtration, however, one may aptly substitute compression through leather or a double cloth, by which we test whether the <term>argentum viuum|Quicksilver; literally "living silver"</term> contains any metallic body within it or not. If indeed something remains in the leather or cloth...

...cannot be passed through, such mercury must be judged useless for the physical work.

<margin>
On putrefaction. 
*The Rosary*, part 2, Chapter 4. 
<note>original: *Ros. [Rosarium Philosophorum]*. A famous 14th-century alchemical treatise.</note>
</margin>
Thus, putrefaction follows solution, according to the witness of Arnaldus de Villanova, <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist.</note> who affirms this very thing with these words: "Take the dissolved stone and place it over a temperate heat, so that it may putrefy and be better digested, namely, for a philosopher's month." <note>A "philosopher's month" typically refers to a period of 40 days.</note> Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> says in

<margin>
*The Codicil*, near the end of the first practical principle.
</margin>
*The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba [Philosophorum]*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "The second step is to putrefy." Raymond Lull also writes to the same effect: "The intention you should have, my son, is to take the dissolved stone and do not delay in placing it in secret dung, <note>original: *secreto fimo*. Decaying horse dung was used by alchemists as a natural, steady heat source for "digestion."</note> so that it may remain there for 40 days, because

<margin>
Book 1 on the Faculty of Simple Medicines, chapter 35.
</margin>
the elements are altered and corrupted toward one another." Such corruption is the solemn generation of our <term>mercury|original: *argenti viui nostri*. Alchemists distinguished their "Philosophical Mercury" from common quicksilver</term>, which cannot be obtained except after putrefaction. Furthermore, it is not at all unknown that putridity thins matter, based even on the testimony of Plato, which

<margin>
Definition of putridity. 
Book 4 of the *Meteorology*. 
Book 8 of the *Method of Healing*.
</margin>
Galen <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> adduces. For speaking of those things which have a sharp flavor, he says: "These same things, sometimes thinned by putridity, enter into narrow passages, and an acidic flavor emanates from them." Aristotle defines putrefaction as "the corruption of the proper and natural heat in every moist thing, by an external heat." Galen, however, says that putrefaction is "a change of the entire substance of a rotting body toward corruption by an external heat." Galen's definition seems to fit plants and animals more closely, but Aristotle’s fits the operations of the Chemists; and Raymond Lull embraced it when he spoke thus in the place cited above: "The effect of putrefaction is the corruption of the proper and natural heat by an unnatural heat." And a little later: "Thus the unnatural heat changes the <term>complexion|The balance of qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that determines a substance's nature</term> that belongs to the substance of the metal into an opposite complexion; yet it could not do this as long as the moisture informed by natural heat remained. Therefore, it is necessary that it first corrupt the natural heat while preserving it." He says "while preserving it" so we may understand that the innate heat is not entirely removed by the external heat that causes putrefaction, but only becomes dull and fails because of the overflowing moisture. Once that moisture is removed by <term>distillation|Purification by vaporizing and condensing a liquid</term> or dried out by boiling, the active elements—rendered sharper and more fiery through <term>calcinations|The process of burning a substance to a fine powder</term>—may exert and demonstrate their powers anew. Therefore, it is necessary that putrefaction precede the division of the elements; for if we seek the division of parts which nature has joined, <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought that decomposition is the only way to separate what nature has fused.</note>

### CHAPTER TWO

...putrefaction is the way to that division. For as mixing, according to the witness of Aristotle, is a union, so putrefaction is a dissolution. <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica* was a primary source for alchemical theories on how substances combine and decay.</note> Therefore, all things must putrefy so that, once they are more fully "digested," they may be better separated. Whence Lull says in the *Codicil*: <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a philosopher to whom many alchemical works, like the *Codicil*, were later attributed.</note> "In such simple, corrupted matter there are four composite elements, which are separable and can be resolved into the Water of Mercury after putrefaction." He calls this "simple matter" a "dissolved body," to distinguish it from a body that is solid and hard.

<margin>What the elements of the Chemists are.</margin>
He likewise calls them "composite elements" because true Chemists do not seek simple elements—from which no new life or generation can arise—but rather composite elements. In these, each single element has the other three attached and joined to it, yet with one predominating over the rest. Thus, the Philosophers call it "Water" when the qualities of water prevail, namely coldness and moisture; "Air" when heat and cold <note>original: *calidum & frigidum*. This is likely a scribal or printing error, as the traditional qualities of Air are heat and moisture (*calidum & humidum*).</note> overcome the others; "Fire" when heat and dryness excel; and "Earth" when dryness and coldness predominate.

<margin>The method of putrefactions.</margin>
The method of putrefying is this: the dissolved stone is placed in a closed glass vessel and buried under dung. <note>Decaying horse dung was a standard laboratory tool used to provide a constant, gentle "blood heat" for weeks at a time.</note> Its heat must be maintained for a set time, either by sprinkling it with urine, by laying quicklime beneath it, by adding more dung, or by changing the dung every eighth day.

<margin>Understanding the practice of the art.</margin>
There is also another, more subtle method suggested by Raymond Lull. The entire dissolved composite is placed in dung, which is itself held in a bronze vessel perforated at the bottom and all around. This vessel is then placed inside another similar bronze vessel. In the bottom of this second vessel, there should be water at a distance of six or eight fingers' height below the bottom of the perforated vessel. In this way, the vapor of the heated water rises to continuously moisten and heat the dung in the upper vessel. It should also have a bronze pipe at the side that projects outside the furnace structure, tightly closed with a stopper when necessary. Through this pipe, the artisan can pour in more hot water as he sees fit, measuring the depletion so that he adds as much in the morning and evening as has evaporated. There should also be a bronze lid on top, fitting tightly into the putrefaction pot to restrain and send back the rising vapors; this can be removed or added at will.

<margin>The separation of elements occurs through distillation. The definition of distillation.</margin>
The separation of the elements follows putrefaction. This is done so that each individual part can be better cleansed on its own. This process is carried out through distillation. Distillation is the thinning of the moister parts of any thing into "breath" or vapors by the use of heat, and their sublimation into the air, which [the parts], by the coldness of the alembic... <note>An alembic is the "hood" or "cap" of a still that cools the vapor back into liquid.</note>

<meta>The catchword "for-" suggests the next page begins with a word like *formam* (form) or *foris* (outside).</meta>

### ON THE TENUITY OF MATTER

...striking the arches or the sides of the receiving vessel, and settling there, they are thickened by the cold, gather into drops, and having become a liquid distillation, they flow back and turn into moisture. The definition of distillation handed down by Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in chemistry and alchemy.</note> may seem incomplete to some, as he says distillation is "the elevation of aqueous vapors in their own vessel." But Geber did not look so much at common distillations as he did at the physical <note>In this context, "physical" refers to the study of nature and alchemical transformation.</note> kind, for which this definition was thought sufficient.

<margin>Why it was invented.</margin>
A double reason for its invention is described by the same author. One is purification from dregs; the other is preservation from rotting. For experience shows that everything distilled is made purer and is better preserved from rotting. Philosophers especially required the purest and cleanest water without any "earth" <note>The author uses "earth" to refer to solid, particulate residue or impurities.</note>, so that if at any time "earth" or a cleansed medicine had to be dissolved, they would have a water that would not leave behind any dregs after that resolution, by which the cleansed medicines and spirits could be infected and corrupted.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But someone will object that I taught a little earlier that nothing is generated from simple elements, and now I require pure water without earth, which can hardly happen; for earth is the nourishment of water, just as water is for air, and air for fire.

<margin>Response.</margin>
I respond that the philosophers desire pure water, not indeed without any earth at all, but such that it cannot be perceived during the operation. This is just as I said in Chapter 1: it should be understood as earth being void of all oiliness as far as the senses are concerned, but not in the absolute truth of the matter.

<margin>The threefold types of distillation.</margin>
Skilled craftsmen establish a threefold method of distillation. One is by ascent, the second by descent, and the third by the side or by inclination, which is a middle ground between the two. The last distillation is performed with a curved flask, which they call a <term>retort</term> <note>original: *retortam*; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note>, or indeed a straight flask but tilted to the side, having a narrower neck and a more prominent belly. The middle type [by descent] uses a straight but inverted flask. In both cases, only a receptacle is added to the mouth of the vessel, into which the vapors are immediately driven, enter, and are there condensed into either an aqueous or oily liquor. The first type [by ascent] also requires an upright flask or "matula," but an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: *alembicus*; from the Arabic *al-anbiq*, the cap or "still-head" of the distilling apparatus.</note> or beaked cap is placed on top of it, into which the breaths [vapors] are first carried, dewing its chambers and walls; then, thickened into moisture, they slip down through its channel and beak into the receiver.

<margin>Variation of fire in distilling.</margin>
The method of distillation varies greatly not only by the vessel used, but also by the administration of fire. For one is done by the heat of a <term>bath</term> <note>original: *balnei*; a water bath, often called a bain-marie, used for gentle heating.</note>, another by ashes or sand, and another by the naked fire of coals or flame; I say nothing...

## CHAPTER TWO.

rr
<meta>catchword: necessary</meta>

...fires between these mediums. For through a water bath <note>original: "balneum". A gentle method of heating by placing a vessel inside another containing hot water.</note>, only the more subtle, colorless parts approaching the nature of simple water are raised, for water does not take on ignition; but through an ash bath <note>original: "cineres". A method using hot ashes to provide a more intense, steady heat than water.</note>, colors and coarser earthy parts usually ascend, since they receive ignition. Through an open fire <note>original: "ignem nudum". Direct exposure to flame.</note>, those things are distilled which more stubbornly refuse to release their liquid, either due to dryness and scarcity, or because they adhere more tenaciously to earthy parts due to viscosity and homogeneity. Chemists can use these modes of distillation vessels, provided that in distilling by ascent, the cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped boiling flask.</note> is not too high, its mouth is wide, and the alembic <note>The "cap" or still-head of the apparatus that collects and cools vapors.</note> is large. The philosophers forbid height in the cucurbit so that the water does not stick to its walls and slide back down to the dregs, thus keeping the craftsman occupied with repeated distillation and great labor. For the same reason, they require a wide mouth, so that vapors may be carried upward more easily into the alembic without any sticking; and a large and high alembic, so that the water to be distilled may be further purified.

<margin>In the commentary on the fourth of Plato.</margin>
For a thing is not clarified, as Hamech says, unless its journey in sublimation is prolonged. It is better known than the need to bring forth examples that "sublimation" <note>The process where a solid turns into a gas and then back to a solid, though here used interchangeably with distillation.</note> is very often used by the Arabs for distillation, just as it is by certain moderns.

<margin>On Calcination.</margin>
Just as moist things are cleansed through distillation, so imperfect metals and the fixed and earthy part of the stone are purified and thinned through calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to a high temperature, but below its melting point, to cause thermal decomposition or to remove volatile substances.</note>. <margin>Definition.</margin> It is defined by Geber <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry.</note> as the pulverization of a thing by fire through the removal of the moisture that solidifies its parts. But what do you mean, O Philosopher, by the removal of moisture? Do you want a body to be so deprived of all its moisture that it does not flow, or gives only a glass-like fusion? For you write in the Chapter on Calcination—and truly indeed—that every body deprived of its own moisture gives no fusion except a glass-like one; and yet in the same chapter, you also assert that bodies are purified through repeated calcination and reduction, just as you taught the same in the Chapter on Descent and Purification through pastilles. If, therefore, calxes <note>The powder or "ash" produced by calcination.</note> can be reduced again into bodies [metals], how have they been deprived of moisture? <margin>Explanation of the definition.</margin> I would be stuck if you did not explain yourself, saying: Since the body is solid, and because of the solidity and the hiding of an occult sulfurousness <note>In alchemical theory, metals were thought to be composed of two principles: Sulfur (the principle of combustion and color) and Mercury (the principle of liquidity and metallic luster).</note> in the cavity of the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi". Mercury.</note>, it is defended by it against burning...

### ON THE TENUITY OF MATTER

...it was necessary to break its continuity, so that the fire—reaching every tiny part of it more freely—could burn out the sulfurousness <note>original: "sulphureitatem". In alchemy, sulfur represents the principle of combustion and impurity that must be purged.</note> from it, and so that the structural integrity of the quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui". Mercury, considered the fluid "soul" of metals.</note> within it does not protect it. Therefore, for the perfect calcination of metals, it is not required that the body to be calcined be deprived of all moisture, but only that its physical continuity be divided and reduced into the smallest possible particles.

<margin>The great diversity of things to be calcined. *The Testament*, chapter 66.</margin>
Just as there is a great diversity of things to be calcined, so too are the reasons for calcination varied. For the <term>Philosophical Earth</term> <note>The primary material or "subject" used as the base for the Alchemical Work.</note> is calcined so that it may be freed from all oiliness, and so it becomes open and spongy, allowing water to better enter and carry out its work. As Raymond Lull says, this is done so the material can be expanded by growing, and within that earth, it can be "suffocated," turned over, cleansed, and purified, and finally converted into the earth's own nature.

Metallic bodies that are "imperfect" <note>Base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron.</note> are also calcined, as are "perfect" ones <note>Gold and silver.</note>. Likewise, spirits and other things foreign to their nature are calcined, such as salts, vitriols <note>original: "atramenta". Literally "inks," but here referring to metallic sulfates or "green/blue vitriol."</note>, and alums. We do not deal here with plants or animals and their parts which are reduced to ash or lime, since we do not require them in the Philosophical work.

<margin>Various methods of Calcination.</margin>
We have stated above why imperfect metals are calcined: namely, so that their corrosive sulfurousness—which ruins and burns them—may be removed; and so they may be freed from the coarse earthiness that hinders their penetration and melting; and finally, so they may be unburdened of superfluous moisture that is prone to catching fire or evaporating.

They are reduced into <term>lime</term> <note>original: "calcem". A fine powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures.</note> either by fire alone, or by exposing them to sharp vapors, such as vinegar and similar substances, or with the help of salts, alums, and other corrosive agents. They are also calcined with sulfur or <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmento". A deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note> mixed with their metal plates or filings.

Perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver.</note> do not need calcination to be cleansed of earth, sulfur, or corrupting moisture—which they lack, being already clean and perfect—but only so they may be further thinned and dissolved more easily, because every calcined substance is more easily dissolved. Therefore, the calcination of these is better achieved through fire alone, with the aid of salts, or through the removal of Mercury by means of repeated <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to strip away the mercury.</note> over them.

Salts, alums, and vitriols are also calcined, not because we seek a "tincture" or any perfection in them (since they lack it), but for the preparation of bodies and spirits. <term>Spirits</term> <note>Volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or ammonia.</note> cannot be calcined unless they are first "fixed" <note>Made resistant to heat so they do not evaporate.</note>: the method of calcinat-

<meta>The catchword "nis" completes the word "calcinationis" (of calcination) on the following page.</meta>

# CHAPTER TWO

<sig>rr 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: someone</meta>

<margin>The Summary of Perfection, chapter 28.</margin>
...the nature of these is such; that as they approach **fixation** <note>original: "fixionem"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note>, the fire should be increased successively and gradually until they can withstand the maximum heat. However, the best **calcination** <note>Reducing a substance to a powder (calx) through heat.</note> for them occurs when they are joined with things close and compatible to them and calcined together; in this way, a most excellent calx is formed, whose effect no one can ever sufficiently admire or proclaim. Hence Geber says: *Sulfur is calcined more easily when mixed.* This is also to be understood similarly for other spirits.

<margin>The sign of perfect calcination. The vessel for calcining.</margin>
The sign of perfect calcination, according to Raymond Lull in his *Book on Mercury Alone*, is when the calcined matter dissolves in warmed water; once dissolved and the water evaporated, it coagulates; after coagulation, it melts in the fire, and then coagulates again. The vessel for calcination should be round and flat, like a small dish or bowl, covered and sealed on all sides.

<margin>On solution.</margin>
Closely following calcination is **solution** <note>original: "solutio"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>, both of the metallic body (which we discussed above) and of the purified and calcined earth. In this process, just as the spirit dissolves the earth, it is in turn coagulated by the earth; thus they are united together so that they cannot later be separated, but are gathered and strengthened by the soul, so that they may withstand all the intensity of the fire. Hence, this "Solution of the Philosophers" occurs when the parts of the dry earth are drenched with moisture and become soft, so that their dryness—which is hardness—is turned into softness, so they may flow, gain entry <note>The ability of one substance to penetrate another at a molecular level.</note>, and represent both the power and the metallic form.

<margin>What is to be dissolved. The Summary of Investigation, chapter 52.</margin>
Not only are "bodies" <note>Metals</note> dissolved, but also "spirits" <note>Volatile substances like sulfur or mercury</note>, though only after their prior fixation. Geber is the authority on this when he says: *The reason for the discovery of solution was the refining of those things which have neither melting nor entry, from which the great usefulness of fixed spirits and those things of their own nature was being lost.* Whatever can happen to fixed spirits must also be understood as possibly happening to a body and spirit coagulated and fixed together. All other things reduced to calx or ash and approaching the nature of salts are also dissolved, so that their waters may be purified through filter-cloths <note>original: "per lacinias"; a method of capillary filtration using strips of fabric to siphon and clean a liquid.</note> and then coagulated once more, if necessary. Thus they are joined to spirits and bodies for their purification or refining.

<margin>How solution is done.</margin>
This later solution is performed by means of manure <note>original: "fimum"; a dung-bed used for gentle, constant heat over a long period.</note> or a water-bath <note>original: "balneum"; specifically the "Bath of Mary," a double-boiler system.</note>, with one purpose and no difference in effect. It differs only in that sometimes the moisture becomes part of the calcined thing.

something may be added to make its solution easier to achieve; sometimes, however, it is not added, depending on whether the matter is prone to flow or is sluggish. If anything escapes the first solution, let it be calcined <note>Reduced to powder through heat.</note> again, and let its solution be repeated until everything flows, having been reduced to water.

<margin>
On Sublimation. Definition.
</margin>
The fifth method of attenuation <note>The process of making a substance "thinner" or more subtle.</note> is **Sublimation**, which is defined by **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> as the elevation of a dry thing by fire, with it adhering to its vessel. And by **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were central to medieval science.</note> it is defined as: *The elevation of the most subtle parts from the fixed parts.* Both definitions are correct, except that Avicenna's definition is more general and seems as though it could also be applied to distillation. But he was looking at the goal of sublimation, which consists in the removal of the "earth" <note>Solid impurities or dregs.</note> from which the spirits must be freed. Geber, however, expressed the act of subliming itself more clearly and taught which things ought to be sublimated.

<margin>
What is necessary in sublimation.
</margin>
In sublimation, two things are required: first, that a dry thing be elevated; second, that it adhere to the sides or walls of the vessel so that it does not gather into drops <note>This distinguishes sublimation, where a solid turns to gas and back to solid, from distillation, where gas turns to liquid drops.</note>. However, for a dry thing to be elevated, it must either be of the nature of **spirits**, or contain the nature of both body and spirit within itself.

<margin>
What chemical spirits are, and their types.
</margin>
In this art, **spirits** are called "volatile bodies" which flee the fire and fly off into smoke; there are three primary ones: namely, **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; Mercury.</note>, **sulfur**, and **arsenic**. There are four secondary ones: **sal ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride.</note>, **tutia** <note>A term for zinc oxide crusts collected from furnaces.</note>, **magnesia**, and **marcasite** <note>Usually refers to iron pyrites or similar metallic minerals.</note>.

<margin>
Which things are to be sublimed with dregs, and which are not.
</margin>
Indeed, certain fixed things are added to quicksilver, sulfur, arsenic, and sal ammoniac to hold back their "terrestrial coarseness," lest they rise up together with the substances intended for sublimation and remain as impure as before. Tutia, magnesia, and marcasite do not require the addition of other matter because they contain sufficient—indeed, superfluous—dregs within themselves; the sign of this is the difficulty of their sublimation, which is not completed without intense ignition. If metallic bodies reduced to ash <note>original: "calcem" (calx).</note> are to be sublimated, they will necessarily require a spirit to lift them, namely sal ammoniac—although Geber and others write that certain things can be sublimated by a most vehement fire even without the addition of spirits. Nevertheless, they state that **Mars** <note>The alchemical name for Iron.</note>, on account of the slowness of its melting, requires arsenic, and **Venus** <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note> requires tutia; with these, they are easily elevated due to their affinity and the suitability of their natures. But being content with this brief mention of these more fruitful spirits, we shall pass on to the sublimations of sulfur, arsenic, and **Mercury** (which are called the "principles of nature" in the procreation of metals), after we have first briefly examined the cause for the invention of sublimation and its utility.

<header>CHAPTER TWO.</header>
<sig>rr 3</sig>

# CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>Why sublimation was invented.</margin>
...we have touched upon. This process is twofold, according to **Geber** <note>original: "Gebrum"; the Latinized name of the 8th-century chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note>. One purpose is so that the "oiliness" of sulfur and arsenic—the property of which is to be easily inflamed and to turn black through burning—may be removed. The other is so that these substances, as well as **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, may be cleansed of their earthy excess. Therefore, the entire intent of sublimation is nothing other than this: that by removing the earthiness of the aforementioned spirits, and likewise by casting away their most subtle and smoky part (which causes burning and corruption), there remains for us their "middle substance." This is the part which exists in a state of balance and which allows for a simple melting over the fire without any part of it burning away or fleeing from the heat. 

In truth, "bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to solid metals, while "spirits" refers to volatile substances like sulfur or mercury.</note> are sublimated along with "spirits" so that the density of the elements may pass into rarity through this elevation. Specifically, the dryness of the **earth** should pass into the moisture of **water**, the coldness of the **water** into the color of **air**, and the moisture of the **air** should depart into the dryness of **fire**.

<margin>A Question.</margin>
But someone will think: If water or Mercury is cleansed of its earthiness through distillation, and the earth is cleansed through **calcination** <note>Reducing a solid to a powder through high heat.</note> from the "sulfurousness" that fouls and corrupts it, what need will there be for sublimation? After all, it provides nothing more than the operations already mentioned. Or, if both of these imperfections can be removed by sublimation alone, why do we add distillation and calcination? For it is done in vain through many steps what can be done equally well through fewer.

<margin>The Response.</margin>
I answer: It is true that water is purged through distillation as much as is possible by human wit, and the earth through calcination. However, they are not so thoroughly cleansed that a new corruption does not reveal itself again when the earth is dissolved. This reveals a surplus of earthiness, as well as wateriness and a certain thin and subtle sulfurousness, all of which are removed through ingeniously repeated sublimations.

<margin>Another objection.</margin>
Again, another will say: Many of the philosophers affirm that the entire physical work is performed through sublimation alone. Therefore, calcination and distillation—and whatever other modes of operation are listed—contribute nothing except to the obscuring of the true art and the hiding of the truth.

<margin>Refutation. How the entire work is nothing but sublimation.</margin>
I confess that this has been said by many, and indeed truly, if they are understood correctly. For by the word "sublimation" alone, they encompass all the other modes of operation described by the philosophers. By these methods, the "philosophical matter"—which is vile and rejected in its raw state—is so purified and so highly elevated and promoted that no thing of the lower world (except the rational soul) can be compared to it. Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundational texts of alchemy are attributed.</note>, exclaiming with wonder, says: "This is the [strength] of the whole..." In the **Tablet**. <note>original: "In tabula"; a reference to the famous *Tabula Smaragdina* or Emerald Tablet, a brief, cryptic text highly revered by alchemists. The quote "Hæc est totius fortitudinis fortitudo fortis" translates to "This is the strong strength of all strength."</note>

<meta>catchword: strength- (forti-)</meta>

<summary>This page explains that sublimation serves to purify volatile "spirits" and "bodies" by removing oily and earthy impurities, ultimately refining them into a balanced state. The author defends the use of multiple chemical processes, arguing that sublimation is often used by philosophers as a catch-all term for the entire spiritual and physical elevation of matter.</summary>

<header>ON THE FINENESS OF MATTER</header>

<margin>The power of the physical stone.</margin>
...of strength, the strongest strength. If one were to say that no power in the whole world, no riches, and no treasures can be compared to this Stone, it is because all these things gradually fail and are exhausted; the Stone, however, the more it is refined and its operation repeated, the more it grows and increases in virtue and quantity, should the artisan desire it. A most brilliant authority for my aforementioned interpretation is one **Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A 13th-century Catalan physician and alchemist.</note>, who in the *Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "flore florū"</note> speaks thus:

<margin>What "to sublimate" means among the Philosophers.</margin>
> Our "to sublimate" is not to ascend higher or to be elevated: rather, to sublimate in a philosophical sense is to make a precious thing out of a vile thing, and to make something high, great, and pure out of a low and tiny thing. Therefore, when we speak of "sublimated bodies," understand them to be refined, and converted into a high, pure, clean, and most noble nature. For this reason, since the Stone is purified and refined from the beginning of the work to the end, the whole work is called nothing but sublimation.

<margin>The twofold sublimation of Mercury.</margin>
As for the modes of sublimation for these spirits, the sublimation of **Mercury** <term>quicksilver</term> is twofold. One is that which is done through prepared salts to remove its dross or external impurity; this must be repeated many times, with successive "resuscitations" <note>A process of returning a sublimated substance to a liquid or solid state to process it again.</note> of the same, until it is extremely white and all its natural lividness has departed. In this sublimation, only a small quantity of Mercury is lost, because the salts are easily separated from it through their dissolution.

<margin>The other from the lime of gold and silver. *Summa of Perfection*, chapter 41.</margin>
The other sublimation of Mercury, which is more perfect, is done from the "limes" <term>calx; the powdery metallic oxide remaining after heating</term> of metals. For this is what **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> intends when he says: *He who has sublimated with the lime of one of the bodies, has sublimated well, and was able to cleanse it perfectly with ease.* Regarding which bodies' lime should be taken, he hints sufficiently when he says in the same chapter that the proof of administering the dregs in their proper proportion is that the matter should be chosen with which the spirits to be sublimated most agree, and with which they are most deeply mixed. He adds the reason why such a material should be chosen as most suitable for sublimation: namely, because that substance to which the things to be sublimated are more closely united is more powerful in retaining the dregs of the things being sublimated than a substance to which they are not united. But no metallic bodies agree more with **Mercury** than the "perfect" ones—namely, **gold** and **silver**. He adds this in express words in Chapter 45, saying: *By these (namely salts, lime of eggshells, crushed marble, and similar things) it is cleansed; but by other things having an affinity with it (unless they are bodies of perfection) it is rather corrupted, because all such things have a sulfurous quality which, ascending with it in sublimation, corrupts it.* But should these "perfect bodies," filed down or reduced to very thin foils, be added to the Mercury as dregs? Not at all, for it will be cleansed no better than if it had no dregs at all. This, the experience of things [finds]...

<header>CHAPTER TWO.</header>

...observed, that when he had sublimated **Mercury** <term>quicksilver</term> from gold filings many times, he found it no cleaner. Wherefore **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 9th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note> subtlely adds: "Therefore sublimation from calxes is better than from all other things." Nor does Geber alone command Mercury to be sublimated from the calx of gold and silver, but also **Avicenna**, **Arnaldus**, and **Raymond Lull**, who all assert that the sublimation of Mercury from the calxes of the two luminaries <note>The "two luminaries" are gold (the Sun) and silver (the Moon).</note> is easy, takes less time, and is useful to the artisan. Thus, among others, the venerable Lull says in his *Codicil* <note>original: "Codicil."</note>, in the chapter "On the investigation of the cause why the second dissolution is made": "If you sublimate with the calxes of the two luminaries, you will sublimate usefully and purify it with ease." But I wish these things to be understood concerning the sublimation of common quicksilver, not concerning the **Mercury of the bodies** <note>The "Mercury of bodies" refers to the essential spirit or liquid principle extracted from solid metals, as opposed to common liquid quicksilver.</note>, which cannot be better sublimated than from its own calx, since no other substance is more closely related to it than this.

<margin>
How the 
watery nature 
of Mercury 
is removed.
</margin>
The removal of the superfluous watery nature of Mercury is accomplished when it is mixed with the calxes from which it must be sublimated; it should be ground and mixed with them by **imbibition** <term>the process of slowly adding liquid to a dry powder to moisten it</term> until nothing of the Mercury appears. Afterward, it is treated with a very slow fire, so that the substance of the Mercury does not rise, but the wateriness of the imbibition is removed. As this recedes, the wateriness of the quicksilver also recedes, and the remainder is removed through the repetition of the sublimation.

<margin>
The sign of per-
fect subli-
mation. 
*The Sum of Perfection*, 
chap. 45.
</margin>
Geber indicates the sign of perfect sublimation of quicksilver to us in these words: "If it gives a good fusion, and has a bright and most white color, and is transparent, then you have sufficiently managed the sublimation."

<margin>
Which subli-
mation of 
sulfur and 
arsenic is 
better.
</margin>
The sublimation of **sulfur** and **arsenic** is the same, just as their matter is also the same, differing only in this: that with arsenic the **white elixir** <note>The stage of the Great Work that transforms base metals into silver.</note> is perfected, and with sulfur, the **red elixir** <note>The final stage of the Great Work that transforms base metals into gold.</note>. They are rightly sublimated from prepared salt, or from vitriol, or alum reduced into a red calx, or from scales of iron, or burnt copper, as Geber is the authority, or from the calxes of metals—which is better—until they are perfectly whitened and take on the whiteness of snow. Indeed, the sublimation of these is similar to the sublimation of Mercury; hence Geber's chapter on arsenic.

<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection*, 
chap. 41. 
Which subli-
mation is 
better.
</margin>
Arsenic is **fixed** <term>transformed from a volatile substance into one that can withstand heat without evaporating</term> just like sulfur, and the sublimation of both from the calxes of metals is better. But those do best who join these purified and refined spirits with grinding and imbibition, then coagulate them with gentle boiling, and afterward push them upward with great violence of fire. For they will find them perfectly purified both from earthy dregs and from that thin and smoky part of theirs that causes burning and corruption. And without doubt Geber understood this when, speaking of Sulfur, he says: "He who seeks to draw out the work from it, should not draw it out by preparing it by itself, since with the mixture..."

# ON THE SUBTLETY OF MATTER #

...is perfected, and without it the **mastery** <term>magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work</term> is prolonged even to the point of despair. Nothing, however, is more easily mixed with **sulfur** than with **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term>. This is known to the pharmacists <note>original: "pharmacopœi"</note>, who, when composing ointments or salves from **mercury** <term>hydrargyrum</term>, usually add some sulfur and grind them together; in this way, they both hide the mercury and cause it to be more easily joined with the other simple ingredients entering the same compound.

<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 53. **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> explained.
</margin>
**Geber** teaches this same thing, saying: "Quicksilver is easily mixed with sulfur, arsenic, and marcasite because of their common nature." He also suggests this sublimation in the chapter "On Sulfur": "Sulfur is mixed with Mercury, and from them, through decoction <note>A process of heating or boiling</note>, a celestial and delightful color is made." Understand "decoction" here as that which is followed by sublimation, though Geber remains silent on this point in this passage according to his custom—for he delivers the art in scattered bits across various chapters—but he explains himself in another place when he writes in the chapter "On Sublimation": "Through manifold grinding and gentle roasting, the greater part of the wateriness of quicksilver is destroyed, the remainder of which is removed through sublimation. And when you see it to be of a most brilliant white, exceeding snow in its whiteness, and clinging to the segments of the **aludels** <term>specialized earthenware pots used as condensers in the sublimation process</term> as if dead, then repeat its sublimation without the dregs." What he previously called "decoction," he here names "gentle roasting"; what he kept silent about regarding sublimation there, he adds here. Even if he had not added it, it could still be understood from the effect of sublimation itself, when he says, "when you see it clinging to the segments of the aludels as if dead," which cannot happen without sublimation. Nor should anyone imagine that Geber or his translator understands "celestial color" to mean sky-blue, purple, violet, or artificial **cinnabar**; for in that same chapter 28, he had previously stated that sulfur is joined to mercury and becomes **usifur** through sublimation. Now, the **usifur** of the Arabs is nothing other than our artificial **cinnabar** <note>A bright red mineral, mercuric sulfide</note>.

<margin>
What the **celestial** or **heavenly color** means to the Chemists.
</margin>
Nor do chemical authors use the name "celestial" or "heavenly color" in almost any other way than for that color which, in its whiteness, surpasses all the whitenesses of the entire world, and seems more heavenly than earthly. Thus says the ***Rosary*** <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note>: "Sublimate the Mercury until it possesses a celestial color, that is, until it becomes most white." **Mireris** <note>An ancient authority often cited in alchemical compendiums</note> suggests this wonderful color of whiteness, saying: "If you should see this suddenly, wonder, fear, and terror will come upon you." As if he were to say: "If you see this most white color beyond your expectation, you will marvel as if at a supernatural thing, and you will fear at the same time lest some delusion lies beneath it..."

It cites authorities like Geber and the Rosarium to clarify that this state of purity is achieved by removing the "watery nature" of the quicksilver.</summary>

### CHAPTER THE SECOND ###

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 32.</margin>
<margin>Chapter 45, *The Sum of Perfection*.</margin>
...and vanishes from your eyes. I said "almost" because sometimes a "celestial" color is taken for blue or azure <note>original: "cæruleo siue lazurio"</note>. Just as in Geber, in the chapter on silver, speaking in this way: "Placed over the fumes of sharp things, such as vinegar, sal ammoniac <term>ammonium chloride</term>, and verjuice <note>original: "agrestæ"; the juice of unripe grapes</note>, a wonderful celestial color is produced." Geber also clearly discusses this conjunction of spirits to be sublimated in another place: "Do not be negligent in the preparation of quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, which is performed through sublimation, because as the cleansing is, so shall the perfection follow. Whence it happens that some form iron, some indeed lead, some Venus <term>copper</term>, and others tin; this happens because of negligence in purification, sometimes of that [mercury] alone, sometimes of the sulfur mixed with it, or its companion, namely arsenic." And let these things suffice regarding the methods of sublimation.

<margin>Vessel for sublimation.</margin>
The vessels should be of glass, wide at the bottom and tapering to a point, like the shape which mathematicians call a cone; or they may even be convex and vaulted without a beak, like a blind alembic <note>A still without a pouring spout, used when the substance is meant to circulate or settle on the walls rather than drain out</note>, so that the sublimated spirits may adhere to their chambers and sides. The lower dish should be made of earth, which may fitly receive the upper vessel within its walls.

<margin>The sign of perfect sublimation of sulfur and arsenic.</margin>
The proof of the goodness and perfection of the sublimation of these two spirits <note>sulfur and arsenic</note> is that it be found clear and bright, and not burnt. As Geber teaches in *The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 45.

<margin>Ceration attenuates.</margin>
Among the methods of attenuation <note>making a substance thinner or more "subtle"</note>, **Ceration** <term>the process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax</term> is not the least. By this process, a hard and infusible medicine is prepared for liquefaction, so that it may flow and enter [the metal], which does not happen except through grinding and imbibition <note>soaking or saturating a solid with a liquid</note>. Those things which are imbibed are softened, and the more they are softened, the more the gross and hard parts are made subtle. But because this method of attenuation, its definition, and the reasons for its invention were spoken of abundantly in Chapter One, I did not think they should be repeated here, as it suffices only to have hinted at them.

<margin>The three benefits of thinness. The first.</margin>
Now let us review in general the benefits of the thinness <note>original: "tenuitatis"</note> of the Medicine, which are primarily three. First, if the medicine is not extremely subtle, it will not instantly penetrate the bodies to be transmuted; if indeed it does not penetrate, it will not even be mixed; if it is not mixed, it will not alter nor tint. Therefore, we have taught that all earthiness and gross wateriness must be most accurately removed by certain methods of operation, leaving only the middle substance of Mercury, which is most thin and airy. For the earthy...

### ON THE THINNESS OF MATTER ###
<meta>catchword: brings</meta>

...and it cannot penetrate what is dense, but that which is thin and airy penetrates easily and tints. Hence, a certain Philosopher says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early alchemical text written as a debate between philosophers</note>:

<margin>Thin medicine compared to air.</margin>
> Body does not penetrate body, but a subtle, congealed substance does, which penetrates and colors the body.

The philosophers could not better compare this thin substance of the stone than to air. Thus, the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century collection of alchemical "flowers" or sayings</note> states:

> If this stone were not of an airy nature, it would not be joined to Mercury, nor mixed with it, nor enter into it; but because they are similar, they are mixed and joined together so thoroughly that fire cannot separate them.

In this passage, one must consider that the author of the *Rosary* compares the perfected stone with Mercury—not indeed in its "decoction" <note>the process of heating or "cooking" the substance</note>, which is at its greatest in the Elixir and at its least or non-existent in common quicksilver, but rather in its nature and "root." This is because they consist of the same principles, and because the matter of the Elixir cannot be brought to perfection unless it has been reduced into Mercury and made subtle like common quicksilver <term>argentum vivum</term>, to which the Philosophers attributed no less of an airy nature. 

Thus Avicenna, Lull, and Arnaldus <note>referring to Avicenna, Ramon Lull, and Arnaldus de Villa Nova, three of the most cited authorities in medieval alchemy</note> say of it: Quicksilver is homogeneous in nature, since it either remains entirely fixed in the fire or entirely flies away from it as smoke, as it is incombustible and airy, which is a sign of perfection. Therefore, just as quicksilver can be sublimated and driven into the air, so it is also necessary for the entire matter of the Elixir to be made volatile and become "Mercury," so that it may ascend into the alembic <term>a distilling apparatus</term> or into the aludel <term>a series of pear-shaped pots used for sublimation</term>. Whence Aristotle says:

> Nothing is suitable for our stone that has not been alive, and has not sought the heaven of the air.

<margin>The second benefit of thinness. *The Testament*, chapter 72.</margin>
This airy nature of the Stone brings another significant advantage, as it is the cause of a completely equal and uniform "fusion" <note>the state of being melted or blended</note>, which Raymond Lull ascribes to air in these words:

> If the stone were not of a thin substance, it could not have a uniform fusion, nor a continuous softening, nor would one part follow the other well. And through this property, it is necessary that air dominates in the said substance; that is, that our stone be generated from an airy nature, for otherwise the property of air could not dominate in it unless it were generated from its true substance.

<margin>The third [benefit].</margin>
To these two advantages provided by the thinness of the matter in the Elixir, a third is added of no less importance: namely, that it is the cause of weight. For the thickness <note>original: "spissitudo"; density or coarseness</note> of metals is the cause of their weight, which follows a good mixing of earth with water. However, the thinner the earth and water are, the more and the better they are mixed, united, and thickened—and this perfected thickening brings about weight.

It cites major authorities to explain how this "thinness" facilitates the uniform blending of elements and ultimately creates the density and weight characteristic of gold.</summary>

Geber <note>A Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy</note> himself confirms this, saying: "The cause of great weight is the fineness of the substance of bodies and uniformity in essence.
