The same author, speaking of the nature of gold, says: "Because gold has subtle and fixed parts, they could be condensed greatly, and this was the cause of its great weight." Regarding the weight of quicksilver, the same says: "Even a one-eyed man can clearly see through its appearance that quicksilver has a dense substance, because of the heaviness of its immense weight, since it outweighs gold when it is in its own nature." 

Let these things, therefore, be said both concerning the matter from which the Elixir is forged, and concerning the absolutely necessary thinning <term>attenuatio</term> of the perfected Medicine and the benefits of its subtlety. <header>ON THE AFFINITY OF MEDICINE AND METALS</header>

<margin>
The Alchemical Work is completed through nature alone by the service of the artisan.
</margin>
...nature putrefies, produces, and renews. By these words, the authors intended to show that the chemical work <note>original: *opus Chemicum*</note> is purely natural. It is Nature herself who desires, retains, digests, expels, corrupts, generates, and gives form both to the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary catalyst of alchemy</note> and to the metals through their joining. The artisan <note>the alchemist</note> merely serves Nature by providing the appropriate heat. 

For how does "nature rejoice in nature" <note>A famous alchemical axiom often attributed to Pseudo-Democritus</note> unless by the desire and attraction for what it lacks? How does it "contain" unless by holding onto what it desires and finds familiar? How does "nature overcome nature" unless by digesting what it has held, transmuting it from one state <note>original: *dispositione*</note> to another, and casting out what is superfluous or unsuitable? 

In the same way, Nature putrefies itself; for unless the cause of putrefaction exists within it—arising from an imbalance of the elements or their qualities—the Alchemical Art will struggle in vain to induce decay in a thing. This is clear in the composition of gold: because all its qualities are so perfectly balanced <note>original: *temperiem*</note>, it never suffers putrefaction unless its form is first destroyed by a force brought against its nature; otherwise, remaining in its own composition, it is everlasting and incorruptible. 

Art can indeed sometimes make things decay faster, or perhaps in a different way than Nature would if left alone, yet the corruption of the thing must necessarily arise from its own nature. Ultimately, all things existing beneath the sphere of the Moon <note>the "sublunary" realm of the Earth, which in ancient science was the only place where things were born, died, and changed</note> spontaneously succumb to this. 

By the same reasoning, Nature produces itself. For unless a thing possesses the power of producing and procreating, the artisan labors in vain to instill it. Just as chicks are brought forth from eggs not only by the brooding of a hen, but also by human skill <note>likely referring to early artificial incubators used in Egypt and described by travelers</note>. No one wonders at this, for everyone knows it happens by the power God placed within the egg: when cherished by the right heat, they produce the same species of bird as the egg. It does not matter if that heat comes from the hen, another bird, or even heat stirred up by human industry. 

<margin>
Eels and other small creatures are produced naturally through putrefaction arranged by the artisan.
</margin>
Even more wonderful is that human skill can produce eels or other small creatures <note>original: *animalcula*</note> through the putrefaction of a certain animal, or of several herbs mixed together, or even from a single leaf, when managed in the proper way. Yet "Art" cannot be said to have produced these animals; it is Nature. Unless that power had been inherent in those materials, even when arranged by art, no living animal would ever have emerged. This is most clear because not just any animals or herbs, when putrefied and arranged in the same way...

### CHAPTER THREE

<margin>The Stone kills and revives itself.</margin>
...but from certain things, certain and determined outcomes are produced. In the same way, Nature renews itself. For our Stone <note>original: *Lapis noster*, referring to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical work</note>, no differently than that phoenix known to us from the myths of the ancients, mortifies itself and resuscitates itself through its own nature. For, as Haly <note>Haly Abenragel or Khalid ibn Yazid, an Arabic authority often cited in Latin alchemy</note> says, just as it dies when its spirits are taken away, so it is brought back to life when those same spirits return to it; and thus it is transformed by its very own nature, nor is there any need for it to borrow anything from elsewhere.

The Philosophers have spoken in a similar way: "Nature is not corrected except within its own nature." <note>original: *Naturam non emendari nisi in sua natura*</note> This can be understood both regarding the refinement of the substances that make up the elixir <note>The "elixir" is the medicinal or perfected form of the Stone</note>, and the metals which are to be converted by the Stone. If we consider the "first matter" <note>the raw, primordial substance of the work</note> of the elixir, although it naturally contains its own tincture <note>the "tincture" is the active essence that "colors" or transforms a metal's properties</note> within itself, nevertheless this tincture is not sufficient for transmuting other metals. This is because nature works simply toward its own perfection only, and cannot transcend that degree; therefore it desires to be improved—certainly by the industry and labor of the artisan, but nonetheless through its own nature. This means that the natural tincture implanted within it must be refined <note>original: *subtilietur*</note> and its power increased, which cannot happen unless it is first made "spiritual" <note>meaning refined into a volatile or gaseous state</note> and extracted from the compact, hard, and solid body. 

<margin>All things are multiplied by an indwelling spirit.</margin>
For we see that all things multiply themselves and produce their like through a certain indwelling spirit. And so, although the artisan helps nature and in some way corrects it, nevertheless without nature—which is prone and inclined toward achieving perfection—he accomplishes nothing. For it is necessary that nature works secretly and internally within the Art, while the artisan serves only from the outside. 

<margin>Nature works from within, Art from without. The artisan is the servant of nature.</margin>
Therefore, the artisan is only a helper and servant of nature, refining it and moving and exciting the internal heat (which was dormant and languishing in the matter) by the heat of the external fire. This internal heat then completes the whole work through natural action without the addition of any foreign thing. Although Art may therefore improve nature and sometimes transcend and overcome it, it does not produce a *new* nature, but only refines nature’s power and uncovers and reveals the subtle nature enclosed within a thing. In this way, Art brings out glass from the ash of a fern or another plant; if the substance of glass had not been hidden in the ashes by nature, the artisan would struggle in vain to draw glass from them. For nothing can be brought out of things that is not in them by nature. To this point, Senior <note>Senior Zadith, a famous 10th-century alchemist</note> says aptly and appropriately: "There has not been born, nor will there be born in..."

It emphasizes that the alchemist does not create new properties but merely uses external fire to "awaken" the natural, internal spirit already present in the matter.</summary>

In the *Book of Figures*.

...later, he who could complete this science without nature—a nature divinely endowed and infused into things. And Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note> says: It is manifest that the operation of medicine is the operation of nature, and the medicine itself is that same nature, because the medicine itself is composed solely from nature. If we understand the improvement of base metals by the Elixir through these words—that "nature is not improved except within its own nature" (for we hinted at a double interpretation of this phrase above)—that too happens only through nature, as will be clear from what is said below. Now, let us consider the definition of Nature.

<margin>
Definition of Nature according to Marsilio Ficino.
</margin>
Setting aside evasions and long disputes, we say with Marsilio Ficino <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar and priest who led the revival of Neoplatonism.</note> that nature is a certain force implanted in things, procreating like from like. Likewise, Nature is an invisible fire, or a certain fiery vigor implanted in created things, by which all things multiply themselves, since without heat nothing can be generated. This invisible fire, or this power of procreating its own likeness, consists in the "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or identity of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> of each thing; for through the form of a thing, nature is perpetuated, and its greatest power is seen most of all in procreating its likeness.

<margin>
Every form is drawn out from its own matter.
</margin>
Now, the form of the Stone is the **metallic soul**, which by its heat digests its matter, tints it with dryness, and impresses upon it the form of gold and silver. But since every form must be of the same kind as its matter and potentially exists within its matter (for only the human soul is introduced from outside its matter), it is necessary that this soul giving form to the Elixir be the same as the matter of the stone. Similarly, since the perfected **Elixir** <note>The "medicine" or Philosopher's Stone in its active, transformative state.</note> stands—according to the chemical Philosophers—as form to matter, and as soul to body, it must be of the same kind and matter as the metallic bodies themselves. But all metals consist of "silver" <note>original: *argento*, likely referring to *argentum vivum* or mercury, one of the two primary principles of metals.</note> and sulfur, as all philosophers attest; therefore the Elixir must also necessarily consist of these same principles. 

<margin>
The nature of the proximity between the Elixir and metals.
</margin>
Those things which have the same principles and the same manner of mixing agree most in their root and are most closely related; and this is that affinity or proximity between the Elixir and the substance to be transmuted—adhering to and retaining its like—which Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy.</note> requires in the third place among the properties of medicine. To explain this further concerning the single matter, form, generation, and mutual transmutation of metals according to nature, and how art imitates the same, we look to the writings of the venerable Ramon Llull <note>A Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> in his...

### CHAPTER THREE

...firstly, and following the opinion and authority of **Master Pietro Bono of Ferrara** <note>A 14th-century alchemist and author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella*, known for synthesizing ancient Greek and Arabic philosophical views on alchemy.</note> who most diligently collected the opinions of the ancient philosophers, we will deal with these matters briefly; then we shall teach how the **Elixir**, by its conformity and likeness, enters into metals and adheres to them.

<margin>That the matter of all metals is one and the same is proven by five arguments.</margin>
Firstly, the liquefaction of all metals clearly demonstrates that their matter is one and the same: for indeed, every metal, once it has been melted, displays the nature and accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or state, as opposed to the core "substance."</note> of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi" (mercury)</note>. Hence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the fourth book of his *Meteorology* says: "Lead, when it is melted, is without a doubt quicksilver." Likewise, their solidification, and ductility, and the fact that they are easily mixed together prove this; for all mixing occurs by reason of similarity and identity. Thus water is easily mixed with water, oil with oil, glass with glass, and metal with metal; they join and adhere because of their shared nature. Finally, this is shown by the fact that all metals can be reduced into quicksilver, from which they had their origin, as is established by various experiments of learned men, and even by the confession of opponents who strive to tear down the truth of the chemical art <note>Alchemy</note>, among whom is **Thomas Erastus**, a Doctor of Medicine <note>Erastus (1524–1583) was a famous Swiss physician and theologian who wrote a massive critique of Paracelsian alchemy.</note>. Moreover, that "first matter" of all metals, as we said in Chapter 1, is a viscous moisture, incombustible and subtle, incorporated with a subtle earth, mixed equally and strongly <term>per minima: an alchemical term for mixing at the most fundamental, atomic level</term> within the mines.

<margin>The first matter of metals. The more immediate matter.</margin>
But their more immediate <note>original: "propinquior" (nearer or proximate)</note> matter, as the Philosophers teach, is **quicksilver**, generated from that strong mixing of those elements. But since matter does not bring itself into being, wise and sagacious Nature has joined to it its own proper agent, so that by digesting and cooking it, she may convert it into the form of a metal.

<margin>The most immediate matter.</margin>
Therefore, the most immediate and closest matter of metals is not quicksilver in its raw state, but as it has been solidified by its own agent—namely, **liquefiable sulfur**—and mixed with that sulfur and converted into a kind of earth. From these two thus mixed, a vapor arises, ascending by a most temperate heat and reflecting back <note>original: "reverberans"</note> upon its own earth, until through a tempered cooking over a long time, a certain metallic fixation occurs there, resulting in diverse bodies according to the nature of the place.

### ON THE AFFINITY OF MEDICINE AND METALS

<margin>
...mutually, from which it may be known.
</margin>
...mutually, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy.</note>, **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist who classified materials based on their chemical properties.</note>, and other philosophers are the authors of this view. In those things having a **correspondence** <note>original: "symbolum." In Aristotelian physics, this refers to shared qualities (like heat or moisture) that allow one substance to change into another.</note> in matter, and virtues, and natural powers, transmutation into one another is easy, not only through **art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to alchemy—the human technological intervention in natural processes.</note>, but also through nature. A sign of their transmutation by nature into gold and silver is their mixing within a single ore-vein, and their successive change. Indeed, in many mines of silver and copper, gold is found, just as in mines of lead, copper, and tin, silver is found. These imperfect things are **ripened** <note>original: "decoquuntur" (literally "cooked down"). Alchemists believed metals "grew" and "ripened" in the earth over long periods of time.</note> over time, and are transmuted into gold or silver according to the place of their generation.

<margin>
There is only one perfect form of metals: in gold.
</margin>
For there is one ultimate and perfect form of metals, and that is gold, which nature alone provides in the mines (unless she has been hindered by some accident), and which Art provides outside the mines. If the remaining metals were perfect and complete in that nature in which they exist, then without a doubt they would not be convertible to another, unless they were first reduced to the **first matter** <note>The "materia prima," the formless base substance from which all things are made.</note>—that is, into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum" (mercury).</note> and **sulfur**.

<margin>
The two-fold mode of the generation of gold by nature.
</margin>
But nature assumes a double mode in the generation of gold: one through itself and primarily—namely, because it generates pure gold in its own mines and from its own principles, without the admixture of other metals; the other through itself indeed, but not primarily, because it first generates some of the imperfect metals from those same principles in its mine, and finally converts them into gold.

<margin>
One matter for nature and for art.
</margin>
If, therefore, the intention of Art is to follow nature entirely, and as far as is possible, so that it may make the same gold as nature itself—since every generation happens from suitable and proximate things—whatever and of what kind the matter is for nature, the same will necessarily be for Art. Since the matter is one and entirely determined for nature, and not manifold, then necessarily that same determined matter will likewise be for Art, and not manifold.

This matter which is subject to nature, as we have said, is **quicksilver**, according to all philosophers, both the naturalists and the chemists; therefore, for the art of alchemy, the matter will likewise be quicksilver.

<margin>
The same agent for nature and for art.
</margin>

<margin>How Art follows Nature.</margin>
...of silvers and gold. According to all natural philosophers, it is necessary that some metal be generated from this process at the end of digestion, and ultimately, gold. It seems necessary, therefore, that this same agent [sulfur], when joined in the Art <note>The term "Art" here refers specifically to the craft of alchemy—the human imitation of natural processes.</note>, must be combined with quicksilver so that it may guide, digest, and give it form. When this has been returned to its own earth, it creates a "fixation" <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire.</note> there, and at last becomes a completed **elixir**.

Instead, Art borrows these things from nature. What nature could not provide—as she works simply toward perfection—Art purifies and refines, and by means of artificial heat, finally converts into gold, and further into an <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Elixir" or Philosopher's Stone was believed to be a substance that could "perfect" base metals into gold instantly.</note>. <margin>External sulfur hinders the perfection of metals.</margin>
...it cooks and <term>digests</term> <note>The process of maturing or ripening a substance through steady, gentle heat.</note> the material by turning, revolving, and washing it. But because the sulfur remaining in the metals, or with their <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, renders them impure, porous, and liable to burning—to a greater or lesser degree depending on its quantity and quality—it does not allow them to reach the perfection of gold. This perfection consists primarily in purity, fineness, solidity, and <term>fixation</term> <note>The chemical state where a substance becomes stable and resistant to the transformative power of fire.</note>. Therefore, at the end of its action, Nature separates that sulfur from the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver."</note>, which was Nature's primary focus. Nature then informs it with the "form" of gold, fixes it, and perfects it without sulfur. If sulfur remains before the digestion is complete, the substance degenerates from the substance and form of gold and becomes another [base] metal, or gold mixed with impurities. Thus, it is clear what the material of metals is in the natural world, what the active agent is, and what the ultimate goal is in this operation.

<margin>The material of Art is prepared by Nature.</margin>
<margin>In what way Art and Nature differ.</margin>
Therefore, because this Art <note>The "Art" refers to alchemy, the human imitation and perfection of natural processes.</note> rarely finds anything in the metal mines that is pure quicksilver in its own nature, nor anything that is similarly pure sulfur—for while it is false to say they are never found, they are usually found already generated and mixed together into an earthy state—and because the alchemist sees each of these born separately by Nature in its own proper mine: therefore, Art, in following Nature, does not take quicksilver alone, nor sulfur alone, nor even quicksilver and sulfur joined together haphazardly. Instead, it takes the same mixed material, composed of those same principles, which Nature has prepared for Art, just as a provident mother prepares for her daughter. Nature joins them from the very beginning of the metals' generation, not unlike how butter, cheese, and whey are all contained within milk. But afterwards, Art separates and sets that material apart; then, once purified, Art joins and digests it again using only externally applied heat while Nature operates from within, until that external sulfur is separated from the quicksilver. Once this separation is achieved, the craftsman is necessarily compelled to give the quicksilver the form of the **Stone**, by infusing into it its own proper soul—one taken from its own material and not from something foreign—and so brings the work to its conclusion. For all matter receives its form in its own time, according as it is capable of receiving that form, and neither sooner nor later. But Art and Nature differ in this: Nature perfects quicksilver into gold through a single <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctio," a process of "boiling" or ripening through heat.</note>, whereas Art requires a double decoction to reach the perfection of the **Elixir**. Yet, Art's process is very brief compared to Nature's, and in this, Art wonderfully surpasses Nature. For the operation of Nature does not proceed beyond the form of gold...

### CHAPTER III.

...yields, since that is its ultimate end: yet Art <note>Referring to the practice of alchemy, the "Art" of imitating nature.</note>, not content with this, when it has reached the boundary of gold, cooks it further <note>original: "decoquit," a process of ripening through heat.</note> and colors it more, so that by the abundance of color and <term>digestion</term> <note>The alchemical process of maturing or ripening a substance through steady, gentle heat.</note>, it communicates and impresses the form of gold upon imperfect and base metals.

<margin>The composition of quicksilver.</margin>
I stated above that Nature, after the action of external sulfur is complete, fixes and perfects silver without sulfur. I would not want this to be understood as if <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> lacks its own internal sulfur, since in its first creation it possesses many parts of an actual white, earthy, sulfurous substance. These belong to its material substance, and without them the substance of quicksilver cannot exist. For it is a composite, as is clear from the <note>Aristotle was commonly referred to as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> Philosopher in the fourth book of *Meteorology*, where he shows its composition, saying: "Quicksilver is like water, which is mixed with an extremely fine earthy substance by a strong sulfurous mixture, until it does not rest on a flat surface; and this is due to the great earthy dryness within it, and therefore it does not stick to what it touches." <margin>*Sum of Perfection*, chapter 30.</margin> And also by <note>Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) was a legendary 8th-century alchemist whose writings were foundational to the field.</note> Geber, who says: "Quicksilver, which is also called Mercury by the usage of the ancients, is a viscous water in the bowels of the earth, a fine substance, united with white earth by a most temperate heat in such a union of the smallest parts, until the moist is tempered by the dry, and the dry by the moist, equally." From these sayings of the philosophers, the composition of quicksilver is manifest.

<margin>Gold stripped of all external sulfur.</margin>
Nor do I mean that henceforth a perfect <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence or change its properties.</note> of quicksilver into gold takes place entirely without any sulfur. Rather, I mean that the external sulfur—which was joined to the quicksilver in the beginning and then separated from it—extracts through digestion that sulfur which is visibly white in quicksilver and potentially red. This sulfur then informs the quicksilver itself with the form of gold and fixes it by its action. From the aforesaid, it is clear that both the gold of nature and the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> consist of the substance of quicksilver alone.

<margin>Question.</margin>
But someone may object to me using the authority of Geber, who explains the nature of gold and its composition thus: "Gold was created from the most subtle substance of quicksilver, clear and fixed, and from a small substance of the world's sulfur, of pure redness, fixed, clear, and changed from its own nature, tinting it."

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To these words, Geber seems to assert that gold consists not only of silver but also of sulfur. To which I respond: Geber, by the substance of this sulfur changed from its own nature...

# ON THE AFFINITY OF MEDICINE AND METALS

...it is necessary to collect it: but it must be of the most subtle and pure substance, adhering to it by its own nature. And in the same place <note>Referring back to the works of Geber mentioned on the previous page.</note>: Nature embraces its own nature more friendlily, and rejoices in it more than in foreign things.

<margin>The labors of the **Sophists** <note>In an alchemical context, "Sophists" refers to "puffer" alchemists who used incorrect materials or deceptive methods, rather than the true principles of nature.</note> in vegetables or animals are examined.</margin>

I have shown the generation of gold through nature and how art follows it most closely, and by what reasoning the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The transmuting agent or "Medicine" of the metals, believed to be capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> enters and pervades metals, and adheres to and retains what is neighboring and related to it. Now let us briefly examine the works of the Sophists and those who seek the philosophers' stone in vegetables and animals and their parts or excrements, stones, glasses, salts, and other mineral intermediaries. Let us consider how they attempt to imitate nature, and what affinity their material has with the metals to be transmuted.

In the first place, those who labor in vegetables and animals, their parts or excrements, or things originating from them, have almost one single intention. This is because they find in the books of the philosophers that the Stone must be composed of the four elements purified by art and joined together again. Thus, after preliminary <term>putrefactions</term> <note>The process of rotting or breaking down a substance to release its components.</note> in manure, they receive through distillations first a clear water by itself; second, a white oil, which they call air—while the dregs or "earth" remain at the bottom. In this earth is the fire, or <term>tincture</term> <note>The concentrated coloring or transforming principle.</note>. To extract this, they pour the abstracted water back onto the dregs and putrefy it again. Gradually increasing the fire after the evaporation of the water, they distill a red oil, which they think is fire; or, they receive it after the white oil without any intervening soaking. They "rectify" <note>To purify a liquid through repeated distillation.</note> these elements of theirs by distilling them many times, as they say, and finally they join together all the earths remaining from each distillation and reduce them to lime or ash. They gradually <term>imbibe</term> <note>original: "imbibunt"; to soak a dry substance with liquid until it is saturated.</note> the ash, first with the water (or phlegm), then with the white oil, and finally with the red oil. In this way, with the elements rightly joined, they believe they have composed the elixir.

But when they cast the material prepared in this way upon molten metals, they see it partly vanish into smoke and partly fail to enter—much less induce any alteration or transmutation which they were expecting.

<margin>The cause of the error.</margin>

The cause of the error is manifest: they did not care to investigate or adopt the principles from which nature perfects metals in the mines, but rather used alien and foreign things which are burned and evaporate, and have no proximity to metals. They would more rightly listen to Parmenides saying in the <term>Turba</term> <note>original: "Turba"; refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), an influential early alchemical text written as a dialogue between ancient sages.</note>: "Unless the [natures] of truth..." <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ras," which begins the word "naturas" on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page critiques alchemists who mistakenly attempt to create the Philosophers' Stone from organic materials like plants and animal waste. The author explains that because these substances lack a natural affinity with metals, they simply evaporate when applied to a melt rather than effecting a transmutation.</summary>

### CHAPTER III.

...you should direct [your matters], and well-fit their complexions, and join blood-relatives to blood-relatives, or you work in vain. And a little later: Strive to know which things have near and far relations naturally, and which stone is a friend to which stone, and how they love and embrace each other; with these signs, apply your hands to the work. If you are ignorant of these stated qualities, 
<margin>Question.</margin> do not approach this work. But perhaps someone among those who spend their labor on such trivialities will say that the philosophers affirm the Stone consists of **spirit**, **soul**, and **body** <note>This triad—*Spiritus, Anima, Corpus*—represents the three essential components of any substance in alchemical theory, later popularized by Paracelsus as Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt.</note>: by spirit they mean water, by soul they mean oil or the **radical moisture** <note>original: *humidum radicale*; the innate, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist in all things.</note>, and by body the earth; therefore, since we can demonstrate these same things in our work, what will stop the Stone from being produced from them? For we have water, we have oil, we have also earth or lime <note>original: *calcem*; here meaning the solid, powdery residue left after heating a substance.</note>. You have these, I admit, but they are not only alien to metallic nature, but even to vegetable or animal nature; so that even if you wished to compose the same plant, herb, or animal, or its part or excrement from those same things which you call principles and elements, you still could not do it, although you extracted your elements from them. Much less, then, will you compose a metal from them, or an **elixir** <note>The "Medicine" or transmuting agent capable of turning base metals into gold or silver.</note> for transmuting other imperfect bodies, with which they have no similarity. 
<margin>Solution.</margin> For your elements are disproportionate, nor can you reunite or mix them again by any art so that the oil and water do not abandon their earth and evaporate; whereas in metals, the moisture is so united with the dry that one is never abandoned by the other, but they remain together in the fire, or fly away together <note>The author is describing the "fixity" of metals; unlike organic matter which burns away, true metallic elements stay bound together even under extreme heat.</note>. If, however, the elements of metals or of the elixir are disproportionate—as when clear or transparent water is drawn from them leaving the earth by itself (just as those do who, for women's cosmetics, throw **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyrum*</note> into an oblong vessel heated by fire and catch its "water")—certainly these will be no more fit for producing the stone than the things mentioned above. Furthermore, if it were enough to have water, oil, and earth—since there is nothing in the nature of things that does not consist of water and earth and some radical moisture—then, according to their judgment, metals and the elixir could be made from all things; and not only these, but anything else: animal, plant, or stone. For why a metal rather than anything else? And thus the opinion of those who assert that *anything can be made from anything* <note>original: *quodlibet è quolibet fieri*</note> would grow strong and be renewed.

<summary>The author argues that the Philosophers' Stone must be made from metallic substances, refuting those who claim it can be made from plants or animals simply because they also contain "spirit, soul, and body." He emphasizes that the elements in metals are uniquely and inseparably bonded, unlike the disproportionate elements found in organic matter or cosmetics.</summary>

...how absurd this is—not to say impious toward God, who implanted a specific seed in almost everything created by Him, so that each thing might produce a species similar to itself—anyone can see.

<margin>The preposterous opinion of those seeking the elixir in stones and gems.</margin>
<margin>In what way stones seem to agree with metals.</margin>
But perhaps those who spend their labor on gems and stones find this affinity with metals within their own material. For just as metal is generated in mountains and mines, so too are stones and gems, and thus they share the same place of generation. And just as metal consists of an oily moisture mixed with earth, so too do stones; for unless the moisture of stones were sticky, the dry earthy part would not retain the moisture, nor would the watery moisture existing within the dry part create a continuous whole, but would instead exhale, and the earth would remain dry and crumbly. To this we say: it is not enough for this "neighborly" affinity to share the same place of generation, or the same distant principles distinguished by certain degrees, but those principles ought to be very near and immediate. Moreover, although the viscous moisture of the earth mixed together is the immediate material of stones, it is a very remote material for metals; they do not agree in the manner of their mixing, nor in the subtlety of their substance.

<margin>How the moisture of stones differs from the moisture of metals. Book 10, *On Minerals*.</margin>
For the moisture in the earthy substance of stones is not bound by the dry part in the smallest possible pieces of one and the other, but in coarse parts of the moist and the dry, so that the moist parts lie together with the earthy ones like the hooks of a chain, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop whose writings on the "science of stones" and minerals were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> says. In metals, however, the smallest bit of earth is mixed with the smallest bit of water, and vice versa, and the greatest part of one with the greatest of the other. One is not separated from the other because of the homogeneity of the parts and the union of the elements, which is the opposite of what occurs in stones. For we see their moisture easily vanish in fire, and the stone is reduced to lime <note>original: *calcem*; the crumbly, white powder (calcium oxide) left after heating limestone.</note>, because the moisture evaporates and does not protect its earth throughout. Stones have neither such oily moisture, nor so much of it: for in metals, the moisture overcomes the dryness, and therefore they are melted by fire; but in stones, the moisture is overcome by the dryness, and therefore the stone is ground down. Since, therefore, stones do not melt (except for a few), and since they cannot be extended under a hammer, nor be mixed with metals, their principles cannot be the same; consequently, neither gold nor the elixir can be composed from them.

<margin>The similarity of glass to metals.</margin>
Yet glass might be considered more closely related by some. For just as metals are melted by the heat of fire, so too is glass; and whom...

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>The difference.</margin>
Just as the moisture of metal does not evaporate, so neither does that of glass. Furthermore, glass has an extremely viscous and tenacious substance; for these reasons, the art of glass-making is not inappropriately subordinated to this art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy or the study of metallic transformations</note>, which is why Geber <note>A famous 8th-century Arab alchemist, often cited as an authority in Western texts</note> also advises us to take glass as an example. We cannot deny all these points; however, one will easily see how far glass departs from the nature of metal if they consider that metallic fusion <note>The melting of metal</note> occurs through the preservation of the natural moisture of **mercury** <note>original: *argenti viui*, literally "living silver"</note>, whereas vitrification <note>The process of turning a substance into glass</note> arises from the ultimate consumption of the radical moisture of every combustible thing, which is reduced to ash through burning. Therefore, glass can be made from the ash of almost anything. 

And we see that when lead and tin have been calcined <note>Reduced to a powder through heat</note> and burned by a suitable fire, they are afterwards converted into glass, just as potters do when glazing earthenware vessels. Similarly, regarding the properties and behaviors of metals, they are extended under the hammer; for that properly belongs to metal, since no other thing in the world possesses such moisture as metals do. Glass, however, shatters and is crushed when struck. Even after being heated, if it is quenched in water or kept in cold air, it very easily breaks and cracks, which metal does not do. Likewise, all metals are mixed with one another in smelting because of the similarity of their matter; but glass and all vitrified substances do not mix with metals during melting, but float on top like oil or any fat on water. Also, molten glass yields to an imposed weight, whereas molten metals do not, no more so than mercury. By these signs, it is easily perceived that glass is alien to the nature of metals; therefore, neither gold nor the elixir <note>The "Elixir" or "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the Great Work</note> can be composed from it.

<margin>Caution in the work.</margin>
Indeed, the philosophers warn us that if any worker should by chance produce a vitrified substance during the work, he should stay his hand from it and bring an end to the operation.

<margin>How remote salts, vitriols, and alums are from the art.</margin>
But if glass, which lacks vaporizable moisture, cannot be the material for the Physical Stone <note>Another name for the Alchemical Elixir</note>, anyone can see what should be judged concerning salts, vitriols <note>original: *atramentis*—literally "inks," but used by alchemists to refer to metallic sulfates</note>, and alums. Not only are they very easily dissolved into water by moisture, but their watery and oily humor can also be drawn out by the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>The branch of alchemy focused on the separation and recombination of natural elements</note> through distillations, leaving behind an earth that has no entry into or fusion with metal. This is quite different in metals, which are easily mixed because of their affinity, and their moisture [is not easily separated] from the dry because of their homogeneity and strong [bonding]...

...by the mixture of both it is not separated, but they remain together in the fire or vanish together.

<margin>How marcasite, magnesia, and tutty differ from metals.</margin>
But perhaps someone will think that a different judgment should be made regarding other intermediate minerals, such as **magnesia** <note>In this context, likely a term for various ores like manganese or magnetite</note>, **tutty** <note>Zinc oxide deposits collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</note>, and **marcasite** <note>A general term for various metallic sulfides like pyrite</note>, which participate in the same moisture as metals; for they all consist of quicksilver <note>original: *argento viuo*</note> and sulfur, although they have many earthy and stony parts mixed in. I say that these indeed possess the same moisture, but it is undigested <note>In alchemical theory, matter "digests" or ripens over time to become perfect metal; "undigested" means it is still crude or impure</note> and bounded in another way through their forms, which occur to them because of the different proportion of the mixture of the nearby component elements, even though the elements are otherwise the same. And this can be clearly observed from the specific behaviors and properties of metals, which are fusion <note>melting</note>, ductility <note>the ability to be hammered thin</note>, and miscibility <note>the ability to blend</note>, which are common to all metals. However, these intermediate minerals can neither be extended under the hammer nor mixed with metals through melting. Indeed, their earthy part overcomes the watery part by many degrees, which is the opposite of what occurs in metals. Therefore, considering these things, anyone will easily perceive that these cannot provide us with the material for gold or silver, or for the Medicine <note>The alchemical Elixir or Stone used for transformation</note>.

<margin>Those who seek the Stone in spirits alone do so in vain.</margin>
But some will perhaps think that the Medicine can be more easily drawn out from the metallic spirits alone—namely, Mercury, sulfur, and arsenic—since they have the greatest affinity with metals, given that they are their principles. We also see these things, prepared with slight effort and projected <note>The act of "projection" involves casting a small amount of alchemical powder onto molten base metal to transform it</note> onto certain bodies, induce a certain alteration, although not a perfect one; if they were perhaps properly prepared, they would provide a Stone absolute in every respect. Geber <note>A legendary figure in alchemy, likely representing several authors of Arabic and Latin texts</note> confirms this opinion of theirs, saying:

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 32.</margin>
> Neither the ancients, nor we, nor those who will come after us have found anything that is joined to bodies except spirits alone, or something that contains within itself the nature of both body and spirit.

And in the same chapter:

> Because we have seen adherence to bodies with alteration in nothing other than spirits, we were for no reason excused from them, but it was necessary to have prepared them with their cleansing, which is done through sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify "spirits"</note>.

And in another place:

> Whatever things are altered, they must be altered through the power of quicksilver or sulfur, or things similar to these, since these alone share in nature with bodies.

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 60.</margin>
Granted indeed, we certainly concede that every alteration is brought about through a spirit, and therefore

### CHAPTER III. 647

It does not follow that alteration must necessarily occur through common quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum vulgare*</note>, or sulfur and arsenic, since quicksilver is also called the "spirit" of metals, as is the white or red sulfur drawn from them, which are terms often used by the philosophers in place of sulfur and arsenic. Next, let us admit that even these spirits known to the common people might induce alteration in metals; they will certainly never do so as long as they remain in their own nature, because during fusion <note>the process of melting metals</note> these spirits leave the "bodies" <note>the solid metallic part</note> and do not adhere to them; on the contrary, they flee the harshness of the fire because of their volatility <note>original: *fuga*, literally "flight"</note> which has not been removed from them. 

<margin>On the disadvantage of spirits.</margin>
Therefore, if they are to be changed from their natural state, the causes of their corruption must first be taken away from them: in sulfur and arsenic, this is the inflammable substance; in quicksilver, it is the superfluous wateriness; and in all of them, a burning quality <note>original: *adus-tiua*</note> even without flame, as well as earthy dregs. From sulfur and arsenic, indeed, the inflammability can be removed through **calcination** <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often reducing it to a powder</note>; from quicksilver, the wateriness is removed through **precipitation**. But in this way, they are reduced to an earthy substance that lacks the ability to melt or to "enter" <note>original: *ingressu*, referring to the alchemical concept of a substance penetrating and transforming a metal</note> another body. 

<margin>*The Summary of Perfection*, chapter 58.</margin>
How, then, will they transmute metals if they do not enter or penetrate them? Notwithstanding these difficulties, we say—according to the opinion of all the philosophers, and especially that of **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in early alchemy</note>—that a certain intermediate substance can be elicited from these, which is not prevented from "entry" by its earthiness, which is perfected by good fusion, and whose impression is not easily removed because of its subtlety. But yet, since this intermediate substance of theirs is not "fixed" <note>stable in fire; not volatile</note>—because a fixed thing cannot be produced from something that is not fixed—although its impression does not easily depart, it is nevertheless not firmly lasting. Therefore, since one must necessarily arrive at the Mercury of "perfect bodies" <note>gold and silver</note> to fix this intermediate substance, it would be more advisable to seek the **Medicine** <note>Another name for the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> in them. 

<margin>The medicine of metals must be sought from metals.</margin>
He who therefore seeks the medicine that converts metals, having left behind all the aforementioned things that do little or nothing for the matter, should take metals and search in them for the principles of metals—namely, quicksilver and sulfur—since these are in them by nature, and metals are generated from them. Let him remember, however, that the "form" of gold and silver can give nothing that it did not first possess; therefore, neither imperfect metals, nor quicksilver, nor sulfur can acquire the form and **fixation** <note>the state of being resistant to fire</note> necessary for the elixir, unless they are first informed and fixed by the form of gold or silver. 

Whence **Plato** <note>Likely a reference to pseudo-Platonic alchemical texts common in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> advises in his fourth [book], 2. that we should especially spend our labor on perfect things. For thus he says: "Wherefore, having been calcined and..."

He cites authorities like Geber and Plato to emphasize that only substances already "fixed" can impart stability to an elixir.</summary>

# ON THE AFFINITY OF THE MEDICINE AND METALS

<margin>It is more useful and requires less labor to seek [the stone] in perfect bodies.</margin>
You dissolve other bodies with great labor, when you could find what you seek in these (namely, the perfect ones <note>original: *perfectis*, referring to gold and silver</note>). If you require their use, you must first convert them into the likeness of the two perfect bodies.
<margin>Rosary of the Philosophers, part 1</margin>
> And Hamech, the commentator on Plato, in the same place: These bodies, namely the impure ones, require preparation just like the sun <note>original: *sol*, meaning gold</note> and the moon <note>original: *luna*, meaning silver</note>; then let them be prepared again, until they arrive at that which is necessary.
> And Arnaldus de Villa Nova: If we wished to begin our work in the primary matter of nature, it would be extremely long, and even impossible; great and infinite expenses would be required to complete this. And even when, through a most difficult artifice, a stone has been made from the nature of metals, the physical work would not yet have begun. This is because it is necessary that the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note> be drawn from the nature of the two perfect bodies before a complete **elixir** is made from it, since it is necessary that what becomes the elixir be more purified and <term>digested</term> <note>a process of chemical maturation through steady heat</note> than gold and silver.

He says "before a complete elixir is made from it" in respect to the form of gold or silver, without which the elixir cannot be completed. However, there is no reason to doubt that the matter of the elixir can be sought from other bodies, as we have shown above, and as will be proven more extensively below by the authority of the philosophers.

<margin>Recapitulation of what was said before.</margin>
We have spoken thus far of how the elixir and the metals to be transmuted agree in their principles, and how they are mutually convertible; likewise, how natural gold and the elixir consist of the substance of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> alone once all extraneous sulfur has been removed. Finally, we have discussed how the form of the elixir does not proceed except from its own matter, which can be no other than that which is in metals at the beginning of their creation. And in all these things, the affinity between the elixir and the bodies to be transmuted is most clearly seen. Nevertheless, to increase this closeness, the Philosophers desire something further:
<margin>A part of the body to be converted must be mixed with the elixir.</margin>
namely, that a part of the body to be converted should be placed into the stone. For example: if someone wishes to change lead into gold or silver by means of the physical stone, it is necessary that he first mix the substance of lead with it, so that they become one thing together. The same must be done for tin, copper, and silver. Raymond Lully indicates this very thing expressly in these words:
<margin>Practice of the Testament, chapter 22.</margin>
> When you wish to make the medicine, consider first to what perfection of preparation you propose to lead it, and upon what body you wish to make the <term>projection</term> <note>the final step of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transform it</note>; for from that body upon which

# CHAPTER III.

...[the matter] upon which you wish to perform the **projection** <note>original: *proiectionem*, the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast onto molten metal to transform it into gold or silver</note>, you ought to place within it. And in the *Repertory* <note>original: *Repertorium*, likely referring to a work by Raymond Lull</note>: If you wish to perform a projection upon a body, place its spirit into the **elixir**, and by such a craft, the Medicine shall have entry into it.

<margin>*The Rosary*, chapter 21</margin>
And Arnaldus: If you do not mix into the elixir some of that very body upon which you wish to make the projection, and if you do not soften it, the spirit will not love the body. To carry this out, various paths are proposed to us by the philosophers, all tending toward one end: that the body to be added to the elixir must be made **subtle** <note>refined or thinned into a more "spiritual" or reactive state</note>. But since there are different ways of thinning, as was said above, one might rightly doubt how this body is to be refined.

<margin>Diverse opinions of the philosophers are recounted.</margin>
Raymond Lull, in the chapter cited above, seems to suggest that it is enough for such a body to be **amalgamated** <note>mixed with mercury to create a soft paste</note> with Mercury, by grinding and mixing until it is like butter and none of its parts can be felt any longer; then this **amalgam** should be spread over red or white sulfur, whose vapor will penetrate this amalgam, coagulate it, and convert it into its own nature. This operation is easy, short, and plausible, and we believe the philosopher wrote such things from experience; however, in another place, he says the spirit of the body to be converted ought to be mixed with the elixir.

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 59</margin>
Geber also warns that the body must be dissolved. For he says: It is a good precaution for giving entry to unmixable things, that the body intended to be altered and changed by these be dissolved. Arnaldus de Villa Nova says elsewhere that the body must be reduced to **calx** <note>original: *calcem*, a fine powder or ash produced by heating a substance until it loses its physical form</note>. When you wish, he says, to project the elixir, you shall make a calx of that matter which belongs to the body upon which you wish to project. Although Geber does not expressly mention calx, he nonetheless seems to follow a middle path: namely, that the soluble parts of the body be dissolved, the remaining parts be calcined, and that calx, joined with the elixir, be **imbibed** <note>original: *imbibatur*, a process of repeatedly soaking a dry substance with liquid to saturate it with "spirit"</note> by its spirit. For he continues thus: Let there not be a solution of all parts, however, but of some; then let that body, and no other, be imbibed time after time. For by this benefit, it necessarily has entry into this alone; this does not necessarily happen in just any other body. Unless this were Geber’s meaning, he would not say, "then let that body, and no other, be imbibed." For what body is to be imbibed except its own, and that which remained from the solution, since he mentions no other body? Moreover, nothing can enter the elixir unless it is pure and cleansed of burning "sulfureities" <note>impurities associated with common sulfur that cause metals to char or blacken</note> and earthy dregs, which are most effectively removed through **calcination**: for, according to the philosophers, nothing enters the elixir unless it is clean and...

# ON THE AFFINITY OF MEDICINE AND METALS.

<margin>
All components of the elixir must be **sublimated** <note>original: *sublimanda*; sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to reach the highest level of purity</note>. 
From *On the Intent of Alchemists*, chapter on fixation.
</margin>
...purified of all superfluities. As for why **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in early Arabic alchemy</note> commanded that this body or **calx** <note>original: *calcem*; the powdery residue or "lime" left after a metal has been burned or oxidized</note> be soaked many times, the reason was so that it could afterwards be sublimated and purified even more than before. This is because a calx does not rise upward at all, or does so only with difficulty, unless it is aided by a **spirit** <note>a volatile substance, such as mercury or an acidic vapor, that helps "lift" the solid metal during heating</note>. That the calx of the body must be sublimated—indeed, everything placed in the **elixir** <note>the medicinal substance used to transform base metals into gold or silver</note>—is affirmed in these very words by **Raymond Lull**, **Arnaldus** [of Villanova], **Albumasar**, and others in this manner: "If you do not sublimate everything you put into the elixir, neither the gold nor the silver produced from it will be entirely perfect." And again: "Therefore, it is necessary that the calx placed into the elixir be sublimated, so that it becomes entirely simple and singular."

<margin>
Reconciling the Authors.
</margin>
To reconcile these differing statements of the Philosophers, we believe it does not matter whether the calx or the spirit of the body to be converted is mixed with the elixir, provided that some small portion of it is joined to the Medicine. However, it is an easier and shorter path for the spirit to be mixed with the elixir at the end than the calx, which is better added at the beginning of the work. Nevertheless, both can be done without harm. Still, let everyone remember: only pure things are suitable for pure things. It is necessary, therefore, that the body be refined and purified in the ways described in the second chapter of this book, and only then joined to the elixir.

<margin>
What must be done so that the Stone may transmute all metals.
</margin>
Hence **Marsilio Ficino** <note>a renowned Italian scholar and priest (1433–1499) whose works often blended Neoplatonic philosophy with alchemical theory</note> says: "If you have extracted the more perfect from the imperfect and added it to a more perfect body, why is there any doubt that the whole is made perfect?" Indeed, so that the Stone may pour its virtue into all metals and transmute them, it can be dissolved and increased in turn by the spirit of all imperfect things. Ficino indicates the same clearly with these words: "What stands in the way of a Stone composed of all metals being able to redden the whole world by **tincture** <note>original: *tingendo*; the process of "dyeing" or staining a base metal to permanently change its nature and color</note>?" This should not be understood to mean all things in the world—otherwise, it would dye plants and animals, and every kind of stone and rock, and the very earth we walk upon, which is absurd and far from the truth. Rather, it refers to all the metals of the whole world, using the "container for the contained" and the "whole for the part" <note>referring to the rhetorical device of synecdoche, where "the world" represents "all metals within the world"</note> with poetic license. Bringing this chapter on the affinity of the elixir with the bodies to be transmuted to a close, we say that the simple and composite **roots of minerals** must first be known to the practitioner. For if he is ignorant of the principles of nature, he will be very far from the work, since he lacks the foundation upon which to build his intention. Therefore, let no one cling to this art unless he investigates it thoroughly.

# ON THE RADICAL MOISTURE

### CHAPTER IV.

*In which it is shown that three humors—namely the original (or radical), the nutritive, and the elemental—are found not only in living beings, but also in metals. What the radical moisture of metals is, and by what means it congeals and consolidates the retained parts; and how it can be increased in metals, though not in living things. Furthermore, the alimentary moisture or "spirit of the stone" is discussed, along with its various effects and operations. From where it is drawn, how it is prepared, and whether it can be elicited from things other than metals, is examined.*

It was stated above how the Physical Medicine <note>original: *medicina Physica*; here referring to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone in its role as a "healer" of base metals</note>, through its oiliness, is melted as quickly as possible; how through the thinness of its material it penetrates into the depths of the metals to be transmuted; and how through affinity and a closeness of nature it adheres to its own likeness—namely, to their **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento vivo*; mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" or base of all metals</note>—and retains it. Now, we must further examine how it coagulates and consolidates that which is retained; **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of alchemy</note> asserts in this place that the Medicine accomplishes this through its fiery radical moisture. However, so that it may be better understood what this "fiery radical moisture" is, we must digress a little. Natural philosophers and Physicians have established a threefold difference of humors <note>fluids or essential liquids</note> in all living things, both in plants and in animals.

<margin>Three humors in all living beings.</margin>
And one indeed they call "alimentary" or "nutritive," because living things are nourished and fed by it. Although this humor has already been changed through digestion <note>original: *concoctione*; the internal "cooking" or processing of food by the body</note>, it has not yet been entirely converted into the essence of the living body.

<margin>Alimentary.</margin>
It is watery and cold, differing little from spring or well water if it were evoked by a **vapor bath** <note>original: *vaporario*; a gentle heating method like a bain-marie</note> and collected in a vessel. As long as it adheres to things, it prevents them from burning.

<margin>Original or vital.</margin>
The other they name the "original" or "vital" humor, and also the "radical" <note>the "root" moisture of a thing's existence</note>. It is fatty and oily. Although it escapes the sharpest sight of the eyes, it can nonetheless be separated by art and industry—just like the previous humor—through distillation, appearing in the form of a white or red oil.

# ON THE AFFINITY OF MEDICINE AND METALS

<margin>
Elemental [humor].
</margin>
<margin>
Example of the three humors in one subject.
</margin>
...or of a color between these. Within this, they establish the spirit and the foundation of innate heat, as well as the primary substance, since it is the first and common to all living things, in which the spirit, suffused with heat, first and by itself settles. Different from these is the aqueous or **elemental humor** <note>original: *humor elementaris*; the basic water-like component that holds the physical parts of an object together</note>, by which the earthy parts of bodies are joined together like glue, and which is common to all things formed from the mixture of elements; it sustains the entire genus of inanimate things, whether stones or metals, glued together by this very substance. To better understand this triple kind of humors, everything will be made clearer by an example. If someone puts green wood, recently cut, into the fire, he will see at first that it is set ablaze with difficulty, because it overflows with much moisture that it had drawn from the earth for its nourishment; for it is this which usually flows from its ends while it heats up. Once this is consumed, the flame readily devours the remaining substance, because that fatty part, which has the appearance of oil, remains purer, dampened by no other liquid. When the fire has ravaged all of this, no flame then breaks out or flies away at all; yet in the remaining coals, there is still a solidity of its own from the leftover tenacious and coherent aqueous humor, which they received in the composition of the elements. When this is finally eaten away and dissipated, only the driest ash, as it appears, remains; although even the ash itself is not entirely lacking in that viscous and tenacious humor—subtle and fixed, and not at all flammable—which can turn into glass and provide a glassy transparency.

<margin>
The elemental humor is common to all things.
</margin>
<margin>
Three humors in the stone.
</margin>
<margin>
A comparison of these with the humors of living beings.
</margin>
<margin>
The radical moisture of metals.
</margin>
And indeed, natural philosophers say this elemental humor is common to both animate things, such as plants and animals, and inanimate things, such as stones and all metals; however, they attribute **radical moisture** <note>original: *radicalem humiditatem*; the fundamental "life-sap" or essential energy of a substance</note> and nourishment to living things alone. But the **Chemical philosophers** <note>the alchemists</note>, searching more deeply into the secrets of nature, have investigated and found those three humors not only in living things, but also in metals, and especially in their **Stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>—not indeed exactly as they are in those possessing a soul, but as they are in metals. For first, just as in the oily and fatty substance of those endowed with life, there exists the native heat, spirit, and soul, and the generation of its own kind; so too in the moisture fundamentally fixed in metals, there is their propagation, the internal heat digesting the matter, and the soul...

...is contained. <margin>

The Stone absorbs and digests this, growing in both quantity and power, no differently than an infant who is first nourished sparingly and gradually with water and milk, then slowly grows until it is capable of digesting more abundant and solid food.

# ON THE FIERY RADICAL MOISTURE

...must be stripped of external sulfur before their radical moisture can be reached. But if gold—which is nothing other than mercury <note>original: *argentum viuum*; literally "living silver," referring here to the philosophical principle of fluidity in metals</note> most perfectly matured <note>original: *digestum*; literally "digested," a term alchemists used to describe the "cooking" or ripening of metals in the earth over time</note> by the degrees of nature—possesses so much natural heat and radical moisture (acquired from the quality of its own sulfur) that it is frequently called "pure fire" by the philosophers compared to common mercury, as it digests and ripens its own substance, then what must we think of the **physical tincture**? For the tincture <term>tincture: the "philosopher's stone" in liquid form, capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold</term> surpasses gold in its radical moisture and heat, and is called "pure sulfur" by the philosophers, and in truth, it is. <margin>Testament, chapter 64.</margin> For as Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</note> says: "The metallic tincture is nothing but sulfur, from which multiplication occurs through its own natural heat in the substance of mercury, ripening it and converting the substance of the sulfur through a specific method of maturation." Therefore, the multiplication of the tincture happens only through the increase and multiplication of natural heat, which is sulfur—one that neither consumes nor burns—within the matter of mercury. 

<margin>Radical moisture is nothing other than sulfur.</margin> From these words, it is gathered that the radical moisture, or the natural heat that resides within the radical moisture, is nothing other than sulfur. This is not, however, the external and burning sulfur which is added to imperfect metals in their impure place of birth, but rather the internal, non-burning sulfur that transmutes the substance of mercury applied to it by the artist <note>The "artist" is the alchemist performing the work.</note> and converts it into itself. For just as air, which is the matter of fire, takes on the form of fire within it, so mercury is the matter of sulfur and is converted into it because of their natural affinity. And since that sulfur is nothing but the tincture, mercury ripened by it will also become nothing but the tincture. This tincture, multiplied and increased in many ways, with external heat further ripening the matter more and more, is made of such great power and effectiveness that, by its exceeding fiery heat, it coagulates and solidifies the mercury of molten metals. Whatever is not of its own nature, it consumes or separates.

<margin>The radical moisture of sulfur is called "oil" in certain respects.</margin> Regarding this sulfur, its radical moisture is called **oil** by the philosophers, because sulfur is oily and fatty. (Indeed, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy; he argued metals were composed of sulfur and mercury</note> defines it as "the fatness of the earth thickened by a temperate ripening in the mine until it becomes hardened and dry.") We spoke of this at length in Chapter 1, so we shall speak more sparingly here, noting only that this same moisture is often called **fire** <margin>Radical moisture is called fire.</margin> by reason of its internal heat. Wherefore Raymond Lull says: "Son, impregnate the body by the fire, and multiply its combustion..."

### CHAPTER FOUR

...and you will have a strong **tincture** <term>tincture: an alchemical liquid capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold</term>: <margin>Testament, ch. 19.</margin> where by "fire" he understands nothing other than that radical moisture with which the **stone** <term>stone: the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work</term> is to be impregnated or soaked. <margin>The Rosary, ch. 24.</margin> And Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says: "Fire matures the whole compound, refines it, and makes it red; it mixes and solidifies the air, and binds the coldness of earth and water, so that they return safely to a balanced state of complexion." And Rhodianus <note>An alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval and Renaissance texts</note> speaks no less elegantly: "In the hidden part of our stone is heat and dryness, which heat is the **element of fire**: the oil is also dry, for this dryness fixes [the substance], since the dryness of fire dyes it." Here, although he seems to distinguish the fire from the oil, he nevertheless declares the qualities of this fire—namely heat and dryness—and openly describes its properties. <margin>Why it is called fire.</margin> This moisture, I say, is called "fire" because, as has been said, the heat or fire of nature is hidden within it, just like the **innate heat** of living creatures is hidden in the **primordial moisture** <term>primordial moisture: the "humidum primigenium," a vital fluid believed to sustain life and hold the body's natural heat</term>. The more viscous and sticky this moisture is, and the more abundant, the longer it suffices for the heat, and the more enduring it is. But this innate heat in living creatures is gradually extinguished—specifically, when the moisture it inhabited (and which served as its fuel) is consumed. If this consumption could be halted, the animal could be made perpetual and sustained for unending ages.

<margin>The primordial moisture of metals can be increased, while that of living things cannot.</margin> In metals, however—and especially in the **physical stone**—the opposite is true, because in it the radical moisture is not only preserved but even increased in a wonderful way. And as the moisture grows, so too does the heat, so that it can deservedly be called fire. This fire, by its own heat, digests <note>original: *digerit*; in alchemy, "digestion" refers to a slow, steady heating process that matures a substance</note> the humidity of imperfect metals that has not been sufficiently "cooked" by nature, and by its own overflowing radical moisture, it matures and multiplies their primordial moisture. And for this reason, the stone is said to have no "terminable" <note>meaning "finite" or "exhaustible"</note> humidity; for although it may be dry to the touch, it is nevertheless abundant in an unctuous <note>oily or greasy</note> moisture in its hidden part, which can never be destroyed or driven out. <margin>Interpretation of the aforementioned.</margin> For a greater clarification of the things said above and by Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy</note>, it seemed fit to bring forward what Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> thinks regarding this fiery heat of **sulfur**, writing in this manner:

<margin>Practice of the Testament, ch. 21.</margin>
> "Son, do not wonder when you see things changed before your eyes through the power of **sulfur**, because it is very hot and dry. Therefore, it is necessary that it possesses the property of fire—namely, of opening the parts of the whole body and of **mercury** <note>original: *argenti viui*; literally "living silver"</note>, and of penetrating and delimiting, because through the heat which it naturally possesses within itself, it opens the closed pores..."

# ON THE FIERY NATURE OF THE RADICAL MOISTURE

<page-num>656</page-num>

...and locked. And since fire is substantially bound within a subtle substance, when all of that also enters the whole body as a vapor—since the substance by which it is bound and collected is very dry—it limits <note>original: *terminat*; in alchemy, this refers to giving a fixed, stable form to a fluid substance</note> and congeals the moisture which it has entered, according to the informing pattern of its heat. He says "according to the informing pattern of its heat" because of the double nature of this **sulfur** <term>sulfur: here refers to the active, masculine principle of alchemy, not common brimstone</term> or radical moisture, as we declared in chapter 1. One of these natures is **Lunar** <note>associated with Silver</note>, imparting only the form of silver to the **stone**; the other is **Solar** <note>associated with Gold</note>, imparting the form of gold. This depends on the greater or lesser boiling <note>original: *decoctionem*; a process of refining through heat</note> directed by the will of the craftsman who strives to make silver or gold.

However, no one should think that Raimundus Lullius <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> understands "philosophical earth" or some other external sulfur by the word "sulfur" in this place. Rather, he means only that fiery radical humor of which we speak, which opens, penetrates, and limits the **philosophical matter**—that is, the "earth" and "water," which he calls the "body" and **mercury** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the fluid, passive principle of alchemy</term>—specifically by inducing and fixing its form. 

<margin>Testament, ch. 55.</margin> Lullius himself is my authority for this interpretation, speaking thus: "Radical moistures are limited and completed into the substance of a metal through their natural heat by the stimulation of fire alone; this would never be possible unless they participated in the nature of the metal." 

He previously said that this sulfur opens, penetrates, and limits the "body" and "mercury" with its fiery heat; now, making no mention of sulfur, he asserts the same thing regarding the radical humor. Furthermore, what he is silent about here—namely that the body and mercury must be limited by the heat of sulfur—he expressed above. For it must not be thought that it is limited by itself, but rather in and with its own earth. 

<margin>The radical humor participates in the nature of the stone's metal.</margin> He also affirms that these radical moistures participate in the nature of the metal because, as shown elsewhere from Lullius, they exist between two extremes. One extreme is mercury and sulfur, and the other is the **perfect elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected medicinal substance capable of transmuting metals</term>. If it did not possess the nature of metal, it could not be the perfect medicine for metals. 

Since, therefore, this radical humor is the middle point between two extremes, it must necessarily obtain the nature of sulfur and mercury, just as it does the nature of metal. Because of this, it is more closely related to the metal than the two aforementioned substances, which are quite remote from the nature of metal unless they are first informed and limited by this "second sulfur," from which the "third sulfur" arises. But just as Lullius touched upon the power and force of this primordial moisture within its matter in the preceding sections, so in the following he describes its power...
