# CHAPTER FOUR. 657

<margin>About Mercury alone.</margin> ...of the stone, which is thereafter nothing other than radical moisture and pure fire, he demonstrates clearly and excellently, as always, regarding the conversion of metals. The **Medicine** <term>Medicine: a common alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone or the Elixir that "heals" base metals into gold</term>, he says, when properly prepared and cast upon a molten body or heated **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note>, fixes, cooks, thickens, and unites the metal by reason of its subtlety and fieriness. By thickening and uniting, it provides weight, but it leaves behind the coarser, earthy parts as dross. And let these words suffice concerning the fiery radical moisture which **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most influential figure in early chemistry and alchemy</note> affirms is necessary for the Medicine, so that it may congeal and consolidate the parts retained through the adherence of its own likeness. I pass now to the **alimentary moisture**, which is one of the three principal foundations of the chemical art or elements of the stone, and it is sometimes compared to Air, just as the radical moisture is compared to Fire.

<margin>About the alimentary moisture.</margin> This moisture is called in the art "spirit," "water," "**Mercury**," "wind," "smoke," and "vinegar," and is distinguished by infinite other names by the philosophers, and is very often confused with the radical moisture. I find a definition of the **Spirit** in a certain anonymous author <margin>Its various names.</margin> who, I suspect, borrowed it from **Raimundus Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull, the Majorcan philosopher previously mentioned</note>. There it is said to be a "mineral virtue in which the natures of metals <margin>Definition.</margin> rest." It is called a "virtue" because it is of a spiritual and airy nature, in the chemical way of speaking, and cannot exist without its body or endure the fire. Although it is such in its own nature, nevertheless the entire metallic nature rests within it and consists of it, because a metallic body is nothing other than quicksilver changed from its own nature, coagulated, and digested and shaped according to the property of the sulfur innate to it.

<margin>Various benefits of the spirit.</margin> The effects and benefits of this Spirit are various. For it preserves bodies from combustion <note>burning or oxidation</note>. Hence the Philosopher says in the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* or "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the earliest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</note>: "If a body is placed upon the fire without vinegar, it will be burned and reduced to ashes." It inhibits burning by its own coldness and moisture, which are the qualities of water. Furthermore, it dissolves all metallic bodies—especially gold and silver—with a true philosophical dissolution into the water from which they were made from the beginning. This it achieves through the thinness of its parts, because it has been clearly purified of earthy matter through frequent distillations and long-lasting circulation, as well as by the sharpness of its penetration, which it acquired from the metallic salt digested and elevated with it. Moreover, it washes and cleanses, because it removes the blackness and filth of the dissolved bodies and their earth through washing; hence it is said more than once—

# CONCERNING THE FIERY RADICAL MOISTURE. 658

...it is called the **Soap of the Wise** <note>original: *Sapo Sapientum*</note>, a name drawn from its likeness to common soap, with which undergarments and clothes stained by sweat or other filth are cleaned. 

<margin>Practice of the Testament, chapter 17.</margin>
**Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and reputed alchemist</note> briefly encompassed these properties in this sentence:

> The property which is water cools greatly, dissolves, and washes.

And in the same place:

> **Quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; mercury</note> is an overflowing and flowing liquid, preserving from combustion and burning.

<margin>Contrary operations in the spirit of the stone.</margin>
Furthermore, various and contrary operations are ascribed to this spirit. For it is said to gather and to divide: to gather things of the same kind <note>original: *homogenea*</note>, but to split and divide things of different kinds <note>original: *heterogenea*</note>. The reason for this is that it adheres to those things that are of the same kind and possess a Mercurial nature, but it sets aside things of a different kind—that is, inflammable oiliness and the earthy substance of the body—and does not touch or embrace them as if they were foreign; or, if it does embrace them, it eventually abandons them. 

It is also said to **mortify** <term>mortify: in alchemy, to strip a substance of its outward form or "life" to prepare it for transformation</term> and to **vivify** <term>vivify: to bring back to life or reanimate</term>. It mortifies by separating the soul and the **tincture** <note>the coloring principle or essence</note> from the bodies, which then remain dead, as there is no longer any splendor in them, nor any life (which consists in radiance) and radical moisture, according to the saying of **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist of the 7th century</note>: "When bodies do not retain their souls, they appear dead and dark." It vivifies, however, when it brings the soul—that is, the Mercury of perfected bodies—into a clean and pure earth.

<margin>Testament, chapter 61.</margin>
It is also said to vivify bodies when it converts metals to its own nature—that is, into quicksilver. Hence Lull says:

> Our water makes the whole body spirit, and turns the dead body into a living substance.

Here it is called a "dead body" because it cannot exert its powers as long as it is compact and hard, but only after it has been made spiritual through **solution** <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note>. For similar reasons, it is said to soften hard things and harden soft things. It softens when it dissolves bodies and moistens parched and dry earth; it hardens when it draws out the radical moisture (which was sufficient for the melting of metals) and prevents it from being able to flow any further. 

Likewise, it **whitens** <note>original: *albificat*</note> and **reddens** <note>original: *rubificat*</note>. It whitens by washing, cleaning, and exalting the earth; it reddens by pouring in the tincture of gold or its oil. The author of the *Lesser Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium minus*; a highly influential alchemical text</note> encompasses all these effects of Mercury or the spirit in these brief words:

<margin>Part 2, chapter 20.</margin>
> With this praiseworthy corrosive water, you will be able to resolve in an instant all bodies, both raw and **calcined** <term>calcined: reduced to a powder by heating</term>, all spirits, and all minerals...

It details the paradoxes of the Work, such as how the same substance can both harden and soften, or kill (mortify) and bring to life (vivify) the metallic bodies.</summary>

# CHAPTER FOUR. 659

...as well as precious stones, and to coagulate them whenever you wish. This water has such wonderful and praiseworthy effects: it dissolves the solid and makes it liquid, cleans the unclean, corrodes the superfluous, fixes the fugitive <term>fixes the fugitive: to make a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat</term>, joins the scattered, increases the white and red tinctures <note>original: "tincturam albam... & rubeam"; these refer to the stages of making silver and gold</note> most excellently, penetrates all things, softens the hard and hardens the soft, and reconciles those at odds; it is the key to the entire art. 

When he adds that this water "reconciles those at odds," he says this regarding the soul and the body, which cannot embrace each other because of their great distance, except through the medium of the spirit. Hence Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher whose name was attached to many later alchemical works</note> says: "Souls cannot enter bodies except by the mediation of the spirit." For this reason, it is also called the "dissolving Mercury of the philosophers" by Arnaldus de Villanova <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note>, who says it "performs the marriage." 

And another says: "This water joins different bodies with such a union that fire cannot separate them." It performs the marriage between the body and the ferment, changes one of them into the other, and defends them from being consumed by fire. Just as this moisture makes things white and red, so it is also said to make things black. Hence Marchos says in the works of Morienus: "Our water dissolves bodies, congeals them, and turns them black." It does this by reason of putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the alchemical stage of "blackness" (nigredo) where the matter decays before being reborn</term>, in which all things are rendered black. Hence the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text</note> says: "Water putrefies, and afterward makes new and diverse things sprout." 

The philosophers could not sufficiently admire or praise the nature of this spirit. Hence the Author of the *Lily* <note>original: "Auctor Lilij"; refers to the author of the *Lilium Intelligentiae*</note> exclaims: "O celestial nature, how you turn bodies into spirit! O how admirable is nature, how it stands above all things and overcomes all things!" 

<margin>Why the spirit is called "nourishing moisture."</margin>
And lest he be thought to speak of another element, he adds: "And it is the sharpest vinegar, which makes pure gold to be spirit; without which vinegar neither whiteness, nor blackness, nor redness can be achieved."

<margin>The Codicil, chapter on the sublimation of Mercury & nourishment by multiplication. Question. Chapter on the method of fermenting things to be treated with it.</margin>
Besides the faculties listed above, this spirit also nourishes and feeds the stone of copper or latten <note>original: "lapidem æris vel lotonis"; latten is a brass-like alloy</note>. For this reason, it is not undeservedly called the "alimentary" or "nourishing" moisture. By Raymond Lull, it is called "virgin’s milk," "re-rawed blood" <note>original: "fanguis reincrudatus"; blood returned to its raw, primal state</note>, "whitened menstruation," "nourishment of the infant," "food of the heart," "poison of the living," and "food of the dead." 

And in the same place: "The operation of this spirit is the nourishment or multiplication of the stone in the substance of Mercury; and when it is nourished by the water, it is increased and multiplied just like all other things." 

But someone might say: the same Raymond Lull in another place in the *Codicil* affirms that this...

### OF THE FIERY RADICAL MOISTURE.

...[it] does not generate or increase moisture. For he writes this, wishing to show the difference of the radical moisture from the other moistures of the stone. Do not think this moisture will be secondary, because it is phlegmatic <note>original: "phlegmatica"; in alchemy, "phlegm" refers to a watery, inactive, or dull distillate that lacks the "fire" of the spirit</note>, nor can it generate or increase the stone by its own nature, except only to moisten the parts of the stone, carrying them by way of vapor. 

<margin>Solution.</margin> I respond that this moisture indeed contains much phlegm, which easily retreats from the fire; however, it nourishes and increases the middle substance of the stone until it reaches its due size. However, it also evaporates easily along with its phlegm from the fire unless it is governed by a suitable fire and later held fast by the soul. Therefore, Calid <note>Khalid ibn Yazid (died c. 704), a legendary Umayyad prince and alchemist</note> says quite aptly: Water adds or gives no more weight to the body except as much metallic moisture as it has in itself, because the moisture of the water passes away, while the metallic moisture remains. Now, he calls the "metallic moisture" the middle incombustible substance of Mercury. Because of this property of nutrition, Lull calls this spirit in more than one place "vegetable Mercury," or "vegetable water of Mercury," or "vegetable menstruum" <term>menstruum: a solvent or "mother-liquid" used to dissolve and nourish materials in a flask, compared to the biological fluid that nourishes an embryo</term>, because it vegetates, nourishes, and makes things grow. Again, another will object and say: "Do not Raymond Lull and other philosophers affirm in many places that the radical humor <note>original: "humorem radicalem"; the vital, life-sustaining moisture inherent in all things</note> is the true nourishment of the stone?" For thus says Lull:

<margin>Testament, ch. 14.</margin>
> In the third digestion <term>digestion: a process of slow, gentle heating</term>, the stone is nourished with perfection and increased in growth; the stone is strengthened to perform its actions in restoring what was lost in the white foliated earth <note>original: "terra alba foliata"; a stage in the alchemical process where the matter becomes white and flaky like leaves</note>. Moreover, it is known that the third decoction is made with the radical humor—which is also called the oil and the soul—since by it the stone is animated and tinged; without it, the whitened and clean earth cannot be changed into the perfect medicine, but remains dead and of no effect, or vanishes. 

We admit that indeed, but it does not follow from this that no other humor nourishes. For what is asserted of one cannot rightly be denied of the other.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>Difference between the alimentary and radical humor.</margin>
But Lull establishes this difference almost everywhere: he compares the "alimentary humor" (of which we are speaking) to the *menstruum*, but the "radical humor" to milk. For just as an infant before birth is nourished only by the menstrual blood drawn through the umbilical cord—since it is unable to take in nourishment through the mouth because of its weakness of digestion and crudeness—but after birth is nourished by milk, and gradually by more solid food as its strength increases: so too the stone of the earth, since it is very cold in the beginning, requires nourishment for itself...

If a colder nourishment were supplied to it then, the converting powers within it would be deadened. <margin>Question.</margin>

<margin>Difference between alimentary and radical moisture.</margin>

<margin>From where the spirit is to be sought.</margin>
But it could be asked: from where is this alimentary moisture or spirit primarily drawn? That it is not common quicksilver can be gathered from the fact that the Philosophers say everywhere that "their" Mercury is not the Mercury of the common people. Furthermore, common quicksilver is not effective upon gold or silver...

...to be called animal, or vegetable, or mineral, and thus they establish three stones. <margin>Animal.</margin> **Animal**, if this spirit is drawn from animals; namely, if milk, human blood, urine, or honey is refined by various modes of distillation and circulation until it dissolves gold and silver and reduces them to a liquid. <margin>Vegetable.</margin> **Vegetable**, indeed, if this spirit is taken from vegetables, such as what they consider to be the <term>quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth essence," or the purest and most concentrated essence of a substance, often associated with alcohol or ether</note> of wine, of celandine, of greater <term>honesty</term> <note>original: *lunariae*; moonwort, a plant often associated with the moon and silver</note>, of wheat root, of mallow, and of <term>mercury-herb</term> <note>original: *Mercurialis*; a plant (Mercurialis annua) named after the god Mercury</note>, and of other herbs, shrubs, or trees which are warm or moist by nature. <margin>Mineral.</margin> **Mineral**, however, if gold or silver is led into <term>Mercury</term> <note>here referring to the "philosophical mercury" or the liquid state of the metal</note> by means of quicksilver. Nevertheless, it is vain to believe that <term>chrysopœia</term> <note>the art of making gold</note> or <term>argyropœia</term> <note>the art of making silver</note> can be accomplished by that liquid. And yet, let us grant that Mercury has the nature of a toxin in itself: none of the philosophers ever asserted that Mercury alone, without gold or silver, takes away the impurity of metals and changes them into gold or silver. On the contrary, it is a general axiom of the philosophers that nothing can remove the ignobility of metals unless it was first gold or silver. ### CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>Mercury sheds its poisonous quality through digestion.</margin>
...with which the other extreme cannot be converted, except through their own intermediates, and the intermediates are the metals themselves. Since, therefore, **Mercury** <note>quicksilver, often considered the "mother" of all metals in alchemical theory</note> is converted into silver and gold—by art above the ground, but by nature within the mines—it sheds the specific qualities it possessed before its <term>concoction</term> <note>the process of ripening or maturing through heat</note>, taking on foreign qualities acquired through <term>digestion</term> <note>a slow, steady heating process meant to refine a substance</note>: namely, first those of silver, then of gold, and finally of the **Elixir**, which is 100,000 times more healthful and perfect than gold. Hence, no poisonous quality of Mercury is to be feared any longer once it has been converted into gold and the elixir, which removes the infirmity of both human and metallic bodies.

<margin>Body, spirit, and soul must be united in the work.</margin>
Moreover, according to the testimonies of the Philosophers, the **body, spirit, and soul** must be mixed at the most minute level, and become a single thing before the completion of the elixir. How then will this spirit—whether taken from animals or vegetables—be mixed at the most minute level with the body and soul (which the practitioners themselves confess must be sought from metals), since they are clearly of different natures and are not even comprised under the same <term>genus</term>? Nay, more: how can a spirit of this kind endure even the slightest fire without being separated from the body? When it escapes, the soul must necessarily be separated from the body as well, since the soul penetrates through the spirit and finds its entry into the earth.

<margin>Comparison of the soul of the stone with the dye of dyers.</margin>
Nor is it an objection that the Philosophers compare the **soul of the stone** (or the <term>tincture</term>) to the dye of dyers. They say that the soul is carried in the spirit just as the dye of the dyers is carried by water onto the cloth; the water recedes, and the dye remains fixed in the cloth due to its oiliness. For by these words, the philosophers did not mean to demonstrate the evaporation of the spirit from the body, but rather how the spirit serves as the vehicle for the soul, and how the soul is led back into the body by the help of the spirit. This can be clearly gathered from the words of **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> taken from the *Rosary of the Philosophers*, chapter 11: *"The spirit is that in which the tincture of the air is carried; when it is led back over the white <term>foliated earth</term>, the spiritual water is immediately dried, and the soul remains in the body, which is the tincture of the air."* <note>original: "tinctura aeris"; in alchemy, "aes" (brass/copper) was often used as a code for the base matter, while "air" refers to its volatile state</note>. He calls perfectly purified and whitened **sulphur** the "foliated earth." And lest any doubt should arise thereafter, he expressly adds the following: *"The spirit, therefore, retains the soul, just as the soul retains the body, because the soul does not stay in the body except by the mediation of the spirit; but when they are joined, they are never separated, because the spirit retains the soul, just as the soul retains the earth."* He says three things, the first of which is that the water is dried immediately; but if one...

### ON THE ROOT OF THE FIERY HUMIDITY

...with the soul, it does not evaporate. Second, the soul does not remain in the body except by the mediation of the spirit. If this is true, it necessarily follows that the spirit does not withdraw. Third, he adds that these three are never separated, because one is the **tether** <note>original: "retinaculum"</note> of the other; nor can any of them subsist by itself without mutual support, since these three constitute a physical body just as they do a human one. Thus, no place is left for the fleeting spirit of animals or vegetables.

<margin>The waters of salts, vitriols, and alums cannot take the place of the spirit.</margin>
But perhaps the "water" of salts, vitriols <note>original: "atramentorum," referring to sulfate minerals used to make inks and acids</note>, or alums—procured either separately or together through solution or distillation—can take the place of that solvent spirit? Let us consider if this be true. First, if these are added to metallic bodies or to the **Earth of the Philosophers** <note>the refined material base of the Great Work</note> using the heat of a water-bath or dung <note>original: "fimi"; decomposing horse dung was used as a steady, low-temperature heat source</note>, as soon as they feel the heat of the fire, their most subtle parts will evaporate. They will return to their original state of salt, vitriol, or alum, and thus, due to their density, they will be unable to enter the body. Much less can they dissolve the compact mass of the metals, or be mixed and united at the most minute level. If water is distilled from them individually or together, their **phlegm** <note>the watery, inactive residue of distillation</note> will not differ much from common water. If their spirits are forced by a strong fire and caught in a vessel, they will merely corrode the metals and "mortify" <note>kill or dampen the vital energy</note> the natural heat of the earth with their unnatural fire. This renders the material useless for receiving the soul, without which it cannot persist, nor achieve the form of a metal or the **Elixir** <term>Elixir: the final, perfected substance capable of transmuting metals and healing bodies</term>. And even if they lacked these disadvantages, they still cannot be converted into **Sulphur**—which is absolutely necessary in the composition of the Elixir—both because they have no natural affinity with it, and because they gradually evaporate when exposed to fire.

<margin>The clear waters of Mercury and Sulphur are rejected.</margin>
The same judgment applies to the clear and transparent waters of **Mercury** and **Sulphur**. Even though they are, in a sense, the principles of metals, once they have lost their "earth"—in which their proper balance and metallic power lie hidden—they can no longer endure the fire any more than the substances mentioned above. They cannot be united with the earth again, nor converted back into earth; indeed, such waters are no less corrosive than the others.

<margin>The liquids of stones are of no importance in the Art.</margin>
Regarding the "liquors" of stones, gems, corals, crystals, and the like, the verdict is the same: they reflect the nature of either simple water or salts. These are almost never dissolved unless they are first **calcined** <note>reduced to powder through high heat</note>, and everything that is dissolved, according to the opinion of **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century alchemist</note>, partakes of the nature of salts, alums, and similar things...

<summary>The author argues that only a metallic spirit can truly unite with a metallic body and soul. Mineral acids, salts, and distilled "waters" are rejected because they are either too corrosive, too fleeting, or lack the essential "earth" required for stable transmutation.</summary>

# CHAPTER FOUR.

<margin>Whether common quicksilver can take the place of the spirit.</margin>
...should have the nature of the soul. But perhaps common quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum vulgare"</note>, as it is found in its natural state, can fulfill the role of the physical spirit, since it is the material closest to the nature of metals? How true this might be is clearly explained by the philosophers, who assert that no quicksilver is coagulated by the earth which was not first coagulated. But the mercury of the common people <note>original: "Mercurius vulgi," meaning standard commercial quicksilver</note> was never coagulated in the mines of the earth; therefore, it cannot be coagulated by sulfur or purified earth. For it possesses a substance too crude, coarse, and undigested for it to penetrate the earth and be turned into its nature, or to be mixed with the soul and held within the body. I do not deny, however, that when joined to dissolved gold or silver after proper **digestion** <note>prolonged gentle heating</note> and the methods of **subtilization** <note>refining a substance into a more volatile or pure form</note> used by the philosophers, it can function as the spirit and be converted into sulfur, obtaining all the other qualities of the physical spirit; yet, remaining in its natural state, it cannot do so.

<margin>The mercury of marcasites is rejected in the art.</margin>
But if common quicksilver, as it is in its natural state, cannot provide the spirit for the Art, how will the mercury of antimony <note>a brittle, silvery-white metalloid</note> and other **marcasites** <note>iron pyrite or similar metallic minerals</note>, and **tutty** <note>original: "thutia," a crude zinc oxide formed in smelting furnaces</note>, and **magnesia** <note>likely manganese ore or a specific alchemical base</note> withstand the test? For these are much more ignoble, more contaminated, and less suitable for **fixation** <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>. Indeed, they differ greatly in the proportion and mixture of their elements, and in their very species, from common quicksilver <note>original: "hydrargyro"</note> or the Mercury of the metals. Since these things are so, one must necessarily return to the quicksilver of the metals, as that is the true principle and the only key of the Art. And let these things be said concerning the **radical fiery humidity** <note>the fundamental moist heat that sustains life and metals</note> and the nourishing moisture or the element of water. Now let us hasten to the remaining properties of the medicine and proceed to the fifth.

# ON THE CLARITY OF PURITY

...is reconciled. Here we explore what kind of purity is required in the work, from where the luster of metals proceeds, and a corrupted passage by **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy.</note> is restored to its proper meaning. Then, it is examined whether this "clarity of purity" can be found in other things, and finally, it is debated whether gold and silver produced through the Art exceed the gold and silver produced by nature.

<margin>How the axiom of the philosophers is to be understood.</margin>
The proposition of the philosophers is well enough known: *That which is imperfect cannot perfect, nor can the unclean cleanse.* <note>original: "Imperfectum perficere non posse, nec immundum mundare."</note> This must not be understood as if the imperfect *itself* cannot be made perfect, or the unclean cannot be cleansed; for that would contradict the authorities of the philosophers and the truth itself. For thus says **Geber**: *The perfect assists the imperfect, and the perfect in our mastery is perfected by itself, without the addition of any foreign thing; and the imperfect is likewise perfected by this same mastery. And by God, they alter one another, and they perfect one another, and are perfected, and each is perfected through itself alone without the help of anything else.* <note>original: "Perfectum imperfectum adiuvat... et per Deum, se invicem alterant..."</note> By these words, Geber asserts that the **elixir** <note>The transformative substance, often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> can be composed not only from perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver.</note>, but also from a mixture of these with imperfect ones—and indeed, even from the imperfect metals alone.

<margin>That the stone can be composed from all metals.</margin>
**Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925), a Persian polymath and influential alchemical author.</note> and the chemist **Aristotle** <note>Referring to the "Pseudo-Aristotle," the author of various medieval alchemical texts falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher.</note> say similar things, writing that from any of the metallic bodies, if they are prepared with a perfect preparation, a white or red elixir can be established. **Raymond Lully** and **Master Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>Two of the most cited authorities in late medieval alchemy; Lully (c. 1232–1315) and Arnald (c. 1240–1311).</note> affirm the same along with Geber. Indeed, it would have been in vain for the philosophers to describe such various regimens of the Art, and they would not have been so diligent in teaching the science of vessels and fires, unless the imperfect could be perfected and the impure depurated. It would also be a vain effort to attempt the composition of the Stone—even if we could extract it from gold or silver alone—unless those same metals could be further purified and **subtilized** <note>The process of refining a substance to its most essential, "spiritual" form.</note> by the Art.

<margin>Gold is further from the perfection of the elixir than base metals are from gold.</margin>
For although this perfection of metals may suffice in the degree of nature, nevertheless, if we look toward the sublimity and excellence of the elixir, we will see that gold is further removed from the purity and **digestion** <note>The alchemical process of "cooking" or maturing a substance through gentle, consistent heat.</note> of the elixir than imperfect metals are from gold. This may be gathered from the fact that imperfect metals can pass into gold in a single hour or a shorter space of time through the addition of the elixir, whereas gold can only be turned into the elixir over a long and protracted period of time. Otherwise, if the cleanliness and perfection of natural gold were sufficient, we would simply take it as nature gave it to us. Whence **Arnaldus** says in his *Soliloquy*: *It is necessary that the elixir be more purified and digested than gold and silver, because it must...*

# CHAPTER FIVE.

...convert bodies diminished in perfection into gold and silver, which they cannot do themselves, because they are unable to tint, except as far as their own capacity extends: for nothing whitens except according to its own whiteness, nor does anything redden except according to its own redness.

<margin>A passage of Geber is explained. From *The Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 10.</margin>
Nor does the authority of **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy.</note> stand in the way when he says in another place, *Perfect bodies do not require preparation, since they are perfect, but only that they be more finely ground and thinned.* <note>original: "Corpora perfecta non indigere præparatione... vt magis subtilientur & attenuentur."</note> This is because Geber was referring to the initial preparation required by imperfect metals before they are dissolved. Perfect metals do not need this, as they lack the superfluous, black, and "burning" moisture, as well as the unclean, coarse, and earthy dregs found in imperfect ones. Nevertheless, the philosophers testify that after they have been dissolved, their **calces** <note>A powder produced by heating a metal; the "ash" of the metal.</note> and their **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to the essential fluid or transformative principle of a metal, rather than just the common liquid metal.</note> must be purified just as much as those of the imperfect metals.

<margin>Gold and silver are dissolved so that they may be cleaned further.</margin>
Indeed, everywhere when it is asked why gold and silver must be dissolved, the philosophers give no other reason than that the pure may be separated from the impure, and that their "earth" and Mercury may be cleansed to the very core. Nature could not achieve this level of purification on its own because it works in a simple, direct manner.

When, therefore, we read in the writings of the philosophers: *The imperfect cannot perfect, nor the unclean cleanse*, <note>original: "Imperfectum perficere non posse, nec immundum mundare."</note> we should understand that they mean nothing else than this: nothing can enter into the composition of the **elixir** <note>The transformative substance or "medicine" used to change base metals into gold.</note> unless it is pure and clean. It must at least be in a state of progression toward the highest perfection and eternal stability, which is impossible as long as corruption and impurity cling to the matter.

<margin>Everything unclean is subject to fire. *The Testament*, chapter 51.</margin>

> Know, my son, that since nothing stained with corruption can endure or tolerate fire, and since fire itself cannot tolerate corruption within it, it is necessary that the clean Stone be masterfully extracted and separated from all impurities and corruptible dregs before you attempt to **fix** <note><term>fixare</term>: To make a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> it, until it becomes pure nature.

<margin>The physical Stone is incorruptible and eternal.</margin>

-># ON THE CLARITY OF PURITY<-

...lest a vapor be produced, we have directed nothing of this work, as a certain philosopher says in the **Turba** <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>. And another says: "If the **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the principle of combustion and soul, rather than just the chemical element.</note> has not been sublimated, it will not possess an ingressing substance or a penetrating power, and consequently, it will be of no value for the true **elixir**."

Thirdly, it follows that this clarity must be cleansing <note>original: "mundificatiua"</note>. To better understand this, it must be repeated that all **metals** are pure and clean in their roots, but are corrupted by "accident"—namely, by the place of their generation, or by the addition of external, impure sulfur. 
<margin>On the Investigation of Perfection, last chapter.</margin>
**Geber** <note>The Latinized name of the influential 8th-century chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note> affirms this very thing: "The substance of the imperfect and the perfect metals," he says, "is everywhere one and the same: namely, **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum (mercury)</term> and sulfur, which are pure and clean before their union." 
<margin>On the Investigation of Perfection, chapters 3 & 5.</margin>
Through this, we find that the corruption of imperfect metals has happened accidentally, giving a new and corrupt form to the matter. Since the corruption of the imperfect metals is accidental and not radical <note>meaning the corruption is on the surface or "accidental" rather than part of its essential "root" nature</note>, and since the stripping away of these accidents is possible (as **Geber** also testifies), the **elixir**—which is nothing other than the most pure, gleaming, and splendid matter of fixed quicksilver and excellently digested sulfur—apprehends and retains only the most clean metallic substance, which is like itself. It leaves behind the earthy and sulfurous matter, which does not belong to the primary composition of the metals. As soon as this substance is stripped of its related superfluities, it emerges no less gleaming and bright than the elixir itself, since it is clear and clean by its own nature—created from the purest and thinnest vapors in the bowels of the earth—were it not for the fact that its splendor had been obscured by combustible sulfur and impure, dreggy earthiness. 
<margin>Requirements in the Elixir.</margin>
The medicine therefore cleanses by adhering to what is similar and close to it, and by separating the superfluous and foreign material that is not of its nature.

Fourthly, it is required that it provide an eminent splendor. It gives this, specifically, by removing the contrary substance that was darkening its brightness and casting a shadow. By "eminent splendor," we mean one that is not like the splendor found in most metals; for all metals, especially when polished, contain some brilliance. We mean a splendor that excels and stands out, such as that found in **gold** and **silver** <note>original: "argento & auro," or the alchemical Sol and Luna</note>, which surpass the remaining metals in their brightness, just as the **Sun** and **Moon** surpass the other stars in the firmament.

Fifthly, it is required that this purity be non-burning <note>original: "non adurens"</note>. That is to say, it must lack the sulfurous quality that causes burning, since all external sulfur burns and is burned. Instead, it preserves the substance from combustion by its radical and fixed **mercurial** moisture, which protects the quicksilver of the metals so that fire cannot act upon it, and even thickens...

->### CHAPTER FIVE<-

...now and it may fix it: for such moisture alone overcomes fire, and is not overcome by fire, nor does it allow itself to be divided into the equal parts of its composition. This is because it remains standing in the fire with its whole substance, rests amicably within it, and rejoices in it; furthermore, it preserves those things with which it is joined. Whence **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy whose works emphasized the mercury-sulfur theory of metals.</note> says: "Whatever we see saved most from burning <term>adustione (the process of being consumed by fire)</term>, we consider those things to possess more of the nature of **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum (mercury)</term>." Therefore, it follows that quicksilver itself is the perfecting agent and the preserver against burning, which is the ultimate stage of perfection.

<margin>A variation in the text.</margin>
The mention of the word "burning" brings to mind how the manuscripts vary at this point in the reading. The common reading holds thus: "The cleansing clarity of purity, giving eminent splendor to that which exists in combustion, not burning." For after the consolidation of the purified parts, that which remains is what the actual fire must burn away—namely, all foreign, unconsolidated superfluities. If this reading is genuine (which I do not think it is), the phrase "not burning" <note>original: "non adurentis"</note> seems to refer back to the preceding word "purity." We are to understand that this purity is not "burning" or cleansing through the process of combustion—as sulfur, salt, bricks, and similar things are purged with the help of fire—nor is it achieved through some chemical work, such as **calcination** <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to cause oxidation or a change in texture.</note> and reduction, or cleansing through pellets or **cementation** <note>A process of purifying gold by heating it with granulated materials like brick dust and salt.</note>. Rather, it is purely natural and proper to the **elixir**, which joins itself to its own similar and pure nature once the superfluities (which are subsequently consumed by the fire) have been separated. The phrase "To that which exists in combustion" refers to the metal or body exposed to the fire and placed in danger of burning, either because of the abundance of external sulfur naturally attached to it (which forces even the fixed **Mercury** to vanish along with it), or because of the rawness and lack of fixation of the Mercury itself—unless, perhaps, by "combustion" we are to understand the fire itself. Another manuscript reads in this way: "Purified purity and clarity, giving eminent splendor to that which exists in combustion, not added <note>original: "non adiunctis"</note> after the consolidation of the purified parts which remain, because the fire, etc." It is as if he were saying "not added," meaning the external elements are separated; these do not consolidate with the pure parts but are instead consumed by the fire.

<margin>How the passage should be restored in the Author's judgment.</margin>
And in a certain way, this latter version is more correct. However, although both copies most consistently retain and read "to that which exists in combustion" <note>original: "in combustione existenti"</note>, I nevertheless believe a mistake has crept in. I think it can be corrected if it is written: "preserving from combustion, not burning." This is according to the mind of **Geber**, who in Chapter 1 of the same book, speaking of this same purity, uses these words: "this oiliness becomes of such purity..."

<meta>This page continues the technical debate regarding the "clarity" of the elixir, specifically grappling with a difficult passage attributed to the medieval authority Geber. It transitions from theoretical definitions of purity to a practical comparison between metallic substances and organic (animal/vegetable) substances.</meta>

# ON THE CLARITY OF PURITY

...of the essence of purity, and artificially cleansed from every combustible or burning thing, so that it does not burn all those things with which it is joined in its smallest parts, but rather preserves them from burning. Otherwise, I confess I do not sufficiently understand what **Geber's** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of alchemy.</note> interpreter means by these words: "giving eminent splendor to that which exists in combustion" <note>original Latin: "dans splendorem eminentem in combustione existenti"</note>. For the interpretation I brought forward above is forced, nor does it satisfy me, although hardly any other can exist if the common reading is to be retained—which I leave to be judged by more discerning minds. However it is to be read, **Geber's** intention is nothing other than that the **elixir** <term>elixir (the medicinal "stone" or agent of transformation)</term> should not only be pure and clear, but also that by its superabundant purity and clarity it should induce an eminent and shining splendor. This occurs by the purer parts of imperfect bodies being glued to it as things similar to itself, while the foreign superfluities are separated—those which are not of the first composition of **Mercury** <term>Mercurij (quicksilver, the philosophical root of metals)</term> but have been added from the outside, which the fire then consumes. What the superfluities of metals are can be gathered from other places in this book, so there is no need for repetition here.

<margin>
Now, whether eminent splendor may be found in things other than metals.
</margin>
Now let us consider whether other foreign things can communicate this eminent brilliance to the viler metals, and let us first examine animals and vegetables and those things originating from them. In these, we do not deny there is a subtle aqueous part, clear and pure, and we admit it therefore has a transparent nature, which is properly the matter of color. But since that moisture of theirs is not condensed or bounded when separated from the earthy parts, it cannot be shining and splendid, much less induce brilliance or splendor in imperfect metals. That their moisture cannot be condensed is evident from this: by no skill or art can their earth be united or joined again to its own moisture once it has been separated by art. This is the opposite of **mercurial moisture**, which never abandons its own earth. Since earth cannot ascend and be **sublimated** <term>sublimari (the process where a solid is heated into vapor and then purified back into a solid)</term> unless mixed with moisture, and that which is not sublimated must necessarily remain dark and foul, surely their earth cannot be shining and clear. Consequently, even when mixed with its own water, it will darken it, however clear and pure it may be, and will hinder the splendor. 

<margin>Question.</margin>
But someone will say that the dregs of wine, honey, and likewise urine, and perhaps certain other things, once reduced to **salt** <note>In alchemy, "salt" often refers to the non-combustible solid residue of a substance.</note>, become clear and are sublimated; therefore, one could condense its own clear and transparent moisture and induce brilliance into it. 

<margin>Solution.</margin>
I respond: these salts, when dissolved, pass into the nature of water so long as they are liquid, and the water cannot be so condensed through these that they are not separated from it:

<summary>The author argues that the elixir's purity allows it to grant splendor to metals by removing external impurities, while dismissing the idea that animal or vegetable substances can achieve the same effect due to their inability to permanently reunite their "earth" and "moisture."</summary>
<keywords>Geber, elixir, Mercury, sublimation, superfluities, metallic vs organic, alchemical salt, moisture and earth</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of why certain substances cannot impart "clarity" or "brightness" to metals. While the previous page addressed the definition of splendor in the context of Geber's writings, this page examines specific materials—salts, vitriols, and gemstones—and explains their physical incompatibility with the internal structure of metals.</meta>

### CHAPTER FIVE.

<margin>
Salts, vitriols, and alums cannot communicate brightness to others.
</margin>
...because the water evaporates, and the salts separated from it retain a coarseness and density which prevents them from entering metallic bodies; indeed, volatile salts of this kind, when cast upon bodies melted by fire, withdraw. If, however, they remain with their moisture, they evaporate together and do not enter, because they are foreign to the nature of metals, and can impart no alteration to imperfect bodies. The same is to be judged regarding **salt gem** <note>original: "sale gemmae"; likely rock salt or high-purity sea salt</note> and **sal ammoniac** <term>sal armoniacum (ammonium chloride, used as a flux and cleaning agent)</term>, **vitriols** <term>atramentis (literally "inks," but in alchemy referring to metallic sulfates or vitriols)</term> and alums, and others of that kind, however transparent and shining they may be, or approaching transparency or luster. These, retaining their density because of their coarseness and a substance different from metals, cannot enter or penetrate them; instead, they **calcine** <term>calcinant (reducing a metal to an oxide or powder through high heat)</term> and burn them. If, however, waters and oils are distilled from them, their earth remains at the bottom, never again miscible with its own water so that they can be united together; the water, therefore, will evaporate without the earth, and the earth will not enter without the subtlety of the water. And therefore all salts, alums, and vitriols are useless for inducing brightness in perfect metals, since their earth—even if it previously had some luster and clarity from the transparency of its water—loses the same through abstraction. And even if it had not lost it, it is nevertheless more coarse and thick than before it was joined and united to its water, which can be known from the fact that afterwards it melts neither by water nor fire, except perhaps by **vitrificatory fusion** <note>Melting into a glass-like substance</note>. Nevertheless, we know that imperfect bodies and their **calces** <note>The powdery remains of a metal after heating; oxides</note> are purged by these from foreign sulfur and superfluous earth, and that a more intense red or white color is reconciled to gold and silver; but they do not, for that reason, change the internal substance of the metals.

<margin>
Stones and gems cannot infuse clarity into metals.
</margin>
But will gems, pearls, corals, crystal, and glass or **metallic fluxes** <note>original: "fluores metallici"; substances used to promote melting</note>—some of which are transparent and splendid—impart brightness to metallic bodies? Certainly no more than the things mentioned before, for because of an essence and coarseness dissimilar to metals, they not only cannot penetrate them, but cannot even adhere to them. If indeed they are calcined, they lose their splendor and are reduced to ash or salt, which will penetrate no more than the things previously named; if, however, after calcination they are dissolved, by the application of heat they will return to a body and retain their previous density. But the matter of the **elixir**, the more it is worked by fire through the industry of the skilled craftsman, the greater clarity and subtlety of penetration it acquires.

<summary>This page argues that salts, minerals, and gemstones cannot permanently brighten metals because their physical "coarseness" and lack of affinity for metallic substances prevent them from penetrating the metal's core. In contrast, it notes that the true alchemical elixir gains greater clarity and penetrative power the more it is refined by fire.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 675, which examined why salts, vitriols, and gemstones cannot impart metallic luster, this page moves into a discussion of "middle minerals" like marcasite and the volatile "chemical spirits" used in alchemy.</meta>

-># ON THE BRIGHTNESS OF PURITY<-

<margin>
Whether **marcasites** <term>marchasitae (iron pyrites or similar metallic sulfides)</term> can impart brightness to other substances.
</margin>
But perhaps marcasites will impart this brightness to imperfect metals, for they possess weight and splendor, or at least certain brilliant and glowing sparks reflecting a metallic nature. Yet even these surely cannot, for they consist of a dense body reflecting the nature of both stone and metal; for this reason, they are most appropriately numbered among the **middle minerals** <note>Substances that occupy a middle ground between stones and true metals</note>. As long as they remain in their dense state, they will float atop liquefied metals and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento viuo"; mercury</note> and will neither enter nor alter them. If, however, we wish to refine them by fire, the stony part is reduced to **lime** <term>calcem (a powdery oxide produced by heating)</term>, the sulfurous part is burned away, and the mercurial part vanishes; for they do not truly melt, since they possess only the raw material and color of a metal, not its actual species or essence. Thus, when reduced to lime, marcasites lose their splendor, and it is as if they never possessed it; furthermore, they are not made any more capable of penetrating other substances by this method. Therefore, one seeks their brilliance in vain, and labor is wasted in trying to refine them. But if the splendor and brightness required by **Geber** <note>A reference to the famous alchemical author, likely the 13th-century Latin pseudo-Geber</note> is not found in marcasites, it is found much less in other middle minerals of that kind—namely, **magnesia** <term>magnesia (here likely referring to manganese ore or a similar dark mineral used in glassmaking)</term> and **tutty** <term>thutia (zinc oxide found on the walls of smelting furnaces)</term>, or even in **boraxes** <term>bauracibus (alkaline salts used as fluxes)</term>, which do not have such luster and cannot be purified at all.

<margin>
Whether **chemical spirits** can give brightness and splendor to base metals.
</margin>
But will the chemical spirits—namely sulfur, arsenic, and quicksilver—induce the splendor of brightness in cheaper metals? For they possess in their nature something shining, which can also be intensified and increased through art. However, we have often said that these, if not **fixed** <term>fixos (made resistant to heat so they do not evaporate)</term>, cannot usefully adhere to metals, because they easily flee the heat of the fire; and what is worse, sulfur and arsenic burn all metals. If indeed they are fixed, they are reduced to an earthy substance that is neither flowing nor penetrating. If, however, they could be fixed without being converted into earth, so that they provide a metallic fusion, there is no doubt that a certain **stone** <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or a "tincture" capable of transforming metals</note> for dyeing metals could be made from them. For so Geber says of

<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 29.
*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 30.
</margin>
**sulfur** and **arsenic**: "Arsenic is a tincture of **whitening** <note>original: "albedinis"; the white stage of the alchemical work</note> with ease, but of **reddening** <note>original: "rubedinis"; the final red stage</note> with difficulty; but sulfur is a tincture of reddening with ease, but of whitening with great difficulty." And concerning quicksilver, the same Geber says: "It is fixed and is a tincture of the most exuberant restoration of reddening, and of glowing splendor, and it does not withdraw from that which is mixed with it, so long as it is in its own nature." But since these works are of the greatest labor, of intolerable stench, and of most dangerous experiment, I would rather advise with the philosophers that each person [should seek this] in gold and silver...

### CHAPTER FIVE.

...should spend his labor on this: in which, as those same authors assert, there are shining rays that **tinge** <term>tingentes (the alchemical process of "dyeing" or fundamentally changing the color and nature of a substance)</term> other bodies with true whiteness <note>silver</note> and redness <note>gold</note>, according to how they have been prepared.

<margin>
Imperfect bodies cannot grant clarity to others as long as they contain some degree of corruption within them.
</margin>
Even though **imperfect metals** <note>Base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron</note> contain something of brilliance in their first composition—since their matter is no different than that of gold and silver, namely consisting of the most subtle and clear fumes—they have nonetheless been so corrupted by the addition of external sulfur and terrestrial filth from the nature of the mineral site that **Geber** <note>The influential 13th-century author of the *Summa Perfectionis*</note> testifies that nothing brilliant is to be found in them. Therefore, one must consider that a shining substance—which might "tinge" and illuminate the matter of the **elixir** <term>elixir (the transmuting agent or "Philosopher's Stone")</term>, that is, the **Mercury** and **Sulfur**—can hardly, if at all, be drawn from them. If this is true, we shall strive in vain to induce brilliance in one thing by means of another.

This must be understood, however, to apply only as long as they retain some degree of filth within themselves. For when they have been perfectly cleansed of it, they can be brought to the perfection of gold and silver and to a clear and shining nature, even by the testimony of Geber himself, whose words are these:
<margin>
From *The Investigation of Perfection*, chapter vii.
</margin>
> When we have seen, through our experience and our ingenuity, that the imperfect bodies have been prepared, cleansed of all superfluous corruption, and liberated from fleeting and terrestrial uncleanness, we have found them to be of greater clarity, brilliance, and purity than the naturally perfect bodies themselves. <note>original: "Cum corpora imperfecta per nostram experientiam... inuenimus ipsa maioris claritatis & fulgoris seu puritatis quam ipsa corpora naturaliter perfecta."</note>

<margin>
Whether the gold and silver of Art exceed those of Nature.
</margin>
He says "of greater clarity, purity, and brilliance," not because he means that base metals transmuted by the elixir exceed the purity and brilliance of gold or silver generated by nature—which is impossible, since **Art** <note>The practice of alchemy</note> can only imitate **Nature** with great difficulty, and it is enough for the gold and silver of Art to be in the same degree of perfection as the natural ones—but because their prepared and cleansed matter can become an elixir. This elixir is much more perfect in its principles and abounds more in purity, clarity, and brilliance than the silver or gold of nature, yet only with the help of the "oiliness" and "soul" <note>Metaphorical terms for the vitalizing chemical principles</note> sought especially from the perfect bodies, as we have said. Otherwise, if Geber had wanted to indicate that imperfect metals transmuted into gold or silver by the elixir were of greater purity and brilliance than naturally perfect bodies, he would not have mentioned "preparation" and "cleansing," but would have said, "when we have seen the imperfect bodies converted," or "changed," or something similar.

<margin>Question</margin>
But someone will object and say: the Philosophers often assert that their gold and silver are not the gold and silver of the **common people** <note>original catchword: "vulgi"</note>...

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
I respond: A transition from one extreme to another does not happen except through intermediates. Therefore, **Mercury** and **sulfur**, which provide the matter and are the extremes of the stone on one side, cannot become a complete **elixir**—which is the other extreme—unless they first pass through the intermediates, which are the metals. Wherefore, they must first be converted into silver <note>the lunar stage</note> and then into gold <note>the solar stage</note>. Since these are on the path and in the motion of attaining greater perfection, and must finally become the medicine which converts the imperfect, they are rightly said to be the silver and gold of the philosophers. Indeed, they exceed mineral gold and silver because they are clearly purer and more subtle, and—that upon which the hinge of the whole matter turns—they are **spiritual** <note>Meaning they have been refined into a non-solid or "living" state</note>. Thus, their perfection can be intensified in a marvelous way according to the will of the craftsman, a power which is taken away from common gold and silver. For common metals are "dead bodies" and can perform no action unless they are first made spiritual, purified, and digested, just like these metals of the philosophers. The philosopher **Aros** <note>Likely referring to Arisleus or a similar authority cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> clearly indicates this same thing when writing to King Nephet in this sentiment: "In our stone are the **Sun** <note>gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>silver</note> in virtue and power, and even in nature; because if these were not in the said stone, gold and silver would not be made from it. And yet the Sun existing in the stone is not like common gold, nor is the Moon in the same way like common silver, because the Sun and Moon existing in the said composition are better and more subtle than those remaining in common nature." # CHAPTER FIVE.

...of the corn poppy or the wild poppy, or of dried saffron, to come upon it, so that he may clothe himself in the king’s garment and keep it <note>This refers to the final stage of the alchemical process, where the substance takes on a deep red color, symbolized by a king's royal robe</note>.

<margin>Another objection.</margin>
But another will shout out besides, and will mock my interpretation by bringing forward the words of Master Arnaldus de Villanova <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist</note> taken from the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* or *Rosary of the Philosophers*, a classic alchemical text</note>, where he says thus: "Throw one weight of it (namely the Lunar elixir) upon a thousand parts of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij"</note> washed with salt and <margin>Part 2, chapters 27 and 28, and the following chapter of the same book.</margin> vinegar, and it will become pure Silver <term>Luna (the Moon or Silver)</term>, better than that from the mine. And throw one weight of it (the Solar elixir) upon a thousand parts of Silver or Mercury washed with salt and vinegar, and it will become the truest Gold <term>Sol (the Sun or Gold)</term> in every trial, and much better than that produced from the mine." By these words of Arnaldus, repeated twice, it seems that the interpretation of the words of Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry</note> which I brought forward could be weakened, and it could be shown that gold made by art and through the addition of the elixir is better than the natural kind.

Indeed, the words of such a great Doctor could move one who is unpracticed and ignorant of the philosophers’ ways of speaking from their original opinion.

<margin>The Refutation.</margin>
But I shall make it, as I hope, so that it appears clearly to everyone what the philosopher means in these places. All professors of this science affirm, and Arnaldus himself also, that one weight <margin>Rosarius, chapter 29.</margin> of the perfect elixir tints <term>tingere (to "dye" or transform the quality of a metal)</term> a thousand thousand parts of **Mercury** or any imperfect body into true silver or gold, which he also proves by an example in chapter 31, saying: "Take a hundred parts of **Mercury** washed with salt and vinegar, and place it over the fire. When it begins to boil, place one part of the prepared elixir upon those hundred parts of **Mercury**, and the whole will become a medicine for other washed **Mercury**. Then, throw one part of this congealed medicine upon a hundred parts of **Mercury** boiling in a crucible on the fire, and the whole will still be a medicine. Afterward, place one part of this last congealed medicine upon a hundred parts of washed **Mercury**, and the whole will become gold or silver in every judgment, according as the first elixir was prepared and composed as red or white." Arnaldus proposes three projections <term>proiectio (the act of casting the Stone or Elixir onto molten metal to transform it)</term> of the stone (which some mistakenly judge as multiplications, not seeing that the power and potency of the elixir is diminished immediately at the first projection, and much more so at the second). For first (I take a certain weight for an uncertain one), he throws one drachm of the elixir over a hundred drachms of washed **Mercury**. Secondly, he multiplies these hundred drachms a hundred times—

...multiplies, for he says: "Cast one part of this congealed medicine upon a hundred parts, and thus ten thousand drachms <note>A drachm is an ancient unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce</note> are made." Thirdly, he multiplies these ten thousand a hundredfold. From which calculation, one drachm of the elixir is found to convert ten hundred thousand <note>one million</note> drachms of Mercury. Now, since in the previous chapters Arnaldus says that by one part of the white or red elixir, a thousand parts of silver or **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij"</note> are converted into silver or gold better than what is produced from the mine, he does not mean the ultimate and final conversion of **silver** <term>Luna (the Moon)</term> or **Mercury** into gold or silver that is compact and dense—such as gold or silver melted in furnaces and reduced into a body or mass—but only that those thousand parts of Mercury or silver are reduced into a powder by the force and virtue of the elixir; or as Arnaldus says, into a "medicine," which is nothing other than gold and silver, but in the form of a powder. This powder can further exert its power, and each of its parts can still be diffused into a thousand others, and thus grow to the perfect number of the elixir, which is one million. And with that intention alone, Arnaldus says in the aforementioned places that this gold and silver is "better" than silver and gold produced from the mine. Therefore, beyond the reasons already mentioned, they are called the **gold and silver of the philosophers**: since, as our Arnaldus adds, there is a great addition in these **tinctures** <term>tincture (a potent alchemical substance that "colors" or transforms base metal)</term>, and they persevere in the fire, and even possess greater virtue and utility in expelling illnesses than the gold and silver of the mines. These things are sufficiently proven by the words of the same Arnaldus described above. For after he shows the ultimate virtue of the elixir and its final **projection** <term>projection (the final step of alchemy, casting the elixir onto base metal to transform it)</term>, he simply adds: "it will all become silver and gold by every judgment," which is true.

Therefore, one should not think, as many do, that gold and silver made through the Elixir are better than natural ones, but rather that they exist at the same level, can endure the same tests, and possess the same faculties, neither more nor fewer. We have now explained the fifth condition of the **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>, namely the clarity and brightness of its purity; it remains for us to deal with the sixth, which we will do in the following Chapter.

<header>CHAPTER SIX.</header>

# ON THE FIXING, TEMPERATE, thin, fixed, incombustible EARTH, etc.

## CHAPTER VI.

*In which the third element of the Stone, namely Earth, is discussed, along with its definition and properties: where it may be sought, by what means it can be acquired, and how it is afterwards cleansed and prepared. Its necessity in the Art is proposed, and it is examined whether it can be extracted from anything other than metals. Likewise, fixation and the methods of fixing are treated, and it is shown how all elements of the Stone must eventually be turned into earth.*

<margin>The duties of the body.</margin>
Just as active principles cannot demonstrate their powers unless they are joined to passive ones as **Spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus"; in alchemy, "spirits" refer to volatile substances that easily evaporate or act upon other materials</note>, so too mineral spirits cannot act unless they are united with **bodies** <note>original: "corporibus"; "bodies" refer to the solid, physical mass of a metal or mineral</note>. The duty of the spirits is to dissolve, wash, cleanse, and vivify the bodies; conversely, the duty of the bodies is to coagulate, mortify, and fix the spirits.

<margin>What kind of earth is desired in the Art.</margin>
By "bodies" or "body" in this context, I understand nothing other than the **Earth** <note>original: "terram"</note>, which our Author desires to be fixing, temperate, thin, subtle, fixed, and incombustible—granting the permanence of **fixation** <term>fixation (the process of making a volatile substance stable so it does not evaporate when heated)</term> in a solution adhering to itself, standing firm and persevering against the fire. He calls it "fixing" by a certain fixation, yet not a perfect one; indeed, it is rather fit for fixing, as he says in the first Chapter—specifically at the beginning of the work. At that stage, the earth is quite raw and undigested, and it is not yet able to fix the other volatile part of the Stone, but only to coagulate it. This is because the earth itself is not yet fixed or incombustible, but remains subject to corruption and burning.

Whence the Philosophers carefully warn us to beware of a violent fire at the start of the work: for this earth must be digested and accustomed to the fire by degrees, so that afterwards it can endure the most intense heat. This happens once it has been made fixed and incombustible through its cleansing and refinement. Thus, it becomes capable of granting the permanence of fixation to the spirit adhering to it in solution, which it could not do before its own fixation. 

And **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century figure in alchemical history</note> indicates this most skillfully, as if ascending by certain steps. He calls it "Temperate," once the appropriate digestions and **decoctions** <term>decoction (the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or mature it)</term> have been performed, because this earth, as **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical texts were attributed</note> witnesses, in the beginning of [its] birth-

<meta>The catchword "natiui-" at the bottom of the page suggests the next page begins with "nativitatis" (of the birth).</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Earth as the third essential element of the Philosophers' Stone, explaining its role as a "body" that stabilizes and "fixes" volatile mineral spirits. It emphasizes that the Earth must be gradually prepared and purified through heat to become incombustible before it can successfully complete the alchemical transformation.</summary>

<margin>Testamentum, chapter 54.</margin>...[persevering] <note>Completing the word "perseverantem" from the previous page.</note> in its nativity, it is cold and dry in the fourth degree <note>In the medieval system of "degrees," the fourth was the highest and most intense level of a quality.</note>, and its substance is bitter and astringent; but through proper digestions and cookings, it is changed from nature to nature, and from flavor to flavor, until at last it emerges as most temperate.

<margin>Cold earth, at the start of the work, becomes temperate through digestion.</margin>
By **Thin**, we mean that which, through the suitable regimens of the Art, has shed all thickness and bodily density, and has cast off its earthy dregs. Thus rendered subtle, it may very quickly penetrate and alter molten metallic bodies through its own fineness. By **Fixed**, we mean when it is joined with its own **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture (the essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist within all matter)</term> and with its ferment—namely, the white or the red—as the heat of the fire is gradually increased. By **Incombustible**, we mean after the removal of the "fatness" and oiliness which previously hindered the spirit's coagulation within it, polluted the earth itself, and made it vulnerable to burning. By **Granting the permanence of fixation in a solution adhering to itself**, we mean that it fixes the spiritual and volatile part of the Stone with every kind of **fixation** <note>original: "fixio"; the process of making a substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note>; this volatile part adheres to the earth by being dissolved, and is mixed with it in an inseparable union. 

Or, by "solution," you may understand the melting of metals, which is a term sometimes used by the writers of this Art. Specifically, it refers to when the perfect **elixir** <note>The "elixir" is the final medicinal or transmutative substance produced by the alchemist.</note>, having been reduced to earth, penetrates the **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the volatile principle in metals.</note> of the lesser metals while they are melted. It leaves behind the external **sulfur** <note>In alchemical theory, sulfur was the "clogging" or corrupting principle that caused metals to be base or "sick."</note> that causes corruption; the mercury, sensing a nature friendly and close to its own, gladly adheres to it and is mixed with it.

<margin>Variety of books.</margin>
At this point, the Reader must again be warned that the manuscripts vary. It is commonly read as: *giving the permanence of fixation in the solution of that which adheres with it.* But, to speak frankly, I do not understand what is meant by "adhering in the solution"; furthermore, I do not see what the two small words "with it" refer to. Another book has: *giving the permanence of fixation, adhering in the solution, standing with itself and persevering.*

<margin>How it should be read, in the author’s judgment.</margin>
Yet even that does not seem to be the genuine reading, though it may lead the way toward unearthing the truth. For even if we admit the reading "adhering in the solution"—meaning that the earth adheres to the substance that dissolves it—I do not know what the scribe intended when saying the earth "stands with itself and perseveres." Therefore, I believe it should be read exactly as I wrote above: *in a solution adhering to itself*—meaning adhering to the spiritual thing, or the part of the stone, or the mercury of the imperfect bodies, as I have said. I leave the judgment on this matter free to others, however, since one should not rashly set one's hand to correcting alchemical books.

### CHAPTER SIX

->**ON THE FIXING EARTH**<-

...[per]severing against the fire, he means the same as he did above when he called it fixed and incombustible. He writes this a second time for greater certainty, so that everyone may know that this earth is perfect and entirely complete. This earth is nothing other than the **elixir** <term>elixir (the "medicine" or "tincture" used to transform metals)</term>. Just as the earth itself is fixed and resistant to fire, it is likewise able to transmute <note>original: "commutare"</note> imperfect metals into true gold and silver, both of which can endure the trials of the fire. Let these remarks suffice for the exposition or explanation of the text and words of **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure regarded as the father of chemistry/alchemy.</note>. Now, let us further consider the definition, properties, cleansing, and fixing of this "earth," and where it may be obtained.

The Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists.</note> understand nothing else by the name **Earth** than **sulphur**. Along with **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, sulphur is said to be the material of all metals. By the same reasoning, it is the material of the elixir, since the elixir is made from the very same matter from which gold and silver are formed—though the elixir is purified to a much higher degree, which is why it excels over gold and silver.

<margin>Why the Philosophers call sulphur "earth."</margin>
The Philosophers call this sulphur "earth" for several reasons. The first is that, at the beginning of the work, it possesses the qualities of earth—namely, extreme coldness and dryness, as has been said—although it later becomes temperate. Indeed, at the end, it approaches the action of fire and, in a way, transforms into fire in terms of its power. The second reason is that just as the physical earth was condensed from the thickness of the other three elements (especially water) and became the subject and foundation of the rest, so does sulphur function in the Art. The third reason concerns the goal: all things that are "fleeing" <note>original: "fugientia"; volatile or easily evaporated</note> and not fixed are turned into the "fixing and fixed" earth. The fourth reason is that the Philosophers could not describe or teach the composition of the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> more aptly than through the division of the elements. In this system, the heat of fire, the moisture of air, the cold of water, and the dryness and weight of earth are understood as specific categories.

<margin>There are four elements in the Stone, though only two are visible.</margin>
Furthermore, although the four elements come together in the mixture of the Philosophers' Stone—indeed, in every mixture—two of them are "enclosed," namely fire and air; and two are "enclosing," namely earth and water. Therefore, in every mixture, earth and water are found in abundance. These two are seen and felt, and their power and work are known and recognized (as is stated in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>). The other two, however, are neither touched nor seen, and their power is only perceived within the first two. Fire and air are the more **formal** and moving principles, while water and earth are the more **material** and quiet principles... <note>The author uses Aristotelian terms here: "formal" refers to the active, shaping force, while "material" refers to the passive substance being shaped.</note>

<meta>The text ends with the catchword "faci-", which would likely complete to "facientia" (making/causing) on the following page.</meta>

It details the four reasons for this naming and describes how the four elements interact within the Philosopher's Stone, distinguishing between visible (earth/water) and invisible (fire/air) components.</summary>
