# ON THE FIXING EARTH

...factors contributing to and aiding in **fixation** <term>fixation (the process of making a volatile substance stable so it does not evaporate in fire)</term>. However, just as the power of a form does not manifest except within the matter in which it is enclosed, so too fire and air do not appear except within water and earth. Therefore, when the enclosed elements <note>fire and air, often considered the "active" or "spiritual" elements</note> are strong, but the enclosing elements <note>water and earth, the "passive" or "material" elements</note> are weak, then the mixture is easily corrupted. This is because the formal principles—through which form, color, taste, smell, and similar qualities are given—evaporate, and only the material parts remain, even if they are not entirely deprived of heat. 

If, on the contrary, the enclosing elements dominate the enclosed, the mixture is not easily destroyed, because the enclosed parts are not easily released due to the strength of the containers. But if both are weak, then one part of the element cannot hold the other. When, however, the elements are made equal in strength and power, according to every possible way of nature, then they equally contain and are contained by one another. Every tiny part of that balanced temperature is bound and held by its match and its opposite equally; all things become one without any division, and the mixture is made everlasting. In such a state, there is no resistance among the component elements, nor any contrariety, but rather total identity and homogeneity. For this reason, **gold** was created by nature to be incorruptible because of its balance and the equal composition of all its elements; fire, which consumes all other things, does not diminish it, nor do air, water, or earth defile or destroy it. Following this example, the **Stone** <note>the Philosopher’s Stone</note> must be guided and composed through the Art, so that all elements may come together in a true equality according to every possibility of nature.

<margin>The Book of the Perfect Mastery <note>original: "Lib. perfect. magist."; likely referring to the "Summa perfectionis magisterii" attributed to Geber.</note></margin>
Regarding this, **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rhasis"; a celebrated 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist.</note>, speaking of the visible elements of the Stone—namely water and earth—says: "When they are alternately married in a suitable manner, a balanced substance is generated from them, which the violence of fire cannot overcome, nor the filth of earth spoil, nor the muddiness of water contaminate, nor the touch of air overshadow."

<margin>A simple element is of no use in the Art.</margin>
Therefore, neither earth nor any other simple element contributes anything of use to the Art, but all purified elements must be joined and equalized forever. This cannot be done unless the craftsman thoroughly understands the simple elements before he begins their division and composition; without this knowledge, all the labor of craftsmen is in vain. We say, therefore, that in this Art the elements that are visible and tangible are the moist and the dry—that is, water and earth—and that within the water is air, and within the earth is fire.

But there is an ancient controversy as to which element is the first and root-

...is radical in the art, from which the remaining elements draw their origin. <margin>Which element is first in the art.</margin> For some have said it is water, in respect, as I indeed believe, to the liquefaction <term>melting or becoming liquid</term> of metals, and because they were water before they were coagulated; but others say it is earth. Whence Hermes says: "Earth is the mother of the elements; all things are made from earth, and to earth they are returned." And Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist often quoted in Latin translations</note> says: "Earth is the mother of elements, and the mother of colors, and the mother of the two smokes <term>the two vapors—sulfurous and mercurial—that rise during heating</term>, and it is the whole, and from it is drawn the whole which we need in the work." Raymond Lull <note>A famous Majorcan philosopher and reputed alchemist</note> says: "In earth you must fix the elements, into which it is necessary that the smoke of our gold be carried as if to the first element, which is the subject and foundation of all others." He says in another place: "The substance of air came out from the substance of water, just as the substance of water came out from the substance of earth. Wherefore it appears that the whole wonderful substance of our stone came out from the earth." I am more inclined toward their opinion, for viscous water—which is the first matter of metals, or quicksilver—would be of little use to us unless it had been coagulated and reduced into the appearance of earth. However, the opinion of others is not to be rejected, if it is understood correctly.

<margin>Definition of Earth:</margin> Therefore, speaking of earth, we say with Raymond Lull that it is a "metallic being in which the power of the mineral spirit rests." <margin>Explanation of the definition:</margin> I said "metallic being" to distinguish it from common sulfur or any other earth sought from middle minerals, stones, animals, or vegetables. For although this earth is called "sulfur" in respect to the first matter of metals along with quicksilver <term>mercury</term>, yet it is not sulfur in its whole nature, but possesses certain qualities of sulfur in the beginning (namely, a combustible oiliness and a foul odor, whence it is not infrequently named the "stinking menstrual water" <note>original: "menstruale foetens"; Lull used this term for the base solvent or "first matter" that must be purified</note> by Lull). These, however, being accidental and not innate in its nature, are removed by artifice.

<margin>The Testament, chapter 56.</margin> Hence Raymond says: "Our sulfur is not sulfur in its whole nature, because if it were sulfur, it would burn the substance of the quicksilver by the excellence of its dominance. And therefore the power of sulfur does not dominate over the power of quicksilver, nor can it consume its specific metallic clarity, but only congeals it and fixes it up to the degree of the power of its virtue while preserving the mineral species." Furthermore, if this substance of earth or sulfur is metallic, it must necessarily either be a metal or be drawn from metals. He calls the "mineral spirit" the water or quicksilver, whose power rests in the earth when it communicates its power to the earth by making...

Properties of the Earth.

Whence, the body—that is, the earth—is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or *Assembly of the Philosophers*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note> to have greater power than its brothers, namely, the spirit and the soul. ...dryness. Hence Pythagoras says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Know that the thing which the philosophers have described in so many ways follows its companion without fire, just as iron follows the lodestone <note>original: *lapidem magnetis*</note>." And in the same place, Theophilus says: "It must be noted that if there is a closeness between iron and the magnet, there is an even closer affinity between copper <note>original: *æs*</note> and the permanent water <note>original: *aquam permanentem*, a term for the stable alchemical solvent</note>." Likewise, Belus says: "Theophilus has shown you that there is a closeness between the magnet and iron, and similarly between the copper of the philosophers <note>original: *æs philosophorum*</note> and their permanent water, both of which are attractive to the other."

<margin>What "copper" means to the philosophers.</margin>
Now, the "copper" of the philosophers is nothing other than sulfur and earth, although it is often taken to mean the metallic body from which sulfur is extracted. Concerning this, Eximenus says in the *Turba*: "Know, sons of doctrine, that there is no true tincture <term>a substance capable of transforming metals</term> except from our copper, or even from the quicksilver itself, or the water of the stone." As Hyargus says in the same place: "The copper of which the philosophers spoke is not the common copper nor the common tin, but rather our body, which must be mixed with the body of magnesia <note>original: *magnesiæ*, a symbolic name for the raw material of the Great Work</note> so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness." In this passage, he calls quicksilver a "body" for the reason that it can be touched, felt, seen, and contained in a place—all properties of bodies—even though for other reasons the philosophers very often call it a "spirit." And a little later: "Hence, cook it and grind it with vinegar <note>original: *aceto*</note>, and call both—either the copper itself, or the vinegar, or the water—by the name of 'copper'." Zimon also says in the following discourse: "You have said, Hyargus, that the philosophers are accustomed to call both things that enter into the mixture 'copper,' and rightly so." Thus, sulfur and quicksilver enter into the mixture, and so each is sometimes called the "copper of the philosophers."

<margin>The reason why the earth retains [it]. *The Testament*, chapter 24.</margin>
The earth retains its quicksilver by the same cause of affinity by which it attracts it. Hence Raymond Lull says: "We cannot bind the spirit through the body unless it is held by its own nature, which is the property of their bond." This is also by reason of a vacuum, because this earth, after its calcination <term>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder</term>, is broken apart and filled with pores, being very thirsty and desiring to restore its lost moisture. For this reason, Lull often calls it a "deserted earth," depopulated of its spirits. And in the *Turba*, the stone is called "hollow, spongy, and deceptive" because of the porosity of the earth, and because it drinks up its own water out of thirst.

<margin>How it both dries and coagulates.</margin>
Furthermore, it dries and coagulates what is retained, due to its bitter <note>original: *ponticam*, referring to a sharp, astringent quality</note> nature and the power of binding with which it is endowed. Hence Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist</note> says: "The earth is the thing that binds the compound, preventing the fluid elements from their raw fluidity, possessing within itself fire symbolically in its dryness. It fixes [it] because of..."

# CONCERNING THE FIXING EARTH

...natural fixation: both its calorific and its fiery power, which it acquired through calcination <term>heating a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile components and reduce it to a powder</term>, because every kind of calcined substance is more fixed <note>stable or resistant to evaporation by fire</note> than that which is not calcined, as Geber <note>Jābir ibn Hayyān, an 8th-century polymath and foundational figure in alchemy</note> says.

<margin>In the *Apertorium* <note>An alchemical work traditionally attributed to Raymond Lull</note>.</margin>
Hence Raymond Lull says: humidity is converted into its dry place, that is, into its own earth, because that is the proper place for the generation of sulfur. And this then becomes clearly apparent, for that earth does not do this before its preparation and calcination, and yet it does so after calcination because of its own natural heat, which was strengthened by the removal of the humidity that was mortifying it and totally submerging it. It purifies for the same reason that it is purified: for just as water washes the earth, taking away its blackness and stench, so the earth in turn holds back the dregs <note>original: *fæces*</note> of the water, so that they do not ascend together with the water, because dregs cling to dregs, and the thicker and denser part of the water falls into the earth.

<margin>
From where earth is to be sought.
*Book of Furnaces* <note>original: *Lib. forn.*</note>, chapter 18.
*On the Investigation of Perfection* <note>original: *De Inuest. perfect.*</note>, chapter 3.
</margin>
Having described the effects or powers of sulfur, it might be asked from where it is most effectively drawn out. We say: from metals, both imperfect <note>such as lead or tin</note> and perfect <note>gold and silver</note>. For Geber expressly affirms this in these words also cited above: **"Mercury and sulfur can be extracted from both imperfect and perfect bodies that have been properly prepared."** He suggests the same elsewhere in this manner: **"From whatever the white or red elixir <term>the transformative substance; white for silver, red for gold</term> is made, it is nonetheless nothing other than quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum*</note> and sulfur, one of which does nothing without the other."** And later he adds: **"And because all metallic bodies are composed of quicksilver and sulfur—pure or impure—which have grown into them by accident and not in their first matter, it is also possible for them to be removed through suitable preparation."** As if he were saying: In the making of the elixir, we have need of quicksilver and sulfur no less than nature does in the generation of metals; but because these two principles are impure and filthy in certain things, they must therefore first be purged and cleansed of superfluities before they enter the composition of the elixir. This is possible because they have come upon the bodies accidentally and not radically <term>meaning they are surface impurities rather than part of the fundamental essence of the metal</term>. Now, the stripping away of accidents is possible, as he says in chapter 5 of the same book.

The illustrious and eminent Doctor Raymond Lull confirms Geber's opinion in many places, and especially in the book *The Compendium of the Transmutation of the Soul* <note>original: *li. de compend. transmut. animæ*</note>: **"The modes,"** he says, **"of mixing elements with sulfur happen in nature in two ways, because they are made either with its own earth, or with a foreign earth. With a foreign earth it happens in many ways—namely, as many as there are modes of mixing."**

<header>CHAPTER SIX</header>

...the nature of sulfur, when they come to the pleasure of the artist <note>the alchemist</note>. By these words, Lull <note>Raymond Lull, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> sufficiently indicates that the spirit or water, and the sulfur or earth of the elixir, can be sought from various metallic bodies. For example: if the spirit of the stone is drawn from perfect bodies <note>gold and silver</note>, its sulfur can be sought not only from those, but also from imperfect ones <note>base metals like lead or copper</note>; and for this reason, he distinguishes between proper earth and alien earth. Proper earth is that which is drawn from the same body from which the other elements—namely water and air—were extracted; alien earth, however, is that which is sought from another body. And because metallic bodies are multiple, the mixture of the elements is also multiple. For one mixture is of water drawn from silver with the sulfur of copper or lead; another with the sulfur of iron or tin; although the sulfur of all metals and their Mercury are one and the same in their root, yet they are distinct and varied by accidents <note>external characteristics or impurities</note>; however, through art, after a suitable cleansing, they can be reduced to a single pure substance.

<margin>On the Intention of Alchemists <note>original: *De Inte. alch.*</note></margin>
The same Lull says: "Sulfurs created from imperfect bodies ought to be illuminated by the tincture <note>the coloring and transforming power</note> of the Sun and Moon <note>Gold and Silver</note>, that is, from their oil, because they need no other." And in another place in the same book: "My son, you will be able to make the elixir from the sulfur of whatever body you wish, either for the white or for the red <note>referring to the 'White Work' to make silver or the 'Red Work' to make gold</note>." From these three cited passages of Raymond Lull, setting others aside, it is clear enough that the sulfur of the art can be sought from imperfect metals.

<margin>From where the earth may be sought most easily and most directly.</margin>
Since this is true, we may nonetheless rightly doubt from where it might be drawn most directly and easily. I respond that while it can indeed be drawn from all, it is drawn more easily from copper and iron than from others, but best and most easily from copper alone. Concerning which, Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century Dominican friar and author of the massive encyclopedia *Speculum Maius*</note> says in his *Mirror of Doctrine* <note>original: *spec. doctrin.*</note>: "Copper is mixed with gold and silver, and receives the tincture, and from it is made the elixir of whiteness and redness, nor does its tincture flee <note>it remains stable and does not evaporate under heat</note>."

This is not to be understood as copper in its natural state, because that would be false, but rather as the "body" or philosophical earth produced from copper, as will later appear more clearly from the same source regarding the lime of copper <note>calcined copper reduced to a powder</note>, which is nothing other than sulfur or earth. He affirms the same concerning iron. Iron, he says, serves the mastery, for it can be prepared so that it enters and becomes a body: but it is only dissolved with difficulty, and with great mastery. Here, by "body," he understands nothing other than the sulfur or earth of the art, which alone, after proper preparation, has entry into metallic bodies. But because its preparation is more difficult than that of copper, philosophers have used it more rarely. But why in these...

# ON THE FIXING EARTH

<margin>Two reasons why "earth" <note>the stabilizing alchemical element</note> is sought primarily in copper and iron.</margin>
Two reasons are proposed why sulfur <note>the active principle of stability and combustion</note> should be sought especially in these two metals. One is that these two bodies contain a "fixed" sulfur within them, which is what we seek; for unless the sulfur of the Art <note>alchemy</note> were fixed, or had the nature of something fixed within it, it could not perform the act of "fixing" <note>the process of making a substance resistant to heat</note>. That these two metals are endowed with fixed sulfur is clearly evident from how difficult they are to melt: for those that contain more fixed sulfur melt more slowly, while those with non-fixed sulfur receive fusion more easily and quickly. <margin>*The Sum of Perfection* <note>original title: *Summa perfectionis*</note>, Chapter 63.</margin> As Geber <note>a legendary 8th-century figure, though these texts were likely written by a 13th-century European alchemist</note> tells us, and experience demonstrates. Yet we do not deny that the sulfur of other metals can also be "fixed" through the Art and brought to this same nature.

The second reason is that "soft" bodies, such as those of Jupiter <note>tin</note> and Saturn <note>lead</note>, easily return to a metallic state before their perfect cleansing (which is done by calcination <note>heating to a powder</note>) because their sulfur is not fixed. These [copper and iron], however, withstand the force of the calcining fire until the earthy substance contaminating their sulfur is removed and pulled away; for this reason, we primarily calcine imperfect bodies. But if we wish to remove the earthy substance of the soft bodies by calcination, they must be managed most attentively and skillfully, lest their "calxes" <note>the powders resulting from heating</note> be reduced back into a metallic body before perfection, thus causing the craftsman intolerable labor and the weariness of starting over. Since this is the case, when the Philosophers teach secretly where the substance of sulfur is to be sought, they sometimes named iron itself, but most often copper, as could be shown by infinite examples which I omit for the sake of brevity.

<margin>The difference between white and red sulfur.</margin>
There are, however, those who place this difference among the impure metals: they think the sulfur for the "white elixir" <note>used to make silver</note> should be drawn only from Jupiter <note>tin</note> and Saturn <note>lead</note>, but the "red elixir" <note>used to make gold</note> from Saturn, Venus <note>copper</note>, and Mars <note>iron</note>, following that saying of Geber: "We extract the paste to be fermented from imperfect bodies." <margin>*The Book of Furnaces* <note>original: *Liber fornacum*</note>, Chapter 19.</margin> And from this, we give you a general rule: that the white paste is extracted from Jupiter and Saturn, while the red paste is extracted from Saturn, Venus, and Mars.

By "paste to be fermented," however, he understands nothing other than the "body of the stone," in which the remaining elements are fixed—which we call sulfur or earth. This must afterward be fermented and "animated" <note>brought to life or activated</note> by the ferment, that is, the solar or lunar "oil" <note>liquid extracts of gold or silver</note>. However, as shown above from Raymond Lull, this difference is not permanent, since it is agreed that one and the same sulfur of metals—regardless of its type—must first be turned black through "corruption" <note>chemical breakdown</note> and then turned white.

### CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>Why some seek the "Earth" <note>the stabilizing alchemical element</note> in perfect bodies.</margin>
Many people, fearing the foulness and impurities of the imperfect bodies <note>base metals like lead or copper</note>, believe it is safer to seek the "sulfur of the Art" <note>the alchemical principle of stability and color</note> in perfect bodies <note>gold and silver</note>. They prefer this because of their purity, and because the alchemist does not need to labor through the initial stages of calcination <note>heating to a powder</note> to remove the combustible sulfurousness and earthy dregs which these metals lack, being already perfect. However, when these seekers encounter the difficulty of breaking these metals down <note>original: *resolutione*</note>—owing to their uniform and strong composition—they easily give up on their purpose.

<margin>Interpretation of the words of Avicenna.</margin>
Among those who assert that the sulfur of the Art must be sought from gold and silver, the clear leaders are Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose works were foundational to Latin alchemy</note> and Master Arnaldus de Villanova <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>. For Avicenna says the following:
> White and red sulfur are made from one single material of metals that has been fully purified, though cooked and digested in a different manner. Therefore, in silver there is white sulfur, just as in gold there is red sulfur. And there is absolutely no such sulfur on earth, neither white nor red, except for that which exists in these bodies. And for that reason, the bodies must be prepared subtly, so that we may obtain from them their sulfur and quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, from which gold and silver were originally made beneath the earth.

Although these words of Avicenna may seem plain and open to those reading them for the first time, they are actually quite ambiguous and deceptive if we weigh them more exactly. For although he says that white sulfur is in silver and red is in gold, it does not necessarily follow that the sulfur of the Art is not found in other metals. For first, he says that white and red sulfur are made from "one single material of metals" <note>original: *ex una metallorum materia*</note>, that is, a material common to all metals—unless perhaps by "one" we understand it to mean "the only one," suggesting he wants sulfur sought from metals alone, which is unlikely to be what he meant, even if it is otherwise true. But if sulfur is made from a material common to all metals, surely that material will be the same in both perfect and imperfect metals alike; therefore, sulfur will also be in those same base metals. Because of this, he adds "fully purified," namely: either by the benefit of nature, as in the Moon <note>silver</note> and especially the Sun <note>gold</note>, or by art and human industry, as in the imperfect metals. Furthermore, his addition "cooked and digested in a different manner" can also refer to the imperfect just as well as the perfect: for sulfur is cooked and digested one way in copper and iron, and another way in lead and tin, not only in gold and silver. Nor do his following words confirm that [restrictive] opinion any further, when he says:
> And there is absolutely no sulfur on earth such as that which exists in these two bodies.

By "such as," I understand it to mean "so perfect and clean,"

However, they can reach this perfection through nature in the mines over a long and protracted time, or above ground in a shorter time through the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the practice of alchemy</note>. Finally, when he <note>Avicenna</note> says that the bodies must be prepared subtly so that we can have their sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum*</note>, since he uses the general term "bodies"—which can refer to both the imperfect and the perfect—he seems to suggest both the former and the latter. Arnaldus expressed his opinion much more clearly.

<margin>
*The Rosary of the Philosophers*, Part 1, Chapter 7.
</margin>
"From the bodies of the Sun and the Moon," <note>Gold and Silver</note> he says, "is extracted sulfur that is exceedingly white and red, since in them exists the purest substance of sulfur, highly purified by the ingenuity of nature. This is more certain and subtle, because in its purification, Art is weaker than nature, nor does it catch up to it, however much it may labor." However, although others also occasionally say that the purest substance of sulfur is in gold and silver, let the student of the Art remember that these things are not always to be understood as if sulfur must necessarily be sought from gold and silver. Rather, it means that their substance, once dissolved <note>original: *resoluta*</note>, is most excellently converted into sulfur and becomes sulfur. For there is no reason we should value the digestion <note>The alchemical "cooking" or maturation process</note> of the sulfur of gold and silver so highly, since their sulfur—no less than that of the other metals—must be returned to a crude state <note>original: *reincrudari*; the process of "un-making" a metal so it can be transformed</note> and corrupted if we wish to work the elixir from them.

<margin>
The sulfur and quicksilver of the elixir must be purer than those of gold and silver.
</margin>
For it is necessary that the quicksilver and sulfur constituting the elixir be purer and more subtle than the sulfur and quicksilver found in gold and silver. Moreover, they cannot be purified and made subtle except after "corruption" <note>the breakdown of the metal's form</note>; otherwise, they would not transmute imperfect things into the elixir, but would simply return to the gold and silver they were before. This is affirmed by all the philosophers, whose opinions I shall refrain from citing. However, this advantage is gained from the sulfur of gold and silver: one does not have to labor in their cleansing before dissolution, as is required in the preparations of imperfect bodies <note>base metals</note>, which consume much time and bring the greatest toil to the craftsman. Therefore, the sulfur of gold and silver can indeed be obtained by a shorter path, but at a greater expense, if the craftsman is less certain about the method of the work.

How the earth is extracted.
</margin>

To explain these words, we must remember that all things that are sublimated are sublimated in two primary ways: either by themselves, because they are spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, and arsenic that vaporize easily</note>, or with others, because they incorporate themselves with spirits. Therefore, mercury, tutty, and marcasite can be sublimated by themselves because they are spirits; but the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery oxide or ash left after a metal has been roasted or "calcined"</note> of bodies—especially hard ones—is not sublimated unless it is incorporated with some spirit. 

<margin>
What is required for sublimation.
</margin>
But since all things to be sublimated must be joined to things most similar to them in nature, as is clearly gathered from Chapter 40 of the *Sum of Perfection*, Geber says in chapters 48 and 71 of the same book that if copper <note>original: *Venerem* (Venus)</note> is to be sublimated, it requires tutty; and iron <note>original: *Martem* (Mars)</note> requires arsenic, with which they most closely agree. 

In this place, however, he asserts without distinction that either metal can be sublimated through tutty or marcasite. For he seems to suggest this difference in drawing out the earth or sulfur from the bodies of metals: namely, that the earth of the two [hard metals], copper and iron, is drawn out through their sublimation with spirits; but the earth of soft metals is drawn out through washing with quicksilver. 

We will present both methods and add a third used by the philosophers for the "perfect bodies" <note>Gold and silver</note>, which does not differ from the first in its manner of operation, but only in the change of the spirit to be added. For just as copper and iron abound in much sulfur, they also have need of a thicker, earthy spirit similar to them for their elevation. But for silver and gold, because there is a very great abundance of quicksilver in them, a similar Mercury is applied to them. If [this Mercury] were mixed with copper and iron, it is to be feared that it would ascend alone because of its subtlety and the dissimilarity of its nature, leaving the bodies at the bottom.

Otherwise, we would seek the sulfur or the "earth of Venus" <note>Copper</note> in the dregs of <term>marcasites</term> <note>In this context, various metallic sulfides, likely iron pyrites</note> in vain. Geber would also be incorrect in saying that its greater part is quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury</note>, since he admits in *The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 48, that it possesses superfluous dregs. 

Let the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery ash left after a metal has been roasted or oxidized</note>, mixed with <term>tutty</term> <note>Zinc oxide collected from furnace flues</note> or marcasite, be ground and soaked several times with distilled vinegar so that they may be more deeply united. Afterward, once the wateriness of the soaking has evaporated, let the tutty or marcasite be sublimated from it with a fire sufficient for the elevation of tutty. This should be repeated until a large quantity of it has adhered to the calces and become united with them. 

Then, let them be placed in a sublimation vessel that can endure a very fierce fire. However, use caution: the quantity of material to be sublimated should not be too large, and the bottom of the vessel should not be concave but flat. This allows the body or "calx of Venus" <note>Copper ash</note> to be spread evenly and thinly upon it so it can be elevated equally, as a thick mass would hinder the process. From the very beginning, they should be driven by a most vehement fire so that the spirit might immediately elevate the part of the body most suited to it—namely, the mercurial part—leaving behind in the bottom the earth or sulfur which we seek. 

The same procedure must be followed with the "calx of Mars" <note>Iron ash</note> until a suitable quantity of arsenic remains with it. Then, by the fire of fusion and ignition, let them be pushed forward into the <term>aludel</term> <note>A series of pear-shaped earthenware pots used for condensing vapors in sublimation</note>, and the "earth of Mars" <note>the purified earthy essence of iron</note> will remain. 

The "soft bodies," namely "Saturn" <note>Lead</note> and "Jupiter" <note>Tin</note>, do not require the addition of the aforementioned substances, since they can ascend by themselves with a very strong fire, as Geber teaches in *The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 48. Nevertheless, these may also be washed by the admixture of quicksilver, and in that way, the earth can be drawn out from them.

This is performed in the following manner: Let the calx of Jupiter or Saturn be taken, having been perfectly cleaned, and onto it pour eight times as much quicksilver that has been previously purified through sublimation. Let these be ground together in a marble mortar until the grit of the metallic calces can no longer be felt, but they are instead reduced to the likeness of quicksilver. Then, let there be added to them distilled vinegar or another similar liquor, such as <term>spirit of chalcanthum</term> <note>An early name for sulfuric acid or vitriol oil</note>, in a quantity sufficient to cover them. 

Pour this into a glass dish or glazed earthenware, and placing it over hot ashes, stir it with your fingers continuously and diligently until the whole mixture is reduced to the appearance of a white powder. Once the vinegar has evaporated, the whole will return again to the appearance of quicksilver as before. Then, collect the black or ashen powder that floats on the surface with a horn spoon, or by—

...[parchment], as best you can, and keep it. Repeat this same work until you have as much "earth" as is sufficient for composing the <term>elixir</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or the agent used to transform base metals into gold</note>. A large quantity of this is not needed; the weight of one <term>scripulum</term> <note>A small Roman unit of weight, roughly 1.1 grams</note> or two <term>obols</term> <note>A tiny weight, usually half a scripulum</note>, or even a little less, is enough.

Whoever seeks another way of extracting the nature of sulfur from "imperfect bodies" <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper</note>, or who desires to know more, should read the *Natural Magic* of Ramon Lull, specifically the chapter on the natural calling forth of bodies from their spirits. However, the method for drawing <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, internal "soul" or "fire" of a metal</note> out of "perfect bodies" <note>Noble metals, specifically gold and silver</note>, which was omitted in this place by Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note>, is as follows:

<margin>The third method.</margin> The <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or oxidized</note> of silver or gold is soaked in mercury, ground, and <term>digested</term> <note>Heated gently over a long period to encourage chemical change</note> with a slow heat for several days, so that the substance of the mercury does not ascend <note>Evaporate</note>. Then, the mercury is <term>sublimated</term> <note>Heated until it turns to vapor and then collected as a solid to purify it</note> from it using the most moderate fire possible. This sublimated material is again mixed with the calces, ground, and roasted as before, until the mercury has notably adhered to it; this will be easily perceived by the weight.

Then at last, return the mercury—which has now been sublimated several times from the calx—to the same, and drive it upward with a "fourth degree" fire <note>The most intense heat in the alchemist's four-stage scale, equivalent to a blast furnace</note>. For in this way, the mercury will carry with it all the "quicksilver" <note>original: *argentum viuum*</note> of the gold or silver remaining in the calx, leaving behind in the bottom of the vessel the sulfur, or the "earth of silver or gold." Many have sought this until now, but only a few of the more diligent and vigilant ones, who were less weary of the labor, have found it. A smaller quantity of this earth is found in these bodies (especially in gold) than in those mentioned before, but it is somewhat superior in power if the craftsman knows how to use it properly. 

<margin>Chapter 11 of the *Correctorium*.</margin> Richard the Englishman <note>Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century alchemist</note> intended to teach this method of drawing out sulfur when he said:
> If you do not resolve the body through mercury into mercury, you will not be able to have the hidden power from it, namely the sulfur digested and cooked by the work of nature.

<margin>The necessity of Earth in the art.</margin> The philosophers worked greatest in the investigation of this "earth" moved by this primary reason: they saw that nature does not proceed except through intermediaries. Wishing to imitate nature, and knowing that a transition cannot be made from the softness of quicksilver to the hardness of metal, the philosophers studied how to compose a "middle substance" through art. This substance participates in two properties—namely, incombustible sulfur and inextinguishable quicksilver—and is suitable in its natural homogeneity and proportion. It would have the power of binding together the soul of the <term>stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> with the spirit, so that from the three joined together, a perfect elixir might be made. However, they could not reach this unless the earth first...

It explains that this extracted earth acts as a vital intermediary "middle substance" required to bind the soul and spirit together to create the final elixir.</summary>

### CONCERNING THE FIXING EARTH
<note>original: DE TERRA FIGENTE</note>

...they might have a metallic [substance] in which they could fix the volatile elements of the Stone, and which would attract and retain the middle substance of Mercury, once its superfluous moisture had been cast off. They valued this so highly that they called it the base and foundation of the whole work more than once. And Ramon Lull <note>Raimundus Lullius: A major 13th-century philosopher and alchemist to whom many influential texts were attributed</note> earnestly warns everyone before they begin the work that they must first know how to divide the sulfur from the metals, because in it lies the whole power of the mastery, as he says in the *Compendium of the Transmutation of the Soul* <note>original: compend. animæ transmut.</note>. All the labor and weariness lies in the division of the elements and the sulfur, and in their purification; for afterwards, in respect to these, almost nothing more remains to be done. Nature completes the rest, and the craftsman can rest from his labor.

<margin>How sulfur is to be cleansed.</margin>
But it is not enough to have the earth or the sulfur, unless one knows how to purify and cleanse it exactly. For no one should think that the sulfur of gold is so pure that it does not need human assistance; for although it is clean compared to other metals, if we consider the perfection of the <term>elixir</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or the agent of transformation</note>, we will see that it differs more in impurity and is further from it than silver is from gold. Indeed, as has often been said, the medicine must be purer, more subtle, and more <term>digested</term> <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow application of heat to mature a substance</note> than gold is in its own nature. Therefore, sulfur, from wherever it is extracted, contains these causes of corruption within itself: a blackness, which is also its death; a combustible oiliness; and an earthy dross. The first is accidental; the other two are internal. For the blackness arises from <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The breakdown of matter, often called the "nigredo" or black stage of the alchemical process</note> and from superfluous moisture which killed its natural heat, so that it could not sprout; for great coldness extinguishes a small heat. Hence the *Rosary* <note>original: Ros.; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text</note> says: "Drive out death from the body."
<margin>Chapter of the Testament.</margin>
By this saying, he understood nothing other than that the superfluous moisture arising from putrefaction must be removed, which was suffocating the heat of the sulfur and preventing it from being able to generate. Lull indicates the same thing in other words, but more clearly, in this manner:
<margin>The double death of sulfur.</margin>
"Cast away the moisture where the dragon is submerged, until it becomes a tiny body from the celestial spirit." By the "Dragon," however, he signifies the earth, as other masters of this art sometimes do. And this is the dragon which, after cleansing, devours its own tail and head—that is, the spirit and the soul <note>The "Ouroboros" or tail-eating dragon is a classic symbol of the cyclical nature of the work and the union of opposites</note>.
Yet there is a twofold death of the body: one which we have described leading to corruption, unless it be removed; the other leading to life and a glorious resurrection, which bodies cannot reach except after death...

## CHAPTER SIX

...those things, however, having been brought back to life, will be everlasting. This "death," <note>Alchemists often described the chemical breakdown of a substance as "death" or "mortification," followed by a "resurrection" into a purified state.</note> moreover, happens to it from the withdrawal of its fertile moisture through <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its composition or make it brittle/powdery.</note>. And in the *Mirror of Doctrine*, <note>original: In spec. doctrin.; referring to the "Speculum Doctrinale" by Vincent of Beauvais, a massive 13th-century encyclopedia.</note> just as the cause of the first death was an abundance of cold humor, so the cause of the second is thirst and a lack of <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential, life-sustaining fluid thought to exist in all things.</note>, which nevertheless is later restored to it in abundance. Highlighting this calcination, **Vincent** says: "To calcinate bodies is nothing other than to extract the corrupting moisture and to introduce a rectifying fiery moisture, through which is their life and essence, afterward standing firm in the fire of examinations." Moreover, this calcination is different from that which I cited in Chapter 2, because this one pertains only to the "philosophical earth," while that one generally encompasses all mineral bodies.

<margin>How the combustible oiliness is to be removed from the body.</margin>
The philosophers commanded that the "combustible oiliness" <note>original: Vnctuositas cremabilis; the flammable or greasy part of a substance that alchemists believed caused it to be consumed by fire rather than transformed.</note> be washed with waters that are—as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy.</note> says—subtle, extremely sharp, biting, and pungent, having no dregs. They commanded that the sulfur be boiled for so long until clear and bright water flows from the decoction itself. Afterward, these washings are to be distilled, and what remains at the bottom of the vessel is to be cast away; the distilled water is to be poured back on again, until all the combustible oiliness departs from it, and only the subtle oily substance that withstands the fire and is non-combustible remains. This is exactly what **Ramon Lull** wished to indicate with these words: "Understand that the nature of such sulfur is very bright, strongly clean, and brought to purity by the power of strong and very sharp washings, in such a way that it has in itself no burning combustible oiliness, nor any vaporous or phlegmatic moisture."

<margin>The "sharp waters" of the philosophers. *The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 52.</margin>
**Geber** indicates in express words what these "sharp waters" are with which the sulfur must be washed, and among them he names distilled vinegar, <term>verjuice</term> <note>original: omphacium; the acidic juice of unripe grapes.</note>, as well as the "water" (juice) of sour pears and pomegranates. And the *Lesser Rosary* <note>original: Ros. minor; a famous alchemical text titled "Rosarius Minor."</note> adds purified human urine, the water of blood, of salt, and of alum, which must be distilled and circulated so many times until they leave no dregs at the bottom.

<margin>How the earthy foulness is to be taken away from the sulfur.</margin>
It remains for us to teach the removal of the earthy dregs of the sulfur. This is done in two ways: namely, through calcination and <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, leaving heavy impurities behind.</note>, but nonetheless simultaneously and at once in the same vessel, and in a single operation. This process is as follows: let the "earth of the stone" be soaked and ground with **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver; used here as a solvent or agent to help the solid "earth" lift or vaporize.</note> that has been previously cleansed. For by itself, the earth could not ascend, but it needs the help of a "lifting spirit." Let it be boiled over a slow fire in a water bath for three days so that the Mercury does not rise; then let it be sublimated from it by a strong application of fire near the end, so that nothing of the volatile Mercury remains within it.

Argen- <note>Catchword for "Argentum" (Silver) on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page describes the purification of "philosophical sulfur" through two main methods: washing with "sharp waters" (like vinegar or fruit juices) to remove combustible oils, and sublimation with Mercury to strip away earthy impurities.</summary>

<page-num>698</page-num>

# ON THE FIXING EARTH

Restore the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: Argentum vivum; mercury.</note> to the earth, grind them together, boil them down, and <term>sublimate</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then collects again as a solid in the upper part of the vessel.</note> as before. Repeat this nine or twelve times, always increasing the fire at the end, until the earth—through frequent sublimation and the power of the <term>calcinating</term> fire—emerges white, and its more subtle and "spiritual" part, having been refined, begins to rise somewhat from the bottom of the vessel and adhere to its sides. When you see this, have good hope: use a feather to brush the earth that has risen back down to the bottom, and moisten it again by adding Mercury. Mix and grind it, and boil it for the prescribed days until you see the greater part of the earth adhering to the sides of the vessel, leaving the earthy dregs and black slag <note>original: scoria nigra</note> at the bottom—worthless and to be cast away, for in them dwells neither life nor light. **Vincent the Monk** <note>Vincent of Beauvais, the 13th-century author of the *Speculum Maius*.</note> touches upon all these aforementioned operations in a few words.

<margin>In the *Mirror of Doctrine*.</margin>
> He says: "The brass <note>original: æs; in alchemical contexts, this refers to the base metal or the 'body' being worked upon rather than modern brass.</note> is washed so that its filth may be removed; it is calcinated so that its matter may be refined; it is washed again in the lime with the strongest waters <note>likely acids or specialized solvents</note> so that it may recover the moisture it lost in the lime. It is sublimated so that it may be further refined, and it is mixed with quicksilver so that its nature may be prepared." If any of the purer parts remain in the earth—which you can recognize by a certain glimmering whiteness—do not grow weary of mixing it once more with the same Mercury, boiling the earth, and finally sublimating it as described, until no more of the purer essence remains within it. The sublimated earth must be placed back into the vessel, and in the third degree of fire, if any Mercury remains in them, it must be driven upward into the <term>alembic</term> <note>The top part of a still used for distillation/sublimation.</note>, and all the earth should be gathered into one and preserved until it can be put to use.

<margin>Why the earth must be sublimated.</margin>
Moreover, this cleansing of the earth which is performed through sublimation is entirely necessary before one begins the "physical work." For if it has not been sublimated, it will not possess a subtle and penetrating substance; because, remaining in its physicality and density, it will not admit the <term>spirit</term>, nor will it have the power to penetrate, and consequently, it will be useless for the true <term>elixir</term>. Indeed, it will not mix with the metals to be tinged, nor can it transmute them into the form of a perfect body. Therefore, before its composition with the water, let the earth be washed by quicksilver, and the quicksilver drawn away from it, so that it remains as a most pure lime or ash. For the philosophers do not command the earth to be sublimated except so that it may be reduced to a subtle matter and nature, and so that it may become like a spirit, and afterward penetrate and "tinge" <note>To change the color and nature of a metal, usually to gold or silver.</note>—specifically, after its fixation.

<margin>On fixation.</margin>
Regarding this fixation, it remains for us to say something, since **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and Western alchemy.</note> requires the earth to be "fixed" and to grant the permanence of fixation to those things clinging to it.

<summary>This page details the iterative process of purifying "philosophical earth" using mercury and sublimation to separate the pure "spiritual" essence from black dregs. It emphasizes that this refinement is essential for the earth to eventually penetrate and transform base metals into a perfected state.</summary>

# CHAPTER SIX.

<margin>Five modes of fixation.</margin>
But let us begin with its definition. <term>Fixation</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance—one that normally evaporates or "flees" when heated—stable and resistant to fire.</note>, according to **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most influential figure in early alchemy. The works cited here, like the *Summa Perfectionis*, are now often attributed to a 13th-century European author known as "Pseudo-Geber."</note>, is the suitable adaptation of a thing fleeing from the fire to the fire. I find a fivefold mode of this adaptation in the books of the Philosophers. One is done through <term>Calcination</term> <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air until it becomes a dry powder or "lime."</note>: for every kind of calcinated thing is more fixed than the uncalcinated, as Geber says in the chapter on Calcination and elsewhere. Through calcination, every "fugitive" <note>original: fugitivum; refers to volatile substances that evaporate easily.</note> thing is destroyed. And another says: Everything calcinated in its kind is fixed. The reason is clear, because through the calcination of metallic bodies, the natural humidity—which caused them to flow, and melt, and move in the fire like water, and held their parts together—is removed, so that they cannot be melted or liquefied except with difficulty, but remain in the fire like ash or the lime of stones. Likewise, through calcination, the burning sulfur—enclosed deep within the substance of the bodies, diminishing the bodies through inflammation and turning them into smoke—is removed, however much good and <term>fixed quicksilver</term> <note>original: argentum vivum & fixum; mercury that has been stabilized so it no longer evaporates.</note> may be in them. And this is what Geber meant when he said,

<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 76.</margin>
<margin>Chapter on fixation.</margin>
> Bodies diminished from perfection are fixed through their calcination, because they are freed by it from volatile and corrupting sulfurousness.

<margin>The second.</margin>
The second mode of fixation occurs through slow and long-lasting <term>decoction</term> <note>Heating or boiling a substance steadily over a long period to refine it.</note>, because every volatile thing, after its cleaning, is fixed by the help of the fire with temperate and continuous heat. For temperate heat, as Geber says, is a thickener of humidity and a perfecter of the joining; but a violent fire is a consumer of humidity and a disturber of the melting.
<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 75.</margin>

<margin>The third.</margin>
The third results from the two previously mentioned and is declared by Geber in the chapter on calcination in this sense. The mode of calcination for <term>spirits</term> <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that can be vaporized.</note> is that, as they approach fixation—namely through slow roasting—fire should be administered successively, increasing it little by little so they do not flee, until they can eventually tolerate the greatest fire.

<margin>The fourth.</margin>
The fourth mode is that purified spirits be <term>sublimated</term> with the pure "limes" <note>The powdery residues left after calcination.</note> of bodies until they are fixed; that is, that the lime of the bodies be imbued with some spirit, which is drawn away from it so many times until they remain together and tolerate the harshness of even the greatest fire, and do not flee from it. The reason is because spirits are of the nature of the bodies, and agree with them greatly, and adhere to them, and are mixed more deeply. Therefore, when they are joined with those limes and are slowly decocted together, it cannot but happen that they feel a friendly society and nature, and some part of them is gradually applied to them, until finally through reiteration... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the word "imbibition" on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page defines fixation—the process of making volatile substances heat-resistant—and outlines the first four of five classical alchemical methods to achieve it, citing Geber as the primary authority.</summary>
<keywords>fixation, calcination, Geber, decoction, spirits, limes, Sum of Perfection, volatile sulfur, quicksilver</keywords>

# ON THE FIXING EARTH

...[of inhibition], <term>decoction</term> <note>A process of heating or "cooking" a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its properties</note>, and <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify or stabilize substances</note>, all things are fixed at the same time. This is what the author of the *Minor Rosary* <note>An influential medieval alchemical text, often attributed to Arnaldus of Villanova</note> intended to indicate when he said:

> "If spirits are sublimated with impure things, they are made impure; if they remain with adhering things, they remain more fixed with the <term>tincture</term> <note>A substance or "elixir" capable of transmuting or coloring metals</note> below, which is what we seek."

<margin>
Fifth.
*The Sum of Perfection*.
</margin>
The fifth mode of fixing is by the addition of a fixed thing. Therefore **Geber**, when he wishes to teach the hardening of <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for Lead</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for Tin</note>, so that they might more closely approach the melting point of the perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver</note> when heated to redness. Their preparation is, he says, that we contrive to mix with them the fixed substance of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; Mercury</note> in their depths, or of fixed sulfur, or of its equal, or with hard and non-fusible things, such as the <term>lime</term> of <term>marcasite</term> <note>Iron sulfide; "lime" refers to the powdered form after heating</note> and <term>tutty</term> <note>Crude zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</note>. 

<margin>
*On the Discovery of Truth*, ch. 13.
</margin>
For these things are united and allied with them and harden them, so that they do not melt until they are heated to redness. And in another place: "With talc and <term>precipitated Mercury</term>, or more usefully with pure <term>Moon</term> <note>Silver</note> brought to this state by calcining and dissolving, we arrive at the ignition and complete hardness of these two (namely Saturn and Jupiter), with unspeakable splendor." By the "fixed substance of quicksilver," Geber means nothing other than the two perfect bodies [gold and silver] consisting of fixed mercury, which it will be necessary to join to other less fixed bodies, or to spirits purified and cleansed by sublimation, if it is decided to fix them. Therefore, **Lully** <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval philosophy and alchemy</note> also rightly says:

> "He who does not coagulate quicksilver extracted from bodies into white sulfur that can endure fire through the addition of it with gold, certainly finds no path to the redness <note>The "redness" refers to the Red Elixir, the final stage of the Philosopher's Stone</note>."

It should be known, however, that these fixed bodies must be prepared according to the intention of Geber and other Philosophers, if we wish to use them, before they are joined with other bodies or spirits, because if they remain in their solid and coarse state, they could not be easily mixed. They must therefore be <term>calcined</term> <note>Reduced to powder by heat</note> and dissolved, or reduced into very thin foils, and <term>amalgamated</term> <note>Blended with mercury</note> with common Mercury in the manner of goldsmiths, until they are made like a paste. And so, finally, they are added to the bodies or to Mercury that has been coagulated by the vapor of sulfur, 

<margin>
*Practice of the Testament* ch. 22, 23, & 24; and in the *Codicil*; 4th practice; beginning of the *Rosary* ch. 25.
</margin>
as **Raymond Lully** and **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> teach more extensively; you should consult them. This mode is different from the previous one, because in this case there is no need for repeated sublimation, but only decoction, and toward the end, calcination. There are indeed other ways of fixing—namely, when spirits or metallic bodies are reduced into "earth" through calcination, or violent precipitation to the bottom of the vessel when heated to redness, or into glass—but since "true" <term>Alchemy</term> <note>The author likely distinguishes the "Great Work" of transmutation from more common chemical tasks</note> does not care for these, we also pass over them deliberately.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "Earth" required for alchemical transmutation. ### CHAPTER SIX

<margin>
Whether sulfur can be sought from sources other than metals.
</margin>
It remains for us to discuss whether this "earth" of the <term>elixir</term> <note>The transformative substance sought by alchemists to achieve the Great Work of transmutation</note> can be sought from things other than metals. It is clear indeed from the principles of nature that every combined body is composed of water and earth: thus all animals and vegetables, and those things originating from them, contain within themselves their own earth, and after the removal of their moisture, they can be turned into earth and ash.

<margin>
Why the earth of vegetables and animals is useless for the Work.
</margin>
But because any simple earth whatsoever does not suffice—otherwise we would merely take the very ground we tread upon with our feet—but rather that which has the power of attracting, retaining, and <term>coagulating</term> <note>The process of turning a liquid or vapor into a solid or semi-solid state</note> its own water and converting it to its own nature, the earth of vegetables and animals (and all things originating from them) will rightly be useless for the physical work. For in whatever way it is prepared, it cannot retain its water, much less make that water conform to its own nature. Since the water is <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>Different in kind or nature; not matching the substance it is paired with</note> to its own earth, it will evaporate upon feeling even the slightest heat, leaving the earth abandoned and deserted; the same must be thought regarding the oils extracted from them. 

Furthermore, the earths of all the aforementioned things are burned through <term>calcination</term> <note>A process of intense heating to reduce a substance to a dry powder or "lime"</note> or the violence of fire, and are turned into ash once their <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential, fundamental fluid alchemists believed was the root of life and stability in any substance</note> is lost. Thus, they cannot be melted or made to flow by any method of preparation unless they are converted into glass. Once turned to glass, they have no way to enter into metals; instead, when those metals are liquefied, the glass floats upon them like oil on water because of its alien nature. The earth of metals, however, does not desert its native moisture even after calcinations; for unless some part of it, however imperceptible, remained within, the <term>spirit</term> <note>The volatile, vaporous essence of a substance</note> would be neither received nor retained by it.

<margin>
A Question.
</margin>
But someone will say: the Philosophers more often make mention of salts, and call their earth "salt." For thus **Raymond Lully** <note>A 13th-century polymath and philosopher to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</note> says in a certain place: 

> "That which remains in the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower, gourd-shaped vessel of a still used in distillation</note> is our salt." <note>original: "Quod in cucurbita remanet, est sal noster."</note>

They say furthermore that their earth ought to become volatile. Whence the same Raymond Lully says: 

> "Take the earth which flies above your head." <note>original: "Accipe terram quæ volat supra caput tuum"</note>

However, we find certain salts of this kind in vegetables and animals, or things reflecting their origin. For "salt of tartar" <note>Potassium carbonate, often derived from the crusty deposits in wine barrels</note> and that extracted from the dregs of wine can be made so volatile that it rises together with the spirit of wine; likewise salt drawn out from honey, and salt of urine, and perhaps some others. I respond that these things are indeed true; yet salts of this kind, in whatever way they may be prepared, cannot coagulate their water or spirit (which is altogether necessary), nor <term>fix</term> <note>To make a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates</note> it; rather, they themselves pass into the nature of water and volatile spirit.

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>
We say also that they are always separable from their waters or spirits,

<meta>catchword: ter- (likely beginning the word "terra" or "terrena" on the following page)</meta>

It addresses a counter-argument involving the works of Raymond Lully, clarifying that while organic salts can be made volatile, they cannot achieve the permanent "fixation" necessary for the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Earth" (the solid, stable principle) of the alchemical Elixir. Following the discussion on why vegetable and animal sources are unsuitable, the author now examines why common salts, minerals, and stones also fail to provide the necessary "Fixing Earth" required for transmutation.</meta>

# ON THE FIXING EARTH
<meta>catchword: quo-</meta>

However, the earth of the art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note>, imbued with its own oil and cooked according to the prescriptions of the philosophers, remains with them in the fire and is <term>fixed</term> <note>Fixation is the process of making a substance volatile (likely to evaporate) stable and resistant to heat</note>, and can in no way be separated or divided afterward. Next, let us grant that such salts are not separated from their waters; nevertheless, as long as they remain in that liquid state, they can be stopped by no art so that they might endure in the fire. Even if they did endure, since they have no affinity with metals, they could not enter into them because of their dissimilarity. Much less could they alter them and convert them into gold and silver, for they are alien to that nature, and there is no fixation or <term>tincture</term> <note>A substance capable of imbuing other bodies with its properties, particularly color and quality</note> in them.

<margin>The earth of salts, alums, and vitriols is to be rejected.</margin>
The same must be judged regarding other salts, whether artificial or natural, such as <term>alums</term> <note>Astringent mineral salts</note> and <term>vitriols</term> <note>original: "atramentis" — literally "inks," referring to sulfate minerals used to make pigments</note>. Their oils or waters, drawn out by distillation, are no more united with their earths, nor congealed by them, than those previously mentioned. Instead, it happens that they are driven out by the fire; and even if that did not happen, they do not have the power of elevating their earth. This is because nothing enters the <term>elixir</term> unless it is made pure and spiritual, having cast off the grosser dregs which block the way of entry and penetration.

<margin>The ash of stones and gems is useless.</margin>
The same logic applies to stones, gems, glass, and mineral <term>fluors</term> <note>Flux-like minerals or spars</note>, which turn into a non-fusible <term>calx</term> <note>A powdery residue left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined"</note> when their moisture is dissipated and consumed. That moisture was previously the cause of their binding, and it is impossible for it to be returned to them so that it might be inseparably united. Even if their moisture were not separated from the earth, they would be prohibited from entering metallic bodies due to their density. If indeed, through calcination, they are reduced to the nature of salts and resolved into a liquid, the more watery part will evaporate from the fire, and the other will thicken into a salt. This salt would not be far removed from the aforementioned salts, whether prepared by art or nature, and therefore it would be no more suitable than they are.

<margin>Why the sulfur of marcasites is less open to the art. The Sum of Perfection, chapter 6.</margin>
Nor will <term>marcasites</term> <note>A term often used for iron pyrites or other metallic sulfides</note> supply us with this earth, since their earth does not differ from the nature of stones. If anyone should argue that they contain within themselves sulfur and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum" — Mercury</note>, which is confirmed by the authority of <term>Geber</term> <note>A famous, though often pseudonymous, Arabic alchemist whose "Summa Perfectionis" was a foundational text in Europe</note>, and therefore the latter can hold the place of the spirit and the former the place of the earth, I respond: their sulfur and quicksilver are <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>Different in kind or nature</note>. They can in no way be so joined that they do not separate, burn up, or flee from the fire. Or, if they are fixed, they are reduced to an earthy substance of no virtue or value. Magnesia...

<summary>The author argues that common mineral salts, gems, and marcasites are unsuitable for alchemy because their components separate under heat or lack the "spiritual" purity needed to penetrate and transform metals.</summary>

### CHAPTER SIX.

Also, tutty <note>original: *thutia*; a crude zinc oxide deposit found in smelting furnaces</note>, even though they have **sulfur** mixed with **quicksilver** <note>Mercury</note>, nevertheless differ from metals in the proportion of their principles. They possess elements that are more earthy and polluted, which cannot be separated from one another except with the total destruction of their substance. Thus, they offer little utility in the art <note>Alchemy</note>, because their matter is much cruder than that of metals, and therefore less suitable for preparation. The venerable and distinguished **Ramon Llull** <note>A 13th-century Majorcan polymath and mystic to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</note> 

<margin>Four things necessary for the physical earth.</margin>
requires four things in the "physical earth." First, an **attractive power**; second, a **likeness or affinity** with that which is being attracted; third, a **natural heat** hidden within it; fourth, a certain **vapor** emerging from the earth—imperceptible to sight or touch—which is the primary cause of the **spirit’s congelation** <note>The process of turning a liquid or vaporous substance into a solid state</note>. These are his words: "In our stone, the spirit moves and is moved just as in its own body, operating both by the attractive power of our stone and by the likeness which the said spirit acquired with the whole substance of our stone in the first mixture. This is aided by a power closer at hand—namely, the natural heat of the stone—which regards nature in the greatest proximity of metallic genus and nature. Similarly, it is aided by the power of our imperfect, perforated, and porous stone, which, through the continuous resolution of its body, has caused an imperceptible and untouchable [vapor] in it through a certain operation." And truly, regarding the description of the physical earth, nothing more apt or true could be said by anyone. Since all the aforementioned earths—and indeed any others that can be imagined—lack these marks, it is certain that they cannot enter into the physical work. The same Llull, 

<margin>Impediments to the earth of the wise. Chapter on the three specifically different humors.</margin>
in another place, adds a fifth to these four faculties or signs of the philosophical earth: namely, **subtlety** <note>refinement or fineness of substance</note>. For thus he says in the *Codicillus* <note>The "Codicil," a major work in the Pseudo-Lullian alchemical corpus</note>: "If you wish to know the reason why our earth is more effective at penetrating and congealing quicksilver than the earth of the **Sophists** <note>Here, "Sophists" refers to false alchemists or those who use superficial, non-philosophical methods</note>, know that it is because the dryness of our earth was produced through the **digestion** of complexional heat. Therefore, it is more fitting and penetrates more subtly into the depths, not only of the substance of quicksilver, but also of the other bodies to which it is applied. The coldness of the Sophists' earth cannot achieve this penetration because it is neither fitting—being of a different complexion—nor does it penetrate, because it does not possess those virtues and subtlety through heat." By these words, he describes three impediments which exclude all other earths from the art: namely, **coldness**, by which they are unable to attract, retain, and coagulate the water

# ON THE FIXING EARTH.

...likeness <note>original: *Similitudinis*; continuing from the previous page's discussion of the four requirements</note> of nature, they cannot [retain] their own; that is, the dissimilarity of nature, by which its water is unable to adhere to its earth and glue itself to it; and the coarseness, by which it is prevented from entering into **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> and imperfect metals. Since these conditions are reversed in the **philosophers' earth** <note>the sought-after "base" or "womb" of the alchemical work</note>, that alone must be investigated by the artist.

<margin>Whether the earth can be drawn out from spirits.</margin>
But perhaps the primary **chemical spirits** <note>original: *spiritus chemici*; the volatile substances: sulfur, arsenic, and mercury</note>—**sulfur**, **arsenic**, and **quicksilver**—will supply us with this earth that is so greatly desired? Yet we have often said that these are uniform in nature, so that their earthy parts cannot be separated from the watery or oily ones, or only with great difficulty and through their total consumption. This is proven true by experience; for if they are placed for **sublimation** <note>the process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid upon cooling, used for purification</note>, their entire substance rises, leaving no dregs in the bottom of the vessel. If, however, they are **fixed** <note>original: *figantur*; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</note> through calcination <note>reduction to powder by heat</note> or precipitation, much of their substance is lost and scattered, so that out of a hundred pounds of sulfur, barely three remain. These are reduced to an earth that has neither the ability to melt nor the power to penetrate, and which rejects quicksilver as something foreign to its nature. Furthermore, since the philosophers' earth must "fix" its Mercury (or its water), and nothing can fix anything else unless it is already fixed or possesses the nature of stability within itself, it is surely in vain to seek something fixed within these fleeing <note>volatile</note> spirits. We do not deny, however, that by adding naturally fixed and dissolved bodies, they can sometimes be fixed, provided it is done with great caution and skill.

<margin>The Sum of Perfection, chapter 30.</margin>
Regarding **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, **Geber** <note>original: *Geber*; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most authoritative figure in medieval alchemy</note> admits this in express words. He says: "It is fixed, and it becomes a **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; a potent substance used to transform or 'dye' metals into gold or silver</note> of most abundant restoration." In the same chapter, he sufficiently indicated how it is fixed with these words: "It is friendly and agreeable to metals. But nothing is submerged in quicksilver except gold." Geber speaks in the same vein regarding sulfur in Chapter 28 of the same book: "He who knows how to mix and befriend it with bodies during preparation will know one of the greatest secrets of nature, and one of the ways to perfection—for there are many paths to a single effect and a single goal." But with what should sulfur be mixed? Clearly with pure and fixed metals; for if it is mixed with impure ones, it will be defiled, and if with those that are not fixed, it will not become fixed.

<margin>The Sum of Perfection, chapter 32.</margin>
Hence Geber says: "Spirits are mixed with gold, and they are fixed by it." The same logic applies to arsenic; for by the testimony of the same Geber, it is fixed just like sulfur, differing only in this: while sulfur is called the tincture of redness <note>used for gold-making</note> and is joined with gold, arsenic—being a tincture of whiteness <note>used for silver-making</note>—

Citing Geber's Summa Perfectionis, the author concludes that these spirits must be stabilized by being combined with "fixed" metals like gold.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the alchemical "earth" as the stabilizing principle and begins Chapter VIII, focusing on the "tincture"—the active, color-giving essence of the Philosopher’s Stone. The first word completes "likeness" (similitudinis) from the previous page.</meta>

->[likeness]<- the tincture is better joined with silver, and is fixed through it—specifically, by a **lunar fixation** <note>a process of stabilizing a substance so it takes on the permanent qualities of silver</note>. Although these things may be true, one might rightly call them into doubt, lest the philosophers understood these things not regarding common spirits, but their own [philosophical spirits]. Nevertheless, it must always be considered that the "middle substance" of these spirits must be coagulated not in their own earth (from which it cannot be separated), but in a foreign one; afterwards, it is to be softened with **oil of the Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note> and fixed. Therefore, he who does not wish to waste his leisure and wishes to achieve the work should seek the **physical earth** in coagulated bodies—that is, in metals. In these, the **sulfur** <note>the active, combustible principle</note> is fixed by nature; and although it may be impure, it can be purified by art. Indeed, in some metals it is already pure, requiring no great labor for sufficient preparation.

But to bring this chapter to a close, we say that whatever is heavy, stable, and fixed in the **elixir** <note>the medicinal or transformative compound</note> claims for itself the name of "**earth**." Thus, when the spirit and the **ferment** <note>the agent that triggers the transmutation</note> are coagulated in the earth, they also take on the names of "earth" and "sulfur." Indeed, the perfect elixir is called "earth" and "sulfur." Hence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says: *Its power is complete if it has been turned into earth* <note>original Latin: *Vis eius integra est, si versa fuerit in terram*; a famous line from the Smaragdine or Emerald Tablet</note>. This means the Stone is perfect and complete if its upper, light, spiritual, and volatile parts—namely the spirit and the soul or ferment—are turned into earth and fixed. From this, the dignity of the **philosophical earth** can easily be seen, as the Stone receives its name from it as its primary part. Its necessity is also easily perceived, since if the earth is neglected, no one has ever reached—nor should they hope to reach—knowledge of the secret Stone, much less its completion, unless they wish to recklessly incur the loss of time, labor, and money.
