### ON THE WHITE OR RED TINCTURE

...its form may be declared, and what is required for a true tincture; finally, why the tinctures of the Sophists <note>Deceptive or fraudulent alchemists who use chemical tricks rather than true transmutation</note> do not succeed, is investigated.

<margin>The form of the Stone is the tincture.</margin>
Up to this point, we have applied ourselves to the preparation of the matter of the Stone; now we must examine how form is given to the same—or rather, how it becomes entirely form. For matter, even if optimally prepared, would be of little use unless it were joined and annexed to form, without which it cannot subsist. Now, the form of the Stone is the **tincture** <note>The active, color-giving essence that effects transmutation</note>, and when the Stone acquires this, it is perfected. Therefore, the Philosopher places it in the seventh and final place among the properties of the medicine. But when I name "tincture," I do not mean just any white or red color, nor that the Stone should be called perfected as soon as a white or red color appears in the work; rather, it must have an intense and exuberant white or red color, so that by its exuberance it can impart that same color of whiteness or redness to other metals without any lessening of its own color or goodness. 

<margin>There are certain degrees of the tincture in the Stone.</margin> 
For the Stone has certain degrees of whiteness and yellowness <note>Latin: *citrinitatis*, referring to the gold-like color</note>, such that at times it is sufficient only for itself and cannot tinge anything but itself. Whence comes that saying of the philosopher in the *Turba*: "Gold does not tinge unless it be tinged" <note>original: *Aurum non tingit nisi tingatur*; from the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical text</note>. At that stage, the Stone is in the degree of gold or silver perfected by nature; but through continuous **decoction** <note>Heating or boiling</note> and the gradual addition of the tinging substance, it ascends. Thus, it first converts a quantity of another body equal to itself, then gradually a greater amount—namely ten times its weight, a hundred times, a thousand times, and finally unto infinity. Among these there are also intermediate degrees, so that one part sometimes converts 110, another 120, 130, and so on, into silver or gold. Wherefore Rhasis <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, an influential Persian alchemist</note> said not without reason: "Therefore its tincture is improved by art, so that some may tinge tenfold, some a hundredfold, some a thousandfold and beyond." 

<margin>What kind of tincture is desired in the Stone.</margin> 
The author of the *Rosarius Minor* <note>The "Lesser Rose Garden," a medieval alchemical treatise</note> wished to indicate the same thing: "Behold the complete red, and the red diminished from its redness, and every redness of the fixed and non-fixed. Behold the whitening white, and the reddening red, and the imperfect making progress." Insofar as the whiteness of the perfect is increased, to that extent it tinges into whiteness; and so it is with the red. But not even just any intense white or red color suffices for the perfection of the **elixir**; otherwise, many tinctures of the Sophists would claim for themselves the name of the "physical Stone." Rather, it is necessary that it grants **lunification** <note>Transmutation into silver (Luna)</note> or **Solification** <note>Transmutation into gold (Sol)</note> to transmutable things, or as he says later, that it be a tincture coloring convertible matter (which can be no other...

### CHAPTER SEVEN

...than quicksilver or some imperfect metal) into true silver
<margin>Signs of true silver.</margin>
into true silver, or gold, with all its certain and known differences. This is so that the metallic body, converted into the appearance of silver, may be white with a pure whiteness, clean, hard, resonant, enduring in the **cupel** <note>original: *cineritio*; a porous vessel made of bone ash used to refine precious metals</note>, extensible under the hammer, ignitable, and fusible. For these are the signs of true silver:
<margin>Signs of pure gold.</margin>
if any body altered in its nature lacks these, it cannot be called true silver, but **sophistical** <note>Deceptive or fake; produced by chemical surface treatments rather than true transmutation</note>. Likewise, if a body converted into the appearance of gold is not yellow <note>original: *citrinum*</note>, heavy, **mute** <note>original: *mutum*; gold does not "ring" or chime like silver when struck</note>, shining, equally digested, extensible under the hammer, ignitable, fusible, and enduring the tests of the cupel, **cement** <note>original: *cæmenti*; a refining process where gold is heated with salts to remove impurities</note>, and antimony, it shall not be called true gold. For nothing can be called gold or silver unless it possesses all the definitions and differences of gold or silver. If anyone desires to know what the test of the cupel is (which today they call the **cupella**) and of cement, and what kind of ignition and fusion perfected bodies admit or undergo, let him consult the final part of the *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: *Summa Perfectionis*</note> by **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though the text cited is likely by a 13th-century European author known as Pseudo-Geber</note>, which is titled "On the Proofs of Perfection." But as for the test of gold by antimony, which was unknown to the ancients, let him search for it in Philip Ulstad’s *The Heaven of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Cælo Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century book on distillation and alchemy</note>. And let these things be said for the explanation of the words of Geber, in which, however, the reader must be warned that a fault has crept in. The common and most vulgar reading is this: 
<margin>How a fault in the text is to be amended.</margin>
"Seventh, after fixation, a brilliant tincture is necessary, and a staining color of another <note>original: *alterius*</note>, or a tincture coloring the matter." In another codex it is read in this way: "Seventh, after fixation, the last staining color is necessary, or a tincture coloring the matter." And this is better in my judgment; for besides the fact that in the first reading the word "tincture" is repeated twice, I do not see to what the little word "of another" refers—unless we wish to understand that a tincture is joined to the Stone by the addition of *another* staining thing, which is not always true, since the philosophers confess that the Stone sometimes contains its own tincture within itself. For so say the *Lily* <note>A reference to the alchemical text *Lilium Inter Spinas*</note>, **Raymond Lully**, and **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a prominent medieval physician and alchemist</note>. Although our Stone naturally contains its own tincture within itself, it nevertheless does not have the motion of itself to become a completed elixir unless it is moved by art and operation. And we have shown above that the lunar elixir <note>The medicine for silver</note>, if it is to become red, requires the admixture of a staining thing, but the solar elixir <note>The medicine for gold</note> does not. Therefore, the little word "of another" seems either entirely needing to be struck out, or read as I have advised.

# ON THE WHITE OR RED TINCTURE.

<margin>
Tincture is considered in two ways in the art.
</margin>
But returning to the matter of the **tincture**, we say that it is evaluated in two ways in the art: one way insofar as the Stone is tinted, and the other insofar as it tints. Likewise, the Stone is tinted in two ways. The first is when, after its purification is complete, it is cooked with its own **water** or **spirit** <note>In alchemy, "water" and "spirit" often refer to the volatile, liquid substances extracted from minerals</note> until it becomes entirely white or red, according to the nature of the spirit. That is, it depends on whether the spirit is suited for decorating the Stone with a white or red color. For the waters of **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> whiten the Stone; whereas the waters of **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, and the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> make the same stone red. However, the water of Saturn—because of its varied **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</note>, by which it is reduced either to **white lead** <note>original: *cerussam*</note> or **red lead** <note>original: *minium*</note>—can be adapted to both the white and the red works, as **Geber** <note>A famous, though semi-legendary, Arabic alchemist whose Latin works were foundational to European chemistry</note> affirms in more than one place. Hence Marsilio Ficino says:

> For the golden sulfur, three reddish spirits are brought back; for silver, three whitening spirits.

<margin>
That the spirit is not lacking in tincture.
</margin>
Moreover, Geber clearly declares that the spirit of the Stone also contains the tincture within itself; for after he had taught the dissolution of Venus <note>Copper</note> into **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, he adds these things:

<margin>
From *The Investigation of Perfection*, Chapter 2.
</margin>
> "Honor this water, with which the elixir is tinted infinitely."

And in the chapter on the preparation of Mars <note>Iron</note>:

> "Honor the dissolved substance—namely, the water of **fixed sulfur**—which marvelously increases the color of the elixir."

But these words of Geber—namely, that these waters can tint the elixir infinitely—are not to be taken as simply as they sound, as if they alone were sufficient for composing and increasing the elixir. This is because an elixir composed solely from the waters of imperfect bodies would be volatile, and the tincture would not remain during the conversion of metals; thus, it would be **sophistical** <note>False or deceptive; a surface-level change rather than a true transformation</note>. Rather, it must be understood that they perform these things after the infusion of the **soul** <note>The "soul" represents the vitalizing principle that grants stability and permanence to the alchemical work</note>, which alone **fixes** the Stone and makes it withstand the fire. For afterward, they can marvelously increase and multiply it. This is exactly what Marsilio Ficino intended to indicate, saying:

> "The philosophers increased the white stone—namely, the fixed one—either entirely with **lunar sperm** <note>original: *spermate lunari*; the essential seed or spirit of silver</note> or by adding other white spirits to it, namely those extracted from Jupiter and Saturn."

<margin>
Objection.
</margin>
But someone might object to me using the authority of **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** in the *Rosary*, chapter 12, where he says:

> "Water only washes and purifies, but oil tints and colors."

<margin>
Solution.
</margin>
By which words Arnaldus seems to suggest that no power of tinting exists within the water. But Arnaldus was looking at the primary effect of water, which consists in moistening, washing, and purifying; he did not, for that reason, take away the power of tinting from the spirit, to which he himself attributes the tincture. For he says thus at the beginning of the cited chapter:

> "There is a difference between the tincture of water and of oil;"

It reconciles conflicting authorities like Geber and Arnaldus de Villa Nova regarding whether these "waters" can truly color the Stone or merely purify it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the alchemical "tincture," moving from the initial preparation of the Stone to the deeper distinctions between different types of tinctures—specifically those of "water" and "oil"—and how they interact with the "body" and "spirit" of the work.</meta>

# CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>The difference between the tincture of the spirit and of the oil.</margin>
He certainly would not say this if he thought that water lacked all tincture. But this is the primary difference between the tincture of water and of oil: the tincture of water cannot be extended into other bodies before **fermentation** <note>The process of joining the Stone with a metal to "seed" it with a specific nature</note>; instead, it is only enough to bring the Stone to its simple perfection of **whiteness** or **redness** <note>The *albedo* and *rubedo*, the final two major stages of the Great Work</note>. However, the tincture of oil, when added to the perfected **elixir**, "fixes" it <note>Prevents it from evaporating or changing when exposed to heat</note>. Thus, it tints so abundantly that it can spread its power even further into imperfect bodies <note>Base metals like lead or iron</note> and **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, converting them into the nature and perfection of gold and silver. Moreover, not only **Geber** and **Marsilio Ficino**, but also other philosophers everywhere affirm that the spirit of the Stone contains a tincture within itself. For instance, **Dardarius** says in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*</note>: "Water ground with the body turns the body into spirit; and thus, when these are mixed and reduced to one, the body incorporates the spirit, while the spirit turns the body into a tinted spirit, just as blood transforms." For everything that has spirit also has blood. He rightly says the spirit turns the body into a "tinted spirit" because it clearly tints its own **earth** <note>The solid residue or "body" of the substance</note>—not with a fixed and firm tincture, but with a volatile one, until it is made firm by the addition of the **soul** and made permanent in the fire. *The Lily* <note>original: *Lilium*, a common title for alchemical treatises</note> says nearly the same: "O heavenly nature, how you turn bodies into spirit! And it is the sharpest **vinegar** <note>An alchemical term for a powerful, corrosive solvent, not literal vinegar</note> which, when mixed with a body and becoming one with it, turns it into spirit and tints it with a spiritual tincture." And **Arnaldus of Villanova** says more clearly and lucidly in the *Soliloquy*: "The body receives the tincture from Mercury (or the spirit) and the soul, naturally according to its degrees." Likewise, **Raymond Lull** and Arnaldus very often mention "white and red waters," not because they appear red to the eye, but because they have the power to make things white or red.

<margin>How the tincture is considered in another way.</margin>
In the second way, the Stone is "tinted" when the **soul** <note>The *anima*, the mediating principle that joins the spirit to the body</note> is infused into the Stone once it is already formed and perfect—perfect in the sense that it is sufficient for itself. This soul is nothing other than the tincture and the fire acting upon the matter that has already been **digested** <note>Slowly heated to encourage chemical change</note>, digesting and cooking it even more until its power is visibly manifested in the stability and **transmutation** <note>The transformation of base metals into gold or silver</note> of imperfect bodies. It achieves this by its fiery power, as we have said elsewhere. This soul is not brought from outside or from things foreign to the Stone, but is drawn out from the very "bowels" of the **perfect bodies** <note>Gold and silver</note> after they have been dissolved. It takes on the form of a spirit until, once implanted in the earth, it fixes the water within it and tints it further—indeed, it tints it so abundantly that it renders it more...

### ON THE WHITE OR RED TINCTURE.

<margin>Definition of the tincture. From the *Book on the Quintessence*, Distinction 2.</margin>
...renders it a thousand times more than before. Regarding this operation, the **tincture** <note>The active agent in alchemy that "colors" or transforms a base substance into a noble one</note> is defined by **Raymond Lully** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> as a composition of "air and fire, silver and gold." Or similarly: the tincture is a composite made of the air and fire of silver and gold. Or in this way: the tincture is a tinting body, arising from and composed of two elements—namely air and fire—of silver for the white, and of gold for the red. By these three definitions, Lully seems to constantly suggest that the tincture of the **Stone** is not granted unless it comes from a **Lunar** <note>original: *Luna*; silver</note> or **Solar** <note>original: *Sol*; gold</note> body dissolved into **Mercury**. He calls it a composite of air and fire not because they cannot be seen or touched due to some spirituality or lack of body, nor because they are exactly like the air or fire in their own spheres—elements of that sort we neither require nor can possess in this Art—but rather to indicate that these two subtler elements provide the Stone with its form and primary tincture, while the remaining elements provide its matter.

<margin>In what way fire is said not to enter the white elixir.</margin>
However, although silver <note>original: *Luna*</note> dissolved in the manner of air (or as air) operates only in the Stone—because silver is much less "digested" <note>An alchemical term for being "cooked" or matured by heat</note> than gold, in which fire already dominates in its active state, manifesting as a lemon-yellow <note>original: *citrino*</note> and red color—this fire exists only potentially in silver, just as it does in the stone of silver. This can be discerned from its whiteness, which is still "crude" <note>unrefined or under-cooked</note> in comparison to the yellow and red colors. For this reason, the philosophers say that fire does not enter into the **white elixir**, and that the white elixir is completed in "three wheels" in which there is no fire, whereas the **red elixir** is completed in "four wheels" in which there is fire. Nevertheless, neither the silver nor the white Stone is entirely lacking in that internal fire of theirs. This is because in every composite there is a "fire of nature," which moves matter toward a certain form for which it is most suited by the course of nature, and according to how the craftsman knows how to shape it. Therefore, the philosopher calls the Tincture a tinting body composed of the two elements of air and fire for this reason: because it is necessary for the tincture to be material, otherwise it could not manifest its fire in action. Yet, although this tincture is corporeal, it is nonetheless nothing in its power but fire mixed with air—or rather, carried within the air—because air is water that has been lightened and reduced to the nature of air. Just as the material of fire is air, which is like its food and fuel, so too the material of air is water; and the entire Stone must be reduced to this nature of air before the tincture of fire or gold can be infused into it.

<meta>catchword: To</meta>

It also explores the distinction between the white elixir (associated with silver and air) and the red elixir (associated with gold and fire), noting that fire is the active force that matures the substance.</summary>

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

<margin>*Rosarium Philosophorum*, part II, chapter 9.</margin>
To the point, **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: Air is distilled with fire because it is itself "tinted water," and its **tincture** <note>The coloring or transforming principle in alchemy</note> is fire; for fire is the body and air is the spirit that carries the fire. And **Raymond Lully** says in the *Codicil*: The soul is fire in appearance and a hidden fire, carried in the belly of the water; from these, air results, which is "tinted water," and its tincture is nothing but fire. And fire itself is nothing but a body refined to the ultimate degree, and the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is fire carried in the belly of the air.

<margin>The tincture of the stone must be increased so that it may tint further. *Rosarium*, part 1, chapter 8.</margin>
It should be noted, therefore, that although the perfected Stone contains its own tincture within itself, this tincture is not sufficient to tint other metals. It is necessary for a greater tincture to be added to the **elixir** than what it naturally contains in itself. Hence **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic and European alchemy</note> and Arnaldus de Villanova say: For this reason, the operation is performed on our Stone so that its tincture may be improved in it more than in its natural state, and so that the Elixir may become—according to the allegory of the Sages—a condiment, an antidote, a medicine, and a cleansing agent from clear species, for the purging of all bodies and their transformation into true **Gold-making** <note>original: *Solificum*</note> and **Silver-making** <note>original: *Lunificum*</note> substances.

<margin>From *The Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 5.</margin>
And Geber says: The tinting agent must be multiplied upon that which is to be tinted, until the tincture appears in the body or the medicine. The author of the *Lesser Rosary*, part 1, chapter 21, states: The more the tincture is increased with auxiliary aids, the more deeply it tints. **Senior** <note>Refers to Senior Zadith, an influential Arabic alchemical author</note> says: Unless you put gold into gold, you have nothing. Gold, however, is called the elixir when, through long boiling, it has already attained the color or redness of gold. This must also be understood regarding silver <note>original: *argento*</note>—namely, when the spirit is joined to its earth and coagulated, it ends in whiteness. Once this is done, if we wish to increase the tincture of the elixir, it will be necessary to add gold and silver to it further: gold to the red stone, and silver to the white stone. This is done not just once but many times; and the more often it is done, the more perfect and subtle the medicine becomes, converting imperfect metals at a greater weight.

<margin>Gold and silver must be refined before they are joined to the elixir.</margin>
But gold cannot make the medicine more subtle or more colored unless it has first been **refined** <note>original: *subtiliatum*; the process of making a substance less dense and more "spiritual"</note>, its dryness converted into moisture, and its coarseness into simplicity. For the Elixir—after many sublimations, distillations, and boilings—is rendered entirely spiritual and simple; it does not receive anything except what <note>original: *quod*</note> is of its own nature. Dense and corporeal things do not join well with simple things. For this reason, Raymond Lully says with good cause: A perfect body remaining in its coarseness cannot have the power of converting an imperfect mixture.

...to its perfect nature: it is therefore necessary that the perfected body be refined before it possesses such power. Now, it is refined when it is reduced to **Quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury in its liquid state</term>, and since the Quicksilver of a perfected body is fixed, it fixes the unfixed Quicksilver of an imperfect body. Therefore, first dissolve gold and silver in the "water of its own kind," if you know it; if not, do so through salts, as we have indicated, for it is sufficient to reduce perfected bodies into **Mercury**. Then, gradually join it to the **elixir**, by watering, cooking, and subliming, until its color and power are pleasing; for in each watering, calcination, and sublimation, you will gain something. This is done as much for the sake of the **tincture** <note>The transformative coloring principle</note> which is increased in the Stone, as for the sake of the digestion. For the more the Stone is digested and cooked, the more active the fire enclosed within it becomes, and the Stone increases in quantity and power, not unlike an infant who, nourished with suitable food, grows daily and becomes stronger, and finally emerges as a perfect man.

<margin>Second way. The Stone is called the tincture and form of metals. Definition.</margin>
In another way, the tincture is considered as the "form" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, the "form" is the essential nature or blueprint of a thing</note> of imperfect metals, and as that which tints them into the **Sun** <term>Sol; alchemical gold</term> and the **Moon** <term>Luna; alchemical silver</term>. And then it is defined by **Richard the Englishman** <note>Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century alchemist</note>:

> A substance which, by tinting, transforms the tinted thing into its own nature, and makes it remain with itself without any separation, teaching nature to fight against the fire, so that the nature of the fixer, the tinter, and the tinted are in harmony.

From this definition, it is gathered that nothing can be called a tincture unless it tints. Therefore, natural gold, although it hides the whiteness of silver mixed with it in a certain proportion, cannot be called a tincture; likewise, neither can silver that has copper mixed with it, because although these metals receive the other into themselves and in a way hide them, they do not provide a color to them unless that color is taken away from themselves. Hence gold that has silver mixed with it, or silver that has copper mixed with it, suffers a reduction of its own perfection.

<margin>Gold cannot be called a tincture.</margin>
For pure and unadulterated gold of twenty-four degrees—or **carats** <note>original: *carattorum*</note>, as they call them—descends by one degree and becomes worse through the admixture of one twenty-fourth part of silver, and thereafter is judged to be only twenty-three carats. Similarly, silver which was established in its perfection at twelve **pence** <note>original: *denariorum*; a standard of silver purity used by minters</note> is judged, by the addition of one penny of copper, to be no longer twelve as before, but only eleven; and one must judge in the same way concerning other proportions. Furthermore, since the tinter [transforms] the tinted into its own nature...

# CONCERNING THE WHITE OR RED TINCTURE

...true redness, according to how they have been prepared. **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; refers to the works attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational authority for medieval Latin alchemy</note>. Gold is the tincture of redness, because it tinges and transforms every body. He says the same: Silver is the tincture of whiteness. In which it must be considered that the philosophers often say gold and silver tinge the remaining metals or bodies with true redness and whiteness—not because gold or silver, remaining in its own nature, possesses such a power (the opposite of which we have asserted), but because they are the efficient causes of the tincture and, as it were, the formal principles of the **Elixir** <note>The "Stone" or medicine of the metals in its active, liquid-like state</note> itself. This is because they impress the **form** <term>forma; the essential nature or "blueprint" of a substance that gives it its specific properties</term> of gold or silver upon its matter, without which the elixir is not completed, nor are imperfect metals converted into gold or silver, since the entire effect depends upon the form alone.

<margin>What more is required in a true tincture.</margin>
Furthermore, there is a need in a true tincture for the "tingeing" <note>the agent of change</note> and the "tinged" <note>the substance being changed</note> to remain together inseparably and become one, and not flee from the fire. Therefore, in the definition, it is added that the tingeing agent makes the tinged substance remain with it without any separation and teaches it to fight against the fire. Now, two things distinct in form cannot become one thing unless they agree in **genus** <term>genus; the broad category or family of a substance, such as "metallic"</term>. Since, therefore, the elixir and the metals to be converted agree in genus and nature—because both draw their origin from **Mercury** <note>Philosophical Mercury, the "primal matter" believed to be the root of all metals</note>—even though a cause of corruption later overtook the imperfect metals, the metals will easily mix and unite with the elixir because of their affinity. And because the elixir is **fixed** <note>stable and non-volatile; it does not evaporate when heated</note> and tolerant of all fire, since it was born in fire and is in a way the "son of fire," it therefore rejoices in fire, which serves as its nourishment and preservation. And because it is born from the purest matter of the metals, it first seizes the purer substance of the other metals; it completes and fixes what is joined and united to it through the exuberant and exceeding **digestion** <term>digestio; a process of slow, continuous heating that matures the substance</term> which it possesses, and makes it remain with it in the fire. And so, finally, the nature of the fixer, the tingeing agent, and the tinged substance agree amicably, which is what is required in the elixir—that is, the tincture.

<margin>Whether the former tincture is found in other things besides gold and silver.</margin>
Now let us examine whether this double tincture we mentioned—namely, that which tinges the elixir and that which tinges the metals—is found in animals, vegetables, or other things. It is certain that the former is not found, because this tincture is nothing but a composition of two extremely subtle elements, namely **Fire** and **Air**, extracted from gold and silver. Since these can only be elicited from gold and silver, it is sufficiently clear that animals and all vegetables, or those things taking their origin from them, are not able...

### CHAPTER SEVEN.

...to be able to supply it, unless they have first been converted into the proximate nature of metals—that is, into Mercury and sulfur—and then into gold and silver. Although these transformations are possible through nature or art, it would be a vain effort to attempt them, since we already possess these metals perfected by nature.

<margin>Only gold or silver provide the form to the elixir.</margin>
Concerning stones, gems, flowers <note>Likely referring to chemical sublimates or "flowers" of minerals</note>, salts, vitriols <term>atramentis; metallic salts or sulfates, historically used in making inks and dyes</term>, alums, marcasites <note>pyrites or other metallic minerals</note>, magnesia, tutia <note>zinc oxide</note>, sulfur, and orpiment <term>auripigmento; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term>, as well as other intermediate minerals and even the four imperfect metals: the same judgment applies. Unless these first transition into gold and silver, they will not be able to provide the tincture or the **form** <term>forma; the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a substance what it is</term> of the elixir. This is because it is the property of the form of gold alone to generate gold within the "matter" of gold (which is common to all metals), and the property of the form of silver alone to produce silver. Therefore, since these forms exist only in gold and silver, it is clear that no other thing under heaven can claim this property for itself.

That the creative form of gold or silver is present in none of the things named above is evident from this: Whatever thing possesses the form of gold or silver must actually *be* gold or silver. For whatever is endowed with the form of a human is a human; of a lion, a lion; of a cedar, a cedar; of a magnet, a magnet; and so on for the rest. For it is the form that gives being to a thing—it is what makes the thing what it is and gives it its name—and when that form is absent, the thing ceases to be what it was before. But neither animals, nor vegetables, nor stones, gems, flowers, salts, alums, vitriols, marcasites, magnesia, tutia, sulfur, orpiment, quicksilver, or the imperfect metals, or anything similar in the nature of things, is actually gold or silver. Therefore, none of these is endowed with the form of gold and silver. Consequently, one cannot infuse the tincture—which is nothing other than that very same form—into the Stone, unless that substance has first been converted into true gold or silver by the benefit of nature or art.

But lest we seem to contradict ourselves, we stated in Chapter 1 that imperfect metals contain a certain highly **radical moisture** <term>humoris radicalis; the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist in all things</term>, which can also provide the tincture of the elixir, though not as abundantly as the oil of gold or silver. Since this oil is in truth gold and silver, retaining all their qualities and properties (however small the quantity), no one could rightly deny that it can provide the form of gold and silver to the elixir.

Accordingly, when we affirm that imperfect metals cannot supply the form of gold and silver to the Stone, this must be understood concerning the to-

<header>ON THE WHITE OR RED TINCTURE.</header>

...from their entire substance, however purified, and not just from cleaner fixed parts, but from their secret interior parts.

<margin>Four conditions of a tincture.</margin>
<margin>That there is no tincture in animals.</margin>
<margin>A deceptive experiment of the art.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But perhaps a tincture understood in the latter way—by which imperfect metals are converted into gold and silver—could be made from animals, or their parts, or any other things derived from them. Let us briefly examine whether this is true by looking at the individual properties of this tincture. First, in a true philosophical tincture, the **fixation of color** is required; second, an **affinity and harmony** between the dyer and the dyed; third, an **inseparable union** of the coloring agent with the colored object; and fourth, the **transformation** of the dyed object into the nature of the dyer. Therefore, although certain beautiful colors can be made from animals or things originating from them—such as from eggs, blood, or similar things—which, when infused into water, milk, wine, or oil, might change their color, they cannot be called "tinctures." This is because the colored object is not converted into the nature of the coloring agent, nor is it united with it; for water, after its coloration, remains water as before, and is not turned into the nature of the coloring agent, nor indeed is the coloring agent turned into the nature of water, because after the evaporation of the water through distillation, the color remains at the bottom of the vessel.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But someone will say: does not the smoke of human hair stain a suspended leaf of silver with a certain lemon-yellow color? So be it, but by no means with a lasting or fixed color; for it only yellows the surface and does not penetrate the interior of the silver. By rubbing, or by heating, or by immersion in a suitable water <note>original: "aquam convenientem"; likely an acid or solvent used in cleaning metals</note>, its former color is restored to it—to say nothing of whether it could withstand melting or the assays of gold. Furthermore, a **material tincture** is required in the elixir. For although the perfected Stone is called the "form" of imperfect metals by the philosophers, nevertheless this form is grounded in matter, since it is corporeal. However, the smoke of hair does not have a body or material substance; and since the dyed object ought to be turned into the nature of the dyer, the silver—by a ridiculous experiment—would have to be converted into a smoke similar to that which colors it, or at least into hair, which no one has ever desired. Therefore, such a yellowing <term>citrinatio; the alchemical process of turning a metal gold-colored, often the third stage of the Great Work</term> is not a tincture, but a deceptive experiment of the art <term>experimentum artis sophisticum; a "sophistic" or fraudulent trick used to mimic true alchemy</term>, and entirely useless.

<margin>Tincture is sought in vegetables in vain.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Likewise, in vegetables, certain beautiful colors are found through nature, and others can also be made through art, as can be seen in saffron <note>original: "croco"</note>, and many other things that imbue things mixed with them with their own color; and in sugar extracted by art, which, when mixed with wine or its distilled water, [provides] no...

<header>CHAPTER VII. 717</header>

...once the dregs are sent to the bottom, it colors it. We see also that ignited copper <note>original: "æs ignitum"</note> often immersed in oil of tartar <note>A solution of potassium carbonate, used in early chemistry to clean or treat metals.</note> takes on a certain silvery whiteness; yet it is certain that a <term>tincture</term> <note>The "tincture" is the agent that supposedly changes the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver.</note> of metals cannot be made from these. This is because a tincture must not only be **fixed** and not subject to the violence of fire, but it must also grant the permanence of that fixation to the object being colored; indeed, the colored object must pass into the nature of the coloring agent. Since, therefore, the purpose of the Chemists is to convert metals into gold and silver, and not into vegetables or other things similar to them which are consumed by fire, colors extracted from vegetables cannot be called tinctures.

<margin>Stones and gems cannot provide the tincture.</margin>
But perhaps stones, gems, corals, minerals <note>original: "fluores"</note>, and colored earths will provide the tincture longed for by the chemists, for some of these are distinguished by beautiful colors through nature. But these, remaining incorporeal in their mass, do not enter into metals; consequently, they cannot alter them. Even if they were to penetrate them, since they do not possess an exuberant color, but only enough for themselves, they cannot dye other bodies. If indeed we attempt to diminish their coarseness through fire, they will be reduced to <term>calx</term> <note>A powder produced by heating a mineral or metal; an oxide.</note>, and thus they will lose the colors with which they previously shone; indeed, they will not even be more subtle then than they were before. And although a more subtle color can be elicited from certain earths, gems, pearls, and corals by means of spirit of wine, distilled vinegar, and other liquors, nevertheless, since this is foreign to the nature of metals—having no proximity or harmony with them—it will neither mix nor unite with them. Finally, since it is necessary in a true tincture for the colored object to be transformed into the nature of the coloring agent, and we do not seek earth and stones but gold and silver, it seems not without reason that these colors are rejected by all students of the art in the **metamorphosis** of metals.

<margin>Salts, alums, and vitriols lack the tincture.</margin>
The same judgment shall apply to salts, alums, and <term>vitriols</term> <note>original: "atramenta" (literally "inks"); historically used for sulfate minerals like green or blue vitriol.</note>. Although these are able to induce some alteration through <term>cements</term> <note>A mixture of corrosive minerals used to refine or color the surface of metals.</note>—for example, so that the color of copper is wonderfully increased and brightened, such that when added to gold in a small quantity it presents the same appearance—nevertheless, since it is not truly united with the gold, but is separated through the trial of the cement and the <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cineritii"; a vessel made of bone ash used to refine precious metals.</note> or by some other means, or is burned away by fire, that tincture cannot be called **fixed**. Likewise, although the redness of gold can in no way be intensified by artifice, it is too weak while remaining in its own nature to be able to dye other bodies, because through frequent fusion and melting that color vanishes, leaving...

...body in its original state. I do not deny, however, that certain transmutations and some wonders are sometimes accomplished through the things mentioned above; 
<margin>Transmutation of iron into copper.</margin>
for we see iron pass into copper through a <term>cement</term> <note>A powder used in a heating process to alter the surface or nature of a metal.</note> of calcined <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfate minerals; here likely copper sulfate which, when dissolved, can deposit a layer of copper onto iron.</note>, or through its thin, glowing plates frequently quenched in oil of vitriol <note>original: "chalchāti oleo"</note>. But for this reason vitriol, although it may change the nature of iron, will not be called a "philosophical tincture," which must not transmute a base metal into another less precious one, but into gold and silver, and this instantly through mere melting and the prior mixing of the <term>elixir</term> <note>The perfected substance that acts as a catalyst for transmutation.</note>: just as any other transmutations discovered by the industry of craftsmen, even if somewhat profitable, are not tinctures unless they possess all the distinctions and characteristics of the definition provided above.

<margin>Whether the tincture can be found in intermediate minerals.</margin>
But in <term>marcasites</term> <note>A general term in this period for various metallic sulfide minerals, such as iron pyrites.</note>, magnesia, <term>tutty</term> <note>original: "thutia"; a crude zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note>, sulfur, <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auri pigmento"; arsenic trisulfide, used as a yellow pigment and in alchemical experiments.</note>, and other intermediate minerals, this tincture of the Philosophers might be sought. For we see copper <note>original: "æs"</note> mixed with <term>calamine</term> <note>original: "cadmia"; an ore of zinc.</note>, and melted with it, lay aside its natural redness and take on a firm and lasting lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinū"</note> color. The weight of the copper is also seen to increase in a wonderful way, which is a sign of a true union of the coloring agent with the colored; for the weight of copper, perhaps 100 pounds before its boiling with calamine, afterward weighs 130 or 140 pounds or thereabouts, and with its name changed, it is called <term>aurichalcum</term> or, by some, <term>orichalcum</term> <note>The ancient and early modern term for brass, which is an alloy of copper and zinc.</note>. I cannot deny that these things are true; nevertheless, for that reason we can never call calamine or anything similar that alters copper or iron a "tincture." 
<margin>How calamine is seen to dye copper.</margin>
For first, calamine increases the weight of copper because it contains much copper within itself, which, when melted by fire, associates itself with its like, leaving behind its earth in which it was contained before melting. And because this same earth includes parts not sufficiently "digested" or "cooked" by nature, but rather still participating in the nature of Mercury and sulfur—both of which exhale a white smoke—during the melting of the copper, these spirits seek to escape. Hence it is necessary that their flight be through the molten body, and thus they <term>citrinate</term> <note>Turn to a yellow or golden color.</note> it, because this smoke of spirits is temperately white, and a white mixture of this sort joined to red suppresses the redness, and "citrination" occurs; 
<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 60.</margin>
which according to <term>Geber</term> <note>A famous, though likely pseudonymous, 13th-century Latin alchemist writing under the name of the earlier Persian polymath Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note> is nothing other than a determined proportion of red and white. That the spirits or vapors of these spirits enclosed in calamine turn copper yellow is evident from this, because both <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and hermeticism.</note> and all alchemists testify that the same can be done with tutty. Tutty, however, is a smoke raised upward in metallic meltings and [adhering to] the walls and chambers...

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Summary of chapter 7, etc.</margin>
...clinging to the furnaces. Or, as <term>Geber</term> <note>An influential 13th-century alchemist (often identified as Pseudo-Geber) whose works, like the *Summa Perfectionis*, established much of Western alchemical theory.</note> says, the smoke of white bodies, or the smoke of a mixture of <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for tin.</note> and <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note> clinging to the sides of furnaces and the furnaces themselves. Thus, <term>cadmia</term> <note>A term for zinc ores or the zinc oxide that collects as a crust on furnace walls.</note> does not truly dye, but it extinguishes and masks the natural red color of copper: Whence Geber says: *The redness of Venus is removed with tutty and it is whitened, but because the whitening of tutty is not sufficient, it only yellowed* <note>original: "citrinat"</note>; and any yellowing is akin to whiteness. Furthermore, in a true tincture it is necessary for the thing being dyed to be transformed into the nature of the dyer; however, copper is not changed into cadmia, but rather conversely, the copper-like parts of cadmia are converted into copper, the earthy parts are separated, and the spiritual and volatile parts evaporate.

<margin>The tincture must be homogeneous.</margin>
Lastly, the Natural Tincture must be homogeneous so that a part does not differ from its whole: if, however, in any substance there are diverse parts—earthy, metallic, sulfurous, and mercurial, as is manifest in cadmia—it cannot be called a tincture, since it is impossible for a metal to be transmuted into such diverse, heterogeneous, and dissimilar parts.

<margin>Sophistical experiments of the art.</margin>
By a not very different reasoning, arsenic, <term>orpiment</term> <note>Arsenic trisulfide, a bright yellow mineral.</note>, sublimated or precipitated <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note>, or mercury raised several times from a precipitate, and <term>litharge</term> <note>Lead oxide, a byproduct of silver refining.</note>—whether each is prepared by itself or some are joined together—whiten copper and iron. Sulfur also turns silver red, although by a very difficult and laborious work. Some also harden quicksilver or tin so that it appears to be silver; finally, I do not doubt that through these mineral means a thousand deceptions can be committed. Yet all these colors are <term>sophistical</term> <note>Deceptive or false; in alchemy, this refers to a change that only affects the surface or appearance without changing the substance's essence.</note>, and they recede when exposed to fire, with the bodies remaining in their original state, or sometimes vanishing together. Since these colors are not <term>fixed</term> <note>Stable under heat; "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance endure the fire.</note>, they cannot fix other imperfect bodies, nor make them endure during testing and repeated meltings; for they are merely smokes penetrating the bodies due to a similarity, but quickly departing, since they do not have a fixed and fixing material subject that is united with the bodies to transform them into its own fixed nature.

<margin>Question.</margin>
<margin>Summa Perfectionis, chapters 28, 29, & 30.</margin>
But someone will say: Are not sulfur, arsenic, and quicksilver called "tinctures" by the Philosophers? For thus Geber says of arsenic and sulfur: *Arsenic is the tincture of whiteness, and sulfur is the tincture of redness.* Likewise: *Quicksilver is fixed and is a tincture of most exuberant restoration and shining splendor.*

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
I respond: If anyone understands these things regarding common <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur often represents the active, combustible, and "masculine" principle of matter.</note>, <term>arsenic</term>, and <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver; the fluid, volatile, and "feminine" principle.</note> exactly as they exist in their natural state, they are not a little mistaken. However, I do not deny that sulfur mixed with <term>quicksilver</term>, and quicksilver mixed with sulfur or arsenic—provided they have all been purified and <term>fixed</term> <note>Made non-volatile so they can withstand the heat of a furnace.</note> by the Art—may pass into an <term>elixir</term> <note>A substance capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</note>; but I assert that none of them, by themselves, are or can become a <term>tincture</term> <note>The coloring or transforming power of the alchemical medicine.</note>. <term>Geber</term> confirms this in the same chapters, saying: *Let no one think that sulfur by itself completes the work of Alchemy, for this would be nothing but a vain belief.* Also: *Sulfur and arsenic are not the perfecting material of this work, for they are not complete unto perfection; however, they may offer support for perfection in certain cases.*

<margin>
That the
perfected
medicine
is sometimes
called sulfur,
arsenic, and
Mercury.
</margin>
The same is said of quicksilver: *It is not our medicine in its natural state, but it can likewise help in certain cases.* Next, it is noteworthy that the Philosophers [alchemists] frequently call their completed Stone "sulfur" and "arsenic"—specifically, they call the red elixir "sulfur" and the white elixir "arsenic," because of the power of the red or white sulfur dominating within it. Likewise, they not uncommonly call the same Stone "Mercury" or "quicksilver," because its entire substance is mercurial. We have not deemed it worthwhile to prove these things through the authorities of the Philosophers, since they were discussed in another book. <margin>In the Mirror of Doctrine.</margin> <note>original: "In speculo doctrinæ." This refers to the *Speculum Doctrinale*, part of a massive 13th-century encyclopedia by Vincent of Beauvais.</note> In a similar way, the Philosophers sometimes say that the elixir and tincture are made from <term>imperfect bodies</term> <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper, as opposed to the "perfect" gold and silver.</note>. Just as <term>Vincent</term> <note>Vincent of Beauvais.</note> says regarding <term>copper</term> <note>original: "ære." This can mean copper or bronze.</note>: *It receives*, he says, *the tincture, and from it comes the elixir of redness and whiteness, and its tincture does not flee.* <note>Meaning the color is permanent and does not evaporate under heat.</note> The same says of lead: *And from it is made the greater elixir of redness and whiteness, and even the "waters" by which quicksilver is retained.* <margin>On the Investigation of Perfection, chapter 2.</margin> <note>original: "De Inuestig. perf." This title is usually attributed to the Latin Geber corpus.</note> Geber also, after describing the causes of perfection and imperfection in metals, and showing that imperfect bodies must be prepared by the removal of superfluities and the supply of what is missing, concludes that after these have been sufficiently prepared, they are fit for the white or red elixir to be made from them. But these things are not to be understood as if the spirits or imperfect bodies alone and by themselves can provide us with the tincture to dye other bodies—since they possess only a little of it—but rather because their Mercury and sulfur can be prepared so that they may receive a larger and more abundant tincture from gold and silver. Therefore, Vincent rightly said that copper receives the tincture, although these words of his could also be understood as referring to the copper and lead *of the Philosophers*, which is their "earth."

<header>CHAPTER VII.</header>

<margin>Another sophistical work.</margin>
But let us return to the point from which we digressed. Certain men have been found who, by a marvelous craft, have so subtly joined gold with burnt copper or iron—prepared and macerated in <term>waters of separation</term> <note>original: "aquis separationum"; these are corrosive acids, like nitric acid, used to dissolve and part metals.</note>—and combined them through the smallest parts, so that the mixture appeared to have transformed into the likeness of gold and to be inseparably united with it. However, experience finally detected the deception of this vain labor, because there was no true change of the <term>form</term> <note>In the Aristotelian sense, the "form" is the essential nature of the metal; changing the color without changing the form is considered a "sophistical" or fake result.</note> in the copper and iron, nor a true union, but only a certain "painted" or superficial mixture. Therefore, we advise all students of truth to avoid and heartily abhor such frivolous and <term>sophistical</term> <note>Deceptive or fraudulent.</note> works, as they are unworthy of a nobleman or a philosopher, and are instead the proper domain of thieves and impostors—especially since investigating them requires no less labor, time, and expense than the work of the philosophers, which fears no test.

<margin>Which tinctures are useless.</margin>
But to conclude this chapter, and indeed this book, we say with <term>Avicenna</term> <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational in Europe.</note>: Tinctures do not succeed, either because they are burned up (such as those taken from animals, vegetables, and everything originating from them); or because they are not <term>fixed</term> <note>To "fix" a substance in alchemy is to make it non-volatile so that it stays in the crucible even under intense heat.</note> but fly away and flee, like the <term>spirits</term> <note>Volatile substances that evaporate when heated.</note> prepared in any manner—the primary ones being sulfur, arsenic, and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note>, and the secondary ones being <term>magnesia</term>, <term>tutia</term> <note>Zinc oxide collected from furnace flues.</note>, and <term>marcasite</term>; or because they do not "enter" the metal, like all earths and stones or things of their nature; or because they do not remain in a fixed state but are separated in some way, such as glass and things of its nature which turn into glass; or because they do not protect the gold and silver produced by the art from being burned by those things that burn other imperfect metals, such as copper and lead. This is because, at their root, they are not gold and silver, but only exhibit a counterfeit appearance of them, nor do they possess the cause of perfection within themselves—which is <term>Mercury</term> rightly thickened, pure, and fixed, which is not corrupted or destroyed by sharp and burning substances, but protects and defends its own bodies.

<margin>What the Tincture of the Philosophers is like.</margin>
<margin>From *The Investigation of Perfection*, penultimate chapter.</margin>

# CHAPTER VII: ON THE WHITE OR RED TINCTURE

...a fixative substance, and that it is not consumed by those things which do not consume gold and silver, and that it brings about <term>consolidation</term> <note>original: "consolidationes"; the process of making the metal solid and stable.</note> and proper weight when tested by a due and perfect <term>ignition</term> <note>original: "ignitione"; testing the substance by heating it to a high temperature to see if it vaporizes or remains stable.</note>. 

<margin>Conclusion.</margin> 
He who desires to possess these conditions or properties of the tincture should take those things in which they exist by nature, disregarding all other things which are not found within the property of a metallic nature. But because these matters have been sufficiently declared in the preceding parts, bringing this book to an end, I pray for the grace of the Holy Spirit and a happy success in their labors for all faithful Catholics and pious <term>artists</term> <note>original: "artistis"; in this context, "artists" refers to alchemists practicing the "Hermetic Art."</note> of good will. 

And I ask that if anything has been written here which seems to differ from the common opinion of other Philosophers, they should consider that it was done for this purpose: so that the student of the art could not be instructed in a more convenient way or a better path, or be introduced more effectively into this science. Indeed, one should believe the professors of this art who adapt their doctrine and precepts to actual experience, rather than the disputes and naked arguments—however subtle they may be and drawn from the innermost chambers of Philosophy—of those who have never "smelled" anything of this science <note>A common alchemical idiom for those who have no practical laboratory experience.</note>.

I also ask that if anything has been said or explained less clearly in certain places, they should attribute it not to the Author's <term>envy</term> <note>original: "invidiae"; a technical term in alchemical literature (the *invidia philosophorum*) referring to the intentional concealment of secrets to prevent them from falling into the wrong hands.</note>, but to the accepted custom of the professors of this art and to the dignity of Alchemy. Yet let those who read find in this little book what others have scattered and hidden in long and almost innumerable volumes. I have explained the secrets of an art so obscure in such manifest words that I do not doubt that the study of chemistry will hereafter be much easier. Indeed, I fear lest I might sometime be called guilty of a sin, because—contrary to the custom of the art—I have compressed the vocabulary and elements hitherto held at a high price and

# *To the Student of Hermetic Philosophy*
## JUSTUS A BALBIAN OF FLANDERS,
### From Aalst, a Lover of Chemistry, sends greetings.

When I consider, kind reader, that those who bring the works of the ancients out of hiding into the light and wish them to be public deserve almost no less praise than those who labor on and publish some new work of their own—and this is true in other sciences, but especially in this one which concerns Alchemy <term>Alchemy: The ancient art and science of transforming matter, particularly the pursuit of turning base metals into gold and discovering a universal medicine.</term>, because hardly anything can be said about it that has not been said before—it seemed not at all foreign to my purpose to bring to light these seven chemical treatises by unknown authors.

I do this especially for the sake of those who have devoted themselves to the study of Hermetic philosophy <term>Hermetic philosophy: A tradition of knowledge based on the writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, blending philosophy, alchemy, and spirituality.</term> and apply themselves entirely to this art—an art which, in my opinion, should not only be held in high value, but even venerated for the wonderful secrets <term>arcana: Hidden or secret knowledge or "mysteries" known only to initiates.</term> it contains. 

However, a double-layered obscurity—and thus no small difficulty—is presented by the philosophers who handed down this art. One layer concerns the things themselves, and the other concerns the words. Because the subject matter is so great and almost divine, they wished to teach it under marvelous coverings <note>original: "inuolucris" — referring to allegories, veils, or metaphors used to hide deep truths from the uninitiated.</note>, and to hand down the highest of such secrets and mysteries of wisdom only through intricate riddles and figures. 

In their words, they used for the most part very obscure terms, borrowing their vocabulary from various languages, not so much to frighten away honest men as to keep out the wicked; for this knowledge is reserved only for the pious and for true philosophers (that is, lovers of wisdom) by God, the highest giver of all good things.

Furthermore, among those who wrote about this for posterity many years ago, I believe few exist who mixed fewer obscurities and difficulties into their writings than these authors. But let the judgment of this be yours, you who hold such monuments in your hands and read them through often, attentively and with discernment. I have taken these, moreover, from a very ancient manuscript, written by someone of that era who was most unlearned and ignorant of this art—

Furthermore, since I have spent nearly my whole life in this field of study, if I take it upon myself to correct such errors here, I believe I may claim this right as my own. I certainly could have attributed some of these writings to myself by altering much of them—as many do in these times—but I have never considered it the mark of an honorable <note>original: "ingenui" — referring to a person of noble or free-born character.</note> mind to seek personal glory from another’s hard work. Whatever labor and effort I have spent in correcting <note>original: "emendandis"</note> these texts, I hope that you, kind reader, will receive it kindly. Farewell.

# FIRST TREATISE
## OF THE ABBRE-
### VIATED ROSARY.

->From a most ancient manuscript.<-

Take note, dearest friend, that what follows is most true to those who understand. The first preparation and foundation of the art is **solution**, that is, the reduction of the body into water—which is into **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: The common name for mercury (Latin: argentum vivum), considered by alchemists to be the fluid, "feminine" principle of all metals.</term>—and this they called solution when they said: "Let the gold be dissolved, which is hidden in the body of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: Not the modern mineral, but a symbolic name for the "first matter" or the raw mineral substance that contains the hidden essence of the metals.</term>, so that it may be reduced into its first matter, to become **sulfur** and **quicksilver**," not so that it might turn back into common water. For our solution is nothing other than the body returning to a moist state and being resolved into the nature of quicksilver, and the "falseness" of its sulfur being diminished—this divine sulfur, abstracted from two sulfurs, is formed when the spirit meets the body. 

The second preparation occurs when the water passes into the body; one is not dissolved unless the other is coagulated, because the body, in conceiving the quicksilver, coagulates it and is itself coagulated by it, and becomes **earth**. This is the "word of opinion" <note>original: "verbum opinionis" — likely referring to a specific philosophical tenet or widespread maxim.</note> of which the **Philosophers** <note>Philosophers: In alchemical texts, "the Philosophers" refers to ancient authorities and sages like Hermes Trismegistus, Geber, or Aristotle.</note> say, "Water is procreated from earth," because water becomes earth when the qualities of earth overcome it, and earth becomes water when the qualities of water overcome it. For the solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit occur so that they have a single operation, and they become a single **bronze** <note>original: "aes" — used here metaphorically for the alchemical alloy or the "base" state of the material before transformation.</note> to which nothing external is added, except that superfluous things are removed during the preparation with the apparatus. 

The third preparation: the earth is plowed and watered, and by the will of God it is carried out in fire and water; and this is the "third word" of this work. For the Philosophers say: "Earth putrefies with water and is purified," then with God's help, once the mastery <note>original: "magisterio" — the skilled application of the alchemist's art.</note> is left behind, it continues to the end. For the earth does not sprout without frequent watering and without prior drying; and both children and women know this, as they lead their seeds and fruits to perfection in gardens. Therefore the Philosophers said: "The operation of nature is nothing but the **work of women** and the **play of children**," <note>original: "opus mulierum, & ludus puerorum" — a famous alchemical aphorism suggesting that while the theory is complex, the physical labor is simple and follows the natural laws of growth.</note> and for this reason the body is soaked as many times as it is dried in turn, for weight must be applied to every weight, measure to every measure, and labor to every labor. And now the correct **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: The stage of breaking down or "rotting" the substance, often associated with the color black (nigredo), to allow for new life or transformation.</term> of the Philosophers follows, and their putrefaction is nothing but the death— <note>The text ends mid-word "morti-", which completes on the next page as "mortificatio" (mortification or the "killing" of the metal).</note>

<summary>This page introduces the first three stages of the alchemical Great Work: solution (reducing the body to mercury), coagulation (stabilizing the spirit into earth), and putrefaction (a natural process of cleansing compared to gardening and household work).</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, solution, coagulation, putrefaction, quicksilver, sulfur, Magnesia, work of women, play of children</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Abbreviated Rosary" from page 725. The previous page ended during the discussion of the second preparation (coagulation). ...unification <note>original: "ficatio"; likely *unificatio* (unification) or *fixatio* (fixation)</note> of the moist with the dry, because the moisture is only held back by the dryness; and although the cold-moist substance flees from the fire, it is nevertheless retained by the dry substance, which is unable to flee. This is because heavy things cannot be drawn upward except by the help of light things, nor can light things be thrust downward except by the company of heavy things—unless it be with the scorpion <note>The "Scorpion" may refer to the astrological timing of the work or a specific corrosive solvent used to "pierce" the metals.</note>. 

### The Fourth Preparation: 
Nature rejoices in nature <note>original: "gaudet natura cum natura"</note>, for when nature is glad, nature overcomes nature; for it contains nature, for it follows and embraces nature, and by the will of God the work is perfected. This is the fourth truth of this work, and it can be called **sublimation** or **assumption** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again, used here to describe the "ascent" of the material's spirit.</term>, concerning which the Philosophers say: "The water itself is made airy, whereas before it was thickened and coagulated with the earth." This happens by the meeting of its own kind—that is, its close relative—and therefore nature rejoices and is glad with nature. For the thing that contains it is its own kinship; indeed, the proximity between nature and nature is as great as that between a magnet <note>original: "adamantem"</note> and iron, or even greater. This is because they are one in their root and not many; they are also one in power, because the spirit is the "killing" <note>original: "mortificatio"</note> of the other body by an imperceptible death. Therefore, nature overcomes nature—namely, by killing the body and then bringing to life that which was radically within it. It is converted into itself, augmented, and multiplied; thus God extracts many from one. Therefore, nature contains nature and nature follows nature, and it is completed by the will of Jesus Christ.

### The Fifth Preparation: 
Our spirit is the carrier <note>original: "delator"</note> of the virtues of the soul, because our brass <term>Brass: (Latin: aes) In alchemy, this rarely refers to common brass, but rather to the "metallic body" or the base matter of the Stone in a specific state of transformation.</term>, like a man, possesses a spirit, a body, and a soul. This is the fifth truth of this work, of which the Philosophers say: "For its spirit is water, its soul is the **tincture** <term>Tincture: The spiritual essence or color-giving power that transforms base metals into gold.</term>, and its body is earth." Yet the spirit remains a spirit: and just as the body is the bond of the soul itself, so the body is a fixed, dry thing, containing the spirit and the soul. Thus, the spirit penetrates the body, the body fixes the spirit, and the soul joins, whitens, and colors them. 

### The Sixth Preparation: 
It varies and changes from color to color, until it reaches the goal of whiteness and redness. Concerning this, the Philosophers say it turns yellow many times, and turns black many times, and many times it is dried out and melted. 

Take note that the **Philosopher's Stone** is composed of two natures, one of which is moist and the other truly dry; when they are cooked, they become one, because neither leaves the other, and they are called "one nature." As long as the moisture lasts, it turns black <note>original: "nigrescit"</note>, because heat acting upon the moist generates **blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem"</note> first. Heat acting upon the dry generates **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"</note>, and in the white, it generates **yellowness** <note>original: "citrinitatem"</note>...

<summary>This page outlines the final stages of alchemical preparation, focusing on the union of opposites (moist/dry, spirit/body) and the symbolic color changes (black, white, yellow) that signal the maturation of the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>
<keywords>sublimation, nature rejoices in nature, spirit, soul, body, tincture, albedo, nigredo, citrinitas, Philosopher's Stone, alchemical colors</keywords>

...just as it appears in lead when we make minium <term>Minium: Red lead (lead tetroxide), used here as an analogy for the chemical transformation from a dull metal to a vibrant red pigment.</term>. Note that the moisture of our stone is a most sharp vinegar <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"; in alchemical terms, this usually refers to the 'mercurial' solvent or "acid" that dissolves the base matter</note>, which must be guarded against most carefully, lest it turn into smoke because of excessive fire and the mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the perfected process or the Great Work itself</note> perish. For when the earth is dried, the blackness recedes and it is whitened; then the darkness perishes and the moisture is diminished, and approaching dryness takes its own governance for itself. The smoke has penetrated its body, and the spirit is bound in the dry; then the deformed blackness appearing will cease, and it will become white, lucid, and clear. 

Then, if the white woman is wed to the red husband <note>The 'white woman' and 'red husband' are allegories for Mercury (lunar/cool) and Sulphur (solar/hot), whose union is central to alchemical theory.</note>, she soon embraces and enfolds him; and then the king, crowned with a diadem, cries out: "I am the white son, the black and the red, both the son of whiteness and the man of transformation." And for this reason the Philosophers say: "Cook them until they become black, then white, then yellow <note>original: "citrini"</note>, and then, as a tinting agent, they become a venom <note>original: "venenum"; here used not as a poison, but as a substance so potent it 'infects' or transforms everything it touches.</note>." 

For the more they are cooked, the more they are dissolved and blackened; and the more they are cooked, the more they are dried and whitened. Thirdly, the more they are cooked, the more they are reddened, until the work is perfected. In dissolution, however, let the fire be gentle; in sublimation <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance into vapor and then cooling it back into a solid, used to purify the material.</term>, moderate; in coagulation, tempered; in whitening, continuous; and in reddening, strong. Truly, whoever errs in these things through ignorance will very often weep over their failure. Therefore, the thing whose head is red, feet are white, and eyes are black, is the mastery. If the triangle is perfected within the quadrangle <note>A geometric metaphor: the triangle often represents the three principles (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) or the Soul, while the quadrangle represents the four elements or the physical Body.</note>, then the stone is adorned with honor.

### The Seventh Preparation: 
The blessed stone is multiplied and perfected when the sum of the fixed is fixed with it until it flows. Therefore, the Philosophers have said that you should make the already fixed stone volatile <term>Volatile: Capable of being evaporated or turned into gas.</term> by means of sublimation, joining them philosophically through their smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; an early concept of atomic or molecular interaction.</note>, so that the whole subtle part is raised in the vessels, and then fixed. 

But if this does not happen, let there be added to it a quantity of the non-fixed part, so that the sum of the volatile exceeds the sum of the fixed, until it suffices for its elevation; for if it overcomes the sum of the fixed, it will fly; and if it does not overcome it, it will flee with the matter. Therefore, let the sum of that which was raised be repeated in its turn, until the whole is fixed through this sublimation and congelation <term>Congelation: The solidification of a liquid or vaporous substance into a stable form.</term>. Moreover, when the whole has been fixed, then repeat the part of the non-fixed, and soak it with as much quantity as before, by the skill known to you, until the whole is raised. At last, let it be fixed again until it provides a fusion as easy as wax <note>original: "ad modum cerae"; a classic alchemical marker of success, meaning the stone melts easily without evaporating, allowing it to be projected onto other metals.</note>, and it is transformed into a Solar and Lunar completion <note>original: "Solifico & Lunifico"; meaning it can now transmute metals into Gold (Sun) or Silver (Moon).</note>.

# TREATISE I.

Thus, by as much as you have prepared through the repetition of the process, so many degrees of alteration and goodness result in the medicine from the multiplication, so that it may convert every one of the imperfect bodies—and even Mercury itself—infinitely into true silver-making <note>original: "Lunificum"; a substance capable of producing silver</note> and gold-making <note>original: "Solificum"; a substance capable of producing gold</note> material. And therefore, in conclusion, the Philosophers must remain near the vessel and behold the wonders when it transmutes itself from color to a color better than can be described, until it arrives at the goal of whiteness and redness. The entire governance in the regimen of this work, therefore, lies in the tempering of the fire.

Then, cease the fire and allow it to cool, and you will find the stone: a pearly body in the color of the wild poppy. This substance is waxing <term>Incerans: From "ceration," a process of softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax, making it ready for fusion.</term>, liquefying, and penetrating; and a single weight of it falls upon a thousand times a thousand-thousand, and two hundred times a thousand <note>This describes a projection ratio of 1 part medicine to 1,000,200,000 parts base metal—a common way for alchemical texts to emphasize the near-infinite potency of the perfected Stone.</note> [parts], immediately converting the whole body into the finest gold or silver, according to the specific property of the elixir. 

This medicine, moreover, will melt very quickly in fire and congeal in air; for when the smoke senses the air, it will penetrate the body and the spirit will be constrained in the dry. It shall become a single fixed body—clear, white, or red, depending on the medicine and the ferment—which shall remain incorruptible as long as the world stands. 

By way of conclusion: note that the quicksilver, lead, copper, minium, and sulfur [mentioned here] are not the vulgar <note>In alchemy, "vulgar" refers to common, everyday materials, as opposed to the "philosophical" versions purified through the Great Work.</note> kinds. Rather, our sulfur is a divine sulfur, extracted from two sulfurs, which is called "sulfur of sulfur," and a quicksilver from quicksilver, termed by the Philosophers "the sharpest vinegar" <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"</note>. These two—namely, sulfur and quicksilver—are really and essentially present in the aforementioned vinegar; that is, within the aforementioned moisture of our stone is the single nature of the stone itself. 

Gold, indeed, and silver, lead, minium, and copper, and things of this sort are essentially and really contained within the common physical body; you will find its proper name in the aforementioned seven doubled propositions. Therefore, let him who has ears to hear, hear; and let him who has eyes, see the stone known in the seven propositions, and praise God.
