<header>SECOND TREATISE.</header>

# ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE.

->By an unknown author.<-

Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "species" refers to the essential form or identity of a thing, which was traditionally thought to be unchangeable.</note> of metals cannot truly be changed, which is indeed true, because species in themselves are not subject to sensory actions, since they are entirely incorruptible: but the subjects <note>The "subjects" are the physical matter or individual instances that carry the form of the species.</note> of these species can be very well changed, because they are corruptible. However, the subjects of species cannot be changed unless they are first (as follows from the sayings of Aristotle) reduced to the first matter <term>Prima Materia: The formless, primordial substance that is the foundation of all physical things; alchemists sought to strip matter back to this state to rebuild it.</term>, and thus they are changed into another form than they were before. Moreover, reason does not stand against this, because when one form is destroyed, another is immediately introduced, as is clear in the works of country folk, who make lime from stones and glass from ashes.

So much more strongly can the wise student destroy the individuals of a species and introduce a new form to them, because the intention of his operation is nothing else but that Mercury <note>In alchemy, Mercury often represents the "spirit" or the metallic principle of fluidity and transformation.</note> be bound in the said bodies, since the elixir of the Philosophers consists only of these. And of these operations, some are medicines of gold, which happen to share in silver in some aspects, and to differ in others. For in the first part of their composition, the work of gold and silver agree in everything; but in the final stage of their fermentation <term>Fermentatio: The final stage where a small amount of gold or silver is added to the "Stone" to give it a specific direction or "flavor" for transmutation.</term> they disagree, because the ferment of gold is gold, and the ferment of silver is silver, nor are there other ferments upon the earth.

Indeed, it is possible for other bodies to work, but they will not be as good as those aforementioned, because they cannot give a purity which they do not possess. And therefore the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle.</note> says: "Why do you need to use other bodies? Since you can have in these what is of greater temperance and less dross?" If you truly need their use, it is necessary that you first convert them into the likeness of the two aforementioned bodies, which will never happen until the Sun and Moon <note>Sol (Sun) and Luna (Moon) are the standard alchemical ciphers for gold and silver.</note>, reduced into the one sought-after medicine, are projected upon them; because Mercury, since it is by its nature convertible, becomes each thing with the individual bodies whose nature it embraces: for if it is joined with lead, it will be lead; if indeed with 

<meta>catchword: iron</meta>

<summary>The author explains the theoretical possibility of transmutation by arguing that while the 'form' of a metal is fixed, its physical 'matter' can be reduced to a primordial state and rebuilt. It establishes gold and silver as the only true ferments for the alchemical work.</summary>
<keywords>species, first matter, Aristotle, fermentation, Mercury, Sol and Luna, transmutation theory</keywords>

<page-num>730</page-num>
<header>TREATISE II.</header>

...to iron will be iron <note>original: "ferro erit ferrum"</note>, but if it is adapted with those two rays <note>These "rays" refer to the transformative powers or qualities of the medicinal elixir mentioned in the preceding text.</note>, it becomes a perfect elixir. Therefore, one must work only with that noble matter, because things are not made except according to their nature: let no one, then, seek from nature what is not in her, for he will weary his soul in vain, bringing back nothing from it but labor and the loss of things and time. Therefore, this medicine of ours is not prepared in the bowels of the earth, but is perfected by art and operation, because nothing is useful from the said stones without preparation and governance. Indeed, there are four principal modes of governance <term>Regimen: The systematic management of the alchemical process, often divided into stages or "reigns" of different operations.</term>: namely, dissolving, washing, joining, and fixing. To dissolve is to corrupt, to divide, and to reduce into the first matter <note>original: "materia prima"</note>. To wash is to bury, to distill, and to calcine <note>Calcination involves heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note>. To join is to impregnate, to whiten, and to redden. Truly, to fix is to ferment, to wed, and to wax <note>The "wedding" or "marrying" is the chemical union of opposites, like sulfur and mercury.</note>. Solution converts the stone into its first matter, namely into water; washing into air; joining into fire; and fixation into earth. Whence Aristotle says,
> When you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then you will have the whole mastery, because then you have the four elements well prepared in one part.

Moreover, of the elements, two are stony and two are aquatic; the stony ones are fire and earth, while the aquatic ones are air and water: you shall extract water from the moist substance, and air and fire from the dry substance. Do not worry about the earth from which the substance is made, provided that it is fixed, for earth and fire drink, dry, and fix the air; while water and air wash, dye, and perfect the earth and fire. Therefore, it is necessary that there be much water and much oil, because the magnitude of the tincture <term>Tincture: The potent substance or "dye" capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</term> will be as great as the magnitude of the oil was. Therefore, the stone is dissolved little by little, so that it may be converted into Mercury, and divided into the four elements, so that its first matter may be entirely obtained. Then it is washed, so that its uncleanness may be removed, and it may return to the color of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note> as it was at the beginning, and the falseness of its sulfur may be diminished. Afterward, it is calcined, so that its matter may be made subtle, and it may be able to be converted from the coarse to the slender, and from the thick to the subtle; then it is washed with the water of Mercury, so that it may recover a greater moisture than it lost in the lime <note>The "lime" is the powdery residue left after calcination.</note>. From there it is sublimated <note>Sublimation involves heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then collects as a purified solid on the cooler parts of the vessel.</note> so that its thinned matter may be more purified, and all this thinned matter—as clean sulfur and quicksilver—may be held upon the earth, from that matter out of which gold and silver were made beneath the earth. Then there is added to it

## THIRD TREATISE
# ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL
## ORE.

->*By an unknown author.*<-

There is one stone, one medicine, in which the whole mastery of the art of Alchemy consists; to which we add no other foreign thing, nor do we take anything away, except for the removal of superfluities during preparation. For you do not need to use any other body in this work except the purest Sun <note>Gold</note> or the best Moon <note>Silver</note>, but it is necessary that you labor over their inward solution and perfect refinement. The first step of their preparation is that you make quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> from them; and when they have been "mercurialized," they will be of manifest liquefaction and hidden refinement. Thus you should understand that the work is directed in four ways: the first way is the dissolution of the stone; the second, purification; the third, feeding <term>Cibation: The process of adding liquid to the dry alchemical matter to sustain its growth, often compared to feeding an infant.</term>; the fourth, betrothal <note>original: "desponsatio" — the symbolic marriage of the masculine and feminine principles.</note>. As far as the first is concerned, the stone is dissolved through frequent grinding and gentle roasting. Therefore, with God’s help, take a little Mercury washed with salt and vinegar, and afterwards distill it through an alembic <note>A pear-shaped vessel used for distillation.</note>, and throw away the dregs you produce. Let this be done a second time, and you will have a deadly poison <note>Alchemists often called the potent, corrosive forms of mercury "poison" because they "killed" or dissolved the metals.</note>. Then place in different vials one part of the purest Sun and three parts of the aforementioned poison, and cook over a slow fire, until...

When the earth has been well calcined and emptied of all air, it will be pale in color and ready for impregnation. If the spirit remains in it, it will be like black earth and will receive the nourishment of its water. When you have done this, you will have the four elements well rectified and purified.

Because it is necessary first to nourish the earth with a little milk, and later with more, just as is seen in the nourishment of an infant. <note>In alchemy, "philosophical milk" refers to the addition of white mercury or "virgin's milk" to the dry "body" to encourage its growth and transformation.</note> Note that the washing of the earth is done through the distillation of water, and the coagulation of that water is achieved through philosophical imbibitions <term>Imbibition: The process of a dry solid soaking up a liquid until it is saturated.</term> of water upon that earth. 

Therefore, wash the "earth of the earth" in the philosophical manner, and cook it until it has drunk as much of its water as it possibly can—specifically, as much as its own weight. For the more often it is well washed in this work, the better and more beautiful it will appear; and if it has not been well washed, it will not be clean, nor will it return to its true color. 

Note that you should have as much air in the separation as you received of water—namely, the first weight of the body, and the first and second weights of the water of the body and of Mercury, as at the beginning. Likewise, wash the earth in the philosophical manner, and cook your work in air, so that it drinks from it accordingly, just as it did from its aforementioned water. Let this be done often until it has drunk a quantity of air equal to the water integrated within it, and always cook and calcine gently for eight days. 

If you truly wish to work toward the red stage <term>Rubedo: The "reddening," the final stage of the alchemical Great Work, representing perfection and the completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, it is necessary to embrace the whole composition with a stronger fire, so that it is reduced to ashes. You must not hold these ashes in contempt, because it is necessary to return them to the work for the nourishment of their fire. Therefore, place the aforementioned ashes in their fire until they melt and drink their fire, and then your composition will be sweet, mild, and red like blood. 

When you have truly reddened the earth in its final reddening, a red tincture will appear with the nature of a poison <note>original: "venenum"; here used to mean a substance with extreme power of penetration or transformation, capable of "infecting" other metals with its own nature.</note>, because it penetrates, and its color is like a glowing coal. Because the operation pierces like a poison, join weight to weight and the composition will be a red tincture in the color of coral; this is the sign of complete digestion, perfection, and the completion of the tincture in its operation, by whose tincture all other things can be stained <note>In this context, "stained" or "tinged" refers to the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note> infinitely.

...four wheels, where the fire can least be delayed, if you first place oil into the air and afterward earth, the oil would be killed <note>original: "mortificatum"; in alchemy, 'mortification' refers to the temporary destruction or "death" of a substance's previous form so it can be reborn in a higher state.</note> in the earth when the water entered. Never make the fire, but make the place where the fire may be; open the door of its fire, and the surrounding air will enter. Fix the water with the earth, so that it adheres to it. And know that if you kill one element out of the four, all are dead; and if one should have more of the soul <note>original: "anima"; the vitalizing principle that connects the spirit to the physical body of the metal.</note> than the other elements, the work will be worth nothing. Understand what I say, for I commend you to God. 

Note the fermentation <term>Fermentation: The final stage where the "Medicine" or Elixir is "leavened" with a purified metal to give it the power to transform other metals.</term> of the Elixir, by casting it upon such a body as you took at the beginning, most excellently purified. In the first marriage <note>original: "desponsatione"; the symbolic union of the "medicine" (the active elixir) with the "body" (the base metal).</note>, there is less of the medicine than of the body—for instance, three parts of medicine and four of the body. Afterward, if you wish, take one part of the medicine with two, three, four, or more usefully according to what you find to be the power of the medicine; and this is the fourth work. 

The fourth work, therefore, is to marry it through the mixing of its first body, because it has been made substantial. For the understanding of this: namely, that the elixir is a fixative <note>original: "fixamen"; a substance that makes a volatile or "escaping" spirit stable and resistant to heat.</note> in the very body from which it was extracted at the beginning. For when the spirit dissolves the soul, it likewise dissolves the body, so that they are reduced to its form. Let it not be fixed and let it not die unless you have occupied it in its own court, because its "occupation" is its fixation achieved through fermentation. You must join it to its body prepared at the beginning, since it will be "occupied" in that body because of the suitability of the form of the spirit mentioned before to the essence of the body. Do not join it to any other body, because it converts the nature of any body; rather, join it to that body from which it drew its origin. If you do this, the whole thing which you join will be elixir. 

Truly, the purpose of many workers fails after the completion of the work because of ignorance of this secret. Note these words: for if you cast your work upon gold or silver, or any other body, it does not convert the nature of that body into the nature of a *different* body, but converts that body into its *own* nature. And if you cast that body upon another body, that body upon which the projection <term>Projection: The act of casting the finished Elixir or Stone upon a base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</term> is made will be an elixir moving the whole toward its own kind. Thus also you should understand that if you cast it upon silver, it will not move that...

# FOURTH TREATISE,
->*which is called*<-
## A USEFUL COMPENDIUM FOR
## BELIEVING the Experience of 
## Meditations.

**T**he experience of our meditations bears witness to the belief that spirits <term>Spirit: In alchemy, a "spirit" is a substance that can be vaporized by heat, such as mercury, sulfur, or arsenic.</term> are more closely assimilated to bodies <note>Metals</note> because they are more intimately united with them; for they agree with those bodies in nature more amicably than other things do. Therefore, through this primary discovery, it has been found by us that the spirit is the true medicine for the alteration of bodies, especially since, when searching among other spirits, we see no other spirit besides *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurium"; also called quicksilver.</note> that is friendly to the natures of metallic bodies. Therefore, by focusing our work upon it, we have found it to be the true medicine of alterable things in its completion, bringing about a perfect transformation. And certainly, the defect in imperfect bodies <note>Base metals like lead or tin.</note> is the scarcity of the quicksilver existing within them, and the improper thickening of the same. Therefore, the completion in these same imperfect bodies will be the multiplication of the quicksilver, along with its proper thickening and permanent fixation <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance (like mercury) stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates.</term>. This is perfected through the medicine created from it—that is, created from quicksilver—which, by the benefit of its own clarity and splendor, hides and covers their darkness by cloaking it, and leads them into splendor, converting them into a brilliant glow. 

Truly, since quicksilver is fluid and fleeting, it does not change without the administration of the nature of its own alteration; and therefore we found that it must necessarily be prepared so that its substance becomes such that it may be mixed in secret, even into the depths of the alterable body, without ever being separated. This cannot be done unless it is inwardly refined in a specific preparation through many repetitions of sublimation <term>Sublimation: A process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor, then allowing it to solidify again, used here to purify the mercury.</term> from dry, burning, and desiccating materials that possess no sulfurous quality. Its entry <note>Into the metal</note> does not remain unless it is fixed, nor does it illuminate unless the most radiant substance is drawn out from it, and it does not provide a proper flow <note>original: "fusionem"; the ability to melt and mix.</note> unless the greatest caution is applied in its fixation. Therefore, imitating nature as much as possible, we sublime it many times from unclean and drying calxes <note>original: "calcibus"; the powdered remains of a metal or mineral after it has been burned or oxidized.</note> until it is most perfectly cleansed of its superfluities, and rendered most white...

...takes on a dung-like color <note>original: "fimum"; referring to the dark brown or black color produced by the gentle heat of a "dung-bath" or horse-manure heater.</note> which is completed sometimes in seven, sometimes in nine, and sometimes in twelve turns. Therefore, when you see the substance as if it were dead, and adhering to the segments <note>original: "spondilibus"; the joints or ribs of the vessel.</note> of the aludel <term>Aludel: A pear-shaped ceramic pot or series of condensers used in the process of sublimation.</term> like the whitest snow, we then divide it into two parts. One of these we keep below, so that we may use it to lift (sublime) the earth-stone; the other we throw into flowing water until it returns to quicksilver. In this—as the masters teach—we dissolve the purest parts separately by distilling once: that is, gold, sulfur, silver, and arsenic, by cooking them gently until they are entirely dissolved and their fiery nature has emerged in the color of blackness.

For heat acting upon a moist substance generates blackness <term>Nigredo: The 'black' stage of alchemy, representing the initial corruption and 'death' of the old form.</term>, while acting on a dry substance it produces whiteness <term>Albedo: The 'white' stage, representing purification and spiritualization.</term>, and upon the white it produces yellowness <term>Citrinitas: The 'yellow' stage, the dawning of the final transformation.</term>. When, therefore, it has been dissolved and putrefied, we then divide it in a water bath, first by distilling gently; afterward, the air mixed with fire is distilled—those elements which are more fixed—over the fire. 

Then we burn the black earth remaining at the bottom of the aludel with a swift or quick fire—that is, we calcine <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder, removing volatile components.</term> it—until it is clean and whitish. From there, we rectify the water and the air—that is, by distilling each one by itself seven times. Afterward, we grind their "fire" <note>The most volatile or energetic portion of the substance.</note> which has been collected and set aside, and we soak it with its own water, and gently roast it, repeating this many times until it is dried out and colored with a redness like urine. 

Then we set aside these well-prepared elements; nevertheless, we join the calcined earth with the white sublimated quicksilver by grinding them together continuously, soaking the mixture with its own water, and gently roasting it until they are incorporated and mixed into one. When the moisture has departed, we light a small fire and sublime it until the earth is lifted up entirely with the white sublimated quicksilver. 

If, however, anything remains unsublimated at the bottom, we add to it in turn a quantity of sublimated quicksilver—first, such a quantity that the amount of the volatile substance exceeds the amount of the fixed substance, until it is sufficient to lift it. And so, turn by turn, we repeat the sublimation upon it until, for a second and third time, it is totally elevated. Afterward, we repeat its sublimation until, through this repetition of the process, it is "fixed" <term>Fixation: The process by which a volatile substance is made stable under heat, so it no longer evaporates or escapes.</term> at the bottom. 

From this point, we repeat the work of calcination, solution, and coagulation over the whole work at least four times, and finally, we fix it until it rests stable even in the harshness of the fire. ...the white and red body, because that is the "foliated earth" <term>Terra Foliata: "Leafy earth," a technical term for the purified solid matter that remains after the initial stages of distillation, often appearing in thin, leaf-like layers.</term> used for fermentation. Therefore, we divide it into two parts: one we reserve for the white work <term>Opus Album: The stage of the Great Work resulting in the "white stone" or "white elixir" capable of turning base metals into silver.</term>, and the other for the red work <term>Opus Rubeum: The final stage resulting in the "red stone" or "red elixir" capable of turning metals into gold.</term>.

Furthermore, regarding the part previously reserved for the red work, we dissolve it in its red water and immediately coagulate it; then we apply to it the red fire of the stone, repeating the entire work of grinding <term>Contritio: The physical breaking down or pulverizing of substances.</term>, soaking <term>Imbibitio: The process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated.</term>, and roasting <term>Assatio: Cooking or drying the substance with heat.</term> many times, until it is dry and red. This, through the previously described method, we sublime <term>Sublimatio: Heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then back to solid on a cooler surface.</term> in turn with sublimated and reddened Mercury—which is not fixed—until the whole has been raised a second and third time, becoming as red in color as is customary. Afterward, by the same method, we fix it so that it remains stable; from here, indeed, we dissolve and coagulate it turn after turn, and reserve it for fermentation for the red work of the Sun <note>original: "Solis opere"; "The Sun" is the standard alchemical symbol for gold.</note>.

Then we dissolve the white earth reserved for the white work, and to one part of it, we join three parts of the purest Moon <note>original: "Lunae"; "The Moon" is the standard alchemical symbol for silver.</note>, which has been similarly dissolved. Joining both these solutions together, we grind and roast them until the whole becomes one body, to which we add enough of its white oil, repeating the grinding, waxing <term>Inceratio: Softening a substance with liquid to give it a wax-like consistency, making it ready for fusion.</term>, and roasting many times so that they are better incorporated. 

From here, with repeated effort, we continue the sublimation upon it, always returning what ascends to the top back onto that which remains fixed below, until the whole is fixed at the bottom; this is completed sometimes in four, five, or seven turns, which is the final stage. Nevertheless, at every turn, we incorporate the whole through grinding, waxing, and roasting, and thus with repeated effort, we sublime the non-fixed from the fixed until everything has become fixed. Then we kindle a very strong fire upon it for a whole day, and by the grace of God, the elixir is complete—stable, dyeing, penetrating, strengthening, and enduring—of which one part converts a thousand parts of any body into the truest Moon <note>i.e., pure silver.</note>. 

Furthermore, we dissolve the whole again in its white oil and coagulate it; then we dissolve it again and join it with the non-fixed part, subliming it in turn until the whole fixed part is completely raised with the non-fixed. When it has been raised, we repeat its sublimation until, through the management of repetition, the whole is fixed; and when it has been fixed, we dissolve it again and sublime it again until the whole is raised once more; then we fix it again through the continuous repetition of sublimation upon...

Therefore, we divide the stone and its matter—which at first is quite unworkable—so that we may make the elements clean, and hold them in purity. 

Then we join them, because in that very hour they incorporate themselves with the body, which they could not do before because of their coarseness; and this is one reason why we divide the stone into its four elements. The desirable desire, the priceless price, set forth by all the Philosophers—which is never set aside nor assumed to have been poorly proposed—we shall here briefly unite into one sum from the books of the ancients. -> May it please our Lord Jesus Christ to send into us the spirit of His understanding. <-

All works of divine goodness are circular and perfect, rotated spherically toward Him from whom they proceeded. From the beginning, before the origin of His creation, setting nature before all things, God made four simple bodies <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>, from which He afterwards constituted all mixed bodies. Of these mixed things, however, He made some intellective, some sensitive and vegetative, some only intellective, and some He created only from the rarity <note>In this context, "rarity" refers to the subtle, thin, or spiritual nature of the higher elements like Fire.</note> of the elements. Therefore, "our heart is restless until we return to Him," <note>A famous reference to St. Augustine’s Confessions.</note> for the rarity of all elements ascends to the fire which is above the stars; therefore we too, created by that rarity, rightly strive upward toward God as toward a single principle. 

Sensitive and vegetative things, however, being composed of the density <note>original: "spissitudine," thickness or corporeal mass.</note> of the elements, are distinguished into diverse species; hence, when they are dissolved by death, they return not without cause to the earth and water, as if to their mother, for the density of the elements naturally tends downward to its center, namely the earth. Yet for all things of a constant nature, there is a fixed limit of size and growth, so that within their species they may increase their own like; and some of them are of dissimilar parts, such as from flesh, blood, and bones, or from wood, bark, and leaves. Some are of similar parts <note>original: "consimilibus," homogeneous; parts that are the same as the whole.</note>, as those which are of one essence throughout, as is seen in metals. 

Now, those which are of dissimilar parts possess their own seed within themselves, from which, fixed in the earth, they multiply and grow, as is seen in shrubs and herbs. But those which are of similar parts do not multiply unless they are reduced to their first matter <term>Materia Prima: The formless, original substance from which all things are made; in alchemy, metals must be returned to this state before they can be changed.</term>; wherefore the Philosopher Aristotle <note>A reference to a famous (though likely spurious) quote attributed to Aristotle in the "Meteorologica" or "De Mineralibus," which became a foundational rule for alchemists.</note> says: "Let the craftsmen of Alchemy know that the species of metals cannot truly be transmuted, unless perchance they are reduced into the first matter, and then indeed they are transmuted, and are well-changed into something other than they were before." Indeed, nature by itself does not build a house nor prepare an electuary <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or conserve made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term>, because it does not have the motion within itself to do this. Therefore, nature must be assisted by art in that which is omitted by nature, because there is no difference between nature and art except that art acts outwardly, while nature acts inwardly; for art, like a tool, administers the motion, while nature itself acts of its own accord, since it strives toward its own perfection. Furthermore, every body is either an element or composed of elements, but the generation of every composite must consist of the four simple elements; wherefore it is necessary that our stone, reduced to the first origin of its Mercury and sulfur <note>original: "Mercurij & sulphuris," the two primary principles of metallic composition in alchemy</note>, be divided into elements; otherwise it cannot be purified nor joined, because its smallest parts cannot enter except into the smallest parts of the body. When divided, however, it is purified and joined again, and it works the elixir which we seek. 

For the experiment <note>or "practical trial"</note> destroys its specific form: but before the division of the elements, nothing of them is seen or felt except earth and water, because air and fire are nowhere seen, nor are their virtues known, except within the aforementioned prior elements; for they are entirely rare <note>meaning subtle or thin</note> and simple, wherefore they cannot be seen at all by corporeal eyes. Therefore, do not worry about that, since it is enough for you to reduce the matter to a simple state of purity.

...[none] of those elements is joined to another except through a medium. Therefore, that which is not contrary to itself is naturally unifying: thus heat and dryness are united of their own accord, since they are in no way contrary to each other, and for this reason the element of air results from them <note>The author here associates Air with Heat and Dryness, though standard Aristotelian physics usually assigns Heat and Dryness to Fire, and Heat and Moisture to Air.</note>. Neither are cold and dryness contrary when joined, from which the element of earth is generated; nor even cold and moisture, from which the element of water is gathered. 

But heat and cold are not united except through a medium—namely, through the moist or the dry—since by themselves they refuse to stand together, as one blunts <note>original: "obtūdat"</note> the other on account of their contrariety. Therefore, heat and cold gather and disperse things of the same kind by dissolving and coagulating, but moisture and dryness are gathered and dispersed by constricting and wetting. 

Simple generation and natural transformation are the operations of the elements; for heat and cold produce things when they overcome matter. When the active forces are overcome, it is clear that a certain violence and "indigestion" <note>In alchemy, "indigestion" refers to a failure of the internal heat to properly mature or "cook" the matter into a perfected state.</note> occurs. It is therefore evident that all changeable things are, through heat and cold, both simply generated and naturally transformed. 

Furthermore, from any specific thing its own specific kind is made, because there is no generation except from things that agree in nature. For indeed, man begets man, and the lion a lion; thus each thing generates its like. However, nothing that comes from diverse kinds ever looks back to itself nor generates its like; the same is true of all things procreated from a different genus. It is necessary, therefore, that the elements be of one kind and not diverse; otherwise, they would have no action or passion toward one another, as one would not even touch the other.

Therefore, a doubt is raised concerning the Stone of the Philosophers <term>Lapis Philosophorum: the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine</term>, as to what it is or what sort it is, since it is never openly named by any of the philosophers. Regarding this, different men have decreed different things; but since the truth consists in one thing alone, we cherish it and teach to avoid all others. For it is clear through the writings of the philosophers that the matter is one single thing, and nothing foreign should be joined to it. Nothing suits a thing except what is closest to it and of its own nature; for things do not produce anything except what is like themselves, nor do they bear fruit except their own fruit. Therefore, since things are of one kind, their roots are one. 

The diversity of things is caused by the diversity of their parts: know, therefore, the clean from the unclean <note>The "clean" (pure) and "unclean" (impure) refer to the state of the alchemical matter; the goal is to strip away accidental impurities to reach the essential "clean" substance.</note>, because nothing gives what it does not have. The "clean" is of a single essence, free from alterations; the "unclean" is diverse and [composed] of...

...united by contrary parts, it is susceptible to easy corruption. The proof of this is found in the Sun and Saturn, because Saturn is entirely corrupted, while the Sun is not at all <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold—the incorruptible metal—while Saturn represents Lead, which is easily oxidized and considered "sick" or "imperfect."</note>. Therefore, a knowledge of the contrariety of bodies and the principle of their creation makes this <term>magisterium</term> <note>The "Mastery" or Great Work; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> easy; for filth adheres to filth since they are of the same kind, but the pure overcomes the nature of the impure, not suffering from any defect in the mixing. Therefore, do not look in nature for what is not there, because things do not happen except according to their own nature, and there is greater corruption in a passive thing than in an active one. Use, therefore, the nobler and simpler member, and it will be enough for you; yet the member of the heart is of the body, just as the member of the brain is of the head, because the power of the rational soul resides in the heart. 

Of these things, however, that which has fewer angles is closer to the nobler and simpler thing, just as a triangle is closer to the simple than a quadrangle <note>A square.</note>, since it has fewer boundaries. The circle is a simple body having no angle. Therefore, leave aside the composite and use the simpler, because that is the "genus of geniuses" and the "form of forms," for it is first and last among the planets just as the Sun is among the stars. I shall therefore transfer my discourse to those things that are homogeneous <note>Of the same kind or nature.</note> in nature, even if they are strong; for among those things that share a <term>symbolum</term> <note>original: "symbolum"; a shared quality or affinity between different elements that allows them to transform into one another.</note>, the transition is easier. 

Therefore, since your search concerns the nature of both luminaries of the world <note>The Sun and the Moon, or Gold and Silver.</note>, one must choose that which is homogeneous to them; and certainly, when this kind is assigned to light, we know much, because the work is not perfected except through it. The crowns of kings are decorated with precious stones, by whose beauty the sight is aided, the soul is delighted, and dignity is adorned; and by their power, the most serious ailments are expelled from bodies, without which all medicine is of little effect. For this reason, physicians use them in their medicines to drive out the most heavy diseases. 

Furthermore, it is the truest argument of the learned that the "best stone of all stones" is the most effective for the expulsion of all infirmities—note here that this "best stone of all stones" is to be understood as gold. Gold was believed to be "digested" by the heat of the earth until it reached perfection.</note> and is nearest to the fire, which sustains the fire the longest and is broken by the fire most slowly. For this reason, precious stones such as Rubies and Sapphires are more powerful than other stones, because they are generated in this hotter state, closer to the Sun with greater heat. # ABBREVIATED ROSARY

Gold, however—since it is made of an earthy substance mixed with water through its smallest parts—is homogeneous with fire on one side of its two extremes, and it is coagulated with cold after the action of heat within it. For this reason, it can be hammered and is improved in the fire, for it is proportioned to a better, equal, and nobler composition than all other precious stones. Immediately after that is silver; therefore, take silver also for the stone.

And certainly, gold is the lord of stones, the noblest of bodies, their King and best head; for it is not corrupted by air, nor by water, nor by earth, nor does fire diminish it. Indeed, fire moistens, decorates, and rectifies it, and burning things do not burn it, nor do corrupting things corrupt it, because its complexion is tempered and its nature is directed in equal heat and cold, moisture and dryness; there is nothing superfluous in it, nor anything diminished. 

Therefore, no stones, no matter how great the price for which they are sold, prevail over gold; even though some may be more expensive than gold, it is not because they exceed the value of gold, but because they are found more rarely and in fewer numbers. Of all the things of this age, therefore, gold is worth more, since it is the ferment of the Elixir, without which the work is never performed. ### FIFTH TREATISE

...as dough, and like the rennet of milk in cheese, and like musk among good aromatics. Justly, therefore, gold encompasses the upper **Solar** part, and silver the lower **Lunar** part; wherefore, unless I saw the Sun and Moon, I would say for certain that the <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium" — the Great Work or the secret process of alchemy</note> was not true. But because I see the Sun and Moon, I know most certainly that the mastery is true: for everything increases its own kind, and all these things are homogeneous in nature. Therefore, it is necessary that their increase be just as it is for the growth of plants in nature. 

The Sun, therefore, is the <term>tincture of redness</term> <note>A substance that can transform other metals into gold.</note>, which transforms every body. The Moon, however, is the tincture of whiteness, since she is the mistress of moisture. Spirits are mixed with the Sun, and they are fixed by it through great skill—a skill that does not reach a stiff-necked craftsman. For a spirit <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances like mercury or sulfur that can evaporate.</note> turned into its own nature dies, and seems like one dead; from there, it later comes back inspired, is multiplied, and grows like all other things. 

Therefore, *unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:24, used here to explain that the "death" (breakdown) of a substance is necessary for its rebirth into a higher form.</note>. Where it seemed to have lost what it was, from there it begins to appear as what it was not. He who is ignorant of its destruction, therefore, must necessarily be ignorant of its construction through the act of nature. 

It is <term>calcined</term> <note>Reduced to powder by heat.</note> and dissolved with the greatest labor; therefore, why do you use other bodies without utility? Why use them when you can have in these [gold and silver] that which is of greater temperance and less dross? If you require the use of those [base metals], they must first be converted into the likeness of the others mentioned before, and only then may you begin the operation upon them. They do not enter the work until they are as subtle in their composition as the perfect bodies.

## THE ABBREVIATED ROSARY

...they return to it: for it is certain that every thing is made from that into which it is resolved. Ice is resolved into water by means of heat; it is clear, therefore, that it was water beforehand. In this same way, all ductile metals <note>Metals that can be hammered or stretched without breaking.</note> can be resolved into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>; therefore, they were quicksilver in the beginning. Note here the resolution of bodies <note>In alchemical terms, "bodies" refers to the solid metals.</note> into quicksilver. 

Blessed and sublime, therefore, is the Lord of nature, who has granted humans the reason to discern and to reduce every thing back to its first matter and nature—namely, bodies prepared back to the first origin of their **sulfur** and **mercury**. Thus, through them, we may accomplish upon the earth in a few days what nature has worked beneath the earth in only a thousand years <note>Alchemists believed that metals "grew" slowly in the earth over centuries; the laboratory was meant to accelerate this natural process.</note>. Hence, if we had no other benefit from quicksilver except that it makes bodies finer and more subtle according to its own nature, this in itself ought to be enough for us. 

For it is friendly and agreeable to metals, and a medium for joining <term>tinctures</term> <note>The transformative substances or "dyes" that change the properties and color of a metal.</note>, because it receives into itself that which belongs to its own nature, but rejects what is foreign. This is because it is of a uniform substance, homogeneous in all its parts. It is this indeed which overcomes fire and is not overcome by it, but rests friendlily within it, rejoicing in it. Because of the excellent way its parts cling together and the strength of its mixture, if its parts are thickened <note>original: "inspissentur"</note> by fire in any way, it does not allow itself to be further corrupted; nor, through the entry of a smoky flame, does it allow itself to be raised further into smoke. This is because it does not suffer its own thinning out <note>rarefication</note> on account of its density and lack of <term>combustibility</term> <note>original: "adustionis" — the state of being burnt or scorched.</note>. 

Therefore, we truly suggest that those bodies which contain more quicksilver are of greater perfection, and those that contain less are of lesser perfection. Certainly, the deficiency in imperfect bodies <note>Such as lead or tin.</note> is a lack of quicksilver and a failure to thicken it correctly; therefore, their fulfillment will be the multiplication of quicksilver, its proper thickening, and its permanent fixation. 

Therefore, when you are at work, strive in all your operations to master **Mercury** in the mixture. If you can perfect it through Mercury alone, you will be a seeker of the most precious perfection, and you will rejoice in the summit of that perfection which surpasses the work of nature. For you will be able to cleanse it inwardly to a degree that nature cannot reach, and thus, as a result, you will be able to create a work from it that will surpass all of nature. For there is no difference whether this is done in natural organs <note>The earth's "womb."</note> or in artificial ones <note>The alchemist's glass vessels and furnace.</note>. From these things, therefore, you should draw out the secret: our medicine must necessarily be taken from those same things which most closely adhere to quicksilver...

# TREATISE THE FIFTH

...however, when it has been ground and made into one single thing, it possesses within itself every **tincture** <term>a substance capable of coloring or transforming other metals</term> that can endure the fire. Therefore, when the body has been so colored by the spirit, it colors other things, and it possesses and bestows every tincture within itself. For this reason, those who prepare the staining venom from the **Sun** <note>original: "Sole," referring to gold.</note> and its shadow—that is, the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna," referring to silver.</note>—perfect our stone. Truly, unless the stone possessed qualities from both one substance and the other, they would not have action and passion toward each other, and the one would not color the other.

A stone and a piece of wood, for example, have no operation between them because they are made of different matter, just as it is with all things that differ in matter. Thus, it is necessary that the **agent** <term>the active principle that causes change</term> and the **patient** <term>the passive substance that receives change</term> be one and the same thing in genus, but distinct and diverse in species. This is just as a woman is distinguished from a man; for although they agree in one genus and nature, they nevertheless have a distinction between them and a distinct operation, as is fitting between the agent and the patient. For matter undergoes the action, while form acts, making the matter like unto itself.

Therefore, matter naturally desires form, just as a woman desires a man, or the ugly desires the beautiful; so also the spirit willingly embraces the body, so that it may arrive at its perfection. Know, therefore, the **mineral roots** <note>The fundamental metallic constituents, likely mercury and sulfur.</note>, and perform your work from them, since we cannot express our stone by naming it in any other way, nor name it by any other name; rather, we name it through a description of its parts based on its roots.

Rightly, therefore, our stone is called "every thing" by the philosophers, because it has within itself and from itself everything necessary for its own perfection. It is called by every name because of the excellence of its nature and its hidden and diverse action. It is found everywhere because of its participation in the elements; it is most vile through **putrefaction** <term>the stage of decay and blackness (nigredo) in the alchemical process</term>, but most precious because of its virtue. It is black, white, and yellow <note>original: "citrinus," referring to the xanthosis or yellowing stage.</note> according to the change of its colors. Therefore, set aside the multitude of its various names, because in whatever way it is named, it is nevertheless always one single and same thing.

Certainly, the philosophers do not care for names, but for the properties of names, because through one they allow the other to be understood; for the thing is not subject to the word, but the word is subject to the thing. There is, then, no essential difference between the white medicine and the red medicine, except in this: that the red medicine requires a greater refinement, a longer **digestion** <term>the slow heating of a substance to mature it</term>, and more heat from the fire in its **management** <term>regimen: the controlled sequence of the alchemical operation</term>. Its base should have a small circumference with flat walls and a wide head, so that the substance to be **sublimated** <term>the process where a solid turns into vapor and rises</term> may ascend through it more freely; in this way, when necessary, fire is applied below and above so it may be better heated. 

Truly, no material other than glass is suitable, unless perhaps it were of a substance similar to it. This is because only glass—and things like glass whose body is clear, transparent, and lacking pores—is able to contain the **fleeting spirits** <note>original: "spiritus fugaces," volatile substances that evaporate or escape easily</note> so they are not driven out by the fire. It also allows the colors appearing in the work to be seen, so that the operator does not err in his management. Other vessels will not do because they have opaque bodies—that is, dark and porous—through which the spirit, passing gradually (that is, little by little), would vanish into smoke. 

It is indeed the nature of spiritual vapors to ascend and not descend; therefore, let the cucurbit with its weak spirits enter into its alembic as far as the rim. Let the joint be cleverly made and well-fitting so that nothing can fall through it; let it also be closed tightly and continuously so that nothing can exit or enter. For if air or a foreign moisture enters, it corrupts the process; but if its **flower**—that is, the white smoke—should escape and flee, the whole work is deprived of its effect. 

The management of our stone is but one: to cook the substances constantly and continuously in their vessel without interruption, until you achieve the desired end. The Philosophers, however, have set down many technical terms out of reverence for their art, such as continuation, concealment, and **purification** <note>original: "mundificationem," the cleansing of the matter</note>, so that nothing filthy or unclean is introduced...

# THE FIFTH TREATISE

### Page 752

...to mix, to cook, to hydrate, to putrefy, to **whiten** and to **redden**—these are many names, yet their **management** <term>regimen: the controlled sequence of the alchemical operation</term> is only one, which is simply to cook; and therefore it is nothing other than **women's work and children's play** <note>original: "opus mulierum & ludus puerorum." This common alchemical phrase suggests that once the heat is set correctly, the process is as simple as laundry or a game, requiring patience rather than complex labor.</note>. Grind, therefore, cook, repeat, and let it not weary you to repeat this many times; for if the philosophers knew that a single **decoction** <term>the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</term> and a single grinding sufficed for them, they would not repeat their sayings so often. Indeed, they did and said these things so that the compound might be ground continuously and cooked without intermission.

Furthermore, its entire management lies in the tempering of the fire, because the variety of its procedures arises from the variety of the degrees of fire. For in **dissolution** <term>solutio: the turning of a solid into a liquid state</term> the fire will always be gentle; in **sublimation** <term>the process where a substance heated in a vessel rises as a vapor and solidifies again at the top</term>, moderate; in **coagulation**, tempered; in **whitening**, continuous; and in **reddening**, strong and continuous. If, however, you err unknowingly in these matters, you will very often lament your wasted labor.

It is most advisable, therefore, that you insist diligently on the work, nor should you leave the work truncated; for you will acquire neither knowledge nor profit from an abandoned work, but rather loss and despair. You also need to be learned in the science of **natural philosophy** <note>In the medieval and early modern periods, this referred to the study of the physical world and its laws, the precursor to modern science.</note> and advanced in skill, so that you may be able to remedy an error at the critical moment through knowledge; for you could not amend it by natural ingenuity alone, for art is aided by genius and genius by art.

Similarly, it is expedient that you not be ignorant of the principles of this art, for he who is ignorant of them will not find the end. Do not strive to find a false goal for the work, but intend only for the true completion of the **stone** <term>the Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy</term>, lest perhaps God, in whose power our art is reserved, deny its truth to you forever. Note therefore deeply concerning the disposition of our stone, which is the whole work.

The disposition of our stone is only one: it is to be placed in its vessel and cooked continually in the fire until the whole rises dissolved. Then the fire is to be strengthened until it has exhausted its moisture, and it becomes dry and very white. Thirdly, the fire is to be strengthened until it is lemon-yellow and very red. But if you are negligent in working, you will see none of these colors; study, therefore, when you are at work, to store in your mind all the signs that appear in any decoction and to investigate their causes. These are very necessary for the craftsman and suitable for the completion of the whole work, because those who are ignorant of the cause must necessarily be ignorant of the effect. ...and not multiple times; and although it is said many times by the philosophers, "put it in its vessel and close it firmly," it suffices nevertheless to put it in and close it **once** until you have completed the whole **mastery** <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process</term>. Therefore, all the rest is set down for the concealment of the art; and certainly, for the generation of man and of every growing thing, the seed is never placed in the womb except **once**. If it were introduced at another time, then that would destroy the other seed because of the rawness of **indigestion** <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow heating of a substance, analogous to how a stomach breaks down food or a womb develops an embryo. For this reason, women who expose themselves to many men very rarely conceive, and if it happens that they do conceive, they give birth to an abortion. So, by adding **cooked** things to **raw**, and **undigested** things to **digested**, men do not nourish the work but kill it, because the fetus is nourished only by that blood of the mother and lives until it is brought into the light. 

From these things, therefore, it is clear that we do not need many things for our work, nor does it require great expenses, since there is **one stone, one vessel, and one management**, and one disposition of the same for both the **white** and for the **red** to be made successively—that is, step by step. 

Therefore, if you have truly and beautifully directed the **natures**, and well-fitted its composition, and joined kinsfolk to their kinsfolk suitably, you will complete the whole work. For natures meeting their own natures follow them and are exalted in them; for they putrefy and give birth, because our nature is ruled [by it]: **nature directs nature**, melts it, and turns it into powder, then **nature restores nature**, gives birth, and renews it, until it brings about the end of the work. 

Truly, because forms are given according to the merit of the matter, it is not at all appropriate to work with nature that is unprepared. The best mode of **preparation** is to take away the superfluous and supply what is absent; for in this way, both the whole and the corrupted are renewed to a perfect state. 

And that is indeed how you must highly **sublime** <term>sublimatio: the process of vaporizing a solid to purify it</term> **Mercury** from false things that do not agree with it at all, until it has taken on a **celestial color** <note>likely a reference to a bright blue or shimmering silver-grey color indicating purity.</note>. Moreover, the seeds of all things growing from the earth are not multiplied nor grow if their generative power is taken away by too much external heat. Certainly, this nature is not multiplied if it is prepared in an improper manner; therefore, do not take nature itself unless it is **pure and clean**...

In this context, it refers to the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them.</note>, you shall dissolve the **silver-nature** <note>original: "lunaturam." For the first step of its preparation is that it becomes **Mercury**, and this does not happen until you soften it through the dominion of water and the continuous movement of heat.

It is necessary, therefore, that there be much water and much oil, because the greater the quantity of water, the greater the quantity of the **tincture** <term>tinctura: the transformative essence or "dye" that changes the color and nature of a metal</term>. We dissolve **gold**, however, so that it may be reduced to its **first matter**, which is to say, so that it truly becomes **sulfur** and **quicksilver**. We do this because we can then best make silver and gold from it once it has been converted back into their basic nature. Therefore, it must be washed and cooked so that it becomes true sulfur and silver <note>meaning quicksilver/mercury</note>, for according to the philosophers, these are the **first matter** of all metals.

And certainly, our **solution** is nothing other than the returning of the body to a moist state, so that the nature of quicksilver may be revealed within it and the false properties of its sulfur may be diminished. It is not, however, returned to "cloud-water" <note>original: "aquam nubis." Likely referring to common rainwater or simple distilled water.</note> as some fools have thought; for if it were returned to such water, it would then become dry by force and not by nature—much like salts and alums—and thus, when placed in the fire, they would be converted into glass. Therefore, their work is false.

Now, note most carefully regarding the **solution**: Our solution is that you hand over **Gabricus** to **Beya** so that the marriage may be performed. And truly, Gabricus, lying with Beya, dies immediately and is transformed into her nature. Then, after many days have passed, he rises above Beya, transforming her into his own body. Although Beya is the female, she nevertheless improves Gabricus because he originates from her; and even though Gabricus is more precious than Beya, we know that no generation happens without her, because no proper birth occurs except from the male and the female.

Therefore, join our **red servant** <note>Gabricus, representing the solar/sulfur principle.</note> to his **sweet-smelling sister** <note>Beya, representing the lunar/mercurial principle.</note> and they will beget the art between them. Once they are placed in their vessel, close it most diligently, cooking them continuously with a gentle fire until they become a **thick broth**. For it is clear from natural principles that every thing whose root is earth and water may be dissolved and become flowing. Certainly, according to the **Philosopher** <note>A standard reference to Aristotle.</note>, earth becomes water when the qualities of water overcome it, and water becomes earth when the qualities of earth overcome it. 

Thus, the **solution of the body** is the **congealing of the spirit**, and the congealing of the spirit is the solution of the body; for they share a single operation, such that one is not dissolved unless the other is congealed. Join, therefore, your leaf to the **poison**,

...yours, and the beginning of the work will be verified for you in it; however, from the rotation of the heavens, both fortunate and unfortunate things germinate in earthly matters. Therefore, at the beginning of your work, unite the solution by means of the **Sun** <note>original: "per Solem." In alchemy, the Sun represents Gold or the masculine, hot principle.</note>, for the effect will appear from there, and because the superior is depressed when the inferior helps, or let the superior things conquer, since they rule over the inferior. 

Be patient, therefore, in the management of the work, close the vessel firmly, and do not stop, because no generation or corruption of things occurs except through continuous motion, excluded air, and tempered heat. An example of this is a woman’s womb, for when she has conceived, the matrix is immediately closed, and the fetus is generated by the heat and moisture of the blood; yet it never receives external breaths until it is born. 

In the same way, let our **Stone** remain continually closed in its vessel until it has drunk its own moisture and has been perfectly nourished by the heat of the fire; for then the **white stone** <term>albedo: the second major stage of the Great Work, characterized by purification and whiteness</term> is born, and the breaths of the air do not harm it. 

It is therefore highly necessary to continue the operation, moderate the fire, exclude the air, and especially until the **whiteness** is reached. Therefore, burn our **copper** <term>æs: in this context, "our copper" refers to the base alchemical starting material, not necessarily common metal</term> with a gentle fire, just as in the hatching of eggs, until its body is broken down and the **tincture** <term>tinctura: the soul or transformative essence of the metal</term> is extracted. 

However, it is not all extracted at once, but little by little it comes out every day until it is completed over a long time. That which is dissolved always ascends to the top, even if the residue is greater; therefore, always beware of a large fire, lest you reach the solution before the necessary time, because this leads the work to a "distant removal" <note>meaning a failure or a regression in the process</note>, depriving it of sense, operation, and motion. 

Note well, therefore, concerning the gentle heat and the **philosophical grinding** <term>contritio: unlike physical grinding with a mortar and pestle, this refers to the chemical breakdown of a substance through heat</term> which is done by our fire and not by hands. 

Intense heat destroys the compound, and coldness puts it to flight, but gentle heat nourishes and preserves it. Therefore, once placed in a tempered **bath** <term>balneum: a water bath or "bain-marie" providing indirect, steady heat</term>, grind it with fire and not with hands. Wash it with the moisture of its own water, so that its fiery power is not scorched, nor its **sulfurous substance** burned; for this sulfur comes out first in the separation, since it is lighter and more worthy of the operation than the virtues of the other elements. 

Now note the signs of true **dissolution**. Continue the tempered bath over it until it is dissolved into an impalpable water and the whole tincture comes out in the color of **blackness** <term>nigredo: the first stage of the work, representing putrefaction and the death of the old form</term>, which is the sign of true dissolution. For heat acting on the moist generates blackness first, and in the dry it works whiteness, and in the white, **yellowness** <term>citrinitas: the stage between whiteness and the final redness</term>, just as can be seen in lead when **red lead** <term>minium: a red pigment made from lead, used here as a physical analogy for alchemical color shifts</term> is made from it. Therefore, govern it continuously with a moist fire <note>original: "humido igne." In alchemy, this often refers to a water bath (balneum Mariae) or a gentle, indirect heat that provides moisture.</note>; do not hurry, and do not stop the work until the whole is destroyed and becomes a completely spiritual powder. That which has become spiritual powder ascends to the top of the vessel, while that which remains thick and coarse stays at the bottom. Note, therefore, the sign of the true **grinding** <note>original: "contritionis." While this literally means grinding or crushing, in alchemy it refers to the chemical breakdown of a solid into a fine state through heat and moisture.</note> of the body with the spirit: unless you turn everything into a spiritual powder, you have not yet ground them. Therefore, continue to grind until they are converted and everything becomes powder; and note how this is done by **fire**, not by hands. This grinding, then, is a result of boiling <note>original: "decoctionis."</note>, not of the hands; it can only be achieved through gentle boiling, moist putrefaction, and continuous grinding by fire and not by hands, for we have no need for the grinding of hands.

**Alkien** <term>Alkien: a term derived from the Arabic "al-kiyān," referring to the internal nature, essence, or the formative "virtue" within a substance that directs its growth and transformation.</term> certainly performs this and is perfected through it, because the **Alkien** of the earth—that is, a certain secret generation within the earth—is like the **Alkien** in a human being. By its own preparative power, it always clarifies and divides just as it knows how; and rightly so, for nature is wise and sufficient for itself in all things it requires. Indeed, it is part of its work to convert earth into water, and water into earth, according to various compositions.

Note first: the earth is to be dissolved with water. Second: the earth will coagulate the water, and this will occur within one hundred and forty days. At first, the water strives to dissolve the earth so that it may have a subtle nature like its own; but secondly, the earth will coagulate the water so that it may sustain the fire within itself. This is the **dissolution of the body** and the **coagulation of the spirit** by the gentle boiling of the fire in one hundred and forty days. Perhaps the **whiteness** <term>albedo: the stage of purification where the matter turns a brilliant white.</term> will appear in forty days, but the former timeframe is better, as it signifies the temperance of the fire and the goodness of the preparation.

However, nothing acts upon the **gold** except our **sulphur** <note>original: "sulphur nostrum." That which is blackened is that which opened the door to the "one who does not flee," and the "non-fleeing" is turned with the "fleeing" <note>This is a classic alchemical riddle. The "fleeing" or volatile substances (like Mercury) are fixed by the "non-fleeing" or stable substances (like Sulphur/Gold).</note>. Yet the torturer does not torture with harm or corruption, but rather with unification and utility. For if its torture were harmful and improper, the gold would not be embraced by it, nor would it extract its colors, which we have called the **water of sulphur**.

Therefore, we say that what first turns black is the **key of the work**, because it does not happen without **blackness** <term>nigredo: the "blackest black," the first stage of the Great Work signifying putrefaction and the death of the old form.</term>. For this is the very **tincture** we seek, with which we may dye any body; it was formerly hidden in its **copper** <term>æs: here referring to the base "starting matter" or "raw body" of the stone, not literal metallic copper.</term> just as the soul is in the human body. The intention of the philosophers, therefore, is that the body—already dissolved into a black powder—should enter its own water and the whole become one. If you ask how powder becomes water, know that this powder is nothing but the water of sulfur, dissolved by the heat of fire. By its own merit, therefore, water receives water as its own nature; for unless everything is turned into water, it can in no way reach perfection.

Note, however, that nothing should be added in the mixing, nor in the whole **management** <note>original: "regimine." For its power is **spiritual blood**, without which nothing happens. It is converted into a body, and the body itself is turned into spirit by it; for when they are mixed together and reduced to one, they turn each other. For the body incorporates the spirit, but note that the spirit colors the body with the color of fire. 

The spirit, therefore, turns the body into a tinted spirit like blood, because everything that has a spirit also has blood. Therefore, that blackness rising above its water must be constantly occupied by a gentle fire until it is reunited in its water, and water becomes water in water—that is, until the whole becomes one water. When one water is mixed with another water, then water embraces water so that they cannot be separated from one another. But the ignorant, hearing "water," think it is water from a cloud <note>That is, common rainwater.</note>. But if they had reason, they would certainly know it to be the **permanent water**, which nevertheless cannot be permanent without its body, with which it is dissolved and made one. The whole work consists in the vapor and <term>sublimation</term> <note>In alchemy, sublimation refers to the process of heating a substance so it rises as a vapor and then solidifies again, which was seen as a way to "spiritualize" or purify the matter.</note> of its water. However, you must take the greatest care in every sublimation, liquefaction, or breaking, against the **vitrification** <note>Vitrification occurs when the materials fuse into a glass-like state and stick to the vessel, making them impossible to work with further.</note> of your vessel; for if you light the fire so much that the water rises to the top of the vessel, it will enjoy the coolness there and stick to that spot. Thus, it will not be able to complete the sublimation of the elements, because it is necessary for each of them to be pressed down and raised up many times by a **spherical rotation** <note>This refers to the "circulatio," where vapors rise, condense, and drip back down in a continuous cycle, often performed in a specialized vessel called a "Pelican."</note> on its own. Indeed, what ascends by violence does not descend without violence.

Therefore, let the fire be gentle, so that the whole work may rise and descend freely by itself, without sticking to the vessel. For unless we thin the **body** with fire and water until it ascends like a spirit, we accomplish nothing. As it climbs, however, it is born in the air and turned into air; life becomes one with life so that one is not separated from the other, just as water mixed with water. Therefore, that which is born in the air is born wisely, since it is made entirely spiritual.

Understand further that we perform sublimation for three reasons: 
1. The first is so the body may become a spirit of a <term>subtle</term> <note>Refined, thin, or non-material.</note> nature. 
2. The second is so the spirit may incorporate itself with the body and become one with it. 
3. The third is so all things may become white and clean, and the "falseness" of the **sulfur** <note>Original: "falsedo sulphuris." This refers to the combustible, impure parts of common sulfur that must be "burned away" to reach the "Philosophical Sulfur."</note> may be diminished, for during sublimation whatever was combustible within the work is burned away.

And certainly, it is highly necessary for us that the elements become **simple**, so they can be joined to one another. Yet they cannot become simple unless they are separated into parts; therefore it is necessary to sublimate both vapors many times, until the water descends in the sifting. We therefore sift the matters with a spherical sieve seven times, so that all things become clear, limpid water. For the body never allows the **soul** to be separated from itself—which is its equal in simple proximity—and therefore we repeat their sublimation, so they may be reduced to a subtle nature. 

In truth, some wisely believe the separation is done in many ways; do not worry about this, because you will prosper by reducing the operation to the equality of a "simple," and not by separating each element individually. And certainly, it will not be difficult to reduce everything to the simple state of **whiteness**. 

Its father is the **Sun**, and its mother is the **Moon**; the wind carried it in its belly, and the earth was born from it. <note>This is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus," one of the most famous foundational texts of alchemy.</note> And that which you received by distilling water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth; for by many iterations of sublimation the soul, ascending with the water, is purified, and its coarseness, descending to the bottom, is "turned to moon" <note>Original: "lunatur." This suggests the matter is becoming fixed, white, or silver-like (Luna).</note> in the earth. Thus, therefore, you shall make earth from fire, and water from air, which you shall return upon the earth, for its power is whole if it has been returned to the earth: turn therefore the earth into

# FIFTH TREATISE #

[...you must turn] water [into fire], and water into fire, then truly fire into air, hiding the fire in the innermost parts of the water, and the earth in the belly of the air; you should mix the hot with the moist, and the dry with the cold. In this way, therefore, you should perform the mixing, because there is no passage from one extreme to another except through a middle state. The **Eagle** <note>original: *Aquila*; in alchemy, the Eagle symbolizes the volatile or "spiritual" part of matter that rises during heating.</note> flying through the air and the **Toad** <note>original: *bufo*; the Toad symbolizes the "fixed" or heavy, earthy part of matter that remains at the bottom of the vessel.</note> walking upon the earth is the mastery of the work. Therefore, you shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, by gently distilling with great skill. 

It ascends from the earth to heaven, and descends again to the earth; it receives the superior force of the spirit and the inferior force of the body <note>This passage is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus," a foundational text for alchemists that describes the unity of the macrocosm (heaven) and microcosm (earth).</note>, because it overcomes every subtle thing by congealing it, and penetrates every solid thing by altering it. In this way, it rules over both higher and lower things, because it works as much in spirits as in bodies. 

Here note deeply concerning the **spirit**, **soul**, and **body**. It is clear, therefore, that our **copper** <term>æs</term> <note>While *æs* usually means copper or bronze, alchemists used "our copper" to refer to their specialized starting material, often a metallic sulfide or "living" metal.</note> has a spirit, a body, and a soul. The spirit is its water, its soul is its <term>tincture</term> <note>The "tincture" is the essence or color-giving property that the alchemist seeks to extract and use to transform other metals.</note>, and its body is its earth. Yet the spirit is the carrier of the soul's virtues to the body, just as the dye of the dyers is carried through water onto cloth. The soul is the bond of the spirit, just as the body is the bond of the soul; the body is fixed and dry, containing the spirit and the soul. 

The spirit, therefore, penetrates; the body fixes; the soul joins, dyes, and whitens. In these three are smoke, blackness, and death, which will not be permanent unless they are removed. Therefore, one must expel the smoke from the water, the blackness from the soul, and death from the body through frequent dissolution, which must not be delayed. 

In these matters, those who have not made "two sulfurs" from sulfur know nothing. The two sulfurs are those which are <term>sublimated</term> from the mixed or joined stone into a tincture; these indeed dye and "flee" <note>To "flee" means to evaporate or vaporize when heated.</note>, but they are contained by sulfur so they cannot flee, because sulfur is the connection of all fleeing things. 

Therefore, mix the **eggs of black hens** <note>This likely refers to a specific chemical precursor, perhaps organic matter or a dark mineral like antimony, rather than actual poultry eggs.</note> with the copper, and you shall have as much gold and silver as you desire. For the **Vulture** flying without wings over the mountain cries out, saying: 

*“I am white, black, and red; the truthful white and yellow son of the red, and I do not lie. Join me, therefore, to my mother and to her breast, because I cause her substance to be contained. Do not, therefore, introduce anything foreign to us, nor cease from the work, for every nature is united with its own partner and is perfected through it. My mother bore me, and through me she herself is born; for she first ruled over me, but henceforth I shall rule over her, because I have become the pursuer of my mother, before I received flight from her, yet she favors me in the best way she can, like a devoted mother...”*
