[...it] cherishes and nourishes the son whom it brought forth, until it arrives at a perfect state. Therefore, place me in a **moist fire** <note>original: *humido igne*; often referring to a water bath (balneum Mariae) or gentle, indirect heat that provides moisture as well as warmth.</note> continuously, which increases the heat of my moisture and forbids the burning of dryness, until it brings about the end of the work. Then draw out my redness and my shadow by themselves, until you persist in the third part; for the boiling diminishes me, but the grinding increases me, and what is diminished after fifteen days is increased after thirty; this is the beginning and the end. 

Therefore, guard the **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury, considered the "living" spirit of metals.</note> in its innermost bridal chamber in which it was coagulated, for from the repeated turn of the sifting, the white water ascends with the soul to the **alembic** <term>alembic: a distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used to purify substances by evaporation and condensation</term> and the body gradually descends to one point; and this itself is the quicksilver which is called the "residual earth" which receives the water and drinks it, because it is the connection of the **tinctures** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a substance capable of infusing its color or properties into another, specifically the power to transmute metals</term>. 

Preserve, therefore, the vessel and its seal, so that you may be powerful in the preservation of the spirit; for the water that was previously in the air now dwells in the earth. If it cannot escape, then return it to the higher parts, and through its own limits—not unsuitably—join it then to its red body previously chosen by you. For wherever the body is, there also the **eagles** <note>original: *aquilae*; a symbol for the volatile spirits or vapors that rise during the heating process.</note> will gather, because if it ascends without violence, it will descend upon it without violence; but if not, then no. 

Therefore, tie the hands of the nursing woman behind her back so that she does not flee from **Gabricus** <note>original: *Gabricum*; a symbolic name for the solar/male principle (often sulfur), who must be "married" to the lunar/female principle (Beya) to produce the Stone.</note>, that is, the husband; place near her the son she brought forth so that she may suckle him, for when the woman has died, there will be a thick **toad** <note>original: *bufo*; the Toad symbolizes the heavy, "fixed" dregs or the "blackness" (nigredo) of the matter that remains at the bottom of the vessel.</note> made of milk; then cut the toad through the middle, offering it to the **hen** <note>original: *gallinae*; the "hen" is a metaphor for a specific degree of heat or a stage of "digestion" where the matter is further refined.</note> so that she may eat it. 

Bring the water back to the earth, administering a tempered fire until it has taken root in its own nature, knowing for certain that it must first be nourished with a little milk, just as is seen in the raising of an infant; for it is nourished with a little milk and fire while it is small, and the more it grows, the more it needs food and heat, until it has drunk its own moisture; for the first of the moistures is cold, therefore a fire must be taken which is an enemy to cold. 

If you place the body upon the fire without **vinegar** <note>original: *aceto*; not common table vinegar, but "Philosophical Vinegar," a potent solvent or acidic agent used to dissolve and protect the matter from scorching.</note>, it is burned, and that which is sought will not be produced from it; because if the fire does not find moisture to dry out, it burns the body; but the vinegar applied to it prevents the burning of the fire, drying itself along with the body so that it suffers no injury. And the more the flame of the fire takes hold, the more [the matter] is hidden in the depths of the water, lest it be burned by the heat of the fire. 

Here note concerning the proportion and weight of the water and the body. I command you, therefore, not to pour in the water all at once, lest the **elixir** <term>elixir: the supreme goal of alchemy, a refined substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or curing all diseases</term> be drowned, but rather pour it in little by little so that always...

### FIFTH TREATISE ###

The **body** <note>original: *corpus*; the solid material or base metal being transformed.</note> should be boiled with three parts of its own water; for if it is prepared without the proper weight, death will come to it, and when this happens, the result will be considered a failure. However, if it is managed properly, it is pacified with its own water over the fire. But because the body initially has little of the **radical source** <note>original: *radicis*; likely referring to the "radical moisture" or essential life-force of the matter.</note>, the power of which is not equally abundant in all parts—just as the brightness of the Sun is not equal among the planets—patience and delay are necessary. Through the long duration of boiling, the water must win the battle against the fire. Indeed, by the gentle boiling of the fire, the water is congealed, and the corruptive humidity is drawn out, the heat of the **radical moisture** <note>original: *humoris radicalis*; the essential, non-volatile liquid within a substance that preserves its life.</note> is increased, and the burning of the dried parts is prevented.

I command, therefore, that our fire be gentle in the beginning, until the water is congealed into a stone and the whole thing settles at the bottom; for within the space of forty days, all the water will be turned into earth. Therefore, when you see the water congealing itself, then be certain that the science is true; for the body congeals its own moisture into a dry state, just as the **lamb's rennet** <note>original: *coagulum agni*; the enzyme from a lamb's stomach used to curdle milk.</note> congeals milk into cheese. 

Therefore, cook the body with the **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; in alchemy, this refers to a potent solvent or distilled spirit, not necessarily alcohol.</note> by congealing it gently at the fire until it becomes thick and very dry, because when it is dry, it quickly drinks the remainder of its moisture. Then apply more water, cook it gently at the fire, close the vessel diligently, and do not hurry nor cease from the work. 

The water, however, is to be divided into two parts: by one part the body is congealed, and by the other it is **putrefied** <term>putrefaction: the process of breaking down or rotting a substance to its primal state so it can be reborn or purified</term> and liquefied. To congeal is to reduce the watery substance into earth; to putrefy is to resolve the congealed parts again. For putrefaction does not happen except from the moist and the dry; in this way, the spirit will penetrate into the body, and the mixing will occur at the most minute level. 

Let the fire administered from below be tempered, and take care also that it is not removed from its vessel too hastily; for it might perhaps die, since the exit will never be open to the infant until it breathes out the airy vapors. Therefore, keep it continually closed, surrounded by dew, taking every precaution so that its **flower** <note>original: *flos*; the most subtle or volatile part of the substance.</note> does not escape as smoke. Grind it, cook it, repeat it; and do not let it weary you to repeat this same thing many times. Nevertheless, rule everything in the work by weight and measure, so that as often as the body is soaked, it is just as often dried out. 

Yet do not eat hastily, nor eat what you do not drink, nor drink what you do not eat; let the drink come after the eating, not the eating after the drink. Otherwise, you will make the "belly" moist, and it will not receive dryness. Eat, therefore, and drink one after another according to reason—I say one is three—and so proceed up to the **twelve faces of the Moon** <note>original: *duodecim facies Lunae*; likely referring to twelve cycles or stages of the process, corresponding to the zodiac or lunar months.</note>. This number runs from the multiplication of three into four, which makes twelve, and...

# THE ABRIDGED ROSARY #

The **ternary** <note>original: *ternarius*; a group or set of three.</note> number is made from one into three, and there are three **segments** <note>original: *falfaturæ*; likely referring to geometric divisions or "folds" of the material's proportions.</note>, each of which is divided into another three segments, and there will be twelve. Turn therefore the **square into a circle** <note>original: *quadrangulum in rotundum*; a classic alchemical metaphor for finding the perfect balance and unity between the four elements and the infinite spirit.</note> and you shall have the **Masterwork** <note>original: *magisterium*; the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note>: and this indeed is done if the square has three equal angles in each of its arms. Make a circle, and in the middle of the circle a center, then in each arm of the circle make three angles from the center of the circle; let there be an equal line from the first center to the other points, and let it be equal, and let one be the measure of all the ternaries. Count the ternaries and you will find twelve, over which you should draw your compass, and you will find that it touches each ternary. Therefore, through twelve triangles, a round circle will emerge; thus the Masterwork is composed, because in this way all the arms converge at the center of the compass.

In this way, the whole **water** <note>the liquid solvent or "mercury" of the work.</note> is to be reduced to its own **body** <note>the solid matter.</note> through its ternaries; for if it is diminished by one, its power will be lessened. **Hunt** <note>original: *Venare*; the alchemist is often depicted as a hunter seeking the elusive spirit of the matter.</note> therefore the souls, since their dwelling is in the earth; if they cannot flee, do not be anything but slow in your hunting, taking care lest they turn into smoke through too much fire. If they flee, they will not be caught with a **falcon** <note>a metaphor for swift, violent methods of distillation.</note>; but if they are enclosed and do not flee, then they return to the body from which they went out, because the body attracts its own moisture to itself just as a magnet attracts iron.

Grind the earth, therefore, boil the water, and repeat the operation until one of the three ternaries is turned downward; for if you have killed one of the three, all are dead, because if one is fleeing and the other is enduring the fire, both joined together will endure the fire. Note here what it is that **fixes** <note>original: *figit*; "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> the spirit. I say that one then contains the rest because of the closeness of its nature, and this indeed is our **coagulation** <note>original: *coagulatio*; the thickening or solidifying of the liquid matter.</note>, which keeps every volatile thing from fleeing. Nevertheless, this is not achieved by human hands, but nature works toward it in a circular fashion, because nature dissolves and coagulates itself, whitens and adorns itself with redness, makes itself yellow and black, weds itself and conceives from itself, until it brings about the end of the work.

Therefore it is clear that this preparation is not a manual operation, but a change of natures, and a marvelous connection of their heat with cold, and of moisture with dryness. Take therefore the **submerged flying volatile** <note>original: *volatile volans submersum*; the gaseous spirit trapped within the liquid matter.</note> and tame it so that it answers you, not by flying into far regions, but by a flight that stays within you; **for that which is below is as that which is above, and that which is above is as that which is below** <note>original: *quod est inferius est sicut superius...*; the most famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, expressing the correspondence between the macrocosm and microcosm.</note>. Therefore, our **blessed water** <note>original: *aqua nostra benedicta*; the purified alchemical solvent.</note> comes to water its own earth, to cleanse the blackness, and every...

...is transferred into many colors by the operation of nature. Note the union of spirit and soul with the body, through which the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>lapis: the legendary goal of alchemy, a substance said to be capable of transmuting base metals and restoring health</term> is fixed. 

The spirit and soul, therefore, are not united with the body except in the **white color** <term>albedo: the second major stage of the alchemical work, representing purification and the "whitening" of the material</term>, because as long as the dark blackness appears, the **female** <note>original: *femina*; in alchemical theory, this usually represents the moist, receptive, or volatile principle</note> dominates. Indeed, she is the first power of our Stone, since unless the matter has been black, it will not become white nor red; for the red is composed of black and white. Nevertheless, a temperate heat acting upon the moisture produces **blackness** <term>nigredo: the initial stage of the work, involving the symbolic death or "putrefaction" of the substance</term>; let it dry the moisture and remove corruption. Conversely, an intensifying heat produces redness, puts moisture to flight, and generates and causes corruption <note>In this context, "corruption" refers to the dissolution of the previous state to allow a new form to emerge</note>. For this reason, it is clear that if the composition is governed more than is proper, it is immediately extinguished, and that which is sought will not be made from it. 

One must take care, therefore, lest the water be turned to flight by too much fire and flee; for this reason, let there be a battle of water and fire through the length of the cooking. For just as water is dried by the heat of the Sun, so by the gentle boiling of the fire, the water—coagulated into earth—holds itself against the assault of the fire. Let the water, therefore, overcome the battle of the fire through the long duration of cooking, thickening, and coagulating itself. If you perfectly knew its nature, you would surely endure the length of the cooking until you found your purpose, since the goodness of this venerable nature is proven most especially in the "bodies," because for no reason of destruction does it allow itself to be divided into the parts of its composition; for it either recedes from the fire with its whole substance, or remains standing in the fire with its whole substance. Therefore, the cause of perfection is necessarily noted in it.

Here, note the governance of the congealing of **Mercury** <term>Mercurius: the fluid, volatile principle of the work</term> with the **Sun** <term>Sol: representing the fixed, masculine principle or gold</term>, because it is said that it is clean water and a true **tincture** <term>tinctura: a potent substance used to imbue other materials with its specific qualities or colors</term> when it is patiently governed by ascending and descending until it is coagulated into white. Patiently govern this nature, then, by gently coagulating the **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: the "living" or metallic spirit of the matter</term> which rains down upon it from our **copper** <note>original: *æs*; this term rarely refers to literal metallic copper in these texts, but rather to the 'body' or base matter of the Great Work</note>. Bitter clouds ascend, and rains fall upon the earth, because every heavy and dense body always slides toward its own center. 

Truly, the quicksilver sublimated from our copper, from which all things are made, is clean water and a true tincture that wipes away the "shadow" of the copper. It is likewise the **white sulfur** <term>sulphur album: the purified, active principle reached during the albedo stage</term> which alone whitens the copper and by which the spirit is contained so it does not flee. Yet that sulfur could not whiten unless it had been whitened in the prior work, for the reason that only sulfur whitens copper; therefore it is clear that the beauty of the copper will be as great as the whiteness of the sulfur. Therefore, if you wish to arrive at the true tincture, gradually impose upon it the moisture which it cast out through constant cooking.

-># FIFTH TREATISE<-

<page-num>768</page-num>

<meta>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of moisture and heat.</meta>

...until it puts on a more beautiful color, and as often as it is soaked, let it be dried in turns, until it is turned into the white that is sought; for when the "waxed" material <note>original: *inceratum*; a stage where the matter is softened to the consistency of wax</note> is dried, it contains itself, and if one part is fixed <term>fixed: a substance that has been made resistant to fire so that it no longer evaporates</term>, the rest is also fixed. If it is white on the outside, it is also white on the inside: therefore, do not cease to soak it, cook it, and gradually dry it, until it is soaked with all of its own moisture. 

Prepare it with **permanent water** <term>aqua permanens: a symbolic alchemical solvent that does not wet the hands; the "spirit" of the substance</term>, and cook it with a gentle fire until the blackness perishes and recedes. Soak it continually with the **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitae*; here referring to the purified alchemical distillate</note> as much as you see is sufficient to the eye; roast and cook it until it drinks all the moisture. Know that the purple color is not dyed except by the cold, nor does it become white except by the dry, nor red except by the hot. 

Therefore, cook this **copper** <note>original: *æs*; in alchemy, this rarely refers to the literal metal, but rather the "base" matter or the "body" of the Work</note> by roasting it with its remaining moisture until it makes itself germinate; then, drying it in the Sun, grind it until it is totally turned downward <note>likely meaning "ground into a fine powder"</note>. Venerate the **king and his wife** <term>rex & uxor: symbolic representation of the dual principles—often sulfur and mercury, or the fixed and the volatile—whose "marriage" creates the Stone</term>, and do not burn them, lest they flee by too much heat, since you need patience and long-suffering, which refine the king and his wife in their governance. Cook them until they become black, then white, afterward red, and then it becomes a **poison** <note>original: *venenum*; in alchemical Latin, this often means a transformative "tincture" or "elixir" that "attacks" and changes the nature of a metal</note> dyeing into gold. 

For our copper, first, the more it is cooked, the more it is dissolved, and it becomes a more spiritual water; second, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened, and it becomes a powder of a whiter color; third, the more it is cooked, the more it is colored, and it becomes a **tincture** <term>tincture: a concentrated substance used to "stain" or transform the properties of another material</term> of greater redness. And this whole operation is nothing but the extraction of water from the earth, and the returning of that same water upon the earth. 

Therefore, when all the water is exhausted and contained in the earth, leave it to putrefy for certain days—that is, for sixty—in its vessel over a gentle fire, until the most precious white color appears upon it. Let the heat, however, be gentle until the whiteness is reached, because if intense heat creeps in, it produces a black vapor and the white escapes the composition. For that vapor is white; therefore, if it is fixed with the copper, it whitens it inside and out; but if it flees from it, it turns into a red that is of no use. 

And certainly in the stage of **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the symbolic "death" or decomposition of the matter, necessary before it can be reborn in a purified state</term> the spirits are dried within it, since unless they are dried with the copper, the colors of the soul will not appear. For putrefaction is nothing but the **mortification** <note>original: *mortificatio*; the killing or stilling of the volatile properties</note> of the moist with the dry; for when the moisture is coagulated by the dryness, then only does the cold putrefy the moisture. But our putrefaction does not happen without the moist and the dry, because the moisture is only contained by the dryness. Although the cold moisture naturally flees the fire, it is nevertheless retained by the body so that it cannot flee, since heavy things cannot be raised higher except by the company of light things, nor can light things be thrust down except by the company of heavy things...

...below, and both are the beginning and the end of the work. Therefore, let there be diligent management, let unrestrained expectation be absent, let the explanation of all things return, and thus your desire will come to pass. Guide the operation continually, cook without intermission; do not hasten, nor cease from the work, because unless the moisture and heat of the womb were continuous, the seed would not remain nor would the fetus be completed; for if the mother dies, the fetus also dies due to the encroaching cold. 

Therefore, God established that blood and heat of the womb for nourishing the fetus until the time of birth; so you must guide the work with continuous heat until the whiteness <note>original: *albedo*</note>, for only in the white color are the spirits united with the body so that they cannot flee; wherefore it then begins to live, nor do foreign winds <note>original: *flatus*; likely referring to outside air or impurities</note> harm it, lest it might proceed more poorly toward the redness <note>original: *rubedo*</note>. Note here most inwardly concerning nourishment by a very gentle fire, regarding which let the heat of the fire be like that of eggs under the belly of hens. 

Therefore, a bath of intense heat causes the work to perish, while the cold puts it to flight, but a tempered heat cherishes and preserves it; for that reason, it is necessary to guide it gently, as for the hatching of eggs, until the whole has become white. Wherefore it is commanded to **whiten the laton** <term>laton: or "latten," a term for an impure, brass-like base metal that the alchemist seeks to purify into "white" silver</term> and to **break the books** <note>original: *rumpere libros*; an alchemical idiom suggesting that one should stop following literal texts and look to the actual transformation of the matter, or that the physical structure of the matter must be broken down</note> lest hearts be broken; for the earth putrefies and is cleansed with water, and when it has been dried, the blackness recedes and it is whitened. 

Then the dark dominion of the woman shall perish, and then the man, ascending over the woman, himself takes away the kingdom; then the smoke shall penetrate into the body, and the spirit shall be constrained in the dry; then the corrupting, deforming blackness shall cease, and it shall become white, shining, and clear; because heat acting on the moist generates blackness first, thus acting on the dry it generates whiteness, and in the white, yellowness <note>original: *citrinitas*; the transitional stage between the white and red work</note>. Let an example be in kindled wood when they make it into charcoal; so also with the substance of our Stone: first, the more it is cooked, the more it is dissolved and blackened; second, the more it is dried, the more it is whitened; third, the more it is cooked, the more it is reddened until it is perfected. 

Therefore, the thing whose head is red, feet are white, and eyes are truly black, is the **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the finished alchemical Stone or the perfected process</note>. Now, that it is necessary for the work to be blackened first is proved by this: that the generation of one thing does not occur except through the corruption of another, and corruption does not occur except through putrefaction and heat acting on the moist; and heat acting on the moist produces blackness, wherefore it is clear that the beginning of our work is the **crow’s head** <term>caput corvi: a symbol for the black stage (nigredo), representing the death of the base material before its rebirth</term>. It is likewise necessary for it to be putrefied, because nothing was ever born, nor growing, nor animated, unless it first passed into putrefaction. For if it has not been putrefied, it cannot [be melted...]

### FIFTH TREATISE

<page-num>770</page-num>

...it will be able to, nor will it be dissolved; but if it has not been dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing. It is clear, therefore, that **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the chemical process of decomposition, viewed by alchemists as a necessary stage of death before a substance can be reborn in a purified state</term> is necessary for us for every generation. Our putrefaction, however, is not filthy nor unclean, but is a commingling of earth with water, and of water with earth, through the smallest particles until the whole becomes one body. Cook, therefore, the **male and wife** <note>These terms usually refer to the chemical principles of Sulfur and Mercury, or the fixed and volatile components of the work</note> together until both are coagulated into a dry state; for unless it is dry, the diverse colors will hardly appear, because it will always be black as long as moisture dominates.

Therefore, closing the mouth of the vessel diligently, cook it at the fire until the whole is turned downward; then let it be the **dragon eating its own wings** <note>original: *draco alas suas comedens*; a famous alchemical symbol representing a substance that stabilizes itself by consuming its own volatile parts</note>, and then it emits various colors. Indeed, in many ways and at different turns, it will be moved from color to color until it reaches a firm **whiteness** <note>original: *albedo*; the second major stage of the Great Work, associated with silver or lunar energy</note>. For all the colors of the world will appear when the blackening moisture has been dried up; but do not care about those colors, for they are not true colors, for it often turns yellow <note>original: *citrinescit*</note> and red, and often dries and melts before the true whiteness. The spirit, however, is not **fixed** <term>fixed: a state where a substance becomes stable and no longer evaporates or changes when subjected to heat</term> with the body except in the white color; wherefore it is clear that the whitening <note>original: *dealbatio*</note> is always to be expected, since it is the completion of the whole work, nor does it change afterward into a true color except into the **red** <note>original: *rubeum* or *rubedo*; the final stage of the work, associated with gold or solar energy</note>.

In every degree, therefore, observe how the water coagulates itself, and how the composite is changed from color to color; for if it is guided ignorantly, none of its colors will be seen, and thus you will very often weep over your labor, because you will be unable to know at which degree the fire must be moderated—which cannot be known except through the colors appearing in the work. The colors, therefore, will teach you what to do with the fire; for they show for how long and in what manner the **first, second, and third fire** <note>Alchemists used different grades of heat, often categorized by the intensity of the source, such as a lamp, a sand bath, or a direct flame</note> is to be made; hence, if you are diligent, the colors will teach you what ought to be done.

Note, therefore, well concerning the fire and its proportions in its degrees: because the fire in solution and coagulation will always be gentle, in **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material</term> it will be moderate, and in the reddening <note>original: *rubificatione*</note> it will be strong. But the more the colors change, the more the gentle fire is to be continued until it reaches the goal of whiteness; for we do not apply much fire to the white, because it is cold, raw, and half-cooked. Let there be, therefore, a gentle fire in the whitening, so that the vapor may be fixed with its body; otherwise, if you intensify the fire, it becomes red before the proper time, which is not useful, because the red is composed of much white and a very small amount of black with great heat. If, therefore, you have well-measured the fire and the operation...

# THE ABBREVIATED ROSARY
<note>original: *Rosarium Abbreviatum*; this is likely a shortened version of the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, one of the most famous illustrated alchemical treatises of the late Middle Ages.</note>

### [ABBREVIATED ROSARY]

<page-num>771</page-num>

...you have sparingly governed [the heat], first reaching a white color; and when it has become white, you shall then light a stronger fire. Apply to it, both below and above, a dry heat for a period of several days until the whole is fixed below, and no exaltation of the spirit ascends upward. This is the sign of **perfect fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term>; then the fugitive shall not fly away from that which does not flee, even though the fire be scorching. This is because **magnesia** <term>magnesia: a term used by alchemists to refer to the "materia prima" or the foundational mineral substance of the Stone, rather than modern magnesium</term>, when it is whitened, does not allow the spirit to flee, nor does it allow the "shadow of copper" to appear—which does not burn. For this is the **white fixing sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur fixura album*; sulfur was viewed as the "active" or "combustible" principle that gives color and form to metals</note> which tints every body and perfects it, converting it into true silver.

Wherefore, if it were pure **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury (argentum vivum)</term>, the power of this white sulfur will coagulate it into silver; and this is the best thing that those practicing alchemy can receive, so that it may convert the matter into silver, because then nature contains nature, and they are joined to one another in a **true marriage** <note>Alchemists often used the metaphor of a wedding (the Chemical Wedding) to describe the union of opposing elements like Mercury and Sulfur</note>.

Truly, there is nothing but a single nature, which in each step of its operations is turned into another nature, because **nature rejoices in nature, nature overcomes nature, and nature contains nature** <note>These three axioms are among the oldest in alchemical literature, often attributed to the Hellenistic alchemist Pseudo-Democritus</note>. It teaches the substance itself to fight against the fire; nor are they then diverse as they were before, but truly there is only one nature, having within itself all the natures and things by which it suffices for itself. Therefore, the work is begun and finished in one single order.

There is, however, a twofold manner of composition: for one is **humid** <note>moist/liquid</note> and the other is **dry**. When they are cooked, however, they become one, and one does not leave the other—and rightly so, because the humid easily receives an impression and easily loses it, while the dry receives an impression with difficulty and loses it with difficulty. Therefore, when the humid and the dry have tempered one another, the dry acquires from the humid the ability to receive an impression easily, and the humid acquires from the dry the ability to firmly retain every impression while enduring the fire. Thus, on account of the humid, the dry is prevented from its separation, and on account of the dry, the humid is prevented from its fluidity.

An example of this is the work of a **potter**, who, binding the earth with water, cooks it in the fire so that one does not leave the other. Do the same with our **mastery** <term>mastery: (magisterium) the completed alchemical process or the Stone itself</term>, disposing the earthy substance through humidity and heat until they agree and are joined, and they do not disagree nor are they divided.

Note, therefore, the two operative virtues of water and fire in which the work is completed. Then, join to them the two operative virtues, namely water and fire, and the mastery will be finished; because if you permit the water alone, it will whiten, and if you add the fire, it will turn red. Note also well that the **white work** <note>original: *opus album*; the stage resulting in the creation of Silver</note> is completed in three wheels [or cycles] in...

<note>original: *Tractatus Quintus*</note>

...in which there is no fire; but the red is indeed completed in four, in which the fire can least be delayed. Therefore the white is completed in three cycles <note>original: *rotis* (wheels); these likely refer to the rotations or circulations of the matter in the vessel</note> in which there is no fire, but the red is rotated in four cycles. And this is indeed the **elixir** which tints with its **tincture**, is joined to its **oil**, and is fixed by its **lime** <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a substance has been heated or "calcined"</term>. The oil is indeed the joining and aggregating agent between the lime and the water; yet the water is the carrier that brings the tincture upon the lime, and when the lime is fixed, the water is fixed with it because of the intensity of the mixing. 

The **soul** <term>anima</term> is the bond of the **spirit**, just as the **body** is the bond of the soul. Nor is this bond like a bond of nature, but rather like a composite; for the composition of nature happens through the entry of opposites, but our composition happens through the **fixation** of the composites. And then the body is the cause for retaining the water, and the water for the oil (which is not burned by fire), and the oil is the cause for holding the tincture, and the tincture is the cause for making the color appear, and the color is the cause for demonstrating the whiteness, and the whiteness is the cause for retaining every volatile thing from flight. 

For when the body has been whitened, it does not permit the spirit to flee, nor the blackness to appear any further. He, therefore, who does not liquefy and coagulate errs in many ways; wherefore, blacken the earth by separating its soul, and afterward make the water return upon the earth, whitening the whole, and you hold the **mastery** <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process</term>. For he who blackens the earth, and dissolves and coagulates the white with fire until it is in color like a **bared sword** <note>This "bared sword" description refers to a brilliant, shimmering metallic white or silver luster</note>, shall be delivered from the darkness. And he who, once the whitening is complete, brings in the soul and—after the whole has been liquefied—fixes it in a rapid fire, will deserve to be called happy and to be exalted above the circles of the world.

You have now learned, dearest friend, how to perform the **white work**; now, therefore, you must know how to perform the **red**. However, unless you have first performed the whitening, you will be unable to make the true red, because no one can arrive from the first stage to the third unless he has first been in the second. Thus, you cannot arrive from black to yellow <note>original: *citrinum* (citrine); the stage of citrinitas often preceded the final red</note> except by way of the white, because yellow is composed of much white and very little black. 

For just as the year is divided into four parts, so also is our blessed work: 
*   The first is **winter**, a moist and cold time. 
*   The second is **spring**, dry and flowery. 
*   The third is **summer**, a hot time. 
*   The fourth is **autumn**, the time of fruits. 

Govern the tinting natures with this arrangement until the natures bring forth fruit at your will. Truly, the winter has now passed, the rain has gone, the night has retreated, and the day has approached; for flowers have appeared in our earth in the time of spring. But standing upon the **white rose**, we seek the **Sun** <note>The "white rose" represents the White Stone (silver-making), while the "Sun" represents the Red Stone or gold-making stage</note>, because it alone attains the full effect...

<note>original: *ROSARII ABBREVIATI*</note>

...every sick body into true silver. When, therefore, you see that whiteness appearing and surpassing all else, be certain that the redness is hidden within that whiteness. At that point, you must not extract the whiteness, but rather cook it until it becomes red. And certainly, the redder it is, the more it is worth; and the more it is cooked, the redder it becomes. Therefore, that which is cooked more is more valuable, and thus consequently, that which is cooked most is of the highest value. 

Indeed, the red color is caused solely by the completion of digestion. For blood is not generated in a man unless it is first diligently cooked in the liver. Similarly, in the morning when we see our urine is white, knowing we have slept little, we return to bed; once sleep is taken, digestion is completed, and our urine turns yellow. Thus, through cooking alone, you will arrive at the redness after the whiteness. You cannot go wrong if you maintain a dry fire over it. 

Do you not see that seed is not generated from blood unless it is first diligently cooked in the liver until it possesses an intense redness? If it were not so, nothing would be generated from that seed. Likewise, our **copper** <term>aes: here referring to the alchemical base material, not common copper</term> is not turned red unless it is diligently cooked. Truly, only the heat of the liver turns the liver's **chyle** <term>chylus: the milky fluid produced during digestion</term> red, and only the heat of a kindled fire turns the white **sulfur** <term>sulphur: one of the two primary alchemical principles, representing the active, masculine, and combustible element</term> red. For the first digestion of the stomach whitens everything, but the second digestion of the liver turns everything red, because heat flourishes in the liver alone, just as dryness flourishes in the stomach. 

Therefore, with dry fire and dry **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to purify it or reduce it to a powder</term>, cook the dry matter until it becomes like **cinnabar** <note>original: *cinabrium*</note>, that is, purple. From then on, you must not add water or any other thing until the red is completely cooked. For in the season of summer and fruits, a flood of rain corrupts the **mastery** <term>magisterium: the alchemical process or the Great Work itself</term>; thus, you must burn it with dry fire without fear until it is clothed in a most brilliant red color. 

Do not cease, even if the redness is somewhat slow to appear. For with the fire increased after the whiteness (the first of the colors), you will obtain the redness. However, in the time between those colors, yellow will appear, but that color is not stable, because after it, the red does not delay in coming. When that arrives, be certain that your work is complete, for then it will have the power to turn the female into the male, and everything incomplete into the true **Sun** <term>Sol: the alchemical name for gold</term>. 

Therefore the philosopher says: "If there be a pure, excellent sulfur with a bright redness, containing within itself the power of a simple and non-burning fire, that is the best thing that [human bodies] can receive..."

# FIFTH TREATISE
<note>original: *TRACTATVS QVINTVS*</note>

<page-num>774</page-num>

...those practicing alchemy, so that they might make gold with it. For this **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" of all metals</term> converts every imperfect body into gold; whereby it is clearly manifest that this alone is our true white and red **sulphur** <note>In alchemy, Sulphur and Mercury are the two primary principles; "white sulphur" creates silver, while "red sulphur" creates gold</note> for which we search, with which we tint any body into the truest silver, better than that produced from a mine. 

When, therefore, you have led each species from the parts of the work, just as we have shown you how to direct them, then bring back the spirits to it and sublimate the whole, for it will be sublimated as something bright, clear, and unable to be mixed with the elements. And that indeed is so that you may take the purest part of that known **Stone**, and through a subtle method of ingenuity join it by the smallest parts so that the whole is raised. If this does not happen, let a quantity of the non-fixed part be added to it, so that the sum of the volatile overcomes the sum of the fixed, until it suffices for its elevation. 

For we have seen in those modes of experience which we have used, that things which are mixed with water and stirred vehemently—if the sum of the volatile defeats the sum of the fixed—the fixed will fly with it. Therefore, when it has been elevated, its sublimation shall be returned, until through this reiteration of sublimation the whole is **fixed** <term>fixetur: the process of making a volatile substance solid and resistant to heat</term>. 

When therefore the fixed has been joined with the non-fixed, repeat sparingly, quantity after quantity; imbibe it through the ingenuity known to you until the whole is raised again. Then the whole is fixed again until it provides an easy fusion, **melting like wax**. This indeed is the standing, dyeing, penetrating, consolidating, and persevering medicine, of which one part converts a thousand parts of any body into the truest gold or silver, according to whether the white or red **elixir** was prepared. 

However, the quality of this **multiplication** <note>the process of increasing the power and quantity of the Alchemical Stone</note> depends on nothing except the multiplied reiteration of the sublimation and fixation of this medicine. For the more times the order of this completion is repeated, the more its abundance is multiplied, and the quality of its perfection is greatly increased, until it changes every body diminished from perfection—and even quicksilver—into infinity. This is true **Gold-making** or **Silver-making** <note>original: *Solificium vel Lunificium*</note>. 

For as often as you have sublimated the perfected medicine in the usual manner and dissolved it, so often you will gain each time. One part is to be projected over ten; and if at first they fell over a thousand, the second time it will fall over ten thousand, the third over a hundred thousand, the fourth over a million, and the fifth over infinity. Therefore, the more the elixir is refined, the more it tints; therefore, in as much as you have elevated [it]...

-> # ABBREVIATED ROSARY <-

...your work, it will be worth so much more, because it will work more abundantly and convert a greater quantity of metal; and this is certainly what **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the legendary father of Arabic alchemy, whose Latinized works were foundational to European alchemy</note> said, who was the master of masters in our mastery: "Work with your stone and I will work with mine, and my stone will be worth more than yours; for if you project one part over a thousand, I will project one over ten thousand, and it will all be good. But if you project one over ten thousand, I will project one over ten million, wherefore my stone will be worth more than yours, because in the transmutation of many thousands it transcends your stone." 

However, Geber does not say this except to mislead us, because our stone and his are one and the same; but he dissolved the whole and **sublimated** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then collecting it as a solid to purify it</term> it many times, so that one part of his work transcended ten of ours. Therefore, the more it has been sublimated, the more power of conversion it will have; thus, that which is most refined is the most potent. 

Do not, therefore, fail to refine your **elixir** <note>The final, perfected substance capable of transmuting metals</note> and make it as light as you can; and certainly the cause of its swift melting is the final refinement of its parts by fire. For whatever is led from **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> in its own nature toward **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable in heat so it no longer evaporates</term> is more refined and more easily dissolved, so that it becomes supremely potent. 

And for this reason, the completed elixir grants a very rapid melting like wax, more so than any of the metals; for it is nothing but the purest substance of quicksilver led into fixation, and fixed from a most subtle and clean matter, which took its origin from quicksilver and was created from it. And this is because, since quicksilver is volatile <note>original: *fugitivum*, meaning likely to evaporate or "flee" the fire</note>, it easily requires a **medicine** <note>Another term for the elixir or catalyst</note> which suddenly—before its flight—might adhere to it in its depths and be joined to it in its smallest parts, and thicken it by its fixation and preserve it from flight in the fire, converting the whole by its benefit in a moment into true **Gold** or true **Silver** <note>original: *Solem vel Lunam*, literally "the Sun or the Moon"</note>, according to that for which the elixir was prepared. 

If, therefore, it were not easy to melt, it would not be fused before the flight of Mercury, nor would it retain it. Note this secret well. If, however, the medicine were not of the same nature as the Mercury, it would not adhere to it in its depths, nor would it be joined through its smallest parts; for quicksilver does not receive into itself except what is of its own nature, nor will anything else fix it. And if it were not most pure, it would not convert Mercury nor other bodies into gold and silver, because nothing gives what it does not have, since nothing is found in a thing that was not in it before. -> ### FIFTH TREATISE ### <-
<note>original: *TRACTATVS QVINTVS*</note>

...our medicine must necessarily be of the most subtle and pure substance, adhering to **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento viuo*; Mercury</note> by its own nature, and of the easiest and most delicate liquefaction <note>melting</note>, like a "fixed water" against the assault of fire; for this will coagulate the quicksilver and convert it into a **Solar** <note>Gold</note> or **Lunar** <note>Silver</note> nature. Now, therefore, we have completed our medicine, which is equally tempered in heat and cold, moisture and dryness. Thus, whatever is added to it becomes of the same complexion as the medicine itself: if you add water to it, the whole will be dissolved into water; if fire, the whole will become fire. This is the reason why the medicine can be multiplied to infinity.

Therefore, it is like fire in wood, and like musk among fine spices, growing more the more it is put to use. For this reason, you must always leave a part behind, since you have been enriched by it, just as one who possesses fire is enriched by it. Take deep note, therefore, regarding the **multiplication** <term>multiplication: the process of increasing the quantity and potency of the alchemical elixir without needing to start the whole Work over</term> of the elixir.

It is multiplied either through **solution** <term>solution: dissolving a solid into a liquid state</term> or through **fermentation**. Our medicine is increased more slowly through solution, but more quickly through fermentation, because a dissolved substance does not work well unless it is first **fixed** in its own ferment. However, a dissolved medicine works much more abundantly than a fermented one because it is more subtle, although it can be multiplied infinitely through fermentation alone. This is because the ferment draws whatever is added to it into its own nature, color, and flavor in every way. For it whitens the mixture, inhibits burning, holds the **tincture** <note>the coloring principle that changes the metal's appearance</note>, does not "flee" <note>evaporate or volatilize</note>, lightens the metal bodies, and makes them enter into and join with one another. This is the end of the works, and without it, the elixir is not completed—just as dough is not fermented without leaven.

Therefore, when you have fixed the elixir by **sublimating** it, return the prepared "body" <note>the metallic base</note> upon it. Let it be mixed and liquefied through the "secret of natures" in the **philosophical vessel** <term>philosophical vessel: a specialized, airtight glass container, like an alembic or retort, used to prevent the escape of the "spirit"</term>. For when they have stood for a length of time, the stronger of them will prevail, converting the whole into a spirit like itself; and because it is powerful over the bond, it does not remain still. 

Here, note the **betrothal** <note>original: *desponsatione*; a common alchemical metaphor for the chemical union of masculine (sulfur) and feminine (mercury) principles</note> of the spirit with the body from which it was originally extracted. Join it, therefore, so that it may generate a body like itself. Do not join it with just anything else in hopes of conversion, but only with that from which it originated in the beginning. If you do this, the joined substance will become an elixir for others. The reason why it ought to be joined with its own likeness is that **sulfurs** <term>sulfurs: the active, combustible, and "soul" principle of a substance in alchemy</term> are contained by sulfurs...

<page-num>777</page-num>
<header>THE ABBREVIATED ROSARY</header>
<note>original: *ROSARII ABBREVIATI*</note>

...and moist with a similar moisture; for the spirit that converts **sulphurs** <term>sulphur: in alchemy, the active, masculine, or combustible principle of a substance</term> into a spirit similar to itself has been made so that both are volatile. These aerial spirits, climbing together into the air, love one another. The philosophers, seeing that the spirit did not flee when joined with things that are volatile, repeated this "fleeing" act with a similar body that does *not* flee <note>i.e., a "fixed" or stable substance</note>. They brought the spirit into that very substance from which it could not escape at all, because of the close agreement of their internal natures. 

Note, therefore, that this is the truth regarding the entry of the spirit into the body. Certainly, a soul enters its own body more quickly than if it were sent into another; if you strive to force it into another, you will labor in vain, because there will be no communication between darkness and light. Therefore, these spirits return to a body similar to the bodies from which they were first extracted, and thus the work is completed. If the "coloring" <note>original: *tingens*; the agent that imparts color or quality</note> and the "thing to be colored" <note>original: *tingendum*</note> are made into one single **tincture** <term>tincture: a potent alchemical liquid or soul-essence capable of transforming base metals</term>, do you not believe that this substance—which colors others and does not vanish—is the true tincture of the philosophers?

Because sulphurs provide color and do not vanish if they are joined to a similar **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento viuo*; Mercury</note> of their own kind, it is necessary to mix the sulphur with white or red quicksilver of its own species. This contains the spirits so they do not flee. For this reason, we command you to mix quicksilver with quicksilver until they become one single, clean water composed of two quicksilvers. However, in the joining of these, you must place a small amount of the "work" <note>the refined elixir</note> upon a large amount of the "body" <note>the base material</note>, so that you have the power to convert it into medicine; otherwise, the whole mass would be turned into a volatile spirit similar to itself. 

If, however, you project a small amount of the work upon much of the body—say, one part upon four of the other—it will become, after some delay of time, a powder. Its heat <note>or "color/glow"</note> will be white or red, depending on the **ferment** <term>ferment: a substance, often gold or silver, added to the elixir to "digest" it and determine its final transformative direction</term> upon which you projected it. This powder is the completed **elixir**. 

And certainly, the elixir ought to be a simple powder, among the best things of this world; both the body and the ferment which you mix with it must be a subtle, fine powder. Note here that when he says "one part of the work over four of the body," the work should be dissolved by itself before they are joined. You should not attempt a total mixture of them until each has been separately dissolved into "water" <note>a liquid state</note>. This is because he who dries a substance before he saturates it does not join them "by the smallest parts" <note>original: *per minima*; a microscopic or atomic level of union</note>, nor does he truly refine them. Indeed, it is more complete to separate a thing from earth than from water. 

Note, therefore, that when a body has been dissolved in water, it is never again separated from its water; rather, when water is mixed with water, then water receives water, and they are never separated from one another. Therefore, if you are **dropsical** <note>original: *hydropicus*; suffering from an excess of water or "thirst." A metaphor for the alchemist's greed or his struggle to balance moisture in the work</note>, drink deeply of this saying and you shall be healed.

A note on **saffron** <term>saffron: Latin *crocus*; here used as a physical analogy for the alchemical tincture’s power to spread its color through a medium</term> and on the multiplication of the **medicine** <term>medicine: the alchemical elixir or Philosopher's Stone in its potent, transformative state</term>. Every **tincture** <term>tincture: the active essence capable of "staining" or transforming the quality of a metal</term> will color a thousand times more in a liquid substance than in a dry one; this is evident with saffron when it is placed in liquids. If it were cast into dry things, it would color very little, but if it is first dissolved and joined with a small amount of liquid, then this small amount will color a great volume infinitely. This, therefore, is how you shall perform the **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of the Great Work, where the elixir is cast upon base metal to transmute it</term>: first multiply ten by ten, and there will be a hundred; and a hundred by a hundred, and there will be ten thousand; and ten thousand by ten thousand, and there will be a hundred thousand; and a thousand thousand by a thousand thousand, and there will be a number beyond counting. This is to say: place one part upon ten, and one of those upon a hundred, and one of those upon a thousand, and so on similarly with the rest.

Again, according to another philosopher: place one part upon ten parts of prepared metal, and one part of this upon a hundred, and it will be converted by a fixed and lasting conversion, if God wills. If, however, at the very first time, you were to place one part upon a thousand parts, it is to be feared that it might be consumed by excessive heat and exhale before it could penetrate and be completed. But when you place one upon ten, it penetrates and mixes quickly, so that it is not necessary to strengthen the fire nor to continue it, but it ought to be taken off the heat quickly. When it has cooled, it already holds itself together with that substance and adheres to it because of the "agreement of nature" <note>the alchemical principle that substances of similar spiritual or elemental makeup naturally bond</note>. Therefore, if you then cast one part of this upon a hundred, the substance of the **stone** is retained by that with which it was mixed, adhering to it until it has transmuted the whole.

Therefore, mix prepared **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury; here described not as the primary matter, but as a stabilizing agent</term> with the "oils" <note>likely referring to the liquid alchemical essences</note>—not because it is the primary matter of all metals, as some affirm and many believe, but because through its coldness it holds the medicine upon the fire until it is mixed, so that it does not exhale. Guard this, therefore, and you shall be fortunate upon the earth.

The cause of all these things is threefold: goodness, necessity, and perfection. The cause of goodness is so that it may color more perfectly and abundantly, that it may bring things to a better state, and convert very many things. The cause of necessity is so that it may be better colored, better "fixed" <note>original: *figatur*; rendered stable and non-volatile</note>, and that it may generate gold or silver like unto itself. For perfection, however, the perfect number is ten, a hundred, and a thousand. Therefore, you shall perform the projection from the first to the last; for if something so small were to struggle simply against something so large, it would be overcome by it on account of its own scantiness.

Note in the following regarding the foundations of the medicine. All the foundations of our medicine must be greatly refined and "colored" <note>original: *tingenda*; imbued with the transformative power</note>, for the more they are refined, the more the **elixir** is colored,

For when the smoke feels the fire, it will penetrate the body, and the **spirit** <note>the volatile or gaseous part of the substance</note> will be constrained in the dry matter; it will become one fixed, clear body, white or red, according to what the medicine and **ferment** <term>ferment: a substance, often pure gold or silver, added to the alchemical medicine to "tilt" its final transformation toward that specific metal</term> were. Then, remove it from the fire, allowing it to cool, because a single weight of it cast upon a thousand parts of any imperfect body has the power to convert it into the finest gold or silver, according to the **elixir** that was projected. Truly, the white medicine requires a white ferment, just as the red requires a red one, because in the red work nothing shall enter except the red, just as in the white work nothing shall enter except the white. Therefore, what you do in the white, do also in the red, because the operation for both is one and the same; but that which completes the tinctures and spirits is their ferment. 

From this it is clear that he who does not join white **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>, which endures the fire, to pure silver (that is, silver in its unadulterated state), has chosen no path to whiteness; and he who does not join red quicksilver, which sustains the fire, to pure gold, has chosen no path to redness. Therefore, let him not tire his body in those things which he cannot reach, because it will profit neither himself, nor another, nor the world, until the greater part in the high mobility of nature shall rest in the incorruptible, as if it were not subject to decay. 

Now we subjoin a recapitulation of the entire work. Because too much talk overwhelms the mind’s understanding and increases errors, we shall relate the whole completion of this work with brevity of speech. It is this: let a sufficiently known **stone** be taken, and with the persistence of the work, let the perfection of **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance to a vapor and then solidifying it again to achieve extreme purity</term> be applied to it repeatedly, so that by this it may be cleansed inwardly. Let the stone be refined until it reaches the ultimate purity of subtlety and finally becomes volatile; and this indeed is the first step of the administration. From this point, let it be fixed by the methods of **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term> until it rests calmly in the harshness of the fire. Thus, the **Work of the Moon** <note>The alchemical process for creating silver</note> becomes exceedingly white, and the **Work of the Sun** <note>The alchemical process for creating gold</note> becomes exceedingly red; for the white is the work of winter, and the red is the work of summer; therefore, for the greater par—

<header>TREATISE THE SIXTH</header>

...it requires sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the "spirits" of the matter</term> of the spirits <note>The partial word "tium" likely completes *spirituum* (of spirits) or *corporum* (of bodies) from the previous page</note>, through its own specific methods, digested in a greater boiling <term>decoction: a prolonged heating or boiling process to extract or refine the essence of the materials</term>, until it assumes a deep red color. In this alone consists the goal of the second degree of perfection. 

But in the third degree is the completion of the whole work: it is when you make the now-fixed Stone volatile <term>volatile: a substance that easily evaporates or "flees" the fire; here, it refers to making the solid Stone capable of being dissolved or transformed again</term> through the methods of sublimation, and then make the volatile fixed, and the fixed dissolved, and the dissolved fixed once more, until it flows and transforms in the certain goal of being gold-making <note>original: *Solifico*</note> or silver-making <note>original: *Lunifico*</note>. From the repetition of this preparation in the third degree, there results a multiplication of the transformation and of its goodness in the medicine, so that it may convert every one of the imperfect bodies into infinite, true Gold or Silver. 

Furthermore, it possesses an effective power to heal every infirmity above all other medicines. It gladdens the soul, increases strength, preserves youth, and renews old age. It does not permit the blood to rot, nor phlegm to dominate, nor yellow bile <note>original: *cholera*</note> to be scorched, nor black bile <note>original: *melancholia*</note> to be exalted too highly. Rather, it increases the blood beyond measure, purges the vessels in the spiritual parts <note>referring to the vital organs like the heart and lungs</note>, and preserves all members of the body. Generally, it cures both hot and cold illnesses more quickly than all other medicines. For if a sickness has lasted one month, it heals it in one day; if for a year, it heals in twelve days; and if it is more ancient and of long duration, it will heal it in one month. It expels all bad humors <term>humors: in medieval medicine, the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determined health and temperament</term> and brings in good ones. It also bestows the love of those to whom it is offered, and provides security, boldness, and victory in palaces to those who carry it. In this is completed the greatest "Secret of Secrets" of nature, which is precious beyond everything else in this world.

...mercury <note>The text begins with the end of the word *Mercurium*</note> into pure Gold <note>original: *Solem*, literally "the Sun," the alchemical name for gold</note>, and all metals. Know that when the soul is joined to the body, the body is quickly consumed and changed into a form other than it was before, because in the first sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance into vapor and then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</term> the body will be black, in the second more clear, in the third more so, and thus up to fifteen times, by dissolving and congealing. In every congealing, take care that the body does not taste anything of the salt, and then wash it again and again. 

If our Stone is whitened, it whitens; if it is tinted, it tints; it possesses spirit and soul, and it even turns itself red, and kills itself and brings itself back to life. There is no thing more wondrous in this world, which is why the philosophers honored it; and when it is whitened, it whitens all bodies and leads them to a proper balance <note>original: *temperamentum*</note>, and spirit retains spirit. Know this: that our Stone is from a living thing <note>original: *re animata*</note>, for it hardens soft things and softens all hard things; it melts crystal and similarly colors it, and reduces all bodies first into Silver <note>original: *Lunam*, literally "the Moon"</note>, and afterward into Gold. 

Know that salt can be made from every thing, and afterward Mercury is made from that salt through various operations. Dissolve and congeal, and make every species with its own species, and every genus with its own genus, and you shall rejoice, for nature delights in its own nature. 

Know that oil distilled seven times returns Mercury into pure Silver, which happens thus: place the Mercury in a glazed vessel over the fire so that it becomes well-heated, and afterward add some of your powder and it will be melted. Know also that the Stone, dissolved three times and coagulated again, rectifies arsenic, sulfur, and mercury. Know that when sulfur is dissolved three times, it dissolves all things and whatever it wishes in one hour; and know that many secrets are in "living sulfur" <term>living sulfur: *sulphur vivum*, or native sulfur, believed to be a primary active principle in alchemy</term>. 

Note that you should give the same weight to its soul and its body during the dissolution and coagulation, until it is fixed and becomes a powder and does not smoke; and this is the best proof of all: when the body does not smoke, you may hold that as a certainty. Know that the Greeks greatly praised the "work of the four spirits" and said it was the truest elixir <term>elixir: a substance capable of changing base metals into gold or curing all diseases</term>, one part by weight over a hundred. Know that each element must be preserved by itself in the governance of the Stone—namely water, oil, fire, and earth—and when all these are joined together at once, there results from it a certain balanced thing which performs various operations in imperfect bodies, and similarly in the human body, of which there is no doubt.

# SEVENTH TREATISE,
# SHORT BUT WEIGHTY
### ON THE
# PHILOSOPHER’S STONE.

"I rolled back the stone, and I sat upon it." <note>original: *Reuolui lapidem, & ſedebam ſuper ipſum*. This is a biblical allusion to the angel at Christ's tomb (Matthew 28:2), used here to metaphorically describe the "resurrection" or discovery of the Stone's secret.</note> Let him be thrust into the pit of punishment who reveals this to the powerful or to a fool; but I reveal it to the good, because I have seen many perish in their labor because they were unable to attain the knowledge of the art. In the name of the Lord, take <term>Alkabrick: an alchemical term of Arabic origin, typically referring to sulfur or a "sulfur of the philosophers"</term>, and human moisture from a healthy vein <note>likely a cryptic reference to blood</note> and mix them in equal parts; extract the water through smoke <note>original: *fumum*, referring to distillation or the collection of vapors</note>, then the air through fire, and finally burn the dregs <note>original: *fæces*</note>, calcine them <term>calcine: to reduce a substance to a powder or ash by heating it to high temperatures without melting it</term>, and mix them in equal parts with the urine of a boy and extract the salt. Then you will have all the stones about which the philosophers have experimented, for they tint <note>original: *tingunt*, referring to the power of the Stone to "color" or transform the nature of base metals into gold</note> marvelously; and they "cook" the material so thoroughly that the nature of fire can do no more. Likewise, this salt resists Mercury <note>original: *Mercurio*</note> when it is soaked and dried with the first stone, and thus a union of the fixed body is made upon a firm rock. May he not see the face of God who reveals this to the powerful or to a fool.

->(*_*)<-

->*End of the short and final Treatise.*<-

# THE MOST NOBLE AND MOST TRUE SECRET
## *Of the Venerable Man, Lord Iodocus Greverus,*
### *Priest.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral motifs.</image-desc>In honor of the holy and indivisible Trinity, and of the blessed mother Mary ever-virgin, as well as for the consolation of the pious, the relief of the poor, and the guidance of those practicing philosophy, I, Iodocus Greverus, Priest and the least of the Philosophers <note>original: *Philosophorum minimus*, a traditional expression of humility used by alchemical authors</note>, proceed to describe the most secret Stone of the ancient Philosophers—which many seek with much error, expense, labor, and even the loss of life. Despairing in nothing of Divine grace and mercy, and fortified by the help of God himself, I undertake this beautiful and perfect work; one that is true, not mutilated, nor obscured by the ambiguity of words. This art was granted to me out of His immense goodness by Him who alone has the power of giving and taking away this most secret art to whom He wills. 

So that His glory—He who bestowed such grace upon me, an unworthy sinner—might through me become known and celebrated among all posterity, specifically among those whom He has called and even chosen for the hidden mysteries of this admirable <term>Philosophy: in this context, "philosophy" refers specifically to Alchemy, often called the "Hermetic Philosophy"</term>; I shall reveal the whole matter in order and clearly. I will use plain speech that is true, yet corresponds to the reasoning and custom of the Philosophers, without any deliberate concealment. For I know well that no one can claim these things for themselves unless God Himself has granted them; He alone illuminates the darkness of these mysteries or obscures their clarity, so that no one may understand even the plainest things unless enlightened by Him, nor may anyone attain even the most obscure things if they have not been illustrated by Him. 

I adjure you, however, whoever shall possess this writing of mine, that you do not communicate it to the unworthy, or the greedy, nor to those who would apply it to the disadvantage or even the oppression of their neighbors—such as men who are tyrants, unjust, adulterers, <insert>the</insert> soft <note>original: *molles*, typically referring to those lacking moral discipline or "effeminate" in the historical sense of being devoted to luxury</note>, and those whose belly is their God <note>original: *quorum venter sibi Deus est*, a reference to Philippians 3:19, describing those driven only by physical appetites</note>. Therefore, place your hope in the Lord God, creator of all things, and work with fear of Him for the benefit of your neighbor according to my writings, expecting a blessing from the Lord in heaven. 

In the first place, know, most dearly beloved, that our art is an imitation of nature: and

Just as nature by itself produces trees and plants, which a gardener then multiplies by sowing their seeds or grafting their shoots; so nature generates metals in the depths of the earth and mountains, such as <term>Gold: referred to in the text as *Sol* (the Sun)</term> and <term>Silver: referred to as *Luna* (the Moon)</term>, which the artist multiplies by grafting or sowing them into the proper earth or a suitable trunk. Therefore, you must know above all else what the seeds of gold and silver are, which are the trunks, and what the earth is. We say, then, that the Sun and Moon contain their own seeds within themselves; and that <term>Saturn: Lead</term>, <term>Jupiter: Tin</term>, <term>Mars: Iron</term>, and <term>Venus: Copper</term> are the trunks; but the earth of all these is <term>Mercury: Quicksilver</term>. Let this be held as a stable foundation toward which you direct your entire intention, adapting the likeness of one thing to the nature and suitability of the other. Indeed, God, the author of nature, has granted us the ability to understand and perfect this part of <note>original: *huius Philosophiæ*, referring to alchemy</note> through this kind of contemplation. We communicate this in this writing to those who are worthy and chosen, so that I, and many others with me, may offer perpetual glory, praise, and due thanksgiving to God Himself.

Therefore, just as the Philosophers are accustomed to seeking similarities for the <term>Stone: The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical "Great Work"</term> by contemplating the operations of nature—drawing parallels from animals, plants, trees, eggs, offspring, and the union of male and female, and almost infinite other things of that kind—so we also, to pave a way toward a clearer understanding of this <term>Particular Work: An alchemical process intended to produce a specific result or metal, rather than the "Universal" medicine that heals all things</term>, shall follow in the footsteps of nature itself and take from her the legitimate and necessary applications. Although this work is "particular," it possesses such a degree of truth that if anyone looks deeply into the causes of things, they will realize it is very close to the Great Triumphal Stone in its certainty, truth, and power. 

Truly, what that matter is from which the principles of this work must be taken, we have already shown to the wise in the aforementioned comparison. To place it even better before your eyes, we say that just as a human is generated and comes from a human, a donkey from a donkey, a hen from a hen’s egg, and wheat from wheat, so from every like thing its like is made: from gold, indeed, gold; from silver, silver. From this, therefore, you understand what matter you ought to take and treat in this work. A man or woman languishing in illness will not procreate a human through mutual intercourse, nor likewise will a weak puppy produce a dog, nor a sprouting or rotten herb produce a herb; but rather a mature and healthy man, with a similarly mature and healthy woman, will generate human offspring; and other animals likewise within their own species; and the seeds of mature plants equally mature. Therefore we say that just as farmers diligently select the seeds of crops, herbs, and trees, and accept none but the mature, and likewise also designate the most intact shoots from trees for grafting; so you also will judge that it must be done in the business of this work. For the <term>common gold: ordinary metallic gold used in commerce, which alchemists considered "dead" or "fixed"</term> does not enter into this work, nor the common mercury, nor common silver, nor anything else common, but rather the gold, mercury, and silver of the Philosophers: the meaning of which saying is clearly evident from what was said above. 

What has been said about seeds must also be said about the earth; namely, that not all earth is suitable for producing these or those plants. This very thing even the divine <term>Maro: Vergil, the Roman poet famous for the *Georgics*, a masterpiece on the art of farming</term> warned in his *Georgics*, and we see it always observed by farmers and gardeners. Therefore, most dear friend, you must discern which earth is suitable for receiving the seeds of the <term>Sun: Gold</term> or the <term>Moon: Silver</term>, lest if you choose an unsuitable one, you miserably lose both the seeds and your labor and expense. 

Therefore, both the seeds and the earth must be chosen with great judgment: moreover, the chosen earth must be cultivated in all ways; just as the earth of fields and gardens is cultivated by plowing, or digging, manuring, harrowing, watering, and other ways of that kind. This selection and cultivation of seeds and earth is what <term>Geber: An 8th-century Arabic alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan) whose Latinized works were the foundation of Western alchemy</term> and the practitioners of this divine work call <term>Preparation: The initial stage of purifying and "awakening" the matter before the actual alchemical transformation begins</term>, without which neither the Sun of the Philosophers, nor the Moon, nor the earth can be obtained, nor is any entrance open to the inner chambers of such a great art. For common gold is mostly impure, contaminated by the mixture of other metals, sick, diseased, and for that reason even sterile; and silver similarly, whereas on the contrary the Sun and Moon of the Philosophers are most pure, defiled by the intervention of no foreign mixture, healthy, vigorous, and abounding in generative seed.
