Indeed, they select seeds, and once selected, they sow them not in common soil, but in cultivated fields or garden plots. Once sown, they finally commit them to the heat of the Sun and the kindness of the sky and earth, awaiting the proper fruit at the right time. In a certainly similar manner, the Philosophers <note>alchemists</note> also, before they begin the work, must judge the common gold and silver they have taken into their hands to see whether it be healthy or "sick." And if they find it to be sick, they should restore it to its proper health with a suitable medicine, which is the preparation itself. This gold, thus medicated, healthy, and purified, is the <term>Sun of the Philosophers: Gold that has been chemically "opened" or purified so it can react, unlike common "dead" bullion</term>; and the same must also be understood regarding the <term>Moon: Philosophical Silver</term>.

Once the Sun and Moon of the Philosophers are held as good seed, the earth itself <note>the mercurial medium</note> must be purged of all its impurities and useless weeds, and refined with diligent cultivation. Into the earth thus refined, the aforementioned seeds of the Sun and Moon must be cast, and continuously committed to the heat and the kindness of the sky and earth. They must not be pulled up by the roots before the lawful time; rather, the mature fruits must be awaited, appearing after the leaves and flowers.

From this it is now clear enough that although the Philosopher may take up common gold, silver, and <term>Mercury: Quicksilver</term>; nevertheless, he does not put them into this work before he raises them from the common soil to the <term>physical grade: the state of being "physica," meaning "natural" or "living" in an alchemical sense, as opposed to inert commercial metal</term>. Some people, indeed, wrapping these things in great obscurities, have cast no small doubts into the minds of those practicing the art. So that you may be able to dissolve all these doubts, always observe this general rule which we give: namely, that nothing enters into the "physical" work without legitimate preparation, the power of which is such that it makes common things "physical." Therefore, nothing impure, nothing sick, and nothing uncultivated enters into our work—even though we may start with the impure, the sick, and the uncultivated before the work begins.

From this, certainly, it appears what the duty of the Philosopher is, and what is the duty of Nature itself, whom the Philosopher serves. For it is the Philosopher’s part to take the material given by nature and to prepare it in the proper way; also to choose and cultivate the proper earth; and afterwards to cast the seeds into it and supply a suitable, continuous heat. It is Nature’s part, however, to rot and dissolve the seeds cast into the earth, to strike roots, to draw out the juice of the earth, and to successively produce branches, leaves, and flowers, to conceive the fruit, and to perfect and ripen it. At this boundary nature rests, and proceeds no further unless she is moved by the Philosopher, who [directs] the progress of nature not in deceptive...

opinions, but he must recognize it correctly through certain signs. Now, another point arises from this contemplation that must be weighed: the various intervals of time in which the generations of natural things are completed. For plants indeed have an annual sprouting and reaching of maturity; trees mature by the fifth or sixth year; some animals reach the maturity for generating sooner, others later. Furthermore, just as we see farmers bury seeds by harrowing and enclosing them, or binding grafted shoots to trunks with wax or clay—things which are not of the nature of the tree, but are intermediaries and aids, so that the sap of the trunk is carried nowhere else but into the inserted shoot—so also in this work a certain "wax" or "clay" <note>This refers to the "Lute of Hermes," a sealant used to make glass vessels airtight</note> must be applied, which does not permit the **sap of the earth** <note>The volatile mercurial spirit</note> to exhale elsewhere, but contains it within. This wax is usually bound with a small cloth by farmers so that it is not cast down from the trunk by the force of rains or winds before the proper joining of the inserted shoot. Thus, we have brought such a comparison to our operation from things daily appearing before our eyes; if anyone considers this diligently, he will easily be freed from many errors and will attain the desired end of our work. But lest we be too long-winded, we will now set down the **practical application** <note>original: *praxim*</note> itself in order: first, we shall speak of the instruments and materials required for this work; afterward, of the preparations; then, of the method of sowing and maturing; and finally, of the reiteration of the sowing, which is the completion of the work.

Choose, therefore, for this work gold that is "new," which has not been subjected to the many labors of the goldsmiths, but has come recently from the mine and has not experienced many fires. It should be of the best color, at 24 carats or close to it; and in this kind, the best is that which is found by its own nature "raw" in small chunks, smelted within the earth itself and as if melted together. If you can obtain such gold, you need no other preparation for this work than to beat it out into the thinnest possible sheets with a hammer; and you should consider the same to be said for silver. If, however, you cannot have such gold, take gold from Hungarian florins <note>These coins were famous for their high purity and consistent weight</note>, and purge it—or have it purged—by melting it through antimony into a <term>regulus</term> <note>The 'little king'; a button of purified metal found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note>, just as the craftsmen do who produce gold leaf; for antimony has the property of purifying gold from every superfluity. But if by chance you do not know the method of purification through antimony, you may burn it in cement for 24 hours, and afterward restore it to a body and hammer it into the thinnest sheets. But lest we hand over a flawed work to you, we shall describe the method of purifying gold through antimony, which is as follows: Take 1 ounce of gold, or as much as you wish, and five times that amount of antimony in respect to the gold; place the gold with the antimony in a crucible, and once placed among burning coals, allow it to flow for one hour or half an hour; then have a tool...

...an iron or bronze instrument shaped like a pyramid, hollowed out on the inside, which is made very smooth within and heated by the fire; grease the inside with tallow or a candle. And afterwards, taking the gold with antimony from the fire, pour it from the crucible into this <term>mold</term> <note>original: "infusorium," a vessel for pouring or casting</note>, and by lightly striking the bottom of the mold so that the gold settles separately, then allow it to cool in this way. Afterward, invert the mold and extract the pyramidal mass from it, the tip of which contains the <term>regulus</term> <note>original: "regulum"; the metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note> of gold. This time also you shall separate the regulus, if there should be any, which you will join with the first regulus separately. You may also repeat this a third time if it seems necessary, which you will know by the size of the second regulus; or leave it thus, if the regulus of the second melting was small. Keep this, therefore, aside, and proceed with the reguli in this manner:

Take a piece of an earthenware roof tile, such as are usually found on the roofs of churches and ancient towers, and make a small pit in it suitable for your reguli; place this in a dry spot and surround it with coals, putting the reguli into its pit. Then light the coals and allow the antimony to evaporate from your reguli as smoke. When the smoke ceases, cover it carefully with coals, and finally blow from above with a bellows until you see no spot nor film upon your gold, but that it becomes beautiful, like <note>The "greening" of gold in the fire is a traditional description of the "blick" or flash that occurs when the metal reaches high purity and reflects the light in a specific way</note> greening grass in the fire; and this usually happens after two or three hours. And then, having removed the gold together with the piece of tile in which it was purified, quench it in clear urine, and thus you will have perfectly cleansed gold. This is fit for our work, so that from it very thin sheets may be made by <term>hammering</term> <note>original: "malleationem"</note>, which should be kept wrapped in paper until the proper time. 

Otherwise, if you find fine gold leaf in sufficient quantity either in <term>apothecaries' shops</term> <note>original: "apothecis"</note> or at the painters', you may use that as pure gold, with no other preparation applied. ### *Preparation of Silver.*

Silver, just like gold, is better if it comes fresh from the mine, or if it has not been worked many times by craftsmen, but only <term>cupelled</term> <note>original: "capellatum"; refined in a shallow vessel to separate precious metals from base metals</note> with <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturno"; the alchemical name for lead</note> in a shard or cupel. If, however, you do not have such silver, take what you have; and if you suspect there is copper or any other impurity mixed into it, purify it in a <term>refining furnace</term> <note>original: "cineritio"; literally "in the ashes," referring to the cupellation hearth</note> with double or triple its weight of black lead, until it is cleansed of every impurity. Then you shall make from it the thinnest possible sheets, and keep them very clean in a fresh paper until their time.

### *Preparation of Quicksilver.*

You must choose <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; mercury</note> that has not been manufactured by artifice from lead or any other metal, but that which comes from its own native ore, such as from mountain cinnabar or from <term>marcasites</term> <note>original: "marcasitis"; iron pyrites or similar sulfide minerals</note>. You shall prepare such quicksilver for this work in this manner: Take one pound of it, three ounces of <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolo"; metallic sulfate salts, likely iron or copper sulfate</note>, two ounces of saltpeter, two ounces of <term>Yemeni alum</term> <note>original: "alumine iameni"; a high-quality alum traditionally sourced from Yemen</note>, three ounces of quicklime, and one pound of yellow wax. Grind the vitriol, saltpeter, alum, and quicklime in a mortar and mix them. Afterward, put the wax into a glass <term>urinal</term> <note>original: "vrinale"; a round-bottomed glass flask commonly used in alchemical distillation</note> the bottom of which has been <term>luted</term> <note>original: "lutatus"; sealed or coated with a protective paste</note> with clay mixed with horse dung and worked together. Place the flask on a furnace in a <term>sand bath</term> <note>original: "capellam arenam"; a container of sand used to distribute heat evenly</note>, and apply a fire that is slow at the start, so the glass does not break from sudden heat, until the wax melts in the glass. Meanwhile, agitate the quicksilver in a glass or glazed dish with the aforementioned ingredients, mixing them very well, having poured in a little strong wine vinegar. When the wax has been liquefied in the flask, the quicksilver mixed with the aforementioned powders should be put in gradually. Let it cook over a moderate fire in that wax for three hours, always agitating and turning it with a wooden spatula. When the three hours have passed, allow it to cool in the flask, and with a clean rod, press a hole into the wax before it hardens. In this way, keep your Mercury very well prepared for this work—namely, as a fit vessel in which
->the Sun and Moon may be sown.<-
<note>In alchemical allegory, "the Sun" refers to gold and "the Moon" refers to silver. The prepared mercury acts as the "soil" or medium for their transformation.</note>

### *Preparation of Antimony; which is the joining agent.*

Antimony, which enters into this work as the bond of the two <note>likely referring to the union of the "fixed" gold/silver and the "volatile" quicksilver</note>, you shall prepare through <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "sublimationem"; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid on a cooler surface</note> in this manner: Take one pound of it and grind it into a powder in a mortar; place this in a sublimation pot, and set an <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "aludel"; a pear-shaped vessel or pipe used to collect the vapors of sublimation</note> on top of it with a side hole. This aludel must be open on both ends—both at the wider part and the narrower part—just like the other aludels. Then, you should secure the joints with tenacious clay mixed with horse dung; in this order, join all six aludels together in a row, so that the narrower part of the lower one fits into the wider part of the one above it, with the joints firmly sealed everywhere with <term>lute</term> <note>original: "lutatis"; a specialized paste or cement used to seal alchemical apparatus against leaks</note>. The topmost aludel, however, must have a smaller hole than the others, about the thickness of a finger and no wider; this is to be plugged with dry wood that fits it perfectly. When this is done and the joints have dried, let this sublimation tower be placed in its furnace and secured with tenacious clay so that it does not wobble back and forth, leaving four holes around the circuit through which the furnace may be freed from smoky vapors.

Then, let the coals in the furnace be lit, and the fire gradually increased until the powder of antimony melts. You will know this for certain if you insert an angled iron spatula into the sublimation pot through the side hole of the lowest aludel. Therefore, when you feel the antimony powder has melted in the pot, then incessantly turn and move the antimony with that iron spatula of yours, providing a strong fire beneath, so that the bottom of the sublimation pot in the small furnace glows entirely white-hot. Thus you shall continue the fire and the constant turning of the antimony until you feel the antimony is entirely sublimated and no longer rises. You can be more certain of this if, upon opening the wooden plug of the topmost aludel, you see no smoke exhaling from that hole. At that point, gradually cease the fire and carefully wrap a damp cloth around the joint of the lowest aludel; when the joint has drawn in all the moisture, carefully remove the sealant and take away all the aludels. Collect from them the <term>white sulfur of antimony</term> <note>original: "sulphur album antimonij"; scientifically known as antimony trioxide, which appears as white crystals after sublimation</note>, which has sublimated onto their sides in the form of the whitest flour. For this sulfur is of admirable effect in this operation, because it is a friend to both <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio"; quicksilver</note>, the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Soli"; gold</note>, and the <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Lunae"; silver</note>. It is the bond of the body and the spirit, and the marriage of the spirit and the soul; it, I say, is the vehicle of the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tincture"; the transformative essence sought by alchemists</note>, and it is that wax

->*The Casting of the Seed into the Earth.*<-

Now you have, dearest craftsman, a great part of your labor completed; it remains that you entrust your seeds to the earth for <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefaciendum"; the process of decomposition that alchemists believed was necessary for a substance to be "reborn" in a higher form</note>, so that they may bring forth the desired fruit—twofold, threefold, a hundredfold, and a thousandfold. Take, therefore, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, one ounce of gold leaf <note>original: "auri foliati"</note>, or as much as you truly wish, and four times as much of your well-cultivated earth, which is in a glass <term>urinal</term> <note>original: "urinali"; a rounded glass vessel used for digestion or circulation</note>, enclosed under a "bee-dome" <note>original: "apum testudine"; likely a bell-shaped cover or a specific furnace lid</note>. Divide the plates of either metal into small pieces, and cast them into the said earth in a cold crucible, stirring continuously with your fingers or a wooden or glass pestle, until all the plates are wrapped in the powder of our earth.

Then have another clean crucible, which you place among burning coals; when it begins to glow white-hot, remove it from the fire and place it in a safe spot between two or three bricks, so that it cannot be easily overturned. And have at hand a clean glazed pan in which there is pure water. Then, while the fired crucible is still hot, cast into it your plates wrapped in your earth. And with your mouth covered <note>A vital safety warning; the "smoke of the earth" likely refers to toxic mercury or arsenic vapors released during heating</note> so that the smoke of the earth is not drawn in by breathing, stir them with a wooden stick so that they enter well into the earth, which usually happens quickly indeed. And when you know they have been well received into the earth—because you feel no lumps or globules under the wooden stick—then pour it without delay into the pan of pure cold water. And by this method, you have cast your seed into your earth. ->*The harrowing of the sown field.*<-

Dearest friend, you should know that this part of the work has been called "impregnation" by some Philosophers, and "perpetual disposition" by others; we, because of the similarity introduced from our beginning <note>referring to the recurring agricultural metaphor of sowing and harvesting</note>, do not call it "harrowing" <note>original: "occatio"; the agricultural process of breaking up clods of earth to cover seeds</note> without reason. Repeat this as many times as necessary, until you see that your amalgam can absorb nothing more of the said whiteness of the sulfur of antimony.

### *The Sprouting of the Germ.*

The Philosophers, taking a likeness from the egg—just as we have from the sowing of plants—taught that the first management of the egg is putrefaction <note>the chemical breakdown or "death" of the material, which alchemists believed was necessary for new life to emerge</note>, which they extended all the way to birth, and not only to the formation of the chick in the egg, placing nutrition after birth. We, following the likeness we have adopted a little differently for a clearer understanding, shall speak of these things in the following manner. Just as we see that the seeds of herbs do not pass entirely into rot and a complete mixture with the earth, but first become wet and softened by the moist juice of the earth, then send forth a germ, the ear of grain grows up, and it pushes forth umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note>, soon it blooms, at last forms seeds, and finally, once they are formed, it ripens. In the same way, even in this particular work, we believe those intervals must be observed in the mind, and we urge that the logic of the heat be adapted to the likeness of the months.

For from the sealing of your Philosophical Egg <note>the glass flask containing the alchemical mixture</note>, while you still see the snowy whiteness of your earth remains, you are advised to administer "Martial heat" <note>original: "Martialem... calorem"; heat associated with the planet/metal Mars, usually signifying a specific intensity, though here described as very slow</note> that is very slow. By the help of this heat, that snowy whiteness passes into a gray or ashen color, which indicates that the germ arising from the earth is now sprouting, and testifies that the strength of "April" is present. Then, by the power and heat of "May," the sprouted germ gradually grows up and is augmented with leaves and shoots. Then indeed, under the pressing heats of "June," it puts forth and expands ears and umbels, from which, as "July" scorches, it forms flowers; as "August" glows with heat, it forms and connects the seeds, which are ripened partly by the same month, but most of all by the service and heat of "September." 

Therefore, I have no doubt that what the management of heat in this work is like will be manifest to an industrious man from these things I have now related. Nevertheless, so that the less experienced may also be consulted, let us declare each part a little more clearly in order.

Let its depth be six or seven finger-breadths, in which you should place a layer of either fresh horse dung or very soft hay to the thickness of two fingers or a little more. Upon this, place your glass egg, and surround it with dung...

Indeed, the growth (*augmentation*) of the sprout happens before the multiplication of the seed within it. Do you not consider the progress of all natural things? Where have you seen the multiplication of individuals of any species before that same seed has germinated, sprouted, and increased in its parts? And [before it] brought forth ears of grain, umbels, or clusters, from which they finally flower, and from the flowers seeds and fruits are formed, and once formed, they ripen by the service of the proper heat? Must you not collect these many seeds formed from that one seed after they have legitimately ripened, purge them of their husks, separate them from the chaff, extract them from their pods, and finally sow them anew? And [must you not] wait until maturity through the same degrees of generation by which it was previously moved by nature; and then for the first time see and possess the multiplication of individuals? 

O fools, why do you rage? Abandoning both the reason and the works of nature, and following the irrational fantasies of your own heads? Did **Geber** <note>original: *Geber*; likely referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century alchemist whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> not tell you that every natural action has its own determined time, in which, over a greater or lesser span, it is finished by producing its effect? And indeed, when we received those things by hand from a most venerable priest of advanced age, we were sworn and bound by oath never to hand them over to anyone in writing; and through that same man, a place was shown to us in the writings of **Calid the Philosopher** <note>original: "Calid Philoſophi" — referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince traditionally regarded as one of the earliest alchemists.</note>, where he attempted to write them but was divinely prohibited. For through those two things, and in no other way, is the desired effect of this most hidden art achieved. Therefore you also, my son, when you wish to work according to our words—which are entirely true, without any ambiguity—should walk in this royal way which we show, so that you may deserve to consider and understand the remaining two things by the inspiration of God, as if they were handed down by hand. For He Himself, if your heart is right before Him, will send to you in the opportune time—just as He sent to me, an unworthy priest—someone who will hand those two things to you by hand, and will leave them as a father to an hereditary son. Therefore, from the beginning of your work, always remember that there are two things which are only handed down by hand to those to whom God, the creator of nature, has granted them. And being reminded by this memory, proceed most cautiously with great fear of God and reverence for nature, exalting your work from step to step, so that when you have your augmented **sprout** <note>The developing chemical matter within the vessel.</note>—namely, led from a white color to a dark red—and your **earth** <term>earth</term> <note>The solid residue or "body" at the bottom of the flask.</note> is suitably dry, you may soon hasten to the end of this "precipitate spring" and resolve all the **clouds** <note>Vapors or steam condensed on the glass.</note> that are in your air into **rain** <note>The process of condensation where vapors drip back down to the bottom.</note>, so that they may irrigate your field, lest the plants now growing die from excessive dryness. Here, therefore, after four natural days of rain have passed, in the same regime of heat, govern your **egg** <term>egg</term> <note>The "Philosophical Egg" or *ovum philosophicum*, a round-bottomed glass flask used for long digestions.</note> with the irrigated earth in a **dung bath** <term>balneum fimi</term> <note>A source of gentle, steady heat provided by the fermentation of horse manure.</note>, and diligently note in your mind how many and what kind of exhalations rise again from your earth. ...damp, so that the **clay joint** <note>original: "iunctura lutea" — a seal made of "lute," a paste of clay, dung, or glass used to airtight alchemical vessels</note> may be more easily loosened; once it is softened, remove the whole warm bath from the furnace, and immediately place your pan with sifted ashes, sealing it with diligent care to the walls of the **small furnace** <note>original: "furnelli"</note> with suitable clay, as before. > Cook it down with a slow fire, which should be a fire like the most burning fire of June.

Now, the signs by which you shall know the umbels or spikes have come forth are these: the blackish **redness** <note>original: "rubedo" — a reference to the final stage of the alchemical Great Work.</note> which was there just now will now reflect a clearer redness, and it will hide the blackness that previously appeared within the red; furthermore, a few **exhalations** <note>Vapors or steam rising from the chemical mixture.</note> will ascend from the earth into the air. Then you shall wait no more than two natural days with continued heat, and you will turn your clouds into rain, which will irrigate your field so that it may bear its fruit in its season.

What the dragon’s tail signifies according to the ancients

For what we said a little earlier concerning the turning of clouds into rain, the ancient **Philosophers** <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" usually refers to earlier masters of the art, such as Hermes Trismegistus, Geber, or Rhazes.</note> described as the **dragon's tail** <note>original: "cauda draconis" — a symbolic term that can refer to the descending or volatile part of the matter, or a specific stage of refinement.</note>; some spoke of it as an increase, some as multiplication, and others as the addition of **new Mercury** <term>Mercury: in this context, "Mercury" refers to the "spirit" or the volatile, liquid principle of the alchemical work, not necessarily the common metal quicksilver.</term>. They wished to signify this, though they did not correctly examine the works of nature.

<note>A handwritten bracket in the left margin marks the following section.</note>

Some have even named our **earth** <note>The solid matter or "body" at the bottom of the alchemical vessel.</note> "water," and when they ordered our earth to be watered frequently, they took new Mercury and not only watered the whole field but even submerged it. They did not understand that this kind of watering must happen through natural **exhalations** <note>The process where vapors rise from the heated matter, condense on the glass, and drip back down, mimicking natural rain.</note> from our earth itself, not from the pouring in of "foreign water." Nor could they understand this saying of the Philosophers, though the whole crowd of Philosophers cried out that one must take care lest our earth be submerged and the seeds perish in the flood.

Therefore, my son, you must be cautious and follow nature as your guide everywhere. The most certain sign of these flowers will be a **metallic redness** <note>original: "rubedo metallina" — the "red stage" or Rubedo is traditionally the final and most important phase of the Great Work.</note>, displaying a metallic luster; and where there were once many rising vapors, there will now be only a small amount. Does its own flower not prove the **eyebright** <note>original: "euphrasiam" — a medicinal herb; the author is arguing that just as plants are identified by their flowers, alchemical substances are identified by their colors and crystalline forms.</note>? ### BY JODOCUS GREVERUS, PRIEST.

Do not break off the work before its mature perfection. Be patient and great-souled, waiting for the appointed time. Listen to Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar and the most famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note> saying that the art cannot be perfected in a short space of time; and therefore patience, delay, and the adaptation of instruments are required in the artist. But what instruments, if not fire alone? Indeed, since fire itself is the sole instrument of all instruments in all natural things, and even more so in this most occult art.

Learn therefore, my son, the governance of fire with the greatest zeal, and do not be negligent in its administration. Nor let the continuous decoction <note>original: *decoctio*, referring to the slow, steady heating or "cooking" of the alchemical substance to induce chemical change.</note> weary you, for the decoction of the proper fire promotes nature and our work from state to state, from color to color, and from a lower degree to a higher degree. Nor do we need any instrument besides it to perfect our egg <note>The "Philosophical Egg" is a common name for the hermetically sealed glass vessel—the *ovum philosophicum*—in which the Great Work is performed.</note>. For decoction softens the seed by rotting it; decoction pushes forth the sprout; decoction lifts up the shoots and stalks; it expands the flowers; it forms the seeds; finally, it digests those same formed things to the expected ripeness. It does all this in one and the same vessel, and by a single operation of the artist, which consists in the administration of the coals. 

O most occult art! O most secret science! O most difficult operation! How much sweat, I ask, does the successive adding of coals require? Is it not children's play and a joke? <note>A famous alchemical paradox: the work is called *ludus puerorum* (child's play) because once the heat is set correctly, the artist supposedly has nothing to do but watch and maintain the fire.</note> O son, compose your egg from the yolk and the white, wrap it in a membrane, and restrain it with an outer shell. Place lit coals beneath it, and when you notice they are failing, add new ones. And thus carry your labor forward from the beginning until it is finished at the end. And when it has been sufficiently well-cooked, do with it as God shall have taught you. But now let us describe the series of maturation in order.

Do not think, my son, that we teach things contrary to the sayings of the **Philosophers** <note>In alchemical texts, "The Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval authorities of the craft, such as Hermes, Geber, or Arnald of Villanova.</note> when we teach that the glass must be cooled before its luting. For if you attempted to surround the glass with lute while it was still hot, the glass would immediately shatter into cracks upon contact with the cold and wet lute. Nor indeed do the sayings of the Philosophers requiring "continuous heat" <note>original: "continuum calorem"</note> mean that you should think your seed is immediately destroyed if the fire slackens even slightly, or burns more than is right. For when the Philosophers require continuous heat, they do so to explain the method of moving the work forward, while simultaneously teaching that those workers are inept who abandon the work they have begun in the middle of its course and do not continue until the very end, but leave it imperfect.

But you, my son, consider nature and look at the movements of the heavens. Is not the heat of the air and the warm loosening of the earth varied repeatedly, both in spring and summer, and likewise in other parts of the year? Does it not often happen in mid-summer, when the days ought to be clear and very hot, that with the Sun obscured by clouds and with storms of rain and wind, we have very cold days? Yet do the crops and plants not die off immediately? 

Nay, rather, if the continuous heat of the Sun burned without relief, and if heat and cold did not in turn refresh the plants by mutual succession—so that the subsequent heat might digest the moist and cold nourishment, and the cold succeeding the heat might again bring nourishment with its moisture—would not the earth, I say, gap open with such continuous heat, and the herbs, trunks, and crops perish from their roots? Likewise, if in the same way clouds and constant rains were to take the Solar heat away from vegetables for a longer time than is right, would not all things swell with **dropsy** <term>Dropsy: a historical term for edema or fluid retention; here, Greverus uses it to describe plants becoming waterlogged and rotting.</term> and fall into decay through putrefaction? Thus, a just temperance and a due measure of heat...

Indeed, it is a very rare vessel that lasts from the beginning to the very end of the work. Yet, do not think that the **Philosophers** <note>Referring to the established authorities of alchemy, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note> have lied when they say the mastery is perfected in a single vessel. For when you hear this said, think immediately of the *species* <note>original: "specie"</note>—the type or kind—of vessel, not the specific individual container, and in this way, you will grasp the truth.

...nourishes the battle; indeed, the middle part has **red** and **black dragons**, whose perpetual battle is with insatiable **chaos** <note>In alchemy, "chaos" refers to the *Prima Materia*, the raw, unformed state of matter before it is purified.</note> and the winds. And when the fury of the red dragons has flared up, stimulated by the oppositions of the winds, they truly perish by their own heat, and that chaos receives their corpse. Lest that eternal battle have any rest, black dragons succeed the red ones just as they are about to perish; these too, burning with fury, catch fire. They perish just as the red ones did, with others immediately succeeding them, as has been said. And at no time is this battle ever ended, for neither are the chaos and the winds finite, nor again does the offspring of the black dragons ever fail. 

For the guardian and lord of the mountain, searching everywhere for the offspring of the black dragons, sends them into the middle of the mountain at certain times: indeed, the summit of the mountain has a threefold variation each year. For in **winter** it seethes with the most glowing embers, like Mount Etna; but in **spring**, with all that previous hidden fire, it overflows with stagnant hot springs and marsh reeds. Furthermore, in **summer**, the waters of the hot springs having been completely absorbed, their ash—still lukewarm, but sometimes even very hot—is raised up, which can be believed to have been burnt by the winter fire. But in **autumn** the ashes disappear again, and a very fine sand, of fervent heat and somewhat reddish, forces itself into their place; this I consider to be the remains, or at least the sediment, of the waters that had stagnated in the springtime. 

In this very mountain, my son, I believe you have seen the royal **gardens of the Hesperides** <note>A reference to the mythical garden of Greek mythology; in alchemy, it represents the final stage where the "golden fruit" of the Philosopher's Stone is harvested.</note>, in which golden and silver roses, and likewise golden and silver pomegranates, come forth and bear annual fruit. Access to this garden is difficult, entry is more difficult, but to pluck those very golden or silver apples <note>original: "mala"</note> is by far the most difficult.

...before winter is finished, you may be able to cross. Moreover, a great danger truly looms from so many fires and such great heat of the flames. Therefore, for one intending to enter here, the **medicines of Medea** <note>original: "Medeæ sunt acquirenda medicamina." In Greek mythology, Medea provided Jason with an ointment that protected him from the fire-breathing bulls; here, it serves as an alchemical metaphor for a protective substance or process.</note> must be acquired, which she herself once handed over to **Jason** when he was attempting to enter this garden. For if you only pass them by, and do not cross through them, you will never be allowed to enter the garden.

And I indeed, while I was held by a great greed and desire for the garden, and saw that I could not cross the flames without danger, nevertheless did not wish to leave before I waited to see if someone might come by chance to show the way of passage, or if by chance the heat of the fire might diminish. And at that time, no one came after me, and already the end of winter was at the very doors: but behold, in the meantime, a great movement of that tower suddenly occurred, and the flame began to diminish, which was extinguished not long after, and the tower and the ramparts were, as it were, swallowed up. 

When this was done, immediately at the same hour where the tower had stood, I ran toward the garden, somewhat astonished by these things which I had seen happen. And when I had approached near the garden, I was hindered from entering by **stagnant hot springs** <note>original: "stagnantibus thermis." But both the waters and the garden itself were surrounded on the outside by a brick wall: I saw, however, three steps of a certain narrow path, through which there was hope of access, and without delay I began to follow them, and the brick wall was opened to me. And when I was on the first step, as if offended by a certain stench of **rot** <term>putredinis: the "Nigredo" or blackening stage, where the matter must decompose to be reborn</term>, I was forced to linger for some time.

The garden, moreover, was in the midst of the ashes, toward which there were three channels of pits, whose heats were different; for that which was closer to the garden was likewise much hotter than the others. I labored so much until I now ascended to the mound of the third channel: when...

Again, after a tremor occurred, the mountain was shaken and enveloped the ashes in a dark gloom; in their place, burning sand followed, surrounding the garden on all sides with a single rampart. And here I conceived the best hope that the end of my labors was near, just as it indeed happened. For when I contemplated the most pleasant flowers of the garden from the rampart, and saw such great miracles as are not permitted to be spoken, I was struck with such great astonishment that it now scarcely occurs to me how a certain **Elder** <note>original: "Senior." In alchemical literature, the "Senior" is often a figure of ancient wisdom or a personification of the chemical process itself.</note> introduced me into the garden. That same Elder held **seven keys** <note>The seven keys typically represent the seven metals of antiquity (Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead) or the seven planetary influences.</note> in his hand, with which I believe he had meanwhile opened the locks of the garden gates while I stood astonished on the rampart. This venerable old man led me to the **tree of the golden apple** <note>A reference to the Garden of the Hesperides; in alchemy, the golden fruit symbolizes the completed Philosopher's Stone.</note>, near which a certain dead **dragon** <note>original: "draco." The dragon often represents the volatile "First Matter" that must be "slain" or fixed to achieve the goal.</note> lay, having been slain not long before, and the golden apples were stained with its blood. Indeed, my soul burned with the desire to pluck the golden apples; recognizing this, the Elder looked at me calmly and said: "Lay aside, my son, the allurements of worldly desires—"

"—for these fruits are given only to Divine minds." I would have thought entirely that I had seen a dream, had I not held both the golden apples and the powders in my hand, and remembered all the words so exactly. But whether I truly entered the garden then, or was carried there only in a vision, or whether I saw a dream, blessed be His name forever, who deigned to open such great mysteries of nature to me, and did not take His gift away from me, an unworthy sinner. Let the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God, be praised, blessed, and highly exalted, forever and ever, Amen.

### C O N C L U S I O N ###

You have here, my son, the entire process of our work, without any omission and without any superfluity, expressed in a fitting style of speech. Prepare your heart, therefore, so that you may find grace in the eyes of God. For it is a gift of God, containing the mystery of the indivisible union of the Holy Trinity. 

O most noble science! Which is the **theater of all nature** <note>The "theatrum naturae" is a common Renaissance metaphor for the world as a stage where God's secrets are revealed.</note>, its **anatomy** <note>original: "anatomia." Here meaning a deep, structural analysis or "dissection" of the natural world.</note>, and **terrestrial astrology** <note>original: "astrologia terrestris." A Hermetic concept suggesting that the minerals and processes within the earth mirror the movements and influences of the stars and planets above.</note>; it is the proof of God’s omnipotence, a testimony of the resurrection of the dead, an example of the forgiveness of sins, an infallible experiment of the future judgment, and a mirror of eternal blessedness! Truly, there is none more excellent than this: inasmuch as it alone embraces and contains all sciences, while it is itself understood by none of them. To You, O Ineffable Majesty, be eternal thanksgiving, praise, and blessing, because You did not hide Your grace from me, nor the mysteries of this most secret art—

## TO THE KINDLY READER.

### JUSTUS À BALBIAN, A FLE-
### MING, SENDS GREETINGS.

*When I first came across the sayings of Alanus* <note>Alanus de Insulis (Alan of Lille) was a 12th-century theologian and poet to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>, *I began to read them (as was fitting) more attentively, and indeed more frequently; for although this writing was small in its size, it was not small in its weight* <note>original: "pondere." The author means the text is physically short but contains heavy, profound meaning.</note>. *What shall I say? It pleased me immensely. And why not? Since it discusses that Chemical art* <note>original: "arte Chemica." In 1598, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were not yet distinct; here it refers to the transformative pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> (*which it professes*) *very clearly. The booklet itself, which I had obtained, was written in the German tongue. Whether the author published it in that language or not, I am still uncertain. This being the case, I did not think it foreign to my purpose to translate it into the Latin language. Nor did I do this to hunt for some small glory from such a little labor; but because I desired to gratify my fellow philosophers with my small effort; especially those who might be ignorant of that language* <note>German</note>. *I have therefore seen to it that this be joined to the little work of Jodocus Greverus, because they are of the same subject; so much so that Greverus seems to have borrowed most of his ideas from Alanus. It seemed fit to add a small commentary on Lully* <note>original: "Lullium." Referring to Ramon Llull, a Majorcan polymath whose name was associated with a vast body of "Lullian" alchemical texts.</note> *by some unknown author, and a letter by John Pontanus, a most excellent philosopher, even though it has been printed before; as well as several records by various authors written in verse that is certainly not very polished, composed in that former age by men most skilled in this art. Furthermore, why I have done so will be easily judged by those who have even the slightest knowledge of this science. As for what others may think, who neither know nor tolerate this art, I deem it should be a matter of indifference. Enjoy these things, kind Reader, while I prepare something else by my own hand. Read, read through, read again, and repeat: nor will you regret the labor, I hope. Farewell and take this in good part. Given at Gouda* <note>A city in the Netherlands, famous at the time for its printing industry.</note> *on the Calends of April* <note>April 1st</note>, *1598.*

# THE SAYINGS OF ALAN THE PHILOSOPHER
## CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE,

->*Translated from the German tongue into Latin*<-

->BY<-

->JUSTUS À BALBIAN<-
->OF AALST.<- <note>Aalst is a city in modern-day Belgium; Balbian was a Flemish physician and alchemist.</note>

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a central face surrounded by ornate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

**Turn** your heart and mind toward God, my son, even more than toward the art; for the art itself is a supreme gift of God, and He bestows it upon whomsoever it pleases Him. Therefore, love God with all your heart and all your soul, and place all your hope and trust in Him alone. In this way, without any doubt, you shall enjoy this most noble art with joy, while in the meantime imposing a silence upon your tongue with compressed lips. Furthermore, there is no reason for you to persuade yourself that when we mention sublimation, or even when we perform it, we are separating the part which is above from that which is below. For in our sublimation <term>sublimation: in alchemy, the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again; Alanus argues here that it is a spiritual/physical unification rather than a simple separation</term>, the fixed parts are not raised up, but rather the parts that are not fixed. We must therefore fix the body and the spirit together, so that they may be made of an easier flow. 

Now, if heat acts upon moisture, a black color appears first; but if heat acts upon dryness, the white color appears, and within that white color, the red color is hidden. Thus, let the students of Alchemy and the seekers of this hidden art establish that the forms of metals cannot be changed unless they are reduced into their first matter: which first matter of metals is none other than Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius." In alchemy, this often refers to "Philosophical Mercury," the essential liquid principle of all metals, rather than just the common element quicksilver.</note>. However, although this reduction of metals into their first matter—that is, into Mercury—is believed to be impossible by many seekers of the art, it must nevertheless be judged possible because all metals are generated in the earth from Mercury and sulfur. Since, therefore, metals have their origin from Mercury and sulfur, it must be said that it is possible to reduce metals through Mercury into Mercury. For every thing is most especially convertible into that from which it took its origin. Furthermore, the first work of this divine art is the solution of the dry stone—namely of the Sun or the Moon <note>original: "Solis vel Lunae." In alchemical shorthand, the Sun represents Gold and the Moon represents Silver.</note>—into Mercury,

# THE SAYINGS OF ALAN THE PHILOSOPHER

### [Page 812]

...blackness, or the reduction of either of the two into their first matter <term>first matter: the "prima materia," or the original, undifferentiated substance from which all metals were thought to grow</term>, and in that way the dry stone is dissolved in it, and joined with it, so that henceforth they never permit separation, since everything like rejoices in its like <note>original: "vnumquodque simile gaudet suo simili" — a fundamental alchemical axiom suggesting that substances of a similar nature naturally combine</note>. And this is done so that if the solution of the body occurs alongside the coagulation of the spirit of Mercury, by one and the same work the coagulation of the spirit of Mercury occurs through the solution of the body. Then it becomes the "One Thing" of which the Philosophers speak everywhere in their books, saying: "It is one single thing," which exists as our unique and only Mercury, containing in itself the property and nature of all metals. For this reason, it is called the "Stone of the Philosophers" by most. And although in truth it is not yet the Stone, it is nonetheless the unique key of metals; it lacks, however, the power of tinting <term>tinting: the ability to change the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver</term> by itself, unless it is first "tinted" with the soul of the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the Moon <note>Silver</note>.

Therefore, no spirit acts upon another spirit, nor does any body act upon another body. Furthermore, this Art consists in the spirit alone and the soul of the body, namely of sulfur and Mercury: for the soul of sulfur exists as a certain corporeal essence. For this reason, he who does not know how to extract the soul from the body of the Sun or the Moon, and to restore the same to the body in the projection <term>projection: the final stage of the alchemical work where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transmute them</term>, should know that he is wandering entirely from the path.

This, however, is done in the following way: The soul of the body—namely of the Sun or the Moon—is elicited or extracted by means of the spirit of Mercury. By this reasoning, the spirit of Mercury is exalted and improved, and the soul is joined in conformity with the spirit. The body of Venus <note>Copper</note> or Jupiter <note>Tin</note> afterwards receives this union of soul and spirit into itself, and from that it receives the life of perfection; and thus, imperfect bodies are led away from their imperfection toward perfection and are brought back to life, and this is by the power and benefit of our Stone.

Therefore, as it has been said, our Stone is made from one single thing, by only one mastery and governance. For our Philosophical Water dissolves the bodies of the Sun and the Moon; indeed, our water exists as "living water," and because of its exuberant perfection, it contains within itself everything that it needs. This substance, once found, is assigned various names among the Philosophers. For it is that pure and transparent water in which the bodies of the Sun and Moon are dissolved; nor can this properly happen in any other thing in this world. Listen to the Philosophers on how this is so: "Our Stone," they say, "namely the body of the Sun or Moon, dissolves itself in the Spirit of Mercury, which coagulates itself together with it..."

<summary>Alan explains that the Philosopher's Stone is a "One Thing" derived from Mercury and the "souls" of Gold and Silver, which together can perfect base metals like Copper and Tin. He emphasizes that the secret lies in using a "living water" to extract the soul of the metal and unite it with the spirit of Mercury.</summary>

# ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE

### [Page 813]

...it blackens, whitens, and reddens; and by itself it receives the soul of the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and weds itself with it, fixing itself in the soul of the Sun or the Moon. Lucianus the Philosopher <note>likely referring to a pseudo-epigraphical alchemical author</note> says: "Our stone is airy and volatile, cold and moist on the outside, but hot and dry on the inside and in its hidden part."

However, its cold and moist exterior, which is visible, is a certain watery smoke, a destruction, alteration, and a kind of blackness corrupting itself and everything else with it; and this same moisture and coldness flees and spurns the fire. On the other hand, the hot and dry quality hidden within it is gold, or certainly that most pure oil penetrating the body, neither fleeing nor fearing the fire.

In Alchemy, however, nothing "tints" <term>tints: the alchemical power to transform the color and nature of a substance</term> except for the hot and dry. Therefore, ensure that the cold and that watery moisture appearing on the outside becomes conformed and similar to the hot and dry hidden on the inside. See to it that they become "one thing," and are made homogeneous, or of one nature in essence. That is to say: let the spirit of Mercury become the soul, and let the soul of the body become the spirit; in this way, you will certainly obtain the force and power of tinting and penetrating.

Therefore, it is necessary for the moisture to be disturbed or altered through certain degrees of fire—namely, by a slow and moderate fire. Furthermore, our stone is made in this way: Take Mercury. For without it, not even nature itself is able to work, as Rhasis <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and famous alchemical authority</note> testifies, saying: "Through Mercury alone can we perfect our work, so that it surpasses all nature."

For Mercury is easily associated with all metals, and is the unique medium through which the "tincture" is acquired. In truth, the nature of Mercury snatches to itself from the ores of gold or silver that one thing which belongs to its own nature, along with that which is conformed to the spirit of Mercury in its entire property. Thus it becomes the earthy Stone of the Philosophers—natural, incomprehensible, and called by many other names by the Philosophers.

This blessed stone, the more and the longer it is decocted <term>decocted: the process of refining a substance by heating or boiling it in a sealed vessel</term>, the more it dissolves the body of the Sun or the Moon, and it is blackened in that solution. The more it dissolves, the more it is dried and whitens; and after the whiteness, the more it is decocted, the more it becomes red—and this is beyond any doubt. Thus, our stone is exalted from a discarded and vile thing into a most precious thing and treasure. For Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most celebrated figure in early alchemy</note> says: "This is done only through our Mercury, through our fire, through [our...]"

fff

# THE SAYINGS OF ALAN THE PHILOSOPHER

### [Page 814]

...our water, through our vinegar; that is, through the unique Mercury joined with its own body. Therefore, take one part of gold or silver leaf, of the kind that painters are accustomed to using; the thinner or more subtle either of these is, the more quickly it will be converted into Mercury. Place it into a hermetic furnace constructed as you know how, adding to it twelve parts of Mercury appropriately purified; and make an amalgam <term>amalgam: a mixture of mercury with another metal, often creating a paste</term>, placing the well-sealed vessel in sifted and dry ash, so that the ashes cover the material.

Afterward, apply a slow and moderate fire, cooking it continuously for as long as it takes until the sayings of the wise are fulfilled, which are recognized by the signs. When it has stood in the "fire of wisdom" for one whole month, black clouds arise, gradually dispersing and vanishing: that is, color gradually consumes color, until at last one remains: and this is the Mercury of the Philosophers and the perfect blackness <note>original: "nigredo perfecta," the stage of putrefaction where the old form dies to give way to the new</note>.

Furthermore, if you take only three parts of Mercury with one part of the body <note>the gold or silver leaf</note>, you will have too little Mercury, which would barely suffice for three months of putrefaction; and so, faster than is proper or than the nature of Mercury itself desires, the water of Mercury will be consumed by the soul of the Sun <note>Gold</note> or Moon <note>Silver</note>.

It is better, therefore, to take twelve parts of Mercury with one part of the body right from the start, and to place it in the ash in a sealed vessel: from here, allow it to be cooked for a space of three months. Then, indeed, what was hidden—namely, the soul—becomes manifest, and what was manifest—namely, the Mercury—becomes hidden. Furthermore, this kind of extraction of the soul through the spirit of Mercury does not happen all at once or in a single instance, but in many turns, throughout every time and day; and even in every single hour and moment, a little bit at a time, until the work has been led to perfection, as was also written above. This is attested to by Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist often cited in Latin translations</note>, who says:

> The soul does not exit from the body in one single instance, but is drawn out in many; nor is it dissolved all at once in the vessel containing the solution, or in which the body is dissolved; but every day a little bit is dissolved in it, and again at other times a tiny amount, according to the governance of the worker and of nature.

Do not think, therefore, that the dissolution of the body happens all at once, but rather through the passage of time and gradually, as the sayings of the Philosophers clearly attest above. It is, therefore, essentially necessary for the seeker of this art, and the one practicing it, to be of a constant and unchanging mind and will. And that...

## ->ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE<-

fff 2

<meta>catchword: since</meta>

Above all, let the operator take care that he does not start one work and then, leaving the first behind, attempt to try another. For this Art does not consist in a multitude of species or ingredients, but in the body and the soul. In truth, the medicine of our stone is a single thing, one vessel, one union, one regimen, and one decoction <term>decoction: a method of extraction by boiling or steady heating</term>. Indeed, the entire mastery is begun with a single thing—namely, Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; here referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the supposed universal base of all metals</note>—and it is finished and perfected with that same thing, Mercury. Although the Philosophers, for the honor of the Art, may point to many other paths—such as continuous decoction, mixing, sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of turning a solid directly into a gas to purify it</term>, grinding, drying, liquefying, firing, whitening, and reddening, and by whatever other names it might be called—it is nonetheless nothing other than a single regimen, which might rightly be called "grinding and cooking." For just as Mercury grinds or breaks down all things, so the fire cooks them into perfection. For this reason, Rhasis <note>Rhasis: Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and influential figure in early alchemy and medicine</note> says: "Cook, and do not let it weary you; do not hasten, nor torment your mind with empty thoughts, but wait for the desired end with diligence and patience."

Furthermore, Longanus <note>Longanus: likely a reference to an alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a name like Johannes or a specific Arabic source</note> says: In this work, take care that the vessel is always perfectly sealed or closed, and that it maintains a continuous and uniform heat; for nothing in this world is brought to perfection without heat and continuous motion. If you are diligent in the operation, you will carefully observe whatever signs of the cooking appear and fix them in your mind. Finally, you must ensure that the vessel is buried in the ashes up to its midpoint, while the other half remains visible, so that you may inspect it daily.

Moreover, after a period of forty days, a certain blackness usually appears like pitch, which is nothing other than the sign of the body now being dissolved. For whatever has been made spiritual seeks the higher parts or the heights, and everything earthy remains at the bottom; everything light tends upward, and everything heavy tends downward. When the body has been dissolved by its own water into blackness and an incomprehensible essence, then the tincture <term>tincture: the transformative essence or "soul" of the stone</term> of the solution is present in that blackness. Thus, finally, the four elements come together as one. For with air you have water, and with fire you have earth. Yet take care (as I have warned quite often) not to believe that the tincture is drawn out or extracted in one single turn; rather, it happens steadily, a little at a time, or day by day as the blackness is completed by the passage of time. Whatever...

### ->SAYINGS OF ALAN THE PHILOSOPHER<-

When it has been dissolved with Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; here meaning the "Philosophical Mercury" or universal solvent</note>, it raises itself up again, even though a greater portion remains continuously below. This blackness <note>original: "Nigredo"; the first stage of the alchemical Great Work, symbolizing death and putrefaction before rebirth</note>, moreover, is assigned thousands of names. For it is called fire, soul, cloud, and the "raven's head" <note>original: "caput corvi"; a traditional alchemical term for the dark, pitch-like appearance of the matter at the start of the process</note>: and this blackness joins the soul to the body. Indeed, our calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to effect a change in its physical or chemical constitution</term> produces a cloud of this sort, as Avicenna <note>Avicenna: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on chemistry and medicine were foundational to Western alchemy</note> attests: "Our beginning," he says, "is called calcination when the body and spirit, already joined, are combined during the work." 

The Philosophers, directing us toward this kind of calcination, command us to take an example from wood. In green wood, three types of moisture exist: first, that which preserves the wood from burning; another, quite fatty and oily, which provides the cause for ignition and burning—these two lack a distinct odor and are consumed by fire; however, a third moisture, greasy but small in quantity, remains in the ash—it is subtle and eternal. In a similar way to the wood just mentioned, we are commanded to calcinate our stone of Mercury and the body. From this, finally, you will learn to expect blackness first, and after that, whiteness: which, if it is digested in our fire for its proper time, will arrive at the greatest perfection. 

In the books of the Philosophers, you will find only two fires: one dry, and the other moist. They called the dry one that common elemental fire which consumes everything; however, they called the moist fire the "horse's belly" <note>original: "ventrem equinum"; a method of providing gentle, consistent heat by burying the vessel in a pile of fermenting horse manure</note>, in whose moisture a hidden heat is reserved. If, however, the moisture in it is diminished or consumed, the heat is also diminished. 

The philosopher Phiares, treating this fire, says: "It is characteristic of the fire of the horse's belly not to destroy, corrupt, or diminish gold, but rather to increase it because of its moisture; whereas otherwise, any other kind of fire would alter and corrupt it because of the dryness it contains." For this reason, the philosopher Alchidonus speaks thus: "Our medicine," he says, "must truly be hidden in the moist fire of horse dung, which is considered the 'fire of the wise' by the masters." 

The *Turba* <note>original: "Turba"; likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> recounts that our Mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver"</note> is the fire, because it possesses a greater power to burn, corrupt, and kill bodies than any other fire, even the elemental fire itself. Calid <note>Calid: Khalid ibn Yazid (d. 704), an Umayyad prince credited as an early alchemist</note> also asserts this: "There is," he says, "a certain fire that consumes everything, so that it may even be ground down." Senior <note>Senior: refers to Senior Zadith (Zadith ibn Hamun), a 10th-century alchemist</note> says the same: "Our water is fire, burning gold more than elemental fire, and our water..."

...is more powerful than any fire; indeed, it converts gold into spirit, which elemental fire <note>original: "elementalis [ignis]"; the common fire of a hearth or furnace</note> is unable to provide, no matter how much that fire may also suit the work. For then our water penetrates the body and converts it into earth, and afterward into powder or ash. Therefore, unless blackness <note>original: "nigredo"</note> appears in the beginning, no whiteness <note>original: "albedo"</note> shall follow. And when the blackness has appeared, know that it does not last beyond forty or fifty days; and this is the putrefied body. 

The putrefaction of the body, therefore, is the beginning of the work, and it is accomplished by a very small heat, lest anything should seek the summit <note>i.e., evaporate or sublime too quickly</note>. For if anything happens to ascend, then a separation of the Mercury from the body occurs, which is not helpful until the husband and wife—namely, the Mercury and the soul—become one thing, and are joined or mixed into one perfect black essence. This perfect conjunction of the two—namely the spirit and the soul—will appear perfectly from above, as a true and certain sign of the solution <term>solution: the process of turning a solid into a liquid state within the alchemical vessel</term>. 

O son, dear to my soul, for this reason be diligently intent upon the putrefaction or solution, which must occur by a small heat, namely in a "horse's belly" <term>horse's belly: "ventre equino"; a term for a digestion vessel kept at a low, steady heat, traditionally by being buried in decomposing horse manure</term> of small heat; that is, in Mercury, with the help of a slender heat. 

That quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is indeed "horse dung" is made clear by Senior <note>Senior Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist often cited in medieval texts</note>, who says: "To the dissolved body, which was dissolved on the seventh day, dung—that is, Mercury—must be renewed every four days"; that is, it must be added. This renewal or addition is specifically called **imbibition** <term>imbibition: the process of "feeding" a dry substance with liquid until it is saturated</term>, **maceration**, **solution**, and **penetration** into the solid and hard parts of the gold or silver, penetrating their pores so that, by that reasoning, we may be able to draw out the soul from them through our spirit of Mercury. 

Establish this as certain: immediately after the solution, that which is pure receives an increase in its own likeness, as is clearly seen in kernels <note>original: "nucleis"; seeds or pits</note> which, if they are committed to the heat of the earth for some days, swell and putrefy; and that which exists as pure and good within them finally emerges and comes forth from them, grows, and is multiplied a thousandfold and receives an increase. That which is impure, however, perishes and vanishes. 

Therefore, we also digest our matter so that it may swell, and so that what is pure within it may grow and receive an increase, while the superfluous part vanishes. In our mastery <note>original: "magisterio"; the Great Work or alchemical process</note>, therefore, nothing is necessary except the solution of the body into Philosophical Water. For unless the kernel of the body of the Sun <note>original: "Solis"; gold</note> or the Moon <note>original: "Lunae"; silver</note> is raised up, or reduced into its first essen- <note>catchword: "essen-" for "essentiam" (essence)</note>

### ->THE SAYINGS OF ALAN THE PHILOSOPHER<-

...essence or matter, you will have spent all your labor in vain and to no purpose. For the body by itself accomplishes nothing unless it has been properly dissolved, as has already been said quite often; truly, it cannot be dissolved otherwise than with its own Mercury. For every thing is destroyed by the same cause through which it grows; nor is anything more in accordance with nature than that every thing be dissolved and freed from the bonds by which it is bound by means of that thing from which it took its origin, namely Mercury.

Furthermore, the ways and modes of dissolving any body are various and manifold: some occur in a cold and subterranean, humid, or even sandy place, just like mercurial waters; another, more excellent than the former, occurs in dry heat, which does not happen in mercurial waters <note>Alan is distinguishing between "common" mercury and the "Philosophical Mercury" or "mercurial water" prepared by the chemist</note>. This water of ours, however, is produced in dry ash in a closed and sealed vessel, and it is the way that both holds the first rank and is far better than all others; the other way, which we mentioned above, is uncertain and destructive.

For this reason, therefore, the Philosophers say their solution is unique, which converts the dry body into water, as if they were to say: "Make Mercury through Mercury," or "through mercurial water." For thus the dry body receives its own proper moisture of Mercury, and so the two things both become and are named as one, because we add nothing foreign to them. For in that union, nothing remains over, nor is anything missing that could give occasion for destruction. But if you attempt to convert your matter into "cloud-water" <note>likely referring to condensation or distilled water from the air</note> in some cellar or moist place, it will receive destruction from that source, because the matter is infected and poisoned by a moist environment.

You may find many people saying many things who are utterly ignorant of this art and clearly unacquainted with the species of metallic principles, slandering and scorning this divine art by citing these words of Aristotle from the 5th book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "è 5. Meteororum"; a reference to a famous passage often used by medieval skeptics to argue that alchemy was impossible</note>, because he says in the aforementioned place: "Let the searchers of the art know that the species of metals cannot be changed—such as making silver or gold out of copper, tin, lead, or iron—so that it may be done." And it is just as they say: for no change will take place unless the metals are first reduced and resolved into their first matter and the essence of mercurial water, and thus are reduced into a different essence than they were before.

Hear what follows: Our mastery <term>mastery: "magisterium"; the perfected chemical process or the Philosopher's Stone itself</term> greatly destroys the form of bodies: for we have seen bodies converted into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>, which many men believe to be impossible.

...fall away, and the sole cause is their own supine ignorance, because they do not know that all metals are generated and take their origin from Mercury and sulfur. Furthermore, if all metals lead their origin from Mercury, what—I ask—stands in the way of them being able to be reduced back into Mercury through Mercury? Take an example of this possibility: just as ice is turned back into water by heat, so also all bodies grow, and all living things receive increase, which is visible in trees and plants as well as in animals; for we see a single grain or pit produce some thousands of thousands, and one tree produce innumerable shoots. If, therefore, metals are also born from the earth and grow in it, it is surely likely and believable that growth and increase can be given to them as well, as with the others. We consider that enough and more than enough has already been said by us concerning the conversion of things; and the possibility of conversion is now sufficiently proved and known to all from the things said before: which is the very thing that led the Philosophers to say:

> Whoever knows how to destroy gold or silver in such a way that they cannot afterwards be reduced back into gold or silver, he has reached the mastery. <note>original: "magisterium." This refers to the ultimate achievement or "Great Work" of alchemy. The "destruction" mentioned here is not the loss of the metal, but its reduction to its primal, formless state—the only state from which it can be evolved into the Stone.</note>

For it is easier to destroy bodies, or to convert their forms, than it actually is in truth; as we see happening, namely that copper receives the tint of gold and becomes brass <term>orichalcum|A golden-colored alloy, typically copper and zinc, which mimics the appearance of gold</term>, and from lead is made white lead <term>cerussa|lead carbonate, used as a pigment</term> and red lead <term>minium|lead tetroxide, a bright red pigment</term>, and from red lead, glass, while the essence of lead always remains. And so each thing remains in its own proper and inconvertible essence. From this, every prudent person will easily gather that no right solution of a body can be made except in its own blood; nor can any utility or advantage be obtained unless the body has first been dissolved: the way and method of which solution follows clearly in brief.

Take, in the name of Almighty God, Mercury seven times optimally sublimated, and revivify the same again through one part of quicklime <term>calx viva|calcium oxide, a caustic substance used here to reactivate the mercury</term>, and a half-part of the same weight of crude tartar <term>tartarus crudus|potassium bitartrate, the sediment found in wine casks</term>, and thus it will be optimally purged; or purge it by whatever best way you know and as you judge convenient. Take three parts of this purified Mercury, and one part of gold or silver reduced into very thin plates or leaves, such as painters are accustomed to use; place them in a solution bowl or dish, and let them be optimally ground and mixed together so that an amalgam <term>amalgama|a soft, putty-like mixture of mercury and another metal</term> is made from it. ### *A summary conclusion for the understanding of the Testament or Codicil of Ramon Lull, and his other books; as well as the quicksilver, in which the whole intentional intention hangs, which is otherwise called the Repertory of Ramon.* <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher. Here used to describe a watery distillate or a specific thickness of the substance that protects it from being scorched by the fire.</note> preserves the whole work from combustion, through the skill of the craftsman. However, you should know that its whole substance—namely, the phlegmatic one—is separated from the whole composite by decoction. Our phlegm is, however, a middle substance, and the "first water" of Mercury, in which the beginning of the stone is found; namely, its dissolution. Nor does it enter into the final product with the stone, although the natures embrace each other in a bond of nature, acting only as a phlegm moistening the parts of things, and not generating or increasing them. ...is boiled down with moisture <note>original: "phlegmate." In alchemy, "phlegm" refers to a watery, often volatile or tasteless liquid obtained during distillation, representing a specific stage of moisture.</note> by a demanding fire, it is all the more adorned by the parts grafted into it, and is thus rendered more fit, so that a manifold fruit may be generated from it. For this is called the **middle nature**, and the **Mercury stone**, and **arsenic** <note>In this context, "arsenic" refers not just to the chemical element, but to a "volatile spirit" or a transformative substance.</note>, and a **subtle spirit** sharing in two extremes: **white and red sulfur**, which binds Mercury and converts it into a silver better than that found in a mine.

But the moisture in which our sulfur—which is called **gold**—is boiled, is that in which moist, spiritual air is intercepted within the substance of Mercury, until its middle part is condensed into water through the action of the body’s heat. For the metallic body, like an acting power, works as the **male**; and it does so because it is its own property, since its heat is enclosed in the airy moisture. When this heat enters the pores of the cold Mercury, it undergoes a gradual and steady alteration. And so, that which is digested through natural heat is resolved into water by the smallest parts, because it is the property of every element to have a contrariety within itself and to act upon its opposite. 

Those parts, however, which are not resolved into water, remain in the form of quicksilver <term>amalgamated</term> <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal.</note> with the body; these cannot be resolved unless they are further refined through <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material.</note>. Therefore, if you wish to resolve the "mud" by coldness, you will only coagulate it further. The heat of the body indeed digests and resolves the Mercury, insofar as it is thickened into water along with its parts of Mercury dissolved elsewhere. 

Thus, our moisture consists of three essential substances. These essences of the elements are directed toward one another in such a way that the greatest part of each meets the greatest part of the other, and the smallest part of each meets the smallest of the other, altering one another by their respective qualities. Whence **Alexander** <note>Likely referring to Alexander the Great, to whom many medieval alchemical works were apocryphally attributed, or Alexander of Aphrodisias.</note> says: 

> They perform the mixing of the elements because the elements work certain effects better in a mixture than in a simple state.

And this is because in such a mixture, the proper essences of the elements remain, which are the proper operative virtues. This is evident through our **Philosophical water**, which is called **metalline**, because it is generated from the metallic genus alone. In this water of sulfur, there is a middle disposition between softness and hardness, through which the transition is made from the softness of quicksilver to the most perfect hardness of metal. From this, I say, it is produced through a determined dissolution...

...born nature, which participates in two contraries: nor is that disposition essential to quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui."</note> and sulfur in their substance or nature, but is only a part of them, from whose alteration of the essential parts one arrives unanimously at a middle earthy substance.
