Therefore, to take up the moisture, condense the air through the hot and dry, and rarefy the dry, and you will have the hot and moist. This airy vapor is spiritually taken up in the **matter of gold** and of other mixtures, and therefore they are more quickly resolved into it. 

Indeed, our **water**, after its separation by the **alembic** <note>A distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cap to collect vapor.</note>, is clear in color like common water; and in the beginning of its operation through the filter, it is pale in color, like the color of wheat chaff. And before it is separated by the filter, it is black: the cause of which is the earthly corruption of the dark body, covering the brighter parts of the spirit in a corrupted form, although it is not truly so in its essence. 

And after its boiling <note>original: "decoctionem."</note> is complete, which happens through rarefaction, it is white in its hidden part: which whiteness is nothing other than the spirit resolved from the body and carried away by the moisture. Indeed, the moisture varies in color; whenever the spirit varies, the moisture varies just as often, because the moisture does not vary except in form. For the spirit, in any boiling, varies in color; and certainly the matter also increases in weight, in virtue, and in power. 

For when the black matter is soaked with water after separation by the filter, the black matter turns white upon the **porphyry stone** <note>original: "porphyde." A hard, purple-red stone used by alchemists as a surface for grinding and mixing materials.</note>; but immediately when the matter is ground, the whiteness is hidden in the matter, and it continues to do this until the power of the water overcomes the power of the earth. Nevertheless, before it reaches its true end in the "color of the earth," many and almost infinite colors will appear, concerning which no one could most certainly give a full explanation. For the earth, in its boiling with its own water, creates many kernels or swellings like little bubbles, in which all the colors of the world appear, so shining that one would hardly believe it unless he sees it or has experienced it. 

Indeed, the substance of this water is the bright and illuminating spirit of the bodies, which in the root of nature was united with the metal and coagulated with fire, namely...

While the previous page (812) focused on the purification of "mercurial water" and the color changes during digestion, this page (823) explores the relationship between the active and passive principles—represented by Sol (Gold), Luna (Silver), and Quicksilver—and how they must be balanced through a "middle" substance.</meta>

<page-num>823</page-num>

<header># ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE</header>

...by mineral virtue, and when it has been coagulated, it is found to participate in two natures and extremes; for it is partly fixed and partly volatile. Therefore, it is called a "middle," in which resides a fixative power: and while it is being fixed, it follows the proper nature of the metal. This is called **sulfur** and a **hard liquor** <note>original: "liquor durus." This likely refers to a substance that appears solid but has the potential to flow or melt, or a concentrated chemical essence.</note>, sublimated into a powder in the manner of a spirit. Indeed, liquidity can never be created in any matter except by the mediation of this liquid spirit. 

This spirit is generated from the substance of two contrary humors—regarding heat and cold—which are of one single kind regarding their root. One of these is **Sol** <note>The alchemical name for Gold.</note> and the other is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; Mercury.</note> in one degree. In another degree, however, it is **Luna** <note>The alchemical name for Silver.</note> and quicksilver. Nevertheless, this quicksilver differs in a certain degree when it is joined with Sol; since it is not quicksilver in its [common] nature, it possesses stronger virtues, which are of heat. 

Quicksilver, acting as the passive matter, is joined to Sol as the agent. However, Sol is not joined with quicksilver as a male with a female; rather, it is the reverse. In reality, the "middle nature" of the quicksilver dominates the matter of gold and **corrupts** <note>In alchemy, "corruption" is a necessary stage of breaking down a substance's form so it can be transformed or "perfected."</note> it, as if it were acting upon it like a male. It does not only corrupt it, but by altering it, it enters the fixed and hot moisture of Sol with its own spirit. This occurs by means of that spirit in which the seed of both is carried; hence Sol is not joined with quicksilver, nor quicksilver with Sol, except through a middle substance. 

Nor does one "love" the other except through such an affinity of nature, where their substance is one. Specifically, the substance of quicksilver exceeds the substance of Sol by four parts, and that of Luna by two parts, because it is colder than Sol—since the active virtues are greater in Sol than in Luna at the beginning of the **confection** <note>original: "confectionis." The process of "putting together" or preparing the alchemical Stone.</note> of the stone. Nevertheless, the quantity of the matter of Sol does not truly exceed the value of one gold coin <note>original: "unius aurei."</note>. The Lunar matter, however, exceeds it more in weight, because it is of a more earthy nature and a more fragile virtue; therefore, it is strengthened by the nature of gold, and without it, it is weakened. 

For although Luna is considered cold by everyone, it is nevertheless hot in a certain degree, but it does not have enough power to act upon the passive matter of quicksilver unless it is aided by a more active matter. And for this reason, the earth of sulfur is prepared with arsenic just as quicksilver is with...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the preparation of the "Sulfur" or the active principle of the Work. While the previous page (823) discussed the balance between the agent (Sol) and the patient (Quicksilver) through a "middle nature," this page describes the specific preparation of this Sulfur, the nourishment of the "metallic germ," and the requirements for the alchemical vessel.</meta>

<page-num>824</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>TREATISE</header>

...with our sulfur. The preparation of the **sulfur**, however, is this: if it is cooked with its own oil and a small amount of **ferment** <note>In alchemy, a "ferment" is a small amount of a perfected substance—like gold—added to a mixture to "leaven" it and guide the transformation of the whole mass.</note>, it will return within eight days into a most brilliant red powder, **tinging** <note>original: "tingentem"; refers to the alchemical power of a substance to instantly transform the color and nature of another metal.</note> silver into gold.

->Where the sought-after matter should be kept.<-

The separation of the waters, why they ought to be placed in the work, and what must be done with them has already been described, and is found more than enough in the books of the Philosophers. I have said that the **sought-after matter** <note>original: "materia quæsita"; the essential substance of the Philosophical Stone.</note> is reserved in a protective **phlegmatic** <note>original: "phlegmatico"; refers to a moist, watery, and cool consistency, similar to the bodily humor of phlegm.</note> moisture, and the **putrefaction** <note>The stage of "death" or breaking down of the matter, usually characterized by a black color.</note> occurs with its own thickness in the secret furnace of the Philosophers.

->How the distillation is performed.<-

Distillation is performed through the **veins of the glass** <note>original: "venas vitri"; likely referring to the tubes or the neck of a glass still or retort.</note>, without the separation of the materials; rather, it is done with their union in our secret furnace, and this is our **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again; here, the author emphasizes that their "sublimation" is a unified process within the vessel.</note>. Enough has already been said regarding the natures of the physicians.

->How the bodies are nourished.<-

The **bodies** <note>In this context, "bodies" refers to the solid metals used in the process.</note> are not nourished [directly], but only their **germ** <note>original: "germen"; the embryonic "seed" or life-force within the metal.</note> within themselves is nourished by the varying heat of the fire, for the practical work must be observed in this. For the bodies are nothing but the food of their own germ, since it is certain that the bodies are changed, altered, and reduced to the nature of the **spermatic germ** <note>The "seed-like" essence that allows metals to "grow" or multiply in quality.</note>. The germ itself is increased by **congealing** <note>Turning from a liquid to a solid.</note>, and it nourishes itself by expanding, just as a child is nourished by its mother's milk; so too the bodies, like its meals, are dissolved and converted into the germ. Likewise, the dissolution of the bodies occurs when the **spirit** is congealed and changed, and the congealing of the spirit occurs when the bodies are dissolved. The **coagulation** of one nature does not happen without the **dissolution** of the other, nor vice versa. And the form of that which arrives cannot be made without the **corruption** <note>The philosophical idea that for a new form to arise, the old form must first be destroyed or "corrupted."</note> of the form that existed before. Indeed, the form of the bodies gives way because of the arriving form of the spirits, and the entire substance of the bodies yields to the nourishment and the **substantial form** <note>The essential nature or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note>. Thus every solution is a **mortification** <note>A death or killing of the initial state.</note>, just as every coagulation is a **vivification** <note>A bringing to life.</note> and the most immediate cause of life.

->Concerning the form of the vessel.<-

The form of the artificial **vessel** <note>The laboratory glassware, such as a flask or cucurbit.</note> in which the said work is perfected is this: it is exactly equal to the form of the **natural vessel** <note>Likely a reference to the womb, as alchemists often sought to mimic the natural "gestation" of metals in the earth.</note> with its long veins, in which the separation of the pure from the impure takes place.

<summary>This page explains the final preparation of the Red Sulfur, the biological-analogous process where the 'germ' of the metal consumes the 'body' of the metal to grow, and the design of the alchemical vessel intended to mimic nature.</summary>

<header>CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE</header>

method: nor is it of any other form, and it is a single vessel with two horns, for in this we must especially imitate nature.

->*How the ferment is made.*<-

Now the **ferment** <note>In alchemy, a "ferment" is a small amount of a perfected substance—like gold—added to a mixture to "leaven" it and guide the transformation of the whole mass.</note> is made after the birth of the **child** <note>original: "infantis"; a common alchemical metaphor for the Philosophical Stone in its developing or newly created state.</note>, so that the best nourishment may be administered to it, so that the body—which in its entire substance is weak—may be supported more and more and led back into a stronger nature. For the ferment is nothing other than **nutritious food** <note>original: "cibus cibalis"</note>, convertible into the essence of the child, so that the entire work is made of a single nature. Nevertheless, the preparation of this food must come first, for this nutritional fermentation must be of its own nature and be assimilated to itself: since unless it were assimilated to it, it would never be incorporated into their nature, nor converted into the nature of **sulfur** <note>In this context, sulfur refers to the active, combustible, and "seeding" principle of the Stone.</note>.

->*Why the ferment should be prepared.*<-

Indeed, it is prepared and refined so that it becomes purely nutritional and easy to convert. Then such is the nature of our stone, that it is preservative and strengthening. Therefore, the more we prepare the ferment, the more capable it will be for converting and digesting.

->*In how many ways the preparation is made.*<-

The preparation is done in many ways. In one way, through dissolution into the "water of the stone" and through reduction; in another way, through **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note> and washing with **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, and the rising up of its middle substance. Next, through the dissolution of the stone and the joining of the waters, and by this method it is easily convertible. In another way, through the **waxing** <note>original: "incerationem"; the process of softening a dry substance into a waxy, meltable consistency.</note> of the lime, and through its dissolution. In another way, by the removal of its earthy nature, which is hard and compact. For our stone is the union of the **Sun** <note>Gold, or the masculine principle.</note> and the **Moon** <note>Silver, or the feminine principle.</note>, until the Sun has drawn the substance of the Moon into its own nature and color. This indeed happens with the "fire of the stone." Then it is continued until it is perfected with things of its own kind.

->*How the medicines may have entry.*<-

Now the medicines, both the **white and the red** <note>The "white medicine" transmutates metals into silver, while the "red" transmutates them into gold.</note>, can have the same entry into that which is joined to them **through the smallest parts** <note>original: "per minima"; referring to the theory that substances must be broken down into their most microscopic components to truly combine.</note>. If, however, you wish to perform **projection** <note>The final act of casting the finished Stone or "elixir" onto base metal to instantly transform it.</note> upon a body, place some of its spirit in the elixir, and through such artistry it will have entry into that matter. In this lies the practice used by many. Note that when the union of the Sun occurs

->*The letter of Johannes Pontanus, a supreme Philosopher, in which*<-
->*he treats of the stone which they call the*<-
->*Philosophers' Stone.*<-

I, Johannes Pontanus, have traveled through many regions so that I might recognize something certain about the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>Philosophers' Stone: A legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life or health.</term>, and circling almost the entire world, I found false deceivers and not Philosophers. Yet always studying and doubting in many ways, I found the truth. But when I recognized the matter, I erred two hundred times before I had found the true matter, operation, and practice.

First, I began the operations of the matter, the **putrefactions** <term>Putrefaction: A stage of decay (often called the Nigredo or "blackness") where the matter is broken down to its base state before transformation.</term>, for nine months, and I found nothing. I also placed it in the **bath of Mary** <note>original: "balneo Mariae"; known today as a bain-marie or double boiler, used for gentle, indirect heating.</note> for some time, and similarly I erred. Indeed, I placed it in the fire of **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note> for three months, and I worked badly. I handled all kinds of **distillations** <note>Purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back to liquid.</note> and **sublimations** <note>The process where a solid turns directly into vapor and back to solid, used to purify "spirits" or volatile substances.</note>, just as the Philosophers—such as **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most influential figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note>, **Archelaus** <note>A legendary Greek philosopher often cited as a source of alchemical wisdom.</note>, and almost all others—say or seem to say, and I found nothing.

Finally, I attempted to perfect the subject of the entire art of Alchemy by every method that can be devised: those done through **dung** <note>Decomposing horse manure was used as a steady, low-temperature heat source for months-long alchemical processes.</note>, the bath, ashes, and other multiple kinds of fires which are found in the books of the Philosophers; but I found nothing good. For this reason, I studied the books of the Philosophers for three continuous years, especially in **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition and alchemy.</note> alone, whose shorter words encompass the whole Stone, even though he speaks obscurely of the upper and lower, and of heaven and earth.

Therefore, our instrument—which brings the matter into being in the first, second, and third works—is not the fire of a bath, nor of dung, nor of ashes, nor of the other fires which the Philosophers have placed in their books. What then is that fire which perfects the whole work from the beginning until the end? Certainly, the Philosophers have hidden it. But I, moved by piety, wish to declare it to you, together with the completion of the whole work. The Philosophers' Stone is therefore one, but it is named in many ways, and before you recognize it, it will be difficult for you. For it is watery, airy, fiery, earthy; phlegmatic, choleric, and melancholic; it is sulfurous, and it is similarly **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>

<header>OF THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE</header>
<meta>catchword: that (original: ille)</meta>

...[resid]ue, and it has many superfluities, which through the Living God are converted into the true essence, by means of **our fire** <term>Our Fire: Also known as the "Secret Fire," this is a central mystery in alchemy. It is not common fire but a specialized heat or catalytic agent that transforms matter without destroying its internal "spirit."</term>: and he who separates anything from the subject, thinking it necessary to do so, truly knows nothing in Philosophy. This is because the superfluous, the unclean, the base, the drossy, and indeed the entire substance of the subject is perfected into a fixed spiritual body, by means of our fire. 

And this the wise have never revealed: for this reason, few arrive at the art, thinking such a thing to be superfluous and unclean. Now it is necessary to draw out the properties of our fire, and [to see] whether it suits our matter, according to the manner I have stated—namely, that it be transmuted—since that fire does not burn the matter, nor does it separate anything from the matter; it does not segregate the pure parts from the impure (as all Philosophers say), but converts the whole subject into purity. It does not sublimate as **Geber** <note>original: "Geber"; refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary alchemical authority. Pontanus is criticizing Geber's method of "sublimation," which involves vaporizing and recollecting substances to purify them.</note> does his sublimations, nor like **Arnold** <note>original: "Arnoldus"; refers to Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, and others speaking of sublimations and distillations to be perfected in a short period of time. 

It is mineral, it is equal, it is continuous; it does not evaporate unless it is over-excited; it participates in sulfur; it is taken from elsewhere than the matter; it destroys all things, it dissolves and congeals, and likewise it congeals and calcines; and it is artificial to find; it is a shortcut without any expense, or at least a small one: and that fire is of a moderate burning, because with a mild heat the entire work is perfected, and at the same time it performs all the proper sublimations. 

Those who would read Geber and all other Philosophers, if they lived a hundred thousand years, would not understand it, because that fire is found only through deep and profound thought; then indeed it can be understood in books, and not before. The error of this art, therefore, is failing to find the fire which converts the whole matter into the true **Stone of the Philosophers**. 

Study therefore for yourself, for if I had found this [fire] at first, I would not have erred two hundred times in the practice upon the matter; therefore I do not wonder if so many and such great men have not arrived at the work. They err, they have erred, and they will err, because the Philosophers did not set down the proper agent, except for one, who is named **Artephius** <note>Artephius (c. 1150) was a highly respected alchemical author. Pontanus credits him as the only one who spoke truthfully about the "Secret Fire."</note>, but he speaks for himself: and unless I had read Artephius and sensed his speech, I would never have reached the completion of the work. 

The practice indeed is this: Let it be taken and, as diligently as possible, be ground with physical grinding, and let it be sent to the fire, and let the proportion of the fire be known—namely, that it only excites the matter, and in a short time the fire

He identifies the author Artephius as the only one who truly revealed this "proper agent" of transmutation.</summary>

that [fire] <note>original: "ille"; referring back to the "Secret Fire" discussed on the previous page.</note> without any other application of hands will certainly complete the entire work, because it will rot, corrupt, generate, and perfect [the matter], and it will make the three principal colors appear: the black, the white, and the red <term>The Three Colors: Known as the *nigredo* (blackness/decay), *albedo* (whiteness/purification), and *rubedo* (redness/perfection), these are the standard developmental stages of the Alchemical Work.</term>. These things, therefore, I wished to say, and to warn the prudent, lest they consume their money uselessly, but that they may know what they ought to seek: **in this way they shall arrive at the truth of the art, and not otherwise. There is a certain noble art, called Alchemy,
Which the fickle man, or one dwelling in fantasy, should not seek.
For it requires a most industrious scholar,
And rarely a layman, unless he be supremely gifted.
Leave aside corruptible things, salts, and vitriols <note>original: "atramenta"; literally "black inks," but in alchemy, this refers to various metallic sulfates or vitriols.</note>,
And many other things which are destroyed by the cementing furnace.
There is a firm tincture <term>Tincture: A potent liquid or substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver.</term> latent in Mercury,
Destined to remain in the fire, shining like the Sun or the Moon:
Yet not the common [mercury], but that which grows like a plant.
The wise man must contemplate these words:
The soul is extracted by means of the spirit,
And it shall be cleansed with the cooperation of fire.
This is the *Lunaria* <note>original: "Lunaria"; literally "Moon-plant." In alchemy, this refers to a symbolic plant or substance associated with the silver-making process.</note>, with its trees and leaves,
Bearing various names, climbing through glass vessels.
Which, when it is sublimated clear and clean,
From it is distilled a permanent wave <note>original: "vnda"; often used to describe the "mercurial water" or the solvent of the philosophers.</note>,
With which, even if a small particle of our copper is colored,
It is of cheap price, yet within it lies the whole.
Many are ignorant of this; to the Philosophers, it is known.
The Stone is threefold and one: spirit, body, and soul.
It is a god-like gift to know these names well.
This is a true comparison of the Trinity itself,
And there is no deviation in respect to its unity.

### *By Another.*

ALCHEMY stands as a creative art,
As is evident in its practice.
Neither powder, lime, nor water
Dyes <term>Tingunt: Literally "to dye" or "tinge," in alchemy this refers to the transmutation or coloring of base metals into gold or silver.</term> metallic bodies.
Alums, salts, sulfurs, or earths
Cannot transform bodies.
The way of the art is not physical <note>Likely meaning "not through mundane physical materials" or "not following the laws of common physics."</note>;
But neither are the roots of herbs, nor worms,
The basilisk, nor the spotted lizard [used]:
But this dyeing thing, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> says,
Hides only in Mercury.
If herbs do not dye, nor liquids,
What do you wish to dye other than Mercury?
Not the mercury of the common people <term>Common Mercury: Alchemists often distinguished between "vulgar mercury" (the liquid metal quicksilver) and "Philosophical Mercury," a refined spiritual substance that acts as the "root" of all metals.</term>, but that which bears the flowers of gold,
And which exists purer than gold itself.
This is the true and perfect elixir,
Dyeing gold into something even better.

### *By another, most ancient.*

If you desire to be made happy, so that you may obtain the blessing of the Philosophers,
As God lives forever, let this truth live with you.
You shall observe an Egg <term>Philosophical Egg: A symbol for the sealed vessel (alembic) or the primordial matter containing the potential for life and transformation, much like a biological egg contains the seed of life.</term> in the world, which is properly called the Egg of the Philosophers.
It remains in a shell <note>original: "testudine"; literally "tortoise shell" or "vaulted chamber," here referring to the protective vessel.</note>, containing the white and the red.
One is called the male, the other is named the female.
Animal, vegetable, mineral—nothing like it is found.
It has an active and passive power, a dead and a living substance;
It has with it a spirit and a soul, which the ignorant person calls a most vile thing <note>original: "rem vilissimam"; a common alchemical trope is that the true "stone" is found in common or discarded materials that the uninitiated ignore.</note>.
It contains the four elements held within its own bosom.
It is everywhere, it is found everywhere, it is held in common by all.
It is bought for a small price; a pound is had for a single shilling <note>original: "vno solido"; referring to a coin of little value to emphasize how common the raw material is.</note>.
It ascends by itself and turns black; it descends and turns white;
It increases and decreases; it is a thing which the earth produces.
It descends from heaven, turns pale and turns red,
It is born, and dies, rises again, and afterwards lives eternally.
It tends toward the end through many ways: but its cooking <term>Decoctio: The process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or mature it.</term> is done by fire.
It is slow, modest, strong, and is increased,
Until, by resting more securely, it is turned red.
This is the Stone of the Philosophers, spoken of according to the seeker's prayer.

Extracted from the kidneys, taken from the body of the womb,

Break down the matter you have captured, using a suitable water <note>original: "lympham." In alchemy, "lympha" often refers to a pure, watery solvent or the "mercurial water" used to dissolve the initial matter.</note>,

So too it should ascend, only to tend back toward the depths again <note>This describes the process of "reflux" or "circulatio," where vapors rise, condense on the lid, and fall back down to the bottom of the flask.</note>:
Thus let it be sublimated; thus let it be purified by its own action.
Then the water of whiteness, purged from the vat of liquid,

Thus let that which is seen to distill be dried out.
No fruit ever rises without a seed;
In which, while the seed dies, it then bears fruit.
The water must be divided for the sake of purifying the body,
One part must be saved to cleanse the cooked materials.
A pregnancy, confirming the change, promises the closing of the gap.
From here the menstrual flow <note>original: "menstruus." In alchemy, the "philosophical Menstruum" is the universal solvent that dissolves and "nourishes" the stone during its development in the vessel.</note> feeds it until its time is up,
Thus the fountain will drip, thus it will pour out its draughts by itself,
It joins the noble water, the earth, and the fire.
The fountain must be taken and ground with quicklime <term>quicklime: calcium oxide, a caustic substance used in alchemy for its drying and heating properties.</term>:

<meta>This page continues the alchemical instructions from the previous page, detailing the internal chemical and symbolic transformations within the "vessel of philosophy." With the parts properly adjusted, boil down the <term>Virgin’s Milk</term> <note>original: "lac virginitatis." A symbolic term for a white, mercurial liquid produced during the distillation process.</note>,
Let it grow warm with a gentle fire, lacking any harsh heat;
And when it is dried, in a similar way the <term>Lime</term> <note>original: "calx." The powdery residue left after a substance has been heated or "calcined" to its core.</note> is moistened.
The wave of its own fountain drips from the mountain's peak,
One fountain and then another for the source of this river.
Just as food in the stomach receives what is pure within,
Let it bring back all the pure essence, and fit it through the limbs.
It is a pleasing sight, yet let the moistening be moderate,
Lest the lime be disturbed as if it were thrown into the sea.
While you join the lime, it will react with opposing signs,
So let the slowest fire dry it using light wood.
When these things are thus dried by the embrace of virginity,
Let the lime again drink the pure wave of the first fountain,
Let it receive the honeyed liquid driven by its own <note>original: "testudine." Literally a tortoise shell, but here referring to the vaulted lid or dome of the chemical vessel.</note> vault,
And let it grind the pure, dried wave of blood.
Then the water, saved and purified by dripping distillation,
Should be poured in so that the submerged lime is covered,
And let it be dissolved, so that it is made clear;
Let it be dried, and let this be repeated nine times.
Certainly it draws to itself the divine oil of its own fountain;
Just as a magnet is seen to draw in hard iron.
But when the dripping fountain dissolves the bloodless snake <note>The "snake" or dragon often symbolizes the raw, volatile matter or Mercury that must be "tilled" or killed to be transformed.</note>,
Let the fire rise from beneath the dung <note>original: "ignis sub fimo." This refers to the "dung fire" (venter equinus), a technique of using the steady, gentle heat of fermenting horse manure to warm a vessel.</note>, lest it dry out from the bottom:
For death will be removed if it is washed in the living fountain,
Which, by dripping, restores, nourishes, and most pleasantly purges,
It washes, corrects, renews, waters, unites, and floods,
It sprouts, and the earth breathes out the scents of flowers.
Therefore, food is given to it, and let it be satisfied with drink,
Let it be merged in the river, and patiently perfected;
And when it is dried, let it be satisfied with the living drink,
Until it becomes full to the brim, serene with a bright whiteness.
Thus it must be roasted and alternately watered,
Until, by absorbing, it dries its own divine oil:
Let it be poured in so that the liquid is entirely drunk up
And then dried, until the whole is turned to ash.
Then the lovely <note>original: "Veneris vena." While Venus usually represents copper, here it refers to a refined "vein" or quality appearing in the whitening matter.</note> vein of Venus from the glowing fountain,
Though still full on the outside, let it become serene under the Sun:
Let the fire fade, so that the whole shines white:
Let it increase sweetly, until, dried, it rests,
A fire kindled, a stronger fire burns.

836
<header>ON THE ENIGMATIC EPITAPH</header>

# BY NICOLAS BARNAUD, OF CREST-ARNAUD IN DAUPHINÉ, PHILOSOPHER, and Physician,

## ON A CERTAIN ENIGMATIC EPITAPH AT BOLOGNA, THE SEAT OF STUDIES, INSCRIBED MANY CENTURIES AGO
-> on a marble stone, the words of which follow immediately. <-

-> <term>D. M.</term> <note>original: "Dis Manibus." A traditional Roman funerary invocation meaning "To the Divine Shades" or "To the Spirits of the Departed."</note> <-

> AELIA LAELIA CRISPIS, NEITHER MAN NOR WOMAN, NEITHER HERMAPHRODITE NOR GIRL, NEITHER YOUNG NOR OLD, NOR WHORE, NOR CHASTE WOMAN, BUT ALL OF THESE.
> TAKEN AWAY NEITHER BY HUNGER, NOR BY THE SWORD, NOR BY POISON:
> -> BUT BY ALL OF THESE. <-
> SHE LIES NEITHER IN THE SKY, NOR IN THE WATERS, NOR IN THE LANDS, BUT SHE LIES EVERYWHERE.
> LUCIUS AGATHO PRISCIUS, NEITHER HUSBAND, NOR LOVER, NOR KINSMAN, NEITHER MOURNING, NOR REJOICING, NOR WEEPING, [ERECTED] THIS, WHICH IS NEITHER A MOUND, NOR A PYRAMID, NOR A TOMB:
> -> BUT ALL OF THESE. <-
> HE KNOWS, AND KNOWS NOT, WHAT HE HAS PLACED FOR WHOM.
> THIS IS A TOMB, HAVING NO CORPSE WITHIN;
> THIS IS A CORPSE, HAVING NO TOMB WITHOUT;
> BUT THE CORPSE IS THE SAME AS THE TOMB FOR ITSELF.

---

-> **A Brief Commentary.** <-

From the time I happened upon this Epitaph—which has been printed by many others—I asked of my own accord whether any man, imbued with the spirit of <note>Oedipus was the legendary hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; an "Oedipean spirit" refers to someone gifted at solving difficult puzzles.</note> Oedipus, had taken it upon himself to explain

<meta>catchword: this</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the famous "Aelia Laelia Crispis" enigma, a mysterious Latin epitaph from Bologna, which the author Nicolas Barnaud intends to interpret through an alchemical lens.</summary>
<keywords>Aelia Laelia Crispis, Bologna, Nicolas Barnaud, enigma, riddle, epitaph, alchemy, Oedipus, Lucius Agatho Priscius</keywords>

--- Page 846 ---
<meta>This page continues Nicolas Barnaud’s introduction to the Aelia Laelia Crispis enigma. He critiques previous interpretations—such as those claiming the riddle refers to the soul, rainwater, or a eunuch—and begins to frame the mystery as a coded alchemical recipe (the "Trismegistic" path) based on his thirty years of study.</meta>

837
<header>A BRIEF COMMENTARY.</header>
<sig>ggg 5</sig>

...this mystery, I understood—not without great joy of my soul—that certain brilliant minds of our time have not hesitated to devote diligent labor to unraveling the secret that lies hidden beneath the fictitious words of this epitaph. Nor were those lacking who, having grasped what is covered in general (so to speak), yet when they took it upon themselves to interpret each word, left the principal parts untouched and examined the rest so superficially that anyone who reads their writings should not be ashamed to say either that they had something else in mind than what they professed to perform, or that they were ignorant of what they had undertaken to do. There were also others who, as I hear, contended in their writings that the **Human Soul**, others that the water of the clouds <note>Referring to rainwater, often used as a metaphor in early chemistry/alchemy.</note>, others—as I understood here from a man well-deserving of letters—that a certain **Eunuch**, and others that various other phantasms were treated in this epitaph. When I understood these things, pitying those who serve in the camps of the more hidden philosophy <note>That is, practitioners of alchemy.</note>, I thought I would perform a worthwhile task if I attempted to open this Trismegistic <note>Trismegistic: relating to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy; implies a profound, hermetic secret.</note> epitaph to them. Therefore, I have gladly taken this duty upon myself. It is now for you to lend me both ears, benevolent **Chemiologists** <note>A term used by Barnaud for alchemists or "chemical-philosophers."</note>: for in a few words, I hasten to teach you what I have obtained through many manuscript books and through much tireless experience of thirty years and more; provided, however, that I first advise those (I speak to those who have no doubt about the metamorphosis of all things existing under the lunar sphere, but especially of metals) that if I were in **Bologna**, I would be the author of a proposal to the **Magistrate**—appointed by the **Roman Bishop** <note>The Pope</note> in charge of Bologna—that he should examine that entire marble tomb, its base, and its surroundings so thoroughly that not even the smallest part would remain untouched, lest by chance something hidden in its bosom long ago, which smells of "everything," should lie buried any longer. Indeed, when I read "**ALL**" here, the story of the truly ancient Roman and profoundly pious philosopher **Morienus** <note>Morienus: A legendary 7th-century alchemist said to have been the teacher of King Kalid.</note> comes to mind. When he had prepared the medicine of the wise for **King Kalid** <note>Kalid ibn Yazid: An Umayyad prince traditionally regarded as the first Arab alchemist.</note> out of his goodness, departing secretly from that king, he depicted the vessel in which he had left that medicine with this inscription: **HE WHO HAS ALL WITH HIM, NEEDS NOTHING**. When that King noticed this shortly after Morienus’s departure, he obtained what he was most seeking: namely, **ALL**, which is truly sought by philosophers—that is, the **STONE** <note>term: Lapis Philosophorum (The Philosopher’s Stone). The goal of the alchemical Great Work, said to transform base metals into gold and grant longevity.</note> which he calls "the philosophers’ stone." And so, it would not be out of place if that entire site of the tomb were examined by officials perishing from the "sacred hunger for gold" <note>original: "auri sacra fame." A famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, often used ironically to describe the desperate search for wealth.</note>. So—

For such treasures are sometimes hidden away and kept secret, so that someone worthy of them is scarcely found; hence it happens that, once the treasure is buried, they entrust the matter to God the giver. This secret has been handed down and commended to the sons of wisdom in various ways, yet always truly, by various philosophers scattered everywhere but agreeing on this one thing. ### ON THE ENIGMATIC EPITAPH

...beyond memory, both because other **chemists** <note>In this context, alchemists.</note> among their authors—whose names they otherwise preserve diligently—nowhere make the slightest mention of this one. As for me, even if we were to scout all the histories most thoroughly, I do not think we could know who or what sort of man he was. Indeed, I am persuaded that these names were entirely fabricated and used by some upright man to whom that ancient and perennial truth of our **art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy.</note> had shone forth among the ancients. 

This man, since he did not wish to become known by his own name or his family name (for times have always been dangerous for those like him; and as the common saying goes, "he who carries treasure publicly invites robbery"), wished to teach posterity by these names—which were not falsely chosen, but imposed upon himself. He intended to show that he who wishes to handle these sacred secrets ought to be a **LUCIUS**, that is, a man of the most subtle, most lucid, and most clear-sighted intellect in investigating the natures of all minerals, semi-minerals, and metals, and in fishing out their families. Furthermore, he should be not only a **LUCIUS**, but also **human**, endowed with that ancient goodness, and to say it in a single word, he must be a pious and truly upright man, as the word **AGATHO** <note>original: "Agatho"; from the Greek *agathos*, meaning "good" or "noble."</note> implies, and a man who fears God, who neither:

> ,, sins, nor rejoices in joining himself 
> ,, to the worst of mockers:
> ,, But with a pure mind loves the laws of God
> ,, and meditates upon them always,
> ,, whether the night brings lovely sleep, 
> ,, or the bright sun waters the earth with light. 

For wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, unless perhaps—as sometimes happens—an angry God grants to the ungrateful and the disobedient what he has otherwise denied to pious men when asked. If those [wicked] men should ever happen to attain such a gift of God, you might call it a drawn sword carried in the hands of a madman, prepared chiefly for their own destruction. Nor yet (to speak with **Thomas Aquinas**) <note>The influential medieval theologian and philosopher (1225–1274).</note> would I deny that this science is accustomed to make the man who possesses it holy, and to turn him from the most reckless into the most prudent man—one who might say with another, having bid farewell to the world:

> ,, I have found the harbor; hope and fortune, farewell;
> ,, I have nothing more to do with you; now play your games with others.

This author of ours, therefore, who set up this monument, was **AGATHO**, that is, "the Upright"; he was also **LUCIUS**, that is, "the Enlightened" by the light of nature and the divine; and he was **PRISCIUS**, <note>From the Latin *priscus*, meaning "ancient" or "venerable."</note> that is, born in that golden age, not in this most corrupt age of ours. He, therefore, following **Plato**...

in the letter to Dionysius <note>Likely referring to the Second Epistle of Plato to Dionysius, often cited by alchemists to justify secrecy.</note>, he decided that one must write about this matter through circuitous routes and riddles, so that if the writing should happen to be tossed about, anyone who reads it might not understand it. Therefore, whoever wishes to understand the sayings of the philosophers must surrender himself entirely to God, and look toward the possibilities of nature rather than the mere sound of words. For these philosophers treated this sacred and hidden **art** <note>The "Art" refers to alchemy.</note> under metaphors, fables, and obscure words; they hid it by design so that it would not be exposed to the impious and the unworthy.

Now let us see who this heroine of ours was, to whom the monument was dedicated. For on the very frontispiece, the letters **D.M.** were placed—that is, "To the Spirits of the Dead" <note>original: "Diis Manibus"; a standard Roman funerary dedication.</note>—after the custom of the ancients. This memory was established by our LUCIUS to show that this heroine was at one time living and then dead. However, as we shall see, he affirms that she was later gifted with a better life and immortality, so that she might be able to impart light and life to her kinsmen—namely, to **Mercury** and the impure metals—and to us "little men" in the matter of our health. Let us now prepare ourselves to interpret the primary and "juice-filled" <note>Meaning substantive or essential.</note> words. She was, therefore, and is, our Goddess:

### AELIA.

Solar, beyond doubt, as the name indicates <note>Connecting "Aelia" to *Helios*, the Greek word for the Sun.</note>, or the daughter of the sun; or rather, she is the substance, essence, ray, and virtue—and indeed, that invisible virtue—of our "Sun," lest anyone wrongly imagine her to be born from the common sun of the masses. Yet there are some who think she was born from Saturn (the son of Uranus and Vesta) and his sister Ops; they recall how, when Saturn had received many children from her and devoured them, only to vomit them back up immediately, Jupiter was saved, and a stone was presented to Saturn in his place as if Ops had given birth to it. They think she was born from them. But whatever the case, she is **AELIA**, or solar; yet (such is her greatness) she does not walk clothed only in that star, the "eye of the world"; she is also accompanied by the other, lesser light, the Moon, which is under her feet. Therefore she is also called:

### LAELIA.

As if a "friend of the sun," and as I interpret it, a lunar power and essence, but not the "moon" or "silver" of the common people. For the older philosophers did not use the common sun and moon in this **magistery** <term>The "Magisterium" refers to the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>. Thus, they proclaimed that the "man of the philosophers" does not require great expense, and they affirmed that this work can be undertaken and perfected by the poor as well as the rich (provided God is present). This would be far from the truth if it could not be accomplished without common gold and silver, since those are precious and not easily accessible to the poor; although it is not...

And those two primary tinctures, the red and the white, are **AELIA**, or if you prefer, **LAELIA**, buried in one and the same subject. They have not been led by nature to their "completion" (as they say), but they are to be led there through our mastery, by making a separation of them from the earthly muddiness and the dross of that substance in which they lie hidden. These then, according to their own nature, become so miscible with pure earths—the red and the white—that they are rightly held in the place of a **ferment** <note>In alchemy, a ferment is a substance added to the work to "leaven" the matter and direct it toward the nature of gold or silver.</note>. Nor are they said to need anything foreign, since this whole thing is one, born from the same image, containing within itself its own co-essential parts; it would be absurd if common gold and silver were required for its composition. 

Yet I do not deny that philosophers can very well dissolve mineral gold and silver with radical things of their own kind, which are as yet least completed by nature, and thus can reach the summit of this art, if one may believe Ripley the Englishman. But truly this operation is not for everyone's talent, and moreover, it is suited to Princes who abound in gold and silver. However, this way which we are treating is more pleasing to philosophers and fits them better, and is much easier. But someone will say here: if this way is as easy as you say, why then is it finally called by LUCIUS...

# LITTLE COMMENTARY

I am forced to frankly confess that for many years I labored in vain regarding the investigation of our "matter" <note>The *materia prima* or starting substance of the alchemical Great Work.</note> and its preparation, though it was perhaps already known to me. Yet I still believe that our entire mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>The complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> could be most easily performed—so to speak—even by women and children, if they once understood it; if, I say, there were someone to teach them what can be taught in a single hour, as the saying goes. But the reason our matter is now called *CRISPIS* <note>Latin: *crispis* means curled or wrinkled; here it implies something "tangled" or complex.</note> and "involved" is partly because it is held back by its own dross and shackles, from which it longs to be liberated by a skilled craftsman; and partly because the "knots" <note>Metaphorical difficulties or riddles.</note> found in this art seem to me to have originated from the philosophers themselves. In their efforts to hide the art, they call themselves "envious" <note>The *philosophi invidi* were alchemical authors who intentionally used obscure language to prevent the "unworthy" from discovering their secrets.</note>, so that what is

->NEITHER MAN, NOR WOMAN<-

remains hidden. These and similar terms, I say, render the matter tangled, arduous to know, and very difficult for those who cling to the literal word rather than the spirit. For such people see this subject of ours called by some "Adam"—that is, the "red man"—who carries in his bosom his wife "Eve," whom they make "white." This is the source of those verses:

> *If the white woman be wed to the red husband,*
> *Soon they embrace, etc.* <note>original: "Candida si rubro mulier sit nupta marito, / Mox complectuntur &c." This is a common alchemical metaphor for the union of Mercury (white/female) and Sulfur (red/male).</note>

And there are many similar sayings which I will omit for the sake of brevity. But when the poor wretches read here that it is "neither Man nor Woman," do they not know whom to trust? However, those who have perceived the true mind of the philosophers do not allow themselves to be led into believing that any animate creature <note>Latin: *animale quid*. Barnaud is warning that the "man" and "woman" are chemical metaphors, not biological reality.</note> enters into our mastery—unless perhaps metaphorically, and in that way in which all created things are said to agree with one another by a certain innate likeness. Therefore, when they hear our subject named "man" and "woman," or called by others "the red servant who embraces the white woman," they think of nothing else but the Sun and Moon <note>Alchemical ciphers for Gold and Silver, or the principles of Sulfur and Mercury.</note>—or, if I may put it this way, their "seeds" and influences—existing together with Mercury in our subject. Since it is said here that it is "neither Man nor Woman," it is easily understood: even though they know that Body, Soul, and Spirit are present in it, they agree with the description. This is the same as when it is said:

->NOR ANDROGYNE,<-

is it said to be. For some half-learned person might have doubted whether this divine "AELIA"—even if she were neither man nor woman—might nevertheless have been both, sharing in each sex. But Probus <note>Likely referring to a grammarian or a specific commentator on the enigma.</note> warns us, to prevent this error, that it was nothing of the sort, even though it contains the "seed" of the male and female within itself; indeed—

<meta>catchword: NOR</meta>

# ON THE RIDDLE EPITAPH

->NEITHER GIRL, NOR YOUTH,<-
Whether you look at its form or its age;
->NOR AN OLD WOMAN,<-
If you consider the passage of time or its grayness.
->NOR A PROSTITUTE,<-
If you calculate its way of life, because it has not yet coupled, nor thought of coupling; and yet,
->NOR CHASTE,<-
Because it desires a husband and carries its own "sulfur" <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</note> with it (which serves in the place of a male), though it remains unmixed; for this reason, it is called *Rebis* <term>Rebis</term> <note>From the Latin *res bina*, meaning "double-thing," a common name for the alchemical hermaphrodite or the union of opposites.</note>. It follows:
->BUT ALL THINGS.<-

That is, as I interpret it, this "Aelia Laelia Crispis" of ours is Man, Woman, Hermaphrodite <note>original: *Androgina*</note>, Girl, Youth, Old Woman, Prostitute, and Chaste. It is, was, and shall be—though for different reasons, as they say—and this is attested by the entire school of philosophers. If I wished to cite their locations and opinions, a year would hardly suffice. Therefore, I wish for you to decide for yourselves, benevolent Chemists <term>Chemiologi</term>, that this substance is "All Things," has all things within itself which it needs for its own perfection, and that all things can be predicted of it, and it, in turn, of all things. For "One is the All," as the greatest Chimes <note>Likely referring to Zosimos of Panopolis, an early alchemist often called "Chemes."</note> says, "because of which all things exist; and if the whole did not contain the whole, the whole would be nothing." Now it remains to see by what fate this marvelous heroine perished; for indeed, it is she herself who was:

->TAKEN AWAY, NEITHER BY HUNGER NOR SWORD,<-
->NOR BY POISON; BUT BY ALL.<-

And this, as it is right to believe, happened before the eyes of the author; for it befits the man who handles these mysteries to be present at the work perpetually, lest he allow any error. Therefore, since death is called the "gate of life," it was necessary for this Heroine to die as well, in order to perform those stupendous miracles of the "One Thing." <note>A reference to the *Emerald Tablet*, which describes the "miracles of the one thing."</note> Here, however, Agatho <note>A Greek name often appearing in alchemical literature, sometimes associated with a legendary philosopher.</note> warns that she was taken away and handed over to death neither by hunger, nor sword, nor poison alone, but by all these things combined. That is to say: she was dried out <note>The alchemical process of desiccation.</note>, reduced to a fixed powder <term>fixed powder</term> <note>A substance that has been rendered stable and resistant to the heat of the fire.</note> resembling a corpse, and extinguished by her own "good poison." Yet, as the author says, she did not perish from hunger because she had that which could nourish her; she was powerful enough to provide herself with native food and drink from her own substance, aided by the craftsman. Nevertheless, she was finally oppressed by hunger and thirst because she had exhausted all her moisture through various "drinkings" <note>The cyclical process of evaporation and condensation within the alchemical vessel.</note>...

# A SHORT COMMENTARY

In accordance with custom, it was necessary for her to perish, and to be killed by iron—if you interpret "iron" (as I believe it should be interpreted) as that very red powder, similar to saffron of iron <term>crocus ferri</term> <note>original: "croco ferri"; a red iron oxide. In alchemy, this represents a state of the matter reached through intense heat.</note>, into which she was finally turned by continuous fire, thus obtaining the name of "the dead." Then, she was also killed by poison—that is, by her own purest sulfur, specifically the solar sulfur <note>The active, masculine principle associated with gold and the sun.</note> that lay hidden and innate within her. By its power, she was fixed <term>fixata</term> <note>To "fix" a substance in alchemy means to make a volatile spirit stable and resistant to fire.</note> and handed over to death; that is, she was turned into earth, as Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> says, while still possessing her powers whole. Therefore, she was not extinguished in the way one might think, but rather:

->NEITHER IN HEAVEN, NOR IN THE WATERS, NOR IN THE LANDS,<-
->BUT SHE LIES EVERYWHERE.<-

The power and potency of our Heroine is, without a doubt, wondrous. Though she has been taken away, the author himself affirms that she "lies everywhere"—that is, she has her seat everywhere. Was our friend Probus <note>A reference to a supposed author or commentator on the riddle.</note> perhaps one of those "Ubiquitarians"? <note>A "Ubiquitarian" was a person (usually in a theological context) who believed a body could be in all places at once; here Barnaud uses it as a metaphor for the universal presence of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> I can hardly believe such an error had been born in his time. But I would have you notice here, studious reader, that our matter—after its preparation and conjunction (of which you will find hardly a word in all the books of the philosophers)—is turned into powder by a gentle and continuous cooking <term>decoctione</term>. Thus, while appearing dead to the eye, it exists not only in Heaven (that is, in the soul), or in the lands (which are various, namely in its earthly body), or in the waters (which are also manifold, namely in the spirit that usually carries the soul), but "everywhere." This means it is simultaneously in heaven, lands, and waters, as the "whole in the whole," and the whole in any individual part. Indeed, those parts, which were otherwise separable, can never be separated from one another after they have been made one. From this, the entire Law and Chemical Prophecy seems to hang. Now, since we have heard who, what sort, and how great this Goddess of ours was, and what happened to her, let us hear, I pray, what the author says about himself:

->LUCIUS, AGATHO, PRISCIVS, NEITHER HUSBAND,<-
->NOR LOVER, NOR KINSMAN.<-

We stated at the beginning of this little commentary what sort of man this author was; namely, a man gifted with a most brilliant mind, numbered among those upright <term>probi</term> <note>A play on the name "Probus" mentioned earlier; "probus" is Latin for "upright" or "virtuous."</note> ancient philosophers. Now let us consider and weigh what drove him to build a tomb for this heroine. For since we hear that he himself was neither Husband, nor Lover, nor Kinsman of this deceased heroine of ours (which we easily grant him, as an upright man who...

<header>ON THE RIDDLING EPITAPH.</header>

One is not accustomed to devote oneself so much to any thing, or to marry it, or to love it so desperately that they decide they must necessarily enjoy the desired object. And since these are the primary causes—namely the Bed <note>Latin: *Thorus*; referring to marriage or sexual union.</note>, Love, and the bond of Blood—which move a person to dedicate a column to someone deceased in the "temple of memory" (if I may speak thus), and yet none of those reasons apply here, I would wish, O son of wisdom <term>fili sapientiæ</term> <note>A common alchemical address to the reader or initiate.</note>, that Agatho <note>Referring to Lucius Agatho Crispus, the name of the person who supposedly dedicated the monument in the riddle.</note> could not be said to have attempted this elegant deed without purpose (for upright men, imitating God and nature, are not accustomed to undertake anything in vain). I would wish, I say, that you were here with me in searching out the reason for this undertaking of our Lucius. For as far as it concerns me, I believe (unless you feel otherwise, then say so) that our philosopher Lucius foresaw that a very famous Academy would one day exist in Bologna (for most philosophers are also prophets). And since he felt that he had obtained such a great and stupendous Gift of God (for he professes to know all things, as you will hear shortly), he did not want the account of his "buried talent" <note>An allusion to the biblical Parable of the Talents; he did not want to hide his knowledge.</note> to be demanded of him by God the Best and Greatest. Therefore, openly and before the eyes of all who trade in good letters, he ordered "ALL THINGS"—that is, the art teaching all things, the most precious of all—to come forth onto the stage, dressed in this riddle. To this art and true science (after that most sacred knowledge of God and Christ, in which the salvation of us all is placed), as the most worthy of all, our Lucius erected this monument to entice students to investigate it:

->NEITHER GRIEVING, NOR REJOICING,<-
->NOR WEEPING.<-

As becomes a constant man—a smooth, well-rounded, and intrepid philosopher—he erected this:

->THIS, NEITHER A MASS, NOR A PYRA-<-
->MID, NOR A TOMB;<-

For these things are woven together and built by the hands of stonemasons and some industrious architect; neither the consideration of a physical mass, a pyramid, nor a marble tomb could ever have been useful to anyone.

->BUT ALL THINGS.<-

That is to say, he placed these very words which you read engraved here—hardly unlike the words of the Emerald Tablet of Hermes <note>The *Tabula Smaragdina*, the foundational text of Hermetic alchemy, which uses similarly paradoxical language.</note>—and furthermore, that supreme and universal medicine <term>medicina catholica</term> <note>The Panacea or Philosopher's Stone, capable of curing all diseases and perfecting all metals.</note> for all human bodies.

<summary>Barnaud argues that the creator of the riddle, Lucius Agatho Crispus, was a prophetic philosopher who left the inscription as a hidden guide to the "Universal Medicine" for future scholars in Bologna. He interprets the monument's description not as a physical tomb, but as a symbolic representation of alchemical perfection and equanimity.</summary>

<header>A BRIEF COMMENTARY.</header>

...thoroughly healing bodies, then also elevating impure metals to the sphere of the sun <note>original: *sphæram solis*; referring to the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note>, and creating precious stones (if one has led the work to its highest degree), it follows:

## HE KNOWS, AND KNOWS NOT, WHAT HE HAS PLACED FOR WHOM.

He knows, surely, the whole art—the medicine of the first, second, and third order, to speak with Geber <note>Geber, or Jabir ibn Hayyan, was a legendary 8th-century figure regarded as the father of alchemy; the "three orders" refer to the stages of medicinal or alchemical potency.</note>. He knows, moreover, that he has thus placed that Philosopher’s Stone. But *what*—that is, how much—he has placed, he does not know, for it is likely he did not weigh it; nor does he know for *whom* he placed it. Therefore, it does not seem unreasonable to me (as I suggested at the beginning) if, as the current times permit, all these things were placed for that great Roman Prince <note>Likely referring to the Pope or a high-ranking official in Bologna who might have the authority to excavate the site.</note>; since it is in his power to see that the entire burial site is inspected and every stone be turned, so that it may finally be known how much or what Lucius placed there.

## THIS IS A TOMB, HAVING NO CORPSE WITHIN.
## THIS IS A CORPSE, HAVING NO TOMB WITHOUT;
## BUT THE CORPSE IS THE SAME AS THE TOMB FOR ITSELF.

For although many interpretations of these words could be given, I—setting all others aside—believe that Lucius, with these first words, *This is a tomb, having no corpse within*, spoke the literal truth and indicated the reality of the matter: namely, that no vile <note>The author distinguishes between a common "vile" human corpse and the noble alchemical "corpse" or fixed matter.</note> corpse was buried in this tomb. Unless, perhaps, the whole Stone (intended to be multiplied by some other philosopher) was left in its vessel and buried by our Lucius—a possibility that seems to me all the more reason to perform an "anatomy" <note>A thorough investigation or excavation.</note> of that place. In the subsequent and following words, Lucius seems to point directly to this very thing when he says:

> *This is a corpse, having no tomb without*
> *But the corpse is the same as the tomb for itself.*

Indeed, our "matter" <term>res nostra</term> <note>The substance undergoing the alchemical process.</note> is said to be its own tomb. To be brief—for "here lies the hare" <note>original: *in hoc iacet lepus*; a Latin idiom meaning "here is the heart of the matter."</note>—they say: "Bury each thing in the tomb of the other." For since Sulfur, Salt, and Water (or the Sun, Moon, and Mercury) are in our matter, we are commanded to extract, join, bury, and mortify them—that is, to turn them into ash. Thus it happens that the nest becomes a tomb for the birds, and in turn, the birds receive the nest into themselves and coalesce with it. It happens, I say, that soul, spirit, and body; male and female; active and passive—placed in one and the same subject within the vessel, cherished by their own fire and [aided] by external [fire]...

# THE PROCESSES
# FOLLOW

*These are not to be despised, nor are they to be followed literally—whether one considers the matter or the operation—by which the studious investigator (as one book is wont to open another <note>A common alchemical maxim suggesting that one text explains the secrets of another.</note>) will be able to acquire for himself not a few things that pertain to the matter, if not indeed All things, by the favoring grace of God Most High.*

## THE FIRST PROCESS,
->*Which I mentioned at the beginning.*<-

Take two ounces of refined gold <term>obrizi; pure gold that has been tested by fire</term>, mix it with a tenfold amount of Mercury elaborated with great study of the art, and dissolve it with a gentle fire <note>original: *vulcano*; referring to Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and the forge</note>, until the Mercury expires, and the weight of the gold placed within

<page-num>849</page-num>
<header>CHEMICAL PROCESSES</header>

...let it remain, reduced into a black powder, which nevertheless, once melted, cannot be converted back into the former nature of gold. From this powder, by means of fire, draw out the Mercury with the water of a containing vapor, until the powder turns into a snowy calx <note>Calx refers to the powdery oxide or residue left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined."</note>. Sprinkle this seven times with water which has been drawn from it just as many times by evaporation, and work it with all care, so that by this frequent impulse and excursion they may thin themselves out and emerge most pure from all filth and dregs, and receive the power of things above and below, by descending into the earth and ascending again, as is read in the *Emerald Tablet of Hermes* <note>original: *Hermetis smaragdina tabula*; a foundational Hermetic text that describes the relationship between the macrocosm and microcosm.</note>. This water is the Azoth <note>original: *Azoth*; a term for the "universal solvent" or the essential spirit of Mercury believed to be the transformative agent in the Great Work.</note>, the living spirit; the Earth is the ferment. The water is the male, the Earth or calx is the female, from whose embrace the infant is born: the Stone.

But a woman does not conceive at just any time, but only when the womb has been prepared by nature for conception. Therefore, putrefy the purified calx—or the Sun of the philosophers <note>original: *solem philosophorum*; a term for the refined alchemical gold or the perfected matter.</note>—in a sealed vessel, or set it aside to digest for forty days until it melts into a white and thick humor. Into this, at the proper intervals of days, gradually pour the water; this is the joining of the male and female, which are united in a wondrous way, and the female is completely melted by the love of the male; this is the solution. Leave it until it recovers its strength again; then let them come together once more, and do this as many times as necessary until the calx has drunk up all its water. Then let the womb be closed, so that nothing may escape; for then the infant grows, and from that frequent coagulation and solution, the Stone grows. 

The philosophers explain which colors are produced; this powder shows these things to be true. Place it upon Mercury in a new crucible—though in such a way that the Mercury has air—and to two drachms add a twelfth part of a grain. Apply a strong fire, and afterwards add borax; you will have one drachm of gold. If you know the multiplication, you will have no need of the Stone; you will find the complete process with me, if you are fortunate, with all its circumstances—though this one may suffice if you are diligent, for nothing is missing. Farewell, and you are unhappy if you are drawn away from this.

## THE SECOND PROCESS

A certain old leader called Duenec <note>Duenec is an alchemical pseudonym, often interpreted as a representation of antimony or lead, or the "melancholic" stage of matter.</note>, when he saw himself despised in the assembly of the great, and because of his profound melancholy <note>In alchemical allegory, melancholy is associated with the planet Saturn and the metal lead; it represents the heavy, "dead" state of matter before transformation.</note> he was of the lowest authority and held in no respect, he entered into counsel with certain of his more faithful friends, as to how he might guard himself against this atrabilious temperament and clothe himself in the sanguine <note>The "sanguine" temperament was considered the most balanced and noble, representing the transformation into a perfected, "golden" state.</note> temperament, the most excellent of the rest.

Friends having been called to council, and having considered the Duke's riches, they deliberated on summoning the supreme physician Pharut. Having been summoned, he came and was led to the Duke; after greeting him with the respect due to his dignity, the Duke addressed the physician thus: "Pharut, Prince of Physicians, who knows the natures and temperaments of all living things, and as I hear, can change them; you have heard who I am, whom I rule, and how great my lineage is in the whole world. You see this calamity imposed on me by the Gods, that I am overwhelmed by perpetual melancholy <note>In alchemy, melancholy corresponds to the *nigredo* or "blackness," the heavy, initial state of the matter associated with lead and Saturn.</note>, which makes me unpleasant and hateful to all the great ones. For I would gladly rejoice, but the continuous and sad motion of my brain forbids it; I would frequent banquets, but the sorrow of my soul prohibits it, and there is no rest in my heart. From this, O Pharut, come my tears; from this, I say, comes contempt and the perpetual wasting away of my body. If you can change this, if you can renew my temperament, I will ensure you immediately understand how much honor and benefit will come to you."

To this, Pharut replied: "Greatest of Dukes, what you ask of me is serious and difficult to do; however, taught by my own misfortune, I know that the requests of rulers are the same as stern commands. Therefore, to satisfy you, I shall undertake this work—difficult, long, and one that fails almost all who strive to imitate me; however, on this condition: that you be obedient and grateful."

At the appointed time, when the aspect of Saturn was opposite the Sun <note>This astrological timing signifies the opposition of the "dark" metal (Lead/Saturn) to the "bright" metal (Gold/Sun), a crucial moment for beginning the transformation.</note>, Pharut ordered everyone to leave the Duke’s house, except for a certain little fool <note>original: *stultulo*; the fool in alchemy often represents the "First Matter" or a catalyst that remains through the process.</note> dressed in various colors, whom he kept there to entertain the Duke. Then he placed the Duke in a clean bed covered with the whitest linens, and covered him thoroughly so he could not breathe, nor be killed by the smoke of a nearby furnace. He treated the Duke through the ordeal of healing with clear and diaphoretic <term>diaphoretic: a substance used in medicine to induce heavy sweating</term> water. From this, he broke out into foul-smelling sweats, yet they were clear, and they stained the white linens with various spots.

Seeing these things, Pharut blushed with joy. After the Duke no longer belched out foul vapors and the black bile <note>original: *atra bilis*; traditionally the "humor" responsible for melancholy, here representing the impurities of the *nigredo* stage being purged.</note> was dissolved throughout the Duke’s entire body, he prepared a firm little bed with the fool; Pharut adorned it thus: First, he placed a large pillow made of the feathers of a young black eagle <note>The "Black Eagle" is a common alchemical symbol for the volatile spirit or the "mercury of the philosophers" that dissolves the body.</note>, then a bolster of swan feathers <note>The swan represents the *albedo* or "whitening" stage, following the blackness.</note>. He covered these with a blackish cloth and, having carefully lifted the Duke from the first bed, placed him here; he covered him with a very white shroud and closed all the air holes tightly, so that he could not breathe in any way. With the Duke warmed in this new bed, Pharut [anointed] his body and feet with foul oil...

## THIRD PROCESS.

Certain things are so composed by nature that they consist of similar parts, such as all metals; these do not multiply, nor do they grow, unless they are led back to their first matter <note>original: *primam materiam*; the theoretical "prime matter" from which all substances are formed.</note>, which is a water containing fire and salt in its belly. It is necessary to "corrupt" or break down these metals so that Art, imitating Nature, may give birth to a new form. For Art is the rival of Nature; sometimes it surpasses it, as can be seen in the smelting of glass, etc.; but at other times, Art only acts as a handmaid and servant to Nature, so that a weak nature may be assisted and an imperfect one may be perfected. In this, Art acts from the outside and manages the movement, so that Nature, which acts from within, can be led to its own perfection—a thing which Nature herself greatly desires. 

Therefore, take note that our Matter, having been led back to its first origin, must be divided into elements, and these must be doubled: namely, into water and earth. The earth contains fire within itself, while the water contains air. These must be purified <note>original: *depurari*</note> and joined together again so that what is sought may be achieved: namely, peace between enemies <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the stabilization of volatile and fixed elements.</note>. Moreover, to this matter of ours—which is unique and named openly by no one—nothing from the outside is added; for a proper generation does not occur except among things that are compatible in their nature. Only superfluities are to be removed, so that we may use the simpler substance, which is like the "genus of genera," having the "form of forms" within itself. 

For the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> is one; the Medicine is one, the vessel one, the regimen one, and the disposition one—namely, a continuous and slow cooking <note>original: *coctio*; the application of heat to transform the substance.</note> in its own vessel. For it is enough to place the stone in its vessel once and close it, until the whole Mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the completion of the alchemical work.</note> is finished; anything more than this is from error. Therefore, the stone remains continually closed until it has drunk up its own moisture and becomes white; for then...

The blasts of the air do not harm it. When, however, the water has been turned into earth—which usually happens within a space of forty days—add more water. Cook it gently; do not hurry, nor cease from the work. Saturate it as often as it is dried out, but take care that you do not make the <term>belly<gloss>the central part of the substance or the vessel</gloss></term> too liquid. Nevertheless, you shall lead all the water back to its body through its <term>ternaries<gloss>triplets; likely referring to the three principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</gloss></term>. And when one of its ternaries is turned downward and thus "killed," all are dead. 

But this is not done by human hands; rather, Nature itself performs this in a circular fashion, <term>blackening<gloss>original: denigrans; the nigredo stage of decay</gloss></term> itself, <term>whitening<gloss>original: albificans; the albedo stage of purification</gloss></term> itself, and <term>adorning itself with redness<gloss>original: rubore decorans; the rubedo, or final stage of perfection</gloss></term>, until it reaches the end. When all the water is exhausted and turned into earth, let it <term>putrefy<gloss>rot or break down through gentle heat</gloss></term> in its vessel for several days over a mild fire, until a precious white color emerges upon it. In this white color, the spirits are united with the body and are unable to flee. 

Regarding this, we are commanded: "Whiten the <note>original: *lotonem*; likely a reference to the 'washed' or 'purified' matter</note> and break the books." <note>This is a common alchemical maxim suggesting that once the practitioner reaches this stage, they should trust the physical evidence of the work rather than textual authorities.</note> All the colors of the world will appear in it when the blackening moisture has been dried away, before it reaches full whiteness. Therefore, observe diligently how the water coagulates itself, and how the compound is changed from color to color. 

And when it has been adorned with a true whiteness, light a stronger fire. If necessary, let there be fire both below and above for a space of two days, so that everything remains at the bottom and nothing is <term>exalted<gloss>sublimated or evaporated</gloss></term>. For he who—once the <term>whitening<gloss>original: dealbatio</gloss></term> is complete—introduces the soul into it, and fixes the whole thing in a rapid fire after it has been melted, will deserve to be called happy and to be raised above the clouds. 

Therefore, when in the season of summer and fruit a flood of rain corrupts the <term>mastery<gloss>original: magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process</gloss></term>, it is necessary to burn it with a dry fire without fear until it is clothed in a most deep red color. Do not stop, even if the red color is somewhat slow to appear; for just as the first digestion of the stomach whitens everything, so the second digestion of the liver reddens everything. <note>This draws on Galenic medicine, which taught that the stomach turned food into white chyle, and the liver then turned that chyle into red blood.</note> 

Finally, take a part of that well-known <term>stone<gloss>the Philosopher's Stone</gloss></term> and join it with a suitable quantity of the "non-fixed" part and <term>sublimate<gloss>heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</gloss></term> it. Then <term>fix<gloss>make a volatile substance stable under heat</gloss></term> it; and join it again with other non-fixed parts, raise it, fix it, and repeat the process until it achieves an easy fusion, like wax. This is the <term>standing medicine<gloss>original: medicina stans; a stable, perfected substance that does not change further</gloss></term>, tinting and persevering, one part of which turns a thousand thousands of any imperfect body and of <term>common mercury<gloss>original: Mercurij vulgi; ordinary quicksilver as opposed to the 'philosophical' mercury of the alchemists</gloss></term> into the true <term>sun<gloss>original: solem; gold</gloss></term>.

<summary>This page describes the transition from the "black" stage of the alchemical work into the "white" and finally the "red" stage. It provides specific instructions on heat management, the union of spirit and body, and the final "fixation" of the Philosopher's Stone to enable the transmutation of base metals into gold.</summary>
