### ->FOURTH PROCESS<-

The Introit of the mass, to the melody of "Let us rejoice" <note>original: *gaudeamus*</note>, etc., is to be sung. The foundation of the art is truly the solution of bodies, which must be resolved not into cloudy water, but into <term>mercurial water<gloss>the philosophical solvent; the animated "living" mercury of the alchemists</gloss></term>, from which the true <term>philosopher’s stone<gloss>the legendary goal of alchemy, capable of transmutation and healing</gloss></term> is generated.

Verse. The entrance of <term>vitriol<gloss>a metallic sulfate used to create strong acids</gloss></term> and <term>salt of glass<gloss>original: salis vitri; likely sandiver or glass-gall, a byproduct of glassmaking used as a flux</gloss></term> in equal parts, giving witness of the solution: Glory to the Father, and to the Son, through the Holy Spirit.

> Lord <note>original: *Kyrie*</note>, fountain of goodness, inspirer of the sacred art, from whom all good things proceed to your faithful, have mercy.

> 
> Lord, divine fire, aid our hearts, so that for your praise we may likewise unfold the <term>sacraments of the art<gloss>a metaphor comparing the chemical secrets of alchemy to the holy mysteries of the Church</gloss></term>, have mercy.

Glory in the highest, to the mighty God let it be sung to the double tone.

> Collect. God, the giver of all goodness, who especially at the end of times, by your goodness and wisdom alone, has inspired the light of the sacred art of alchemy in your servant N. N. <note>The standard placeholder for a name in liturgical texts</note>, not for his preceding merits, but by your ineffable piety and preventing grace: grant, we pray, that what he has received from the gift of your majesty may benefit the health of his body and soul. Mortify all vices within him and pour in the grace of virtue, so that he may faithfully employ this same sacred art solely for the praise and glory of your name and for the propagation of the Christian faith, through our Lord Jesus Christ, Amen.

Epistle. O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God.

Gradual. Arise, eagle, and come, south wind: blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow.

Verse. He descends like rain upon the fleece, and like droplets falling upon the earth. Alleluia.

O happy creator of the earth, whiter than snow, sweeter than sweetness, fla— <note>The text breaks off mid-word</note>

O Saving Medicine of mankind, which cures every ailment of the body in a short moment, and grants the limit of a long-lasting life; you renew human nature, drive away poverty, bestow riches, restrain sadness, and preserve life in safety. O sublime fountain from which truly gushes the true <term>water of life<gloss>original: aqua vitae; here referring to the universal solvent or the elixir of immortality</gloss></term>, into the estate of your faithful, Alleluia <note>original: *Alleluia*; a song of praise</note>.

The sequence of the holy gospel is to be sung to the tune of "Hail, most brilliant" <note>original: *Ave praeclara*; a famous medieval hymn to the Virgin Mary</note>; which I wish to be called the "Testament of the Art," because the whole chemical art is hidden within it through tropical <note>metaphorical or figurative</note> words, and blessed is he who understands this sequence.

Hail, O beautiful radiance of heaven, radiant light of the world; here you are coupled with the moon; let there be a <term>martial coupling<gloss>a union involving iron or the planet Mars, signifying strength or a specific metallic reaction</gloss></term>, and a conjunction of Mercury. From these three, chiefly through the bed of the river, is born that **strong giant**, whom thousands upon thousands seek through the mastery of the art. These elements are dissolved—not into the water of a cloud, for by that our <term>gum<gloss>original: gummi; a term for the thick, viscous substance during the early stages of the alchemical process</gloss></term> is never refined—but resolved into <term>mercurial water<gloss>the "living" or philosophical mercury used to dissolve gold</term></term>. This, our blessed gum, once dissolved by itself, now bears the name of the "seed of the philosophers." Now, even now, it seeks to be coupled; to be betrothed to the virgin bride, and to impregnate her in the bath through the temperance of fire. But the virgin is not suddenly impregnated unless a kiss is bestowed upon her through frequent embraces; then, she conceives in the <term>matrix<gloss>the womb or the alchemical vessel where the "seed" grows</gloss></term>, and thus a happy offspring is procreated; and this is by the order of nature. Then, at the bottom of the vessel, appears the **strong Ethiopian** <note>original: *Aethiops*; in alchemy, this refers to the *nigredo* or "black stage," the stage of putrefaction and death of the matter</note>, burnt, calcined, discolored in hue, and utterly dead, lacking life. Now he begs to be buried, and to be moistened by his own moisture, and to be gently calcined, until from the strength of the fire he appears most brilliantly white <note>the *albedo* or "white stage," signifying purification</note>. But often he first takes a drink, which entirely climbs to the heavens <note>referring to sublimation, where the substance vaporizes and rises</note>, since he is already well washed by himself in the perseverance of the fire. Now at last he is made pleasing, reborn by his own sweat, and the body, which was previously darkened, is returned washed.

Behold the wonderful regeneration or renewal of the Ethiopian! Henceforth he claims for himself a new name through the **Washing of Regeneration**, which the philosophers call the <term>sulfur of nature<gloss>the active, combustible principle of the stone</gloss></term>, and their son, who is the **Philosopher's Stone**. But behold the "darkening of fools," who are deceived through ignorance of natural philosophy by the various resistances of the fire.

Behold, the thing is one, the root is one, the essence is one, to which nothing foreign is added, but only the superfluous is removed through the mastery of the art. Finally, it seeks to be strengthened, to be fermented by its own nature,

## THE FIFTH PROCESS.

I saw a clarified Old Man rising, holding in his hand a closed book, sealed with seven seals <note>a reference to the Book of Revelation 5:1</note>; and raising my eyes, I saw him covered in white silver garments, overlaid with golden leaves. At the top of his garment was a golden ring, covered with silver, in the circumference of which were written these words: **Spirit, Soul, Body.** From which ring hung seven chains, both of gold and silver

sealed, they surrounded the whole book, and with a backward-looking gaze, revolving through the whole book, they all returned to that ring. Here the old man, when questioned by me what that might signify, responded that the golden ring itself, covered with silver, signifies the **philosopher’s stone**, which in its depth <note>its inner essence or "profundo"</note> is golden and masculine, and in its outward appearance is silvery and feminine. The seven chains revolving around the book are the seven operations <note>the stages of the alchemical process, such as calcination, solution, etc.</note> which surround and complete the entire mastery.

When I questioned the old man about what the writing on the ring signified, he replied: "This writing is wonderful, and it is the entire secret of Philosophy, which is seen to be contained within a short compendium. For the **spirit** denotes <term>Mercury|In alchemy, Mercury represents the volatile, spiritual principle of a substance</term>, which, entering the body itself subtly, brings it to a simple disposition, extracts the **soul** from it and, elevating it upward to the air, carries it away with it. Later, once the body itself is prepared to the nature of the **fifth essence** <note>the *quintessence*, or the purest, most refined state of matter</note>, which is a simple reduction, he pours the soul back in, and the body, embracing it, rejoices with it. Moreover, the soul is that **non-burning sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur non urens*; a technical term for the fixed, stable principle that does not evaporate in fire</note> which congeals the Mercury into a **Lunar** <note>silver</note> or **Solar** <note>gold</note> body, meeting in the place of nature. This soul is the mediatress between body and spirit, and she binds and joins them in an inseparable union. Nor can the spirit be joined with the body except through the soul, which is the <term>tincture|A substance capable of transforming or "coloring" base metals into gold or silver</term> of the Sun and of the Philosophers; for without it, nothing can be done or completed. By these things, understand that our **Sulfur** is not the sulfur of the common people, which is fatty and burning, infecting and corrupting everything. But the **body** denotes the Sun and Moon themselves, which the soul herself rules over, like a form within its subject; and after the separation of the soul, it is called a "dead body," until it becomes perfect through the entering soul; then it is called a "living, immortal, and resurrected body."

Looking again upon this description of the ring, I saw on the first part of the golden chain a Seal with silver letters, saying: *In the warm and moist place me; and from those feed me because I am weak.* Then I asked the Old Man what this meant. He replied that it is the first key, or operation of this stone, which is called **Putrefaction** or **Digestion**, which is done...

I saw finally the second chain, silver at the beginning and golden at the end, and on the silver part was carved a seal with golden letters saying: *Having been lightly digested, I am animated; therefore, exalt me from the heavier things.* And when the Old Man was asked what it was, he said: "That is the seal of the second operation of our stone, which is called <term>Distillation|The process of purifying a substance by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into liquid</term>." The third seal is the third golden chain, written with silver letters saying: *Separate the tincture from the said thing—that is, from the air—and command the air to be exalted through itself in the moist state many times.* This is the third part of this operation.

Then I saw the fifth chain, golden and silver, but black on the surface; and in it was the fifth seal, written with silver letters, saying: *I thirst, I fail, give me drink; and intoxicate and whiten me.* The Old Man, when questioned about these things, replied to me saying that this writing was of great importance, because the inanimate and <term>calcined body|Matter reduced to a fine powder or ash through intense heat</term>, with a part of the animated spirit, is more quickly disposed toward the nature of the <term>fifth essence|original: "essentiæ quintæ"; the quintessence, the purest and most refined state of matter</term>, and reaches it more quickly.

Beholding the sixth chain, both golden and silver, I saw in it the sixth seal, written with golden letters saying: *We are widowed and orphaned, and distanced from our own home; therefore lead us back to it, so that the body, embracing us, may become friendly to us.* To these things, the Old Man, when asked, said: "This is the reduction of water and oil upon the dead body, because the soul cannot..."

# THE FIFTH PROCESS

...can stand without the body, and vice versa; and it is the sixth operation of this mastery.

The seventh and final operation is the seventh chain, both golden and silver, which I saw; in it was the final seal, sealing all things, written in both golden and silver letters, saying: *Gently friendly with fire, act so that water, by its own violence, cannot separate us* <note>original: "Leviter cum igne amicabilis, fac & aqua, sua violentia, nos separare nequeat"</note>. When the Old Man was questioned, he said this was the final stage, namely <term>fixation|the process by which a volatile substance is made stable and fire-resistant</term> and <term>nourishment|the stage where the alchemical "stone" is fed or augmented to increase its power</term>; which is to make the dissolved material fixed, and it is the seventh and final <term>key of the philosophers|A fundamental secret or stage in the Great Work of transformation</term>.

I have chosen to add these five processes for your sake, studious reader, so that those more advanced might judge, use, and enjoy them to the glory of God; while the younger ones, newly initiated into these sacred mysteries, might have something to contemplate, attempt, and experience—yet not without the greatest discernment and care, lest they act, as the saying goes, "against the will of <term>Minerva|The Roman goddess of wisdom; to act "invita Minerva" means to work against one’s natural talent or without divine inspiration</term>"; lest, as the proverb says, they "waste their oil and labor" <note>original: "Oleum, & operam perdant"; a common Latin idiom for wasting time, effort, and money on a fruitless task</note>. 

I could indeed have added more processes to these—and not contemptible ones either, which I keep by me in manuscript form—but these seemed sufficient for now to open an easier path for you toward attaining the "Epitaph" <note>original: "Ephitaphium"; likely referring to the "Epitaph of Hermes," a famous alchemical allegory, or the completion of the work</note>. For these were of no small use to me while I was experimenting with various things, and they opened the way to deeper secrets by the grace of God. If, however, I understand that these labors of mine, such as they are, are welcomed by you, a student of chemistry, then whatever I find hereafter in my philosophical storehouse that can be shared without breaking the celestial seal, I will gladly impart to you in due time, while you enjoy these. Farewell.

### ELEGANT POEM.
->*In the name of the Living and Life-giving God.*<-

->I.<-

Earth gave me my body, fire provided my strength:
I seek a high home, yet my seat is always at the bottom:
And the moisture that quickly leaves me washes over me.

II.

<meta>This page continues the "Chemical Processes" section, moving from the descriptive narrative of the "Fifth Process" into a series of alchemical riddles or enigmas. These poems use paradoxical language to describe the properties of the Prime Matter and the stages of the Great Work.</meta>

<page-num>958</page-num>

# CHEMICAL PROCESSES

### II.

I have tears, yet there is no cause for sorrow:
There is a journey to heaven, but the heavy air hinders me:
And he who fathered me, is not himself born without me.
<note>This riddle likely refers to the "philosophical mercury," which "weeps" as it condenses and mediates between the "father" (sulfur) and the "son" (the stone).</note>

### III.

Fine dust of water, fallen with a slight weight,
Wet in the sun, flowing in summer, dry in the cold,
About to create rivers, I first occupy all the lands.

### IV.

I shall tell you of the wonderful origins of our life:
I was not yet born, nor was I then in my mother’s womb,
Even when the birth was completed, no one saw me born.
<note>This refers to the "hidden" nature of the <term>Prime Matter|The formless, initial substance required for the alchemical work</term>.</note>

### V.

I cannot be born, if I have not killed my mother:
I killed my mother, but the same end awaits me.
My death suffers the same fate that my origin already created.
<note>A common alchemical metaphor where the raw material must be "destroyed" or decomposed (the death of the mother) to produce the refined substance.</note>

### VI.

Life for me is death, I die if I begin to be born:
But the fate of death comes before the origin of light:
Thus I lead the shades themselves as my only parents.

### VII.

I am not great indeed, but the greatest power resides within me,
The <term>spirit|The volatile or gaseous essence of a substance</term> is great, although in a small body,
Nor does my seed have any harm, nor my fault any shame.

### VIII.

We are both stones, we are one, we both lie together:
How sluggish one is, as much as the other is not slow;
This one remains unmoved, that one does not cease to be moved.
<note>This describes the union of the "Fixed" (stable) and the "Volatile" (active) principles, often symbolized by the King and Queen or the Toad and the Eagle.</note>

### IX.

No one can split me, though many can cut me down.
But I am multi-colored, destined eventually to be white.
I prefer to remain black, for I shall fear the final fate less.
<note>This refers to the <term>Nigredo|The 'blackness' or initial stage of decay in the alchemical process</term> which must precede the <term>Albedo|The 'whiteness' or purification stage</term>.</note>

### X.

No form is certain for me, no figure is foreign.
A brilliance is within, shimmering with a radiating light,
Which shows nothing, unless it has seen something before.

### XI.

I do not die immediately while the spirit departs.
For it returns constantly, although it also often recedes:
And for me now there is a great capacity of the soul, now none at all.
<note>This describes <term>circulation|The process of repeatedly vaporizing and condensing a liquid in a sealed vessel to spiritualize the matter</term>.</note>

# THE LITTLE BOOK OF LAMBSPRING, THE NOBLE ANCIENT GERMAN PHILOSOPHER,
## CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE.
<note>Lambspring is a legendary figure in alchemy; his "Little Book" is famous for its beautiful emblems depicting animals like deer, fish, and dragons to symbolize chemical stages.</note>

->*Rendered into Latin from the German verse by Nicolas Barnaud of the Dauphiné, a physician and most devoted student of this science.*<-

My name is Lambspring, born of a noble family,
And I bear this coat of arms with praise and right.
I have read philosophy, and understood it well.
Through the learning of my teachers, I reached the foundation,
Which God in His grace bestowed upon me,
Giving me a spirit with understanding.
Therefore I have become the author of this book,
And I have set it down in this noteworthy order,
So that the poor and the rich may understand.
Truly, nothing like it is found on earth,
In which (God be praised) I have not forgotten myself.
For I have attained the true foundation and the truth:
Therefore, keep this book in silence,
And do not regret reading it often.
In this way you will learn and receive the truth,
And you will turn this great gift of God toward the good.
O God the Father, who art the beginning and the end of all things,
We beseech Thee for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ,

The author, Lambspring, asserts his noble lineage and divine inspiration, positioning his work as a spiritual and practical guide to the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

### ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE
iii
<meta>catchword: FIRST</meta>

That You may enlighten the senses of our reason and our thoughts,
That we may praise and celebrate You without ceasing,
And that we may complete this book according to Your will,
And likewise that You would deign to direct all things toward the good,
And preserve us in Your immense mercy.
May Your Holy Majesty grant this through His immense clemency:

With divine aid, I will recount this art to you,
And I will hide nothing of the upright truth from you.
After you have understood me rightly and well,
At last, you shall be free from your error:
For there is nothing more than one single thing
<note>original: "nihil plus est quam unum" — a core alchemical belief that all matter originates from a single primordial substance, often called the <term>Prima Materia|The formless "first matter" which contains the potential to become any substance.</term>.</note>
In which all things lie hidden.
Therefore, do not lose heart:
For cooking, time, and patience are necessary for you,
If you wish to enjoy the noblest fruits.
Do not let the time and labor grieve you,
For seeds and metals must always be cooked by you in moderation,
<note>original: "coquenda" — <term>Coction|The alchemical process of slow, constant heating, often compared to digestion or the incubation of an egg.</term></note>
Day by day and for several weeks.
Then, in this single, cheap thing
<note>original: "vili re" — A common alchemical trope is that the Stone's source is a "vile" or common substance that the ignorant would step over in the street.</note>
You will find and perfect the entire work of philosophy.
This indeed seems so impossible to all men,
Since it is such an easy and lowly labor.
But if we were to show it to others and bring it to light,
We would be laughed at by men, women, and children.
Therefore, be modest and secret;
Then you will be in peace and without care,
Namely toward God and your neighbor,
Who gives the art and wishes it to be hidden.
Now we will omit the preface
And begin to describe the true art;
And in rhymes and figures, truly and plainly,
Without trifles or lies, we shall bring it to light,
Giving thanks to the Creator of every creature.
And now follows the first figure.

## THE FIRST FIGURE.

->Pay close attention and understand rightly that two fish<-
->swim in our sea.<-

->*The sea is the body; the two fish are the spirit*<-
->*and the soul.*<-

The Philosophers say in general,
That there are two fish in our sea,
Without any flesh or bones.
Let these be cooked in their own water:
Then from them shall come a vast sea,
Which no man can describe in words.
This is the decree of the philosophers:
The two fish are but one, this is the truth;
Yet they are two and nonetheless one
Body, spirit, and soul.
<note>original: "Corpus, spiritus, & anima" — The alchemical triad. Alchemists believed that for the "Stone" to be created, these three aspects of matter must be separated and then perfectly reunited.</note>
Now certainly I say to you:
Cook these three together,
So that it may be the greatest Sea.
Afterward, it will be made known to you
When you have received great increase.
Therefore, cook sulfur with sulfur well,
<term>Sulfur|In this context, sulfur refers not just to the chemical element, but to the active, "combustible" soul or essence of a substance.</term>
And do not speak many words about that matter.
Keep silent and hide these things for your own great benefit,
Thus you will be free from all poverty.
Restrain your mouth well;
Thus your labor will be known to no one.

## THE SECOND FIGURE.

->Here, observe quickly the black beast<-
->in the forest.<-

->*Putrefaction.*<-
<term>Putrefaction|Also known as the "Nigredo" or blackening; a stage where the material is broken down by heat, symbolizing death and the stripping away of impurities.</term>

The philosopher says at present
That there is a beast in the forest,
Completely covered in blackness.
If anyone cuts off its head,
Then it will lose its blackness entirely;
And it will choose the whitest color.
If you desire the true understanding of this,
The blackness is called the head of the raven.
<note>original: "caput corvi" — <term>Caput Corvi|The "Raven's Head," a classic alchemical symbol for the dark, chaotic beginning of the Great Work.</term></note>

As soon as this [the blackness] has vanished,

This then at last is called the "one stripped of its head"
<note>original: "capite spoliatum" — This refers to the alchemical stage where the "black head" of the crow (the symbol for the initial stage of decay) is removed, signaling the transition to the white stage, or *albedo*.</note>
When the black cloud has perished, believe me.

# THE THIRD FIGURE.

->Next, know without worry that in the forest<-
->the deer and the unicorn hide.<-

->*In the body are the soul and the spirit.*<-

The Philosophers say stoutly,
That there are two animals in this forest;
One is praiseworthy, beautiful, and swift:
A great and robust deer.
The other is a unicorn, as the Philosopher shows:
These two hide entirely within the forest.
But blessed shall that man be called
Who shall snare and capture them.
The masters, with clear words,
Signify to us here and in all places
That these two animals wander in the forests.
(Yet understand the "forest" as a single thing.)
But if we look to the foundation,
Then the forest shall receive the name of the "Body."
<term>Body|In alchemical theory, the "body" is the physical matter or the vessel that holds the volatile "soul" and "spirit" during the transformation process.</term>
Then also, surely and rightly, it will be found
That the Unicorn is the Spirit at every hour;
The Deer, indeed, desires no other name
Than the Soul: a name which no one shall take from it.
Now it is also right that he be called a Master,
Who by that art shall lead and restrain them,
To lead them into the forest and bring them out again.

### THE FOURTH FIGURE.

->out of two lions.<-

Faithfully the philosophers teach us
That two robust lions walk,
Namely the Male and the Female, in a dark and horrible valley.

Horrible, with a cruel face and appearance,

<note>In alchemical symbolism, the two lions represent the volatile and fixed principles (often sulfur and mercury). ### THE SIXTH FIGURE.

This is truly a great miracle and a clever deception: that in the poisonous dragon the supreme medicine exists.

*Mercury correctly and chemically precipitated, or sublimated, and dissolved in its own water, and coagulated again.*

A horrendous dragon inhabits the forest,
Supremely poisonous; it lacks nothing.
When it sees the rays of the sun and the bright fire,
Then it pours out its poison and flies so monstrously
That no living animal can stand before it;
Even the <term>Basilisk</term><note>The Basilisk was a legendary serpent-king said to kill with a single glance. Here, the dragon is described as even more formidable.</note> itself is not its equal.
He who knows how to wisely kill it
Will escape from all dangers.
All veins and colors are increased in its death,
And from its poison is made the supreme medicine.
It suddenly consumes its own poison,
For it devours its own poisonous tail. <note>This describes the "Ouroboros" or tail-eater, a symbol of the cyclical nature of the alchemical work and the "fixing" of the volatile substance by its own power.</note>
All these things it is forced to accomplish in itself,
And a laudable balsam then flows from it.
At last, they will see these powers,
And wonderfully all the wise shall rejoice over these things.

### THE SEVENTH FIGURE.

Two birds are named in the forest, yet only one is to be understood.

*Mercury, having been frequently sublimated, is finally fixed, and can no longer escape or fly away through the power of fire. For the sublimation must be repeated until it becomes fixed.*

A nest is found in the forest
In which <term>Hermes</term><note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy. His "chicks" represent the chemical components in the early stages of the Great Work.</note> has his chicks.
One always tries to fly,
The other delights to stay in the nest,
And the one does not let go of the other. <note>The bird that stays represents the "fixed" principle (solid), while the bird that flies represents the "volatile" principle (gas/vapor). Their struggle and eventual union represent the stabilization of the matter so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>

### THE EIGHTH FIGURE.

*Let the body be placed again for digestion in horse manure <note>original: "fimum equinum." Through this operation, the body has become white; but the spirit has become red by the alchemist's art. In India <note>Alchemical texts often refer to "India" or "the East" as a metaphorical land of origin for hidden wisdom.</note> is found a most pleasant forest,
In which two birds are bound together:

This power was given to it by God,
That it might live forever in the future and never die.
It has acquired for us riches and a safe life,
So that through this we may perform great miracles,
Just as the true philosophers clearly describe to us.

### THE TENTH FIGURE

->The Salamander lives in the fire, and the fire has changed<-
->this creature into the best color.<-

*Reiteration, gradation, and improvement of the tincture or of the stone of the philosophers; or rather, let it be understood as augmentation.* <note>Augmentation refers to the process of increasing the quantity or the potency of the Alchemical Stone after it has been created.</note>

All the fables tell us these things:
That the Salamander <note>In alchemical lore, the Salamander is a symbol of the "fixed" or "incombustible" part of the matter that can withstand the highest heat of the furnace without being destroyed.</note> arises from the fire,
In which it has its food and life,

The Salamander traverses all of these and is cleansed in them;
From here it hastens to its pit,
And on the journey itself it is captured and pierced through,
So that it dies and gives up its life with its blood.

### The Ancient
# FRENCH PHILOSOPHER OF
# the Dauphiné, anonymous
### BOOK
## OF THE GREATEST SECRET OF ALL
## worldly glory.

Divine aid must be implored in even the smallest matters. What then, dearest son, must we do in the difficult and greater affairs of this world? And since it is so that our intention revolves around the greatest and grandest secrets of the world—as shall be demonstrated through logic below—therefore, invoking the immense goodness of God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, we shall begin in His name and that of our Savior, with His Spirit leading us. In the year 1447, on Monday the 7th of January, on the day following the usual festivities <note>The author is referring to the day after Epiphany, or Three Kings Day, a major feast in the medieval calendar.</note> held in our kingdom—as it is our custom among us to rejoice in commemoration of those faithful kings who, with joyful hearts, came from various lands to one place to worship our Lord and Savior—I have decided to depict with my pen and reveal the secrets that have usually been handed down under a veil and in a nearly hopeless form. Yet I do so in such a way that those who are clever and initiated into these matters may profit from this little work and fully acquire worldly glory. However, I exhort you not to abandon eternal glory for things that pass quickly away from you, knowing that all corruptible things ought to be left behind for the sake of the incorruptible. 

With this preface, for the benefit of all faithful Christians—especially our Lord King Louis <note>While Louis XI became King in 1461, in 1447 he was the Dauphin (prince); the author may be writing retrospectively or using the title as a mark of high respect.</note>, the most serene Lady Queen his consort, and their son, my Lord the firstborn Dauphin—we say that there are seven planets, seven days, and seven metals; although, as far as I am concerned, I count only six, namely those which can be extended under the hammer <note>The author is referring to the "malleable" metals (Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead), excluding Mercury from the count of finished metals.</note>. These [metals] and those [planets] are known, and the former are named after the latter due to the influence and participation between them. Mercury <term>Mercurius: Quicksilver. In alchemy, it represents the fluid, passive, and material principle of all metals.</term>, however, is not properly a metal, but the principle of metal; and that which is the principle of something is not the whole thing itself. For Mercury serves as their matter, while sulfur <term>Sulphur: The active, masculine, and "fiery" principle that acts upon Mercury to create specific metals.</term> serves as their form. Indeed, we have seen metallic bodies, with the witness of our own eyes, resolved into Mercury and multiplied within it; but Mercury will never be a metal unless it has been coagulated by the power of sulfur. By "sulfureity," we mean every natural heat—

...is twice necessary, for that reason we say quite often that this is not the **Mercury of the common people** <note>original: "Mercurius vulgi"; refers to ordinary quicksilver used in trade, which alchemists believed lacked the "philosophical" spark needed for transformation</note>. Because just as the smallest parts of dry earth are overcome by the addition of water and by thorough mixing—as is evident in the work of a potter—similarly our earth, or our sulfur, is divided into the smallest particles when it is thickened by the addition of its own water. This water is the raw, clean Mercury extracted from the mineral; for quicksilver itself is infinitely more piercing and penetrating than the **strong waters** <note>original: "aquae fortes"; corrosive acids like nitric acid</note> of the **sophists** <note>here meaning "false alchemists" or "deceivers"</note>, which you must avoid.

Similarly, quicksilver, as it is seen by the common people, is very volatile, mobile, cold, moist, and white; yet in its hidden interior, it is hot, harsh, terrible, and is proven to be a **deep red** <note>original: "rubetum"; likely referring to the red oxide or a "toad-like" earthy state in the process</note>. It is also a "white fire," and metallic bodies are melted and liquefied through it much faster than by the fire of a furnace, as is shown by experience. Likewise, it is turned into red through our **procedure** <term>regimen</term> <note>the specific, controlled sequence of heating and cooling in the alchemical process</note>. Furthermore, it is fixed by its own power with the help of our sulfur, which is our fire. This itself is the work of nature, and its virtues are not seen; for that reason, they are not recognized by the common people.

Let there be a window wide enough, positioned above the furnace, so that in times of necessity you can see your actions and recognize the colors appearing in the work. ...of one foot or more. Let there be an iron grate in the middle, round in shape, and four flue-channels arranged in a cross <note>original: "quatuor viæ in cruce ventriculares"; likely referring to air vents or heat channels arranged in a cruciform pattern to ensure even heating</note> corresponding to the said furnace, running from the outer edges to the said grate. In one corner of the said furnace, there shall be a sufficiently thick channel, always filled with coals, as high as the length of one reed <note>a "canna" or reed was a historical unit of measure, often around 5 to 10 feet depending on the region</note>, or five feet, or more or less, corresponding to the grate. In the circumference of the grate, there shall be four earthen hoods <note>original: "capellæ"</note> in the shape of **alembics** <note>the teardrop-shaped glass or ceramic lids used in distillation</note>. In the middle, there shall be one hood; however, unlike the others, it shall hang in the air, while the other four will rest upon the foundation. The fire shall be made as described, and the mouth of the furnace shall be opposite the coal-channel (namely, in the corner). There shall also be the necessary iron instruments for cleaning the grate and for extracting the ashes.

There is, however, one **regimen** <note>a "regimen" is a specific set of rules or stages in the alchemical process</note>: namely, that the substance be placed in its own vessel and in its own furnace, and be cooked continually without interruption. **Take** <note>original: "℞," the symbol for "recipe"</note> one pound of the best **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note>, and let it be placed in a mortar with coarse salt and the best vinegar, and let it be incorporated into the form of a paste. Then, by sprinkling it with warm water, **revive** it <note>original: "viuifica"; refers to the process of cleaning the metal so it regains its bright, "living" luster</note>. Do this two or three times until its blackness vanishes. Finally, cause it to pass through leather <note>squeezing mercury through chamois or soft leather was a common way to filter out solid dross</note>, and it will come through like milk. Then, into one ounce of **our sulfur** <note>alchemists used "our" to distinguish their secret prepared materials from common minerals</note>, put four ounces of Mercury. Place this in a glass vessel sealed with the **seal of Hermes** <note>original: "sigillo Hermetis"; a "hermetically sealed" glass neck, melted shut to prevent any vapors from escaping</note>. Then, let it be placed in its secret furnace, and let the fire be kindled there. It multiplies, it grows, and it is made into a flowing fountain of wisdom. Oh, well said! The sea of wisdom ebbs and flows; it boils and it rests. If you wish to act safely, always act with patience; continue, and do not let the work weary you. You must not hasten, nor cease from the work, until the whole assumes the form of a **dry stone**. For since it is **fixed sulfur**—a coagulant already coagulated—it naturally coagulates its own Mercury through long and frequent **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects again as a solid</note> over it. Therefore, guard these: namely, the earth and the water; for when the water is mixed with the earth, the earth absorbs it with its dryness, thickens it with its tenacity, and makes the water like itself through its own density. This is because every dry thing naturally desires its own moisture. For this reason, **delay** and **tempering** are said to be necessary in the **mastery** <note>original: "magisterio"; the "Magistery" or the "Grand Operation" of the alchemists</note> of the philosophers. Nature cannot bypass its own movement unless it is hindered by haste. Therefore, ensure that all things are **dissolved**, and take care lest the spirits flee through the violence of the fire, for then the whole mastery would be lost. Know, dearest son, that our whole mastery is nothing other than making a right solution and...

BOOK OF THE GREATEST SECRETS.

...perfect solidification <note>original: "congelationem"</note>. Dissolve our stone, and afterward solidify it, and let nothing more be sought. The humidity of our stone is dried out little by little through habitual exposure to its own fire. In our stone, there are only two things, and they are of one nature: one is dry and firm and incombustible; the other is moist, volatile, and incorruptible. Therefore, it is necessary that these two be tempered together so that one does not leave the other. For if you wished to provide heat according to the needs of the fixed thing <note>the "fixed" or stable part of the matter</note>, the volatile thing would not be able to endure it; and if you wished to provide heat according to the needs of the volatile thing, the fixed thing would always be dulled by the coldness of the other, and the work would never be perfected. It is necessary to provide heat according to the motion of the whole, namely of the entire compound, so that everything may be dissolved and become one permanent water. Therefore cook, cook, and cook again; and let not the long cooking weary you; be long-suffering, patient, and constant, and insist only on the completion, disregarding all else.

The first color of our stone after a good continuation, when it begins to coagulate, will be black <note>this stage is traditionally called the "Nigredo" or blackness</note>, and it will last for forty days; and then the stone will be made white <note>the "Albedo" or whitening stage</note>. And then the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol," representing Gold</note> will work with its white sulfur, converting **Mercury** into pure **Moon** <note>original: "Lunam," representing Silver</note>. And if it has a greater digestion <note>a "digestion" refers to the prolonged application of gentle heat</note>, it will work with its red sulfur, converting Mercury into the best gold. By this, you ought to consider that the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> is a hermaphroditic body—that is, containing within itself two virtues, the Lunar and the Solar—because gold was silver before it was gold.

Note, however, that once our matter is fixed at the white stage, it can never be destroyed by fire; and therefore you can give it as much fire as you wish, because its <term>tincture</term> <note>the coloring or transforming power of the stone</note> will always be improved in the process, and it will be made most red, like parched blood or the syrup of pomegranates. If you wish to <term>multiply</term> <note>the process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical agent</note> it with the ferment from which it came in the beginning, the whole will be converted in thirty days into a pure medicine, white or red according to what the ferment was. Finally, you shall take one ounce of its powder and cast it upon ten <note>ounces</note> of any metal, and it will be pure gold or pure silver. Again, you shall take one ounce and cast it upon that which is already converted, and it will be pure medicine. And you shall repeat this as often as the medicine flows like wax or oil; and then it is called oil of gold, **drinkable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary medicine thought to grant longevity</note>, balsam, the fountain of life and the river of paradise, the treasure of the whole world, and the hidden secret.

Of our art, only one thing exists, to which, as much in the beginning as in the end, nothing external is added that is foreign to its nature: and it is the nature of the purest quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi", literally "living silver" or mercury</note>, from whose smoky resolution—both in the bowels of the earth and in the philosophical vessel <note>original: "alveolo", a small trough or cavity</note>—an oily vapor is generated. <header>EXTRACT</header>

<margin>Opinion —</margin>
The philosophers describe various stages, namely sublimation <note>the process of turning a solid into vapor through heat</note>, distillation, calcination <note>burning a substance to a fine powder</note>, solution, coagulation, fixation <note>making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, and ceration <note>softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency</note>. Yet the stone is one, the medicine is one, the vessel is one, the furnace is one, and the labor and operation are one: and thus the philosophers have always spoken of "the one," commending unity and rejecting diversity. For it happens to those who spend their lives in travel that they have many lodgings but no true friendships. A plant that is moved too often does not grow strong. A wound to which frequent and different medicines are applied does not form a scar. When our "body" is placed in "water" <note>the alchemical solvent or "mercury"</note> to be dissolved, it immediately turns black; and it is also immediately separated into its smallest parts, immediately calcinated, immediately dissolved, and sublimated. Through dissolving and sublimating, it is joined with the spirit. If there should be anything foreign mixed into the body, it will not dissolve, but will remain at the bottom of the vessel; and all of this happens in a single hour. At the end of the mastery <note>original: "magisterij", the completion of the Great Work</note>, the soul rises and abandons its body, and the body itself remains totally dead at the bottom of the vessel. If you do not return the soul to the body by means of the spirit and the will of the practitioner—and if you are ignorant of this "key"—then you are in despair, and the entire mastery is hidden from you. Once you have seen the "Whiteness," cool your work, for by cooling the Moon <note>original: "Lunam", representing silver or the white stage</note> you will find the heat of the Sun <note>original: "Solis", representing gold or the red stage</note>. Stay near the vessel and behold the wonders, for it turns white and yellow faster than in three hours of this day; yet the germination of this thing is green. If you see this suddenly, wonder, fear, and terror will come upon you; for at last, a Whiteness will appear that surpasses all the whitenesses of the world.

### The Whole Art.

<margin>brevity +</margin>
**T**herefore, receive in the name of the Lord our Bronze <note>original: "Æs", likely referring to the base metallic matter</note>, which you must join with "nine eagles" <note>a symbol for nine sublimations or nine parts of volatile mercury</note>. Grind it so that it becomes entirely spiritual <note>vaporous or refined</note> without any remaining dregs. Place it in its vessel and set it in the furnace so that it adheres immovably to it. Then the "blackness of putrefaction" <note>original: "nigredo putrefactionis", the first major stage of the work</note> will appear and dominate for a long time. After the blackness, whatever color appears is praiseworthy. I ask that you cook it without ceasing, and perform the "work of women" <note>original: "opus mulierum", a traditional term for a simple, patient process like cooking or washing that requires gentle heat</note> until it begins to sprout in a green color. Then, by means of the spirit, return the flying soul to its body from which it first departed, so that it may be joined to it in a most white color; once joined, let it be cooled. Now you have the perfect stone, fearing neither fire nor air, which—once formed and fixed—you may lead forth by fermenting it from both sides: the fixed into the volatile, and the volatile into the fixed. Guide it, then, until it is reduced to ash and turns red, having the color of burnt blood, or...

...of the dragon, or of aloe, or of the liver <note>original: "epatis," likely referring to "hepar sulfuris" or liver of sulfur, a liver-colored chemical compound</note>. And cast it upon the body whose generation you wish to obtain, and cast this upon other imperfect bodies. Therefore, in our work, the body must become spirit by means of dissolution, and conversely, the spirit must become body by means of coagulation. In this way, the body acquires fluidity from the power of the spirit, and the spirit acquires stability <note>original: "fixionem," the ability to withstand fire without evaporating</note> from the power of the body; and in this lies the perfection of the art. Dissolve, coagulate, and tinge <note>to "tinge" is to transform the color and nature of a metal, usually to gold or silver</note>, and you shall have what you desire. Our stone has a spirit, a soul, and a body; it is a stone, yet not a stone. If you dissolve it, it is dissolved. If you coagulate it, it is coagulated. If you make it fly, it flies. It is, moreover, volatile, white, hollow, deceptive, and hairless, which no man can touch with his tongue. If you say it is water, you speak the truth. If you say it is not water, you lie. In the philosophical work, the raw mineral spirit is joined like water with its own body, dissolving it in the first decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid</note>: It is then called the <term>Rebis</term> <note>From the Latin "res bis," meaning "a double thing," representing the union of opposites like male and female or spirit and body</note>.

### THE SECRET OF THE PHILOSOPHERS,
#### formerly written in hexameter verse
#### by a most learned man.

->*In the name of the living and life-giving God.*<-

<margin><unclear>to carry up twice</unclear></margin>
->I.<-
The earth provided me a body, the fire provided me strength,
I seek a high home, yet my seat is always in the depths:
And a moisture drenches me, which quickly deserts me.

->II.<-
I have tears, but there is no cause for sorrow:
The path is toward heaven, but the heavy air hinders me:
And he who fathered me is not born without me.

->III<-
A thin powder of water, falling with little weight,
Moist in the sun, flowing in summer, dry in the cold;
About to create rivers, I first occupy all the lands.

->IV.<-
I shall relate to you the wondrous beginnings of our life:
I was not yet born, nor was I then in my mother's womb;
Even when the birth was completed, no one saw me as a newborn.

->V.<-
I cannot be born, if I do not kill my mother:
I have killed my mother, but the same end awaits me.
My death suffers that which my origin has already done.

### VI.
My life is death; I die if I begin to be born:
But the fate of destruction <note>original: "lethi," referring to Lethe, the river of forgetfulness or death</note> comes before the origin of light:
Thus I consider the spirits of the dead alone to be my parents.

### VII.
Indeed I am not large, but within me is the greatest power,
My spirit is great, though in a small body,
My seed holds no harm, nor does any fault bring a blush <note>In alchemy, the "blush" or "redness" (ruborem) often refers to the final stage of the work, but here it implies a lack of shame or impurity</note>.

### VIII.
We are both stones, we are one, we both lie down:
As sluggish as one is, so active the other goes;
This one remains unmoved, while that one never stops moving <note>This refers to the "fixed" and "volatile" principles in alchemy—substances that resist fire and those that evaporate or change</note>.

### IX.
None can split me, though many can cut me off.
But I change colors, destined to be white at some time.
I prefer to remain black; I shall fear the final fates less <note>The "black" stage (nigredo) represents the initial state of putrefaction or "death" of the matter, which must occur before it can be purified into the "white" stage (albedo)</note>.

### X.
No shape is certain for me, yet no shape is foreign.
Within is a brilliance, flashing with radiant light,
Which shows nothing, unless it has seen something before <note>This likely describes the reflective or mirror-like quality of purified mercury or the "glass" of the philosophers</note>.

### XI.
I do not die immediately while the spirit departs.
For it returns constantly, although it also often withdraws:
And now I have a great capacity for life <note>original: "animae," soul or breath of life</note>, and now none at all.

### XII.
I have endured more than one body ought.
I had three souls, all of which I held within.
Two have departed, but the third has almost followed.

It cannot be denied more clearly than by saying, No.
And it cannot be affirmed more clearly than by saying, Yes.
To whom it has not been given, he does not understand. For every gift is from on high <note>This reflects the common alchemical belief that the "Great Work" is a *Donum Dei* (Gift of God) and cannot be mastered by intellect alone</note>.

->*You will seek much and you will not find,*<-
->*Perhaps you will find when you are not seeking.*<-

# OF NICOLAUS BARNAUD
### By
### Christa Arnaud of Dauphiné, philosopher and physician
## A BRIEF ELUCIDATION
### of that
## SECRET OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

->In the name of the living and life-giving God.<-

The author begins, whoever he may be, with an invocation of the most high God, as is fitting and becomes a Christian man.

<margin>Psalm 25</margin>
> *But is there anyone anywhere who dedicates himself to God?*
> *Rare indeed, but he is blessed.*
> *For whoever is of this kind shall have the most high God*
> *as Master and Guide,*
> *who may show him the way he should choose for himself.*

Let no one ever think he can attain this rule unless God inspires him, or a teacher instructs him, or through manifold experience with the greatest labors and no small expense. Now he begins to narrate entirely in riddles, as much as is permitted, the acquired knowledge of the philosophers' secret, saying:

*The earth is my body*] The author introduces Mercury speaking through personification <note>original: "prosopopoeiam," a rhetorical device where an abstract thing or inanimate object is represented as a person</note>—not indeed as the Mercury used for preparing or dissolving our substance, but as the one who dyes it and is himself dyed. He affirms that his body is earth, as it truly is; earth, I say, in the beginning and in itself dead, but toward the end of the work revived and glorified. He begins to teach the path of this glory by which he arrives at it, saying:

*Fire has provided my strength*] For it is fire that prepares the body for dissolution <term>dissolution: the breaking down of a solid into a liquid state, a key first step in alchemical work</term>, without which nothing happens; it is fire that coagulates, that dyes and fixes <note>In alchemy, "fixing" means making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note>, and completes the entire work. However, this should not be understood as just any fire, but as the natural fire that resides within every thing, which is also called the "sulfur" of the body in this matter, though it is invisible. By its benefit—mixed in its Mercury (which is also fire) and assisted by a gentle external fire—the substance is dissolved, digested, killed, and awakened, finally emerging crowned with glory and honor. Meanwhile, he says:

*I seek a high home*] For the soul ascends from the earth into the heavens while it is being cooked, with the spirit as its leader and the help of the external fire, which they call the fire "of the Sun."

*My seat is always in the depths*] Because it descends again into the earth, which

<meta>This page continues the "elucidation" by Nicolaus Barnaud, specifically interpreting a series of alchemical riddles through the lens of the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus. It connects the physical processes of distillation and sublimation to a symbolic "journey to heaven."</meta>

...is called the nurse by Hermes <note>original: "nutrix ab Hermete vocatur." This refers to the line from the Emerald Tablet: "The earth is its nurse."</note>. This ascent and descent, however, is nothing other than the primary part of the philosophers' **sublimation** and **distillation**. It follows:

*[And the moisture which quickly leaves me drenching me]* Since Mercury <term>Mercury: In alchemy, this is not just the liquid metal (quicksilver) but the "spirit" or volatile principle of the matter</term> ascends very swiftly, he is said to leave the earth; but when he descends in the same way, seeking the earth, he is said to drench it. Thus says Hermes in the *Emerald Tablet*: "It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and so it receives the power of the things above and the things below" <note>original: "ascendit à terra in cælum, iterumque descendit in terram, & ita recipit vim superiorum & inferiorum"</note>.

*[Tears are mine, indeed they are mine]* Namely, while I descend from the sky to the earth—that is, when I am carried downward after many sublimations—I seem to myself to shed tears.

*[But there is no cause for sorrow]* On the contrary, I rejoice greatly in that matter, and I congratulate myself because those very tears strive to renew and expand me, and to extract my **tincture** <term>tincture: the potent, concentrated essence capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold</term>.

*[There is a journey to heaven]* Arnald of Villanova <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist</note> in the second chapter of the book *Of the New Light*, says of this journey to heaven:

> Let attention be paid to this, for in this elevation—if it be done correctly—something permanent is found, which must be brought by force above the overflowing volatile; that is, it must be raised, and what has been raised must be returned to the part which remains from the same, until the fugitive becomes whole. Then the aforementioned earth remains from both, converted into a hard, very lemon-yellow stone. Nor is that aforementioned volatility sufficient until the entire mass of the aforementioned stone, raised by fire and returned to its vessel, continuously ascends through the same, so that nothing unclean or filthy remains from it at the bottom of the vessel. When it is thus most perfectly elevated, that which is held by Hermes will be fulfilled in the completion of the philosophical work: *It ascends gently with great skill from the earth to the heaven*, as was said by us above.

But, so that our speech may return to where it digressed, I cannot help but wonder how it came into the mind of this thing of ours to say the journey to heaven is a cause of sorrow to itself. For since every thing desires to be perfected, and the journey to heaven aims at perfection, it is a wonder, I say, that our Mercury (who acknowledges heaven itself as his parent) does not instead greatly desire it. He adds the cause, saying:

*[But the heavy air hinders me]* As if he were saying: "Gradually, and by the hour, helped by my native fire and that of my brother <note>The alchemical "brother" often refers to Sulfur or a stabilizing agent that works with Mercury</note>, and assisted by external fire, I am made heavier, hastening toward **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term>. Therefore, since the feathers of the wings of my brother (whom he calls both father and sire) are nearly consumed, I am hindered from that easy ascent which would have been more familiar to me in the beginning." It follows:

> *[And he who begat me is not born without me.]* <note>original: "Et qui me genuit sine me non nascitur ipse."</note>

For neither can the dissolving **Mercury** <term>Mercury: In alchemy, the "spirit" or volatile principle, often acting as a solvent</term>, who may be called the father, be discerned or seen without the **Sulfur** <term>Sulfur: The "soul" or fixed principle that provides color and stability; here identified as the "tinging Mercury"</term>, who calls himself the offspring here. This is because they have now become one thing, as appears in the first conjunction. Furthermore, there are metals from which, in which, with which, and through which—as Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous physician who emphasized the "Three Primes": Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt</note> also testifies—perfect metals are made. These are, I say, hermaphroditic bodies <note>A reference to the alchemical Rebis, a figure combining male and female traits to represent the union of opposites</note>, as that ancient poem concerning Jupiter testifies:

->*Almighty Jupiter is called both father and mother.*<- <note>original: "Iuppiter omnipotens genitor, genitrixq; vocatur."</note>

Therefore, what can be said of Mercury also seems to be said of Sulfur, and vice versa. For this substance of which the philosophers speak is nothing other than *sulphureous Mercury* and *mercurial sulfur*. In this dual thing, which is yet a single thing, Sulfur acts as the male, while Mercury acts as the female. Again, the former holds the place of the father, the latter the place of the son, in one and the same body. Since both are of an indivisible society—both the begetter and the begotten—they are said to be born and to come forth together. But he continues, saying:

> *[A fine powder of water fallen with small weight, / Dripping in the Sun, flowing in summer, dry in the cold.]* <note>original: "Puluis aquæ tenuis modico cum pondere lapsus, Sole madens, æstate fluens, in frigore siccus."</note>

Here he calls it "powder," which he previously called "moisture" and "tears," about which enough has been said above. He makes this powder "dripping in the Sun" and "flowing in summer," so that you may see with how light a fire our work is accomplished; for when the fire is silent, the powder dries. Who, I ask, has ever seen such a powder?

> *[About to make rivers, I first occupy all lands]* <note>original: "Flumina facturus totas prius occupo terras"</note>

Unless this Mercury is excellently mixed and—as they say—**amalgamated** with the "body" in the proper proportion, and placed in its vessel and furnace as is fitting, and cooked with the **fire of Egypt** <term>fire of Egypt: A term for the gentlest, most constant heat, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen or the sun's natural heat</term>, it can never be seen as standing water, nor occupy the "earths." I believe we must strictly conclude, along with almost all philosophers, that only two "earths" of one kind are present in our work. It follows:

> *[I shall tell you of the wondrous beginnings of our life]* <note>original: "Mira tibi referam nostræ primordia vitæ"</note>

Here our Mercury seems to open up about his origins, wanting to say who or what kind of thing he is. Yet he does nothing of the sort, unless perhaps he begins in his usual way, enigmatically. Meanwhile, he prepares to relate the beginnings of his life, which are indeed admirable. Since he says here that he was a participant in "life," who would not at least count him among the class of living beings? Especially when one hears from the philosophers that he [possesses] a body,

...to have soul and spirit. But what, I ask, if he should finally hear of this substance: that it not only lived, but was even born again, and from its resurrection imparted everlasting life to its brothers <note>In alchemical terms, the "brothers" usually refer to the "base" or "imperfect" metals (like lead or tin) which are "perfected" into gold by the Stone.</note>; likewise to plants, that they might be forever green; and indeed to us poor mortals, that we might enjoy a healthy and sound life under the hand of God, if we grant that it can be used in the proper dosage. What, I say, would he say of such a great matter, which the true philosophers <term>Philosophers: In this context, "philosophers" refers to alchemists, the "philosophers by fire."</term> treat? Would he not candidly confess it to be a heavenly and almost divine secret? Furthermore, the substance itself proceeds, speaking of itself:

> *[I was not yet born, nor was I then in my mother’s womb]* <note>original: "Nondum natus eram, nec eram tum matris in aluo"</note>

How could it happen that he was born, who was not yet in his mother's womb? In this place, as the following parts also seem to show, the author hints that it is **Sulfur** <term>Sulfur: The active, masculine principle of "soul" in the alchemical work.</term> of which he speaks, which is most often used in the place of **Mercury**, and vice versa, as we touched upon above. This Sulfur, remaining in the form of a vapor, had not yet entered the womb of its own vaporous Mercury. These things especially regard the generation which is done by nature alone in the mountains and subterranean places; since that generation precedes the one where nature is the servant of art <note>The alchemical "Art" or "Great Work" seeks to speed up and perfect the slow natural processes occurring deep within the Earth.</note>, and because the latter emulates the former, these things can be said and interpreted concerning both.

> *[Now that the birth is complete, no one saw me born]* <note>original: "Iam posito partu natum me nemo videbat"</note>

Whether it was in the tunnels of the earth and the element of water, in which it is certain that minerals and metals are born, or in the philosophical vessel <note>The "alueolo philosophico" refers to the glass flask or "philosopher's egg" used in laboratory work.</note>, in which the union and generation happen invisible to the blink of an eye.

> *[I cannot be born if I do not kill my mother]* <note>original: "Non possum nasci si non occidero matrem"</note>

The author returns to this; and he says these things concerning the beginning of the extraction of the **Philosophers' Tincture**. Since this must be done through "Living Mercury," whom he calls the mother, once the tincture itself is extracted—that is, the body being dissolved—the Mercury is "killed." The philosophers hint at this in other words, affirming that the **solution** <term>Solution: The process of turning a solid "body" into a liquid "spirit."</term> of the body cannot happen without the **coagulation** <term>Coagulation: The process of thickening a liquid into a solid state.</term> of the spirit; for that reason he says:

> ->*I killed my mother, but the same end awaits me.*<- <note>original: "Occidi matrem, sed me manet exitus idem."</note>

> *[My death suffers that which my origin already did]* <note>original: "Id mea mors patitur, quod iam mea fecit origo."</note>

With the mother—that is, the Mercury—having been killed, the dissolved body also dies, and both are clothed in a mournful and black garment <note>This refers to the *nigredo* or "blackness" stage, the first major goal of the work, symbolizing decay and the stripping away of old forms.</note>. Therefore, since he killed his mother at his birth, it is just that he himself, as a matricide, should also die.

> *[Life to me is death]* <note>original: "Vita mihi mors est"</note>

He has this in common with man, and especially with the Christian, who as soon as he begins to live—that is, to know God and Christ—so soon does he also proceed to die <note>A reference to the spiritual concept of "dying to the world" or "dying to self" in order to achieve eternal life.</note>. And therefore he says:

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the alchemical poem began on page 886. ### THE PHILOSOPHICAL SECRET

> *[I die if I begin to be born]* <note>original: "Morior si cæpero nasci"</note>

Indeed, in that celebrated union of **Gabritius** <term>Gabritius: The masculine principle, often associated with "Philosophical Sulfur" or the "King."</term>, as they call him, with the shining maiden **Beia** <term>Beia: The feminine principle, "Philosophical Mercury" or the "Queen." Their union represents the joining of the fixed and the volatile.</term>, Gabritius dies almost as soon as he is first born.

> *[But the fate of death comes before the origin of light]* <note>original: "Sed prius est fatum lethi, quam lucis origo"</note>

Our most powerful and most holy Savior, **Jesus Christ**, predicted this very thing when speaking of himself: *Unless,* he says, *a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it brings forth much fruit.* <note>A reference to John 12:24, a common alchemical justification for the stage of "Putrefaction," where the substance must turn black and "die" to be reborn as the Stone.</note> In this place, however, the author declares that the origin of light follows the fate of death. Thus it follows:

> *[Thus I take only the spirits of the dead as my parents]* <note>original: "Sic solos manes ipsos mihi duco parentes"</note>

These are the ones, evidently, who will finally raise me from the tomb to the royal throne.

> *[I am not great, indeed, but within me is the greatest Virtue: / The spirit is great, though in a small body]* <note>original: "Magna quidem non sum, sed inest mihi maxima Virtus: Spiritus est magnus, quamvis in corpore paruo"</note>

**Count Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist whose works emphasize the "fountain" in which the King bathes.</note> explains all these things clearly, though in different words, in the fourth part of his little work. He says the King is killed by the very fountain [that washes him] and is revived by it; thereafter, from the substance of his kingdom, which is divided into the tiniest parts, each of his subjects receives a portion. And however tiny a particle anyone may have, he is made equal in wealth, strength, and power to the King. See what a great force the great spirit has in a small body. It follows:

> *[Neither does my sprout have harm, nor does my fault have a blush]* <note>original: "Nec mihi germen habet noxam, nec culpa ruborem"</note>

Here, he declares that the sprout is most pure, and he clears the red **tincture** <term>Tincture: The transformative essence of the Alchemical Stone, capable of "coloring" or changing base metals into gold.</term> from any crime, because they are neither in fault nor do they deserve harm. It follows:

> *[We are both stones, we are one, we both lie down]* <note>original: "Ambo sumus lapides, Una sumus, ambo iacemus"</note>

In this place, he does not hide the number of the species and their **fixation** <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</term>. Since these things do not happen without divine will, as my personal motto suggests, I judge it right that he who has received such a great gift from God, the Best and Greatest, should give thanks to such Majesty and serve Him perpetually. He adds:

> *[As sluggish as one is, so active is the other; / One stays unmoved, the other never ceases to move]* <note>original: "Quam piger est Vnus, tantum non segnis it alter, Hic manet immotus, non desinit ille moueri"</note>

Since he has already said that both are stones, it might seem strange how it happens that he now makes one moving and the other unmoved. This seems to be said concerning the **body and the spirit** <note>In alchemy, the "body" is the solid, fixed part (the "sluggish" one), while the "spirit" is the volatile, vaporous part (the "active" one).</note> before perfect fixation, as they call it. For the "envious" <note>A term alchemists used for authors who intentionally obscured their writings to hide secrets from the unworthy.</note> are mostly accustomed to putting those things last which should rightly come first, so that they may deceive the unwary, and vice versa. But he says:

> *[None can split me, though many can cut me off]* <note>original: "Findere me nulli possunt, præcidere multi"</note>

A point by its very nature is entirely indivisible and cannot be cut; and this matter of ours...

...brought to the highest peak, it yields red celestial-earthly atoms.

*[But I am many-colored]* <note>original: "Sed sum versicolor"</note>
Doubtless many and various colors appear during the work, of which three are primary: black, white, and red.

*[In time to be white]* <note>original: "Albus quandoque futurus"</note>
For after the blackness <term>nigredo: The first stage of the alchemical work, representing decomposition or "death."</term> and the other fleeting colors, whiteness <term>albedo: The second major stage, representing purification and the washing away of impurities.</term> follows—and indeed an most intense whiteness—which transforms all lower metals into the finest **Moon** <note>In alchemy, "Moon" (Luna) is the standard term for Silver.</note>. But our subject here says:

*[I prefer to remain black.]* <note>original: "Malo manere niger."</note>
To what end, you envious one? For you would be fit for use neither for yourself nor for anyone else.

*[I shall fear the final fates less]* <note>original: "Minus vltima fata verebor"</note>
You fear what you ought most to desire: namely, to ascend to that kingdom which nature and art have prepared for you alone. Proceed.

*[No shape is certain to me, no shape is foreign.]* <note>original: "Nulla mihi certa est, nulla est peregrina figura."</note>
He plays and alludes to another who said:

->*By what means may I hold Proteus as he changes his features?*<-
<note>A reference to the shape-shifting sea god Proteus. In alchemy, this represents the "mercurial" nature of the matter, which takes many forms before it is fixed.</note>

All these things, however, can be applied quite well either before the first fixation or before the final **Work of Three Days** <term>Work of Three Days: A symbolic period or a specific rapid procedure mentioned in late medieval alchemy for the final perfection of the Stone.</term>.

*[A brightness is within, flashing with radiant light.]* <note>original: "Fulgor inest intus, radianti luce coruscus."</note>
In this place, to give us hope and add courage, he indicates what is hidden within himself—what is concealed from the common people, who look only with eyes of flesh—namely, that a most splendid and invincible heavenly (not to say divine) brightness lies hidden within.

*[Which shows nothing, unless it has seen something before]* <note>original: "Qui nihil ostendit, nisi si quid viderit ante"</note>
For many things must precede before that brightness reveals itself. But he continues, saying:

->*I do not die immediately while the spirit departs.*<-
<note>original: "Non ego continuo morior, dum spiritus exit."</note>

*[For it returns constantly, though it often recedes]* <note>original: "Nam redit assidue, quamvis & sæpe recedat"</note>
These things have been explained by us clearly enough above when we were discussing the **tears** <note>A common metaphor for the vapors produced during heating that condense and "rain" back down into the flask.</note>, which he here calls "spirit." The philosophers teach that these are emitted (though few) during the Work of Three Days.

*[And for me now the power of the soul is great, now nothing]* <note>original: "Et mihi nunc magna est animæ, nunc nulla facultas"</note>
While the compound is dissolved, the power of the soul can be said to be nothing, except insofar as it is joined to the spirit to bring about the dissolution of the body; but when it is joined to the body, then it is at its most powerful.

*[I have endured more than one body ought to]* <note>original: "Plus ego sustinui quam corpus debuit vnum"</note>
The envious one brings these things forward to flatter himself, but hear what the other affirms about him, so you may know how childishly he complains.

### To the Sincere Reader.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' featuring a seated figure within a landscape with classical architecture in the background.</image-desc> A few months ago, I handed over for publication the *Chemical Trio* <note>original: "TRIGAM CHEMICAM." A "Triga" is a chariot drawn by three horses; here it refers to a collection of three treatises.</note> in which nothing was by my own hand except for a Latin translation of the German work by Lambspring <note>A famous, though semi-legendary, German alchemist whose work is known for its emblematic poems.</note>, an elegant explanation of the Stone in certain Chemical Verses, and the remaining works of an ancient French philosopher. Now, I bring forward the *Gold-Bearing Quartet* <note>original: "QUADRIGAM AVRIFERAM." A "Quadriga" is a four-horse chariot; here referring to a collection of four treatises.</note>, in which not even a single word originates from me. (For what, I ask, could I ever devise or say in this philosophy of metals <term>metallorum philosophia: Alchemy, specifically the study of transmuting base metals into noble ones.</term> that has not been said before? To do so would be "to act upon what is already done.") Therefore, I send it out into the light exactly as it came from the authors, with nothing added or deleted. 

I do this especially for the sake of the French, English, Germans, Italians, Poles, Bohemians, Prussians, Swedes, and the Dutch <note>original: "Batavorum"</note> (who were born for miracles), and the Confederate Regions. By the blessing of God, while practicing medicine <note>original: "medicinam faciens"</note>, I have several times traveled through the kingdoms, dominions, and lands of all these people, and I have compared my studies with many philosophers known to me. It is for the sake of all these that I do this. (Forgive me, Spaniard—whose kingdom I both saw and traveled through forty years ago—if nothing is sown or reaped for you here. You have gold-bearing ships won with much of your own and Indian blood; you have no need of this chariot. Rely on your ships for now, while you are still permitted.) 

Into the bosom of these other good men, I say, I bring forth and hand over these four wheels. You, sincere men born of God, mount up, and gather the most ample fruit from the wheels, in the wheels, through the wheels, and with the wheels, while the Spirit of God dwells in the midst of your hearts. But if this chariot should not satisfy some (though a few things suffice for the intelligent), let them wait for the horses and the driver, who will lead them to the highest Parnassus <note>A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; here used as a metaphor for the pinnacle of alchemical achievement.</note> of the chemical muses, though not without divine aid. These, I, by God's favor...

*...I will prepare [these works], etc. If I see that these have pleased eminent men, I shall release them shortly. Barnaud makes a theological pun here, identifying the "Philosopher's Stone" sought by alchemists with Jesus Christ, the "cornerstone" of the Church.</note>, *the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who, when he comes (and he is expected soon with great joy by the pious) with his glory, and all the angels with him, shall sit upon the throne of his glory, and all nations shall be gathered before him. He will separate you one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. To those on his left, he will say: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me."* <note>A direct quotation of the Gospel of Matthew 25:31–43, emphasizing that the "fruits" of alchemical knowledge must be used for charity.</note> *Let them remember, I say (lest they, like the foolish virgins, become wise too late), to use these extraordinary gifts of God for his glory, for the honor of the Church of Christ, and for the aid of any neighbor, but especially for the faithful. That they may do this, let them pray with David:* <note>Likely referring to a poetic paraphrase of King David’s Psalms.</note>

> Teach me, I pray, O Supreme God,
> The doctrine of your 
> Most holy Law, and I shall 
> Keep it for all time.
> Grant me that 
> Wisdom of yours, by which I may understand
> Your decrees; and diligently 
> I will obey you continually.
> At last, sweetest Father,
> Lead me onto the narrow path
> Which leads to your kingdom,
> Than which nothing is more desired by me.

*With these few words, I wish you well, honest reader, and I pray that God may favor your studies as he does mine. Fare well, and remember us. From our little chemical study* <note>original: "museolo nostro chemico." A 'musaeum' or 'museolum' was a private place of study, contemplation, and scientific work.</note> *in Leiden* <note>original: "Lugduni Batavorum," the Latin name for the city of Leiden in the Netherlands, famous for its university.</note> *in the month of July, 1599.*
