<header>SECOND GATE</header>

### *On multiplication, the eleventh gate.*

I now prepare myself to explain multiplication, which the philosophers define as follows: It is the increase of the Elixir in both quality and quantity, for both the Red and the White <note>The "Red" and "White" refer to the two grades of the Elixir: one for transmuting metals into gold, the other into silver</note>. Multiplication, as they describe it, is that process which causes the increase of the medicine in every degree—in color, in scent, in potency, and in quantity. And the reason you are able to multiply your medicine infinitely is this: it is like a fire, which, once ignited, never dies but always dwells with you, just as a fire in a home, or like musk in aromatic mixtures, of which a single spark can ignite a greater fire of multiplied power. The same occurs in our medicine. A man is rich if he has fire, whether more or less, because it can be increased as much as he wishes; likewise, he is rich who possesses even a small particle of our Elixir, because it can be increased infinitely.

There is one way: if you dissolve our dry powder and perform frequent congelation <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid or thick mass</note> upon it, you will then achieve an increase in its potency. A second way is to multiply it in both quality and quantity through repeated fermentation, as I clearly showed you in that chapter through various modes of natural operation; and likewise in the chapter on our cibation <term>cibation: the "feeding" of the alchemical matter with liquid (often called "milk" or Mercury) to sustain its growth and volume</term>, where you can learn how your matter is infinitely multiplied with Mercury.

But if you wish to dissolve and ferment all at once, it will increase in quantity as much as in potency. In this way, you can multiply it so that it grows within the glass in the manner of a tree, which we call the **Tree of Hermes** <note>original: "Hermetis arborem"; a visual phenomenon where metal crystals branch out in a glass vessel, resembling a plant</note>, most beautiful to behold. One grain of this will be multiplied into a thousand if you wisely know how to perform your projection <term>projection: the final act of casting the alchemical Elixir onto a base metal to achieve transmutation</term>.

For just as powdered saffron <note>original: "crocus"</note>, if tempered little by little with liquid and then added to a greater quantity of liquid, tints far more of the liquid in quantity than if it were whole in its thick substance; so our Elixir, the more refined it is made, the more widely it will spread itself with its tincture <note>The "tincture" is the transformative color and quality that the Elixir imparts to base metals</note>. Therefore, cover your fire in the evening as well as in the morning, so that you do not need to go searching for it from door to door among your neighbors to borrow from them. The longer you retain it, the more you will gain. Always multiply it more and more in your glass, nourishing it with Mercury for as long as you live, and thus you will have more than you need—this is most manifest. There is no reason for me to write more clearly; use reason as your guide, and do not let loose the reins to sin because of this wealth, but serve the Lord your God more attentively for as long as you live...

...and do not forget to store these things in your mind. Reflect that you must one day stand before the tribunal of God; therefore, dispose of your gifts and your treasures uprightly and piously. ->*On projection, the twelfth gate.*<-

IN projection, it will be proven whether our practice is useful. I must advise you of certain secrets regarding this: if the <term>tincture: the active transmuting agent or "dye" that changes the nature of a metal</term> is true and stable, you will prove it with a small quantity of your medicine. Upon metal or Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, it will adhere like pitch and tint during projection so that it withstands all fire; it will enter and spread itself most widely.

But many have destroyed their work through ignorance when they perform projection upon impure metal; for their tincture vanishes because of the corruption which they did not remove from the "bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the base metals being acted upon</note>. After such a projection, the results are brittle, dark, and black. Therefore, so that the tincture can endure perpetually, see that you first project your medicine upon the <term>ferment: a substance, often gold or silver, used to "prime" the medicine for a specific result</term>; then that ferment will become brittle like glass. Project that brittle substance upon cleansed and very pure bodies, and immediately you will see them curiously colored with the tincture, which will withstand all trials.

And so, calculate from the Psalms of David to make a useful and perfect projection <note>The author uses the titles of Latin Psalms as a mnemonic code for the ratios used in the projection process</note>. Upon the Psalm whose beginning is *Foundations* <note>original: "fundamenta" (Psalm 87)</note>, project *Now let depart* <note>original: "Nunc dimittis" (The Song of Simeon)</note>. Upon *My words* <note>original: "verba mea" (Psalm 5)</note>, project *Foundations*. Then *My words* upon *I will love* <note>original: "diligam" (Psalm 18)</note>, and *I will love* upon *Give ear* <note>original: "attendite" (Psalm 78)</note>. In this way, make three, four, or five projections, until the tincture of your medicine begins to decrease. Then it is time to make an end of the projection.

By this mystical speech, I mean nothing else than that you should first project a smaller amount upon a larger, always increasing the number—as the wise say—and keep this secret to yourself. Be eager for learning; it will not be a burden to you. For he who joins the <term>Elixir: the perfected alchemical substance</term> to "sick" <note>i.e., unrefined or impure</note> bodies knows little of what projection truly means. If you multiply ten first by ten, that number makes a hundred; if you multiply a hundred again by ten, that number is called a thousand; if likewise a thousand by ten, they make ten thousand, which again multiplied by ten make a hundred thousand. Now you have overcome these twelve gates and you govern the whole citadel at your pleasure; keep these secre- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing to the next page</note>

->*The recapitulation follows.*<-

To reduce this treatise into an Epitome <note>A brief summary or distillation of the core principles.</note>, attend diligently to the breadth of our <term>stone: the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</term>, and begin in the West, where the **red male** and the **white spouse** shall become one, betrothed by the spirit of life, so that they may live in love and quiet, with earth and water being equally proportioned; and one part of earth for three of spirit is also a good proportion, which is twelve parts of spirit for four parts of earth or "body." You must take three parts of the female and one of the male, and the less there is of the spirit in this betrothal, the sooner you will complete your <term>calcination: the reduction of a solid to a powder through heat</term>. Then proceed into the North through the darkening of the red man and his spouse, which is called the **eclipse**, dissolving them and altering them between winter and spring, converting the dark earth into water; from there, ascend through various colors into the East, where the Moon will appear full during the day. Then the purgatory and its course have passed. For there the Sun rises appearing white and bright; there is summer after winter, and day after night. Then earth and water, after the blackness, are converted into air, and the clouds and shadows have passed, and all things appear bright. And just as the West was the beginning of this practice, and the North the perfect middle of the deep alteration, so the East is the beginning of the speculative <note>The stage of the work where the internal nature of the matter is observed rather than physically manipulated.</note>, but in its course, it soon reaches consummation in the South; there the elements are converted into water by circulation. Then, there is no reason to doubt that you will obtain your desire, for you have turned the wheel of our philosophy. Nevertheless, you must circle your wheel twice more, in which are comprised the secrets of our philosophy declared in the **12 gates**, if you have rightly conceived how you shall perfectly calcine the bodies, dissolve, and putrefy them, and all other secrets of our "lowest astronomy" <note>original: "infimæ astronomiæ"; a common alchemical term meaning the study of "terrestrial stars" or metals, as opposed to celestial astronomy</note>, with a perfect understanding of all the poles shining in our heaven with inexplicable colors; never have more beautiful ones been seen: the pale and the black, the false yellow, the imperfect and the red, the color of the **peacock's feathers** <note>original: "pauõis plumarum color"; the *cauda pavonis*, a stage of shimmering, iridescent colors indicating the transition to the White work</note>, most elegant, the rainbow which shall also pass, the varied color of the Panther, the **green lion**, the **Crow's beak** black as lead—these shall appear before the perfect white—and many other colors; and after the perfect white, the ash-gray, and the false yellow, and afterwards the **red blood** shall appear.

If, therefore, you wish to prepare this thing for yourself by this art, **hide the height** <note>original: *altitudinem*. Your **red elixir** must be divided into parts before you perform the <term>rubification: the final stage of the Great Work where the substance turns red</term>, and these parts you shall place in two glasses. If you wish to have a double elixir of the **Sun** (gold) and the **Moon** (silver), do this: with your **Mercury**, multiply it immediately into a great quantity. If in the beginning you have only enough to fill a single spoon, you will be able to multiply it—into both white and red—so that even if you live a thousand years, you shall have more than enough. 

Therefore, carefully dissolve your base and convert it into a **perfect oil**, which must be achieved through <term>circulation: the process of distilling a liquid and allowing it to flow back into the base substance repeatedly</term> according to our purpose. These oils will fix crude **Mercury** into perfect **Sun** and **Moon**. This fixed and pure oily substance, **Raymond** <note>Referring to Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a famous philosopher and reputed alchemist. Many texts were attributed to him to grant them authority.</note> called his **basilisk** <note>In alchemy, the "basilisk" refers to a powerful, transformative substance or a "king" of chemicals capable of transmuting other metals.</note>, of which he never provided such a clear explanation.

Remember that man is the most noble creature in earthly composition that God ever created, in whom there is a **neutral Mercuriality** <note>A balanced state of the "Mercury of the Wise," the essential spirit of matter.</note> of the four elements proportioned by nature; it costs absolutely nothing and is produced by art from its own mineral. For our metals are nothing other than our two minerals of our **Sun** and **Moon**, as Raymond wisely notes. The splendor of the bright Moon and Sun descends secretly into these two minerals; although the splendor is hidden from your sight, you can use art to make it appear clearly.

Putrefy this **hidden stone**, this one thing; wash it in its own liquor until it turns white: then ferment it wisely. 

And thus you have the sum

# THE THIRD WHEEL,
## *The Book of*
# MERCURY AND THE PHILOSOPHER’S
# STONE BY GEORGE RIPLEY,
## English Canon.

Dearest son, I shall instruct you in this blessed science, which was hidden by the ancient sages, upon whom God deigned to bestow such great grace. Understand, therefore, that our matter is the highest of all things on the earth, yet of the least value or price, as will later appear more clearly to you. For if water incorporates itself with earth, it will be the lowest of all water; and unless it be fixed with fire, it will ascend higher. In this way, it can be seen how water can be both the highest and the lowest. 

That it is of the least value is indeed true. For in our earth and water, and in that foul earth, you shall find pure and clear water, which is our <term>sperma: the seed or reproductive essence of the work</term> and <term>quinta essentia: quintessence, the fifth element or purest substance</term>. Then, however, that foul earth is worth nothing more and is of no value. 

Indeed, what I said about water being the highest will appear in many ways: understand, son, that without water we cannot make bread, nor anything else that God created in the nature of things. Here you will easily perceive that water is the <term>prima materia: the "first matter" or the primitive, formless base of all substance</term> of all things born or generated in the world. For it will certainly be manifest to you that nothing grows or takes increase without the four elements. Therefore, whatever is composed of elements by the virtue of the four elements, it is necessary that the origin of all things being born or growing should come from water. 

However, do not understand this to be said of [common] water, but of that water which is the matter of all things, from which all natural things are produced in their own kind. So you shall understand that first, air is generated from water; from air, fire; and from fire, earth. 

Now, however, I shall speak to you even more familiarly and kindly; I will manifest this mystery to you further, step by step, lest by too much haste it happens to us according to the proverb: "He who hastens too much often arrives home too late." <note>original: *Quod qui nimis festinat, sæpe nimium fero veniet domum.*</note> Now, therefore, to satisfy your desire, I shall speak of the first mat- <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page to be continued on the next.</note>

<summary>George Ripley begins the "Third Wheel" of his treatise, explaining to his student that the base material of alchemy is both the humblest and highest substance, identifying a specialized form of "water" as the primary source of all elements and growth.</summary>

[mat]ter, which the Philosophers call the <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence," a pure, celestial substance latent in all things</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"</note>, and they call it by many other names, the more to hide it. In this certainly are four pure elements in their exaltation. Therefore you should recognize that if you wish to have the quintessence of man, it is necessary that you first have a man, and from that matter you will have nothing else, and see that you notice this well. For I tell you that if you desire to have the <term>philosopher’s stone: the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting enlightenment</term> <note>original: "lapidem philosophorum"</note>, it is necessary that you first have the quintessence of that same stone, whether mineral, or vegetable, or animal. Join therefore species with species, and genus with genus, and not one without the other, nor anything contrary that might be outside its own species or genus. Beware, therefore, of all foreign and strange things. For stones are not made from bones, nor are geese born from cranes.

If you have considered this well, you will find fruit, through the mediation of divine grace; with that helping us, we shall proceed further to speak of this blessed water, which is called the **water of the Sun and Moon** <note>original: "aqua Solis & Lunæ"</note>, hidden in the concavity of our earth. Concerning which earth you should also understand, that everything which is generated must necessarily have a male and a female, from which arise action and passion, without which generation never occurs. But from things differing in genus you will certainly never have profit. Nevertheless, if you have this **water of the Sun and Moon**, it will attract other bodies to its own genus, and through the mediation of the power and heat of the Sun and Moon, it will make them perfect: just as an infant in the mother’s womb, through the <term>decoction: the process of heating or "cooking" a substance to refine it</term> of temperate heat, converts the <term>menstrual fluids: here referring to the biological matter provided by the mother to form the fetus</term> <note>original: "menstrua"</note> into its own nature and genus—that is, into flesh, blood, bones, and life, with the other properties of a living body, of which it is not expedient to say more.

And from this it will be given to you to understand, that our water converts itself into a perfect genus, with things of its own kind: for it will first congeal itself into a substance similar to oil; then that oil, by means of temperate heat, it will turn into a gum; finally, by means of the perfect heat of the Sun, into a stone. Now, therefore, understand that from one thing, you have three: that is, oil, gum, and stone. Understand also that when the water is turned into oil, then you have the **perfect spirit**; but when the oil is turned into a hard gum, then you have the **perfect spirit and soul**; and when that perfect spirit and soul are turned into a stone, then you have the **perfect body, soul, and spirit** together, which is then called the stone...

When indeed, after the union that comes from marriage, it generates the water of life and the philosophers' milk, with which you will increase and feed your stone forever.

I could tell you much more, my son, about this <term>first matter: the fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made</term> <note>original: "prima materia"</note>; but let these things suffice you so that, having set aside wordy obscurities, we may at last proceed, by the favor of divine mercy, to the actual practice of the <term>philosophers' stone</term> <note>original: "philosophi lapidis"</note>. If you are ingenious, let these few things suffice for you, so that you may investigate many more things and perceive my understanding. Therefore, consider well, my son, that according to the ancient proverb: *He has not earned the sweet, who has not tasted the bitter.* <note>original: "Dulcia non meruit, qui non gustauit amara."</note> Now truly, that we may say something further regarding our **brass** <note>original: "ære" (aes). In alchemy, "brass" or "aes" often refers not to the common alloy, but to a specific stage of the metallic matter or a "philosophical" metal.</note>, understand that brass signifies permanence, or permanent water. Whatever else must be considered in the nature of the name of brass, you will easily perceive from its **Tetragrammaton** <note>meaning "four-lettered name." While usually referring to the name of God, the author here uses it to describe a four-lettered alchemical code.</note>—that is, its four-lettered name—taken from the English word for brass using these four letters: **B, R, A, S**.

First, therefore, by **B** is signified the "first body" of our work, which is our sweet and bitter olive, and our brass remaining permanent in its own form.

By **R** is signified the "root" of the work's name, and the spring of the **permanent radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the fundamental life-fluid or "innate heat" believed to exist within all matter</term>, which is our red tincture and our red rose, which purifies—and purifies all things—within its own kind.

**A** signifies our father **Adam**, who was the first man, from whom the first woman, **Eve**, was born; from which you can understand that therein is the male and the female. Know, therefore, that our brass is the beginning of our work, our gold, and our olive, for it is the **first matter** of metals, just as man is the beginning of man and woman.

**S** signifies the "soul" of our life, and the spirit of life, which God breathed into Adam and into all creatures: which spirit is indeed called the **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: the "quintessence," a pure, incorruptible substance beyond the four physical elements</term>.

Furthermore, my son, by these four letters we understand the **four elements**, without which nothing is generated in the nature of things. They also signify the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold/the Male principle, and the Moon represents Silver/the Female principle.</note>, which are the cause of all life, germination, and the growth of all things born in the world. In this four-lettered name, therefore, consists our entire work. For in our brass is the male and the female, from whom arises he who is called the "begotten."

Pay close attention, therefore, my son, to what is signified by our "sweet brass," what is called our **sandiver** <term>sandiver: also known as "glass gall," the scum or salt that forms on the surface of molten glass</term>, or the salt of our nitre; what is meant by **dragon’s blood** <note>A common alchemical term for various red substances, often cinnabar or a specific red resin used as a metaphor for the final "red" stage of the work.</note>, what the Sun and Moon are, our Mercury, and our **water of life**, and many other things about which the Philosophers have spoken obscurely and in riddles.

Understand then, my son, that our **first matter** is neither common gold nor silver, nor is it made from corrosives or such foreign things, which those wandering and groping in the darkness use today. Beware, therefore, my son, lest you admit anything contrary into the kind; for be certain of this: *whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap.*

Moreover, understand that when our stone is completed in its own kind, it will then be a hard stone that is not easily dissolved. Nevertheless, if you add his **wife** <note>original: "vxorem suam". In alchemy, the "wife" usually refers to the feminine principle or a specific solvent, such as mercury, needed to "marry" the solid stone to make it fluid.</note> to him, he will be dissolved into an oil, which is called the **oil of the philosophers**, the **incombustible oil**, and by many other names.

Understand therefore, my son, that there are different types of **fermentations** <term>fermentation: the process by which the alchemical "medicine" is matured or multiplied in power</term>, both physical and spiritual—namely, physical in quantity, and spiritual in quality. Physical fermentation increases the weight and the quantity of the medicine, yet it is not of such great power as the medicine itself. As for spiritual fermentation, it only increases the medicine in quantity, but not in potency. But spiritual fermentation increases it in both. And where the physical fermentation rules over a hundred, the spiritual rules over a thousand.

Furthermore, as long as the medicine is fermented with spiritual qualities, it is called a **medicine**. But when it is fermented with a physical substance, it is called an **elixir**. Thus, there is a different method of fermenting and a distinction between the medicine and the elixir; for one is spiritual, while the other is physical. Understand also that as long as it remains a spiritual ferment, it is a liquid oil and a **gum** <note>original: "gumma". Refers to a resinous, semi-solid state of the matter.</note> which cannot be easily carried from place to place. But when it becomes physical, then it will be a stone which you can carry around in a purse. Now, therefore, you see the difference between the medicine and the elixir.

Nor is there less of a difference between the elixir and gold or silver; for gold and silver are difficult to melt, but the elixir is not so, for it flows easily at the flame of a lamp. From this, you will easily perceive how varied are the differences of our composition and temperament.

Finally, to say something of their food and drink: understand that their food is of **airy stones** <note>original: "lapidibus aereis". This likely refers to volatile substances or the "spirit" captured from the air.</note>, and their drink is extracted from two perfect bodies: namely, from the **Sun** and the **Moon** <note>The Sun and Moon are standard alchemical code for Gold and Silver.</note>. The drink which is extracted from the Sun is called **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile". A legendary liquid form of gold believed to grant longevity.</note>, while that which is from the Moon is called **virgin’s milk** <note>original: "lac virginis". A common term for a white, mercurial solvent or a specific stage of the white work.</note>.

Now, my son, we have spoken to you in sufficiently plain language—provided that divine grace does not fail you—for the drink extracted from the Sun is red, while that from the Moon is white. Therefore, one is called potable gold, and the other virgin’s milk. One is also masculine and the other feminine, even though both derive their origin from a single image and a single kind. Think, my son, on my words; otherwise, if you wander in darkness, evil will come to you from the lack of light. See to it then, my son, that you are diligent in the turning of the **philosophical wheel** <term>philosophical wheel: a metaphor for the repeated cycles of distillation, sublimation, and circulation required to refine the matter</term>, so that you make water from earth, and air...

### THE GOLDEN CHARIOTS
## FOURTH AND FINAL
### W H E E L.

*The writing of an honest and well-learned man, whose name has been lost, treating the elixir of the Sun <note>The "Sun" (Solis) refers to gold, the most perfect of metals.</note> of Theophrastus Paracelsus.*

DISSOLVE gold with its entire substance by means of a corrosive, for as long as it takes until it unites itself with the corrosive. Nor should the mind shrink from this method of treatment: for to gold—if indeed it is gold—the corrosive is beneficial, and without the corrosive, gold is dead. Now it follows that this dissolution should be removed again through putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the alchemical stage of breakdown or "death," usually represented by the color black, which allows for the spiritualization of the matter</term>, although truly the corrosive cannot easily be removed: for if it is naturally inherent in gold that it must preserve the human body and cure it from every illness, and not allow it to be corrupted, how much more will it provide this for itself, and that without any infection of its own. For gold corrects and improves whatever is not pure. Therefore, the corrosive in the gold should by no means be called a corrosive. For the power and virtue of its secret <note>original: "arcani"</note> overcomes every poison. Indeed, all Realgar <term>Realgar: a toxic red arsenic mineral; here used to symbolize poisonous or "raw" mineral qualities that the alchemist must "kill" or transform</term> in the elixir of gold is forced to die, and passes into the most excellent and distinguished medicine and tincture. In this manner also, drinkable gold <note>original: "aurum potabile". A legendary liquid medicine made from gold, believed by Paracelsans to be a universal cure-all.</note> is prepared after putrefaction. These are the words of Paracelsus, literally.

*There follows a brief proof from my own work that the aforementioned elixir and tincture can be made.*

FIRST, I take the due matter, which the author himself also names—namely, gold. This I dissolve by a corrosive, which the author chose to call by this name here (although elsewhere it has infinite names) because as long as it remains in its specific form, it thoroughly corrodes and despoils metals; hence he calls it both "enemy" and "robber" elsewhere; not otherwise than a glue, on account of the equal proportion of their union...

<header>THE GOLDEN CHARIOTS</header>

I dissolve this matter, or gold, not only with its entire substance, but I use for this dissolution a corrosive of such a kind that it can (as this author intends) unite and bond itself with the gold. It is well known that nothing can be united or bonded to it unless it is of the same nature; for "nature rejoices in nature" <note>original: "natura enim gaudet natura." This is a fundamental alchemical axiom suggesting that only substances with a shared "radical" essence can truly combine.</note>. Now, we know that metals are of the nature of minerals; therefore, this corrosive—if indeed gold is to be united with it—must also be of a mineral nature. Minerals contain many more and better "spirits" than metals do, and it is these spirits that assist in the processes of addition, gradation <term>gradation: the alchemical process of intensifying the color, weight, or purity of a metal</term>, and fixation. For as the philosophers say, they contain within themselves "tinctures" <term>tinctures: the spiritual essence or coloring principle capable of transforming base matter into gold</term> and colors.

If we now consider the veins of the earth where gold is born, and look at which "enemies" or corrosive minerals surround it (regarding its superfluity or unequal proportion), we will chiefly find the spirits of **sulfur**, **salt**, and **mercury** <note>These are the "Three Primes" or *Tria Prima* of Paracelsus, the three fundamental components of all matter.</note>. From these, therefore, one must take and separate a more subtle substance, or "glue"—that is, something that is of the nature of gold, which can be united and bonded with gold, and which can multiply that gold in weight, color, and fusibility. It must unite and bond with it in such a way that it becomes one substance and one form with it, and consequently one inseparable individual entity.

In my own work, I possess such a medium that joins itself with gold in this way, so that it becomes one substance and form with it, multiplying its weight and also increasing its color. This is seen when the gold is sublimated into crystals of the deepest red; these do not lack fusibility <term>fusibility: the quality of being easily melted</term>, as experience demonstrates, for they flow even in the flame of a candle. 

Since my medium unites with gold in this way, and embraces that gold so closely and "amicably"—so that truly, according to the philosophers, "nature receives into itself from nature that which is of its own nature"—I do not hesitate to affirm that I am using a "true corrosive" according to the mind of **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist whose theories dominate this text.</note>. This is especially true since such a corrosive must be so appropriate that it is not useless to the gold. My medium is most useful to it: first, as was just said, it renders the gold "higher in grade" in its color (which is what **Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century Italian alchemist often cited for his work on the dissolution of metals.</note> desires); and second, it makes it heavier (as Theophrastus requires of a "specific corrosive"). While "strong waters" <term>strong waters: "aqua fortis" or nitric acid, used by jewelers and alchemists to dissolve metals</term> typically dissolve metals in such a way that nothing is lost in weight, in my work—by means of my corrosive—not only is no weight lost from the gold, but weight is actually added. Indeed, I always find my gold, after its crystalline sublimation, to be double in weight...

...more ponderous. <note>original: "derosius," likely the conclusion of "ponderosius" from the previous page.</note> Theophrastus <note>referring to Paracelsus, whose full name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim</note> also asserts that without a corrosive, gold is dead, but when united with a corrosive, it lives; it is established that this happens in my work in a similar fashion. For who will deny that those things live which contain a vital spirit? Yet in this work of mine, which I have named so often, because the gold attracts that spirit from the corrosive to such an extent that it seems to rejoice in that spirit alone above all others, and therefore it wishes to be dissolved and coupled, as it were, by this alone. Moreover, it is established that all metals are dissolved through life, and no other dissolution of bodies can occur (according to the testimony of the philosophers) except through life. Who now does not see that this gold, united with the spirit, lives? Especially since the author expressly confesses that without the corrosive, gold is dead. This same union of gold with the spirit is confirmed by that marvelous **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to show the union of spirit and matter</term> which takes place in the fire.

Since, therefore, all the philosophers cry out with one voice: *Dissolve the bodies, and make the fixed volatile* <note>original: "Solvite corpora, fac fixum volatile." This is a core command of alchemy—to break down solid matter (the fixed) into a spiritual or gaseous state (the volatile) so it can be purified.</note>; and I have (by the grace of God) proceeded this far in my work; it remains only that we now **coagulate the spirits**, or make the **volatile fixed**. The author shows that this must be done in this place through **putrefaction**; for "the corruption of one is the generation of another" <note>original: "corruptio unius est generatio alterius." An Aristotelian principle used by alchemists to explain that the old form of a metal must "die" or rot to be reborn as the Elixir.</note>. 

It seems, however, as if Theophrastus suggests that the corrosive ought to be entirely removed through putrefaction. But if the mind of the author is looked into more deeply, he clearly feels differently, which is apparent from these words: *Although the corrosive will not be able to move itself easily,* etc. He indeed wants a separation to occur, but only such a separation that that which cannot and should not be separated—but rather united with the gold to increase it in weight and color—is not removed at all. 

First, indeed, that the corrosive should not be entirely removed is proved from the aforementioned union, which would be in vain if removal were necessarily required; and also from the example cited in the text, where he says: *It is naturally implanted in gold that, by an innate power, it preserves the human body and cures and protects it from all diseases.* If it can provide this for another, it certainly will provide the same much more for itself, and will protect itself from that corrosive. To this he affirms that this corrosive is by no means to be called "corrosive" when it is in the gold; and he confirms this by the reason that all **Realgar** <term>Realgar: a toxic arsenic-sulfur mineral; here used to represent the raw, destructive corrosive agent</term> (and thus the corrosive) is forced to die in the **Elixir of gold**. When it is dead—that is, annihilated—a new generation will occur: namely, a most excellent and most noble medicine and **tincture** <term>tincture: the final, potent alchemical substance capable of transforming both metals and the human body</term>. This also agrees with other philosophers who, all with one voice, only then recognize a perfect medicine and tincture...

...when it reaches its own sweetness, just as apples are not fit for eating until they have reached their perfect maturity and sweetness. Moreover, through **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: a stage in alchemy where substances are broken down by heat/moisture to be "reborn" in a purified state</term>, which the author especially requires in this work, it is well known that many bitter or corrosive things become sweet; finally, many poisons are made into the most excellent medicines. That this single work will reach its own just and perfect sweetness, I am convinced by experience itself, since I have already had this (though not yet perfected) in my hands—had not fate, hostile to good things, and **impious Mars** <note>original: "Mars impius"; a common alchemical metaphor for war or civil strife, likely referring to the Thirty Years' War which frequently interrupted the work of 17th-century scholars</note> envied me such a noble prize. And here, as I mentioned a little earlier, I bring forward all true philosophers as witnesses. Nor does the stubborn opinion of certain people cause me any hesitation—those who will not concede that any medicine to be taken into the human body ought to be prepared by means of a **corrosive** <term>corrosive: a sharp solvent, usually an acid or spirit, used to break down metals</term>. They think correctly [according to their own knowledge], for they are ignorant of the **separation** <note>the process of removing the harmful "stinging" qualities of a solvent while retaining its power</note>, and of that which cannot and must not be separated, but rather must be united with gold: they do not know how to bring out its latent and innate sweetness, which ought to increase in weight and color.

<margin>]</margin> If they knew this, they would not so greatly dread the corrosive, nor would their minds shrink so much from this method of treatment. For indeed, gold, insofar as it is gold, excels by means of the corrosive; and without the corrosive, gold is **dead**. On the contrary, they would rather confess with Theophrastus that **potable gold** <term>potable gold: "aurum potabile," a legendary liquid medicine made from dissolved gold</term> and the Elixir of the Sun are useful and health-giving medicines for the human body, if they are prepared with their due corrosive in the proper manner. For both, according to the mind of Theophrastus, are made in one and the same way after putrefaction. Therefore, even true potable gold, unless it is of exquisite sweetness, ought rather to be considered a "deadly" gold. Having obtained this aforementioned sweetness and brought it to its perfection (than which, God willing, nothing is more certain, since I have tasted the same not only in gold and silver, but also in corals and pearls, each of which manifested their latent sweetness to me by means of my corrosive), indeed, whatever its **tincture** <term>tincture: the concentrated essence or color of a substance that has the power to transform other bodies</term> may be, which the author here

The height of the stone in its fiery quality, shining more than perfect from the **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: also known as the "quintessence," the purest part of a substance that remains after the four elements are removed</term>, is the end of both practice and theory. The Sun holds the fire. Just as Christ—as scripture bears witness—descended from his high throne into the holy womb of Mary for our redemption, so here our stone descends from its high state into the womb of the **Mercurial virgin** <note>original: "virginis Mercurialis"; a symbol for the purified solvent or "First Matter" of the alchemists</note>, so that it may free its brothers from their original filth.

The beginning, or the West, is the latitude of our stone and the entry into practice; it is pale and earthy in quality. Saturn holds the earth. Just as Christ hid his Divinity from our sight when he took our nature upon himself, so also our Sun has left its rays of light here for a time; it has hidden its glory under the wings of its wife, the Moon, and dies bodily so that it may multiply its species.

The dark depth of the stone in the North is purgatory. It is imperfect and watery in quality, variable in color, an **Eclipse of the Sun** <note>original: "Eclipsis Solis"; refers to the "nigredo" or blackening stage of alchemy</note>. Mercury holds the water. Just as Christ our Savior was buried after his passion and death on the tree, and afterward his body was glorified and rose clothed in immortality, so our stone, buried here after the pains of death, has risen from the darkness and various colors, appearing in the East with incomparable clarity.

The Eastern latitude of the stone and the entry into theory is airy. The Full Moon. Jupiter holds the air. Just as Christ ascended from the earth into the heavens in the clouds, up to the throne of his glory, and reigns there as light without end, so also our Sun, having now become our stone, has returned again into its glory, placing its fire here in the south, which can heal lepers and renew youth.

### THE FOURTH WHEEL

...what he rightfully promises here can be much less lacking. Indeed, all true philosophers agree with **Theophrastus** <note>original: "Theoph."; referring to Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist.</note> on this point, for they do not recognize one as perfect without the other. Led by these and other reasons—both because in the work itself every detail agrees so perfectly with the author's own description, and because I see that no other signs are missing from my operation, especially the **blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem"; the stage of *Nigredo* or putrefaction.</note> and the **redness** <note>original: "rubedinem"; the stage of *Rubedo*, the final triumph of the work.</note> which are the principal colors commonly required by the Philosophers—I by no means doubt, in hope and silence, commending the happy outcome of this labor to **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "D. Opt. Max."; a standard abbreviation for *Deo Optimo Maximo*.</note>. May He, upon whom alone all perfect knowledge depends, deign to let this happen most happily for the glory of His divine name and the benefit of our neighbor.

# PROCESS

Let one single thing, or one substance, be made from two; yet first let them be mixed and composed in such a way that the smallest part of one is joined with the smallest of the other, without any hope of future separation. Finally, let it be fixed <note>original: "figatur"; in alchemy, "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> and dissolved again, and this repeated so many times until there emerges a **Medicine** <term>Medicine: "Medicina," another name for the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir, capable of "healing" base metals into gold.</term> that is ductile, meltable, dense, porous, light, and heavy. When placed upon a fire, it should melt like a metal before the "flight" of the **Mercury** <note>original: "fugam Mercurii"; referring to the evaporation or volatility of quicksilver.</note>, and it should adhere to the Mercury itself and to all metals through their smallest parts. It must penetrate them in such a way as if it were of their own proper substance, so that they can never be pulled apart from one another once they have become one.

This Medicine will convert all things with which it has an **affinity** <note>original: "symbolum"; a term used to describe substances that share the same alchemical "signature" or nature.</note> into its own nature. Moreover, the stronger the initial mixing, the more abundant the resulting **transmutation** will be; for the latter depends upon the former and follows it, just as an effect follows its cause. Great care must therefore be taken to follow this path, which can hardly be done without **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the deposit as it cools, used here to purify the "Mercury."</term>, since sublimation is the medium—a sort of transition—that causes such a union. However, it is necessary to cook the sublimate thoroughly until it is fixed and can endure the fire. This will not happen the first time; rather, one must dissolve the fixed matter again and cook it again, until it reaches its full completion of melting, enabling it to penetrate and "infect" <note>original: "inficiendum"; in a laboratory sense, this means to dye or permeate the entire mass with a new color or quality.</note> the metal. This usually happens during the fourth solution and coagulation, though the number **seven** <note>original: "septenarius"; the number seven was considered a symbol of perfect completion in alchemy.</note> represents the total completion.

Therefore, let the sublimated **Physical Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius physicus"; not common quicksilver, but a purified "philosophical" mercury prepared by the artist.</note> be taken, and let a vessel be prepared for it—either of glass or of dense earthenware—that can resist the fire. In this, let two or three ounces be cooked with a continuous fire until the Mercury becomes "metallized" <note>original: "metalleficetur"</note> and sticks entirely to the vessel. It is best to repeat this with new Mercury after the first has adhered, until this too adheres, and until the whole is converted into **Marteck** <term>Marteck: likely a variation of "Martach" (from the Arabic *martak*), referring to litharge or a metallic oxide crust that forms during heating.</term>. When this has been done, let a fire be applied for four or five days, a little stronger than before, until all the adhering material descends to the bottom of the vessel like a mass of tin or lead. This is the **Bronze** and the **Lead of the Philosophers**, and once it is produced, the rest is nothing other than **women's work and children's play** <note>original: "opus mulierum, & ludus puerorum"; a common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the initial difficult stages are passed, the final maturation requires only gentle, easy heat.</note>. Take it, then, and cast away its powdery impurities, if it has any; dissolve it in the remainder of the Mercury—in five, six, eight, or ten parts—and place it again in a suitable vessel, and cook...

It explains the transition of "Physical Mercury" into a stable metallic mass known as the "Lead of the Philosophers," signaling the end of the difficult labor.</summary>

# PROCESS.

Cook it, as you did before, and test the sample taken out to see if it penetrates now, with sufficient fusion: but if not: repeat its dissolution and cooking until you achieve this. And you will have, as the philosophers say, their **egg** <term>Philosophers' Egg: A symbolic term for the sealed vessel (the "Athanor") or the developing substance of the Great Work itself, representing the potential for new life/gold.</term>, and you will be occupied in their secrets.

It remains, Most Sweet Lord Cousin <note>original: "Patruelis"; specifically a paternal cousin.</note>, that with all our heart and all our strength we should humbly approach that Highest God, that he may lead us by his holy spirit through Jesus Christ his Only-Begotten Son our Lord, the true **Cornerstone** <note>original: "Lapidem angularem"; a deliberate pun by the author, linking the "Lapis" (Stone) of the alchemists with the spiritual "Stone" of Christ.</note>, and teach us to understand these sacred mysteries, and to work and perfect them if they seem to serve his glory and our salvation. For He who Is, Who Was, and Who is to come, the Almighty, will pay the due penalties to the former and the most desired rewards to the latter: because God loves the character of the pious, but the one who leads a shameful life He affects with eternal torments. From our little study in Gouda, the first of January, 1601.

<header>THE CHEMIST</header>

...with the aid of divine majesty <note>original: "tatis diuinæ"; likely "maiestatis" or "diuinitatis" continuing from the previous page.</note> and through their own labors, they attained this knowledge. They left it in their books for posterity, just as it seemed fitting to them: yet they wrote under such an enigma of words so that it would neither be opened to the unworthy or the foolish, nor hidden from the worthy sons of doctrine. 

In the exposition of these matters, we trust we shall be guided by a divine governing hand; we shall not exceed the permitted boundaries, but we shall touch upon those things that are appropriate according to their suitability. But lest this volume of our work be extended to an immense size, we do not intend to undertake an explanation of all the books composed by those who have reached the said science through various paths—though one may approach a single goal by many paths. 

Instead, we shall proceed by explaining only the writings of those ancients to whom this science seems to have been especially and most intimately granted and revealed by the hand of divine abundance. These were the masters who were in agreement regarding the work and composition of our <term>elixir</term> <note>The "philosopher's stone" in liquid form, capable of transmuting metals.</note> or "penetrating poison" <note>original: "veneni penetrantis"; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a substance that "kills" or breaks down the base metal to allow for its rebirth as gold.</note> which tints and perfects bodies. This elixir is composed of our <term>Magnesia</term> <note>Not the modern mineral, but a symbolic "prime matter" containing the seeds of gold.</note>, and our <term>permanent water</term> <note>A specialized solvent, often associated with philosophical mercury, that does not wet the hands.</note>, and our ferment, or our air. 

Because of its goodness, its power in operation, its unity, and the unchanging nature of its tint and alteration, the philosophers chose this work as their own above all others. They placed their symbolic figures upon it and spoke of it in various discourses; yet, despite their hidden meanings, they remained in total agreement.

The first of these before the flood were Seth and his sons, and the <term>Scolici</term> <note>original: "Scolici"; likely referring to the "Schoolmen" or specific followers of the Sethian tradition.</note> their followers. After the flood, there was Hermes Trismegistus, the head of the Philosophers; then Moses, and Maria his sister <note>Maria Prophetissima or "Mary the Jewess," a foundational figure in early alchemy.</note>; after these, King Hercules, Stephanus of Astane, Belinus <note>Often identified as Apollonius of Tyana.</note>, Solomon, Democritus, and Rosinus <note>An Arabic-to-Latin corruption of the name Zosimos of Panopolis.</note>. 

Then came others, from whose sayings the *Book of the Assembly* <note>original: "liber turbæ", referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts depicting a debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> was composed, such as Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Zeno, and others whose sayings are described in that very *Book of the Assembly*. Afterward, truly, many others were their followers, who wrote books in this way of working, or mentioned it in some part of their writings, such as Morienus, King Khalid, Miruendus, Alfidius Alexander, Rhazes, Avicenna, Virgil, Geber, and certain others. 

We shall bring forward their sayings as a testimony of truth for the perfect explanation and proof of the things we relate in this book, as the opportunity arises. And indeed, rejecting empty boasting, we do not deny that just as we have, so too might others of sound and subtle intellect—even without the help of this book—attain the goal of perfection through the books of the aforementioned philosophers...

...to perceive and attain <note>original: "tionem percipere"; likely completing "eruditionem" (erudition) or "cognitionem" (knowledge) from the preceding page.</note> knowledge. However, if they persist with perseverance and constancy in the repeating of their reading and the frequency of their experiments, and if the resources for working are available to them, and if this has not been denied to them by God: for we describe nothing else in the course of this little book except what has flowed from the fountain of wisdom of those ancient philosophers. Therefore, we hope that through this labor of ours, the science and the truth of the wisdom of the ancients—to whom the powers of the sciences were specifically granted—may be preserved incorrupt from the arrows of the ignorant and the detractors. We also hope its followers may become more true in their practice with divine help: for if they are not ungrateful to God, and if they understand by reason this exposition which we make, and remain persevering in the work, they will be able to reach the fruit of this truth. 

We will arrange this book through brief propositions in the main text, and we will add to each proposition a sufficient commentary, strengthening the meaning of the aforementioned philosophers with authoritative citations, as well as adding from our own small gift of knowledge whatever seems opportune to us. We give this book the title *The Palm of Divine Wisdom* <note>original: "Theosophiae Palmarium"; "Palmarium" can also imply a "masterpiece" or "prize."</note>, because it reflects the author's name in a certain way and explains to us the <term>Secret</term> <note>original: "Arcanum"; a hidden, powerful mystery of nature.</note> of God's wisdom. 

We think it worthy to begin our little book with this sequence: first, to treat our <term>Elixir</term>, whether it is made from one thing or several. Second, concerning the matter of the components of the Elixir itself. Third, concerning the method and governance of composing and perfecting it. Fourth, concerning its utility and fruit, both in metals and in humans. Therefore, giving praises to God and asking for His help, we subjoin the first proposition, which is as follows:

->*unchanging tincture and most truly perfecting them*<-

This first proposition is seen to be proven through the sayings of many philosophers, especially those who are cited in the book of the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note>, among whom Eximenus <note>A name likely corrupted from a Greek original, often appearing in alchemical literature.</note> says in the ninth discourse: *Know (he says) all you of skilled mind, that there is no true tincture except from our copper <note>original: "aere"; while it means bronze or copper, in alchemy it refers to the specialized "philosophical" metal.</note>: do not, therefore, destroy your souls and your money.* Parmenides, in the *Assembly* in the eleventh discourse, says: *know that...*

The envious <note>original: "inuidi"; a common alchemical term for authors who deliberately obscured their writings to keep secrets from the "unworthy."</note> have treated in manifold ways many waters and broths, bodies, stones, and metals: but leave these, and the gold, and the coins; and make coins become gold, in place of this our brass. Lucas, in his 12th discourse, says that one thing does what many things perform, needing no other things except one; and that one thing, in each individual stage of our works, is turned into another nature. Ictis, in the 15th discourse, says: Know, you seekers of this art, that what is most powerful and sublime among the philosophers is, among the foolish, the most vile of all things—this is what we venerate. Bonellus, in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>, 36th discourse, says: Know, all you seekers of this science, that the entire work and the regimen <note>The "regimen" refers to the specific process of heating and governing the chemical reactions.</note> are produced by nothing but water.

## PROPOSITION II.

->*On the contrary, this Elixir does not consist of only one simple*<-
->*thing, but is rather a composite.*<-

This proposition seems contrary to the first. However, we shall refer the resolution of this and several subsequent points to the eighth proposition; meanwhile, we shall present the sayings of the wise. Bonellus, in the 36th discourse cited just above, says: "The envious have called this composition, when it has been turned into blackness, 'sufficiently black.'" Rosinus, in Question 48, says: "For no stone is generated in the art except this one, which the philosophers have composed from their own things." The same author in Question 2 says: "Unless there were something containing the two thinnest parts, which makes them peaceable, they perish and flee from the fire."

## PROPOSITION III.

->*It follows, moreover, that our Elixir consists of at least*<-
->*two things, since it was previously*<-
->*stated to be a composite.*<-

This third proposition, though it—along with those following up to the sixth—may seem contrary to the first, will be reconciled in the commentary on the eighth proposition shortly hereafter. Now let the sayings of the philosophers come forward to confirm it. Aristeus, in the *Assembly*, 10th discourse: "Take the body which I have shown to you, and fit it into thin plates: and place it in our water, which is the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a technical term for the eternal solvent or "mercury" that does not wet the hands.</note> after it is governed." Diomedes, 29th discourse: "Join therefore the male, the son of the red slave, to his fragrant wife." <note>This is a classic alchemical allegory for the union of chemical opposites, often representing Sulfur and Mercury.</note> Zonon, in the 35th discourse, seems to show this openly, saying: "I signify to you that the art requires two natures. For the precious is not without the vile: nor the vile without the precious." Zenon, in the 26th discourse: "Then the Elixir is composed of the moist and the dry."

### PROPOSITION IV.

->*Further, the Elixir seems to consist of three things.*<-

Parmenides, in the 5th discourse, says: Therefore, dismiss the manifold superfluity, and take the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury, considered by alchemists to be the feminine, receptive principle of all metals.</note>, and congeal it in the body of magnesia <note>original: "magnesia"; in alchemy, this was not modern magnesium, but a name for various mineral ores or the "raw material" of the work.</note>, or in *teambar* <note>A rare term likely referring to a type of amber or a specific metallic alloy mentioned in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> or in sulfur that is not consumed by fire—which three, nonetheless, are the same thing—and make the nature itself white, and put in our brass <note>original: "æs nostrum"; a symbolic term for the alchemical substance at a specific stage of refinement, not literal brass.</note>.

### PROPOSITION V.

->*The Elixir is composed rather of four things.*<-

Menaldus, in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "in turb[a]"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note>, 25th discourse, says: Know that this brass, which I have commanded you to rule, consists of these four bodies. Dardaris, in the 4th discourse, says: Sulfurs are the souls which were hidden in four bodies; once extinguished, they naturally held each other together and provided the tinge <note>The "tinge" or "tincture" refers to the Elixir’s power to transform the color and nature of a metal.</note>.

### PROPOSITION VI.

->*The Elixir also consists of more and many things.*<-

Zenon, in the 26th discourse, says: This venom <note>original: "venenum"; alchemists often used "poison" or "venom" to describe the potent, transformative power of the Elixir.</note> is like a birth and a life, because it is the soul, and it is extracted from many things and applied to coins. Bonellus, in the 49th discourse, says: It should be noted that the clean water which comes from sulfur is not from sulfur alone, but is truly composed of many things, which are made into one sulfur from many sulfurs.

### PROPOSITION VII.

->*Finally, the composition of this Elixir seems to be made from all things.*<-

Aristeus, in the 51st discourse, says: Take the quicksilver from the flower of brass, which they also call the water of our brass, and the fiery venom extracted from all things. And a little later: And know, all you seekers of this art, that every body is dissolved with the spirit to which it is joined; and that all spirits are altered by the bodies.

->*The reduction of the disagreement of the aforesaid to harmony, and their correct determination, through which it is concluded that our tinging Elixir consists of many things or of a composition of many.*<-

To prove this proposition, along with the harmony of the other preceding ones, we say that our Elixir <term>Yxir|A variant of Elixir.</term> consists not of one alone, but of a composition of many, since before the composition of these things, they are diverse in species, and [called] by diverse na- <meta>catchword: names (vocabulis)</meta>

<page-num>947</page-num>
<header>C H E M I C A L</header>

...are called by their individual names; but after they have been mixed together through their own governance <note>original: "regimen"; the specific sequence of heating and treatment required in alchemy.</note>, they are so united to each other that they become one new substance, called by a single name. We can see examples of this in other composite things. For instance, when a certain antidote <note>Likely referring to a "theriac" or universal medicine common in medieval pharmacology.</note> is prepared by art from various herbs, gums, liquids, and many other species—which are each called by different and distinct names on their own—once the concoction is complete, a certain new species results that is different from its components, and it is called by a single new name. Similarly, bread is composed of water and a mixture of flour, yet it is called "bread." The same thing is seen in the building of a house, which consists of stones, lime, wood, bricks, and other such things; yet it is called by only one name: "House." Many more examples could be given. Thus, the philosophers in our work have called the composition from which our **elixir** <note>original: "yxir"; an archaic spelling of elixir.</note> proceeds by only one singular, new name—**Magnesia**—even though they made it from many things. They did so because it is a "great thing" <note>A wordplay on the Latin *magna res* (great thing) and *Magnesia*.</note> in which the greatest secret lies. Astanus says in his 42nd discourse: "When the philosophers have prepared the materials and joined the loving spouses together, the golden water ascends with them." The Philosopher in the 73rd discourse of the *Assembly* <note>original: "in turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or *Assembly of the Philosophers*, a famous early alchemical text.</note> says: "The first composition, namely the body of **Magnesia**, is made from many things, although they have become one single thing; it is then called by one name, which the ancients called the **Whiteness of Brass**." The proof and solution of the six aforementioned propositions is more than sufficiently clear to the intelligent reader from all the points stated above, just as are the doubts regarding the seventh proposition. Therefore, Proposition 9 follows.

### PROPOSITION IX.

> *Although it has been shown that the elixir consists of a composition of many things, its root and foundation is nonetheless our **brass**, which must be brought to the state of elixir through its own governance; for without governance, nothing is changed.*

This proposition is the beginning of the demonstration of the species from which the elixir is made. Moreover, hear Eximenus in his 8th discourse on why governance is necessary: "Know that no true tincture is made except from our brass; do not, therefore, destroy your souls and your money, nor bring sorrow to your hearts. I will add a foundation for you: unless you turn the aforementioned brass into white, and then make it like coins to the sight, and then turn it red, you have achieved nothing." Bonus says in his 37th discourse: "This is our brass, which the philosophers commanded to be washed away by the eternal water." Constans says in his 28th discourse:

# T H E  C H A R I O T E E R <note>original: "AVRIGA"; a title likely referring to the one who "steers" the chemical process.</note>

And know that if you take anything other than our brass, and govern <note>original: "regatis"; the specific alchemical sequence of heating, cooling, and chemical treatment.</note> it with our water, it will profit you nothing.

### P R O P O S I T I O N X.

*The governance of this our brass is such that it becomes a poison, or a staining rust.*

Mundus <note>A speaker in the "Turba Philosophorum," an influential early alchemical text.</note> therefore says in discourse 47: "The ancients believe that he who turns gold into poison <note>original: "venenum"; in alchemy, this refers to a potent, transformative substance or elixir that "penetrates" metals, rather than a literal toxin.</note> has already reached the goal; but he who does not remains in nothingness." Anaxagoras says in discourse 54: "He who can turn gold into rust <note>original: "rubiginem"; refers to a metallic oxide or powder produced during the Work, intended to "dye" base metals.</note> and poison has already found the goal."

### P R O P O S I T I O N XI.

*The rust or staining poison will not be produced from our aforementioned brass unless it is itself stained.*

This proposition is certain and is supported by both reason and the authorities that follow. By reason indeed: because since our brass <note>A philosophical or "sophic" metal, not the common hardware alloy of copper and zinc.</note> can scarcely be corrupted by any common governance without returning to itself unaltered; and when it has been purged by the testing of fire, it does not provide a greater staining power. For all of its color is necessary for its own perfection, nor can it color anything else apart from itself while remaining in its own nature without the loss of its own color; so that if mixed with another, it loses some of its color, and thus there is no profit. Therefore, it remains thus in its own nature unless it is governed by such a regimen by which it is stained with a more intense color, exceeding the color it perfectly possesses while in its own nature. This governance must be such that the brass is turned into a powder which, because of the abundance of intense color, is almost black—like the color of burnt blood, or Tyrian purple, or a deep violet color. And then, because of the excess of its color, the smallest part of it, when mixed with a large body of a "white lesser light" <note>original: "albi minoris luminaris"; alchemical shorthand for silver.</note>, will stain it with the sufficiency of the color of the "true greater light" <note>original: "veri luminaris maioris"; alchemical shorthand for gold.</note>, with a transmutation and staining that is invariable and fixed because of the power and stability it acquired from the governance and the staining agents. Monarchus says in the *Turba*, discourse 25: "Because brass does not color, except for color; because that which is colored colors [others]." <note>Meaning a substance must be saturated with color before it can impart that color to another body.</note>

### P R O P O S I T I O N XII.

*This body is also the Elixir, and the leaven in the dough.*

Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> in the seventh treatise says thus: "Similarly, gold in bodies contains every body within itself and gives them life; for the elixir <note>original: "yxir"</note> is a ferment <note>original: "fermentum"</note>, without which the work is never completed, just as dough is not fermented without leaven."

<note>original: "æs noſtrum (our brass), venenum (poison), rubigo tingens (staining rust), aurum (gold), Anaxagoras, tinctura (tincture), luminaris maioris (greater light/gold), Monarchus in turba, Yxir (elixir), fermentum (ferment), Hermes"</note>

### PROP. XIII.

*Therefore, it shall dye our brass itself, and that which produces the poison or rust; namely, the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens"; the enduring alchemical solvent or "philosophical water" that does not wet the hands.</note>, or the quicksilver and Cambar <note>original: "Cambar"; a technical term often referring to a specific state of mercury or "white lead" in the Turba Philosophorum.</note>, or the quicksilver from the male, or by things called by similar names and the ethel-substances <note>original: "ethelfacta"; likely derived from the Arabic "al-it̠al," referring to the spiritual or fixed essence of a substance.</note>, by which it is mixed and corrected by its own governance.*

All these things which are said to dye our brass, although they are called by diverse names, are the same thing: namely, our water composed of our things, and perfected by its own governance. The governance of this water is, by the will of God, unknown to the common people. And as for the fact that our brass is dyed, listen to Parmenides in discourse 2: "Know that gold is turned into rust by the permanent water." Mosius says in discourse 44: "The quicksilver which dyes gold is the quicksilver of Cambar."

### PROP. XIV.

*Again, by the action of fire, this our brass shall be dyed.*

Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> in the third treatise says: "And this tincture remains red like Kermes <note>original: "Karmes"; a brilliant red dye derived from insects, used here to describe the color of the "Red Work" or final stage.</note>; for our son the King <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the perfected stone or gold.</note> takes his tincture from the fire."

### PROP. XV.

*From the aforesaid, it is concluded that our dyeing elixir <note>original: "yxir"; a variant of Elixir.</note> consists of our brass and our permanent water, and by the governance of fire it is brought to an intense power of dyeing and altering with perfection.*

It is certain that he who knows how to complete the composition of our permanent water and its governance with our brass shall have his intent from them; otherwise, working in vain, he is worn out. For Constantus <note>A speaker in the alchemical text "Turba Philosophorum."</note> says in discourse 20: "If you govern <note>original: "regatis"; to process according to the specific alchemical heat-regimen.</note> our things in such a way, it profits you nothing. But if you govern our brass with our water, you shall find all things predicted by us."

### PROP. XVI.

*And because the said permanent water, without which the dyeing of our brass does not occur, is by no means bought for a price, it is necessary first to demonstrate its composition and governance, as far as is permitted.*

Pythagoras says in discourse 28: "Some who have books read them and think that this composition is bought; it must certainly be known that nothing of the work is bought."

### P R O P. XVII.

*Regarding the preparation of this permanent water <note>original: "aquæ permanentis"; the philosophical solvent that dissolves metals into their prime matter without wetting the hands.</note>, there is a twofold composition which must, in the end, become one.*

The Philosopher in discourse 12 says: The composition is twofold; for one is moist, and the other is dry only. Therefore, let them be cooked so that they become one, and this is called the "good thing of many names" <note>Alchemy is famous for "polyonymy"—using many names (like "our brass," "the dragon," or "the hidden stone") to describe a single secret substance to confuse the uninitiated.</note>.

### P R O P. XVIII.

*The first composition shall be made from dry things alone, which is called the body of Magnesia <note>original: "Magnesiæ"; in alchemy, this is not the modern chemical magnesium, but a "mother" substance or prime matter capable of taking on many forms.</note>, or the whiteness of brass, or the lead of brass, and sulfur, and the brass of Magnesia, and our money, and our gold, etc. The second composition, however, is from the aforementioned dry things with the moist, which is also called Magnesia, although one name is often substituted for the other.*

Rosinus <note>A common medieval name for the Greco-Egyptian alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> in question 8 says: Consider, therefore, those things found in the books of the philosophers: Our Brass, Our Money, Our Gold or Our Lead, and Our Magnesia. These are nothing other than that brass reported to you; for the secret is within it, which is why they referred to it by these names. Similarly, their Lead, which is their Magnesia, becomes the money which is their "body." Therefore, the Brass is a composite thing, which nevertheless becomes the "money" <note>original: "pecunia"; here used metaphorically to mean the valuable medium or "currency" of the alchemical transformation.</note>.

### P R O P. XIX.

*This first composition <note>composition</note> which we said was of dry things, called the body of Magnesia, is a composition of four bodies or four elements.*

Monaldus in discourse 25 says: Know that this brass, which I commanded you to rule, is those four bodies. Democritus <note>The ancient Greek philosopher, often cited in alchemy as a master of "spiritual" physics.</note> in the allegory, distinction 19, says: And no tincture <note>A substance capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold.</note> is made except from joined bodies.

### P R O P. XX.

*These four bodies are called the sulfurs of the earth.*

Dardaris in discourse 44 says: The sulfurs are the souls which were hidden in the four bodies.

### P R O P. XXI.

*Out of these four bodies or elements in the composition of the body of Magnesia, it is necessary to apply an equal proportion.*

The Allegory of the Wise <note>original: "Allegoria sapientum"</note>, distinction 1, says: If you place the medicines equally, you will feel no error. But if you add or subtract, you are striving for a correction <note>The "medicines" are the elemental ingredients; balance is essential for the stability of the Work.</note>.

### P R O P. XXII.

*The second composition, which we said was of dry things with the moist, is quicksilver <note>mercury</note> joined with the body of Magnesia itself, and that composition is called Magnesia.*

Parmenides <note>An ancient philosopher whose name was used in the "Turba Philosophorum," a famous alchemical assembly.</note> in discourse 11 says: Therefore, leave behind the many-folded superfluous thing,

->T H E  A L C H E M I S T<-

...and take quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; the liquid metal mercury, often considered the "spirit" of metals in alchemy.</note>, and congeal it in the body of Magnesia. Either in *kenkel* <note>original: "kenkel"; a term likely referring to a specific alchemical vessel or a mineral variant</note>, or in the sulfur that does not burn. In the Book of Allegories, section 12: quicksilver is the spirit which they wish to be contained by the body of Magnesia; for the body of Magnesia is the body which they dissolve, so that in it they may compose the spirit, which is both spirit and body alike.

### P R O P. XXIII.

*The discovery of this mixture is that the spirit may be coagulated in the body, and the body itself may be dissolved into the spirit, and the whole may become one, which is called Magnesia. And this is to make bodies incorporeal, and the incorporeal bodies.*

Astanus in discourse 42: Incite a war between brass <note>original: "aes"; refers to the "philosophical brass," the starting metallic material</note> and quicksilver, because they tend toward destruction and are corrupted first. For that reason, the brass conceives the quicksilver and congeals it; but the quicksilver, conceiving the brass, dissolves it.

### P R O P. XXIV.

*The perfection of this mixture shall be achieved through the regime of decoction [boiling], grinding, and washing. By the benefit of this regime, the thickness of the body will be thinned, and its impurity will be cured and raised, and its fiery subtlety—hidden in its belly, which is its tincture and soul—will be preserved, hidden in the other spirit.*

It is necessary to mix that thick substance with fiery poison and putrefy it, and diligently grind it until it becomes a spirit, hidden in the other spirit. Plato in discourse 2: For the spirit, separated from the body and hidden in the other spirit, causes both to become volatile <note>original: "fugiens"; literally "fleeing," referring to a substance that evaporates or sublimes easily when heated.</note>.

### P R O P. XXV.

*And for that reason, an old proverb rings out: if you know how to give the fire of fire, then the fire and the aboth <note>original: "aboth"; likely derived from a Hebrew or Arabic term for a vessel or a specific intensity of heat</note> are sufficient for you. Since quicksilver burns bodies and refines them, it separates their coarseness from the subtle part.*

Monaldus in discourse 25: Know that quicksilver is a fire that burns, mortifies, and binds bodies in a single regime.

### P R O P. XXVI.

*This quicksilver itself is also called "fiery poison" in this mixture, because like fire it is diffused through the body of Magnesia, just as poison is spread through the bodies of men.*

Allegory, section 5: The fiery poison is the monied water <note>original: "aqua nummosa"; likely referring to the "our money" or metallic solution discussed in previous sections</note> not yet perfected.

### P R O P. XXVII.

*Therefore, let there be a destruction <note>original: "interitus"; refers to the alchemical 'mortification' or 'killing' of the base metal to release its inner essence</note> for the continuation of the aforementioned regime, until the body has been so thinned and dissolved in the said spirit that it is incorporeal to the touch. Let both be light and impalpable to the touch, like butter or brains. And when it has become thus, it must be exalted through fire in Ethel <note>original: "Ethel"; an alchemical term for the sublimated spirit or the vapor found at the top of the vessel</note> before our brass is mixed in.*
