->T H E  C H A R I O T E E R<-

Astanus, Discourse 42. Copper <note>original: "Æs"; referring to the "philosophical brass," the base metallic matter of the work</note>, which the philosophers—when they have prepared the materials and joined the spouses together, uniting themselves—have caused a golden water <note>original: "aqua aurea"</note> to rise from them. Mundus, Discourse 47. Unless you continue the matter with fire until the spirits ascend, they will vanish into nothing.

### P R O P. XXVIII.

*This sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again in a purer form</note> must be performed with a gentle fire, so that the purified subtlety of the compound—which is the tinting soul <note>original: "anima tingens"; the active essence that gives color and quality to the metal</note>—may be exalted to the highest or uppermost part of the vessel. The coarse earthiness, which hinders the tinting and the penetration, is left behind at the bottom in the Ethel <note>original: "Ethel"; an alchemical term for the dregs or ash remaining after sublimation</note>.*

Monaldus, Discourse 25. Know that the body cannot tint itself unless its spirit is extracted and hidden in its belly; for that which is thick and earthy does not tint, but it is the thinness of nature that penetrates and colors within the body.

### P R O P. XXIX.

*This sublimated material is the quicksilver of Cambar <note>original: "argentum vivum de Cambar"; "Cambar" likely refers to a specific mineral or geographic source used in alchemical nomenclature</note>, and the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a solvent that does not evaporate or change under heat</note>, and gum, and urine—which we have said above tints our copper—and it is called by many other names besides. In the sublimation of our first work, it is the completion. The second work, however, consists in this: that by its governance we may turn our copper alone, by means of this water, into a tinting rust <note>original: "rubigo"; a term for the red-colored state of the material, often signifying the final stages toward the Philosopher's Stone</note>.*

Astanus, Discourse 66. The rust is the second work, which is achieved with gold alone.

### P R O P. XXX.

*The beginning of this governance is to divide the aforementioned permanent water into two equal parts. One of these will be mixed with a proper portion of our copper, so that it may be dissolved and broken down into earth; the second part, however, will be saved for the watering <note>original: "impotationem"; the act of soaking or saturating the dry material</note> of that which was broken down.*

Hence Theophilus, Discourse 22. Divide the poison <note>original: "venenum"; a common alchemical metaphor for the transformative solvent or mercury</note> into two equal parts: with one part, liquefy the copper; save the other part for grinding and soaking. Cerus, Discourse 23. When you have divided the water into two parts: the first will be for liquefying and cooking the body, and the second for cleansing the burnt material and its companion, which have been made one. Nichorus, Discourse 33. For it is necessary to burn our copper with one part, and then to soak it seven times with the remaining water.

Mundus, Discourse 34. Take one part of the gum of the animal of most intense whiteness, and one part of fish gall, and from a white calf

### PROP. 33.

<margin>—></margin>
*For the easier mixing of our copper itself with the aforementioned water; it is necessary for us first to produce the metal in thin plates, and thus to mix it with the water and cook it in it until it is dissolved, and they become one.*

Aristeus, Discourse 19. Take therefore the body which I have shown to you, and fashion it into thin tablets: Then place them in the water of our sea <note>the alchemical solvent or "permanent water"</note>, which is the water remaining after it is governed; then place it over a gentle fire, until the tablets are broken down and become water.

### PROP. XXXIV.

*This composition must be placed in a glass vessel.*

### PROP. XXXV.

*Indeed, in the governing of this, many colors will appear; first, namely, black: second, white, third, saffron-yellow; at last, it will arrive step by step at the intensity of redness, even to the perfection of the Tyrian color <note>original: "tyrij coloris"; a deep crimson or purple dye, symbolizing the final stage of the alchemical process</note>, all of which we shall subjoin in order in their own propositions.*

Diomedes, Discourse 29. Cook them therefore until they become black: then white: then red: then let the tinting poison <note>the substance that has the power to transform other metals</note> be made.

### PROP. XXXVI.

*Truly, because unless our work is first whitened, we cannot make it red: it is necessary in the first stage of the governance to lead it to the white or "money-like" color <note>original: "nummosum"; referring to the luster of silver coins</note>.*

Frictis, Discourse 15. Know that the beginning of the whole work is whiteness, which redness succeeds; then comes the perfection of the work.

### PROP. XXXVII.

Aristeus, Discourse 19. Then place it over a gentle fire until the tablets are broken down and become water. Mundus, Discourse 18. Mix these portions, and cook them for forty days. Pandulphus, Discourse 21. Therefore, cook these four things prudently for forty days.

### PROP. XXXVIII.

> *During the very time of cooking, before the aforementioned whiteness arrives, a blackness will appear on top, which is of the nature of Martech.* <note>original: "Martech"; likely a corruption of the Persian "martak," referring to litharge or lead monoxide, often associated with the "head of the crow" in the black stage of the work.</note>

Pandulphus, Discourse 21. Then cook it little by little; taking it out, look to see if it has become black. Bonellus, Discourse 37. Seeing the blackness hovering over that water, know that the body is now melted.

### PROP. XXXIX.

> *For the said blackness should be purged by washing with salty, and sharp <note>acidic</note>, or sweet waters, without grinding, until it becomes like a molten coin.*

Bonellus, Discourse 37. Wash it, and deprive it of its blackness.

### PROP. XL.

> *After the removal of the blackness, however, the aforementioned whiteness will begin to appear; in the meantime, it is necessary to cook this so that it becomes like a white, coin-like stone, like marble, or similar to salt in its splendor and brilliance.*

Lucas, Discourse 12. Roast it, therefore, for seven days, until it becomes like glittering marble. Philiorus, Discourse 15. If you cook it well and deprive it of blackness, it will be turned into stone, and will become a coin of the most intense whiteness. Theophilus, Discourse 22. Cook it for forty days until the white flower, and the flower of salt <note>original: "flos salis"; likely referring to the purest crystalline form of the substance</note>, appears in its splendor and brilliance.

### PROP. XLI.

> *This stone is called Aiar, or the Boric stone, or the Attic stone <note>original: "lapis Aticos"; likely referring to a high-grade mineral or "Attic salt," used as a metaphor for purity</note> by the philosophers.*

Theophilus, Discourse 22. The philosophers have therefore called this the Boric stone. Pandulphus, Discourse 21. I have shown you the beginning of this stone, which is the Attic stone. Lucas, Discourse 22. And know that when it is coagulated, we call it Aiar.

### PROP. XLII.

> *Up to this limit, indeed, it is necessary to maintain a light fire.*

Lucas, Discourse 12. And so it appears gentle in the whitening, until it is coagulated.

> *In the aforementioned cookings, care must be taken that the vessel is always closed so that the spirit does not flee, but is coagulated within it.*

Lucas, Discourse 12. Beware lest it exit from the vessel: rather, coagulate the humidity within the vessel. Mundus, Discourse 16. Observe the vessel, therefore, lest the compound smoke and flee.

### P R O P. XLIV.

*In the aforementioned decoctions, however, the moisture in the mixture is not entirely held or coagulated: but one or two out of its three parts are separated, which can be saved for the work of the second Cambar.* <note>Cambar: A technical term in medieval alchemy, likely derived from Arabic, referring to a specific stage of the work or the vessel itself.</note>

Hermes in the allegory, distinction 6. "If you consume a third part of your Camels <note>original: "Camellorum"; in the cryptic language of the Turba, this often refers to the volatile spirits or the "beasts" carrying the water</note>, leaving two-thirds, you have already reached your purpose." Balgus in the assembly, discourse 50. "I declare to you that in this cooking of the coin <note>nummus: refers to the flat, disc-like appearance of the solidified alchemical matter</note>, the weight of a third part of the water is consumed; but the remainder becomes wind, in the spirit of the second Combar."

---

### P R O P. XLV.

*After the said composition has been coagulated by the aforementioned governance and turned into a dry white stone, whether coin-like and shining like marble; it is necessary to increase the fire so that it may be broken down, until it is turned into earth, or yellow or greenish ash.*

Pythagoras, discourse 13. "Break the lime and the marble." Socrates, discourse 16. "Cook it with the most intense fire, until the thickness of the body is broken down." Batosius, discourse 24. "Cook it until it is coagulated: then grind it until it becomes a crocus <note>term: crocus; a saffron-colored powder, usually a metallic oxide</note> similar to the color of gold."

### P R O P. XLVI.

*Moreover, this grinding ought to be done not by hands, but by strong fire alone, as we have said.*

Zenon, discourse 35. "And know that it does not happen, except by the strongest cooking and continuous grinding—by fire, not by hands."

### P R O P. XLVII.

*Moreover, when the aforementioned stone has been turned into earth somewhat colored, as has been said: It is necessary to moisten that earth with the second part of the water which you saved: yet not by adding all the water at once, but in several turns: seven at the least. And in each imbibition <note>imbibitio: the process of the dry "earth" absorbing the liquid "spirit"</note> cook it, until the water is dried in it, and the hidden colors in it come forth into the manifest.*

Corus, discourse 25. "Moisten it seven times, until it is broken down." Gregorius, discourse 27. "When you see this shining stone, you must break it by force and turn it into earth, and let it have a little redness, so that you may receive the remainder of the water, which the envious <note>The "envious" (inuidi) was a standard term used by alchemists to describe previous authors who deliberately concealed the truth of the Work</note> ordered you to divide into two parts; and when you moisten it many times, until in that hidden body...

Azaracus, discourse 57. Mixing the ash with water, cook it again until that ash melts, and then cook them and soak them seven times while the water remains, until the composition becomes sweet and red; soak it also until it is moist.

*The moistening* <note>original: "impotatio"; likely a variation of "imbibitio," the process of feeding the dry matter with liquid</note> *of the aforementioned ash is also sometimes performed by the water which had risen from it during the work of petrification* <note>original: "lapidificationis"; the process of turning the substance into a stone-like solid</note> *and the aforementioned breaking down.*

Aristeus, discourse 19. Drink up the Ethelia <note>original: "Ethelia"; a term often used in alchemy to refer to the volatile spirit or the "black sulfur" released during heating</note> or its own water which came out of it. ->### P R O P. LIII.<-

*However, one must take such care against an excess of fire in the work of the said soakings* <note>original: "imbibitionum"</note> *so that the soul is not chased away from the ash; but remains and is fixed within it.*

Diomedes, discourse 29. Return to it its own sweat, and give it to death again, and establish a kingdom for it; and take care that you do not chase it away, burning it with too much fire.

->### P R O P. LIV.<-

*Once the said soakings and boilings* <note>original: "decoctionibus"</note> *of one hundred and fifty days are finished, it must afterwards be cooked again intensely with an intense fire for forty days toward the completion of its coloring and its perfection, so that it becomes a spiritual, impalpable powder of a Tyrian* <note>original: "Tyrij"; Tyrian purple was the most expensive dye of antiquity, here representing the final royal red stage of the Great Work</note> *or purple color, or of a burnt red; which is the perfection of the intention.*

Sobosses, discourse 24. And do not cease to cook and dry it until it is soaked with all its moisture: Then leave it in its vessel for several days, until the most precious Tyrian color comes out upon the top.

->### P R O P. LV.<-

*And so this powder is the elixir* <note>original: "ixir"; a Latinization of the Arabic "al-iksir"</note> *or the poison of the philosophers,* <note>original: "venenum philosophorum"; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a substance so potent it "penetrates" and transforms the nature of a metal</note> *which when placed upon coins stains them; and turns them into perfect gold, by the help of God.*

Barsen, discourse 30. And that which, coming into perfection, stains every body. Mundus, discourse 47. Namely, that poison which the philosopher asserts stains every body.

->### P R O P. LVI.<-

*And this tincture shall not be found wanting by fire or by trial* <note>original: "examen"; the assaying process used to test the purity of gold</note> *but it will be unchanging and firm; and so forth.*

Arsuberes, discourse 14. When the poison penetrates the body, it colors it with an unchanging color, etc. The same author: from sulfur mixed with sulfur, a most precious color is made, which does not change nor flee from the fire.

### PROPOSITION 57.

*The true cause of this effect is this: because, on account of its virtue and the properties it has acquired from both nature and art, it is powerful enough to separate what is superfluous even from homogeneous bodies* <note>original: "homogeneis"; substances that are uniform in composition</note> *with the help of heat. Because of its subtlety, it penetrates through the smallest parts, and it disjoins and destroys the corruptible part, leaving behind only the incorruptible substance of perfection. For the same reason, if it is taken into the human body, it ejects all superfluities of the humors* <note>original: "humorum"; the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient and medieval medicine believed governed health</note>, *bringing the body into a state of balance, protecting it from sickness, and preserving it in perfect health. This is indeed a gift of God and the secret of the philosophers;*
->*which Kings and others seeking find not at all, except those*<-
->*to whom divine goodness grants it.*<-

Barsen, discourse 25. But Kings seeking this do not find it, except those to whom God grants his favor <note>original: "annuit"; literally "nods" or "gives assent"</note>. Rosinus, question 10. No one is able to separate the truth from those things which the philosophers set down ambiguously, except by the inspiration of God or by the instruction of another. Also the same author, question 13. That which God has granted to his prophets and his chosen ones.

### PROPOSITION 58.

*He, therefore, who understands the aforementioned things by reason shall be numbered among the sons of wisdom. Let him therefore offer manifold praises to God, lest he be ungrateful for so great a benefit. But he who does not reach an understanding of them should know that this happens because of divine judgment, or his own ignorance, or sin: because he ought to blame not us, but*
->*himself.*<-

Diomedes, discourse 29. If you who investigate this science understand it, you are blessed; but if not, I have already paid what I owe <note>meaning "I have fulfilled my duty to explain it"</note>: and in brief. And if you are ignorant, God has hidden the truth from you. Do not, therefore, find fault with the wise, but with yourselves. For if God knew there was a faithful mind in you, he would certainly have made the truth known.

*Let us therefore return manifold thanks to Divine Wisdom who, opening secrets to us, allowed them to be unlocked—approved by such valid sayings of the philosophers through the sequence of this our description, as far as was permitted—by Theosophy* <note>original: "Theosophia"; here used to mean divine or sacred wisdom</note>, *without envy. May His name be praised forever and ever.*

->**Amen.**<-

### TO THE READER WHO LOVES CHEMISTRY. <note>original: "Philochimo"; a Greek-derived term for a lover of chemistry or alchemy</note>

*You have here, benevolent Reader, many and indeed remarkable things in this brief letter which I offer to you: namely, what, of what kind, how much, and in what way health can be restored, protected, and cherished. I speak of the true balsam of the celestial stars, which allows no body to fall into putrefaction; and as Theophrastus says, it leaves no leprosy, gout, dropsy* <note>original: "podagram, hydropisin"</note> *or other diseases unexpelled by the administration of a single grain. And if it is fermented with the sulfur of the sun* <note>original: "sulphure solis"; referring to the "soul" or essential heat of gold</note> *and you wish to use this star of Venus* <note>original: "astro Veneris"; the alchemical metal copper</note>, *you will be able to turn the whole body of Venus into the Sun* <note>original: "solem"; gold</note>. *Moreover, so that you may achieve this more easily, I will add something to help you (for one book opens another, and one discourse opens another); I will add, I say, for the sake of the philosophers of all the United Provinces, a most dear little writing of mine containing the revelation of a mystery. I do this, however, under this law and omen (just as I have long since done with the French philosophers, whom I led to the glory of God, the nourishment of the Church of Christ, and the service of the most Christian King HENRY the Great* <note>King Henri IV of France (reigned 1589–1610)</note>): *that if God, in His mercy, deems any of you worthy of such a great gift, he should—with fitting prudence and observance toward God—holily, cautiously, and freely attribute, give, bestow, and consecrate his entire work (I mean the Philosopher’s Stone brought to its highest perfection) to the most serene Prince MAURICE of Nassau* <note>Maurice of Nassau (1567–1625), Prince of Orange and Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic</note>, *governor of these provinces, and to the Most Noble Estates of the United Provinces of the Netherlands. Whoever does this (and he will be doing what becomes a good man, following the Samaritan who led the man wounded by thieves to the inn, etc.) shall be counted among the greatest friends of God and his country, and shall find God and all his fellow citizens favoring him as one. This shall be that Christian Alms* <note>original: "Eleemosyna"; an act of charity or mercy</note>, *to which none similar has been distributed since the founding of the world; by which so many myriads of souls shall benefit, and in these United Provinces they shall rejoice in the highest God, giving perpetual thanks to the Author. Dissolve the fixed in the non-fixed, or in the non-fixed mother. This is not achieved unless they are joined in a vessel that is not wide <note>original: "vaso non amplo"; a narrow-necked flask used to prevent the escape of vapors</note>, lest one flee from the other, and unless they are tormented by fire. Then one works upon the other, and they become one thing, just as they were before; thus they fight against enemies, and the thick part ascends to the upper parts, well-guarded so it does not perish. In this way, the tiny fixed part becomes volatile. Thus white is born in the dry; in the white, citron-yellow; in the citron, red.

## ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,
### *A Letter from a certain Father to his Son.*

The secret of all secrets, the most hidden mystery of this so noble science, I shall reveal to you, dearest son, just as we have touched it with our hands and seen it with our bodily eyes. I adjure you by Him who created all things, that you hand over this most holy and excellent gift to no one, but that you conceal it in the manner of the philosophers <note>The "manner of the philosophers" refers to *VOS* (Virgo, Oratio, Silentium)—purity, prayer, and silence—to keep secrets from the "unworthy"</note>. Do not wonder that I have spoken openly with you, for I have known your errors for many years now; and seeing your most frequent study and your care, I could not resist my own will to hand this over to you, however much I might fear bringing punishment upon my soul. But dearest son, if you keep our commands, you will achieve a good result; and before we come to the practical work, we shall uncover for you certain natural principles, so that knowing them, you may believe what follows below.

The principles of this famous science are the same as those that are natural in metals. Furthermore, these very things are the principles of metals upon which nature is founded in her actions for forming them. Take, in the name of Christ, our blessed Stone, the honored stone, the glorious and incombustible stone, the stone hidden by all philosophers and described in parables—which is <term>Roman vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolum romanum"; likely high-quality iron or copper sulfate, prized for its ability to produce acidic vapors</note> of the highest quality. This is the stone, dearest son, which all philosophers have hidden, and they have written various and diverse sayings about it, so that such a great secret would not be grasped by the foolish and the unworthy. Take, therefore, as much of it as you please and grind it coarsely; then place it in a glazed pot over coals for <term>calcining</term> <note>original: "calcinandum"; heating a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile components and reduce it to a powder</note> alone, so that the superfluous moisture may be breathed out, and there will remain for you a white and yellowish substance. Beware, however, lest the matter be turned red, because you would lose much of our glorious spirit; and this is <term>common calcination</term> <note>original: "calcinatio vulgaris"; the standard chemical heating process known to common craftsmen, as opposed to the secret "philosophical" method</note>, which all philosophers—by hiding the truth—have demonstrated should be done in metallic bodies. Then remove it from the fire and grind it all very finely, until it is reduced to an impalpable powder. When these things are completed, take a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "bocia storta"; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, carefully sealed with clay <note>original: "lutatam"; the use of 'lute,' a protective paste, to seal the joints of the glassware against pressure and heat</note>, and put your powders into it, so that they do not exceed the weight of one pound. Place it on a furnace adapted for this, and gradually light the fire beneath, and in the name of the Lord begin to <term>distill</term> <note>original: "destillare"; the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then condensing the vapor into a liquid</note> with the receiver, its joints well-closed, so that it cannot breathe out in any way. 

Continue the fire in this way, and occasionally strengthen it, until white fumes begin to distill and enter the receiver. Then the fire must be increased, because in the matter itself there is a certain fiery part, which is called the element of fire, and it cannot come out without a great fire. When indeed the white fumes have settled, make a very strong fire once more for one hour, and this is done only so that if any fiery part, which is heavy, could not distill, it may be forced to come out by the stronger fire. When this is done, extract that precious water, and reserve it in another clean vessel, well-closed, so that it cannot breathe out in any way. 

You have, therefore, dearest son, the highest secret: because this water is called by every name in the world, and is named by the wise. For in it are three elements: water, air, and fire. -># THE EPISTLE<-

...from the water bath, but let it drip until it can no longer drip further; then throw away the distilled water, because the spirit has remained with the body. And this is what all the philosophers have said: "That which went out from it, return back upon it, until it is fixed with it, and let them not be separated for eternity," because **nature rejoices in nature.** This operation, as Raymond <note>likely referring to Raymond Lull, a legendary figure in alchemy</note> says, is called <term>conception</term> <note>original: "conceptio"; the stage where the "male" spirit and "female" earth begin to unite</note>, because the earth has begun to retain within itself a small amount of the quicksilver—that is, of our spirit.

Afterward, remove the aforementioned earth from the dried water bath, and know its weight; grind it a little in a glass mortar, then place it in its <term>urinal</term> <note>original: "urinale"; a glass flask with a rounded bottom and long neck, named for its resemblance to a medical vessel for collecting urine</note>. Pour our glorious water over it in an amount equal to the earth itself. Put the aforementioned flask back into the water bath for a day and a night, for there the matter is digested. Once that time has passed, transfer the vessel from the water bath to the ashes <note>a "sand bath" or ash bed used for applying more intense or direct heat than water</note>, adding an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: "alembicum"; the "hood" or cap of a still used to direct vapors into a condenser</note> on top, and distill whatever is able to be distilled. Take care during the drying of the earth that the fire is not too violent, because the entire work would be destroyed and <term>vitrified</term> <note>turned into a useless, glass-like substance by excessive heat</note>.

Therefore, my son, continue this operation—namely <term>imbibition</term> <note>soaking the solid with liquid</note>, <term>inhumation</term> <note>literally "burying," referring to placing the vessel in a warm bath or manure to maintain steady heat</note>, and distillation—until the earth has "drunk" a fortieth or fiftieth part of itself. This will be certain to you if you place a small amount of it upon a glowing-hot metal plate; if it all flies away in smoke, then it is finished.

If, however, the aforementioned sign does not occur, continue the operations again until you achieve your effect. And note that in the second and third imbibition, it will become black and take on the color of <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturnus"; in alchemy, Saturn is the symbol for lead and the color black, representing the "Nigredo" or death-phase of the work</note>. If this does not happen, our work on our stone would be in vain. For that spirit is planted in our earth, and suddenly it is corrupted; then, through the decoction of heat, it grows and multiplies. This <term>putrefaction</term>, my son, is necessary, because **the corruption of one is the generation of another.**

> O blessed Nature, and blessed is your work, for you make the perfect from the imperfect through true putrefaction, which is black and dark; afterward, you cause diverse and new things to sprout with greenness. This is even demonstrated in the Gospel: > **Unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it brings forth much fruit.** <note>Quoting John 12:24</note>

And thus, many and various colors will appear in succession before the earth has drunk its proper weight. When it has its weight, it will arrive at a certain whiteness or "citrinity" <note>a lemon-yellow color</note>. This operation, therefore, is called "impregnation"...

<summary>This page describes the repetitive cycle of distillation and "imbibition" required to unite the alchemical spirit with its "earth." It emphasizes the necessity of the "Nigredo" (blackness) or putrefaction stage, using the biblical metaphor of a dying seed to explain how chemical corruption leads to new growth.</summary>
<keywords>distillation, imbibition, putrefaction, Raymond Lull, Saturn, Nigredo, alchemy, quicksilver, spiritual transformation</keywords>

-># ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY<-

<page-num>966</page-num>

...they call it; because our blessed earth has been made pregnant, and it is the time of her birth, and a son shall be born who will not resemble his parents. And so that we may have the complete <term>magisterium</term> <note>the "mastery" or the completed Great Work of alchemy</note>, let us proceed to the rest. Take the aforementioned pregnant earth and place it in a glass vessel, sprinkling over it a little of our water, and place it in a <term>bocia</term> <note>original: "bocia"; a glass flask or cucurbit with a long neck</note> in the ashes. Light a fire beneath until all humidity evaporates; but when the earth has been dried, increase the fire to the third degree <note>a higher level of heat, often compared to a hot sand bath, used to drive vapors upward</note>, because it will begin to <term>sublimate</term> <note>the process of a solid turning directly into vapor and then back to solid at the top of a vessel</note>, and our glorious and incorruptible sulphur will ascend to the top of the vessel. 

When all of it has ascended, it will be exalted in "foliated earth," or in a "miraculous salt," which is called the **Sulphur of Nature** by Raymond <note>Raymond Lull</note> and other Philosophers. Therefore, my son, take this treasure, because nothing in the world is worthier or more excellent than this; for this is the gem of the wise, a deadly poison, a sublimated arsenic. This is the toad that congeals Mercury; this is the dragon devouring all things and converting them to its own nature. This is he of whom all the Philosophers cry out in the *Assembly*: <note>original: "turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> "Honor our king coming out of the fire, crowned with a diadem, whose father is the **Sun** and whose mother is the **Moon**; let him be nourished by his own milk until he reaches a perfect age." This is the son born to us; let him be fed with his own milk until he is fixed and flows like wax. 

However, you shall perform this mastery, which is called the <term>ferment</term> <note>the substance that "leavens" or transforms the base metal into gold</note> by the Philosophers, in this way: Take, in the name of God, our miraculous water and place it in a water bath to be distilled, and continue the distillation until it will no longer distill. Afterward, remove that vessel from the bath, and in its bottom you will find a certain most red and glorious thing. This done, take the aforementioned red matter and place it in another clean vessel in the ashes, and hide it away by adding an <term>alembic</term> <note>the "hood" or cap of the still</note>. Then, make a very strong fire, because it cannot be distilled in any other way. When the whole matter has been distilled, you shall <term>rectify</term> <note>purify through repeated distillation</note> it seven times. Note that in the seventh distillation, even if it stood in the fire for a year, it would never distill further, but would always remain in the form of oil. This, my son, is the true ferment of the philosophers and nothing else.

And many ignorant people believe that our sulphur is fermented with [metallic] bodies, which is foolish and far removed from natural principles. But our blessed stone calcinates itself; it dissolves itself; it kills itself; it brings itself to life; it disposes itself—

<meta>catchword: made (facti)</meta>

<summary>This page describes the sublimation of the "pregnant earth" to produce the Sulphur of Nature and the subsequent creation of the "Red Ferment" (the oil of the philosophers) through sevenfold distillation. It uses allegorical imagery of a king, a dragon, and a toad to describe the chemical transformations.</summary>

<header>E P I S T L E.</header>

...it nourishes itself, it feeds itself, it ferments itself, but not with anything that was not born from it. If you wish to bring it to the desired end, take our sulphur exalted in the heaven <note>referring to the upper part of the vessel where the substance has collected after sublimation</note>, and ensure you have its weight; place it in a clean <term>urinal</term> <note>original: "vrinali"; a common glass flask in an alchemical lab, named for its resemblance to a medical vessel</note>, adding over it a fourth part of its weight of our aforementioned oil. Mix everything together until it becomes a single substance. Afterward, place that vessel in a proper fire, or otherwise in a dry stove, because there the matter will be digested and <term>fixed</term> <note>rendered stable and resistant to heat</note> by such warmth. When you see your matter is dry, do not be slow to "feed" it, always giving it its prescribed weight of its own "milk," until the whole is fixed and flows without smoke, like wax. When you have achieved this, you have what you desired. Observe this method in <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiectione"; the final stage of alchemy where a small amount of the Stone is "projected" or thrown into molten metal to transform it</note>: namely, take one part by weight of this medicine and cast it upon ten parts of molten <term>sun</term> <note>original: "solis"; the alchemical code for gold</note>; the whole will be converted into a melting and penetrating medicine, healing both metals and all diseases. You have, my son, the most precious secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> which I promised to show you long ago; hand it over to no one. But be upright, praise Almighty God, and let the poor be your care.

<meta>This page continues from the conclusion of the practical instructions for the Great Work. Having described the "feeding" and "projection" of the medicine, the text now transitions into a collection of authoritative "Sayings" (Dicta) from renowned alchemical masters to provide philosophical and traditional weight to the preceding instructions.</meta>

<page-num>368</page-num>

<header>S A Y I N G S</header>

### Geber. <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "Father of Chemistry." His works were considered the foundation of medieval alchemy.</note>

> Where we have spoken most openly and clearly, there we have most hidden the knowledge. <note>original: "Ubi magis aperte & plane locuti sumus, ibi scientiam magis occultauimus." This refers to the alchemical practice of *Deckname* or "cover-names," where clear language often masks a symbolic secret.</note>

### Senior. <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail.</note>

> The philosophers have hidden nothing except the preparation, which is the most difficult of things: and without it, nothing is perfected, nor can it be known except from God, or from a master who may teach it.

### Bonus of Ferrara. <note>Also known as Petrus Bonus, author of the 14th-century "Precious Pearl."</note>

> Whatever is in the midst of movement toward receiving some form can be led to the end of that movement, unless it is hindered. But imperfect metals are of this kind, while <term>gold</term> is at the end of movement. Therefore. <note>Bonus uses Aristotelian logic: if nature intends for all metals to eventually become gold through "movement" or maturation in the earth, the alchemist simply removes the "hindrances" to speed up the process.</note>

### Raymond in the Vade-mecum. <note>Attributed to Raymond Lull, a famous philosopher whose name was later attached to many alchemical texts.</note>

> Whatever the celestial virtue of the elements performs in natural vessels, this same thing it performs in artificial vessels, provided they are formed after the manner of natural vessels. <note>The alchemist's flask is viewed as a "microcosm" or a miniature version of the Earth's womb.</note>

### The Lily. <note>Refers to the "Lilium Intelligentiae," a popular alchemical treatise.</note>

> The Work is not caused by the movement of the heavenly bodies, since it can be achieved in time, provided the matter is placed in a vessel lacking a seam. <note>This emphasizes that while astrology is important, the physical "hermetic seal" of the vessel is what allows the transformation to occur.</note>

### Richard the Englishman. <note>Richardus Anglicus, a 14th-century alchemist often associated with the "Correctorium Alchemiae."</note>

> Art imitates nature, not in that it builds something entirely new: But that it refines the virtue of that nature; to this end, art begins to perfect where nature fails: to uncover and reveal the subtle matter within a confused or corrupt thing.

### Arnold of Villanova. <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>

> Hence it is necessary that what is good in the imperfect body be perfected together with the perfect body, because since the <term>living silveriness</term> <note>original: "argenteitas viua"; a reference to the essence of Mercury</note> of the perfect body is fixed: it fixes its own silveriness upon the non-fixed part of the imperfect body, by which it draws the fixed living silveriness from the perfect bodies, and causes this to penetrate, glorify, and completely perfect it.

### The Same.

> The <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "Materia prima"; the formless primeval substance from which all things are made</note> of metals is a certain smoky substance containing within itself an unctuous humidity, from which substance the craftsman separates the "philosophical humidity"—which is fit for application and is as clear as a tear—in which dwells the metallic <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the "fifth element" or pure spiritual essence of a substance</note>. This is the manageable metal, and in it is the means of joining the <term>tinctures</term> <note>the coloring agents that transform metal into gold</note>, because it possesses the nature of both sulfur and quicksilver.

### Arnold.

> Sun and Moon <note>Gold and silver</note> exist in virtue and power within our stone; if this were not so, neither Sun nor Moon could ever be produced from it.
->The Same.<-

The quotes emphasize that alchemy is the perfection of nature through the manipulation of "living silveriness" and the quintessence.</summary>

<page-num>968</page-num>
<header>OF THE WISE.</header>

->The Same.<- <note>Refers back to Geber from the previous page.</note>

*Every growing or being born thing is multiplied in its own species; metals are not generated except from their own seed, but <term>quicksilver</term> is the seed of metals and their origin.* <note>original: "argentum vivum." In alchemy, Mercury/Quicksilver was considered the "mother" or "sperm" of all metals because of its fluid, metallic nature.</note>

->Pandulphus.<- <note>An authority frequently cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*, a core 12th-century alchemical text.</note>

*Nature rejoices in nature; nature contains nature, and nature overcomes nature.* <note>original: "Natura natura latatur; natura naturam continet, & natura naturam vincit." This is one of the most famous axioms in alchemy, suggesting that the transformation of matter must follow natural laws rather than forcing them.</note>

->Diomedes.<-

*We must revere nature, since nature is not corrected except by its own nature; for it makes itself sprout.*

->Paracelsus.<- <note>The 16th-century Swiss physician and occultist who revolutionized alchemy by focusing on its medicinal uses.</note>

*Only from metals, in metals, through metals, and with metals are perfect metals made: for in other things is the <term>Moon</term>, and in other metals the <term>Sun</term>.* <note>In alchemical code, the Moon represents silver and the Sun represents gold. Paracelsus argues here that the "Philosopher's Stone" must be derived from metallic sources, not organic ones.</note>

->Raymond.<- <note>Raymond Lull.</note>

*The Stone is not made from one thing, but from two together.*

->Constans.<-

*Take care for nothing else, except that you have <term>quicksilver</term> fixed in the air and the fleeing volatile in Mercury.* <note>This describes the central paradox of the "Great Work": making the "volatile" (vaporous) substance stay still, and making the "fixed" (solid) substance flow.</note>

->Eximidius in the Assembly.<- <note>original: "Eximidius in turba." Refers to a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of Philosophers).</note>

*I command you, however, to mix quicksilver with quicksilver until one and the same clean water is made from these two bodies.*

->Senior.<- <note>Senior Zadith.</note>

*Water is not joined together except with the likeness of its own <term>sulfur</term>, nor is anything found in a thing like its own sulfur, except in that which comes from it: sun from sun.* <note>Sulfur and Mercury were the two primary principles of matter in medieval theory; "sun from sun" implies that the gold of the alchemist must come from the inherent "goldness" already inside the matter.</note>

->Raymond.<-

*In water is all our knowing, and the secret, and the desired end.*

->Hermes.<- <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>

*That Stone is the whole secret and the life of every single thing, and every man needs it; and this is the water which is the grain in wheat, the oil in the olive, the gum in peaches, and the fruit in all trees, and the principle of human generation: and from it comes the living thing which does not die as long as the world exists, because it is the head of the world, that is, the <term>moisture</term>.* <note>original: "humor." Hermes is describing the *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul," a vital moisture that alchemists believed animated all of creation, from plants to minerals.</note>

<summary>This page presents a series of aphorisms from alchemical authorities emphasizing that "like produces like." It argues that the Philosopher's Stone must be sought within the "mercurial" moisture that serves as the life-force for all of nature.</summary>
